It's been a while since I played a game that's this lovingly crafted and that felt like it came from such a strong emotional space that exudes throughout the entire journey. Brothers is a game that deals with many different themes, some fantastical in nature, and tackles them head on and with a touch of nuance. It's also a very charming game that overcomes any technical limitation through great art direction.
Its basic concept of controlling the older brother on the left analog stick and the younger brother on the right is one that may turn off some at first but truly comes into its own as the game progresses with a thematic payoff unlike anything I've ever seen in a game before. Brothers also has excellent pacing that carries over into its puzzles. They are simple yet I never felt like they were braindead easy. They're always fresh in some way and play off of mechanics I learned before without ever showing a tutorial on screen outside of the beginning chapter.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons was an excellently developed puzzle platformer that wasn't afraid to go to some dark places but also knew when to highlight a truly joyous moment. And this was all through gameplay. These special moments or sections were rarely shown through cutscenes only. It wants you to experience these parts through gameplay as much as possible, and it very much succeeds at that. But it's a climactic moment near the end that truly brings that idea home. A moment so brilliant and emotionally resonant to me that it'd be a shame if people missed out on this because we're on the cusp of a new console generation transition. Don't pass this game up. It begs to be played.

Let me start by saying though it says I only have 6.8 hours played that couldn't be less true. I only have 6.8 on pc but over 500 on the originial Xbox. This review is based on my sole opinions only but I am trying to keep it as unbiased as possible. Keep in mind this game is old so don't try and compare to anything you may have recently played.
If you don't wish to read alot then just know this is for sure a game you should get. As long as you can patiently deal with the outdated graphics and different fighting mechanics you will be spending 14.99 for easily over 10 hours of game play if you just dive straight through the story and 300 hours if you decide you want to comb the island for its secrets.
Music-9.5/10 only reason its not a 10 out of 10 is because there isn't enough beautiful tracks. The 40 or so unique tracks need to be made into 100. Just because of how hype they get me I want more!
Gameplay (Combat, Character interactions, Movement, etc)-9/10 For its time its very good. Its RNG based combat effected by your skills and such so it might seem nonsensical but its actually really challenging and fun when you understand the correlation. I love the fact that different weapons have 3 different attacks and the damage makes sense based on the weapon. I.e a spear will do more thrust damage as opposed to slash. This changes on how you're moving when you swing. There is a wide variety of different creatures, ememies and character models to chose from. Almost anywhere you go you can find someone to help or talk to and get information from. Explore far and wide. You never know where a secret catacomb is with a legendary ring in it or a hidden sword under a bed that can help immensely. Be you a thief who profits off others success and sneaks around danger. Or a mage with mastery over the arcane. Or a barbarian who would rather charge in axe swinging than negotiate. All play styles can lead to your success or destruction, one as easily as the other.
Story- 10/10 Not many games have ever captivated me for so long or made me crave the next adventure as this one did. This is my favorite story out of all the Elder Scrolls. The lore is far reaching and ties into itself all over the place. There are books all over the place that are just as fun to read as it is to go fight someone. Many a times have I sat in a book store just reading for 30 minutes before I realize what I'm doing. The main quest doesn't grow dull but leaves you in suspense and wonder as you figure out your place in the wide world of Vvardenfell.

Machinarium is a cute and funny game about a robot who have had enough of bullying and corrupt systems. The main robot of the game finds itself in a landfill and after figuring out how to assemble itself begins its quest of getting back home and stopping the evildoers that has been supressing it for so long.
The game features a lot of minigames and puzzles, most of which are classic logic question of geometrical type but also some new and clever ideas that are really challenging. The storyline is a bit wierd and since none of the characters really say anything, it's hard to realize where you should go after you've solved a part of the puzzle. The developers have made a smart solution to this by implementing a "tips and tricks"-help manual that you can only access after you have played a short bit of simple sidescroller.
I've only had the opportunity to play it once, and since it only took me roughly five hours (even with getting stuck and trying many different paths time and again) I do not feel like this is a game that I want to own. Even though there is the option to solve some things in different order, it is a very linear game with few things that are out of the main quest.
Overall I think that Machinarium is a really cute game, a nice challenge for anyone that are new to puzzle solvers or really like playing a lot of them and the design in it is really wonderful.

While I'm not saying that I'm writing this for the Steam Award Achievement, I ain't saying I'm not either.
Nonetheless, Spore is a fun game.
Well balanced and fair at some points? No.
But fun in small spurts? Yes.
There are 5 stages. Cell, Creature, Tribal, Civilization, and Space.
Each focuses on a different scale with what you're controlling being evident by their titles (Space meaning space-ship), and what you do in one stage can give you bonuses for the next. It'd also be nice if they gave you negatives as well, leading to more interesting playthroughs and unique challenges for each combination.
Alas, they do not, and the modding community seems to have left Spore behind with it being both not very friendly to modders, and the unfortunate lack of enthusiasm to improve a game that few people play anymore.
What most people will tell you is that the first 4 stages are just filler, and the last is where the real meat of the game lies, and those people are mostly right. The first 4 are quite short, with achievements for speedrunning them uncomfortably easy to get with the smallest amount of effort, but those are also where the majority of the actual building happens, for creatures, buildings, and vehicles.
The UI for building things is extremely simple and effective. However, it's simplicity also reduces the variability that you'll see. Some of the more unique and facinating creature designs you may imagine up are simply not possible with the Spore Creature Creator. And with the game designed with only land-based creatues in mind, making those creatures anyway would just end up with something that looks pretty when stationary, but ends up looking like an awkward mess once it takes its first step.
That doesn't mean that the first four are boring though! They're plenty fun (well, not Tribal. $%#& that one) and it's nice to see your little creatures fighting their way up the food chain, carefully dealing with the well balanced Maxis creatures and staying the hell away from the completely overpowered and terrible to look at player-made creatures.
Right, forgot to mention that.
Nearly all of the player made creations look ugly either because some 5 year old made it, or someone played it for the very first time and stacked as many weapons and different kinds of feet they could onto the thing to max out its stats.
Due to this, the vast majority of... everything you get from other players looks absolutely terrible. If you want other people's work in your games, look for and add them manually.
Other than that though, the game is pretty fun, and ignoring the absolute mess that is the Spore community it's still pretty solid to this very day.

Your usual adventure game but with a catch. There's no text in the whole game, relying mostly on visuals to tell its basic story and hint what do do next. The latter is the true challenge of the game, which is not new in this genre, but several puzzles will make you go in circles. Fortunately you have a minigame that if beated, it will give you the full playthrough of the screen you're in, so you can work a little extra to get the solution rather just googling it.
The game works in flash and that's probably its main problem. The game runs well, but some inputs can be rough specially as the character has a very limited area to interact with. There's also some puzzles that might feel the game becomes either bugged or unresponsive, so better double check before making assumptions.
If you figure out all its puzzles Machinarium is actually pretty short. But due how vague the game is hinting the next step as well the limited interaction range will force you into, is not a game that you can beat by just clicking everything until the character walks into it.

Resident Evil HD is a complete remaster of the original Resident Evil released on Playstation 1 in 1996.  If you played the original way back when, are familiar with the more recent titles, or haven't yet taken the dive into the series, Resident Evil HD is definitely a game worth picking up.  The game looks fantastic, plays exceptionally well with updated controls, is a heck of a challenge, manages to strike an incredible balance between old-school and new-age, and it's an incredibly fun (and scary) experience!
The Resident Evil series was built to be a horror genre, and - though some of the new-age games might leave your eyes rolling - the classic ones pull off the horror genre perfectly.  You won't find cheesy jump-scares, ear-piercingly loud noises, obnoxiously dark rooms or copious amounts of gore here.  The Resident Evil HD is about
; constant suspense of what kind of enemies you will encounter in the next room, fear of death (and the resulting loss of progress), nervous planning for how to conserve your resources and ammo, and strategic use of weapons and ...
... tactical retreats to make it to checkpoints and stay alive.  Resident Evil HD is a horror game because it truly immerses you in its world, keeps you actively engaged with its one-of-a-kind atmosphere, and does so with beautifully simple grace.
That said, don't come into Resident Evil expecting a "modern 3rd-person shooter", because that's certainly not what Resident Evil is. While it has shooting elements as a core mechanic of its gameplay, at it's heart Resident Evil is a survival-strategy game, with heavy emphasis on puzzles and solving the horror-thriller mystery that your main characters find themselves in.  If I had to compare Resident Evil HD to a modern game, it's more of an "Amnesia" or "SOMA" with the addition of a limited amount of weapons than it is a Resident Evil 5 or Dead Space.
Breathtakingly well.  I remember all-too-well the shooters on first-gen consoles; they were clunky, frustratingly difficult to play, and not exactly the easiest on the eyes.  Resident Evil HD manages to strip its reboot of all the bad things I remember of those days while retaining what made them great.  Controls have been updated to make movement and aiming much more intuitive (I recommend a controller, but mouse/keyboard also works to satisfaction).  Visuals have been completely redone, from textures, to models, to levels, to in-game text and inventory.  Everything is identical from a mechanical and (level/game) design standpoint, but it runs smoothly, plays smoothly, and looks fantastic.  Don't let the simple movement/camera/aim controls fool you, Resident Evil is fun, engaging, and challenging in all of its own right.
While admittedly the story itself isn't the most stand-out, that's not to say it's poorly written.  Resident Evil's story shares the same beautiful simplicity that defines its core gameplay.  You play as one of two main characters, whom you can select at the start of your game.  They find themselves trapped in a mysterious mansion with the undead (and other vicious creatures), with their friends lost, and looking for a way to escape.  Cutscenes are limited, dialogue is concise, and there's only as much story driving the game along as there needs to be; and that's just fine (preferable, even).  The real story here is how the characters are going to survive... or more accurately, how YOU are going to.  You must solve puzzles, explore the mansion, survive with limited resources, and ultimately hope to get the heck outta dodge before the evil there takes you down with it.  Who caused the horror at the mansion?  What is the purpose of this desolate building in the middle of nowhere?  You can only hope to find out as you try to escape.
At $20 this game is some fantastic value for your dollar, is an experience unlike anything else you'll find, and will give you more than a few fun play-throughs. On sale this game is a no-brainer.  As I also mentioned above, the remaster is of the highest quality and it is one of the better optimized reboot/ports out there on PC.  Resident Evil HD is a game that's definitely worth picking up and giving a try for almost any category of gamer, and I have been very pleasantly surprised with just how great it is.

Wonderful remake/remaster, probably the best remake I've seen to this day.
It keeps the same essence as the original Resident Evil, but improves it a lot, specially on atmosphere (to be honest, the original never caused me true fear, even when I was a kid, but this one did with the incredible atmosphere and ambient it implements).
>New puzzles are really welcome, they keep the same style as the old ones, and even the old puzzles that still here are improved in some way (for example, having to do OTHER puzzle to actually solve this "old" puzzle in question). They're all very good and balanced, so you probably won't get stuck for hours on the same puzzle if you pay attention to the files you find and put some effort into it, just like in the original.
>The graphics, well, are amazing, not much else to say about it.
>Only problem I found is that it forces the resolution to 1920/1080 even if you change it in the options (since my PC is not that good, that's a problem). My PC is actually better than the minimum requirements, but inferior to the recommended, but I still had slow motion and lags. Solved editing a file to make the internal resolution the one I want.
>The gameplay is as amazing as the original Resident Evil games, keeping everything we loved and implementing some stuff over it, such as the defense weapon, which are a good additional. Oh, and everything still as difficult as before (the part in the lab where you can't run or shoot because of the chemical you're carrying is really annoying, but in a good way).
>Story you know, great as always, but it gets better as the series progress.
>Camera is good and works well, but sometimes is annoying. I found myself running straight to a enemy a couple of times for not knowing what was before me, right at my face, but I couldn't see it because of the camera. That's a common problem with this type of camera though, and it's not even a big problem, but worth mentioning.
So, this game is true to the horror genre, not relying on jumpscares all the time to make you "fear". It KNOWS what the word "fear" means, using it in a amazing way. The outside part when you walk to the cabin and pass though a cemetary and all, this part scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, one of the best implements in the remake, in my opinion.
Buy it, this is one of the best remakes ever made, if not the best.

I wanted to like this game, I truly did.
I was probably the only person on the planet who was looking forward to this game before release, well I finally got around to playing it and it's just inexcusable.
I'll separate this into thirds because that's how the quality of the game seems to be divided.
1: The first third of the game the writing is trash and the gameplay is great, nothing too upsetting here except the occasional softlock from being trapped behind an invisible wall, this happened to me 3 different times in the first hour of gameplay.
2: The second third of the game the writing is decent, level design, while simplistic, seemed to be free of softlocking potential, and the gameplay was pretty decent to boot. Hour #2 was the best for me personally.
3: The final third of the game the writing is excellent, especially compared to the rest of the game, but everything else suffers. Many objects don't have hitboxes at all, leading to clipping through them; this is especially problematic in the platforming sections, most of my deaths in this game came from falling through an object that was clearly there, and I played on the hardest difficulty. A couple of sections were the generic "kill all enemy" rooms which come standard in many games, but here I spent several minutes running around looking for the final bad guy(s) which seem to have spawned off of the map or something because these scenarios could only be fixed by reloading and playing several more minutes, many of these times only to have to do the same thing again.
All in all the game feels rushed. In the beginning it felt as if the devs were new to making games, because while, yes, there were many problems, it felt as if they were actually trying, then in the middle of the game they were comfortable making the game and poured their heart into it, then we enter the end, where they just♥♥♥♥♥♥out a jumbled mess and gave up.
This is one of those games that makes me REALLY wish Steam had a "mixed" option when reviewing games, because while the game isn't completely terrible, I feel that it was lazily put together, especially in the later portions. My copy was free, so I feel that spending my time on this game was worth it, but paying money? Wait until it's on sale for at least $10, and only then should you even consider buying it.

Allow me to get one thing out of the way first. Bomber Crew is a solid game. Its got all the foundations right for a great experience, and in the short time i played the game, i did have fun with it! It had a great deal of challenge to even the earliest of missions and promised only more difficulty to come. i loved the art assets within the game for customizing your characters as well as the plane itself, including custom made decals.
So why am i not recommending the game then?
In its current state, Bomber Crew has a lot to promise, and a lot of room to grow, but it simply lacks content. The missions will invariably get repetative and it will only take as long as it takes for a refund to no longer be an option to realize that the missions are all the same, just skinned differently. The game just lacks variety right now, once you look past the different descriptions of the target youre supposed to either bomb, take a picture of, or deliver supplies to. I hope that one day that i will catch word of a significant content patch that varies up the gameplay, but until then i await my refund and leave this review as a thumbs down.

Great game, in my opinion, if you manage to setup the microsoft live account. Just search within the game forum and you shouldn't have much problem with the game's functionality.
Campaign:
You play as the Wolf pack, Umbrella's Delta team, special force and must seek and destroy any evidence of Umbrella's experiments following the Dr.Birkin unwillingness to cooperate. External forces are involved with the good doctor, no one must leave alive.
Secondary missions (optional add-on):
You play as the Spec-Ops, sent by the goverment following the total radio silence of Raccoon City. Local info of the population status is sketchy at best, but an epidemic seems to be involved. Investigate and establish the current situation within the quarantine zone.
Single Player :
Pros: The atmosphere is incredible, from the bloody streets to Umbrella's ressearch center. From the simple zombie to Birkin's mutant form, a well defined fan service. Stiff, muddled, and a missed opportunity.
+++PROS+++
The best thing about this game were the characters. They were the "ghostly light up specialist" theme turned way up, and they were very cool, charming, and interesting. Their costumes were fantastic too; you can easily tell who's specialty is what based on their appearance.
---CONS---
***ON THE BOND OF THE TEAM***
I think this game should have been very focused on the main characters of this game, this very cool band of specialists, which seem to have had a disproportionate amount of care in making compared to the rest of the game.
The story is nothing to get too invested in. I could hardly care about how the story of Delta Team fits into the rest of Resident Evil. It is, after all, easily inserted without any loose ends, but also not fitting edges with evidence; the previous games did not leave unanswered mysteries in mind for this game to answer. It could have been very interesting, looking behind the curtain, but there never was any curtain.
As it is, the Delta Team missions are a backdrop to what the story should have been about: the unity of the team and the forces that stress them, including their employers. The game did write in some strain between Delta Team and their employers, but it felt shallow. It was told through some audio lines, so the characters' emotions about the situation were limited in expression; we see our characters standing still, backs turned, as they say these things. There was one cutscene that was nice, as the commander angrily calls Umbrella, but after that, we're back trudging along through chores, following orders. I didn't feel as if this conflict gave me motivation. In the end, it all resulted in a binary and meaningless choice; follow one final order or don't. I think the story could have used more illustration of the bond of the team and the disagreement with Umbrella. How? Cinematics, make the characters feel more life like than 3rd person models. Gameplay, have the characters help each other more; as it stands, you're just playing alongside people rather than with them. As for the Umbrella conflict, perhaps Umbrella could provide aerial or technical support that comes and goes with the story.
The basic idea of throwing zombies into a mix of opposing fireteams can be interesting, but then the game has to be, first and foremost, built around firearm combat. If you want tactical gameplay that requires use of cover, you have to lower the time to kill and plan the covers and positions for smart decisions. Instead, you trudge along your path until find a cluster of fireteam enemies and you take cover and play whack a mole, popping out when they finally pop out, waiting until they're all gone.
The cover system was a mess. I had to run to cover, then back up, then walk forward slowly to enter cover, which tries to go automatically.

I was late to the Elder Scrolls series... to put it into perspective, the first ES game I played was Skyrim. Don't know why, but I just never played Elder Scrolls before Skyrim. So I always struggled to get into Morrowind, and found that it was mostly because the characters and environments looked like relative♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't get me wrong, I still play Ocarina of Time and Mario 64 and have a good time, so I don't have a problem with outdated visuals, but a lot of that is propped up by nostalgia.
That being said I've always wanted to get into Morrowind, so I decided to grab the graphics overhaul mod and push through it. Let me tell you, totally worth it. There are so many things that Morrowind did so right that the later entries in the series have lost. The absence of a quest compass is the biggest. I love having to really read the quest, take directions, and find my own way to my destination. It makes the world so much more immersive and makes you pay attention to it. Rather than looking at a little arrow at the top of the screen, I'm looking at landmarks and following directions. It's nothing short of great, and I hope to see games go back to that in the future. Breath of the Wild did a bit of that.
While Morrowind has a steeper learning curve than the later entries, and is definitely not the same level of visually stunning, it does give you all the tools you need to understand the game and succeed, and with some easy to install mods can have a very charming aesthetic. It is a great game, and if you haven't taken the time to play it, you definitely should.

So.. Machinarium.. This is really one of those games that allready has so many positive reviews that it might not need another one. But here it goes:
Machinarium is set to a universe where there seems to be no humans. Instead there is machines building machines. As you can see from the screenshots posted on the store page of the game, it almost seems like it takes place in a junkyard, where the living machines often are built from scrap metal. Even tho these are machines and don't speak, they have character, and show emotions.
Machinarium follows the old and well known point and click game mechanic. It is a story driven adventure/puzzle game, that has a rather serious story, but manages to add humor to it on several places.
The story captured me from the very first moment that i started playing this. I don't want to ruin the story for those who haven't played this yet, so im not going to cover any part of the story in this review.
As mention above, the characters in Machinarium don't speak, but they show thinking boubles above their head and make noises (an alternative way to give the player hints about what they need to do next). This method, in my opinion works very well.
I have played many puzzle games and i have to say that for me, this was kind of perfect in terms of difficulty. Many puzzle games tend to become to confusing when they try to make it a big and challenging game. Like having a big area with lots and lots of things to interact with, without a single clue on what to do next. Machinarium manages to give you a lot of different options on what to interact with, but at the same time you get enough hints on what your goal is that you for example knows that you have to do someting with this item, just not what.
The levels in Machinarium are great actually. There is a lot of variations and different enviroments through out the game. They also made the levels in a way that you get a feeling of a big living world even outside of the playable areas. You still have to remember that this is a sideview game with limited possibilities of movement. Still, there is depth in the levels, so you can for example walk away and towards the camera.
For me these kinds of games gives me some nostalgia from the time around 2001-2006 when i used to play games like these on flash sites all the time. There is something "calming" about sitting there without any stress, and figuring out these sorts of games. Of course Machinarium is more polished, longer and better than most free flash games out there.
So far in my review, i've only said positive things about Machinarium. But as many other games before it, Machinarium suffers when it comes to bugs and crashes.
I experienced several times during my playthrough that the games just froze with a black screen. I still could hear the music but i had to close it through task manager and restart it to keep playing.
I also experienced that the game just closed for no apparent reason, and sometimes while playing and i clicked on something, nothing happened in-game.
But since this is a very small game in terms of size, and that it practically doesn't require anything to run, it took me seconds to restart and be back in it.
Machinarium is a great game, really.
If you like story driven puzzle games i would recommend you to get this.

FTL in a plane!
Not really, but there's a lot of comparison to be made between Bomber Crew, FTL, Kerbal Space Program and XCOM.
Micromanagement is the name of the game and boy will you be doing a lot of micromanaging.
You take the role of a Lancaster Bomber commander in charge of a crew of 7 specialists conducting reconnaissance, bombing, hunting and rescue missions whilst WW2 plays out around you.
A majority of the time you'll be looking into your plane, micromanaging crew from position to position with each member of the crew having only one (later two) tasks they're competent at and having special abilities for.
The rest of the time you'll be using the other core mechanic of the game: "tagging" which involves hovering a 360 degree camera over environmental elements (which can be movement waypoints, bombing targets, enemies or allies) for a few seconds which will then instruct the relevant crewmember to interact with them accordingly.
Almost all the major interaction your bomber has with the outside world is through tagging.
Pilots will fly straight without a navigational icon being tagged. Gunners won't fire on targets without them being tagged.
This isn't fundamentally bad but it means that you'll be taking precious time in a firefight to instruct your gunners to shoot at targets 20m directly in front of them (sometimes with a view obscured by the bomber itself) whilst trying to contain a fire in the midsection and repair a faulty engine.
This can create VERY tense moments of trying to manage your bomber around hazards, your crew around your bomber and your tears as you forget something in the rush and it causes your bomber to fall out of the sky because you ran out of fuel.
This might sound like a negative review, but it's not. This makes the game challenging and thrilling.
My two biggest concerns though are how janky some moments can be and accessible the game is.
This is a very punishing game.
Crew you've put a lot of time into levelling up can die permenantly.
You don't have backup crew to level on the side and after a certain point it's difficult to grind up inexperienced crew.
A crew can die in amazingly quick fashion; usually through mismanagment but sometimes you'll just randomly blow up because you didn't have enough time to see how much damage an enemy is doing or because several enemies spawned in and took out all 4 of your engines instantly and your crew were too slow to get to parachutes.
There is a soft reset though but it makes particularly random deaths more a waste of time then complete punishments.
A lot of people have said that a tactical pause would make this game better and I agree.
There is an element of "Git Gud" but having the option (and rewarding players who don't use it) would be great.
All things considered, I really liked this game and really recommend it.
Running Duck has done an excellent job with great polish and I look forward to seeing what updates this game gets.

So 20 flights in, and all but two of the "Fire and Forget's" original crew are alive. That's not bad. Actually all in all that's 5 times better than the average for a Lancaster Bomber Tail Gunner's life expectancy. The game really lets you feel that too.
I'm not saying it's hard in the beginning, far from it. The game's tutorial eases you in to things over two missions with some unexpected combat.  Once out of the tutorial though, you spend so mcuh time getting a hang of how to tag, how to navigate, swearing because your landing gear has been down the entire time, that you miss the fact that you've got two engines on fire and you've accidently sent your pilot down to get ammo for the rear gun which has sent your bomber into a nose dive.
Once you get past the frantic "Oh smegging hell get back in the Pilot's seat!" frustration that can come from a close quarter's misclick during that early game frustration, it moves to a more natural "Oh smegging hell, where were those intercepting fighters coming from again?" style gameplay which is more suited for the time period.
Every flight is made with calculated risks surrounding both plane and crew upgrades, as there's never enough money for both. Every time the optional recon photos appear you're making what can often be a live or death decision for your crew over what could be valuable intelligence for the war effort. Every mission in progress gets you invested, keeps you focused and on the edge of your seat.
For all its charm and frantic pacing however, Bomber Crew does suffer from some issues gameplay wise. While mid mission has impact ranging from "Am I going to have to retrain a level 8 tail gunner from scratch?" to "Am I going to have to retrain an entire crew from scratch?" the completion of missions doesn't seem to have any real impact or weight on the game world.
There's a motor factory in Bruges that I've blown up a few times now in what is (by using the life expectancy as a guide) 10 weeks. Now either Belgians build fast, or it doesn't matter save for a buff for a couple of flights. There's no real pentality for choosing to do that mission solely either as the difficulty never really spikes, it just swarms.
Now forcing a choice between the Bruges Motor factory for a buff and say the airfield for stopping a debuff would give the game much more of that "FTL in WW2" feel which for the most part this game is deserving of.
I'd say the only other thing that this game seems to miss is once again in its world building. What I would love to see is your Lancaster taking off in a full wing of Bombers, and watching them whittle down under enemy fire until it's just your crew left to complete the mission. Not all the time, just say for critical missions. It's not much but for all its charm it feels pretty lonely up in the skies on the Allied side.
Small collectibles as your crew wrecks havoc on the Reich, like propaganda pictures (both for and against) featuring your Lancaster or Crew, promotion notifications, or even medals. Little things (complex programming wise I know but still) that would just make it pop just that bit more, and add to the investment of the survival of your crew and your kite more than just skills and a end of mission bonus.
With all of that said Bomber Crew is perhaps for me my sleeper Gem of the Year, and is well worth the small financial and long time investment.
Personally I want to make sure that my crew makes it to be on a History Channel documentary one day.

First of all, I recommend a fast internet connection...not necessarily in order to play, but for the download. After downloading a few gigs on the initial download from Steam, it patched another 11 GB. So... if you do have a slow connection, this one will be one of those "overnight downloads"
Anyway, what can I say about DCUO? I did start playing about 4 weeks after it was launched, and liked it very much early on. I eventually did stop playing, but came back several times. Unfortunately, due to the switch to and from P7S1-Games and an email-addy I cant access anymore, I lost my original account and another one I made.
It's not THAT much of a problem though, as leveling a char to the cap level does not take long at all. You do a few "main story" quests plus some bonus side quests, and in no time, you are there. So, leveling is not as much a part of the game as in other MMOs, unless you wanna level a ton of alts. That is totally ok though, I like leveling, but don't need days of leveling in EVERY game I play.
The game itself is lots of fun, and since I mentioned alts: YOu should try a few, try different builds. The weapon sets (like gadgets, swords, guns, kinetics etc.) are tons of FUN. So is the controller-role IMO... most of the chars I made were controllers.
If you like to, you can build a new char based on your favorite DC char (I made a Batman-inspired gadget-using controller, and on my old account, I made a Flash- and a Green-Lantern inspired char. The latter was pretty easy regarding outfit and powers, as one of the DLCs will give you very nice Lantern-style powers). Or you can go for a totally unique character regarding powers and outfits
The game is fast, think "MMO meets arcade beat em up". The races and challenges are fun, and one thing I liked was that several of the quest bosses and special dungeons you do at cap level especially (and I am talking about solo-instances) are pretty challenging the first few times. It DID feel like a nice little achievement to finally beat some of these encounters, so that was nice.
The game never kept me playing longer than a few weeks, but also, I always keep coming back to it. It's fast, it can be quite tough, but it's tons of fun, whether you are a DC fan or not.

Alright, so this game has (according to Steam) mixed reviews. This may be changed at any time I need it to be.
Here's my input:
Positives:
-The game looks clean graphically.
-The characters have amazing attention to detail in first-person view.
-The gun handling also follows the above.
-You can see your torso and below (better than CoD can do).
-Skills level up pretty quickly.
-Fair and balanced guns, pain, and upgrades.
-Teamwork is not directly shown (most times) but is noticeable.
-Fast map loads.
Negatives:
-Pay-to-win; a lot of features are restricted to veterans-only, and the game constantly advertises for you to get it.
-Player levels gain very slowly (very, very slowly).
-Waiting time for matches usually severely underestimated.
-No immediate prompt for training (First playing, I didn't get a prompt to do the training mission).
-Many things are overpriced/not needed.
-Obtain items by leveling up the weapon (which is tedious since XP is gained slowly).
-Gravity is very low. People jump very high, which could be replaced with more of an advanced feature
-Deploy delay penatly (from
killing yourself is a feature worth destroying computers.
-Cannot sell/decommision items/soldiers (I wasted a good 9700 credits for a negative test).
Intermediates:
-No bullet penetration to the smallest extent (even cloths and thin wood doesn't have penetration).
-Queue time is usually severely underestimated.
-No voices, but I'll let it pass since it's only in Beta.
-No voice chat. I'd wish there was, but I understand its absence.
-Report function is broken but useable. This is a community problem, and it is that some people will automatically report you if you
accidentally TK them (even if you apologize), but most disregard. The pro to this is that people can report actual TK'ers and no (even more flawed) automatic system does it (so people who do know it was an accident don't have to ruin the other's time).
-No Steam friend finder function, which is okay, but makes it harder to find friends.
Final judgement:
A good game if you're looking for a near-realistic WW2 game. Generally, unless you're pretty devoted, I'd say more casual players stay away. Fun game, though. Teamwork is a virtue. Not a bad community, but you always have a small few of bad apples. I hope the Beta pulls through.

Wonderful remake/remaster, probably the best remake I've seen to this day.
It keeps the same essence as the original Resident Evil, but improves it a lot, specially on atmosphere (to be honest, the original never caused me true fear, even when I was a kid, but this one did with the incredible atmosphere and ambient it implements).
>New puzzles are really welcome, they keep the same style as the old ones, and even the old puzzles that still here are improved in some way (for example, having to do OTHER puzzle to actually solve this "old" puzzle in question). They're all very good and balanced, so you probably won't get stuck for hours on the same puzzle if you pay attention to the files you find and put some effort into it, just like in the original.
>The graphics, well, are amazing, not much else to say about it.
>Only problem I found is that it forces the resolution to 1920/1080 even if you change it in the options (since my PC is not that good, that's a problem). My PC is actually better than the minimum requirements, but inferior to the recommended, but I still had slow motion and lags. Solved editing a file to make the internal resolution the one I want.
>The gameplay is as amazing as the original Resident Evil games, keeping everything we loved and implementing some stuff over it, such as the defense weapon, which are a good additional. Oh, and everything still as difficult as before (the part in the lab where you can't run or shoot because of the chemical you're carrying is really annoying, but in a good way).
>Story you know, great as always, but it gets better as the series progress.
>Camera is good and works well, but sometimes is annoying. I found myself running straight to a enemy a couple of times for not knowing what was before me, right at my face, but I couldn't see it because of the camera. That's a common problem with this type of camera though, and it's not even a big problem, but worth mentioning.
So, this game is true to the horror genre, not relying on jumpscares all the time to make you "fear". It KNOWS what the word "fear" means, using it in a amazing way. The outside part when you walk to the cabin and pass though a cemetary and all, this part scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, one of the best implements in the remake, in my opinion.
Buy it, this is one of the best remakes ever made, if not the best.

Resident evil hd remaster is a survival horror game developed by Capcom and was released in 2015 it Is a remaster of the 2002 remake of the 1996 original resident evil.
In resident evil you play as Either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, a member of Raccoon City’s STARS squad which gets sent to investigate murders on the outskirts of town, the team gets separated and eventually you end up in an abandoned mansion in the middle of a forest, from then on you explore the mansion looking for the rest of your squad as well as finding a way to escape, as well as trying not to get killed by the numerous zombies roaming around the mansion. I won’t say much more about the plot, overall I thought the story was quite interesting, and there is quite a good sense of mystery going on that kept me interested.
Gameplay revolves around you exploring the mansion, avoiding zombies, picking up items and supplies and solving puzzles to progress forward. I’ve never played a resident evil game before and I’ll be honest, when I first tried it I didn’t like it that much. However after giving it a second try I learnt the controls, and I took my time to understand the game mechanics I actually really enjoyed it. If you play the game on PC I highly recommend using a controller, you can select between two different control layouts, one is the original tank controls and one is a more updated control scheme that feels a bit more forgiving, I decided to use the tank controls as I feel it adds to the tension of it all. This game is pretty tough for a first timer even on the easy settings, there are zombies and monsters scattered throughout the mansion and you have to deal with them, however at the beginning supplies are very limited so you have to be careful not to use up all your ammo and health items and you also have a very small inventory size plus you can die very easily, but there are item boxes scattered throughout the world allowing you to manage your inventory. Saving is done through the use of ink ribbons and you also have a limited supply of them, however on the easy settings the game is very generous with how many ink ribbons you can find as well as the other supplies including ammo and health.
The game forces the player to think about their surroundings and make smart decisions on how to progress forward, avoiding zombies completely and trying to run past can be a better strategy in the long run as you might need that ammo for later when you really do need it. If you do end up having to kill a zombie, just be sure to actually kill it, you can do this in two ways; either scoring a headshot or burning the corpse, a headshot is never guaranteed however and the kerosene used to burn zombies is also limited. The puzzles in the game aren’t too difficult and is usually just a case of remember what fits where. All these gameplay elements work well together to create an intense and somewhat frightening experience that is also highly enjoyable, once I got the hang of everything and I took it slow and methodically I really started to enjoy the game.
Graphically the game looks quite nice, with some very good use of lighting which adds to horror atmosphere of the game.
The sound and music of the game is fantastic. Hearing the groan of a zombie once you walk into a new room can strike a little bit of fear into you especially if you’re low on supplies. Hearing the ongoing thunderstorm outside the mansion adds to the atmosphere and the echoes of your own footsteps make the mansion feel like a real place. The music is quite dark and atmospheric adding to the tension of it all. Using headphones is a must in my opinion
Overall I enjoyed the game a lot once I figured out all the game mechanics. The game took me around 15 hours to complete. I wouldn’t say its Silent Hill scary but it is still very atmospheric and tense experience and a highly enjoyable one. I’d say this game is a must play, take your time and learn the mechanics and it is a blast to play. There is also quite a bit of replayability with playing as the different characters and playing on the higher difficulty settings. Let’s hope they do an HD remake of Resident Evil 2 and 3.

Do I reccomend this game? Yes... and No.
I'm going for a no response because I'm mainly pointing out the flaws of this game, but I will be pointing out positive things in the game as well.
The game starts you off in a tutorial realm and tells you a little bit about objects, picking up items, crafting and equipping. The game has a lot of content that can be reached, and building isn't extremely complicated.
This game is very confusing and has a high learning curve. You have to remember a lot of different crafting recipes and craft things appropriately, which is sometimes a pain, but luckily all possible recipies are put onto their website, so you can easily control + f and search items that you may want to craft.
One problem I have is the inaccessibility for new players. I've read recently that many players have managed to lose a lot of valuables because of silly paywalls (I will get into more detail about this later) and just general bad mechanics, but from what I believe, this mechanic was fixed. They made it so only people with permission can enter your chests, so setting it to yourself works, which is a good step in the right direction, but took them long enough to realise that this was the only viable idea they've really had.
My BIGGEST problem is the constant pay-to-win premise. I wouldn't mind sitting through ads every 15 time I entered/exited a realm to be honest, but the whole game survives on the "cubics" currency. The cubics are quite commonly found in mining blocks, but only are found as one each (Two after you get a perk, but it's uncommon and it's only until much later on (around your level 10/20, will be discussed later). They are quite cheap to buy, but I don't have money to splurge right now on the game, so I haven't bought any cubics, but the game really emphasises on buying items. Buying anything on the store costs cubics (and often in very hefty amounts) but buying from players often costs cubics. You'd think a good tactic would be buying/selling items, but to even sell items, you MUST have 1000 cubics to spend on a cash register, which is 20 days of quests/mining blocks, and there is NO way to craft this. This isn't just a problem for the cash register, there are a LOT of blocks that cannot be crafted and require cubics in hefty ammounts. The only block I find reasonable is a "construction block" that allows for easy breaking and dismantling which costs 100 cubics for 1000, but any other block is completely a waste of time and money in most cases. It's completely unreasonable to have a good 30% of blocks and 90% of clothes to be inaccessible without spending ridiculous amounts or buying from somebody else (which is the only real method to getting clothes unless you want to overly pay for a chance of a rare item). Sometimes, even renaming your building to something more relevant costs a lot of money, and that is just to RENAME a build.
That's not the only problem. One BIG issue I have is the camera angle. You are forced to have your camera facing upwards constantly and this is really irritating. The devs even have the cheek to make it so you have to craft a complicated item JUST so blocks above you can be seen underneath, and doesn't include blocks at the side. While a Nice idea, this is only accessible IN other people's realms as well as your own (if they have the item crafted in the first place). When mining underground in one of the "mines" areas that can be found on the map, the camera can be a LARGE nuisance when trying to hunt for ores, often meaning you can only mine at the very edge and not inside. This goes for the early parts of the game as well, 5 presents are hidden around underground in your first realm, but this would require you to demolish most blocks in a 30x30 area, though this could be easily solved by just making this a feature not required by items.
The last problem I have with the game is the tag system. You can tag your building with a category to see what that is, but the tags can be exploited. This can make it hard to find maps that are what you want, for example, finding parkour maps can be extremely difficult as this can be anything from a small jumping puzzle in a larger build area or an entire map dedicated to parkour.
One thing I love about the game is the perk system. Most of the perks aren't fully obtainable (some that give you hats aren't available after level 2, so you have to pick then or later, but this perk isn't required), and really makes you feel like you have been making progress in the game, as well as offer some cool buffs for leveling up and playing.
Also, making fun maps can be simple once things are found (having a bottomless pit costs a LOT of money, though, so unless you have the cubics, you'll have to resort to a material like spikes or lava to kill your participants if they fall if you want to make a parkour map), so making a cool building or parkour can be simple and fun to do with minimal stress.
TL;DR this game is pretty good, it's fun and allows for great builds, and the community is sometimes good and bad, but most MMOs have similar members in them. The game is a great sandbox but has many problems to the point where I can't really suggest it to everybody, as it requires a lot of time and patience or money.
Rating: 4.5/10
Positive:
+ Fun Leveling System
+ Easily Accessible Sandbox Game
+ Great Collectables
Negative:
- High learning curve
- Lots of paywalls
- Inaccessability for newer players
- Awkward and unnecessary camera
- Tag System Vague/Can be abused

A handful of games have shaped my life; most were on the original Playstation. Resident Evil I (Biohazard) was one of them. I remember my older brother and his friend playing RE I and II, and how zombies were the first thing in my life to actually terrify me. These shambling cannibals gave me nightmares and simultaneously intrigued me. It wasn't until I read "World War Z" and met Max Brooks in person did I begin to take my obsession with zombies more seriously and begin writing novels on them.
But I digress. This HD remaster is a wonderful addition to any RE fan's library. The graphics are beautiful, the game is just as terrifying as before, and even the voice acting got an update (I believe, I'm not 100% sure). If you like zombies or horror games, this one's a must-have for your library. Highly recommended--buy it now!

To play Morrowind in 2017 visit Morrowind Nexus and begin.
Step One: Morrowind Code Patch
Step Two: Delayed BrotherHood Attacks
Step Three: Official Plugins
Step Four: Watercolored v2
Step Five: Morrwind Graphics Extender XE
Now play the best in the Elder Scrolls series. Seriously, this game is so good that despite its release back in 2002 it still holds up today. Attacks not hitting? Silly noob, this is an RPG, and your first quest giver ALL TELLS YOU TO USE TRAINERS. Spend the gold, get your skills above 50 and watch how often you hit things! Cliff Racers annoying? Please. Skyrim's dragons are significantly less fun and more frequent. Faces scrunched together? Sure, but it beats those creepy baby wax dolls of Oblivion.
Morrowind outshines every other TES game for a few reasons. First you have the world, which is immersive, and doesn't hold your hand at ALL. You are not a badass here. You are technically the chosen one, but its gonna take a lot of suffering before you reach that point. Desperately searching for gold, conserving mana and arrows, and trying to get a few more herbs for a potion are some of the activities that will stick with you. Also. Walking. This game has fast travel, but only via rare and hard to find scrolls and spells. You will be walking, so the graphics enhancements I suggested help. Also the music is outstanding, and unlike Oblivion, Morrowind has literally hundreds of little dungeons strewn about, your quest might be literal hours of walking away, but there is always something new to see and do. Speaking of which, this game is LOOOOONG. Don't worry about not having the right skills, go join one of the many factions and earn some coin, go spelunking, train yourself up. Don't worry about that 5 in shortblades, there is ALOT of money to be made, and you can train most of the skills up in the starter towns. Balmora is love, Balmora is life.
Morrowind is a living breathing place. It may not have the conveniance of Skyrim, the randomness of Daggerfall or the uh...well whatever Oblivion had going for it, but it makes up for it with sheer personality. Immersion, challenge, and longevity, this game has it ALL.

This is a fun, cute, if short game. The puzzles you had to solve were very diverse, which I truly enjoyed, and the controls to select objects to interact with were smooth. I especially enjoyed the use of clasic arcade/board games in some of the areas. The arcade game to open the hints journal was a little too hard to work around each time for me, but I was easily able to find the list of hints posted by the creators online.
The real downfall for this game was that the story felt lacking. It had been so long since I purchased this game that I had no idea when I started it (or indeed until more than half-way through the game) why my character cared about this city that I had been thrown out of or the relevance of the girl who only appeared in memories that I had when I left the screen alone for too long.
For me personally, this worked out great because I was looking for a game that I could have running and play for a few seconds at a time to break up some tedious busy-work I needed to get done on my computer. But, the fact that the story was so disengaging and mostly revealed in thought-bubbles in the very last scene might be cause for caution before purchase for someone else. When the story was finally revealed, it felt that that must be the half-way point and now we are getting down to business. Really, there was just one "fix-all-the-issues" scene followed by a get-away scene and that's it.
So, basically, the story could use some reorganization and I would have LOVED to play this for longer, but over-all, a very nicely constructed click-based puzzle game that perfectly suited my purposes of having a game to play while working, and would probably prvide a satisfying few hours of puzzling for someone who played the game without multitasking.

Curator Review:
This board game, developed by Days of Wonder, is a game of many pieces but also a game in which you are encouraged to slaughter your friends. Pick a race, conquer some regions, go into decline, conquer some more, and make money along the way! The person with the most money at the end of the game wins. This risk-esque game is elegantly designed and a beautiful replica of the physical board game. If you love board games or you just love wailing on your friends, I highly recommend it. 8/10

Writing a review for this game really makes me wish Steam had a "Maybe" button.  Small World 2 is a computerized version of the Small World board game.  The goal of the game is to have more victory coins than the other players by the end of the game.  You gain victory coins based on how many territories your race holds on the map at the end of your turn (plus special and racial bonuses).  The races and specials are randomized at the start of the game and the mechanics ensure that you'll play at least a couple of races each game.  Unlike Risk, players are not defeated and forced to leave the game.  Play proceeds for a fixed number of rounds and everyone participates until the very end.  Only two sources of randomness exist in Small World:  the available race and power combinations and the die roll for the last conquest of your turn.  The rest is all strategy, which is another serious departure from Risk (everyone seems to compare Risk and Small World in reviews so I'll do it too).
So Small World is a great game.  But should you buy this version of it?  There is absolutely no substitute for gathering a group of friends at a table and playing the real thing.  But the physical version of the game does take up a ton of space and is littered with pieces you need to manage and arrange.  The game boards (the map you use depends on the number of players) don't take up much space, but everything else you need to play the game more than makes up for it.  My family and I found it a little awkward to play on our moderately large kitchen table.  It doesn't help that new players will need the large cheat sheets included with the game to figure out what the races and special abilities do.  The big advantage of the digital version is that the computer keeps track of everything for you and there are no pieces to manage.  You also have the option to play against AI opponents which can help you learn the game.
I actually bought Small World 2 so that I could learn the game and practice for playing with my family.  I think that is a fine reason for buying the game.  Given the attention to detail visible in the game itself, the instructions are surprisingly poor.  Having the rules enforced by the game itself makes it easy to get the hang of things.  Games move a lot more quickly too given that there is no need to deal with physical pieces.  It costs less than the physical version of Small World too.
The reason I can't wholeheartedly recommend the game is because it feels cheap.  For all the fun I've had with it, it is actuality a poor port of a mobile game, with none of the optimizations or customization options you would expect from a PC game.  The fact that the tutorial you can access from the game just loads a Youtube video was shocking.  It's a mediocre version of a great game.  Buy it if you want to play the game by yourself or with friends online (but if they live close by, please consider the board game instead).  Otherwise, just skip this and play the real thing.

This is very frustrating and I've seen plenty of other people booted too.  This is not an internet connection issue (for me or for others), but rather a server issue.
As mentioned before the soundtrack is very limited and repetitive.
Good game, but it definitely contains some wonks that need to be worked out, and hopefully these will be worked out soon because I would love to see more people adopt the game and play it online.

Bomber Crew will bring back fond memories of Faster Than Light (FTL). It's hard to not make a comparison. What it has in common with it is frantic micromanagment minus the aliens and gathering scrap. You upgrade your bomber in a variety of ways and you must make decisions based off of weight and funds.
What Bomber Crew is not is any sort of flight sim. You must navigate the plane with a waypoint system. You do not actually fly it. You must manage all of your crew instead.
The game comes with a learning curve that isn't too steep, mostly because it takes a bit to understand what is going on. After making a few impressive craters in the landscape, you will get the hang of it in a reasonable amount of time.
A mistake you can make in this game is grind too much to upgrade to a perfect plane. Part of the strategy on being successful is to not overdo it. Spending hours to lead yourself into a false sense of security only to have your soul crushed by one mission that just went wrong is a bad idea. Getting attached to crew members is a bad idea.
If you are a rage quitter, ready your alt-F4 key press protocols.
With the insane flood of mediocre games being created on a daily basis, this game is a gem. It has nice graphics, sound, and an entertaining atmosphere. Very few miscromanagement games get it right. Bomber Crew gets it right. It's not for everyone, but who cares? Not everyone like nachos, either.
Some people will find the interface somewhat clunky. I did at first, but got used to it in a few hours. The game definately doesn't play itself. Be aware there is no "pause" button that you can use to issue orders. You can push the escape key in case of bathroom breaks, but it wont save you from forgetting where your engineer went. This is a minor issue, and I really don't think the game needs a pause order system. It would break the tension and immersion IMHO. People with a case of OCD should avoid this. However, this game may provide those people with exciting therapy.
If you enjoy games with just the right amount of pucker factor, buy now. If you prefer games where you press "A" to win, you should buy it anyways because I know you want to.

Brothers is a gorgeous adventure delivered through a unique control concept that is perfectly executed throughout its many action, puzzle, and dramatic utilizations.  It is also a remarkably affecting and memorable experience, a confident and heartfelt peer to Journey and Ico.
It is difficult to talk about the game and its design at length without at least hinting at story spoilers.  Suffice it to say that I have always found it interesting when games co-opt their own mechanics to force you to do something dramatic, and Brothers does this in the most thorough and thoughtful way I have ever seen.  The controller requirement is not only key to the game's "solo cooperative" gameplay; it is also, brilliantly, vital to its emotional impact.  To use cautiously vague terms, in its climactic moment, Brothers uses the interactivity uniquely offered by videogames to pull the player into a character's mind in an elegant way not possible in other media.  That is all I will say on the matter.
Aside from being both fun and powerful in its own right, Brothers is also on the short list of videogames that are truly important because of how they explore the medium's potential.  I cannot recommend strongly enough that you play it as soon as you possibly can.

The amount of choice and freedom available in this game is still staggering to this day. You have much more player agency over the world in this game compared to Skyrim. Here, you can actually kill NPCs that give you quests. You can enchant your boots so that when you jump, you can jump 20ft. Or 50ft. Or across the map. You can enchant armor and weapons, use spears, follow signposts and specific directions instead of objective markers, kill someone and live in their house, create your own spells (yup, scrolls and potions too). You can contract diseases on your adventures that you can cure. Oh, and you can become a vampire or werewolf. And that is just some of the more interesting stuff...
You can't shout people to death... but at least there's a lot to make up for with that.
You have an epic quest that the game tells you about at the start, but following it is optional and is really there to give the player a goal in the massive sandbox of a world. You start off as a nobody, and eventually can have god-like powers. The world, atmosphere, and music combine to make you feel like a part of an epic fantasy novel.
Altough graphically dated, if you have patience (and maybe a little of your own imagination) it is a wonderful experience. Or you could just mod it so it looks pretty - the Morrowind Overhaul is a great project for that.

I personally have yet to beat the game, and am not the biggest fan of the levelling system, but there are lots of things to love about this game: All the magics available to you; the old-timey feel of the menus and sound effects; the humongous, gorgeous world to explore; the fascinating, wonderous soundtrack- they've done a great many favors for this game's overall quality! And by far the biggest issue - the aged graphics - have a simple, highly-customizable fix in the form of the Morrowind Graphics & Sound Overhaul mod. Overall, this game's many positive aspects heavily outweigh the negatives, and have earned it my 9/10. Happy questing, and remember kids: Watch out for arrows flying towards your knee! ...Yeah, I know, wrong ES-

No fantasy RPG will ever reach heights as Morrowind did. Many claim that the game did not age well, but they're not keeping mind that the game is over 15 years old at this point. Just compare the game to other games at the time, then judge Morrowind on it's aging. The control scheme is a bit out of wack, but I simply switched the activate and jump key, and the ready weapon and ready magic key, and the game felt like any other Elder Scrolls game I've played.
The best part of the game has to be the immersiveness. The vast variety of skills and attributes makes you really feel like you're progressing throughout the game. The map wasn't the biggest, but there was so much to explore. There was no fast travel so everything felt more in depth and real. Quests felt like quests, not chores, or tasks.
Now, the character customization was very limited, and the animations just looked ridiculous. Each individual body part got it's own 3D polygon shape. There is a simple fix to that error, which would be to install the Better Bodies mod through Nexus Mod Manager.
The combat in the game may be one of the biggest cons, although it gives off a real RPG/dungeon crawler vibe, that was eventually lost throughout time, as more First Person Shooter-like games become popularized. Morrowind will always be my favorite Elder Scrolls game.

Machinarium from Amanita Design is one of the best point-and-click adventure games I’ve played.  Yet there is almost no text, and the cute robots that inhabit the dirty, rusty city you’ll be exploring communicate exclusively through adorable pictograph speech bubbles.  Join Josef the little robot on his journey to save his friend Berta and defeat the nefarious Black Cap Brotherhood.
A beautifully hand-drawn world full of mechanical creatures and robot people is the backdrop to your adventure.  Josef is thrown out onto the scrapheap, and you must get him back into the city.  Collect items and solve puzzles to find your way forward.  You’ll help a lady reunite with her robot dog.  You’ll bust out of prison.  Most adventure games give you the entire screen to search through to find the correct item to click.  Machinarium smartly limits your reach to your own arms, but you can stretch and shrink Josef high and low in order to reach items.  Anything you collect, he will open up his head and shove it into his mouth, in an endearingly cute animation.
Other than the limitations I described, this is a fairly standard adventure game.  Click a bunch of stuff on different screens, in the correct order.  There are no twitchy challenges, though a fair number of puzzles have a fairly lax timed component to them.  There are also no major “fail states” that require you to redo minutes of work.  You usually only have to retry a few seconds worth of action if you make a mistake.  One really cool feature is the hint system.  Rather than just click a button, or spend from some limited pool of “points” to get past a difficult puzzle, you play a little Game Boy-style shooter minigame to get a look at the guide.  There are no limits to how often you do this.  The in-game guide is awesomely illustrated, and you’ll feel good about yourself for having ‘earned’ the hint rather than just giving up.  I never had to consult an outside source to proceed in the game.  Rather, I immersed myself in the world, and let the game itself give me a gentle nudge through some tricky spots.
The music and sound effects are amazing, as we expect from Amanita Design.  Machines clank and buzz strangely, and speakers throughout the city play some hauntingly distorted but still cheerful jazz.  Everything you interact with sounds different, in a good way.  Each environment you explore has its own soundscape, making the world a pleasure to discover.  The soundtrack as a whole has a strange electro-ambient vibe, and I really dig it.
Yet your ears aren’t the only part of you being thoroughly pleasured.  The graphics are outstanding.  Everything has a hand-drawn, cared-for feel.  You sense the love that went into designing this world.  You may be moving from static screen to static screen, but that doesn’t mean these scenes are lifeless.  Graphical tricks give the world unexpected depth, and on most screens there are objects and characters constantly moving and interacting.  The level of detail that went into not just the puzzles, but the space those puzzles inhabit, is really noticeable.
That hand-crafted feel really makes this game stand out in my mind.  It is just such a unique experience.  I found myself wanting to solve the puzzles not just for the sense of accomplishment, but so I could see what was hidden around the next corner.  Some of those puzzles were a little obtuse, and I got quite lost later in the game where the majority of the city is available to you to walk around freely.  Minor quibbles that don’t really influence my opinion on this game at all.
Which is to say, you really should play this game.  It is a shining example of unique, quirky developers making the game they want to make, without the constraint of publishers or focus groups or shareholders to please.  This game stands on its own merits, and doesn’t try to appeal to everyone.  The irony is that by being so unique and innovative, it should appeal to everyone.  The cute graphics combined with the adorable thought bubble cartoons will stick with you for a long time.
Also, you can get Josef and Berta plushies at the Amanita Design store.  I’m trying to convince my wife to let me buy them for our kids.  Really, they’re not for me.  I mean, they can sit on my desk when the kids aren’t playing with them.

Minecraft clones are a dime a dozen these days, but this one really stands out. It's free, but there are no ads, and it runs great on my wimpy non-gaming laptop. I've only played a couple hours so far, but I can already tell that the dev team is active and responsive. The camera controls are simple but more-or-less functional, although they do get in the way. The building tools are fairly intuitive, and the overworld is pretty easy to navigate, although I do wish the tutorial explained the menu.
Each player is given their own "realm" to build in - the entrance to this realm is placed on the overworld map, wherever you decide to stick it. You can change the permission settings for your realm at any time, but the default allows anyone to visit and only you to edit. You can also blacklist or whitelist individual players, and toggle PVP. Blocks are obtained from public mines, each a different biome, accessed in the overworld. You can teleport to whichever entrance you want using the Sky Map on the menu, and visit different "worlds" (continents?) by using the launch pads, which are also visible on the map.
There is in-game currency called cubits that you can buy for real money, but you can also accrue it by mining, which is something you'll be doing a lot of anyway. The drop rate for cubits when mining is pretty fair, and there are no time limits or items essential to buy, so it's unlikely to cause much frustration. You can use it to purchase blocks instead of crafting or mining them, as well as luxury items like hats and game enhancers like new quests or a name change. There's a pretty robust trading system as well, with cash registers providing relatively secure transactions.
There's a platforming aspect that's pretty entertaining. It's clunky (like the platforming in Minecraft), but there's no real penalty to dying, and it's not something you're forced to do. Special blocks like bounce blocks, spike plates, and acceleration rings let players build their own obstacle courses (referred to in-game as "parkour"). The devs seem to be tinkering with adding more features like this - right now they're working on monsters, and blocks that allow you to make secret passages. Using signposts as exposition and dialogue, you can make a pretty basic adventure game with this, which is cool.
Cubic Castles is free, but I'd pay money for it, and I think the devs deserve money - they're even doing a charity promotion for someone who needs a heart transplant right now. If you're on the fence, I'd say pick it up and give it a try.

Creepy Castle lives on highs and lows, though the premise might not seem too attractive to some there's a whole lot to offer. And then there's even more to offer. By the end what it has to offer is certainly cool but also feeling a little stale because you've spent so long getting through it.
To summarize the story is as such, you are Moth, a wandering warrior who one day finds some incredible evil happening within a place known as The Castle of Light and goes to stop it. Along the way he meets many friends and enemies, all with stories that we just don't have enough time to get into. With some heroics and conquest, Moth eventually finds himself in over his head fighting something beyond mere good and evil. By the end you have this overwhelming feeling of amazement and wonder. Just who were these characters beyond this castle? What could come next? So with some excitement you discover that three more scenarios have just opened up, each one boasting a new adventure with the gameplay you've just gotten accustomed to and somewhat mastered. Fast forward ahead a couple scenarios and you STILL wonder who these characters are and are starting to feel a little slowed by the stretched concepts from the dueling system. By the end, as gripped as you are by the story, you might find that it's really the only thing gripping you at this point.
What I'm getting at is Creepy Castle has its flaws. They start out as small stylistic choices, but eventually you have this nagging sensation as you wander back on the path you've gone down several times already that, well, maybe the developers could have developed the maps a little more, maybe they didn't need to have THAT many battles, for goodness sake would it kill the game to expand the overall visibility by a few more blocks?! This is what I'm going to dub the "I'm stuck in scenario three" syndrome but the complaints still extend to scenario two and four. Two is short and interesting, but ends up repeating itself to complete a story with only a small change at the end really being the difference between the two halves. Four is loaded with battles, and as nice as the variation in duels go, it still ends up feeling a bit too stretched.
And really all three situations feel the same in different ways: stretched. Redoing an entire scenario just to experience a slightly different - yet plot crutial - conclusion, stretches the game out. Getting lost trying to find the last couple of things in a near identical looking maze in scenario three - intentional or otherwise - stretches the game out. Fighting a laaarge number of baddies, all utilizing duel schemes you've seen en masse in the previous scenarios, stretches the game out. Ultimately I felt like as expansive of an adventure this game had to offer, I would have preferred it to be shorter.
Compliments where compliments are due though, the duel system is very thoroughly utilized, every enemy has a unique pattern or use of each duel minigame. It only ends up feeling stale because by the end of the game you've done nearly a thousand of them. There's looooads of great pixel art stylized in a retro commodore style and even recolored enemies have unique changes done to them. Every scenario has different musical theming and reused songs are at a low. And the best of all, the writing is frankly spectacular. You wouldn't expect it from a game with such a cute style, but - without getting into too much spoilers - there's tons of great character interactions and motivations. It grips you and doesn't let go because you just HAVE to find out what happens! These guys stretched a concept to near breaking point but frankly it works. That said I will have to dock a few points for making a bunch of interesting characters who seem like they could go past being just simple one-notes - having a large role in the various protagonists' stories - only to not really go ANYWHERE with them. There's a whole lot of story that feels just missing in scenario one that never is brought up again.
So, Creepy Castle gets my recommendation.
