Huniepop is a 2015 (adult) tile puzzle matching and dating simulator game that allows you to strategically match colored tokens for points and successfully win “date challenges” in order to reach the highest goal, a one-night (erotic) stand. Huniepop takes influence of Japanese anime and its visual novels, parodied the genre with great result. You might have heard this game before, probably from hilarious one-line reviews to infamous standing against Steam Terms of Service and censorship. Huniepop got its name and does it capture your attention?
Huniepop does not have a plot, but it does have a bit of lore in regards to character relationships between one and another. The main point is for you (male or female) to sleep with 12 women (9 default and 3 “secret” characters) and…that’s pretty much it. Most importantly, do not take this game seriously. Each of the 12 women have a unique personality and some characters are very memorable (I won’t spoil them; you will have to find out yourself) while a few characters are cringeworthy. The game starts off when you meet a young woman named Kyu, a nymphomaniac fairy who “guides” you on the tutorial section and gives you a few tips on what to do. As you progress into the game, the total points requirement for each puzzle increases, relying on 4-token to 7-token combos and wise tactics to successfully win over dates. When you win a date, you’ll gain Munie (Money) to spend on standard gifts, unique gifts, food, and drinks (alcohol). When you give a woman gifts, you will also gain Hunie points which allows you to spend on traits like romance, sensitivity, passion, and others. These traits will help you on later dates. In addition, giving gifts to a woman will grant you hairstyle unlocks and date gifts (permitting easier solutions to overcome tough puzzle challenges).
Puzzles are not the only challenge, dating simulations are an obstacle if you are not good at memorizing. Each woman would ask you questions about remembering their attributes (age, height, weight, cup size…yes…cup size, and others), and ask preference questions (Examples: Do you like girls who have pubic hair? What is your biggest turn on? etc.) If you get the question right, you get more hunie points; however, if you get the question wrong, the woman would be “upset” and won’t gain hunie bonuses but it does not penalize your relationship with the woman you are currently with. That’s pretty much it about gameplay. The voice acting is amateur, but I prefer it this way for “authentic purposes”. What the game is most famous for are the pictures after completing each date until the climax (four pictures for each woman x 12 women, totaling up to 48). I won’t go in full details about the pictures but I found two pictures from one particular character “unsettling”.
Are there criticism for the game? To be honest, it is hard for me to find legitimate criticism for the game though I had some criticism for one particular (and probably, controversial) character, the high-pitched girl who is a “cat”. I could write an essay on why I dislike or despise this character, but this is for another time. Regardless, I’ve encountered one bug where some women would talk simultaneously as if there are two of them. The replay value range is very low to moderate if you are seeking achievements, enjoy the addicting puzzle challenges, or hear the “voices” at night. Another criticism from me is that this game delivers guilty pleasure. I don’t know why but I really like the game even though I know that playing the game “feels wrong”.
The most difficult part is who I would recommend this game to. Huniepop targets a certain audience, which are gamers who like anime-style genre. However, what attracts me to the game was actually (believe it or not) was the tile-matching challenges. This is very addicting and I appreciate the developers for making the gameplay very unique. The game cost $10, but it is best to get the game around $5 or less (-50% or more) because of low replay value. I can only recommend the game to people who likes anime or can handle adult content but this is certainly my money’s worth and I am looking forward for the sequel as long as the “cat” is not in the next game.

This game is excellent. Really seems to capture the hectic "blown to hell" struggle for survival in the air.
I was hesitant at first because of the points by negative reviews, but after playing for a while I think they missed some key things:
1. Zoom out from your bomber and use the shift key to zoom in. It's really quick and always autocentered.
2. Use the number keys to select your crew members. That will help you avoid clicking on the wrong guy.
3. As you progress the campaign (critical missions) losing your bomber and crew becomes less painful. Your recruits start at a higher level and the airplane starts with some basic upgrades.
4. There is some grinding in this game. You wanna grind crew levels and aircraft upgrades. You should be doing medium risk missions only after low risk is easy. Do high risk only after medium risk is easy. If you bite off more than you can chew, use the pilot's Abort and get the hell home. It's better to fail than lose everything.
5. As your crew levels, the game gets more and more easy. You can autotag fighters so you're not overwhelmed by that. You can get an autoloader for your tail turret so you don't have to reload it. You can call in Spitfires to help you take out the enemy quickly. You can navigate at high altitude to avoid flak and fighters.
This game is not quick and easy. It will take you a while to get fast, but when you do, it becomes very rewarding.

First time I tried to play Witcher, I hated the combat so much that I uninstalled before I finished the tutorial.
Second time, I realized that I was too hasty. The combat isn't really that bad, compared to everything else that's not especially enjoyable about the game.
Basically, everything that everybody says about Witcher is exactly the opposite of the truth. Namely, the combat isn't that big of a downer, but the story is actually kinda dull and unoriginal, and the characters are as bland and two-dimensional as a Dennys menu. It's swords and sorcery fantasy with a "dark" flavor... you have seen it a million times. Maybe you've never had a chance to have sex with as many NPCs, so there's that.
BTW: if you haven't figured it out by now, don't believe any game that promises "serious consequences for your choices" that supposedly make a significant difference in story and gameplay. What you'll usually get is either two sets of skills/companions/endings to play toward (Jedi/Sith, Nord/Imperial, etc), or at best varying degrees of hostility from rival factions (Minutemen-Brotherhood-Institute). The Witcher has a dull cutscene montage that appears at certain transitions to narrate some consequences, none of which are interestingly game-altering.
Most of The Witcher consists of monotonous clicking on enemies, which as I said turns out NOT to be the most boring and repetitive part of the game, That honor goes to the structure of many of the quests, which largely consist of meeting someone at midnight and discovering that you don't have the exact thing that you need for them to talk to you... and then going to get it and discovering that the merchant won't be back for six hours... and then going to find one of the rare places to sleep (I mean meditate) for eight hours... then going to the merchant and buying the Exact Thing... then sleeping for eight hours... then meeting the original guy at midnight with the Exact Thing so that he can tell you how to get to the next questgiver... who can only be met on the other side of the map at 10 pm when there's a light rain and no chickens in the neighborhood. And HE'LL refuse to speak to you until you get Exact Thing #2...
Seriously, it was when I realized that I was literally just waiting for it to rain to get to the next quest stage, I began to have serious doubts that I was ever going to look at The Witcher as anything but a chore. I'll believe you when you say it all pays off in the end. I choose to believe you and move on, rather than continue the torture of proving it true or false for myself. I got it during a sale, and played it for a few days, so I can't really say I didn't get my money's worth. I've played much better games all the way to the finish in that amount of time... so except for the part where I rarely enjoyed myself, The Witcher was a very good value.

Creepy Castle is a game that simply oozes with style and charm in a very vintage way!
In this game, you play as Moth in a world full of other bug-themed friends (and others) who will help you in your adventure through the castle. The supporting cast are all very varied and well written, with very destinct personalities and traits. Some of the characters you will speak to directly, but a lot of the lore and personality of the cast is brought out by the (very funny and well structured) books that are littered throughout the castle. These are all optional if you just want to punch things in the face, but they are usually very helpful, or at least interesting.
The game also has multiple game modes and stories, all lasting a few hours each, to really help bring the world to life! A lot of work clearly went into crafting this game.
Gameplay is typical Metroid-Vania style exploration, get The Thing, use The Thing on The-Other-Thing to open a new path, fight bad guys along the way. Should be very familiar in this sense, but the battles are more akin to a turn based RPG, with some Wario Ware Minigames thrown in. You take turns punching each other in the face, but occasionally you'll get a Minigame battle. Button Mashing to get free of snakes, quick draw anime-style sword showdowns, and a bunch more that are harder to explain, but intuivite once you see them!
I'd very heavily recommend this game, especially if you're looking for a personal feeling story that's full of great characters and wonderfully retro charm and style! There are certainly 'better' exploration games out there in terms of gamefeel, but this was designed to feel like an early video game and it boasts that wonderfully.

I've been following this game from its inception, backed it on Kickstarter, and helped test it, so I may be a little biased because I'm quite invested in it. That being said: I love it. It's sort of a puzzle-game/Metroidvania hybrid, so if you like turn-based action, exploration, puzzle-style strategy, and/or minigames that are often a test of your hand-eye coordination and reflexes, you'll have a blast. If you like thoughtful, emotional dialogue that's still grounded more in a cartoon fantasy realm than in everyday realism, this is the game for you. If you like adorable, varied, and surprisingly detailed pixel art and "retro" color schemes from the early 90s (and before!), it's all right here.
And I haven't even touched the music which is frankly just stellar. RushJet1 (who you might know from 1001 Spikes, the Megaman Remade albums, and the Cave Story Remix project) works really well with Marius and Zach, two of Creepy Castle's developers, to create catchy-yet-multilayered chiptunes that range anywhere from quiet and subtle mood music to fast-paced and frenetic. Honestly, even if you're not huge on the game itself, the music is worth the price of admission alone.
Unlike a straightforward action beat-em-up like Castlevania or Metroid or something like Undertale whose battle system is more akin to a cross between Earthbound and a shoot-em-up or bullet hell game, Creepy Castle's battles are more akin to WarioWare or even old-school physical games like Simon Says, Bop-It!, and timing-based memory games, all accompanied by unique sprite art portraits and animations.
Some are harder than others (at least to me), but I imagine everyone will have their faves and their duds... my personal favorites are Duel and Bullrush. The key, though, is that they switch up constantly. Every enemy has at least a couple attack variations, so you're never stuck doing the same battle minigame for long. If you get really good at one, you still have to be on your toes; it might change up, or the enemy might simply trade hits with you, and you have to strategize when to use healing items (food), special attacks, and bombs. It's surprisingly intense and engaging for what is essentially a series of timing games.
Bosses are made even more intense with the addition of a move timer and the inability to "escape". Some are also resistant to specials, and they all have various quirks and fight gimmicks that make them quite fun to encounter.
The in-game lore ranges from incredibly dry humor (this is some seriously Monkey-Island level dryness, which is right up my alley - see the "Instructional Manuals") to serious contemplations on the nature of love and loss and the purpose of unbidden upswells of (sometimes destructive) emotion. It's all part of a neat space/time-hopping fantasy adventure which is both compelling and good fun, so the changes in tone fit right in.
The game is divided into "scenarios" or "episodes" which you unlock as you progress, so each one can be played as a self-contained game or as just one part of a larger story. Some scenarios are battle-heavy, while others focus much more on exploration, finding secrets, etc. They're helpfully labeled so that you can pick and choose which ones you want to play and in what order based on your enjoyment of the various aspects of the game, and there is some replayability in each because you can select new characters after you complete each one. There's also a neat tracking system on the main menu which shows every enemy you encounter, every piece of in-game lore you find, and every song you hear, so you can see whether or not you've missed anything and go back to find them. Each scenario takes between ~1 and 4 hours to play if you try find absolutely everything which makes for a surprisingly lengthy game experience, but the advantage here is that you can stick to one scenario at a time and portion out the playtime as you need.
I think the game really has something for everyone, and like I said, the music alone is worth the price of admission. Beyond that you have cute, fun, and detailed spritework, alternately funny and touching writing, and a good amount of engaging world-building to look forward to. I highly recommend you give it a play-through.

At the time of writing, I have completed two of the main 4 scenarios and 1 of the remixed scenarios. While I have not seen the entirety of the game, I am confident that I have formed a solid opinion. Creepy Castle deserves both a recommendation and is well worth the $15. I rank CC up there with indie classics such as Cave Story and Shovel Knight.
CC is an indie-retro style side scrolling action adventure game with turn base battle. CC is a genre blending game, with gameplay a blend of metroidvania exploration and a Mario & Luigi game combat system.
The exploration part comes in the form of rather large levels which has to be traversed to find items to allow for advancement. Like any metroidvania games, backtracking is rewarded with extras and secrets. However, one thing to note is that exploration can be slow due to CC imitating how a ZX Spectrum game would have run. Other issues such as generic backgrounds making poor landmark and a featureless map make remembering where things were difficult. But like any other metroidvania game, the sense of progression is great.
Combat are typically 1-1 affair (
) can be categorized with 3 types of turns: regular, duels, and crits. Regular combat is uneventful and results in both  combatant taking 1 damage. Duels involves mini-games where if the player does well they can get hit in with no damage, but may do no damage if they fail. The mini-game are usually fair once you have learn the games rule. Crits are annoying because the game lacks any real stats. There are experience tokens but they are more of a mean to allow for increasing difficulty rather than any player growth. Both player and enemies can randomly land a crit which can do more than 1 heart of damage. You can heal as a free action but being unable to predict crits can lead to unfair deaths. The RNG also factors into duels as duels are not always guaranteed against some enemies, forcing regular combat, forcing more damage. The combat can be forgiven though since it’s pretty easy and the game is generous with healing items.
All in all, the game is still fun. I know I put a lot of negatives out there but if you’re willing to look past that then there’s a lot of positive too.
The graphics and art style are well done and very memorable. CC is a true retro experience simulating the early days of home consoles.
The story is good. It plot isn’t convoluted or bogged down by melodrama. Furthermore, CC has quite a bit of lore with unqiue characters and stories implied in the dialogue. The plot compliments the game by being doled out slowly, encouraging exploration.
The sound design is great. The music does loop but is far from annoying. The jukebox feature is actually nice since the game soundtrack is large with unique tracks for different scenarios.
The game has plenty of secrets and characters to unlock for free play. Free play allows you to replay scenarios with different characters from the game with slight changes to dialogue.
The amount of polish and content in the game is very satisfying and I cannot stress this enough that I think this game deserves to a chance. I hope that the developer Dopterra continues making more content for this game and expanding the world of CC as it is truly something to enjoy.

This game really surprised me.  I went in thinking it would be a small retro style game with some metroidvania elements, and found out the scale of this game is much larger.  In a way, it's the mixing of Metroidvania and Undertale, where battles are fought through mini-games and exploration for power-ups with backtracking play a key role.  What really blew me away was that the game blows out into a much larger story once the initial castle is cleared.  The story branches out in other episodes that follow various characters after the events of the original story.   These side stories expand the story greatly and some of these are quite larger, even larger than the initial episode.
The music in this game is truly one of the best chiptune OST I've ever heard.  As far as flaws, the non-boss enemies each have a small set of mini-game battles depending on their type.  At certain points in the game, I felt there were maybe too many enemies which leads in turn to play the same type of mini-game way too often in a short time frame.  Overall though, it's a surprising large game with a lot of secrets to hunt down.

An excellent port of the board game.
SmallWorld is like Risk, except with much smaller armies, each with a combination of two special abilitys (randomly combined).
Reinforcements are non existent so as your army dies off, you can put that army in decline, score points from territory they still hold, and then grab another army on the next turn.
This is a game of interesting decisions, not luck free, but even in loss your brain will try to work out exactly how you could have done better.
It's not a game you can perfect, like chess, but it can be learned, and it's a good time once your literate with the racial and special abilities.
Excellent digital version of the board game, keeps all the charm and is infinitely replayable!

Resident Evil (1996) was the game that successfully continued the traditions of Alone in the Dark (1992) and strengthened the survival horror as a category. With simplified adventure elements and often dumb(ish) puzzles it concentrated on horror with lots of fighting involved. Using the same fixed camera view/angle as seen in AitD, the game managed to amplify the horror feel, but the fights were often unnecessarily hard because of this (and the scarcity of ammunition).
After some strange murders in the countryside, a team of S.T.A.R.S. (Special Tactics and Rescue Service) officers from the nearby town, Raccoon City are sent to investigate the area. Attacked by zombie dobermanns they run into a nearby mansion that's seemingly abandoned (even though all the lights are on) to seek shelter. Soon all hell breaks loose as they discover the traces (and results) of a secret experiment regarding a mysterious virus that threatens the whole world...
The surviving team members' presence depends on which character we picked at the beginning. We can choose Chris Redfield by default, who is strong, has a lighter and 6 inventory slots. To make things more entertaining, he doesn't have a firearm (he had one in the intro, but nevermind). The other protagonist is Jill Valentine, who can't take as much damage as Chris, her knife is weaker, but has 8 inventory slots so she can carry more stuff around (this involves both quest related items and weapons). She also starts the game with a handgun and soon acquires a lockpick as well (which is only useful for a couple of doors though), not to mention she has access to the powerful grenade launcher.
The game is slightly different depending on which character we chose, there are minor plot twists and additional information revealed, plus both of them meet different sidekicks (Jill - Barry, Chris - Rebecca) throughout the game. We also have to rescue our partner accordingly and there are certain situations where the 2 characters can act differently. For example Jill can attempt to kill the plant monster using a herbicide whereas Chris has to use conventional firearms to destroy it, but Chris can use a flamethrower later against a giant spider while Jill can't and so on. Also there are funny moments, such as the one with the zombie emerging from the bathtub, where Chris just watches and freaks out, while Jill quicky crushes the zombie's head by trampling on it then rushes to the toilet and throws up :)
There isn't much to praise about the plot as it's quite simple (the characters are even more so), but anyone who has heard about Resident Evil already knows this. There are 4 (or 12 to be precise) different endings depending on who we rescue and whether we blow up the secret underground lab or not. Don't expect huge differences though, I'd say the game gets rather boring after 2 (1 with Chris and 1 with Jill) playthroughs (you will need at least 4 if you plan on unlocking all the costumes, weapons and such).
The dialogues are hillariously and notoriously bad (just your average Japanese game), but they became a positive trademark of the Resident Evil games as time flew by. The "You were almost a Jill sandwich!" line for example became quite famous and it's a mystery why they removed it (!) from the game. Were they trying to even out this mistake and make the game more serious? Probably. Well, they could have left this one in for fun and for old times' sake.
Resident Evil HD REMASTER features a fair number of new elements (I'm comparing it to the original RE from 1996, not to the 2002 gamecube version). The most important one is the addition of an extra boss, Lisa Trevor, the daughter of a former employee of Umbrella. With it new areas were also added: the spooky cabin outside the mansion and her lair below. The encounter with the giant shark is also a highlight.
Another new enemy is the "crimson head", a reawakened zombie which is a faster, deadlier version of the shambling, twitching zombies we all know. They usually appear after leaving the corpse of a zombie (with its head still attached to its neck) on the ground and reentering the area. To prevent this from happening we can do 2 things: going for headshots (in a game where it's practically impossible to aim vertically, it's not an option) by lucky criticals, or using kerosene and burn the corpses. Yes, burning them is a new feature too, but for that we'll need a flask filled with kerosene (it runs out after 2 uses) and a lighter (which Chris has automatically, but Jill needs to find and carry around). And yes, this means we need extra inventory space.
We also receive close-quarter self-defense weapons (other than the terrible knife): disposable (because each one can only be used once - don't ask) daggers. Depending on which character we chose, Jill can find battery packs for her taser while Chris uses flash grenades (this one is lethal, because he places them inside the mouth of our foes and the resulting explosion blows their head apart, but it can injure us as well if we stand to close). We are definitely going to be needing these, because if one of the enemies manage to grab us, it'll start biting us immeditely, but with the use of these items, not only we can avoid taking damage, but can also injure or kill our attacker.
The game requires a controller (it doesn't, but it is recommended) and even with that it won't be easy. There are numerous layouts, but I found none of them exactly useful: autorun is handy, but sometimes walking and "tank controls" are more suitable to dodge the zombies' attacks (when they lunge at us and miss, they stand idle for a while which we can use to slip by). Later on as the enemies get quite fast though and we should use the autorun option again. Also, if we don't have any defense items (daggers, etc.) and the enemies grab us, we can only free ourselves by shaking the analog sticks (we're still going to be moderately injured after doing so) or we just simply die. I felt this is important to mention as I did not find any clues for that in the game itself.
The fixed camera angles - while providing the perfect atmosphere - also make our job harder: the game contains far too many action scenes for it to be easily overlooked and the sudden change of perspective can also be disorienting especially during a fight. This was a common problem in Alone in the Dark as well, but it wasn't as combat oriented as Resident Evil. Also the game punishes us for not following a certain pattern: if we venture somewhere we are not supposed to (yet or again) we can quickly find ourselves surrounded by 3+ zombies and this can force players to refer to walkthroughs.
The game is still trying to balance between action and adventure, but does so with little success, as I haven't seen anyone praising RE for its clever puzzles. Most of them are mediocre at best and serve as a bit of a relax period between 2 fights. Mostly we have to look for keys and push crates.
As far as graphics go, I'd call it a lazy port: the character models look good (especially the bonus costumes), but the backgrounds look just plain ugly compared to Resident Evil 0's crisp environments, the contrast between the characters and the backgrounds is visible. The audio is pretty good, but the crows still sound awfully wrong.
To be honest, Resident Evil 1 has never been amongst my favourites: I liked Resident Evil 2 better and now after having played Resident Evil 0 (which I loved and also
) I must say it exceeds this one in almost every aspect. That being said, Resident Evil HD REMASTER is still a very good game, but in my opinion its status in the series is overrated (blame nostalgia).
PROS
+ classic RE atmosphere
+ multiple endings
+ new monsters and locations
+ memorable bossfights
CONS
- controls and camera angles will lead to many deaths
- low quality environments
- no "Jill sandwich"
RATING
7.5/10

A good story, superbly written and told, wrapped in a mediocre FPS, Bedlam is a trip through levels referencing classic games that ends up feeling like playing their non-union Eastern European equivalents (closer to
than Quake 2, in other words).
So, more fun-ish than fun, but the whole thing is held together by great humor, an interesting plot, excellent (and excellently scottish) voice actors and an anything-goes story that makes you curious to see what's up next. It's the execution that's underwhelming.
Besides budget limitations, there are also some conceptual problems that undermine the game's efforts. Physics in a quake2-era level, for example, or an open, "where the hell do I go now?" design on levels referencing Medal of Honor (which were always very carefully guided experiences). The mechanics and feel of the controls stay the same throughout, which is a huge shame as it would have been great fun for them to advance with the games Bedlam is aping.
It's a shame the final game doesn't match the premise's ambition, but it's still worth trudging through the worst of it. Even the seemingly endless final level (complete with shoddy FPS platforming) is worth it for the banter between the protagonist and the title character.
A recommendation, then, with some heavy caveats.

Let me start off by saying gfwl is a major inconvenience;however,if you have enough patience there is a decent game waiting for you. After sorting through Microsofts madness I finally got to relive my childhood but in a much more sinister way. I feel this game caters toward the older audience who grew up with the original playstation trilogy and not to the RE4 and onward crowd. The game allows you to experience the disaster that unfolds in Racoon City but you get to do it with a team of highly trained soldiers/mercenaries(if you play multiplayer). I get a RE Outbreak feel but with much more competent characters and a better battle system. The combat takes on the feel of Gears of War,the characters you play are reminiscent of the Metal Gear series and the story stays roughly along the lines of Resident evil 2/Resident Evil 3(though you can make fate breaking decisions). Personally I don't think the mesh of these series a bad thing at all. The story is lacking but you should already be familiar with it if you're a resident evil diehard. Also,why should soldiers/mercenaries know every little detail? They have objectives and are not emotionally invested in anything except completing said objectives and staying alive. This is also definitely a shooter and should be treated as one. I would suggest you play it with friends or randoms providing you get a chance as the friendly AI is atrocious, the enemies not as much. Speaking of enemies, they seem to be quite resilient and you shouldn't go in guns a blazing until you get some experience under your belt. It was a challenge to me even on normal difficulty but my skills aren't up to par and I'm not a twitch. As far as gameplay goes I only have experience with keyboard/mouse and not with a controller. The game seems responsive and not hard to control asides from item pickup/interact with environment/take cover key being shared(make sure you're dead still before picking up items/opening doors). It hillariously adds to the stress of combat when being overrun as there is nothing better than watching your buddy fly head first into a door when he/she desperately tries to open it. All in all I feel it's worth the price providing you get the full game and go in knowing it's a combat shooter.

Well. First off I'd like to say that I've started the series with the 5th game, Skyrim.
I loved it, so I decided to go back and buy Oblivion. Shivering Isles had me glued to the monitor for a hefty chunk of my free time and the dungeons felt full and interesting (and the physics system with vines and chains dangling from the ceilings? I have no idea why there was less of that in Skyrim),
I thought I'd go even more back, skipped Morrowind (I don't now why) and picked up Daggerfall for free (I do have a thing for old dungeon crawlers, so I guess I was bought immediately).
Then came Arena, played it for a bit, got out of the jail and... That was the end of the demo, I guess. But from what I've heard the game world is randomized, so I don't feel like I'd enjoy it too much, especially that the fighting system had me begging for mercy and biting my nails every time a rat or goblin appeared in front of my camera.
It's a... vast, open ended, huge game. (I'd say even a bit too open ended, at least for me, I'm a simple man, I enjoyed Skyrim, remember?)
It's huge, there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of characters to talk to, no real set rules that would limit what you can and cannot do.
Wanna: Create unique, overpowered weapon/armor and enchant it with a GOD'S SOUL? Go for it.
Create a customized, one of a kind spell that will make you, I don't know, a floating, invincible ball of flame at a low low cost of losing 99% of your current life? (I... Don't know if it's possible, there's levitation and invisibility, setting yourself on fire too, but, I'm not sure)
Kill everyone in a frenzy, calling out to Sheogorath? (You can do that in Skyrim too, but you get my point)
It's an open game, there is the main questline, but you can create your own quests, your own quests for finding the rarest artefacts/ingredients/races (the last living dwemer, for example), your quest for creating a literally godly item.
To wrap it up: It's a great game and with the open source engine overhaul it's probably one of the best rpg games.
Get it. And get OpenMW (Free, open source, fully rewritten engine. Works better and quicker, by default supports widescreen, hd and vast graphical effects), It's a great game and honestly, one that's going to make your library much more... Complete.

The Witcher 1 is not perfect and to sing high praises about it is only to its detriment. As someone who has never played the series, the hype surrounding Witcher 3 has truly overshadowed the issues this first part of the trilogy has when talked about. Hopefully I can present this game in a way that is fair to its successes, but also its failures. This will probably be the longest review I write because I feel there is no other way to fully encapsulate how this game feels.
The Witcher is the story of Geralt, a Witcher who has been brought back to life with amnesia and after a short prologue must deal with the secrets of his mutated species being stolen and a war between Humans and the Scoia'tael. Story is something that is heavily focused on in this game and to great surprise is one of the few games where your choices matter. Choosing who lives, dies and what sides you help will directly affect how certain NPC's deal with you and what directions the plot will take, even if ultimately the overarching plot does not concern these details altogether.
Characters are unique and memorable, you will make allies and find people to hate depending on what kind of player you are. It makes decisions that have no consequence matter because you care about how they will affect the characters around you. However, this is where we get into some of the issues. While it's story and quests are impressive the amount of padding is ridiculous.
Chapter 2 and 3 of this game are some of the most tedious questlines you will find in any RPG. While set up to be a mystery intrigue, things slowly end up as nothing more than a fetch quest featuring two distinct areas: Vizma and its swamp. You will find yourself constantly running between these two places and nothing else. If you also plan to do the side quests which are highly recommended for upgrades, exp and occasional story beats; You can easily double the amount of time you will spend going back and forth.
Not to mention that with the Witcher's freedom of how you go about questing; These chapters suffer the hardest from side quests that relate to parts of the main quest that you may not have started yet. If you take the time to do many side quests before parts of the main ones you can learn details or pick up items that you shouldn't know about yet. In some cases, this can create very confusing plot scenarios where you have already done multiple things that Geralt had no idea that he had to do until he is told about them later.
Despite this, Chapters 1, 4 and 5 have far less of this problem. But even here backtracking is still quite prevalent. This isn't a game breaker, but overall it feels like this game could have been 10 hours shorter with a focused sequence of events. Open ended questing only works when you have enough areas to justify it and Witcher’s level design isn’t good enough to begin with.
What must be praised, are the interactions and wealth of content. Each chapter may be only a small area, but they're filled with things to do and characters to learn from. Some of it may be padding but each chapter creates its own atmosphere and feels fleshed out. You can get very immersed in it's world. This feels like an extension of games like Majoras Mask where every character has a schedule and events happen at certain times of day. These have their own small issues, such as the quest markers not updating characters locations outside of their homes, but most are small nit-picks for a very cool gameplay concept.
While the Witcher is an RPG, it distances itself through its combat, alchemy system and approach towards things such as loot. While many have given criticism to its combat I feel like this is one of the less problematic elements of the game. When it works combat is quite fun if a little hard to get used too. Everything you do is based on an animation system with button presses at the correct times to combo attacks.
Along with this are your two main weapons. Steel and Silver swords. Steel is better for human enemies and Silver is better for creatures. At first this is quite simplistic but eventually you will have to swap between them and their 3 differing combat styles to be effective in each fight. (To get the most out of these systems I played on hard mode to make sure I had to learn how these features properly worked)
What this means is that Witcher ends up as a game that is more about preparation than running into each fight. It’s a great way of keeping the player engaged. The alchemy system also encourages this. Most early game potions have effects that at first will seem odd. The first healing potion for instance heals over time rather than immediately. During the tutorial the game will also teach you that these are better to use before a fight starts, rather than using things mid battle. While you will still find some potions that help in a pinch you can be punished quickly for not being prepared and trying to down potions mid combat.
Sadly while most of the game has these moments; More than once or twice you will be locked into a battle that ether removes your potions effects, or you will enter a room only to be swarmed with enemies and taking damage before you even gain control. These are giant oversights into the core design of the game that are completely out of place.
What doesn't work with the combat unfortunately are the lengthy and sometimes broken animations. While at times combat is tight, fast, and focused. Animations for changing swords, being knocked over, stunned, and swinging a sword can get glitchy and take far too long. This makes Geralt feel unresponsive and causes some unfair deaths. There are a few times where I've been knocked over only for the game to realize two seconds after this and send Geralt to his lying down animation much later than it should.
Another frustrating bug are the multiple crashes you will experience throughout the 40-60-hour campaign. They aren't frequent enough to kill the game, but you can lose hours of progress from a bad crash.
Loot is also slightly underwhelming. Unlike most RPG’s Witcher has more focus on temporary buffs than permanent increases. Most weapons that enemies have are garbage. Swords have -20-30% damage compared to your starting weapon, and other items such as daggers or clubs can’t even be used in the combat system which makes them a waste of time not only for the player, but the developers as well. There are so many unique and interesting weapons and all of them are deliberately useless. It borderlines on sheer obliviousness from the team’s part to even waste time creating them.
Fortunately, there are a lot of parts to enjoy. One of the better gameplay choices is how important knowledge is. To craft potions, collect certain ingredients or bring up certain topics you first must find out about them. It’s an interesting way of letting the lore of the series be interwoven with the moment to moment gameplay.
The story itself, while mostly a normal tale of revenge and a war between two equally bitter sides is backed up strongly by the lore established. You get the sense that you are only seeing a part of this massive world filled with stories and settings. But it also leaves a little to be desired after the ending.
The musical score is great. It gives the game strong individuality, nothing quite sounds like the Witcher besides the Witcher. You can almost understand each environment just from hearing the music before beginning to explore.
Altogether, The Witcher is flawed but decent. The few high points are some of the most interesting you will find in a story-driven RPG, but at it’s more consistent lows it can feel broken and mediocre. It’s not one of the greatest games you will ever play, but it’s certainly worth trying out to see where the series started.

I loved many parts of this game, but it had some pretty major faults. The most glaring fault of this game is the backtracking and just traversing the map in general. There was lots of backtracking in every area of the game. Which wouldn't be too bad except for the fact that some of the areas are set up like mazes and just traversing some of the regular areas can lead to you getting lost with the extremely minimal map system. The map only shows you where you've been and where nearby save points are. I think the game would be GREATLY imporved if the map had only a few changes added to it, such as showing rooms you haven't explored that are ajacent to rooms you have already explored, or adding little marks to show obsticles that you can't pass currently but that you can come back later to advance, or even a destination mark everytime you clear your current objective. Also, you unlock more parts of the story as you play the game, obviously, but there are many parts that requre you to replay the SAME GAME MODE just with a differnt character and very minimal differences: mostly just dialouge changes, which I enjoy but are locked behind too much repetitive gameplay.
However, I still think that this game is overall good, and if the map was better and backtracking was minimized I think this would be a great game. The gameplay was solid, for at least the first run through and I found the gameplay and the characters to be charming. My favorite part was the story, which had beutifully written dialouge and characters, as well as very non-traditional themes that you wouldn't expect to find in a simple video game about talking bugs: such as companionship, whether or not the good in life outweighs the bad, no hero is completely pure, and even a single person can make a significant difference in the world. After finishing the first storyline I found myself more interested in the story than the actual gameplay, which made it especially frustrating that parts of the story are locked behind monotonus gameplay.
Overall I think that this game is worth getting and playing to the end of the main story, but I cant reccomend playing the story again as the supporting characters to piece together the rest of the story because having to go through it all again with almost no difference is just too aggrovating.

With an excellent soundtrack, engaging storyline, and refined battle system, Creepy Castle is a gem to say the least. The colorful unclutterd visuals are a nice throwback to the classic age of video games, and the levels are cleverly designed. There is actually a large amount of humor, even in the item descriptions, and the characters are easily likeable and creative. Although I was unable to join the Kickstarter, I greatly appreciate the amount of inclusion the early supporters could have. It seems that many creations these days lack a sense of "life"; however, Creepy Castle is an exception, and I thank the creators and fellow supporters for this.
It is difficult for me to choose what I like most about this game, as each element is executed very well. If I had to choose, I would say the battle system stood out the most to me. There are a great deal of RPGs that could improve by incorporating elements of this system.

Really enjoyed what I've played so far, nice dialogue and wonderful chiptune music. 8-Bit graphics with a nice flair with the character portraits and event battles. Even if its simplistic, I really like the designs and pixel work, and the CRT / Bloom filtering (both settings you can toggle off if it bothers you) really makes it feel like an old NES game.
Only nitpicks I would have are that it would be nice if the map was more useful, or if it could be scrolled around at least. I found myself getting a little lost, but the areas aren't too big so far that its that much of an issue. Some of the battle events feel a lot harder than others as well, but that might just be me being slow at Parry events or uncoordinated at button sequences. Crits can feel a little unfair sometimes too -- its like, you put in mechanical sequences to avoid damage based on player skill, but there's no stopping or avoiding a crit.
The variety in the battle minigames is pretty nice, and it seems to keep adding more and more to it as the game goes on. BF and Poindexter's tutorial / story entries are adorable too. Remember, you have to punch things in the face before they punch you in the face!
A game that throws you back into the times of 8-bit, throwing puzzles and addicting music right at your face for you to enjoy!

Shallow experience, but interesting.
It's a neat concept, but it forces you into further stages even if you want to stay an animal or a microbe. It's not terribly bogged down with realism, science, or depth, but is a cute sketch of a fantastic history. I played a couple of species up to civilization, but once their brains get bigger, it gets less fun/more wonky to me. The graphics are also showing their age on a game that was never all that good looking (very bubbly, plastic,  and sticky). I'm not big on civ games, and that's what it turns into. But even that is a stripped down version of an alien civ game (with space travel). The building systems are interesting, clever, and the way it animates what you make is really pretty cool. It takes a little extra effort to make things move the way you want them to move, but it works if you think about anatomy the right way. The game deserves A) a remake and B) other companies to emulate this game in different styles with different focuses.
Personally, if this game had real evolutionary consequences and was focused MORE on evolution and divergent speciation, anatomy, mutation, and the microbes you made in the first stages stuck around to compete with you, I'd play it more. I'd LOVE to have my species wiped out by it's distant evolutionary cousin that sweeps through like the black plague! That is deep evolution right there. But that's not the focus of this game. If I had the option of stepping back and just watching for a while, to see what happened as these little buggers did what they wanted, I'd watch more. If it was on a more awesome planetary scale with less arbitrary time jumps, a more informed science, and a little less of the kiddy stuff, colonies with different cultures and politics and forced evolutions via science and augmentation, contiguous procedural fractal-environments and fractal species generation w/evolutionary tracking . . . I'm asking too much.

While the gameplay of the game is enough to warrant attention, the game itself leave a LOT to be desired. It is pretty much nothing else than a huge grind fest which you gamble on a dice roll every single mission. Even with the best preparation and skills, one lucky shot or one unlucky run and you lose EVERYTHING: your bomber, your (now experienced) crew... And you need to start all over again... Unless you just save scum like crazy. Let's be honest here: would you really want to have to play another hour with the exact same missions to get back to where you were just to get shot down three missions later and have to do it AGAIN all over from scratch?
I can still say that the game should have a lot of appeal to a specific audience. People who loved Darkest Dungeon for example (even tho I have no clue why people even like that game) will love playing Bomber Crew just to start over if (when!) they mess up. But for me, considering the gameplay and the price tag, there is no way I'm going to recommend this game in its current state. The game would need another complete layer of complexity or strategy added or at the very least give your crew even a remote sporting chance to survive a crash so you don't have to regrind everything every single time for me to even think this game to be a good one.
Consider this game to be a child game... Which won't appeal to the youngsters anyways due to the sheer frustration factor.
Edit: after giving this game WAY MORE than its faire share of attention and chance to actually come back from the depth... I have done nothing but completely validate my review by now. Many, MANY missions in the last three chapters were re-runs of previous chapter missions (some of which I did SEVERAL times by that moment already. Especially those missions which reduce the enemy efficiency: those are always the same missions but you do get a huge bonus so you'd be a fool to ignore them) which in the end just led to an even more aggravating grind fest. The last chapters are completely impossible to complete without having a maxed or nearly maxed crew along with a fully upgraded bomber and all.
Here is the most critical flaw in this game: you unlock critical improvements, both in crew apparel and in bomber improvements, by collecting intel points. Those intel points add up with time and missions and you need the heck of a ton of those to get the last few upgrades, which you absolutely need to complete the last missions without your crew dying on you. So you have absolutely no choice than to do missions after missions only to get those intel points.
Anybody who would argue that this game is not a grind fest is a moron. The game itself is totally and solely geared toward it. At this point I just pride myself by having a low review approval score since it seem to be the real gage of a real true review. The other day I've seen a one sentence long review approved several hundred times... Says a lot about the gaming scene nowaday. Sad.

This game is great! Buy it if you like FTL and the likes ... if you don't like to read, check out my 3 minute overview video here:
I would call it a world war 2 bomber crew & survival simulation. What looks cute on the outside gets very challenging very fast and the gameplay is surprisingly deep.
First you need a crew. They feature different stats like cold resistance, survival skills and of course how good they are at their main profession. There are gunners, mechanics, pilots, radio operators and navigators. They can level up and gain new skills but be careful: if they die, they die. They are gone and you need to hire a new crew member and re-train it again.
Next up is your bomber. It's a Lancaster and you can customise it in much detail. Add armor, add turrets and paint it in  different color schemes. You can also draw your own logo on the sides. After your done spending your earned money and research points go and select your next mission. Most of the time there are several choices with different risk levels.
Once you're in the air things get hectic quickly. You need to mark enemy fighters for your gunners, refill turret ammunition, open the bomb doors in time, take recon photos, bomb targets, drop supplies for downed pilots, extinguish burning engines and tend to injured crew members. Of course there's lots more to do and you need to do it fast and under fire. Bomber Crew needs a lot of multitasking. If you're are hardcore singletasker you may scratch the game off your list now since you most likely won't have much fun with it.
I was impressed of the game's love for detail. For example there's rain which stops once you pass the cloud layer. The navigator can't see through thick clouds so you need to adjust altitude to find your targets again. Or the bomber´s hull gets accurately punctured by enemy fire and on top of that electical or hydraulic systems may malfunction at any point and stress you out even more … and the list goes on.
I don't know how extensive the game is at the end. Just played for two hours and boy I'm addicted. I want to upgrade my bomber and my crew and I want to see what comes next. The first five missions had a lot of variety with supply drops, bombing runs on buidlings, hunting u-boats, excorting a ship and taking recon photos. Overall the game reminds me of FTL and feels a bit like a realtime version of it. In combination with the nice art style and challenging but fun gameplay we've got a compelling little game here.

An overly complicated modernization of the Risk board game with a mild Fantasy theme. Very difficult to see text. Annoying graphics and animations. Terrible Tutorial (it's a youtube video). Insanely annoying voice acting.
If you like digital Board games, and want a family-friendly one, get Days of Wonder's other title, Ticket to Ride, or Carcassonne, Agricola. A lot of people prefer these games for iPad or Android tablet because of Pass and Play.
If you want more grown up board games try Talisman (kind of DnD lite - has single player against AI plus robust online multi-player and numerous content expansions and updates coming all the time) or Elder Sign: Omens, which is basically a Cthulhu-Horror themed Yahtzee mashed up with a board game. ES: O is single-player only.
Not recommended unless you really, really like Risk.
-----
P.S. I've played this on iOS too, so disregard time. That's just this version, which is worse than the tablet one, which isn't that good either. I've actually played the game for about 3 hours. Resident Evil 1 HD is an example of a game remake done right. Not only it captures all the elements that made the original RE1 famous, but also it ironed out most of the kinks, added new content that resulted in even greater experience, and made sure that this game, even after 15 years of release, is still the quintessential survival action horror on any platform.
The Resident Evil series is far from perfect, but its infamous cheesiness is also its greatest advantage. No game on Steam can showcase this more than the HD remaster of the 2002 Resident Evil 1 REmake, which is considered to be the best in the entire franchise by many (at least until the RE2 REmake comes along).
The game’s secret is the perfect bland of several smaller and larger elements. It mostly takes place in an incredibly unrealistic, giant 1930s horror film mansion filled with ridiculous 1960s spy movie deathtraps. Its script and voice acting—while improving a ton compared to the 1996 original—just revel in the typical B movie cheesiness.
Still, the game is not a parody, and its straight-faced serious approach, interestingly enough, makes everything a lot better. The levels and enemies (chiefly zombies, with some gruesome biological experiments in the mix) are deadly and put most gamers to the test. Especially if you are used to modern autosaves, checkpoints, instant retries, replenishing health, and near-infinite ammunition; this game lacks all of these.
The difficulty also comes from the old-school control system, where the levels use fixed cameras (and stunningly gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds) instead of the more common over-the-shoulder viewpoint. It takes time to get used to it, but the reward is great, because RE1 offers unparalleled replay value within its genre, thanks to its wide variety of game modes, two selectable protagonists, and several paths and endings the player can take.

TES III - Morrowind is an old RPG now. But don't let anyone ever tell you that new games are better than older ones, as this is one game that counters that statement completely.
Probably my most played RPG to date, with at least 1000+ hours on DISC (which I still have) before I decided to get it on Steam. A game despite predating Oblivion and Skyrim, just has something special that the other titles don't have.
SO - Morrowind is an RPG from 2002, and has you, the player, transported into Morrowind on a prisoner's ship (for reasons unknown). You are led to the Census and Excise Office, where you create your class, sign your release forms and then you're kicked out on your♥♥♥♥♥and left to do your own thing. Naturally this can be a little daunting but it also carries the possibilities of carving out your own future ingame, through not having to follow any main quests at any point. You can create your character then spend the next 200 hours running through dungeons, punching skeletons and ghosts to death (don't ask). Or you could join the Imperial Legion, or Thieves Guild, or whatever you fancy. The freedom is unparalleled in comparison to modern Western RPG's, as even though there is a set questline and ending to follow, you're left to figure it out yourself. The game won't hold your hand and lead you to each quest. No it won't. I'll explain.
In the likes of Skyrim, Diablo, Fallout, what have you - You'll be given quests and told what to do and where to go. Simple enough. In Morrowind, someone will tell you to do something. Your character will write it in their journal and off you trot. No quest markers. Unsure as to how to get there? Figure it out. Ask people, follow roadsigns, or pay for a Silt Strider to fast travel you there. (There's no fast travel from map, you can only do it from certain places and you have to pay.) Oh, and there's no way of reliably keeping track of your quests unless you remember to read your journal. If you got halfway through a quest at least 20 hours ago, you'll have to look through each page to find what has been done and what you've to do next. It's a lot less forgiving than being able to bring up a screen that gives you a list of quests you've to do, but it's so much more immersive and unique.
Morrowind also has a much more complex Magic system than the more recent entries of The Elder Scrolls series. You can buy scrolls for one-time spell use, or learn magic which you can use at any time, providing you have the magicka to cast them. But Morrowind also lets you craft your own spells, given some NPC's can offer the service. This can result in some truly hilarious concoctions, such as spells Soul trapping everything within 50m and poisoning, freezing and burning them all at once, or fortifying athletics by 1000, causing you to sprint at a ridiculous rate. Morrowind players will also be familiar with a certain scroll, 'Scroll of Icarian Flight.'
It's also somewhat abusable. This is included in the later titles of the series, but you can use your alchemy skill to craft potions fortifying intelligence, drinking the potions, and repeating this process until you're insanely intelligent, allowing you to craft utterly game-breaking potions. This is optional fun but worth trying for a laugh.
Morrowind itself is a very interesting land. There are all sorts of climates, from the deserts of Ald'ruhn to the Imperial styled city of Ebonheart. In lore, Morrowind is the home of the Dunmer, or Dark Elves, so expect to be meeting plenty of them. YOU N'WAH. Morrowind is also massive, and being unable to fast travel at will encourages you to make your way on foot, where you'll no doubt be sidetracked with the list of locations and sights to see on the way. If you're really invested in the lore then there are many books ingame you can read as you find them in the ingame world, and you'll probably even recognise a few showing up in Skyrim and Oblivion if you've played them first.
The combat is more primitive than Oblivion and Skyrim as it is mostly based on dice rolls instead of the damage you do, like an old-school RPG (which it is really).In Morrowind, having a low weapon skill means you will likely miss your target a lot. Try using any weapon at the beginning of the game when you aren't proficient. You'll be flailing around like a nutter. The weapons themselves do set amounts of damage, it is not goverened by your skill. Being level 10 with long blades and hitting someone with a claymore overhead might do 18 damage, but you'll miss a lot more than if you were level 100 in long blades, where you'll more or less hit every time but still do the same damage. This obviously isn't as engaging as the combat in later titles. Simply put, you will have to min-max at the start of the game and focus on at least one combat skill if you want to survive. When you have it at a high skill, then only would it be worth considering levelling up another skill. Having a bunch of skills at level 20 will not help you at all later on. If you want to really put time into it, then venture out of the settlements and grind on mudcrabs. Or you can pay some NPC's to train you.
The story itself doesn't really unfold until you actually do the main quests, so mentioning much about it would almost be considered spoilers. It's up to you to find out how to progress.
The Steam version of Morrowind is the GOTY version, which means you also get included with the main game, the Tribunal and Bloodmoon DLC's. Even I have not touched these much at all despite my time playing this game, but I highly recommend you leave them until a later level, as they are much more demanding than the main quest in terms of character level and equipment. Unfortunately you don't get the Construction Set with the Steam version but hey ho. You can install a copy of it from Nexus Mods. There's also a lot more on Nexus Mods for Morrowind if you want to take a look, including graphics overhaul mods and combat overhauls. Even to this day mods are being made for the game.
Oh, and Morrowind even has Spears and Medium Armour.
Totally worth it.

A good story, superbly written and told, wrapped in a mediocre FPS, Bedlam is a trip through levels referencing classic games that ends up feeling like playing their non-union Eastern European equivalents (closer to
than Quake 2, in other words).
So, more fun-ish than fun, but the whole thing is held together by great humor, an interesting plot, excellent (and excellently scottish) voice actors and an anything-goes story that makes you curious to see what's up next. It's the execution that's underwhelming.
Besides budget limitations, there are also some conceptual problems that undermine the game's efforts. Physics in a quake2-era level, for example, or an open, "where the hell do I go now?" design on levels referencing Medal of Honor (which were always very carefully guided experiences). The mechanics and feel of the controls stay the same throughout, which is a huge shame as it would have been great fun for them to advance with the games Bedlam is aping.
It's a shame the final game doesn't match the premise's ambition, but it's still worth trudging through the worst of it. Even the seemingly endless final level (complete with shoddy FPS platforming) is worth it for the banter between the protagonist and the title character.
A recommendation, then, with some heavy caveats.

Tried hard to be modern and artsy, but the 'PhyreEngine' unfortunately does not provide magical tricks to remove online delay, hence this 2p-coop-only timing puzzle videogame falls flat as an online experience. From what other reviewers wrote, it doesn't even work properly via LAN.
If it were couch coop only, I'd moan that there's no online MP, but as it stands, I have to moan that the online MP isn't very good. Later levels are just about impossible due to the atrocious lag / delay and random erratic AI behaviour resulting from this.
I sure like the comparably cheap two pack offer, but the bugginess / glitchiness as well as frequent reliance more on perfect timing than clever thinking prevents me from giving this game a positive review. Unlike it apparently was the case for other reviewers, my 1.5 hours of playing time did not include 'lightbulb moments' where I was mesmerised by the developers' astonishingly intricate puzzle design. At all. As far as challenging players with pattern memorisation and perfect timing goes, there are various games on Steam that make far far better use of those gameplay elements (SMB, Rush Bros and I assume Electronic Super Joy as well as SpeedRunners).
Give this game a look if you engage in regular single PC dual gamepad multiplayer games, or if you happen to have a lot of patience for a game's issues when it comes to playing online with a close friend.
P.S.: Voice communication is a must for all but the first few puzzlies. Not gonna be any jolly if you can't communicate while you play.
P.P.S.: When you're STUCK SOMEWHERE due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LEVEL DESIGN, it's impossible to kill yourself to restart from the last automatic save point. Good job, developers.

This game is all kinds of fun. Running around flash style, zipping around buildings batman style, or just superman-ing it up, running around with a unique hero with your own special powers and weapon choices is a total blast. I have quite a lot of hours put into this outside of steam mind you. This is the only game I've ever played that pulled off the ability to FEEL like a super hero/villan.
I could do a pro/con list, but I'm sure you would have seen plenty of them by now, so I'll just give my basic opinion of the game itsself. There is quite a few powers you can choose from, on top of several weapons you can choose from to go with any kind of play style you really want. No one weapon or power is neccesarrily better than the other either, you just have to play accordingly. Which isn't a bad thing, but some people don't get that and assume there is...shall we say "cookie cutter" builds. I'm sure there is certain ways that you can play a specific build to make it better, but it is by no means REQUIRED in any sense. At least in my experience playing with tons of people (raids and pvp).
As far as the F2P (free to play) model, let's all be honest, it could be a whole lot worse. Given it's current F2P model, I think it's fair enough. But ABSOLUTLY DO NOT expect to get the whole game through the F2P model. I heavily recommend just doing the subscription, as it will save you hundreds of dollars up front. Many powers among other things will be LOCKED unless you have the dlc, which all gets UNLOCKED when you get the sub. $15 a month is much more manageable for most people anyways. But again, that's just my preference on the matter. You will not be able to access most end game raids through the F2P model, or most "auction house" stuff (due to the cash cap).
Overall I give this game a 8/10 for ingenuity and enjoyability. It's definitly a gem amongst the many crappy MMO's that are out there, especially the ones following a "F2P" model. At least download it and try it, the worst that could happen is you just not like it and uninstall it anyways. Which I personally doubt if you are even looking at this game and curious if it's enjoyable or not.

In Mount & Blade: Warband, you control an unnamed protagonist on his journey to find out who is leaving messages on his answering machine. Every day, the protagonist recieves a mysterious voicemail-telling him to go to an address and do a job. Once you get to your destination, the game shines through. What remains of Mount & Blade: Warband once you get into the action is a psychadelic, challenging, colorful top-down shooter/beat-em-up with a driving neo-80s soundtrack and the neon atmosphere to back it up. The violence is appallingly fun and simple, and often is overlooked as you rampage through the game's levels floor by floor. Mistakes are swiftly punished with near-instant death: everything is a one-hit kill, for the most part, and that goes for both you and the enemies. With a powerful soundtrack, striking visuals, and addictive gameplay, Mount & Blade: Warband is not the game to miss!

A fun, highly novel sidescrolling RPG set in a cute fantasy world of anthropomorphic insects, backed by a chiptune score of the first water!  Movement is modular, but you can choose smooth or instantaneous shifting, among other customizations.  The give-and-take of classic RPG combat is interspersed with terrific little minigames, or "duels," that can get pretty tough, though you can choose to dampen the difficulty if you want -- but I would only do this as a last resort.  Ever since I played
, I've felt that every turn-based RPG that does not involve tactical positioning should incorporate minigames like these; they make combat so much more dynamic if done well, and this game does them
well!
The game may be cute, but as you play through the chapters, you'll find that
has a pretty epic story and some heady themes to go with it -- like depression, the dubiety of psychopharmacological treatment for such, the search for meaning, and the need for companionship.  I was very surprised to find all this in the game, and even more surprised that these themes are handled so deftly.
will appeal massively to fans of
and
, as it shares tonal and aesthetic similarities with those excellent titles, but it has a sparkling personality all its own.  I love this game, and you should pick it up now!

I would not be playing this otherwise if I didn't feel that was the case.
If you're willing to let some things go, you'll find a pretty charming, modest experience here.

I backed this game on Kickstarter and received a pre-release copy a couple of days before launch, and I can say I am glad I helped support it!
I absolutely adore Creepy Castle and I've only played through the first adventure! It's very charming, cute and funny, and combat is mixed up with a variety of little minigames, ranging from a reflex-based "Press the attack button when you get the signal" game, to pac-man style maze games and even Pipe Dream style puzzles! (I'd also like to note that the dev team were considerate enough to include an 'accessibility mode' which make the duel minigames more forgiving for people who have poor reflexes or are otherwise having trouble with the minigames. There's no punishment for doing this either, it's specifically there to help you enjoy the game!
The graphics are very reminiscent of the SInclair ZX Spectrum, though a variety of palettes are available in the options, and if the tile-based movement is too sudden and jarring you can smooth it out while keeping it looking reasonably authentic.
All in all, definitely give this a look!

Only played it for a couple of hours, and I was a Kickstarter backer, but here is my honest opinion so far:
This game is pretty difficult, but not frustrating. It seems pretty deep and varied, but on the surface it plays very simply.
The gameplay is a more-linear-feeling Metroidvania, where the main goal of each area is to find keys and proceed to the locked doors. There are normal enemies, bosses, and plenty of items (and more importantly, story/lore) to find and deal with.
Fighting is the game's key feature - some battles are very basic Rougelike-style I-hit-you, you-hit-me, but the majority take place as a series of frantic minigames, somewhat akin to Warioware and similar titles. The first you are introduced to is a quickdraw event where you have to hit your key as soon as the screen prompts you to. Others I've encounted range from buttom mashers to DDR-style hit-the-correct-keys-quickly games to Pacman-likes. It's all stuff we've seen before, but it's presented in a way that's fresh yet familiar, and a lot of fun to play.
That being said, you will get hit - a lot - and so far the only way I've found to replenish your health is to eat food found throughout the castle. There's a very limited amount, so if you end up having a lot of trouble with a specific enemy, I'm not sure how you'd manage to survive.
I'm sure I've barely scratched the surface in the couple of hours I've played, but overall I'd say if you're into the aesthetic of the game and like what you see in the trailers, give it a try. It delivers what it promises.

Still, I'd recommend the game for those who loves board games and does not mind said bugs too much -- personally I haven't had any connection problem for several months now and until the issue is fixed, not being able to play with ghouls can be considered as a challenge. :)

The boardgame version of Small World is excellent, and this is a faithful adaptation; so why don't I recommend this one?

Since this is a direct, very lazy port of the tablet/mobile version, there are no options to really configure anything: you can't even fullscreen the game. Playing online with friends is a possibility, but the horrendous UI makes actually connecting to a game a chore (did I mention this is a direct tablet port yet?), and the ingame chat censors you without mercy no matter who you are playing with. The latter could be acceptable if it didn't then immediately result in the game temporarily muting you in chat. Playing with the AI is not any better, since the AI either doesn't know what it is doing, or freezes all together with indecision, never ending its turn (Heroic Halflings in a 5 player game seems to stump the AI regularly for me if a bot gets it). As the game has no turn timers, if the AI decides to freeze in this manner there is nothing you can do to salvage that particular session.

Machinarium is a point-and-click adventure game in the old fashion of "click inventory items against everything on screen until it works". You play the role of a tiny little robot dude whose first task is to rebuild his body, having been unceremoniously dumped into a junkyard.
The story is told without any words, instead using the charming artstyle and clever worldbuilding to convey what's happening. It's a risky venture, especially in story-driven games like these, but Machinarium pulls it off very well; Little Robot Dude's attempts to sneak back into the city are easy to follow and very cute.
Some of the puzzles can be somewhat obtuse, as is the norm for adventure games, which may put off some players, but there is a hint system built into every puzzle which lets Dude give his own insight on the solution. For times when this doesn't suffice, a short walkthrough can be unlocked with some skill at a minigame, which will give the player a storybook guide on what to do next. The wordless presentation makes Machniarum a game that can be enjoyed by all-comers of any language, age, or skill with words.
Finally, the Robot Street Band's performance will stay with you forever.

So I purchased this game because it was reccomended by Steam, and I am definitely pleased. The art style is deceptive, as many games with this style tend to be easy games meant for younger people. This is a very intensive and challenging management game.
The game sets you up as the 'lead' of a Lancaster bomber, and you have to manage each crew member's job. Pilot, engineer, navigator, etc. The action can get very hectic when you are approaching your target, have flak and fighters shooting you, and you see a navigator icon for the next. Many times I had to circle a target because I missed my drop, or even more embarisingly forgot to open the bomb bay doors.
Then you have the dash home, unless you are feeling really brave and want to go get some extra cash with recon photos, where you are trying to mark enemy fighters, heal wounded crewmates, repair the various system, oops your engine is on fire, better send a guy out with an extinguisher, oh and you forgot to raise your bomb bay doors, that is eating your fuel, oh that engine fell off, and finally finally you get to the airfield, only to remember you forgot to lower your landing gear. Hope you have enough fuel for a fly around!

This game is amazing. As a fan of FTL, I was really stoked to try out another crew management style game, and this one just about checks every box for me. Everything is great from the gameplay to the art to the historical theme, and even its well-designed menu screens. People here are complaining a lot about the difficulty, and yes this game is hard. But if you're into the challenge of rogue-like permadeath games, this should not come as a surprise. People that are complaining about things like, "the gunner should be able to reload himself, it's not realistic!!!" are completely missing the point. The game is about testing your skills in managing a scenario where ten things are happening at once, and you need to figure out what decisions are most important at any given time. This is not a hyper-realistic ww2 bombing simulator. This is a super fun and unique management game set in a great ww2 theme. Plus you'll get a chance to try some well-known historical bombing runs (operation chastise, anyone?).
