Now that Umbrella Corps exists, this it he second worst game in the Resident Evil franchise. Fortunately, it wasn't made by Capcom, so they almost get a pass.
I'll be up front with you here. This game....it no good.
Let's get the silliest bits out of the way first. This game still uses GFWL. It still. Uses. GFWL. Moving on. My play time may say 30 minutes. I assure  you I pre-ordered this game on PS3 when it came out and played it there first.
Slant Six did a superb job of creating a believable, enjoyable, and creepy atmosphere for Raccoon City, doing justice to the many different iterations of the town. Cars are wrecked everywhere, there's plenty of blood and everything is on fire, and it's dark. The Umbrella labs beneath the city, especially, I have to say are the most exquisite part and add depth to the facility that makes it far more believable than anything we ever saw in Outbreak, RE2 or RE Chronicles.
Unfortunately that's the most concentrated group of positive things I can say.
The weapons are all broken and disappointing, save for the knife. The knife and melee options make for a fun revisit to a different developers game: Dead Rising - where guns suck and you can melee everything til the cows come home. As far as the guns go, I have literally shot both AI and human players in the head 8 times [and they didn't die] with the .50 cal. Sweet death, or it should be. It wasn't just "Oh maybe it glitched." No, this happens on a reliable basis all the time in story mode and a little bit less in multiplayer. This rifle is used to destroy equipment and disable vehicles. It's not used on human beings. This would literally gib a human being. Yet a human enemy, be it a soldier or another player, does not instantly die when hit anywhere with it. Thus the problem with putting an anti-material rifle in any game, ever. It's SUPPOSED TO BE BROKEN. When it isn't broken, it ruins the game, and so it's then broken in a different way. In 4 years they have not patched any problems with the guns.
Zombies will not reliably attack you unless you are bleeding, which is a good game mechanic for multiplayer, but even when you are bleeding they often ignore you and the same applies to enemies. Hunters will literally run up to you, and troll you.
I'm not joking. A hunter will occasionally run right up to you, be within inches of ruining your life, and then it will suddenly spin around and run away. What the ♥♥♥♥!? That hunter just trolled me! All of the B.O.W.s work on aggro, so, whoever shoots the Tyrants more, that's who it goes after. Admittedly, the AI functions well enough to make the game stressful and harrowing - the way it should be - but more often than not it's just a battle of hopefully directing the NPC enemies away from you long enough for someone else to be the victim.
Some of the actives in this game, much more so than the passives, are complete broken horse♥♥♥♥♥♥ RPG abilities do not belong in shooters, ever, and this is no exception. Lupo especially - she has an active that grants her invincibility (or is it infinite ammo?) for about 20 seconds straight, with pretty much no cool down. It's not fun, at all, to be the one unfortunate enough to be trying to kill her. Vector has active camo that won't reliably fade even after being grenaded. Both Spec Ops teams and USS have the same skills for matching classes, but it seems the majority of the time that the U.S.S has a pre-existing design advantage.
This game does have many good game modes, like G-Virus sample mode, which is essentially capture the G-virus (like CTF). Nemesis is another good mode, though DLC of course - it's an objective match, King of the Hill essentially, where each team can take control of nemesis and he'll murder the other team as long as your team controls the Nemesis panel. All of the game modes, minus Heroes, are fun, they are just crippled by broken weapons. Heroes unfortunately pits two teams of "heroes" against each other - heroes being somewhat canon characters who have THOUSANDS of HP and can take anything but a Grenade Launcher shot to the face, repeatedly, and still kill the other team alone if the other team has lost its heroes - even if not, they can still take on four enemy heroes at once for quite a while. I have had matches where we literally corner♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Jill Valentine for minutes straight, hitting her thousands of times with every weapon in the game, and she did not die.
Story is, of course, irrelevant in this game, as it contradicts pretty much every game that is considered canon, and intentionally so. Even knowing that, the story is virtually non-existent and consists only of a non-stop slew of Ramirezery:
'Wolfpack, do everything. Do everything else. Wolfpack, we're leaving you for dead. Fight us."
which, without being tied together by an overall plot like a similar action thriller novel would be, is just annoying and tedious.
The most disappointing thing about this game is is really, honestly did have a lot of potential. The setting is awesome and the multiplayer shooting in the middle of BOWs is a great idea. It just simply doesn't work. And now another developer is trying again with Umbrella Corp. And Umbrella Corp honestly looks even glitchier and less polished than this game did. I really wanted to like this game.
Sidenote. Slant Six literally came out to the journalists one day and said they don't know why the game is broken or where to start on fixing it. After this, I then got into an argument with a woman who claims she was on the ORC dev team. She claims Capcom was overbearing and caused most of the problems.
Lady. The game is fundamentally, at its most basic gameplay mechanics, broken. That's not Capcom telling you what to do. That's your game being a turd.
If being broken wasn't bad enough, they released an army of DLC for this game including Nemesis mode and several other parts of multiplayer and campaign. Are you joking? Don't buy this garbage unless you find it for less than $10. This is $60 I'll never get back. Right now because of E3 it's on sale for like $7. It's stil not worth it because I doubt the MP community still exists.

As a big fan of the original BATTLEFIELD 1942 I was a bit skeptical of this game since it appeared to be very simmilar yet it was a free to play game.  But I found I really enjoy this game. It has the slower paced World War 2 style gameplay I enjoy, where accuracy and visibility of your opponent are more important than usually found in your standard shooter where everyone has an automatic weapon and spray and pray wins the day. If you are one of those who enjoy charging into the battle with a ragtag assortment of vehicles you will not be disapointed there are plenty of vehicle types to use, including a bicycle.
Pros
-fun slow paced shooting
-decent graphics (Great graphics in the sense of free to play)
-players begin with semi-automatic rifles rather than fully automatic
-upgradeable weapons
-Weapon maintainence
Although this seems like a con, the meapon maintaince mechanic really keeps the game balanced.  For example i could keep spamming grenades, but the the maintaince cost could reduce the in game credits i recieve after the battle to almost 0.
-grenades are effective weapons
Cons
-A LOT OF GRINDING
This is pretty much the central bad thing about this game.  Its comparable the amount of grinding required for free games such as Planetside 2 MULTIPLIED BY 2.  As a result the battles mostly consist of people useing default equipment because it takes so long to earn anything else. I've already play 9 hours and still am only less thank halfway to being able to play the Assault game mode.
-Pay to accelerate game
This is pretty standard of all free to play games.  The members however do not recieve access to any god weapons (as far as i know) but do recieve and extra perk and a 4th carry slot (which seems really unneccesary since you dont need to carry a pistol and/or grenades if you dont want to). Also They recieve additional experience after battles.
Thats all I have to say and I hope you keep this review in mind when deciding on downloading this game. Remember that this game is not for everyone and feel free to form your own opinion.

Hello, this is a non-biased review of The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. Let me start off by saying I having no nostalgia for this game because my first TES game was Skyrim, and I thought I'll give this a try with no mods. I have not finished playing this yet. I will start by talking about the bad, then the good.
First let me talk about what I didn't like. When I first started this game I was TERRIBLY CONFUSED becasue the total lack of any tutorials or explanation of how the game works! I had no idea how the combat system worked and I almost gave up. However I didn't, and I went online and I read a tutorial on how the combat works and I figured it out and it actually makes sense and it honestly is a little fun. Because this game is so outdated there is no quest markers or any indication of where to go. Sure, they give directions in the quest journal, however they can be very difficult to follow, and honestly extremley frusturating. In my opinion the lack of proper markers is what turns many new players off of Morrowind and is a major hurdle that I still haven't fully got past. And of course the "outdated" (to say the least) graphics that make it hard to tell sometimes what is what, and also the lighting in certain places in horrendous and you are barley able to see anything at times when you're in a dark area.
Alright now that I've got that off my chest its time to talk about the good in Morrowind. TES III: Morrowind takes place on the island of Vvardenfell which is a beautiful enviroment if you can get past the graphics. I would even go as far to say that the overall type of land and enviroment in Morrowind is better than both Skyrim and Oblivion (which is saying a lot because Oblivion had a beautiful enviroment)! I love all of the creautres (especially the Silt Striders :D) and of course all the other types of animals! Also who could forget about the AMAZING soundtrack!? It's easily one of the best soundtracks in any game ever in my opinion. Which I happened to notice that the soundtrack is in some parts of Skyrim and Oblivion which is fine with me! Skywind may be just around the corner, but there's still plenty of reasons to play Morrowind.  If you're willing to forgive a sometimes clunky engine and a steep learning curve at the very beginning, then you'll likely find alot of things to love.
By listing the main selling points of the game I hope to show why the game is still dear to so many.  Its easy to be put off by janky trailers and the fact that the game is now 15 years old, but if any of the following sound good to you, its worth giving Morrowind a try.
+ Most exciting location of any Elder Scrolls game - Vvardenfell (the game's setting) is far more alien than that of most video games.  Wizards live in giant cities made of mushrooms, the local God-King has a moon hovering over his Aztec inspired city, and there's a warrior clan living inside the shell of a giant crab.  The dungeons are far more expansive than later games, and the local bus system is a bunch of giant insects.
+ Expanded magic system - create your own spells and magical items, with plenty of freedom to bend the laws of physics through teleportation, levitation, water walking or slowing gravity.  Summon allies and monsters, augment and buff your own abilities, or just blast everything with the elements.
+ Many more skills to level - Throwing Weapons, Spears, Medium Armour, Unarmored, Mercantile, Blunt Weapons, Axes, Mysticism, Acrobatics, Speechcraft, Athletics - none of these skills are in Skyrim, and a few aren't in Oblivion either.  If you enjoy roleplaying your character, this gives you many more options for a unique identity and playstyle.
+ More Guilds/Better Progression - I won't spoil which factions you can join, but there's over half a dozen of them, each with their own politics, aims, and enemies.  Some will ask you to undermine the goals of others, so you'll have to choose carefully.  Unlike Skyrim and Oblivion, progression relies on having a guild's required skills to a certain level, so you can't become an Arch Mage without knowing any spells.
+ Great Story, If you want it - You're free to ignore the main quest completely, just like in Daggerfall, as the game never forces you to start it in order to progress.  This makes roleplaying characters easier, as you're not forced into being the chosen one (Skyrim) or having to pretend you can't see a burning city full of daedra on the horizon (Oblivion).  But honestly, the game's method of telling you lore through differing accounts and giving you multiple perspectives on the 'truth' makes it both realistic and intriguing.  Its up to you to decide what you want to believe and how you wish to go about taking action.
+ Music - Jeremy Soule's soundtrack fits the mood and setting perfectly.  If you've played other Elder Scrolls or games such as Neverwinter Nights and Knights of the Old Republic, you'll already know what to expect. Plenty of really beautiful tracks in here.
+ Active Modding scene - Morrowind's going through some exciting times right now, with huge projects such as Tamriel Rebuilt adding a contintent's worth of content to the game, and the Morrowind Graphics and Sounds Overhaul transforming the game and taking advantage of modern hardware.  There's even a team of modders who've made the game open source, so anyone is free to have a go at drastically altering the way the game plays.
Have a look at the other reviews here on steam to see some of the game's criticisms if you're still cautious about buying the game - after all, the game is pretty pricey given its age (when not on sale), and its always good to take a second opinion on any purchase.
If there's other plus sides to this game you feel I've left out then feel free to leave a comment.  If you want advice/ mod recommendations then thats also welcome!

Bedlam is supposed to be a love letter to classic gaming. It may be a love letter, but it needs proofreading and it's written in crayon.
The story is fairly solid. It's a game that has our plucky heroine, who has been mistakenly digitized into a computer game, fighting through several games paying homage to classics and modern titles, starting with a Quake/Quake 2 clone. It's not the best I've played, and the writing of characters does not impress, but I'll get back to that later.
This fairly competent plot doesn't save us from bad gameplay.
By midgame, you have basically every weapon obtainable in the game, a whopping 17 of them (by my memory). The main problem with this is that you end up with about 3 or 4 that you like, with outclassed weapons staying at the top of the multi-weapon slot. Going from one gun to another is an absolute chore - there's no way to disable fast weapons switch. And because you have so many weapons, there's never enough ammo given for the gun you actually want to use. On top of that, it seems like enemies don't drop ammo.
The guns themselves aren't even all that good. Most of them just feel like hitscanners or projectile weapons that do something slightly different from eachother. The sounds are boring, and in the case of the sword (which uses the same clang-a-clang sound for
), can become downright annoying. There's also no hand viewmodel except during a hard to use melee; the guns just float off to the left of the screen.
Back to the writing. They drop the names of other games like it's going out of style. "I just came back from the Minecraft Archipegalo! Call of Duty is overrun, and everyone in Black Mesa needs to get out as soon as possible!" This was all said at once. (But we'll get it, because we're such cool gamer dudes and gamer grrls, right?)
The ending... ♥♥♥♥ing hell, the ending. After fighting up a tower of the same purple blocks and assorted enemies you've seen between levels for the last 90% of the game,
Final word: 5.5/10.
get it on sale if you like the concept. Or if you like the author. But, if you like shooter games that are fun to play, pass.

Welcome to the fun and interesting game called BEDLAM. Based on the same book of the same name (which I have not read,) throws you through an assortment of retro/nostalgic inspired realms. Originally an Early Access Game then released Oct 2015, this game swooped past my radar sadly at first... But upon finding it in a bundle and getting this game for around 4$CDN and a friend telling me about it, I gave it a try.
I'm avoiding from spoiling anything about the story, so I can't say too much about it, as it all gives slight clues and hints into the story as it goes on. As the store pages says, you play Heather Quinn (aka Athena,) an overworked and underpaid scientist developing medical technology for corporate giant Neurosphere. One day you volunteer as a test candidate for the new Neurosphere brain scanning tech, but then you are trapped inside a video game called Starfire. This is where you start your journey into Bedlam. As you fight off enemies, you are then contacted by another "Player" telling you to make it to a "Glitch" that will allow you to reach to other video game worlds to rejoin with them. The rest you will have to play to find out.
This plays like your standard FPS game, with certain points playing slightly different... And by different I mean it's still a standard FPS. Bedlam takes you on a journey to different games, but does not implement any new or interesting features in them! Each game only offers different weapons and different enemies, with the levels almost having a "reskin" as they all play basically the same. There isn't much that makes certain levels feel "different," which really starts to make the game boring. I also bring up the term that the levels are all "Static" and don't really have anything living in the maps. Plants don't move, flags/banners don't move, most things that you would expect to sway in the wind or move from an explosion, don't move. There is very little things that move like fans. This made the levels feel very empty to me. The Glitch levels are really bad for this on having nothing, and combining platforming as well.
There was 2 parts that were worth playing. The first one being the Unreal Tournament inspired arena map called "Rocket Arena" which played like your average deathmatch. With the added bonus of the hilarious voices of angry teens calling you a hacker and a cheater. The other part is the FPS Pac-man map.
The AI for the enemies is very cheap. I found myself through the entire game being shot from enemies that I could not see. Enemies you can hardly see shoot you with pinpoint accuracy and will always know where you are.
This game offers you too many weapons. When you visit each game world you earn about 3 new weapons, but you can carry ALL of them to every level. This is annoying when some weapons become the same weapons and you start to not use them. This is even worse in the last level when you have to switch weapons constantly and have to cycle through all those weapons to get the one you want... While trying not to die from the aimbot AI. You will also find you will not run out of ammo, as having that many guns means you will always have ammo for your other guns.
The last level is by far the worst thing in this game. Not only is it in the glitch setting, but you will do nothing but platforming, shooting enemies as they spawn in the farther you go, and try not to fall off the map. I experienced 2 MAJOR problems with this level though. Every time I loaded the last level for the first time, the game would glitch out and show my glitched into the wall/floor, with all my weapons out, stuck, and the game chugging at 5 FPS. Thankfully restarting the level/re-loading a save fixes the problem. The other problem was that enemies could WALK THROUGH WALLS AND OBSTACLES, even being able to shoot through them. Not only was this cheap, but it almost made it impossible to kill certain enemies when they happened to be inside a giant rock, and they had a rocket launcher, and I could not hurt them with bullet weapons.
Some people claimed to have a hard time completing this game, but I breezed through it on Hard with very little trouble in areas. I only died about 4 times in my playthrough. This game only took me 6 hours to beat, but my card farming app farmed the game before I could play it, so 3 hours was AFK.
Pros:
- Plays/feels very much like a retro FPS.
- Interesting levels/locations.
- Rocket Arena Map is the best part.
- Good characters with an interesting story.
- Not very long, and not very short either.
- Fun weapons to use.
- Runs smooth.
- Easy achievements. (Only 1 really challenging.)
- Steam Cards.
Cons:
- "Static" levels.
- No secrets in levels.
- Levels can get boring and start to feel the same.
- Enemies can start to feel repetitive.
- AI is all over the place, can be Aimbots.
- Too many weapons.
- Last level is glitchy and horribly designed.
- A HUGE disappointing final boss.
The game is a 5.5/10 from me. This game is more enjoyable if you are someone that likes good writing and enjoys all the nods/references to other games. But because of this, I can't recommend this to everyone. The game had such potential, but they squandered it and left it how it is, which saddens me greatly. If you can look past the problems though and can get it on sale, it is a fun little game that is worth a playthough to experience it for yourself. Because it wasn't completely terrible, the game ran fine, and I was able to complete it, it still gets the Thumbs Up from me.

My co-op partner and I found the puzzles to be minimally challenging for far too long, and I feel like my interest has been lost. Though I really would like to complete the game, I'm not sure that I will find the motivation. For reference, I really like Portal and indie platformers tend to appeal to me, but Thomas Was Alone lost me in a very similar way.
On the plus side the aesthetic has a modern, minimalistic appeal and the animations are well done, and that was a big draw for me when I purchased the game. The game controls well with Xbox 360 / One controllers and the game detected them without issue. Those that appreciate the gameplay should find that the rest of the game is quite well made, though the sparseness of the settings menu can be a turnoff.
I did experience some tiny framerate issues on my system with a mid-end i5, Radeon HD6870, and a solid state drive, but nothing that significantly hampered the gameplay experience. Though I will hesistate to blame the framerate problem on the game since it could be attributable to a problem with my system, I want to note that this PC runs most other games without hickups and it well exceeds the recommended system specs.
Concluding, I think this game has charm and will absolutely appeal to some people, but it was not my cup of tea. Though I can't honestly recommend this game because I didn't enjoy it, I feel that it is absolutely worth a try if you think it might appeal to you.

HuniePop is known for its sexual content, but there is more to this game.
The game you play while on a date is like Candy Crush, but way better. You equip 6 items to use, and match different tokens. Each token has its own effect on the game, making the game more interesting. Outside of the dates you have conversations with the different girls to get to know them better, and earn 'hunie' to upgrade your stats during dates. They quizz you on what they have told you, and you can use the 'munie' earned on dates to buy them some gifts.
There is not much story in this game, some girls have a little backstory. If you're looking for a great story, HuniePop is not what you're looking for. This does not mean there's nothing to do. HuniePop has challenging achievements, and it will take some time to get to 100% completion. There's hidden girls to unlock, hairstyles&outfits unlocked through normal playing,  items to collect for during the dates, and an extra difficult mode.
Concering characters, there's a lot too chose from. There's a HuniePop girl for everyone. I find most of them written very well, and fun to discover. As you talk to them more, and go on more dates you get to know a lot about the girls, and their relations to each other.
HuniePop has a very enjoyable soundtrack. There's songs for each location, including the date locations. There is not a single song in there that I did not like, but a lot of songs that I truly fell in love with. The songs fit the environment they're played in well, and add a lot to the overall atmosphere of the game. You can enjoy each song in the game, but it is definetely worth buying the soundtrack.
The art in this game is masterfully drawn, and I'm not just talking about the lady parts. The locations are drawn in great detaill. The game has an anime artstyle, and one of the best I've seen. The girls themselves are also especially well-drawn. There's their normal sprites, and the pictures they send you. You can see that a lot of work was put into making these pictures look as good as possible. The Digital Art Collection gives you all these artworks
and adds unseen artworks.
Overall, I enjoyed this game a lot, and definetly think it's worth a shot if you liked puzzle games or dating sims.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

So I purchased this game because it was reccomended by Steam, and I am definitely pleased. The art style is deceptive, as many games with this style tend to be easy games meant for younger people. This is a very intensive and challenging management game.
The game sets you up as the 'lead' of a Lancaster bomber, and you have to manage each crew member's job. Pilot, engineer, navigator, etc. The action can get very hectic when you are approaching your target, have flak and fighters shooting you, and you see a navigator icon for the next. Many times I had to circle a target because I missed my drop, or even more embarisingly forgot to open the bomb bay doors.
Then you have the dash home, unless you are feeling really brave and want to go get some extra cash with recon photos, where you are trying to mark enemy fighters, heal wounded crewmates, repair the various system, oops your engine is on fire, better send a guy out with an extinguisher, oh and you forgot to raise your bomb bay doors, that is eating your fuel, oh that engine fell off, and finally finally you get to the airfield, only to remember you forgot to lower your landing gear. Hope you have enough fuel for a fly around!

This game is amazing. As a fan of FTL, I was really stoked to try out another crew management style game, and this one just about checks every box for me. Everything is great from the gameplay to the art to the historical theme, and even its well-designed menu screens. People here are complaining a lot about the difficulty, and yes this game is hard. But if you're into the challenge of rogue-like permadeath games, this should not come as a surprise. People that are complaining about things like, "the gunner should be able to reload himself, it's not realistic!!!" are completely missing the point. The game is about testing your skills in managing a scenario where ten things are happening at once, and you need to figure out what decisions are most important at any given time. This is not a hyper-realistic ww2 bombing simulator. This is a super fun and unique management game set in a great ww2 theme. Plus you'll get a chance to try some well-known historical bombing runs (operation chastise, anyone?).

Resident Evil/Biohazard HD Remaster is a remastered version of the classic survival horror game developed and published by Capcom
This is a prime example of how all remasters should look like. It's a shame that we had to wait for the PC port this long, but even after 15 years of it's original release on the Nintendo Gamecube, it still looks and plays really good
It's a really unique game when it comes to it's atmosphere, and somehow, even after so many years, that clunky gameplay is still very catchy. Inventory management with it's low capacity can be a pain, especially on first playthrough, but in the end, I was also OK with it, since it also adds so much to it's tense atmosphere
It's also worth playing at least twice, since you can choose between playing as Jill or Chris, each with it's own, slightly changed playthrough with different characters and dialogues
All in all it's a very good game and I can't wait for the remake of Resident Evil 2!

OK, I had the original one for PSX back in the day, but I couldn't play it. Being honest, I was a kid and it scared the hell out of me. I remember watching that cutscene where the first zombie appears, turning and watching you. Yes, that was the point my dad said "Not for kids, not at all". So, from that day, I had this idealized idea of this game where it was the scariest one out there.
But I think it would be fair to analyze the game without the nostalgia factor in mind. And, if you do that, man it is bad. Like, bad bad. Why do I say that? Let's summarize:
- Controls are bad. Even with the remastered ones, where you can use your controller sticks in a moder way, in which left means left, not just turn left, the control is confusing. Because the camera system is. So you push forward to advance, the character moves to the next part of the room, where a new camera angle is set and now you are running towards the camera, so left, right, up and down get all mixed up. And the shooting seems clunky for today standards.
- Transitions. These are a house brand. You click a door and a cutscene starts where the door opens and you expect something to be on the other side but it's never there. Well, there is a transition for EVERY SINGLE DOOR. And sometimes you have to go from one side to the opposite one of the mansion and, in the process, get through six or seven doors. I think the main reason for this is to make the game pace slow and to avoid the speedrun feeling. But man, it is way too much.
- Inventory. Six slots and that's it. And for the survival component is fine. I don't like games where you can carry an arsenal with you at any time. But this is plain frustrating. There are times where I shot to spend the ammunition so I could free a slot in my inventory to pick an item. Combined with the transitions nightmare, it is an unpleasant experience indeed. I mean, you are in a room with your inventory almost full. Find a herb and say "why not pick it up?". You do and then you find a quest item. And you can't take it because your inventory is full. So you say "OK, let's head back to the container with all my stuff to make some space". And that's four doors away, so you know it's going to take way too much time. So you curse, throw the controller away and quit the game.
- Bad story. And, if you don't agree, I am sure you have played (and loved) the original one. Because, let's be serious, it is not good. At all.
- Cheap puns. This is the worst and it kills the mood.
But there were good things too, don't get me wrong:
+ The atmosphere. The horror is not constant, but I was tense the whole time.
+ Difficulty. It is a fair game. Even though hard was too hard for me, I think it was fair. It is just that it requires more focus on it that I was willing to give.
+ Eventually, it is over, and you could say "I finished that", and then you uninstall it and forget about it, just remembering the good parts when it pops up in a conversation with friends.

As someone who started the Resident Evil series at RE4, it was cool to experience the origins of the games.
Some of the puzzles are fun, and give you a good feeling of accomplishment when you solve them.
It is a lot more puzzly than a lot of the other games, and some of them have not aged well. A lot of puzzles rely on the player knowing whether or not they interacted with all background objects in the room, and later on in the game where there are multiple rooms with red zones (items not yet picked up), it gets annoying to run back and forth to check rooms.
Locked doors work nicely to limit your search area to check at the start of the game, and focus player exploration.
Another issue is early on in the game, when the game does not keep track of which doors on the map are unlocked by which key, and there are 4 types of locks or more depending on how you include them.
It's honestly one of the scariest RE games I have played. You run past enemies a lot and limited ammo/item slots is always a concern, so it makes just getting around the house incredibly tense. Enemies just off camera can lunge out suddenly, which keeps exploration really exciting.
Limited item slots, even for puzzle items and limited save items, does get frustrating at some points though, as it leads to a lot of backtracking to swap out items.
Overall, I would say that if you are a fan of any of the other RE games or if it is even your first entry into the series, it is definitely worth a try.

For me, this is the definitive open-world RPG. I don't foresee anyone ever making one I like more than Morrowind. Quest markers have since taken away the sense of immersion and adventure that you were given in Morrowind. You're expected to interact with NPC's, get information and vague locations through conversations, and find things by surveying the enviroment around you. It creates a genuine sense of intimacy with the world when you're familiarizing yourself with the geology and lore for the sake of navigation that you absolutely cannot get from following a compass at the top of your HUD.
Character building is everything in Morrowind. You have to be very careful when you're spec'ing your character if you want to kill so much as a kwama forager once you leave Seyda Neen. If you're looking for an RPG with open-ended stat building where you can feel free to experiment, or switch to a different class type after several hours, Morrowind is not the game for you. How you choose your major and minor skills, your favored attributes, and your race determines how you'll play the rest of the game as that character. This may mean some trial and error to new players, I would definitely advise not to get too attached to your first character.
What makes this game so addicting is the empowerment it gives you, and how rewarding it feels to get that power. There is little to no level-scaling in this game. You start out struggling to fight even the rats and mudcrabs, and very slowly become an unstoppable, even literal, god. While it may be too slow for some to retain interest, the slow gradual pacing is more fulfilling than anything Bethesda has released since. There are no hard caps to your power, either, as you can creatively enchant or brew your way to immortality if you've put enough hours in. This sounds overpowered and unbalanced, but the amount of work you have to put in to to reach this status never leaves you feeling cheated of an experience. You earn every increase in strength you get, but no matter how powerful you feel there is always something out there that can kill you if you're not careful. This is because you're not the only god on the island, and no NPC's are so important that they will go unconscious instead of dying.
Dungeons are can be massive and rarely linear. Caverns have intersecting, winding tunnels, some of them underwater, some of them requiring levitation to reach. Each one is handmade, unlike Oblivion, and unlike Skyrim you feel like you're discovering them yourself, instead of tripping over new delves that you could already see on your compass anyway. Many open world RPG's fall into the trap of the world existing soley for the player, like no one actually lived there before you got there. If you don't want to feel like you're the first person to enter any of these 400 crypts in thousands of years, Morrowind will give you a breath of fresh air since everything feels very natural and lived in. Ancestral tombs are littered with offerings from visiting family members who paid their respects before you stepped in, caves are turned into furnished homes by smugglers and thieves, and ancient towers becomes fortresses to powerful archmages. Even when you do feel like you're the first person there in years, it's usually for good reason, with high leveled monsters and the bodies of lesser adventurers on the ground.
Gold is a precious commodity, a design choice that has apparently become out of style in modern open world games. No matter how rich you get in this game, there is always something to spend your money on. Enchantments and skill training can quickly climb to astronomical numbers if you seek true power, but it's there to take if you're determined, unlike later installments in the series where gold essentially becomes useless after just a few hours. The legendary and mythical artifacts and weapons are not likely to bring you tangible wealth either, since no common shopkeeper is going to be able to afford these holy relics. This makes them feel more special, since you can't just sell your Daedric artifacts to some random bumkin in the imperial city for 2,000 gold.
Some say the game has aged too poorly which might be true. The gameplay itself was divisive when it was released so I don't think it's fair to chalk that up to "aging" but the engine is obviously very dated, it can take some tweaking and modding to run on modern hardware and vanilla Morrowind only supports up to 1024x768 resolution. You'll immediately notice how short the render distance is. There are definitely a lot of things that Oblivion and Skyrim did a lot better than Morrowind could. The UI is very clunky. It's almost always obvious that you're playing a very old game.
The most common complaint against the game though isn't the legacy software. It always seems to be about the dice-roll combat and the walking speed, which I think is what ultimately makes or breaks the experience so here's my thoughts on it. For the dice-rolling, people are turned off by statistic-based combat in a first-person view. If, for instance, you're shooting a bow while steathed, the arrow may go through the enemy but it will still roll a dice behind the scenes, in DnD fashion, to see if you miss, hit, how much damage. And there are many modifiers, such as your fatigue, skill level, governing attribute, specialization, etc. You roll misses pretty often and some people don't like this, which is totally valid. I've never seen why the two elements can't coexist or why people think it's inherently a bad design choice, but I do understand why some people would hate it. I've always been under the impression that the fights aren't visually supposed to be literal interpretations of the encounter: I think Morrowind works so well because the game is simple enough to let your imagination fill in the blanks, from the immense text, to the static NPC's, and the rng combat. If you were playing DnD with your friends, you would imagine the fight happening as it corresponds to every miss and hit and critical that you roll. Morrowind evokes the same type of lucid roleplaying where what you're seeing is more of a representation than an interpretation.
As for the walking speed, it IS quite slow. Running uses your stamina which is essential for all combat classes, meaning there are times where you may need to walk if you're expecting combat in the near future. You can make yourself much faster through enchantments, spells, potions, etc. but for much of the early game you will be very slow. There is no fast travel, but there are boats and silt striders and teleportation spells that can take you to virtually every populated area in the game, but you can't open the map and choose a location. This means the game overall is a much slower paced, patient game than other open world games and it drives some people crazy.
Obviously, both the walking speed and DnD combat can be changed to your liking with some very popular, very easily installed mods. With one of the most active modding communities on the internet even after 15 years, there's very little about the game you can't change to your liking at this point, yes even taking away random weapon misses. The buggy mess that Bethesda released in 2002 can now be comepletely polished and tailored to your specific preferences. I personally still play a mostly Vanilla build with only a couple hundred Audio/Visual enhancements with bugs and balance fixes for polish. Why change my favorite game anyway?

Obviously being an older game it has a few issues with Windows 10, like crashing when you try to exit the game. I found switching to Windows 7 compatibility mode works a bit better, but it still crashes from time to time.
Fortunately I've had no problems starting it and playing the actual game, and it actually seems to work very well with WINE under Linux, so that's a huge plus too.
What do I love about Morrowind?
- It's a true open world RPG. By that, I mean you don't click on a gate and wait for a loading screen to enter a town. No, you literally just walk into it. Exploring a game has never been so interesting. I spent an hour trying to find a specific location, but I ended up coming across a few side quests from people along the road, or random caves just off the beaten path full of loot.
- Morrowind will punish you for not being prepared. Sometimes you're required to unlock an object or door in order to proceed, but if you don't have any scrolls, spells, or lockpicks to assist, then you're out of luck. Or maybe having a spell absorb item will help you against some bandits who are branding weapons of paralysis (extremely tough to counter).
- It doesn't hold your hand. In rare occasions, NPCs will mark a location on your map, but for the most part you need to follow their written directions to get there. For example, "Head northeast, then straight north once you're at the plantation". The only fast travel you will find is silt striders, boats, and mages guild teleports. However, these won't just take you anywhere. You will have to plan your route, and sometimes be required to use a silt strider, to a boat journey.
- Vamprism and Lycanthropy actually feel like curses. As a Vampire you are shunned by most people (I believe the mages guild will make exceptions), and being in sunlight will kill you pretty quickly. But don't worry, the game doesn't end there. There are 3 factions of Vampires (Mages, thieves, and Warriors). Depending on which one you contracted vampirism from will determine what traits are boosted when you turn. You are also able to pick up a whole quest line from that coven.
As for being a Werewolf, things function as normal, but every night you will turn into a ferocious Werewolf for several hours with a bloodlust. If you don't kill, then you lose health the following the morning. Turning into a werewolf with the ring of hircine will make you exempt from Bloodlust. The point is, both of these diseases feel like true curses that make you question whether or not you want to keep it. This is how it should have been in all TES games.
- You feel a sense of achievement. As I've said, Morrowind can be a pretty unforgiving land, and punish you for not being prepared. Navigating to a specific place and clearing out extremely tough enemies make you feel like you really accomplished something. Sometimes you're rewarded with some pretty nice loot, too. Other times it's just a "thank you".
- The music. I mean, it's Jeremy Soule. Not much else to say except this guy composes some of the finest scores your ears will ever have the joy of listening to.
Honestly, I could go on, but I think you get the point.
But what DON'T I like about Morrowind?
- The fact that there are only 2 DLCs (Tribunal and Bloodmoon). I can't get enough Morrowind. But don't worry, even the base game itself will keep you entertained for a very long time.
If you've never played Morrowind and try it out after playing something like Skyrim, you may feel a little disappointed about the combat system. Keep in mind that it doesn't just use a "weapon touched X, then hit" algorithm. It uses a fairly complex dice based system in the background, where many of your attributes will determine how much damage you do, and whether or not you'll even land a hit. If you're not skilled in the particular weapon you're wielding, you may perform a bunch of "ghost swings". This can be extremely frustrating, but once you work out how to improve your combat prowess it's very satisfying.
If you don't like Morrowind, then you're wrong.

I picked this game up and playtested it throughout most of its Early Access run up to release. At first I was madly in love with the game, from all the tounge-in-cheek references to old games like Quake 2, earlier CoDs, some DOS classics - it spoke to me as someone who grew up with all those titles. The gameplay was fast and frantic, some of the levels were designed real well, and overall, I was satisfied.
And then I read the book.
Now the game dissapointed me. SO much potential...
But aside from that, on it's own it has some issues. Pretty much all enemy AI just stands still trying to shoot you, the cover-shooter levels leave something to be desired, and a lot of your time is gonna be spent just running around in dead silence, without enough music to fill the void. That being said, high points of this game are in its superb voice acting, with a memorable main-character. You get to carry over weapons from gameworld to gameworld, so you can blast nazis with pixellated buckshot, or fight cyborgs with halo-era tech. The graphical fidelity in each world matches it's era, and it's really neat seeing the progression as you go along.
Gunplay is...relatively basic, as it has to be considering enemy AI, but it's servicable. At points there's a lot of variety in the level design and mission objectives. My say is that you get the game just to try it out (and nostalgia bonus, Quake fans), and if you find yourself interested in the world, pick the book up and read through that - you'll be in for a muuuuch fuller ride.

Ibb & Obb is a delightful indie co-op platforming experience but you need a buddy to play along with. It's strictly a co-op game, so that means either playing with a good friend or with random players. Like classic platforming, you run to the right and overcome obstacles together, the twist being that you have the ability to walk underneath the floor, parallel to the top. Many of the puzzles and enemies must be solved by using this ability, with one player being on top of the world and one underneath. There have been times where we have been stumped at how to progress thanks to this clever little mechanic. Momentum and jumping physics also play parts in the challenges for you to utilize. The game isn't the longest in the world, 3 hours and more for the secrets and collectibles scattered and hidden throughout. Visually, it's simple, using highly vectored and clean graphics with simple enemy design. You will see alot of back drops and paths being re-used with the difference being colours and ambience. The difficulty is pretty tame until the late stages which then ramps up like a bridge. Not a bad thing but you'll find yourself suddenly hitting a wall and being stuck.
Although I have only played with a friend, i can see this being a difficult time with random players. You might have trouble with players who lack patience or rush ahead leaving you behind. There is no in game chat that I know of, with the only intstructions you can give is by moving the mouse around to draw lines and paths if you're trying to show how to progress.
Overall, 3/5.

I recently ran through The Witcher: EE. This was my first experience with the game, and I must confess I was mostly playing it to get to the sequels.
The game has aged relatively well, though you'll need to enable V-Sync on your video card control panel for it to be playable, as it doesn't have an in-game option and will probably chug along without it. Good CPU clock speed will also help, because the game engine doesn't support multi-core processing, from what I've read.
Beyond the graphics, this game also shows it's age with the mode-based point-and-click combat system. It's not the worst thing you've ever played, but you'll need a while to get used to it.
Beneath the surface, The Witcher boasts an intriguing story set in a very rich world. As Geralt of Rivia, you're already a hero of great renown at the beginning of the game, though amnesia allows the player to get up to speed with all of the local lore. You'll slay monsters, woo damsels, and drink your fair share of dwarven spirits. Be sure to read all of the books you find, have plenty of Swallow on hand, and don't forget to brew mutagens with the unique ingredients you get from the bosses. The Witcher also carries over some gear and decisions into the second game of the series when you complete it. Keep your best sword and armor by your side.
Altogether, The Witcher: Enhanced Edition is an excellent start to a storied franchise, and if you're patient with the game's artifacts you'll find yourself enjoying every quest.

Yes I definitely recommend this game!
Even today on its 10th year it's still an incredible RPG with a very deep and engaging story, NPCs which are really interesting, a great protagonist who does not dwarf the other characters and does not make them feel bland.
The graphics are actualy MUCH better than a lot of other games released close to 2007 (compare to Divinity 2-Dev Cut for example) and the cinematics are awesome.
The combat is not really intense, but it's also not tedious nor feels like a chore. It's mostly timing your clicks and changing to the proper sword and spells/potions.
There are plenty of additional features like minigames (card & dice games), brawling, sex cards, alchemy and crafting and a huge RPG element regarding story decisions.
Even the gear and the skills make this feel like an RPG where you are either a fighter, or a mage and not a superhman god who can do everything simultaneously.
There are a lot of quests which will make you backtrack and repeat the same areas, but they almost always have new enemies and some new section unlocked which is a plus compared to other games. Quest items and clues along with puzzles are exactly at the right spot in terms of difficulty. That means no annoying and exhausting alt-tabing every 2 minutes to find the next step of the puzzle, but also not ridiculously "under your nose" easy.
Exploring is a huge aspect in this game and rewards the player properly with hidden quests, spells and bounty bosses and items and not lame rewards like 2 silver-loot corpses or dead ends (*cough* Dragon Age *cough).
There are also a ton of caves, crypts and dungeons with amazing and immersive enviromental effects which can also be quite hard and have you end up butt-hurt, only to explore them later on when your level is higher.
CD Projekt is also putting their products on sale really often and they keep lowering their prices as their games age, unlike some other big-name companies. I bought this for about 2$ during a sale.
To sum it up, this game is a top-tier RPG, one of the best ever made and a MUST PLAY for all the genre fans!
My personal score would be between an 8 and a 9/10, because the combat would have to be better and more engaging for a perfect score.

It took me a while to decide whether I'd recommend this game or not.
I do love some good frantic micromanagement, an this game does that VERY well; the idea of being chased down be a squad of fighters, while trying to reload your cannons and having someone repair a flaming engine is horribly stressful in the best possible way.
That said, core mechanics of frantic flying and trying not to explode aside, the game is a grind once the permadeath kicks in. I had an almost fully upgraded bomber with a near-max level crew manning every station to perfection... Then I didn't. An enemy bomber came up underneath us and peppered our belly with machine gun fire while my ventral gunner was out of ammo. At the same time, a squad of fighters came in above and ripped my level 12 pilot to shreds. I was focused on bringing ammo to my gunner, and didn't reaize that the bomber was taking a nose dive into the ground.
Whole crew was K.I.A. except for, ironically, the pilot. (He died on the next mission with an inexperienced crew)
Overall, a fun, tense game with some rudementary management elements, but it does suffer from a rather intense permadeath mechanic, making it very frustrating to get back to the same level you were at before. I can't fault the game for that, as I myself really enjoy a good game like that, as I enjoyed my time with bomber crew.
Paid $15.00 for it, got 10 hours of enjoyment, and 20 minutes of white hot rage.

Personal, Biased Review:
I didn't care much for this one.  The 50/50, swing-or-miss combat system was a total killjoy for me.  End of story.
Technical Review:
Graphics: 6/10
Really good graphics, but people's hair look like rugs, their faces look like rubber, and glitches abound (characters clip through the floor and the walls, etc.).
Story: 6/10
Although the main quest can be sort of a drag, it is partially made up for by good questlines like the Dark Brotherhood quests, and entertaining side quests.
Sound: 6/10
The game has an AMAZING soundtrack and okay SFX.  Oh, yeah, did I mention the OST is amazing?
Gameplay: 5/10
Immersive and lore-rich questlines and the ability to customize the controls are awesome, but the combat can really kill the fun until you master the system.
Replayability: 7/10
Morrowind will always have you coming back.  Getting bored?  Put the game away and in a few months you'll find yourself having as much fun a child in a candy store (if you can cope with the sucky combat system, that is).
Overall: 6/10 "Okay, but could use work."
Final Word:
The quests are immersive if you find one you like, but the combat is a drag, that can make an amazing quest or questline really tedious instead of what it should be:  fun.
Really good for those who like a challenge or old games made for a DOS-based OS, but for the modern, casual gamer like me, I think it would be best to hold off, or you might walk away with a bad taste in your mouth.

The Best Creation Game Ever

OVERVIEW:
Spore is a game based around progression and growth from the Cell stage all the way to the Space age. You start out as a cell, fighting for your life and eating microscopic rocks and meats. After some swimming, you sprout legs and start a nest. From here the real fun begins. You can both make peace and gain DNA this way (which I have yet to try) or make a person who is made for fighting and strike fear into the eyes of everyone who comes in your way. Or you know, try to.... From here you continue progressing, go to a new stage blah blah blah. THEN BOOM. SPACE. The real fun begins. Moving from planet to planet you storm the galaxy conquering everyone in your way. You continue this until you have made everyone extinct or made everyone your allies by dancing, singing and posing... yeah... that's not a joke. You make friends by perfectly mimicking their actions which always fall in those three choices. No talking or anything. That's all that the game has to offer but there are multiple possible ways to win and SOOOOOO many different choices for making your characters that if you get bored of this game before having at least 50 or so hours on it, you might be brain dead, maybe.
SERIOUS SIDE:
The game does not take itself seriously. At all. It does have serious sides though, as any game would. A lot of the mechanics require thought and making allies and enemies is an absurdly strategic thing as you want to make friends with people who are strong to maybe help you pick on the small guys but if you can't do it successfully they might turn on you. It takes skill to play even though it does have a lot of humor in it.
COMICAL SIDE:
Spore has to be one of the best games when it comes to knowing that it isn't taking itself seriously. And I love that. No, I ADORE THAT. Its character creator is sure to get laughs out of you and you cannot find one play through of it where something stupid isn't created. Try. I dare you. You can't do it. Watch the trailer for the game. IT IS SO FUNNY AND IT KNOWS IT IS SUPPOSED TO BE.
PROS:
COMPLETELY customizable creatures
Progression that feels like you actually did something instead of just taking a step to the end
Satisfying worlds and feel
Simplistic start that leads into a more complex game
Great game play physics
Good combat system and social system
You get to play god
CONS:
Sort of confusing controls
Disappointing Cell stage
STILL NO SEQUEL
DLC that is the price of the base game
DLC that only adds parts
FINAL VERDICT:
Spore is a good game for people who enjoy "sandbox" games and games where you "mimic god."
I would give the game an 8.5/10 rating and all that I would really need for a 10/10 game is a better start to be honest. The beginning sets the game up as a sort of kill or survives game as you have to kill to progress and there is no peace so to speak which, for me, was ok, but could have done with some fine tuning. It makes for a bad start that is otherwise split in the decision to be a peaceful or hostile race. It does make sense in a science standpoint but the game isn't known to be scientifically correct and can't lean on that wall. Once you pass this stage, or spend 20 minutes playing the original Agar.io, you get to have HOURS of fun. The game is wonderful and as a person who likes "god simulators" it is very fun. It needs a new form though. If there was a remake or sequel made, it would be amazing. The graphics are slightly old cough very old cough but can give it a sort of charm.

As an MMORPG, this game gets kinda dull and grindy after you hit the level cap, with everything seemingly geared toward group raids, the gear treadmilll, and free-to-play stuff designed to make you want to pay for a subscription and/or spend money on not-so-micro transactions.
But as a superhero action-RPG, this game is fantastic.   The part you can play for free is one of the best single-player open-world superhero games ever made (with lots of optional opportunities for co-op or PvP).  The game is much more action-oriented than most online RPG's, with movement mechanics, power knockback, and throwing environmental stuff all significant parts of the combat.
With lots of alternate missions depending on your mentor, a bunch of different powersets to try out, and both hero & villain factions, I've enjoyed taking several characters through the Level 1-30 single-player game and even bought some of the DLC to try out a few of the newer powersets.
Also no game does a better job of making you feel like a superhero when you fly (or glide or grapple or speedrun or surf) around the city.
The character creator is somewhat limited, but the way gear works is great.  New gear buffs your character stats and gives you new styles for tweaking your superhero look. Most importantly, you can keep whatever style or look you want regardless of which gear you actually have equipped for stat purposes.
If you enjoy superheroes, just designing a character and flying around  Metropolis or Gotham (which look great) in DCUO is more fun than many entire superhero games.  Even if you don't like MMOs, there a ton of great single-player content here that is completely free.  And maybe you'll enjoy the MMO stuff more than I did.

I've been playing MMORPGs for many years.
DCUO has one of the BEST character creations for a F2P game I've come across.  You can truly setup YOUR hero/villain, just how you want them.
Heros get to choose from Wonder Woman, Superman or Batman as their "mentors".  This determines your starting area, Metropolis or Gotham, and how you experience the story line.
Villains get to choose from Circe, Lex Luthor or The Joker as their "mentors".  Again, this determins your starting area & how you experience the game.
One of the coolest parts, Villain or Hero, you both run around the same areas!  I thought that was really well done.
Gameplay is fluent.  DCUO is available for the PS3 & PS4, so you can definitely feel the button masher style of gameplay, even with a keyboard and mouse.  There are combos for your ranged and melee, then you have your skill department, your "special" powers.  Don't expect to have the same powers or maneuvers as a DC hero/villain.  Player created characters are slightly different.  Based off of heros/villains, but, different.
PvE is immersive!  Just running around Gotham is awesome!  I love it.  There's a feeling like you're right there helping to stop braniac!
Then, you reach the money cap.  F2P is $1,500, Premium is $2,000, and Member is $unllimited.  This may be a concern to a lot of people.  And I keep reading people think this means "pay to win".  No, you can happily play, having a $1,500 cap, and have LOADS of fun!  If you really like the game, buy a 1, 3, 6, or 12 month membership.
They've done a good job making a game that's easy, immersive, immensely customizable, & fun to play.  I wanted to give them money.  So I bought a 1 month membership.  Did I need it?  No.  But, why not?

Pro's:
It opens up not unlike the movie, by infiltrating somewhere and then figure out what is going on, what those that they're infiltrating are up to and what happened are certainly different things.

Cons:
The graphics are still not very good, though certainly decent for their time. A bit like Final Fantasy 8 or so. Almsot everything is static like FF8, anyway.
The game is a 'dark' game, which is to say thre's very little actual light in the gme, likely for the ambiance. Thus, playing in a darker room or with higher contrast is a must, though the former would certainly be more fun.
Controls are wonky as heck. I don't know if it was using my USB game pad (identical to a Playstation controller) or if it's the import from console to PC, or even if it was that bad originally which I confirmed wasn't the case with my original copy, but controls sucked hairy, sweaty bum. It's like the characters run around on a slightly turned grid. It isn't up/down and left/right, but diagonals.
Overall 6/10 (-1 controls, -1 NOT improved graphics as promised or simply slightly better to being only barely noticable, -1 seeming reliance on the jump out of nowhere to scare you factor for the primary fear of the game rather than any sort of actual update and finally, -1 for game being almost too easy. Example, items you need to continue shine brightly like the gems at the beginning.) - I'd still recommend it for anyone from that age of gaming that enjoyed the game style. Otherwise, not really. If possible, choose something like Parasite Eve in place of it, or one of the newer Final Fantasies or the myriad of other FPS's. Bedlam was a blast to play. In a time and age where most FPS are designed to appeal to the masses, few titles evoke the sense I had when I first played DOOM or Quake, unless we’re talking about the recent Wolfenstein game. That said, I’m not saying this is comparable with those games in terms of quality and overall production values, but I do strongly believe that this is an underrated gem and so I’d like to express how this game deserves to be played.
In Bedlam you play as Heather Quinn, or Athena (her nickname). You’ve recently got a new job and soon enough you find yourself trapped inside some sort of videogame. Soon enough you realize the sort of mess you’ve put yourself into and uncover a conspiracy that is placing your digital life in danger. This is what I really enjoy about Bedlam. The game takes place inside various game worlds and is brimming with tons of references that trigger so many memories and filled me with nostalgia so many times.
Throughout the game you’ll play on various different settings, from alien worlds that reminded me of Quake, to medieval villages and a war torn Europe. Each of these sections will give you access to a whole new range of weapons that fit this timeline. This is also one of old school aspects of Bedlam that I really appreciate. The fact that you can have up TONS of weapons and switch between them as you see fit, instead of being restricted to 2 or 3 weapons like in most FPS these days. Weapons range from blasters, a crossbow, a minigun, a railgun, a sniper rifle, you name it, there is something for everyone. Of course, each of these settings will also present you to a new aesthetic and new types of enemies. Therefore, the game manages to keep the levels interesting and fresh by not only changing the graphical style but also the way the levels themselves are designed.
As you could expect, this is an homage and a love letter to the times when the FPS genre was at its height. In that sense, the game is extremely fast paced, there is no walking, you’re constantly on the move, and you need to be so, in order to not be hit by enemies. The fact that you move so fast and have access to such a huge arsenal made the game a lot of fun for me to play, since different weapons would be more suitable to defeat certain enemies.
There is only two complaints that I’d like to mention, the fact that sometimes the enemies would get stuck behind walls and other times they’d shoot behind those walls (still hitting me), and the other complaint is related to the hitboxes of props, sometimes I’d shoot over an object while having my crosshair directly on the enemy but the shot would hit the object in front of me. Besides that, it’s worth mentioning that the game is also somewhat short. It can easily be beaten in 5-6 hours (atleast on medium difficulty).
To finalize, Bedlam was an extremely pleasant surprise. I had it sitting on my library for ages and I’m very glad I went ahead and gave it a go. The soundtrack is mindblowing good and I’m actually sad I can’t find it outside the game. If you’re a fan of first person shooters, especially if you’re a fan of games like DOOM, Quake and Wolfenstein, Bedlam might be worth check out. It is fun, varied, charming, challenging, nostalgic, filled with gaming and geeky references and features a rather interesting and unique storyline. Please give this one a chance!

Be aware of the genre! This is a fast paced, tense micromanagement game. I suspect that a lot of the negative reviews are from people who bought it thinking it was a nice, casual cute-em-up.
I have to admit that I thought it would be a nice 'chill' game and was quite surprised when even the tutorials required quite a bit of attention. But the good news is it's a great game as long as you're ready for the intense micro. You're constantly having to make decisions on what to focus on - the bombing run, the fighters that are chewing your plane up, or the crew member who is bleeding out on the floor?
The only real negative I can give for this game is it has a currency system that doesn't really fit very well. You get British pounds to buy plane upgrades and crew equipment from completing missions, and another type of currency that allows you to unlock equipment before you've earned it. This seems to be to limit the upgrades the player can do at various stages, but I think some kind of point allocation system would have fit the theme better.

Yes, it's entirely possible to lose a veteran crew along with an upgraded bomber by a misclick (just send pilot instead of nose gunner for ammo and take more than a second to realise the mistake). And yes, the game does require some grinding to get to the juicier upgrades. And "pause" button (not just clicking "more help" on tip window) could be invaluable in case real life interferes. Also, ability to multitask is rather usefull.
That being said, it's a good game that can be played in short chunks, stories practicaly write themselves, and the feeling of accomplishment when bomber lands back despite holding on spit and prayer after a succesfull run makes it worth all the trouble.

I rarely review games just because of how much of a hassle it is for me to write a decent review and the amount of time it takes to write one. However, The Fall is truly a masterpiece that brings a excellent mixture of morality and science fiction alongside interesting puzzle elements and a bit of horror as well. In brief summary of this game you are an "ARID aboard a Mark 7 Combat suit". After crash landing on what only we can assume is Earth we realize that our pilot is critically injured and we must seek immediate medical attention. I will not spoil the entire game but I will say that you should be ready for some suprises. A quick rundown of Pros and Cons
Pros:
Great Puzzle game
Beautiful yet, simplistic world design
Compelling story
Science-Fiction (I am a sucker for Sci-Fi)
Cons:
Annoying gun mechanics
Some minor bugs which require a restart
Some rather difficult puzzles
In final, I find this game to be well made and a proper use of Kickstarter funds and for $2 on Steam as of the time this review goes up, why not pick it up and try it yourself.

The Fall is a point and click adventure that mixes light puzzles with short action sequences.
It is interesting in its use of religious allegories, and the story is a reflection on what would artificial intelligence entities consider "right" or "wrong", based on the rules their creators have provided them with. In that sense, the whole game depicts a kind of purgatory, in which both the actions of the player and other characters are constantly analyzed for compliance. Full compliance means validation into an AI heaven of human subservience, while non-compliance means being thrown into the oblivion of decommissioning.
While The Fall deserves a gold star for tackling such heady topics in the short 4 hours max that one takes to finish it, unfortunately the game falls short on execution. Considering The Fall is an actual video game, the "gaming" aspect is not really that good. Puzzles are not that interesting and can be easily solved. Mixing puzzles with combat sequences may have taken a page from other games like Out of This World, but controls are clunky and again, the end result is not fun.
In closing, I recommend this game with some reservations. Get it on sale.

ON THE NEGATIVE SIDE I almost didn't play it. At the begining you are required to press [escape] to activate the your Networking systems. Once in that menu you can't leave. You can't back out, you can't do anything until you activate your systems. You can't go to the setting and look up the button layout or anything, you are stuck at that menu. For the life of me I couldn't figure it out. I pressed every button 2 or 3 times. Then I thought the game was glitched, so I restarted. Same problem. I finally had to Alt Tabbed out the game to look up what I was doing wrong. Turns out Spacebar is the on/off button I needed to push. Its not just a jump button anymore kids.
In the end I am not saying the game is bad because of one problem, but it was fustrating. The game does show you how to play but in this one area it left me in the dark. With this minor road bump I still beat the game and recommend it to other players. And I am sure the sequel will be even better.

In my opinion, Pajama Sam was the best series Humongous ever made, featuring imaginative settings, witty writing, and clever gameplay. Now, I personally think that Pajama Sam 2 isn't quite as good as the first and third games in the series, but that isn't saying much because this is an excellent adventure game. In this entry, Sam decides that he's had enough of a scary thunderstorm, and sets out to put a stop to Thunder and Lightning, who turn out to be sisters in charge of the world's weather. Finding a massive complex called World Wide Weather, he sneaks inside and has an accident that sends the weather operations into turmoil, and now he must find the four missing parts to bring the weather factories back on line, before Thunder and Lightning lose their jobs.
One point of criticism I have is that the big conundrum in the game  is all Sam's fault. That doesn't hurt my enjoyment of the game, but I don't like it when the main objective of game is undoing the protagonist's mistake. It would have been better if Sam had arrived just after things went awry, lending some mystery to what caused the problem; maybe Foster Boondoggle, who never appears in-person in the game, could secretly be the perpetrator who we confront at the end.
Otherwise, the game is just what you'd expect from a Pajama Sam game: exploring a boy's wild imagination, populated by characters who are mostly living furniture and in a fun, nonsensical setting. The game world is a mix of industrial and corporate environments, contrasting with both PJ Sam 1 and 2. You'd think this would be boring, but the game is so imaginative that it's every bit as fun to explore as the other games. Something else that just occurred to me is the first three PJ Sam games each occur at different times of the day: PJ Sam 1 is at night, 2 is during the day, and 3 is during twilight. Having a fourth game kind of screws up that pattern, but oh well.
All in all, this is a great game for kids, and also for any fan of adventure games. In fact, I'd recommend any of the Pajama Sam or Spy Fox games for any adventure gamer, regardless of age.

A prime example of how all Remasters should look like. It's a shame that we had to wait for the PC port this long, but even after 13 years of it's original release on GC, it still looks and plays really good. It's a really unique game when it comes to it's atmosphere, and somehow, even after so many years, that clunky, tank-ish gameplay is still very catchy and I personally also love those (sometimes terrible) fixed camera angles. Inventory management with it's low capacity can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially on first playthrough, but in the end, I was also OK with it, since it also adds so much to it's tense atmosphere. Choosing whether to take more puzzle-related items or keep more ammo was always a big dilema. It's also worth playing at least twice, since you can choose between playing as Jill or Chris, each with it's own, slightly changed playthrough with different characters and dialogues. All in all it's a very good game and I can't wait for remake of RE2, which is already in production.... oh and don't forget to use door skipping mod. It's super annoying with those endless door-opening animations.

Bedlam has a great concept. You play as a woman who gets trapped in a video game and as she tries to escape back to the real world, she ends up jumping from one video game to another.
The writing, humor, story, and voice acting are all fantastic. However, to experience all of that you also have to experience average gunplay, awful level design, a lot of bugs, cheap enemy AI that uses aimbots, among other things. Bedlam is only around 6 hours long with no replay value. And even with its short length, there are several areas of the game that are padded out for no reason.
For a game that was in Early Access for over a year (let's not forget when Bedlam entered Early Access, it was already 50% finished), this is extremely disappointing.
I did enjoy it because the writing and humor was excellent but I'm not sure most people will be willing to sit through the numerous issues this game has to experience the good.
