A puzzle adventure in a stylised world of robots and amazing music.  A robot that has been abandoned by his city in pieces must pull himself together and return to not only confront some rather bad robots, but save his robot girlfriend in the process.
The first thing I noticed about Machinarium, as a first impression, is the music.  The soundtrack by Czech composer
really stands out in the task of impressing a strange new world without alienating the player from what they are engaged in.
Graphically, the art style for Machinarium is quite striking, with hand-drawn animation hauntingly evocative of works by surrealist Jan Švankmajer, and seeming to be another achievement for Dvorský that fans of Amatina Design will be encouraged to see.  With their pencil-and-paper 'living comic' art style, the organic appearance of the background and characters helps to round out the artificial world with a warm and almost human sense, which helps the player to get involved with the characters quite readily.
For an adventure game without dialogue at all, the plot is quite memorable and involving, with the characters having both impact and personality.  By removing dialogue from the game, the designers also allow the game to be accessible to players who do not speak English, using thought bubbles and pictures, authentic instruments and short beeps or buzzes to illustrate what characters are thinking or asking.
Puzzles throughout the game are both thought-provoking and challenging, sometimes requiring the player to think outside the box to complete tasks without pushing for weird feats of skewed logic present in some games of the genre.  Should the game prove to be too much of a bother, an in-built 'hint' system allows players to get some suggestions to how they can complete the task.
For some players, the puzzles will be a bit
challenging, though thankfully a short minigame can help to unlock the puzzles if you are more of a mind to do a reflexive shooter than a point-and-click puzzle solve.
Some players have reported having issues with transferring the game from fullscreen to windowed mode, though this seems to be more of a UI confusion than a bug issue.
None to speak of.
Turn out the lights and enjoy the immersive, imaginative world.
Well deserving of the awards it has recieved, Machinarium is a beautiful game with something special for art and music lovers, as well as fans of the point-and-click puzzle genre.  10/10.

Bedlam is very clearly sold on novelty, which is good because that's exactly what it is, and not much more. It isn't without any merit, the developers clearly had some passion for what they were doing.
As far as video game stories go, it isn't bad, but it isn't anything amazing, either. The voice acting - when they weren't failing at mimicking accents - was serviceable. And barring the odd need for the female characters to remind you of how much they are totally girls and how much they don't get what they think is proper respect in video games (which does make it seem like the writer has some kind of chip on their shoulder), the dialogue is also serviceable.
Which leaves us with the actual gameplay, which unfortunately lacking. The game leads you through a series of mockups of other well-known shooters, but what it fails to do is be a worthwhile shooter itself. The combat wasn't very interesting, the level design wasn't very good, and ultimately the experience was simply bland and dull.
Once the novelty of the concept wore off, the game rapidly overstayed it's welcome and became a chore to finish.

Bedlam is a game where you get to explore and fight through different era's of FPS.  Is it worth the money though?
Story: The story is good and solid but it draws a lot from science fiction movies so it may not be that big of a strech.  You are playing a woman who gets sucked into a game, and as you play you find out more about yourself and the worlds you play in.  Expect plenty of references to games like half life, gta and Quake.  I do see them doing a sequel to this game because of how the story plays out.
Controls: I played the game with a Xbox One controller, if I have the choice its normally more convient if im not at a desk.  The controller worked great in the game with menus even having the controller buttons listed.  I am sure the mouse controls function like  a normal FPS, as I briefly did use a mouse pad.
Gameplay: The gameplay is your standard shooter, pick up guns and kill the bad guys.  There are a few parts where you must solve a puzzle (not that hard), or find something to unlock something else.  Expect older style shooter play such as serious sam or doom as quite a bit of the game requires killing lots of foes.
Overall I did really enjoy this game and I might come back to touch up this review later if need be.  This game does have its humor and I laughed more than I thought I would. I will say some of the voice acting could have been a bit better and some people might be turned away by the voice acting.  I didn't have much problem with it but some people don't like female main characters, and some people don't like accents.  I am a huge fan of shooters and I really enjoyed my time with this game.  I do wish it was longer, and I was able to 100% the game in one playthrough, as only a few achivements are missable and none require a certain difficulty.  I would give this game a 8/10

What can I say?  I started it and finished it in the span of one day.  I couldn't stop playing until I had reached the end.  Was it the best game I ever played?  No.  The story and nostalgia were enough however, to keep me moving through the world.  The gameplay reminded me of my early days of FPS gaming, with nods to Quake, Medal of Honor, Nazi Zombies, and even Planetside.  They also sprinkle in FPS versions of other classic genres.  Some are hits and some are misses but they offer a nice enough variety to break up the game worlds.
Pros:
-Nostalgia.  This is probably the make or break point for most people.  If you are not a 90's era gamer, this will not have the same appeal.
-The early story writing is fantastic.
-LARGE variety of weapons.
-Responsive aim controls.
-Lead voice actress does a wonderful characterization with a lovely Scottish accent.
Cons:
-LARGE variety of weapons. With so many weapons, it requires cycling even using the number keys.  That means getting the weapon you want or need becomes a chore.  Think texting with a keypad to understand the issue.
-Story writing winds down about halfway.  The humor and characterizations become a bit more predictable as we close upon the ending.
-Platforming segments lead to multiple deaths.
Tips:
-Quick save is your friend.  The checkpoint system in the game is unforgiving so do yourself a favor and use that [F5] key to good effect.  It even keeps a couple at a time so you have little chance of quick saving yourself into a corner.
-Health and ammo respawn so make sure you do a run to collect whenever you are faced with a sizable enemy force.

Bedlam is a refreshing little romp that pays homage to some of the iconic FPS titles of the past.
Recommended to everyone who feels a bout of nostalgic longing for a good story-driven game, because let's face it - nowadays, the FPS market is so oversaturated that it most titles feel copy-paste-bland and generic.
Seeing as this is not a major-label mainstream release, I was still impressed with what they pulled off with the resources they had. I'd say the game successfully mirrors the evolution in graphics and gameplay and still makes the whole experience highly enjoyable. Granted, it has its hiccups like getting stuck against objects, but nothing offputting, really.
The voice-acting and story are on point and it even has a few nice twists and turns. Granted, the game is short, but it's also juuuust right.
Last, but not least, I don't feel like I need to highlight that it features a female protagonist (because HELLO, it's 2015) as much as I want to highlight her Scottish accent. A+! (and thank god for subtitles)
tl;dr:
4 out of 5, go get it.

There's nothing wrong with a good nostalgia trip when done right.
, however, does not qualify as such in the slightest; from the shoddy controls to broken gunplay, it deliberates misses the mark on what made the classic FPS so lovable, so endearing after all these years.
It's a fun concept, of course, just wasted on a developer that has no talent in creating a solid FPS of any creed.
p.s. that Unreal-style deathmatch stage was one of the most cringeworthy things I've ever had to endure. I *really* did not to need to be reminded of casual misogyny in online games. Not one bit.

The Fall is a narrative focused adventure game that takes a unique twist on the, by now somewhat well-worn, science-fiction tropes and themes of AI consciousness. It does so in two key ways: most obviously, by not having any human characters directly participate in the story, and instead presenting a small cast of AI in various states of (dis)function, but also more subtly by allowing those themes to be evoked...naturally (for lack of a better word, since we are dealing with computers) through the fascinating dialogues that play out between them, and the actions and decisions they end up making. In the instances that characters do address these themes explictly, it feels earned, and they do so without launching into overwrought pontifications. It's an execution of the "show, don't tell" idea, if you will, although in this case the writing is sharp enough to be part of the showing. This is reinforced by the excellent voice actors all giving powerfully evocative, yet understated performances.
The game's second biggest strength is its atmosphere. You'll never quite be allowed to feel at ease thanks to some truly creepy sound design, and a soundtrack that stays subtle and foreboding for the majority of the time, only coming to the forefront to effectively underscore combat encounters and important dramatic beats. Similar praise can be handed out to the aesthetics and visual design, which play to the strengths of the 2D, sidescrolling plane with moody lighting and great scene composition, allowing for moments that feel succesfully cinematic (which feels like an even bigger achievement for such a small game).
The puzzles are fine, providing respite from the oppressive mood and even some moments of levity through instances of well executed dark and macabre humor. There's also some fun to be found in a combat system that makes use of minimal cover and stealth mechanics. In all of these instances, however, the controls are a bit imprecise and clunky, and might take some getting used to or cause some frustration at the worst of times. It could be argued that, since you are playing an AI that is controlling a suit, this is an intentional design decision, and it does feel that way at first, but as the game progresses, it starts throwing some challenges and obstacles your way that don't fit well with the otherwise slow pace and demand more precision and responsiveness than you're able to reliably achieve. None of these issues ever amounted to anything other than small quibbles for me, but game's main draws are definitely its narrative and atmosphere.
So, while it ends up playing like a fairly standard adventure game with some light action elements, these parts don't get in the way of its strengths, and The Fall never quite stops feeling like something truly special.

This is an amazing game. Technically, it isn't TES III (3), it's V (5). Why do I say that? Well, let's look at the history:
Timeline of release years
1994	- The Elder Scrolls: Arena
1996	- The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall
1997	- An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire
1998	- The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard

2002 - The Elder Scrolls III: Tribunal
2003	- The Elder Scrolls III: Bloodmoon
2003 - The Elder Scrolls Travels: Stormhold
2004	- The Elder Scrolls Travels: Dawnstar
2004 -The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey
2006	- The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion
2006 - The Elder Scrolls IV: Knights of the Nine
2007	- The Elder Scrolls IV: Shivering Isles
2011	- The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
2012	- The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Dawnguard
2012 - The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Hearthfire
2012 - The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Dragonborn
2014	- The Elder Scrolls Online
2016	- The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Special Edition
2017	- The Elder Scrolls: Legends
But, I understand WHY they named it such. It was only due to the fact that it carried the name The Elder Scrolls in the title. Two of the titles above, while BEING
, were actually supposed to be DLCs to TES II: Daggerfall. So, enough of the history. I am sure that 99% of you have already yawned and fallen asleep.
Do I recommend it? Most definitely. Is it a bug free title? Nope. It crashes more often than it runs on modern systems.
on Windows 8 - 10 systems. Windows 7, is more hit and miss on installing.

New in this version is the Widescreen mode and "Alternate" control scheme. Instead of using the classic tank controls (which are sill present), players can instead opt to play the game using a more modern control scheme that makes the character move in the direction of the controller instead of Up = forward, Down = back and left/right is turning (tank controls).
The game is relatively unchanged beyond those points and stays true to the classic nature of this masterpiece of a game. If you're a horror fan, do yourself a favour and buy this game!

Level design is pretty plain and there's not much I can say about it other than the fact that you'll go through extremely typical levels inspired by shooters: there's a bunch of Quake 2 inspired factory/alien planet levels, the obligatory sewer level, and a Medal of Honor war-torn city. They're all exactly as you imagine them to be and there isn't much creativity involved in them. The game tries to have some gimmick levels but they're pretty dull, there's a particular one inspired by Pac-Man which requires you to get every single pellet in a labyrinth while being chased by invencible enemies and it was as tedious as one would expect. Seven or eight levels in I was sent into a level inspired by fantasy games and I had to find a sword. By this point the game was so boring that I had to drop it.
The only good thing I can say about it is that the dialogue is usually decent. However, sometimes it falls prey to thinking that name-dropping other game titles counts as humour.
I got this for around u$8 and even then I thought it was too much money since there's better games on Steam for that price. You're better off watching a playthrough on Youtube for the story and dialogue rather than wasting your time playing it. It's not a ~~bad~~ game but it's extremely dull.

Bedlam should be an incredibly cool game that takes players through a thrilling ride of landmark shooters like Quake, or Medal of Honor while exploring the evolution of video game design. Instead Bedlam mostly just shows us what other great games look like while feeling like a fairly bland shooter itself.
The journey begins when some gamer, known for technical prowess in shooters, realizes that she is in a game. From there, stuff happens and she has to shuffle around to other games. Bedlam tries to explore various video game genre/subgenres but doesn't ever quite commit. The horror game give you some tighter corridors and zombie enemies, but that's similar to the annoying catwalks that fill out the sci-fi inspired shooter levels, and then pretty much every other level just has wide open spaces but with different fillers (tanks in the World War 2 shooter setting, cottages in the fantasy one). Playing through this game is less like actively exploring different games and more like playing a single game with lots of costume changes, which just comes off as weak. Why does a fantasy game feel like Quake-lite, Medal of Honor have no setpieces, and the futuristic shooter have no interesting weapons? Imagine how something as simple as adding a directional damage indicator when jumping into the Medal of Honor section would have been to communicate growth, or adding a regenerating shield in the future settings, mana and light RPG elements in the fantasy setting, and so on, until the player actually feels the difference in settings and genres. Really, the feeling of movement and how resources are managed would have been an easy way to the chart the growth of shooters. It's these little missing details that really would have made the game shine.
None of the mechanics or level designs ever grow, which is a real shame. All the different weapons you get feel pretty much the same and seem to have no qualities attached to them: the crossbow shoots a bit lower and sometimes one of the shotguns feels like it actually hurts enemies more up close, but enemies aren't too picky on what you kill them with so there is hardly any strategy or risk involved. Bedlam doesn't exclusively stick to shooters: there are some levels inspired by Pacman, fantasy RPGs, Warcraft, classic and horizontal shooters.
What probably feels most out of place is the fact that your character is an absolute bullet magnet. Enemies you can hardly see gun you down with pinpoint accuracy so you sometimes just don't have a chance to even see what killed you before you have to reload and hope that you sprint behind cover fast enough to avoid whatever magic bullets are finding you. Due to level design shifting from bland with dull color designs to a nightmarish mess of ramps and platforms full of holes, the AI gets very annoying. However, towards the end of the game, the quasi-platforming steals the show as the most frustrating aspect.
I feel the ending of the game dragged on for a few hours too long. But it probably only felt like that because I was constantly having to reload due to me missing a jump when I just missed it by, who even knows how much, because I cannot see my feet. Platforming without being able to see your feet is like having to race in reverse, or shoot a gun that always fires off-screen. The jump button was also hit or miss on a controller at times. On top of the inaccurate jumping, the game's platforming sections are all designed like a maze with jump pads that are hard to gauge, alternate routes that lead you backwards, platforms full of holes that will drop you sometimes. This is absolutely one of the most annoying combinations I can even imagine. If anything, this should have been the psychological horror section of the game.
The concept is certainly interesting, but the mechanics house little creativity at best and are near-broken at worst. You are better off just popping in the games that Bedlam seeks to emulate. The concept and ambition are there, but too much of what should make Bedlam unique is left at surface level.

The core concept of Bedlam (mixing FPS settings and taking weapons from one to the other) is interesting and can lead to some fun puzzle-solving designs, but this game does not capitalize upon this, instead opting for a perfectly linear shooter with a huge, clumsy inventory.
A perfect example of this is the magic barrier separating Not-Skyrim's lower village from the upper village: the way it's done in-game is via finding the sword and opening the barrier, but I have a rocket launcher.  Could I not just rocket jump over the wall into the upper village (as far as I know, I cannot)?  Could I not just blow up the gate?  With all these weapons at my disposal, I can't use them to defy conventions or find alternate solutions.  It's disappointing.
The game also suffers from writing that's a bit too on-the-nose and it falls apart halfway through.  The end of the Not-Halo section was a particularly egregious low point, as the cloaked enemies are hard to see, hard to hit, and don't telegraph their attacks.  I spent 5 minutes looking for one that was cloaked and refused to do anything, including shoot at me.  This was after spending 5 more minutes looking for two other guys who had bugged out and had not moved from their spawn point.  The final boss is reminiscent of the Nihilanth in Half-Life, except not challenging at all whatsoever.  Once you clear out the mooks that spawn in, you can attack the boss with impunity, and the only possible deaths are from falling off the edge.
The $20 they're asking is too much to pay for a game of this length and simplicity.  If you're truly interested, I would suggest waiting for a sale.

In addition the movement cannot decide which way it wishes to be so it is stuck in a horrible low gravity, low friction limbo that can grind one to a halt on but a small incline or pebble in the road. It feels worst during the many jump pad sections which have more a habit of throwing up more than forward leaving huge uncertainty of making said jump. Like many others I can't help but compare this game to FTL. Where FTL is a near perfect experience from a games design perspective, with each mechanic adding to the experience. Bomber Crew feels as though it is an uncomfortable mash up of Realism and mobile phone like gameplay. This is reflected in its very nice cartoony graphics that are friendly and welcoming, the game itself is very difficult.
Whereas FTL is difficult, a game would typically last not much more than an hour. You would probably die before defeating the final boss and lose everything. It didn’t matter though! You die, you start again, it was designed to be played like this and it worked. Bomber Crew on the other hand has the player die (quite easily) and then starts the tedious and repetitive grind to earn enough money and experience only to die again in the same mission. This is my biggest problem with the game.
The controls seem as though they were designed for something like an iPad, you can pretty much play the entire game with just the mouse. Although this is great for accessibility It makes the experience frustrating and tedious sometimes trying to move the camera and click on things that could easily be done with hotkeys.
I hear a lot of reviews asking for a pause but I respect that they did not implement this. It makes the game more unique and adds something to the pace and excitement of the game. I like the plane upgrades and the progression keeps me wanted to upgrade before taking on a hard mission. The skill upgrades are nice but shallow.
Overall, the game has some amazing ideas but fails to execute them successfully. I feel as though they should have picked realism or a casual kids game. The game feels as though it falls somewhere in the middle and doesn’t work either way. I may improve my score if they fix some of the issues in the future.

Overall it's fun and part of it comes from the chaos of multitasking too many things and the other from its growing difficulty. Which after a certain point in the game is too much, you start to lose experience crew members or the bomber. Replacement aircraft and aircrew to upgrade as the game progresses but they really don't keep up with the mission difficulties.
I would recommend it but I want to warn you about a few things which I really would like the developers to adjust because this game can get very overwhelming quite suddenly. The manual targetting of aircraft becomes a real handicap in some missions where there is just far too much going on for you to handle will leave you with many planes not being targetted. Having to manually require gunners to fetch ammo instead of automatically getting it is annoying. While there are 8 crew positions (once you have a belly turret) you can only have 7 crew still, which doesn't seem right. And having to use up space for parachutes just in case things go badly prevents you equipping your aircraft effectively.

Overall, it was a really good game. The whole concept of it is just unexpected, but it makes you want to finish it

Interesting game. I recommend it, just about, with caveats. At heart, it is an enjoyable and extremely well-made micromanagement game and rogue-like-like. If you like trying to make quick decisions under pressure, this is a game for you. Think FTL without pausing, or silent hunter with much shorter and more hectic mission cycles.
When out in the air you command your crew in each of their stations, and "tag" enemies and new coordinates by pointing your screen at them. Missions give you intel and money. You can spend your money on new equipment for your crew and upgrades for your plane at fixed intel levels.
Each individual mission is generally appealingly tense, and most of the time they can go either way with victory or defeat.
There are three main problems. First, the game is too punishing, when sometimes it is not clear how the player should have been more successful.
A classic example is later in the game, when you get a bomb that must be dropped from high altitude to detonate. The problem is, you must be at low altitude to tag your target from some distance. At the top of high altitude, when your navigator tells you you are at high altitude, you lose your target tag. So how can you actually drop the high-altitude bomb on your target? It turns out, "must be dropped from high altitude" is not entirely accurate - after numerous wonky passes, flapping around like an indecive pigeon, I dropped the bomb from somewhere above medium altitude, but below high altitude, and it worked!
Second, the in-game economy is off. It simply costs too much to upgrade your bomber and crew. Later in the game, your plane is only really viable if it is upgraded to the hilt, and it takes many, many missions to get there. So you end up wasting vanilla plane after vanilla plane on doomed missions, where you complete your objectives but lose your plane and crew. There's no point making one or two minor upgrades if why aren't enough to bring it back.
Finally, the end-game is a chore. As far as I've got it's not entirely clear how I unlock the final mission. I believe it will come eventually after I accumulate enough intel by doing procedurally generated missions over and over again. The final upgrades are the same as the mid-game upgrades, but with higher numbers. As you progress, even easy missions are filled up with faster fighters with more powerful weapons, so it doesn't feel like you're becoming more powerful. The final quarter of a game should not be overly punishing. After all, we've got here because we like playing it, and we want to see the end.
So, given all this why do I recommend the game?
Well, the core mechanics are great. There's a niche out here for a WWII bomber crew game, and any single mission is an excellent example of that. I've got a good ten hours of pure in-the-zone joy from it.
And finally, it's SOO CLOSE to being an excellent game. From the general's frowning expression when you don't take out an enemy ace, to the pigeons dancing around on top of the barracks, to the enemy pilots expertly fitting Queen quotes into their threats, it's clear a huge amount of love has been put into this game. Play it for the love of the beginning and middle, and don't let the end-game spoil it.

I do not have any nostalgia for Morrowind. My first Elder Scrolls game was Oblivion, which back in 2006 blew my mind. Around that time, I also bought Morrowind to further immerse myself in this LOTR-esque world of Tamriel. I played it for a couple of hours, got totally lost (I suppose for the lack of pointers) and lost interest. Occasionally during the next 10 years I would make an ill-fated attempt to play it again, but would soon lose interest.
However, last year I decided to make a serious attempt to play it again. I installed the Morrowind Overhaul mod (or rather a compilation of mods) and set out on a journey to Vvardenfell. What I found was a feeling I have not experienced since playing Oblivion for the first time a decade before.
Morrowind is set on the island of Vvardenfell in the province of Morrowind, a rather remote area of the Empire. In contrast to Oblivion with it's Medieval fantasy setting and Skyrim with its Nordic setting, Morrowind takes inspiration from Egyptian, Japanese, Middle Eastern and I suppose even Mezoamerican cultures. The world is darker, rawer and much more mysterious than the latter two games. If, like me, you play Elder Scrolls games primarily in order to get immersed in another world, no other game of the series is ever as immersive as Morrowind. The settings, often intelligent quests and great sound (from the winds of Ald'Ruhn to the fantastic theme) is what makes Morrowind a fantastic game.
The gameplay, while showing its age, is remarkably well-done. Character customization, spellmaking, enchanting, alchemy are all here, as is levitation (which becomes the best way to travel with a pair of fast shoes...). Only the combat mechanics stand out as archaic, especially in the beginning where your attacks rarely hit. This is less like Skyrim's action-oriented combat, and more like D&D-style dice-rolling. However, as you progress and your attacks become both more powerful and more accurate, this becomes less of an issue.
This is my first review, and I find i difficult to know whether you would like this game. I supppose that if you want a world where you can truly immerse yourself, Morrowind is a safe bet. If you are looking for a game with more focus on fast-paced gameplay (or even just refined gameplay), it is possible that you will find the later installments of the series more to your taste. However, I personally consider Morrowind one of the best games I have ever played.

When I first heard of Clustertruck it seemed like a silly game that would only entertain me for 5 minutes at best.
Boy was I wrong, not only is Clustertruck an extremely fun adrenaline rush with great replayability, but it also got me hooked to the point that I played through all the levels in one sitting. All there is to this game is jumping from truck to truck while dodging obstacles, which can sound quite boring, but the real fun starts when you treat it as a parkour speedrunning game by trying to complete everything as fast as you can. Went through all the levels? Buy some upgrades and do it again. Upgrades sometimes drastically change the way you play by adding interesting mechanics. Completed it again? Get some friends together and challenge eachother, see who can beat a level the fastest.
For being such a simple game, Clustertruck is a surprisingly fun and replayable parkour speedrunning game. I highly recommend anyone who is on the fence to give it a try.

"The Witcher" is a 3rd person RPG. It asks players to make choices that visibly impact the world, gives us engaging combat, and opens a refreshing variety of ways to interact with NPC's. It is also one of the first mainstream RPG's to offer a romantic element-- something which brings a whole new purpose to character motivations.
While unique and well-crafted, "The Witcher"s  gameplay often feels like busy-work, however, creating a narrative that wanders in circles. By the time we finish 7 chapters of wandering, we will definitely have seen amusing and exciting moments sprinkled throughout the game-- but the repetitive and monotonous pace will wear down even the most eager of hearts.
"The Witcher" has a great core that simply does not grow successfully throughout the hours of playtime it asks of us.  Instead, let's just recognize how this game influenced much greater games (Dragon Age Origins, Witcher 2 & 3, even Skyrim) and accept that Its best quality now, is only what it inspired in later games. If you're on a budget try one of those, instead!

Pajama Sam 2: Thunder and Lightning Aren't So Frightening truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself exploring one room for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of not finding the solution is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the worlds are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a puzzle to earn a new area, and you would use that new area to earn more puzzles. In layman's terms, to earn more rooms, you had to perfect current puzzles. They ditched that and added the ability to google the solutions. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock the first room. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many rooms are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging rooms, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to play every variation.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Pajama Sam 2: Thunder and Lightning Aren't So Frightening is its expasive community. There are lots of flash games for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10
BUY THIS GAME.

If you would dare to look at Pajama Sam 2 and say to yourself, 'Well, it's a sequel, it can't be quite as good,' you need to immediately rethink all of your life decisions and then play Pajama Sam 2. While there are some slight changes here and there to keep the game feeling fresh, Pajama Sam 2 is packed with all the distinct features that made the first game so amazing: more pointing and clicking, more item collecting and more existential journeys of self-discovery. Instead of collecting socks, Sam collects a large variety of puzzle pieces, which is likely symbolic of the courage and morality he must piece together in order to confront his crippling fear of thunder and lightning. Speaking of puzzles, Pajama Sam 2 is like a puzzle with every piece in its proper place: with its moving story, well-crafted characters and exciting gameplay, this game feels incredibly polished and complete. Throughout its development, the geniuses at Humongous Entertainment must have known they had a masterpiece on their hands.
If I had to give this game a score, I would give it a 10/10 with a complimentary smiley face.

It's an absolute pain to get the game to actually open, you still have to deal with GFWL, without the DLCs it's only about 3 hours long (the DLCs adding a roughly equal amount of time), and the AI is dumber than Payday 2's.
That aside, even with fragments of GFWL still there connecting to play with a friend works easily, and the gameplay itself is at least a 7/10.
Get the Complete Pack, and then play it with a buddy or two, and you've actually got a pretty solid and enjoyable, if still short game.
Some things to try if you can't get it to open:
1. Make sure it's installed to the same drive as Windows.
2. Uninstall MS GFWL Redistributable and MS GFW Marketplace using Control Panel's Uninstall feature, and then redownload/reinstall GFWL.
3. Go to My Documents/Capcom/RERC and delete settings.dat (This is only applicable if you've gotten the game to run at least once before).
4. Just keep opening it straight from the .exe over and over, lots of times it'll eventually work.

Resident Evil games always try to make traversing the levels interesting due to various mechanics: limited inventory meaning you have to choose which items to bring with you at any time, various locked doors forcing you to search for key items, enemies which you don't have the resources to kill, and doors which are close to breaking or are only usable one way. All those features combined makes traversing the mansion feel like a big puzzle, and this game handles that aspect much better than any other game in the series. It does become a bit too simplified in the later parts of the game, but the first half of the game has excellent level design.
This remaster of the game features a new rendering engine which makes the characters look a lot better, new costumes, a new very easy difficulty (which anyone wanting an actual challenge should avoid), and rather lackluster backgrounds. Unfortuantely, Capcom weren't able to re-render the backgrounds for this remaster, but they tried their best to find alternate solutions. So the result is that you've got some backgrounds which are simply upscaled from their original jpeg renders, some which are touched up by hand,  some which have specific elements replaced with 3D models, and a couple which are fully re-created in 3D. Unfortunately, the vast majority are simply upscaled. Despite this, the game still manages to look good overall.
The original version features slow door animations with a static speed which were masking loading times. Loading times in this version would be virtually instaneously if it weren't for the fact the door animations are still the same length and they're still unskippable. As a result, you'll be looking at doors for potentially hours throughout a playthrough. If this doesn't sound appealing, I suggest looking up steam guides to find a mod which lets you skip all door animations.
This is not just one of the greatest RE games, it's one of the greatest games ever, in general.

Back in the late 90's I remember this game releasing for PS1, and I was a huge fan of it. I purchased the original, the directors cut, every version I could get my hands on.
Fastforward to now, and I decided to tromp through some old stomping grounds. RE HD Remaster is a remaster of the Gamecube version of the game, which includes a few new and revamped areas, and much better graphics. Gameplay has remained unchanged from the original, other than a key fact that you can play without tank controls (hell yes!). Resident evil relies heavily on the "survival" aspect; you have limited inventory space, limited ammo, even limited number of saves. The puzzles in this game can be quite devious, and the game gives you hints, but rarely outright tells you what to do (I played the game with a guide because I'm old and don't have the same memory I once did). Zombies, dogs, every enemy in this game is deadly; a normal zombie can take as many as 10 bullets to kill on Normal. Its a lot more brutal than I remembered as a kid. Top it off that some enemies can follow you around the mansion, its constantly a harrowing experience, especially if you skipped enemies to conserve ammo.
However, the game is not without its flaws. I really wish they would have edited out the "loading" animations of the doors, it adds a lot of unnecessary length. As well, the rooms are not labeled, so sometimes finding where you need to go next can be an absolute chore. I remember one time I was looking for a specific room and it took me 10 minutes combing through google pictures to locate the damn thing. Aiming is incredibly difficult, to score headshots you need to let an enemy almost bite you half the time. As well, inventory management is a real chore, and while it adds a lot of challange to the game it becomes a chore constantly running back to a storage box. I really wish they gave an option to discard things like herbs or ammo, especially if you accidentally picked something up. Lastly, the cheesy voice acting is still here, and the lip sync with the words is HORRIBLE. Its wayyyyy off... why the hell didn't they fix that, I can't fathom.
Pros
------
* Challanging gameplay
* Still a classic
* Graphics are gorgeous
* Storyline is zany, but much more believable than later entries
* Pretty darn long your first playthrough
* Puzzles are clever
Cons
-----
* Antequated gameplay, a lot of the systems don't hold up to the test of time, and some make the game harder by making it more annoying (like inventory management)
* Lip sync is WAY off
* No way to discard items
Overall, I'd give it an 8/10. Call me sentimental, but this game is still awesome.

I don't own the boardgame of this yet but a couple of my friends and I spent several hours playing last night and well play many more in the future. A charming game that is much deeper than its whimsical appearance may suggest with a lot of replayability despite the (at least currently) singular map.
I would love to see more expansions for it, especially the modular map, to come to the PC version and more races and powers means more options and crazy combos. Some of these combinations were laugh out loud funny (flying ghouls, peace-loving barbarians, etc.) so even more of these would enhance the game immensely.
It needs a fullscreen option and we had some minor hiccups getting our games set up (invite friends and bots, the go button wouldn't light up everytime, had to go back to the previous menu then select current MP game and then the button worked) but we encountered no other bugs.
Essentially the objective it to hoard the most coins by fulfilling victory conditions while placing race tokens to conquer land. All races are matched with a power that modifies what they do and helps determine how many tokens you have to use for attack and defense. As your race spreads out it becomes harder to expand anymore so you will usually have to go into a decline and select a new race/power combo. A race in decline will normally be left weak and unable to do much but still accrues coins for you. These race/power combos are on the right side of the screen and you can take the top one or skip down for penalites if a combo isn't to your liking. Players take turns conquering and reinforcing, trying to get more coins than anyone else to win at the end of the last turn.
There's a lot of subtle strategy involved in both the races inherent abilities but also in the power they are attached too and how many tokens they can get. Pushing your self thin can net a lot of early coins but if the others gang up on you it can backfire and some races are much better at this than others. Knowing if and when to go into decline and when to take or skip a race/power combo as well as when and where to attack and is that last possible understrength attack worth risking that die roll for(?) combine to make it an excellent game. Highly recommended.

This is an absolute gem of a gem, and I'm so glad I discovered it. It is simple yet satisfying, and just the right length.
You take on the role of a ghost, whose only goal is to go about the town scaring its poor denizens. After getting sufficiently spooked, they will abandon whatever place you're currently haunting, and your goal is to get everyone to flee all the buildings.
As a ghost, you can float around freely, and the movement is rather quick and elegant. It really is a joy to just fly around the environments as an adorable little poltergesit. To actually scare people, you haunt objects and then perform one of a number of different preset actions, which is just a cute animation that scares any citizens that observe it. For example, you might cause a rocking horse to start rocking back and forth on its own, a phone to start ringing, or a skeleton dinosaur to snap its jaw. There are also some that actually involve some ghost/entity appearing and doing something that would be genuinely creepy if this game weren't so darn cute. You unlock more interactions as the citizens get progressively more terrified. Nothing in this game is actually scary, of course. The art style is playful and cartoonish, and all the animations are adorable (and very smooth).
Besides scaring the pants off everyone you can find, there are also some special inhabitants (a clown, a cook, a boat captain) who you are able to kill by solving very simple "puzzles" (really just special interactions with the environments). Once they are dead, their ghosts become available for you to use, although this doesn't change the gameplay. Still it's a nice addition. Who hasn't wanted to be a ghost clown? If only there was a pirate ghost available...
There are only four locations in the game - a hospital, a boat, a museum, and a theater. They are each unique from each other and all have some great animations to behold, but I found the museum and theater espeically fun (in the museum you can move around as a statue and attack people, and in the theater you can play instruments). Even if you want to see every animation the game has to offer, it can still be beaten in about an hour. You cannot die (you are already a ghost!) or lose in any way. Overall, the game is more like a toy than an actual game, but that's fine. It's a delightful toy, that please 21-year-old me just as much as it would have please 10-year-old me.

The mechanics weren't great. Although polished mechanics aren't

And finally, the art! It was actully a decent style. I will admit that The Fall lives up to it's "atmospheric" tag: the whole experience really felt dirty and gross, which is I'm sure what the designers were going for. The 3D modelling was good, if a bit lacking in polish, but overall things felt cohesive and made sense visually.(7/10)
So, overall, I give it a 6.5/10. Good enough, but not fantastic, probably too short for $10, but with interesting story and decent puzzles behind the whole thing.

I wouldn't say it's a bad MMO. It's a bad *game,* but as far as MMOs go, this is pretty awesome. I wish the quests had some sort of consistent storyline, beyond the short arcs. I wish they'd actually stuck with the "omg Braniac is invading!" arc they were going with in order to explain why villains and heroes could be fighting each other one moment and alongside one another the next. I *really* wish the powers themselves had been free, and that the expansions had been more about in-game content. And, most of all, I wish there were more opportunities to actually interact with the world, rather than just having to behave like a hired thug--it's a little jarring to go through the interesting and complex character creator, only to find yourself in a world that doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about what you do or why you do it at all, beyond the black-and-white "hero or villain?" selection (and obviously there aren't any real ramifications for that action; the voice actors for the villains manage to sound suitably evil, and there are the occasional Kidnap Citizens and Kick Puppies scenes, but otherwise you might as well be punching toasters).
Again, by the incredibly lackluster standards MMOs have been setting for themselves, lately (Black Gold, Onigiri, Eden Eternal, I could name a thousand others), this is a very good game. If you enjoy MMOs, you'll enjoy this. I certainly do, for all its flaws. But it disgusts me that I have to qualify it like that.
If you're having a hard time enjoying it and are unwilling to give up on it for some reason, try bringing some friends along. Unfortunately, the way quests are set up means that if you chose different mentors you'll be doing different quests at different times, but at least you'll be able to do Raids and Alerts together. And for gods' sake, don't turn PVP on unless you like being followed by higher-leveled players all around the field; they'll wait until you're vulnerable, and then they'll eat you and your delicious experience.

As a fan of the Chicken Invaders series, i was quite disappointed with this entry. Even though it's more of the same -which is good- there are some changes this time around which harm the enjoyment a lot more than they help it.
Extending a theme from CI4, your ship often rotates (not freely) to add some variety to the levels, but this time around there is a stronger emphasis on pointing you the wrong way and making you wait until you're able to shoot the remaining foes. Furthermore there is an entire chapter devoted to "reverse" top down shooting; meaning that instead of the foes at the top and you shoot upwards, the foes are at the bottom and you shoot downwards. While it doesn't sound like much, it is so completely against what you're used to in this type of game that it gets annoying very quickly.
The other change related to the rotation is that now the "gravity" goes wherever your engines are pointing, so if you're pointing right then the pickups, eggs and keys will fall to the left. I don't like this change either, at least when gravity was always downward you'd know where exactly to look after destroying foes.
There are a couple of side-scrolling terrain-avoidance levels, these are okay but they're basically change for the sake of change. The new weapons are all rubbish and once you've tried them all out you'll be avoiding collecting them because the older powerups are just better.
It's hard to recommend Chicken Invaders 5 because Chicken Invaders 4 is better in every way, even the story and humour were much better in the previous game. Regardless of if you're new to the series or not, just go with CI4 it's way more fun.

Machinarium is a Point&Click with a brilliant and beautiful universe. Sounds and musics are made with metallic noises. There’s a lot of humor too. The story is about a world of robots; we control a small robot which was thrown to the dump and is going to return in town to repair the insult which was made for it. Dialogues and flashbacks are made in drawn bubbles.
The difficulty is more present than in Botanicula for several reasons: at first, objects to be collected are facing in the background, so they are not easily locatable at first glance and force us to look well everywhere.
Secondly, the robot has the capacity to change its size; what makes that there are actions which we can make only for a certain height and not for an other one.
Finally, the objects which we collect can sometimes merge between them to form only one.
The whole allowing to have riddles a little more complex, increasing the interest and the length of the game.
However, even by being blocked, no need to fetch the soluce on Google. The game integrates itself the solutions of 2 manners: in every area, it is possible to consult a clue, which just gives the main action to realize at one time or another to finish the area. But it is also possible to consult the guide of solutions (which is a comic strip showing step by step what to do to achieve the level), if you manage to play with success to a short shooting game.
Indeed, numerous short games punctuate Machinarium: several puzzles, riddles and games like Space Invaders.
In conclusion, a very good Point&Click game, with a well thought universe and a good level of difficulty!

In brief: A gimmicky idea that doesn't work and should have stayed a novel.
In boxers: Bedlam is an FPS that explores the idea of jumping between different video games that have come out over the years - specifically First Person Shooters, though a couple of others are thrown in later on - and seeing how art styles have evolved over the years. Oh, and there's a plot about being stuck in a video game world that's being destroyed by glitches and stuff, but whatever.
The biggest problem with this is that although the art styles are really fun to see in how they differ, the gameplay remains exactly the same throughout. It almost never varies no matter which game you're in, whether it be the Quake 2 knock-off, the WW2 Call of Duty knock-off, the Left 4 Dead knock-off, the Planetside knock-off, the Fantasy MMO knock-off, the Civilization knock-off or the Unreal Tournament knock-off. It's almost entirely consistant throughout, and it's a HUGE missed opportunity. There are a few levels which deviate from this (knock-offs of Pac-Man, Space Invaders and... uh, a generic Shmup), but they're short and barely have time to register before you're back into standard shooting.
...oh, did you notice I mentioned knock-offs? Yeah, you're playing through games 'inspired' by classic games of the genre. This wouldn't be an issue if all the other characters you talk to over the radio didn't mention games that actually exist. They're off playing through Rayman, GTA and Lego Batman, while you're stuck in... generic fantasy land. The references just make you feel like you're missing out on what could have been.
"What could have been" is a perfect phrase for this game, to be honest. It's full of missed opportuties that would have made things infinitely more enjoyable. Being able to use guns from one game in another is neat, but there's no ammo for them so you just won't bother. The AI is consistantly frustrating - they're always amazingly accurate with their guns and as a result you'll constantly get shot before you even know they're there. The sections in between levels are just sort of broken platforms in space which feature some VERY questionable platforming (don't jump on the tiny platforms, you'll fall right through them). And every single section is generic, repetitive and drags on for far too long.
If there are positives to be had, then it's in the visdual department. The game LOOKS perfect. Every single style of game is fantastically put together and when they do bleed together it usually looks pretty neat. The audio, on the other hand, is much more mixed. The lead voice actress is pretty good (and Scottish, which is a pleasant change), as is the the titular Bedlam, and the villains are suitably menacing. The other characters... not so much. Their acting leaves something to be desired and never really works, so you're pulled out of every conversation they have.
I tired of this game remarkably quickly and by the end I was practically on my knees BEGGING for it to be over. The game has a neat concept but the poor execution and overlong levels means it vastly outstays its welcome. And the absolute kicker is that the game ends on a sodding "Hey, here's a portal, let's see where it leads" cliffhanger. Because, y'know, I wanna play MORE of this.
Maybe if the developers actually tighten the floaty controls and make the different games FEEL different, I could recommend this. As it is though... I really can't.
Oh, and screw the snipers who turn invisible.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥

Before you read this note that I've played and beaten the original Resident Evil.
Not a bad game. I'd personally give it a nice 9/10. It kept me entertained for hours (even though it says I played it for a whole 7 minutes at the time I wrote this), and it had good puzzles. The only thing I didn't quite enjoy was the Crimson Heads. Yes, the infamous, well known, Crimson Heads... Sure I left every last one of them alive through the game, that wasn't a problem. However when they showed up for the first time, I was just thinking, "Really? I killed you already... You're actually kind of boring..." Other than those, the game was fun. The Tyrant fight took a whopping minute to complete. Mind you this is the final boss fight in the game, and arguably the hardest to fight... I don't care who you are, you shouldn't be able to destroy a boss that easily (especially if you're as bad as I am...). I beat the game in a fairly casual time of about 13 hours. Go ahead and say I'm slow, I don't care... All I know is that when I beat the game, I expected "Once Again Mode" to be a sort of New Game+ feature like in Resident Evil 4 where you load your save and continue with what junk you unlocked the first time around (seeing as you save after you beat the game), but no! No, you actually just get a new menu screen, you unlock Hard difficulty, and you can tell more easily what difficulty is what (even though they're fairly obvious). But yeah, I rationed every bullet, gas can, and healing item until the end, just to be told that I can't play with them next round...
All in all, the game was nice, graphics are pretty, the defense items helped, the new music was cool, and the gameplay felt much easier than the original version, but if the New Game+ feature was in this game, I'd give it a solid 10/10, it is that good...

TLDR: Read the book instead.
Do you like unerringly accurate hit scan enemies that can nail you from across the entire level? Do you like assets that have hit boxes beyond their visible boundaries *if* the asset itself properly loads in at all? What about enemies that clip and fire through boundaries? Perhaps you're a fan of auto-saves that murder you if you try to load them, focing you to pistol start the level from the beginning? If you enjoy any of these features, then hot damn, do we have a game for you.
Bedlam is an interesting concept mired by flawed technical execution. Beyond the aforementioned "features", weapons are bland and have no real impact. A majority of the environments are uninteresting save for the glitch zones. These however quickly overstay their welcome since they are used as giant, empty platforming areas in which to spout exposition as . And then when they decide to put action into a glitch zone during the final level of the game, you'd wish they hadn't. It's a sprawling mish mash of assets and enemies from the rest of the game thrown haphazardly together creating a frustrating, overlong slog. The references are heavy handed, random (LEGO Batman is one of them for chrissakes), and sure to become dated VERY quickly. I *really* wanted to enjoy this game, but ended up finding it disappointing.
If you still want to give it a shot, I'd suggest letting it get patched and go on sale first.

The game takes place in Racoon City during the Infamous infection time, (Same time as Resident Evil 2 & 3). You are part of a squad from Umbrella that must follow orders and do missions within the disastrous and unstable Raccoon City.
You are a squadron of 4 deployed by Umbrella, you get to choose your character you play as, aswell as the companions you bring along with you, note the campaign can also be played with 4 other players to have a full coop story experience.
There is a a few different classes and characters, such as Vector(Recon), Lupo, Beltway (Explosive Specialist), Spectre (Marksman), Bertha (Medic), FourEyes (Scientist). They all have different abilities such as Stealth, Seeing through Walls, Plantings explosives, Healing, & all kinds of different perks. Which is nice to be able to choose whom you enjoy playing as the most.
You can unlock new weapons, perks & abilities by buying them with XP which is nice. Though the level system is quite redundent.
The story itself is mediocre, nothing to shabby or to keep you wanting to move forward, you end up just shugging along although it was nice to see characters such as Nemesis, Leon, Claire, Sherry & Ada during your travels in Raccoon City. It was a nice cross-over with Resident Evil 2-3's story although this games story is Non-Canon to the series.
Now well the big part, the Gameplay. I found this game to be entertaining most times. Shooting up zombies and infected, (those Crimson Heads & Hunters sure could be a pain) but I enjoyed having a challenge with B.O.W's which was nice and shooting up zombies on the streets of Raccoon City.

What I absolutely despised about this game was the "Enemy Soldiers", they were literarly your worst nightmare and they were freaking everywhere you go in this damn game. They would be spammed in large numbers and were hard to kill, they would Harass/Aim-Bot/Shoot You Up as if you were trying to land on D-Day. One soldier could literarly murder you within 2 seconds if your not in cover, now imagine 15 of them clumped like a bunker you have to get through (Dying Simulater begins). The Enemy Soldier A.I are ridiculously hard in this game even on Normal and they will kill you.
Remember when I mentioned getting through soldiers is like attempting to get through a bunker with an automated turret?, well imagine that but with 20 zombies harassing you at the same time, is that not enough how about annoying Crimson Heads and Hunters, yea your gonna get real angry during situations like that because this game is stupidly unbalanced.
Ah, so you cleared the area of Zombies & B.O.W's?, well you better watch out because that soldier over there just killed  you. Oh?, not a problem right this game has checkpoints?, Oh did I forget to mention this game has one of the worst Checkpoints systems I have ever seen... If you clear a room of 50 people proceed a bit further and die... well guess what? you gotta clear all that bull crap again, and it will happen ALOT in this game.
But, I have A.I Partners to help me right?, Your A.I Partners are useless as Nipples on a Man. They may get a few zombie kills, but oh boy when it comes to fighting Soldiers & B.O.W's you are the one whos gonna do all the work. Example of treachery: You have Bertha on your team because she's a medic, well she aint gonna heal you when you absolutely need it, you could be right next to her with little to no health and she will prioretize any enemy over healing your behind.
If you got friends you can play with, do it because the A.I are useless, YOU are the one man army here with a bunch of monkeys with guns.
This game has a crappy Auto-Cover system, more reason to die.
Overall, this game can provide entertainment. I had fun playing it, apart from the deaths from soldiers of course. Is it worth its retail value?, Absolutely not BUY IT ON SALE as I did, no more than $10 should you pay for this game.

When Small World 2 functions properly, it's a fun and faster incarnation of its tabletop predecessor. The game is arguably easier to play than its tabletop incarnation because it prevents players from making invalid moves and sometimes indicates possible moves. It also makes it easier for players to keep track of numbers like turns and quantities of troops. The game also captures the aesthetic of Small World very well, and actions are played out rather pleasantly. However, the game crashes or bugs-out frequently. The game is locked at one specific resolution, which cannot be changed (except by maximizing the window, which may sometimes result in letterboxing). There are no settings options whatsoever, aside from game volume and music volume. And finding a game online is horrendous because creating and joining games is tedious, and that's if there's even anyone online to play with (which there more often than not, is not). Many of the UI elements can be confusing, especially since the tooltips (when functional) aren't always informative. Parts of the UI, particularly text, will even change the game's cursor to the system or text cursor, making the entire game feel cheap and poorly made. One would expect many of these issues to be solved, or at least addressed, shortly after the game's release, but since at the time I'm typing this the game has been released for over a year, I believe that it's safe to say that these issues will not be addressed any time soon, if at all. The entire game feels like a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥money grab, and despite the genuine entertainment it may provide, albeit in small amounts, I cannot recommend this game while these issues continue to exist.

*STORY TIME*
'The Longhorn' was a british light bomber plane with a fairly experienced crew that was eager to fight the evil that was present. they trained together, slept together, fought together, and gave each other a shoulder to cry on in these dire moments. they were ordinary people that were drafted to do extraordinary tasks.
they were:
SGT. Dale fleming
SGT. Henry Wallace
SGT. Cynthia Henderson
SGT. Gillian Reid
SGT. Wallace McGregor
SGT. Jean Bruce
F/SGT. Marvin Kerr
'The Longhorn' and her crew were sent out on one particular night to eliminate enemy U-Boats that were causing a problem on the coast, not far from their base. it was a dark and stormy night, but the battle-tested Longhorns were up for the task. they flew into the night sky and rained hell on the first U-Boat they saw. Suddenly, enemy fighters emerged from the clouds and ambushed. Machine gun fire lit up this dark night. The Longhorns fought hard, however, they were still a new crew. Due to a lack of communication, they didn't realize that there were U-Boats that still needed to be destroyed. After scrambling around trying to find U-Boats and fend off enemy fighters at the same time. 'The Longhorn' took heavy damage. But worst of all, she ran out of fuel. propellers stop spinning, the light bomber starts plummeting to the ocean. The pilot gave the order to bail out, but it was too late. 'The Longhorn' and her crew smacked into the ocean.
F/SGT. Marvin Kerr, engineer, was the sole survivor of this failed mission. Kerr swore that there were other survivors and pleaded command to send a search party to find his crew. Command had stated that there were even more airman that are MIA, it would take too much time and resources to find all of them. Those that were MIA were presumed KIA, and Kerr had to join up with a new crew, and that's just what he did. He didn't speak much, but how could he? How could he even begin to replace the voids in his soul that were once filled by his former crew? As Kerr and his crew were gearing up and making necessary upgrades to their bomber. Kerr took it upon himself to paint the words "Never Forget" on the nose of his new bomber. The rest of the crew couldn't even speak. The pilot, Ernest Crawford, saw this and respectfully named his plane 'The Longhorn II'. This lifted Kerr's spirits, and he was able to function, as an engineer. throughout these next missions, Kerr would do anything he could to make sure the mission was complete. He would ride the wing and fix the engines mid-flight, he would heal any injuries that his crew sustained, he even took over the mid-turret after F/SGT. James Wright lost his life. Kerr was a key member of the crew. until one day, 'The Longhorn II' and her crew were sent on a mission to eliminate enemy gun placements. Everything was going as planned, until ace pilot Felix Feder emerged from the sky and started lighting up the longhorns. Navigator Daniel Brown, and Kerr were both hit, they were both down. Bomber Daniel Woodbridge was experienced in first aid too. With only one first aid kit, he had to make a choice, either revive Kerr, who can fix the heavily damaged plane. Or, revive Daniel Brown, who can find our way back to base...
Woodbridge ended up reviving Brown, to ensure that they can get home. Kerr bled out, and died on 'The Longhorn II'. The rest of the crew understood Woodbridge's choice, they all agreed that Kerr would have made the same choice. They gave Kerr a proper burial, and etched his name on the memorial, with the rest of his original crew. That is the story of 'The Lonhorn'. 'The Longhorn II' still soars high in the sky to this day with only four of her original crew still alive. Pilot Crawford swears to avenge Kerr one day, by killing Felix Feder.

Great boardgame gets a great videogame treatment! Local multiplayer makes a great alternative to getting out the box and playing tabletop when kids are around to grab at the 100+ pieces in the game.
As for the game itself:
It's a Risk-esque territory accumulation game, set in a fantasy world, but without the massive luck based elements of risk. Over the course of the game you'll control different factions (elves, orcs, sorcerers, etc.) all with different attributes that tweak the core rules. Each faction gets assigned a random special ability like flying, berserking or dragon master that further tweaks the rules.
Each territory requires 2 soldiers to conquer, with 1 additional required for each additional factor like terrain, fortifications or opponents troop occupation. Eventually your troops will wear thin and you'll have to put your active race in decline; all but one troop in each location is removed from the board. You still collect points for those territories; but special abilities & troop movement are no longer an option. At the start of your next turn you'll be able to select a new faction.
Play continues for 10 rounds with points being accumulated for each territory you control at the end of each turn. It's fast paced, with fun art and concept; and also scales very well. It supports 2-5 players, but has a different sized game board depending on how many people are playing!

Cubic Castles is a voxel building game conceptually similar to Minecraft and others of the genre. I like Cubic Castles for several reasons, which I'll outline below, but in broad strokes it's easy to learn, easy to play, and there is a very pleasant community within the game, here on Steam, and on the official forums for the game.
Pros:
Very polished look. The game looks wonderful, the blocks are crisp and colorful. The mining zones generate in a way that looks plausible and clean. It's easy to tell one kind of resource from another on the screen with different patterns, textures and colors that make each distinct.
Easy control - movement is basically the four cardinal directions along with single and double jumps. Camera angle and elevation control are easy.
Wide variety of craftable items - This is pretty self-explanatory, but if you play the game I recommend having a browser window open in the background leading to
- it's a valuable resource the details how each item is built.
Community - the players tend to be very nice people. I've only encountered one really rude player so far, and I have a decent amount of hours invested. That's rare in any multi-player online game.
Lots to see and do - people build and maintain realms with all sorts of goodies. Some are shops, some are games or metagames, some have puzzles or obstacle courses (known in game as parkour areas, a great co-opting of the word.) People make hangout rooms and places just to see interesting things. Simply hopping from one realm to the next can be fun and also inspire new ideas on things to build.
Cons:
Limited camera angle/not designed for first person view - That's a limitation that carries with it a very specific consequence: It makes it difficult to make multi-level structures that can be navigated easily. For example, I have built houses with two floors, and in order to make the first floor seen I have to make the second floor significantly higher in order for the third person view to allow others to see it. It would be nice to have a first person option, or total camera control, or both.
Limited chat function - generally the chat is limited to local players only. The game makes money in a few ways, one of which is selling "Hollas" which are essentially a global chat broadcast. This is a minor issue, as any game needs to make money to survive, and as revenue-generators go that is a very mild one. A readily available chat option to speak to online friends via a tell or direct message would be nice.
Occasional beggars - players frequently show up in one's realm begging for free stuff. That's not a flaw with the game directly, but as a community issue it is at least something to make note of. The positive item, however, is that you can easily kick-and-ban those pesky panhandlers.
Summary/TL;DR
It's a load of fun with a few issues that are more of a "hmmm" thing than a deal breaker. I recommend the game highly and hope to see you there.

I want so badly to love this game. It has a fantastic aesthetic, interesting premise, and intuitively constructed puzzles. The dealbreaker for me, however, is the controls. It just feels absolutely terrible to play.
Some key issues:
- Aiming is quite off, to the point where my cursor has to be halfway across the screen from what I'm aiming at in order for the gun to make contact. Given the importance of precise timing to the combat, this is very frustrating.
- Jumping feels floaty and unpredictable.
- In order to interact with objects, they must be highlighted with the flashlight. Interactable objects are not visible otherwise. You literally have to be shining a flashlight on an elevator panel directly in front of your character in order to press it. This means the flashlight has to be out most of the time, which slows your movement, and suffers from the same awkward aiming difficulties as the firing does.
Playing this game is largely a question of betting on whether I can get through 10 minutes without quitting in frustration at the horrifyingly bad controls.
If you are someone who has a very high tolerance for control-based problems, and nothing I've listed above sounds like a big deal to you, then you might want to give it a try (for obvious reasons, I can't vouch for any late-game or ending content), but for the overwhelming majority of players, this is just going to make you miserably frustrated.

Experience: Played this in closed beta, and open beta, pre-order, pay to play for a month and got tired of poor world pvp mechanics and quit. It went free to play and I tried it out again much later and it was fun for kicking around in PvE and I leveled a few more toons to the cap level of 30. I have 3 level 30 Villains and 3 level 30 Heroes.
PvE: The grind to get into raiding is more than I have ever seen in an MMO and I have played a lot of them. Game mechanics for raids are very poor. You expect to be leveling a very active controller character and end up standing around with your thumb up your butt just handing out energy to the tanks and healer. The one big raiding guild that I had joined was full of "lifers" (people who had purchased a lifetime subscription to the game) and they added their own drama to the game to spice it up... I was banned for being "a potential spy"...
PvP: The PvP mechanics in the arenas are evolutionary, however severely unbalanced even more than other MMOs. Open World PvP is similar mechanics where there is a mirror world where everyone can PvP no matter your level. Level 30s often squish low level players for kicks.
Social: The game keeps coming out with new paid expansions, however the population continues to dwindle. I still have the game installed because I like the PvE fighting mechanics. It's fun to watch some of the combos and devastation in your wake. Hardly anyone reads the chat, and its near imposable to get into an active guild because most of them are dead.
Opinion: It's fun to tool around with a buddy, just don't expect to be able to play with your friends right away. The introduction to the game is roughly 15-30 mins long depending on your experience with the game. I still keep it installed just to pop in from time to time and beat down some mobs.

It's a shame it took as long as it did to port this, particularly for those that didn't enjoy this gem when it originally came out on the Nintendo Gamecube.  But it's here and is a very solid port.  The only minor issue is that it seems NVIDIA didn't create a profile for it, so for some, their PC will default to integrated graphics.  If the game runs slow, go to your control panel and make sure that the correct GPU is chosen.
This game came out during a really magical time, where the franchise was waning after RE 3: Nemesis.  Nintendo provided the revitalizing RE4, but went a step further by not only releasing the great, but not stellar RE: 0 prequel, porting RE2 and RE3, and most importantly, this excellent remake.  As a whole, that succeeded in introducing Nintendo's audience to the franchise, and also giving it a fresh start that both valued its roots and encouraged further progression.
This remake captures everything that made the original Playstation classic great while modernizing its look and presentation to frighten a new generation of players.  I love the way that each shot manages to provide thrills not only by what it shows you, but also with the style in which it shows you the scene.  Many scenes would be welcome in a terryfing horror film, and add a lot of immersion to the game.
