What's supposed to be a love letter to the FPS genre is instead an unabashedly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game that unironically embraces the worst FPS tropes. That's not a parody, that's just making a terrible game.
When the game first starts you're placed in what you assume is a parody of a low budget FPS game, like some russian made starseige:tribes.  It tricks you. You're having fun enough, Jumping around fast, shooting dumb enemies with simple weapons.  It's not terrible, and there's a little bit of humor to keep you going.  Then you change worlds to a WW2 game.  This is where the warning sirens went off. It's not like any WW2 FPS game. It's not wolfenstein, it's not call of duty, it certainly isn't medal of honor either.  Instead I'd have to compare it to a super linear city level from BF1942, where you're (almost) forced to clear out  building after copypasted building of nazi snipers. There's about one joke in this level.  The WW2 fps genre has so many things you could be parodying and pointing fun at, hell, where's the d-day invasion where you're charging the beach? Instead, like I mentioned earlier you just go through bland city blocks clearing out buildings so aimbotting snipers (with no tracers)  don't murder you. It wasn't fun. It wasn't challenging. It was just awful.
I couldn't make it much farther because I realized that the game wasn't going to improve. You get more guns, but none of them are interesting at all.   Did the developers actually play quake or UT?  There's no silly UI changes between levels, there's not even a BLOOD ALL OVER WHEN YOU GET SHOT SO REALISTIC joke in there.  Instead inbetween levels occasionally you might find an ancient image macro that you might chuckle at (or most likely want to facepalm).
There are a few good jokes in the game, and the protoganist is extremely scottish, but it's just such a bad GAME that none of it is worth slogging through.

The short: While the core ideas are great, the uninteresting and uninspired environments, terrible gunplay which never improves, ridiculously accurate and frustrating omniscient AI, and lousy jumping puzzles in a game that is incompetent at platforming, all add up to a tedious and frustrating game experience.
The long:
I really, really wanted to like this game.  The idea of going on a journey through the history of gaming
a game is great and one of the reasons I loved the first 3/4 of Evoland, before it became victim itself to the genre characteristics it strove to make fun of (RPGs).  This romp-through-gaming-history is what also drew me to Bedlam.  Here however, the genres being mocked are early FPS games, which I thought for certain had to be less tedious than the latter parts of Evoland when it reduced down to a grindy RPG.  However, the great premise, witty humor and writing in the early parts of the game, and even the Scottish female protagonist could not save Bedlam devolving into yet another exercise in tedium.
The graphics and gunplay in the early part of the game is very basic, but the humor of the situation and the voice exchanges between the protagonist and other game characters were enough to keep me amused and interested to see where things would go.  However, after trudging through the levels of this first 'FPS universe', it quickly became apparent that I would have to struggle through the tedious combat and uninspired game environments for longer than I would have liked.
The second game world that is explored in Bedlam seems even less interesting than the first. Lots of buildings and streets full of nothing but empty cloned rooms and textures.  The only thing really occupying this world is the AI opponents - which themselves are also boring and repetitive.
Speaking of AI, let me just say this.  At all times, as long as you are within a certain radius of the enemies, they will know exactly where you are, even if that happens to be up 3 flights of stairs or behind cover.  They are also incredible marksmen and will never miss a target if it stands still for even a split second.  This grew annoying very quickly, and while I kept hope that this game logic was just a way to mock early AI systems, nothing in Bedlam's core game behavior ever changed.  Things actually get progressively worse as the enemies gain access to better weapons.
Oh and about those weapons!  Alright, don't let anyone tell you there is no such thing as having
many weapons.  This game proves that, beyond a doubt, you should not have access to every weapon you've come across at any point in time.  Not only is it terribly difficult to choose a weapon in later stages of Bedlam due to the overwhelming number you have (especially using a mouse wheel), it is also terribly confusing as to which weapons are more or less powerful than one another.  The developers could have easily remedied this situation by restricting access to weapons that are available on any given game 'universe', or at least removing ones that are similar in power to one another.
And now back to the game universes..  I wish I could say that the game worlds that Bedlam visits improve in design, or that the FPS gameplay itself improves, but that would be a lie.  Okay, the one 'low gravity' Unreal-Tournament-inspired level was a bit of fun to play, and actually quite hilarious as the voices of angry teens mocked or reacted to my actions. I'd also give props to the 3D PacMan-inspired level if it was actually any fun to play, but it and the Space Invaders level just feel like early unfinished prototypes that were shoehorned in and wind up feeling just like filler.  Luckily those two non-canon (FPS-wise) levels are over rather quickly.
The game world that annoyed me the most would probably have to be the 'void' that lay outside of all the game universes you visit.  Its this weird fractured landscape that introduces platform jumping puzzles, and really shines a light on just how bad such a thing is inside an FPS game.  Sure, there are probably one or two first person games that do this relatively well, but they are the exceptions to a rule.  However, Bedlam goes one step further here by introducing a delay between the button-press and the actual jump.  Yes, the character actually takes one extra step before jumping, which meant a lot of falling off obstacles to my death. It wouldn't be so bad if this was done only once or twice in the game, or it didn't reset to the beginning of the level, but unfortunately this mechanic is used and reused and becomes a major problem especially on the final levels.  Learn to save often if you find yourself braving these areas of the game!
Alas, there's not much saving grace for Bedlam.  It has a fun concept. It has good writing and humor in early parts of the game. It has a fairly decent voice actress. And it has one fun level. That's it. Terrible gunplay, AI, level design, and yes jumping puzzles all hamper the experience and make it an overly tedious and frustrating game to play. I'd suggest saving your money or buying this at a discount.

For my full review, click here;
The further I got in the game, the higher my frustrations got. Bedlam fails to create the atmosphere of retro shooters or to even properly analyse 90’s FPSs. The experience hides its own flaws behind the guise of being a caricature. Nothing in this game feels modern, and the badly designed levels and gameplay would’ve been considered poor back in the days of Half-Life. The storyline is absolutely structureless, and features one of the worst endings I’ve ever seen in a game. The actors sound bored, the environments feel lazy and there’s very little to bring you back when this ‘homage’ is done. I wouldn’t recommend this game to even hardcore fans of the genre.
There’s a decent enough setup within the game’s world. In Bedlam you work for a company that has designed a machine that can import personalities into digital environments, including video games. Your faithful employer decides you’d be best suited entering the fictional world of “Starfire,” an early 90’s FPS game from your youth. These points are the full extent of the story. Sure, you’ll pick up some emails throughout the game, explaining your love of the “Starfire” franchise, but it doesn’t contribute in any way. The story might be one of the most offensively simple I’ve seen in the past year.
Characters are introduced and are either completely thrown away, built up into nothing, or are clearly the villain; one that turns by their second appearance. You jump from one bad gameplay experience to the next, waiting for Bedlam to evolve or add new elements; but it never does. You’ll travel through a collection of retro shooters in an attempt to escape. Its final level is one of the longest and worst paced finales I’ve ever spent two hours slogging through and ends with quite possibly the laziest boss fight I’ve ever played. I don’t want to spoil anything, but it doesn’t attack you, it doesn’t move, and it requires you to bounce on a jump pad over and over in order to get a shot in on it. Then, the game wipes its hands, leaving you without answers or memories of enjoyment in one of the most unsatisfying endings I ever slammed my keyboard over.
I was really looking forward to playing this game too, because at least on paper the premise seems to work. Evoland 2 did a great job of taking a ton of different tropes and elements from entries in it’s genre, and I really enjoyed that experience despite its flaws. This game however just doesn’t bend these aspects into anything engaging, and ends up leaving the experience feeling as dated as it’s subject. Jumping from space stations on an alien planet to a World War 2 shooter sounds like a winner. It gets even more bizarre when you visit some 2D arcade shooters and even an RTS board with a giant hovering mouse cursor above you. It’s all so delightfully self-aware and inventive. The reason it doesn’t work however is because they didn’t throw any new ingredients into the pot, and it leaves the whole experience feeling repetitive and boring.
You’d think that with so little attention spent on the story, you might actually get some love from the retro gameplay. It was nice to go back to a non-regenerating health bar, but there’s a reason the genre has evolved. Like Duke Nukem Forever, it does nothing to modernize or even make the experience feel smoothed out in anyway. If it was the intention of the designers to recreate the frustration of unintuitive controls, broken assets and game breaking bugs, well congratulations; you nailed it. Having my gun suddenly stop working in a middle of a firefight threw me into a fit I haven’t experience since I was five years old.
The game does feature a large assortment of guns and weapons that you pick up from various points in the game. This does provide moments of bliss when you take a flame sword and shoot fireballs at miniature tanks, or shoot a rocket at spooky scary skeletons. It’s interesting having such a wide assortment, but sadly not all of the guns have their advantages, and some will get forgotten when you get a better version later in the game. As I mentioned earlier, if the guns work. And even if they do, you’ll find moments where you’ve laid five shots into an enemy’s chest, only for them to vaporize before connecting.
Art design is all over the place. All the elements feel purchased, like a hodgepodge of different styles and intent. The environments are barren, and lacking diversity outside of the same six assets. This is one area where I could almost forgive the lack of polish, as amassing a ton of components for a 10 minute section would be overkill, but the game does a bad job of hiding its small library.
Sound design matches the relic-like qualities of everything else. Music is bland and forgettable. The sound effects are average, and aren’t mixed very well. Probably the most grievous oversight however, is that everyone speaks with a heavy accent through fuzzy and digitized filters. It makes sense, given that many of the characters are off-screen in the distant land of “Liberty City” and “Saints Row”, but I can’t make out anything they’re saying over the static. This forced me to read the entirety of the game’s dialogue, and the constant yammering of actors who have no idea what ‘inflection’ means. The performances are simply atrocious.
For “parody” to work, there has to have a clear target and its own sense of enjoyment. If it doesn’t, your take on the subject will come across as a cash-in over an entertaining effort. Nothing feels like there was any effort put into it; to engage the player with questions about why games like Heretic worked. If you want to side with the idea that these faults were intended, to match the subject- be my guest. Me personally, I see it as convenient as writing a movie set from the visual perspective of a blind person. You can call it clever- I’ll call it a radio drama with a movie’s ticket price.

Well, first of all I've got 650+ hours on the game, so I'm pretty experienced to say the least, giving me the right to give an honest review.
This game is somewhat minecraft based, having to craft a majority of items. While also interacting with other players in order to trade goods, or recieve them. There is an ingame currency, however it can also be earnt, and with the right knowledge, you can earn it easily with a marketing eye. For instance, I have a friend who has NEVER brought cubits (ingame currency), and yet always seems to have more than me; Of which, I buy the cubits.
- With that said, I have sent plenty of reports in. They are answered fairy fast, usually in less than 2 days depending on how busy they are with tickets.
- A lot of the players are friendly, willing to help newbies settle in, and even build if necessary. I personally love to help new players, and will donate them a few hats, and wings depending on how many I have in stock/and or spare. I'll ask if they need any help, and try my best to fill in that request. Many other players put themselves out there to do the same.
- There are plenty of events that take place within the game, although there is a forum to keep up to date with this, as well as a facebook page, ect. Easter, Halloween, and Christmas are what I've seen so far. It's nice to know that the devs go out of there way to make it just     that much more interesting. Some of the events include free /limited/ hats, if you're lucky enough to catch the person giving them.

This game is AWESOME.
Ok, before I delve into any more detail, this game is NOT A MINECRAFT RIPOFF. There are a lot of people that are trying to capitallize on Minecraft's success(Believe me, I've seen my fair share on iOS and Android), but this is not one of them. This game's relation to Minecraft(Hereon referred to as MC) is like Unturned's relation to MC: Possibly inspired and similar with blocks and vector-based graphics. JUST BECAUSE A GAME HAS THOSE THINGS DOESN'T MEAN THAT IT IS A MC RIPOFF.
Now that I've got that out of the way, here is my opinion.
This game is like the Mario game series had a child with Minecraft, with Terraria as the godfather, with some awesome F2P buisiness strategy thrown in. It has a focus on platforming and building alike. Now, the F2P buisiness strategy. It is a fantastic model, where you can earn the in-game currency named Cubits through several methods. One, of course, is getting them with real money. Cubits(Often abbriviated to C or c, and will be referred to as CB from hereon) will also occasionally pop up when breaking a block. You can also earn them by doing quests or selling things. Yes, this game has a alive and THRIVING player economy. You can obtain blocks one of 3 ways: Mining them in the mines sprinkled generously around the HUUUUUGE map, buying them with CB(You can buy pretty much every block in the game in the store, as well as a few exclusive blocks) or buying them from another player. You can also complete offers on mobile to get CB. "Wait, what!?!?", I hear you asking. Why yes, the game is also availible on iOS and Android as well. The best part is that you can be playing on the computer, have to go on a trip somwhere, and you can pick up and play the game from where you left off on the computer. That is the icing on the dessert known as the Churpumple: A pie inside of a cake that is a dessert that is sometimes made in my family, but that's beside the point. Refer to the simple chart below for a TL;DR version and my dislikes:
YEAH!:
-Awesome focus on platforming and building
-Epic, thriving in-game economy
-Many ways to earn in-game currency
-Only 1 currency, no gems or tickets or super coins or anything like that
-SOOO fun to play
-You can play on iOS and Android from where you left off on the computer
UGH!
-You have to buy sentries to keep your rooms(Mini-realms that can be put in your realm) safe
-Getting blocks can be really time-consuming
-Hollas, game-wide broadcasts made by players, can be really annoying
-Quests can be as simple as mining 16 blocks of sand or as hard as doing hard parkour
-You need perks to do basically anything in this game, which means you'll have to pick between emotes appearing on your person's face, be able to have 1 more row of items in your inventory without your person slowing to a crawl, or the abillity to use a saw to craft
-Realms decay over time and dissapear(They get put directly back into your inventory though. (Thanks for pointing that out, BJDware!))
VERDICT:
10.1/10
Very good in-game purchase system, not forcing you to pay to win. There isn't a premium membership that costs 10 bucks per month or anything, so it's awesome. Thriving in-game community and economy. Also, may I throw in that you can harvest liquids without any machines and liquids don't flow?(Not saying I WANT to have machines to harvest liquid, but it is kinda wierd)
Decision: Take all of this and put it DIRECTLY into my Steam account.

This game is fun at first, then it gets repetitive after 5-6 hours and in late game it gets annoying and poorly balanced.
To those who are saying that this game needs a pause: no, having no pause IS THE CHALLENGE of this game, it's the key feature. The problems are the interface, controls, difficulty curve and permadeath.
The core gameplay loop is solid and fun but the game needs more polish. It's like FTL with no pause, but with little replayability, and where permadeath means you pretty much lose all your progress and have to go back to grinding, doing the same old missions over and over again. Maybe a better comparison would be Cook, Serve Delicious but with almost no keyboard controls and permadeath (this sounds like a terrible game, but actually Bomber Crew isn't that terrible). Unlike in FTL, this could mean losing 10 hours of progress. It desperately needs normal and ironman difficulty levels separated.
The interface leaves much to be desired. It's a fast-paced game where your success is dependent on your reflexes and speed, yet the interface does a very poor job at providing you information in a way that would let you see what is happening exactly in a split second. Are there any planes attacking you that you haven't tagged yet? Good luck figuring it out, the game doesn't tell you. You can look at the radar and see if all the red circles in the air correspond to all the green dots on the radar, but good luck doing that when you're surrounded by 15 jets.
Want to know if the hazard ahead that you spotted is a radar station or a flak? Well just fly in the middle of it and find out since mr. developer cound't be bothered to create separate hazard icons for these two.
Is the fuel leaking? Well, I sure hope you didn't miss that one 2-second notification from one of your guys in the middle of the fight. It would be too hard to create some icon on the side permanently flashing if you have a fuel leak, wouldn't it?. And you know that a developer is not good with interfaces when the "exit to main menu" botton is located in "options" tab.
The interface as it is now would be good enough for a game with pause, but for this game, a game that's fast-paced and has no pause, the interface is inadequate.
The controls are not good enough for this kind of game. You need to spam your crew's abilities in the toughest moment, yet there are no keyboard shortcuts to activate the abilities, you have to do everything with your mouse. Why? There's no "go back to your station" button. Why? Tagging mode button is a toggle, not press-and-hold and you can't change it. Why? No shortcut to execute a corkscrew or an emergency dive, which you normally do when under fire by 10 enemy planes and fighting fire in the cabin while trying to fix your electrical system all at the same time. There's no time to click these manuever buttons with your mouse, you NEED keyboard shortcuts. Or imagine: CTRL+A hotkey to send my gunner to go grab some ammo and return to the cannon. That would be so nice and so much better than the point-and-click kerfuffle you have to do with your mouse now.
My advice for the developer is to go play Cook, Serve, Delicious. It has a somewhat similar stressful real-time gameplay loop but with great controls. Check out how important great controls are for this kind of game. Bomber Crew feels super clunky  and frustrating to control in comparison.
The difficulty curve goes from just right in the beginning to a bit too easy in the midgame to unfairly hard in the final mission of chapter 7. This is where I gave up. After 30 or so completed missions you start to get bored doing the same stuff over and over again. Less grinding, better end-game balancing and more mission variety would help a lot.
Some minor complaints. So you've completed a mission and you're stuck looking at this stupid debriefing screen where it shows you XP and money gained. The debriefing takes good 30 seconds and you can't skip it or speed it up. You're stuck looking at the game slowly telling you that all of your crew made it back safely, 5 drammatic seconds for each crew member, even though you landed at your home base and there's no risk that some of them didn't return home. Why can't you just press spacebar and speed up this damn debriefing?
Some vests for your crew that you unlock in the midgame and better pretty much in all stats than the vests that you unlock later in the game. Why? Did the developer even check and compare their stats?
With some more polish, interface and control improvements and better balancing it could be a great game, but as it is now it seems as if the developer either rushed it or stopped caring some time before the release. Sad!
As for permadeath... Seriously, don't implement permdeath in a game that doesn't have randomly generated content. For comparison, let's look at two critically acclaimed indie games with permadeath that sold really well, RimWorld and FTL. In RimWorld, you lose even more hours of progress time than in this game but there it feels ok, because you know that a new game will be very different from the previous one. The life and death of your colony is always unique, never the same. In Bomber Crew, you die and you have to play through the same content all over again, nothing will be different, it will be the same crew gear, the same bomber upgrades, the same aces, the same missions on the same map all over again in the same sequence. It's not fun to do the exact same thing over and over again. You don't have randomly generated maps or randomly generated missions or randomly generated bomber parts. Permadeath just doesn't work here.
Unlike in FTL, you lose too much here when you die. In FTL you lose maybe one hour of progress, no big deal. Here you lose ten hours. Unlike in RimWorld, your next run will be 99% the same as the previous one. This is why so many people are saying that permadeath is so frustrating here. You really should implement non-permadeath mode or make it so that on death you lose only one crew member and one piece of bomber equipment or something like this.

If anything should be a commandment of game design, it should be that innovation should never be at the cost of its execution. Unfortunately, The Fall commits this sin almost to the detriment of sacrificing whatever good ideas are left. Something derivative that works will always last longer than something different for the sake of being different to a fault.
Despite a lukewarm reception of as a stand-alone product, the upcoming sequel shows manly combat criticisms have been redeemed, but the sequel should also address its non-combat elements. Alone, it slows down the pacing more than a Catholic wedding; together, the marriage of gameplay and narrative suffers being too traditional.

If the introduction wasn’t as obvious about the themes of The Fall, the game explores various secular and Judeo-Christian allegories transforming the fall of mankind by the capacity of its free-will into the conflict of artificial intelligence governed by its Three Laws of Robotics malfunctioning because of the loopholes resulting in defections. The number of allegorical tools used is nothing the game tries to hide. The intro begins with a body falling from the stars; the first achievement references Plato’s allegory of the cave as you leave the tutorial area; and the amount of Christ-like figures and their usage of blood throughout would make J.D. Salinger blush.  These aspects showcase how much attention to detail was put into the game’s narrative to humanize the conflict of A.R.I.D. to be believable.
However, it’s not the narrative that concern me as much as there being too many game mechanics for the scope of this game. The Fall attempts to blend side-scrolling action and stealth mechanics with the classic adventure-game puzzles when these aspects are all lacking. Stealth basically boils down to holding E to wait for the enemy to turn around for an instant kill. Action boils down to shooting as many headshots with an awful aiming reticle that shifts the screen if you turn around, and when crouched your reticle is always higher than a crouched enemy. Puzzles utilize a janky interface where you must move the reticle on the selected area, hold the mouse button and the interface menu button before you can select the interaction. One area of faults, as a result, bleeds to the others that it creates an inconsistent, diluted experience of its potential.
Even when you strip away the mechanical issues, the lack of focus hampers its ability to communicate the gameplay in tandem with the narrative. For starters, the choice of stealth/action is moot because there is nothing to make the player decide upon using force or pacifism. Puzzles, while perhaps the best at utilizing the allegories for gameplay, are neutered from being more effective because these extra features take them out of focus. They also are not well-made as they suffer too much moon-logic to make solving them not feel convoluted. All of these suggestions could be beneficial in not only making the player more involved with the story but also at communicating the deeper ideas inside the game.
To describe the matter more clearly, the solution of having your cake and eating it too is not to demand for more cakes to fill the void but to take smaller portions to better savor it. As an example of how to utilize a single mechanic for philosophical discussion, The Swapper centers the game around a tool that lets the host swap souls with a cloned body as well as with other hosts, willingly or not. The result of the constant body-swapping mechanic with the puzzles not only emphasizes the psychological horror such a device would possess but also suspends the disbelief of the player from plot-holes and the space-station’s layout. The repetition of this idea cements its believability through playing the game, and as a result the narrative built around that core idea is magnified even to the most clueless of audiences on philosophy.

What is uncommon in my reviews is to follow-up a story-section with another one, but having illustrated my complaints with the gameplay of The Fall previously the only thing left to discuss are the problems with the model, namely its episodic/trilogy design. At worst, these types of narrative designs can leave players feeling apathetic while they wait for the next chapter for a story that feels complete. At best, the storyline can accommodate the design of a trilogy by making each section possess a beginning, middle and end with enough to satisfy the player for the continuation of a larger storyline. The waiting time between episodes depends on the intended schedule of release as well as the amount and quality of content with each release, and it is this aspect that I think is the issue with The Fall’s narrative.
Part 1 of The Fall tells the complete story of A.R.I.D’s decent into becoming an unbound AI through her mission to save her pilot inside her armor. The storyline centered around this conflict is the complete narrative whereas escaping the facility and planet that she landed on is the remaining part of the story left unfinished. In terms of choices, there is only one major choice at the end that may or may not impact future games, so in terms of content and replayability the storyline feels finished for right now whereas the potential choices and gameplay feel like they have only begun. Perhaps the first episode would be excusable if the development cycle wasn’t as long as it has taken to reach the second game.
Originally, Part 2 of the Fall was supposed to be released in 2016, but due to development related issues as well as the Nintendo Switch port priority, the game is now expected to release sometime in the third quarter of 2017. Even with the legitimate reason of prioritizing the port for a living console, I don’t think the wait was reasonable for an expected year-and-a-half development cycle. Due to the fact that the developers haven’t utilized an Early Access model, I can only hope they used that extra time to make something with a decent amount of content and/or replayability if we have to wait for a third game. Otherwise, I don’t think people will be patient enough for the conclusion in two years to three years of another wait.

As an avid supporter of early access games done right with reasonable deadlines for completion, buying into The Fall right now perhaps isn’t the best time to experience the game. When the sequel comes out, hopefully, in the late summer or the beginning of fall, then perhaps consider purchasing Part 1 once all the reviews are out if they react favorably to the sequel and once the developers have given players expectations of how long the third game will take to iron out for its release. I’m rather selective of unfinished products that I support in knowing that they may fail or bust that risks not only monetary value but also disappointment with more lasting consequences. In the case of The Fall, I hope the developers used what they learned from the first part’s shortcomings and continue to create a polished experience that will be as loved by the fans as much as the dedication these developers put into their project in sticking with their game through all trials of its tribulations.
In a closing manner that might equally confuse Christians as well as my secular friends and myself, I think it’s important to end this review with a few words about acknowledging the importance of integrity, especially with the amount of dishonest developers on Steam and the number of failed games that never get the chance to be completed due to conflicts in life.
“[…W]e also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not put us to shame […]” (Romans 5).

PROS

CONS
- Very unpolished and unresponsive movement and combat package, especially for a game that relies on combat for a number of sequences. Character feels like a tank.
- Controls in general are cumbersome - looking and interacting requires using the flashlight and pointing at something and then going through a menu to interact, so it's several buttons for something that's at the core of the game and that you have to do a thousand times.

Machinarium is one of those cute little Indie designs that, due to it's small team or low budget, has to pick up its boots and survive on its charm alone, and while concise and simplistic, it does that in spades. A sombre meander through a beautifully stylized, decaying robotic and alien world.
The reason Machinarium works so well is that it's very simple, what would normally be a flat flash game has been given life with tone, interaction, soundtrack and art style all marrying together to create a truly solid little game.
* The lack of dialogue and the fantastic sound and music, when placed together with the rustic, dystopian art really give the world a strong but still alien character to the world and make you want to explore and see more of it
* Little detailed works like the mini-games for hints add a fun layer of light wonder
* Genuinely none that take away from the game other than perhaps a lacklustre ending
Play time clocks in at 5 hours, and there are better indie titles out there for less than Machinarium, and with more replay value, of which Machinarium has very little, but at £7.49/8.49€/$9.99, it's still a reasonably priced and is a good buy when on sale.

TL DR: Morrowind is a masterpiece in world building. Combat is bad, and there are some really broken systems to be found and enemies you'll just mod out after first sight, but it still has an absolutely incredible world to explore.
The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is a first-person RPG developed by Bethesda. The third main title in the critically acclaimed Elder Scrolls series, it's a departure from both previous and following games in the series, having the smallest world in the series but also the most deep and interesting one.
Morrowind starts with a cutscene showing an ancient prophecy, and your character awaking on a boat. You're a prisoner arriving on Vvardenfell, an inner island to the continent of Morrowind, home to the dark elves of Tamriel. You start off by creating your character, choosing your race, appearance, birthsign and preferred attributes and skills. Afterwards, you're left with the mission to go see an Imperial agent at a somewhat nearby city, and that's it. A stranger in a strange land, you can go wherever you want to after this fairly short introduction.
Vvardenfell isn't huge in size, but the developers cheated for it to appear so. Your starting speed is very, very slow, and there's no fast travel. However, there are lots of lore-respecting means of travel to be used throughout; cities usually have cheap silt strider services which will take you to nearby cities instantly, for example. The game starts out pretty slow, with you having to do mostly fetch quests for a few factions. Luckily, as bad as fetch quests do sound, Vvardenfell is one of the best videogame locations I've had the pleasure to explore. It's a really alien island, featuring swamps, ashlands, sandstorms, giant mushrooms, some used as buildings, and the huge red mountain volcano at the center, blocked on all sides by a magical barrier to keep the evil lord Dagoth Ur from escaping it.
Once you get some levels on your character, exploration starts becoming much easier as you've got more money to travel, more speed, maybe a few teleportation spells.The main quest starts to open up as you deal with both the Great Houses of Vvardenfell and the nomadic Ashkhans who refuse Morrowind's Tribunal religion and believe in the return of the legendary lord Nerevar. Combat becomes slightly less of an affair in missing several times and finally hitting your enemy, though overall it's still bad, and the low point of the game, along with the Wikipedia-like conversations.
Tens of hours in, near the end of the game, you'll no longer be a stranger in Vvardenfell. Quest locations will still be pointed out by somewhat confusing directions, but they feel easier by then. You already know things like what the hell a foyada is, for example. You already know you way around this island, by feet or by magic, because by then if you do use magic you should already know how to levitate and walk on water, maybe even how to jump across long distances in one jump. The main story also reflects this in part, which is great!
What I'm saying is that Morrowind, by throwing you into a world and giving you the time to adapt, turns into into an inhabitant of sorts, who knows the nooks and crannies of a previously alien land. It's a masterpiece in world-building, though brought down a bit by simply bad combat. What is there more to say? Well, the music is great, and even though I'd usually associate such an alien setting to something other than Jeremy Soule epic fantasy stuff, it does fit.
Being a Bethesda Gamebryo game, Morrowind is, of course, highly moddable, though it doesn't have as may mods as later games in the series. This means you can change whatever you don't like about the game, including making combat slightly more actionRPG-like, removing cliff racers (an omnipresent menace in the roads of Morrowind, and an awful one), improving graphics, et cetera. I'd recommend MGE XE, Morrowind Code Patch, watercolor textures if you're into that sort of thing (they're the same as the main game but high-res), any mod to remove cliff racers, and the dark brotherhood delayer (so you don't get attacked by people with the 2nd best light armor in the game by level 1, either dying or completely unbalancing your economy.)
Overall Morrowind's amazing world makes the game very much worth your time, as you're not likely to see something like this anywhere else.

A bit of a first for me here, as I'm completely rewriting and reposting a Steam review from scratch, 'cause...reasons. Very GOOD reasons. And basically, I don't want the rather negative reception for my last review of this product to drag down the approval rating for this one.
In short: this port simply doesn't work for some people. MANY people. I used to be one of those people. Then I got myself a spanking new laptop about a year ago, and lo and behold: the game from 2002, itself a remake of a game from 1996, finally works! (Though granted, not the first time 'round. I'm suspecting that a recent NVIDIA or Windows update has now rendered it playable. On an expensive modern gaming laptop, no less!!)
For the sake of posterity, I'll post my old review in the Comments below, just so you can witness the rage myself and countless others have felt - still DO feel, to some extent - towards Capcom's absolutely appalling customer service policies. (Oh-oh! Probably ♥♥♥♥ed up this review's chances already, seeing what a bunch of butt-smooching apologists the average "loyal" Capcom fan appears to be. Go on, vote me down, you sycophantic bottom-dwellers.)
Anyway, onto my review of the 2015 HD remaster of the 2002 Gamecube remake of the game originally released on the Playstation 1 in 1996. (Still with me? Good. Be thankful I haven't even mentioned the Playstation 1 "Director's Cut" released in 1997. You're welcome.)
I adore this game. Beyond words. It is, simply put, the single most sentimental horror video game in all of history for me. Or at least...the 1996 version is. Though this remake is largely faithful, and mostly just improves on some of the shortcomings of the original, so...I guess I'm sentimental towards THIS, too. Though not quite as much. But you get the idea. The 1996 version is still the product I have the most sentiment towards, but I'm happy to pretend these two versions are the "same game". Which they're definitely not. Though they very nearly are, in a way; at least in MY head, and in my heart.
Rambling aside, this is a game - and version, particularly - which still holds up well in this day and age. Sure, the manipulative (yet oh-so-effective) fixed camera angles remain, but we now have the option to change to a control system which is a tad less "tank-like" than both the original PS1 and Gamecube versions (though still potentially confusing, by modern standards).
The closest thing we had to a genuinely terrifying and highly cinematic horror game before this was Alone in the Dark, and that was...even more clunky to control, and considerably less cinematic and thereby significantly less scary. I also played this before any Alone in the Dark games, so it still seems like "the original" scary horror game set in a spooky mansion...to me, at least.
Hey, ♥♥♥♥ it: did Alone in the Dark have any giant sharks in it? No. No, it didn't. Suck several fat, throbbing ♥♥♥♥♥, Alone in the Dark. Resident Evil got there first.
It's actually very hard to explain to people who "weren't there" how significant the original version of this game was when it came out. The mansion was a truly amazing thing to explore, its denizens a true nightmare to behold. I have not before, or since, experienced anything quite so simultaneously terrifying yet compellingly unputdownable in a video game. Many games have since come close...but none could ever replace the unique place that Resident Evil holds in my heart.
I love you, Resident Evil. I hate you, Capcom. I'm still not going to give this a perfect score, because of the troubles I know this ridiculously under-serviced port still causes for other people. The only warning I can give is: don't be surprised if it doesn't work on your computer, for no good reason whatsoever. A bit of a wonky recommendation I know, but it's regrettably the only one that I can give.
Verdict: 9/10 (10/10, minus one point for the fact that Capcom have no morals whatsoever, and couldn't give two frigs about who their products do or do not work for).

Clustertruck is a stylized game, where what you see is almost what you get.  It is a 3D extreme platformer where you jump on trucks and the floor is lava.  It executes well in the style, it's hilarious in its absurdity.  The physics however, just doesn't seem quite right.  Oftentimes when I missed a truck and restarted a stage, it felt like the game was working hard to keep me from succeeding.  Intertia is strong in this game, and hard to fight.  Normally this would be okay, but it is difficult to gauge exactly where you will land, because you don't have a shadow, and judging distance is extremely difficult here, vs other 3D games for some reason.  Add onto this that it is easy to tap walls or ceilings (also forcing you to restart the stage), and you will become familiar with the game over screen.  I managed to get through most of the game just fine, with deaths here and there.
The levels are short and restarting is easy, so even when the deaths (often) did not feel like I could reasonably succeed with the game's physics.  The last level though, whew.  A miserably long trek, where what you need to do to succeed wasn't clear, and where it is filled with walls, ceiling, and obstacles for you to hit.  I didn't finish the game, and I spent like an hour on the final level, it is an abomination that shows off the worst of the game.  Through most of the campaign I had the mindset of "this is cool, but I don't know if it is great."  At this point though I can confidently say that it is alright if you pay five bucks for it.  Fifteen dollars though is grotesquely overpriced.  It's fine, but it does still need work.

First Impression (Will change when game is done)
So far, I'm not seeing why this game got such immense hate. Sure it isn't the best game in the world, and it doesn't encapture that old Resident Evil feel, but let's be real for a minute. Fans of the series who kept on hoping that Resident Evil would re-encapture the horror of the original 3 are going to be sorely dissappointed. The series moved into a more action oriented genre with 4, becoming more action-oriented with each iteration after 4. So the fact that people are acting surprised that ORC was primarily action based need to get a reality check. Comparing this to any other Resident Evil will basically give you the worst impression of all. This was meant to be a completely stand alone title, giving a non-canon hypothetical scenario that takes place between 2 and 3, where you play as the bad guys basically.
As for the game itself, aside from the terrible friendly AI and GFWL, ORC has some good gameplay to be had. A linear shooter, where it becomes cover-based against humans, and turns into an all out slaughterhouse against zombies, it flips between the two surprisingly well. The story is pretty cheesy and feels a bit half♥♥♥♥♥ but again most of Resident Evil's story telling is not all that exceptional. They all feel like a cheap B movie became a longer than expected series, but never got past its B movie storytelling. But I do cherish that in Resident Evil and can enjoy the stupidity and silliness.
I wouldn't reccommend this game at full price right now, but it is definately worth 10 bucks, especially if you have someone to play with and can deal with GFWL.

REVIEW
The Fall is an intriguing adventure game. The stylized sillhouette graphics set a great eerie atmosphere. The Fall plays pretty much like a classic point and click but as a side scroller. There is a bit of combat, similar to the old Flashback or Blackthorne games, but most of the game is a classic scavenger hunt of puzzles - find the item, to get past the door. I got stuck a few times. I am not sure if the game is logically possible without consulting a walkthrough at times for some of the puzzles. But the story is intriguing enough and the ending is quite mysteriously satisfying for those who who enjoy a good mind bending twist. The Fall is actually the first part of a larger story. This is slightly disappointing as the story isn't concluded at the end of the game. But still worth a playthrough or two.

I wish more games were this length!) I'm super excited for part 2.

The Fall is a brilliant sidescrolling action-adventure about deviant AI.
The art design reminded me of Limbo (although it's actually a real 3D environment) and feels very atmospheric. The game manages to convey a completely desolate feeling. The support cast is written brilliantly, dialogues are intriguing and the entire setting as well as the main theme are unique in a way I haven't seen before in another game.
More than recommended, this is a philosophical and fun piece of art. Can't wait to play the second game.

Pros: beautiful scenery, genuinely intriguing story and world, a very cool take on perspective down to the menu level.  characters are great.
Cons: you will spend the vast majority of your time in this game running in circles, trying every possible permutation of using each item you have on everything you pass and shooting every bit of scenery because the puzzles are not well designed.
Honestly, it feels like a pretty inspired game, held back by a lack of play testing and funding.  The cliffhanger ending reeks of "we ran out of money on kickstarter #1, and now we need more in order to complete the original game".  Which is understandable and just what happens in some cases, but also doesn't leave a great taste in one's mouth.  That said, at least there was a solid product that was followed through to delivery.  Honestly, I hope the devs get backed by a larger company so they can take this game and produce it into a full, polished release.  It definitely hs some solid potential, but given that the vast majority of the 6hrs I spent on it was either afk or running around the same areas repeatedly trying to figure out what I missed, its more of a demo than a full story.
Other notes:  This isnt a combat-based game.  Don't expect it to be one.  Has no replay value, since the game appears to be 100% railroaded.  That said, if you miss the old-school style adventure games and the ridiculous puzzles that came along with them, this is for you.

I haven't played a lot of point-and-click games but I do know that Machinarium is overflowing with charm. The art style looks like it was sketched with colored pencils, the protagonist is a cute little robot that stores items in his belly, and the story is told through little cartoons in thought bubbles. The only reason I can't recommend this game is its difficulty. Perhaps it was intended for veteran point-and-click gamers but I found many of the puzzles to be difficult and confusing. Luckily, the developers decided to included hint for each level in the form of a cartoon bubble to help you understand what your primary goal is in each level. Unfortunately, most of the time I had no idea of how to get to that goal with whatever was placed before me in the level. The developers also included a walk-through for each level in the form of a book which you can unlock by playing a mini-game. The walk-through helps a lot but I found myself turning to its guidance for most of the levels (especially later in the game). It may have just been difficult for me but I don't want to continue playing a game where I constantly have to be taught how to play the game. That being said, you can tell that a lot of heart and soul went into this game. So if you're in to point-and-clicks, you might give this one a try.

I've played for a few hours now (it only says 0.8 hours due to my Steam going offline, trust me I spent far too much time playing this instead of applying for uni this afternoon) and have a few thoughts on the game:
Pros:
- Great, challenging gameplay, with good depth: it really does force you to think and prioritise without letting things get out of hand. The idea and development of crew roles, and skills, is especially good, and I love in particular the presence of a wireless op and navigator, which could have been very easily cut out of the game by the devs to make it easier to play at the cost of historical accuracy. Furthermore, how the game handles is pretty damn good and I'm not going to be too harsh on it, considering how difficult it would have been to translate the concept of a WW2 bomber crew into an actual game.
- Very cute, you do get quite attached to the crew
- Fantastic to see an attempt to introduce bombers, in a goofy yet occasionally brutal sort of way, into the World War 2 genre, rather than just another run and gun or a conventional real time strat game.
- Customisable crews to suit their roles and what you need them to do: You can kit your crew out in a lot of different ways which is great (plus they have actual names, different faces etc which is brilliant!)
Cons
- Getting shot down is brutal: you can lose your entire crew at times, with all their levels, skills etc. and have to start from scratch. Does make the later levels and missions extremely difficult with a brand new gunner or engineer, would recommend that the devs make losing members of your crew less impactful on how hard missions can be, as it can be unplayable (possibly solved by "borrowing" an experienced crew member from another bomber in your squadron, or if you do lose your entire crew, maybe take over another kitted out bomber in your unit, if the idea of squadrons were to be added (detailed further below))
- Variety of missions: The missions themselves do get repetitive, maybe thinking up scenarios, and adding a more fulfilling campaign with focus on the war itself (e.g. with each mission you advance a day/week through the war etc., or maybe every day you have the option to fly on one of the RAF's nightly bombings of Europe). Also, make more use of the medium and high altitudes!!!
- Depth to the game itself: At the end of the day, you're confined simply to your little bomber crew and your trusty Lancaster. While this is a major part of the game's charm, World War 2 is such a historically rich genre, and there are so many, many things that the devs could add to make you really feel like a part of this massive war effort:
-the option to join a variety of particular squadrons from the time, and intel on which German squadron/wing you are up against
-to move from one historical airfield to another, and to be able to see all the other major airfield in the country on some sort of map
-regular raids as part of your flight or your entire squadron, rather than just on your own most
of the time, and a roster of everyone in the squadron, consistently updated with those KIA or MIA
-a campaign that delves into the chronology of WW2 far more than it does currently
-decorations and awards
-More British bombers (if your crew were to be "reassigned" to another squadron using an aircraft other than the Lancaster) or even the option to fly as the American, Germans or Russians in their own campaign, and with their own bombers! I would definitely pay for DLC like that.
- A pause button: Whilst I myself am just fine with there being a no pause button (for me it really does add to the intensity and fun), I do understand the reviews that call for the addition of one (although I personally don't think it is as gamebreaking as some make it out to be); the intensity of the game during mid-air combat is pretty hard to handle.
Just my two cents, hope that the devs will read through these comments and really develop and finish off what is a very fun, very innovative and very promising game with, admittedly, issues that does impact its depth and consequently how much time people are willing to devote to it. Would recommend it though, it is only a few days old, pretty cheap all things considered and for a title that is part of what is a pretty underdeveloped feel, the gameplay is quite polished and enjoyable for a few hours.

I heartily recommend Bomber Crew; a time-management game of cute airmen risking life and limb to strike at the heart of the Nazi warmachine.
While the meta game is fairly thin, it offers up just enough levers to pull and upgrade decisions for them to matter: Should you purchase armored engines or lightweight ones? Prioritize crew survival over upgrading those guns?
Selecting bombing missions in a certain order can also pay off: you could take out the enemy's ammo dumps first to weaken their flak cannons in your next operation.
It's simple, but enough to keep me engaged.
When you take to the skies is when the rubber hits the proverbial road.
You'll find Bomber Crew a hectic game of quick prioritization & task assignment. You'll have to keep an eye out on the goings on outside the plane as well as inside the plane. You'll have gunners running around hauling ammo to their guns and your navigator on the wing putting out a fire, because your engineer is bleeding out in the back from a stray bullet.
It's intense!
And yet, I find the procedure based nature of the game very appealing and almost relaxing. A successful mission meant you stuck to the fundamental procedures of a bombing run. Keep to clear airspace so your navigator can plot a course. Keep your guns full of bullets, an eye on your fuel and the enemy fighter planes tagged.
The game is most often compared to FTL for it's ship-based combat where you command little guys to run around to different stations but that comparison isn't very apt. Bomber Crew isn't a great game for it's tactical depth the same way FTL is.
Bomber Crew is best defined in that moment that your engineer is attempting to repair the hydraulics systems because the bomb hatch won't open and your right wing just got ripped apart by an enemy ace. You have seconds to act.
Your eye the clouds in a faint hope that you could get above them in time. You hover over the emergency landing button  but remember your right landing wheel got blown off along with the wing.
With seconds left you order your boys and girls to grab their parachutes and jump. The pilot got shot grabbing his chute. You hope you brought enough supplies to see some of the others survive behind enemy lines. You could use these veterans for the next run.

The only real annoying aspect is that if your crew gets shot down and your bomber destroyed, you'll have to start basically from scratch... which can be avoided by exiting the game if things start going west... Still, I have had heaps of fun with this game, and it has much room for expansion and DLCs.

This game works so much better when it's flaunting its over-the-top absurdity.  Some worlds have that, others do not.  The other worlds try so very hard to be a skillful speedrunning course filled with obstacles and other things you have to adapt to, but the nature of the random paths of the trucks just make it very frustrating, in the bad way.  I never felt a sense of accomplishment for beating a difficult level, I was just glad that the trucks just so happened to be in the right spot for me to jump on and that the un-fun part was out of the way, as was the case with the entire Ancient, Winter, and Steampunk worlds.
On the other hand, most of the levels involved in Sci-Fi for example exploited just what crazy things you could do while still being a moderate challenge.  Instead of bunnyhopping around random map geometry that will kill you and hoping you don't slip or your truck suddenly explodes, you're being launched airborne for 8 seconds at a time to soar over vast chasms, and climbing up a saturated, falling stream of trucks over an abyss in attempts to survive until the goal.  The Laser world was pretty solid because its gimmicks and traps were more obvious and predictable, so I could actually play around it and not just have a bad hand dealt to me more often than not.
It's cute and fun for a while.  I'm not sure I'd pay full price for it, but the time I spent with it from getting it discounted in a humble bundle was worth it.

Bedlam is a PC FPS with lower-than-modern visuals but a really good reason for it - its story revolves around a person being stuck in cyberspace, going through games trying to escape.  So there are sequences reminiscent of Quake 2, Day of Defeat, RTS games, even Pac-Man and other arcade games.  All in all it makes for a fun game where the graphics don't matter too much. And the story is forcefully told by your character, who really pushes the accent.  It's tongue in cheek and has way more cursing than it really seems to need, but for the most part it does a good job mixing the worlds and experiences well.  Except the last level, which feels like it's half as long as the rest of the game combined, and really could have been shortened significantly without impacting the game.  But that's a minor quibble - if you enjoy old school FPS games, this is a nice diversion.  And be on the lookout for the forthcoming book that shares the world, also called Bedlam.

Original Review:
The art and music are nice, but it is SUPER easy for a point & click adventure/puzzle game. Unfortunately I can't recommend it based on this.
Addition as of 12/5/2015:
To elaborate, Machinarium does not play to the genre's strengths. It does not make many meaningful strides to get you to soak in its lustrous environments. The environments are... not quite lustrous either, which contributes to this disengagement. It needed to utilize the environments way more for it to be considered a really great point and click adventure game. Just see The Secret of Monkey Island: that game makes such excellent use of its environments, backgrounds, and setting, that it's no wonder why it's lauded as one of the BEST point and click adventure games ever made. Machinarium, on the other hand, is very amateur and did not make nearly as great an effort in immersing you within the game world.

Witcher 1 is truly a masterpiece. I was a bit put-off by the top-down perspective as I much prefer to play an RPG in third or first person. But I can confidently say the experience was not brought down whatsoever by that. I long to play Witcher 3 and have yet to, so I cannot compare it to it's latest entry, but then again it is somewhat unique because of it's gameplay.
It features a wonderfully crafted story that is indepth and enjoyable. I found the romance to be wonderfully implemented, something I had never encountered in an RPG before. It has been awhile since I played the game but I cannot think of any sidequest I didn't enjoy as they were all carefully crafted and sometimes challenging. Although certain potions could make the fights hyper simple, such as the last boss fight where I downed a potion to make me immune to knockdowns. The developers are also skilled at writing a story with two, three, or even more issues going on at once. Yet they are all so deftly orchestrated, that you can follow and pay attention happily to them all at once. Many stories and issues cross over eachother adding even greater depth and a higher level of enjoyment to the game.
While it is not a true open-world game like it's latest franchise entry, there is plenty of wandering and exploring to be done. The combat is fluid, I think I poorly understood it when I first played but I got through without much trouble. The characters are all intriguing and memorable. I remember most all of them by personality and role even if not by name.
Lastly it really kicks off the story and sets the mood for the rest of the franchise. I definitely would recommend giving Witcher 1 a try if you ever get the chance, and I hear a mod is now underway for W3 that is W1's story, told through the new game engine and third person perspective.

Side-scrolling Sci-fi game with stealth elements, shooter mechanics, and narrative themes. It had a lot of potential to be really good: The environment is dark and tense complementing the tense scenario that the protagonist finds itself in, the characters seem well created with great voice acting, and the story is compelling and brings up interesting topics, like the evolution of interaction between computers and humans and the way that an Artificial Intelligence manages/manipulates its protocols and directives to complete its task.
Despite this praise, the game's action sequences and gun fights are subpar. The shooting sequences of the game rely heavily upon hiding behind cover, waiting for the enemy to fire a few shots, and then popping it in the head. This interaction between enemies and yourself is not skillbased: waiting is not a difficult thing to do.
These combat areas are further hampered by clunky aiming mechanics: poor mouse aiming control (with no option to adjust sensitivity) limits your ability to aim, meaning that a controller is almost required to play; additionally, you cannot look straight up when you need to. And since this mechanical design carries over to pointing your flashlight and interacting with the environment, the clunky aiming controls follow you throughout the game, leaving most of the game dark and difficult to play.
The Fall has good production quality put into its story, character, and environment design. But the end result of boring combat sequences and clunky controls leaves leaves the player literally in the dark fighting with the controls more than with the threats. Because of this, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game.

I played oblivion and skyrim before this and it took a while to get used to Morrowind. After playing through Morrowind with a few mods installed I can truthfully say this is one of the best elder scrolls games ever. This game is worth it

9.5/10
Absolutely recommend. Morrowind is a unique, one of a kind game that is unlike any other. Taking a lot of freedom from Arena and Daggerfall before it, Morrowind is an open-world RPG game with no hand-holding and freeform leveling.
Unlike Oblivion and titles after it, Morrowind relys a lot of old-school dice rolling and a lot of reading. Be prepared to be lost and fear the world for the first few hours but give it a chance and it quickly becomes an engrossing, engaging land filled with hundreds of quests and things to do.
Do not enter Morrowind if you have not read or experienced any idea of how the game works. It is NOT your typical action/adventure RPG. Morrowind is somewhat in it's own gaming genre kinda like a mix between Oblivion/Skyrim but playing with a D&D style mechanic running in the background. There are no quest markers. Everything must be either found with directions, using clues and journals, etc. Enemies do not typically scale. Locations are unique to levels, early end games items can be found with time and skill, etc. You can and more than likely will become a GOD after countless hours of playtime although this requires actually playing and working for it.
Morrowind is my personal favorite Elder Scrolls title. No nostalgia here either as Oblivion was my first followed by Skyrim. A better magic system featuring spells and schools of magick either nerfed or completely removed from later games. More types of weapons like spears, short katanas, crossbows, throwing stars/knives, etc. Each dungeon being handcrafted (although typically they looks similar, they each tend to play their own story in the background), more fleshed out guilds, the ability to wear clothing under armor and seperate left/right pieces. Just too much to list.
I paid $14.99 USD for the Game of The Year Edition. Considering the amount of content and the current going price for a physical copy, a well spent purchase. The Steam Edition runs beautifuly and is also capable of modding. The same Morrowind as before, nothing new, nothing different.
*TIP!* To play Morrowind in 1080p HD or higher (it looks so much better and keeps the vanilla textures), download 'Morrowind FPS Optimizer' and place it inside the Morrowind folder. Run it and click 'change Morrowind registry settings' then set to your liking. Enjoy!

Being a massive Resident Evil fan, I had high expectations for this game, but I didn't expect how good it would actually be.
For those who don't know, REMaster is a fresher, more detailed version of the Gamecube release, which was a remake of the one and only, Resident Evil 1, which was, in it's time, one of the most popular games on the Playstation One. REMaster stays true to it's former self but at the same time, looks and plays like a totally new game.
Most of the puzzles have been revamped, so much that I found myself searching the forums for solutions. I expected to whiz through this game as I thought my knowledge of Resident Evil 1 would carry me through, this was true in only a couple of occassions.
The game itself is very well built, it ran very well on my laptop (GTX 950m, i5 2.8 GHz, 8GB RAM) and only crashed once. It has full 1080p support, and gives the player the option to use the classic '4:3 ratio) that was utilised in the Gamecube version.
The only complaint I have with the game is that the pre-rendered environment backgrounds look outdated, these were not updated unlike the game's textures.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who is brave enough to play it in it's entirety ;)

SPORE is a game I adored in college.
Yes, that was 8 years ago.
There are games I play that are much, much older than 8 years that I still can play to this day and find no faults with.
Spore is not one of them.
At the time this game came out, it felt like an overambitious mess- but dammit, it was MY overambitious mess.  I loved it, and I played it obsessively between classes.
I bought it a few weeks ago for 5$.  I wish I had spent that somewhere else.
This game doesn't hold up.  The creature creator is fun- it's interesting to see the horrible, horrible monsters you create stumble around awkwardly in the creature phase.
The Tribal phase is where it starts to hurt to remember this game.  It's awful, antiquated, and at it's core- offensively simple.
Then, you get to the planet-wide "City" phase, which is equally frustrating.  Pacifist/Religious route, even on the easiest setting, was painfully hard to micromanage due to the lack of intuitive controls- controls that are more than fine in RTS games that they were clearly trying to emulate.
The game has charm- it has a LOT of charm.  Your creatures coo and chirp and growl and jiggle awkwardly in their little speechbubbles, and the level of customization was truly mindblowing several years ago.
Sadly, it doesn't hold up.  It breaks my heart that I came back to this game with so much nostalgia, only to find that all the negative reviews back when it came out were sadly accurate.  This game isn't fun anymore- I had fun with it when it came out, but it's not worth your time.  Not even for five bucks, sadly.

Great game so far despite its faults, and trust me there are faults. It looks great, sounds pretty good (although the characters speak in a cute little gibberish language that sounds suspiciously like Cantonese at times), and overall is just a great idea: real-time FTL in a WW2 bomber.
Where it falls short is the lack of variation. There is only one bomber and although you can upgrade every part of it in multiple ways, I'd really like to have seen the option of fielding maybe a smaller, more fragile and more agile fighter-bomber, maybe, or a colossal flying fortress or something. The upgrades themselves all have visual effects which is cool but it's all pretty standard "Faster Engine", "Thicker Armour" or "Bigger Gun". This can all be fixed via DLC and if it's priced wisely I don't think anyone would object to that.
The only big, fundamental problem with the game though isn't the difficulty, it's the altitude. You can go between High, Medium or Low altitude, but literally everything happens at Low altitude. Even a high-level Navigator can't navigate properly at Medium or High altitude, so you'll be lost and waste fuel if you spend time doing anything aside from flying a couple hundred feet above the deck - and in a game where a big part of it is catastrophic fires that draw your pilot from his station or engines becoming damaged and needing daring mid-air repairs, being that low sucks because the second anything bad happens you'll smash into the ground and your entire crew is hosed. It feels good on the rare mission where you can fly at Medium or High altitude - remember, gearing up your characters is a mechanic in this game, so preparing them for high altitude and low temperatures is a thing - dive down to Low, drop a perfectly placed bomb, and blaze your way back across the Channel while fighting off those damn Krauts the whole way. It feels
. But the game is designed in such a way that that simply isn't going to work - either you'll run out of fuel blindly groping your way around at High/Medium altitude, or will crash because some BS ace who sets everything his guns hit on fire will knock your engines out and you'll plow into terra firma before you have a chance to do anything because you're only like seventy feet up.
All that said, though? It's fun, it's worth the ten bucks I paid for it, and it doesn't have problems so big that it'll ruin the game. Try it out at least.

Clustertruck is a floor-is-lava type game.  You run toward the goal by jumping on the top of trucks.  Hitting walls or the ground forces you to start over.  There are 90 levels spread across 9 worlds, each with their own theme.  You start in the desert, move to ice, then get surrounded by lasers, transported to medieval times, etc.  The game also features a level editor so you can play hundreds more levels all created by the player community.
There are also two game modes: you can play through the levels with or without special abilities.  The abilities allow you to have one special movement capability and one utility.  Movement specials include teleportation, grapple hook, double jump, and others.  Utilities include slowing time, throwing down your own portable truck, flipping trucks, and an interesting mod called SUPERTRUCK.  Yes, SUPERTRUCK is exactly what you'd expect: trucks only move when you move.  It's awesome!
One point may make or break this game for most players.  The trucks do not follow consistent paths between runs.  They do follow mostly the same path, but sometimes they will move slightly left or right of previous attempts.  With obstacles on the course, this may mean some trucks get destroyed in one run but not in another.  This means you will be unable to memorize a course and unable to try and beat specific replays, but I don't think it is really that much of an issue.  The differences are so slight that it really doesn't matter; your muscle memory and quick reflexes will still enable you to learn and complete a level.
I really appreciate that the game doesn't waste your time in menus between levels or retries.  If you fail, you merely press a single button to get back onto a truck.  If you succeed, it's again just a single mouse click to continue the game.  Considering you will be restarting a lot, this is a smart design choice.
The game is challenging, but it's also a lot of fun.  The unique aspects of each world ensure you're plays don't feel like you're repeating the same courses over and over again.  Plus, adding abilities into the mix gives you new ways to complete every level.  I found myself returning to Clustertruck frequently, always ready to attempt the next few levels.  The design of the game easily allows for play sessions lasting anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours.  If difficult platforming games are your thing, Clustertruck is definitely for you!

Now that I've said that, I can explain how fun HALF of this game is.
Cell stage is a sort of fun indtroductory mini-game more than a full stage. Just imagine alll those games where you eat stuff to get bigger, then eat creatures smaller than you. That's cell stage.
The Creature stage is the best part, or maybe second best part, of the game for me. I loved murdering and consuming all of my neighbours and using their limbs to find new parts to evolve. One annoyance, sometimes I couldn't tell where my species had gone when they migrated.
Tribal stage is meh. It's kinda fun at the start, until everyone else starts dominating you and you get your food stolen every ten seconds.
City stage is boring. More of the same as tribal stage, but with tanks and boats. Get through this stage as fast as possible.
Space stage is just as great as Creature stage, if not better. After being confined to one planet for so long, you finally get to build your spaceship and fly to distant star systems. Make friends with aliens, or hunt those in tribal stage for sport. It's great.
In conclusion, the first two stages of the game and the last stage are great, but Tribal and City just seem shambled together. Oh, and there's NO ONLINE FUNCTIONALITY. Screw you EA. Pick this game up when it's on sale for a fiver or so.

Well, I was having some fun with this game up until the 9th level.  It is very brutal and unfair, with only 1 heath pack that I could find throughout the whole level.  It is a huge level and you can get killed very easily, trying to find anything useful.  There are a ton of empty buildings used to house some enemies, but they only drop ammo and weapons, sometimes...  Other buildings are just empty and are used to lure you to your death from enemies hiding in buildings across from you.
The biggest problem is the fog.  The enemy can see and shoot you way before you spot them.  Plus your sniper weapon moves a LOT and theirs do not.  They are dead on snipers and they will kill you fast!  Without health packs, it's only a matter of time before you stop reloading your quick save and quit playing.
Then there is the problem of not being able to save during the most intense battle in that level.  IMO, that was a game breaker.  They throw so many enemies at you, it's impossible to get through it without dying.  Then you have to take out a tank with almost zero health!  Even if you back track way back, you cannot save anymore.  It's locked into the "NO SAVE ZONE!!!"  It is a very frustrating experience!
If you have killed any of the soldiers that are in the "NO SAVE ZONE:, before you trigger the no save feature, and then save your game…  You will have to kill all of the soldiers again, that you lured out of that zone!  It's so frustrating!!!  Again, don't try to lure them out of the no save zone and then save your game.  If you have to reload your save, you'll just have to kill them all over again…  And you WILL have to reload many times trying new strategies, only to die over and over again…
Keyboard bindings will not let you bind commands to some key's!  Why can't I bind Left-Shift?  Kind of the norm these days.  So crouching can be rough.  And you really need to crouch a LOT!!!  Another game breaker for me!
You also do not stop moving for a second making it hard to judge where you will stop.  This has gotten me killed many times!  Just trying to strafe and shoot is a major chore!   You really need to be accurate and do head shots or the enemy will kill you first!  So movement sucks!  In a FPS, movement is everything!
Collision detection is way off and invisible walls are everywhere. Don't expect to use a vehicle as cover then pop out to shoot.  You'll need to step way away from the vehicle to get past that invisible wall.  I have died too many times trying to kill an enemy 2 feet away and never hit him.  Even with the shotgun!
I really wanted to like this game as I said, I was having fun with the first 8 levels.  I'm stuck on level 9 and will probably not ever play again as I got too frustrated!!!  I may try again when the game is finished, but they really need to fix some game breaking problems for me to play this again.  I'll even change this review if they fix the fog and sniper weapon so I can shoot strait.
EDIT:  I got past that 9th level.  I restarted it and found health packs and armor everywhere.  Maybe the new patch fixed this problem.  Anyway, now I'm stuck in the sewers with no MAP!!!  Silly game IMO...
