TL;DR: Huge battles between two or more sides squaring off and possibly deciding the fate of the world with a crazy amount of freedom and modding community.
Do you like combat? Do you like maps on which you move in real time? Do you like freedom? Have you dreamt of making your own adventure in a medieval world and forging you own fate?
Well then, M&B:Warband is the game for you. In the vanilla game you either start off as a poor noble or a peasant and you forge yourself in the world, along with your reputation and relationships with the various entities in the world. Want to be a bandit and harrass all the major empires, none being able to stand in your way? Done. Want to rise up to the title of ruler of all the known world and have everyone under your yoke? Done. Just a simple trader or mercenary? Also done.
You make your story in this game and your actions will influence the whole world which can progress dynamically just along fine without you if you choose to let it be. The graphics are a tad dated, however that doesn't get rid of the charm of the game. Combat is responsive and great, as each hit you make feels like it connects. You can change the difficulty of the game by changing combat speed, how much damage enemies do to you or you do to them. Want to go in a frenzy where you're a one man army? Lower the difficulty. Want to have a hardcore world where even a single shot will kill you as it is brutally realistic? Increase the difficulty. Both are fun to play and for the player that wants a normal experience, just roll with the default difficulty.
The true beauty of this game, however, comes with its modding community on its forums. There are hundreds of mods which improve, overhaul or add to the game in some way. From adding guns (even without Fire and Sword or Napoleonic Wars standalone expansions) to Ancient Rome to the Sengoku period of Japan. There are purely multiplayer mods which are extremely good and then there are single player mods which overhaul the entire world and create a new story, add events, give even more freedom to the player or make the world brutally realistic and hard as real life was.
Simply said, this game has a lifeblood and huge community that is not likely to expire any time soon. Tens of thousands of players have put in thousands of hours in this game purely simply because of the amount of freedom it allows, modding community and the community behind each mod as well. It is a genre of its own. Who doesn't like having hundred of his troops facing against hundred of an enemy's troops? There's even tactical mods to make you feel like a real general. In the higher difficulties you most definitely will need to stand behind your troops and hope you don't take an arrow to the neck.
The most enjoyable way to play this game would be to play vanilla and afterwards get into mods. Regardless of whether it's an SP mod or an MP mod, you will get your money's worth. Many a friendships have been formed through the MP mods. Some communities are very disciplined, other very lax and friendship forming. This is, after all, your choice of fun.

Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon city is another in a series of attempts at making a multiplayer-capable RE game (the first being outbreak and followed by multiplayer variants in RE 5/6 etc). While the concept is good, the execution is fairly lackluster, marred by flaws in control schemes and gameplay issues. For example, your character has the option to do a running dive by sprinting and pressing the action key and in no way is this ever useful in the game whatsoever except to make you look like a goof while you try and grab that much needed healing item and die for the umpteenth time.
Most of the enemies tend to follow the bullet sponge style of difficulty regardless of whether you are shooting them in their weak points, meaning you have to have a team of fairly competent and focused people to clear harder areas. To add insult to injury, the AI is dumb as toast and the networking is dependant on GFWL which is probably one of the worst frameworks for online play you can find. Other typical issues from previous games present themselves in this series such as not being able to shoot through certain obstacles with clear gaps in them and other somewhat ridiculous engine-related restrictions.
I can't really recommend this one especially since GFWL is pretty much on the way out. While I salute Capcom for making an honest try at a co-op game, this attempt fell completely flat.

The meat you use is important. My favorite roast is the chuck roast; it has wonderful marbling throughout the meat, and when given an ample amount of time to cook, chuck roast winds up being tender and melt-in-your-mouth delicious. To understand the importance of adequate cooking time, you must understand that these tougher pieces of meat have lots of tough connective tissue that will only soften when cooked at a lower temperature for a long period of time. You can’t rush a pot roast; you’ll be disappointed with the result if you try. But if you reach deep down into your soul and find your patience—at least, the patience that was given to you by your Maker to relate to beef-related circumstances in your life—you won’t be disappointed.

Short, yes, but FULL.
I see other commenters knocking this game for its short length - and it is short, granted - but it's a really, really fun short game.    The "haunting" mechanic feels pretty fresh when you're playing it, and it's fun to go around the different locations spooking people.
But where the game really shines is in the fantastic art direction.  This game is a treat to look at, and the screenshots don't really do the game justice - almost every prop is able to be possessed by the ghost, and each one has multiple spooky animations to them, each of which felt unique and distinct.  In most games of this sort, you'd expect to have the same object placed multiple times and each instance would do the same thing, but not this game - each spooky animation felt individually crafted, so much of the game was just the fun of going arouond triggering spooky effects and watching people get scared and run away.
One word of warning is that the game involves killing some people instead of just scaring them.  This game appears to be pretty kid friendly from the art direction, and I was going to share this game with my kids until I realized that was one of the mechanics.  This could be a solid kids' game without that mechanic.  It also feels somewhat at odds with the more whimsical presentation of the game - spooking people away feels lighthearted and fun, and the ghost murdering people undercuts that vibe considerably.  Not everyone will care, but if you have kids, you might want to play through the game once before deciding whether to let them play.
Other than that, though, this game is really fun and polished.  Well done, developers!  Thumbs up.

Let me start by saying that Witcher 1, especially for it's time, is not a "bad game" but this review is LONG. I suggest reading the SHORTER " GOODS"  and " NOT-SO-GOODS" lists directly below if you don't want to read too much.
The franchise has soul and a lot of supporters but I'm afraid this game hasn't aged well... at all. A friend of mine is a huge fan of the 3rd installment and pushed me to check out the franchise. We ended up trying out he first game together (me playing, him watching) and managed to find a lot to critisize. I had fresh eyes with no prior knowledge while my friend had experience of the sequels so we managed to get to the end and make a pretty extensive review of the title. So with that said here's an easy list of GOODS and NOT-SO-GOODS, if you're looking for more in-depth info you can check out the lower section in this review. Thanks for reading!
GOODS
+ The lore and setting aren't unique but have a lot of creative elements which makes the game feel fresh and original. Exploration is limited but I still felt encouraged to do so.
+ Part of this are the many weird creatures you've probably never seen before. I love cool monsters to fight and reading in-depth descriptions of their lifestyles and weaknesses.
+ There's both humour and philosophy to be found in the dialogue though the delivery... we'll come back to that later.
+ Combat style is unorthodox. It'll probably get tedious the longer you spend in the game, but still better then most RPG's where you just click the enemy once and use an ability or two.
+ If there is at least one character in this game you can relate with, it's the main character Geralt. He's like medieval Batman with extra snark.
+ The story is... extensive? The ending was pretty cool? And some characters at least grow... kind of? Most is unclear, as many characters disappear almost as soon as they're introduced and their fates are left unclear.
+ Your 12-year-old brother will love the overabundance of cleavage on literally all female characters save for that one gross old-lady.
NOT-SO-GOODS
- Most dialogue is badly written. Incohesive to the point of feeling completely random at times; as if the people are talking to themselves instead of each other.
- On top of that the voice-acting is absolutely horrible throughout. Sometimes so camp it's funny, but mostly just bad. Thaler and Dandelion are 'passable'.
- Since every one in the game save for you is a (word that steam won't let me spell), it's hard to care about any thing going on to any one in that world.
- 90% of your decisions don't really matter. There are 2 sides to most major conflicts in the game and they're both really, really stupid.
- Too long. The game makes you walk every where, basically no warps. You're required to complete side-quests to advance the plot even though they're often not even related to anything. So there's a lot of pointless back-and-forth running which simply isn't fun.
- Inventory system is rubbish and confusing. Alchemy system looks overly complicated but only has like, 3 usefull potions to make.
- Choosing "skills" mostly consists of " 10% better dodge" or " 15% stronger attacks while bleeding" and it's all just really unimaginative. Which is sad to see for a fantasy RPG.
- My friend told me that the two red-haired harlots who did nothing but order me around and whine were supposed to be ROMANTIC INTERESTS. And if you reject all of their advances? The game STILL acts as if Geralt has the hots for Triss; which arguably has the worst voice acting of the cast. Falls under the " choices don't matter" part I guess.
- Probably the worst introduction of a game I've ever seen. The plot is rushed and confusing. The tutorial is so bad it doesn't even explain you how to attack before throwing 20 bad guys at you and... well just read the bottom if you want to know more.
- Immersion? Sorry, you should look somewhere else for that.
- Some glitches, some that caused crashes. The worst is the ever-persistent one where every one's hairs and beards wildly flap all over the place when you're in conversation with them.
- ALVIN
So yeah, I can't really recommend this game to any one aside from diehard fans who are simply curious as to what the original thing is like. After fully playing it my fan-friend felt he didn't miss much though. Old school RPG fans will miss interesting dialogue and freedom of choice while modern RPG fans will hate the leveling system and lack of streamlined gameplay. I'm sure most Fans of the later games will probably dislike how the characters look and act with this "first installment weirdness" while newcomers will be absolutely confused about what's going on for the first TWO OR THREE HOURS of the game. And that's asking for a big commitment right of the bat. All the while using amnesia as the most overused excuse as to why the main character is ignorant of nearly everything and all the characters feel the need to explain all the things you didn't want to know while leaving out the things you DO want to know. Most dialogue trees are tedious. Half of the side-quests are "Go here, kill that, come back" and the list goes on and on. I would've given up if my friend didn't encourage me.
The "two faction"  system is especially stupid. On one side you have human racists who want all non-humans out of the country while the alternative group is a bunch of NON-human-racists who want to burn absolutely every one. The game even punishes you if you play independent, constantly berating you for being "weak-minded for not being able to commit to a choice" even though as I just explained; choosing either faction makes you a hypocritic racist. And guess what? SPOILERS: By the end of the game every one (save for two or three friends) has backstabbed you, no matter what you chose. So I ask: what was even the point of ANY of this!?
It has heart. It has soul. You can see a lot of work went into crafting a big story in a bigger world but it falls flat on it's face in almost every aspect. The rare moments it shines are too scarce and I can safely say the ending isn't enough to stick around. Maybe in it's time it was respected for all the new things it did, but it has aged terribly since. Some fans tell me Wicher 1 has the best story of all of them. Well I just hope that's not the case as we've noticed many the plot-holes, cheapshots, bad tropes, cliche's, "coincidences" and contradicting world-building in this game already...
So in the end I don't recommend this. Now it's time to get started on Witcher 2 and see how well every thing has improved.

EDIT 1: 25.6.2014 - 2.5 Version
I decided to keep the old review as it was, because it was accurate at the time and a lot of people (20/21) found it helpful, as well as to show how the game has improved in both stability and gameplay.
First and foremost, the crashing issues. At least for me, they appear to be gone. I cannot claim that the game now works for everybody, but for me, I can honestly say that after trying it multiple times today, I haven't experienced any problems whatsoever.
Secondly, the new game features.
In this regard the game has improved dramatically and became closer to the model of Days of Wonder's other digital board game, Ticket to Ride.
- Joining/creating games
The "Search for a game" model has been replaced with a Ticket to Ride-like arena, with a lobby and a "create a game" and "join a game" option. This removes a problem that sometimes occured previously, when in cancelling a search and restarting it (with different or same parameters) you ended up in multiple matches at the same time. It also adds a lot more customization to the game, including but not limited to the number of players (also present before), the amount of time each player has to act, password protected games, ranked/unranked games (previously only matches with your "buddies" were ranked) and the option to play a single session game (fast paced, all players only play one game) or multi session (longer rounds, suitable for those who play multiple matches at the same time, or prefer relaxed long lasting games similar to correspondence chess).
- Gameplay
Before the 2.5 update, you could spend 10 minutes or more waiting for an opponent to make a move, which made a match that could've been finished in 15 minutes, last an hour or more. A situation made worse when after 10 minutes of waiting, you got a message that the player disconnected which automatically aborted the game. The introduction of a timer makes matches run a lot smoother. It makes games (single session) shorter and more active, and the addition of bot replacements for disconnected players, means that the very frustrating situation of ending up with a 50 minute unfinished game is gone.
Conclusion
I'm happy to change the review to a recommendation. Now the game is as it should have been all along. I just hope that new updates won't mess it up again. The only downside of the game right now, is the lack of players, which will hopefully change once the word of it's improvements spreads.
Also a recommendation for potential buyers of the game, who are not already familiar with the board game version. Check out the youtube show TableTop (hosted by Wil Wheaton) and their episode about SmallWorld, and get to know what the game is about in a very entertaining way.

Let me start out by saying that I 100%'ed the game in 7.5 hours.  My first playthrough was pure; meaning I beat every level without using any abilities and I chose to do this before I even knew there was an achievement for doing so.

I consider myself pretty good at going fast and flying through the air as I've spent hundreds of hours rocketjumping and surfing in TF2 and CSGO. So you would think this game was a perfect fit for me, and so did I until I played it.
So why the negative review?  To be quite frank, it comes down to a couple simple principles that I believe in when it comes down to design.
1: Speed should be encouraged. (this is after all a game about going fast) In reality it is about going at whatever speed the game decides because going to fast will result in constantly running out of trucks to jump on making levels unbeatable.
2: The RNG is just painful.  The trucks wildly swerve about and throw themselves off cliffs, and almost all of the stage hazards and mechanics are also entirely RNG based so there is very little actual use of skill and the game devolves into a waiting game for the planets to align and for a run to even be possible to complete.
3: The controls are weak and the physics are poor. Much of my experience in air control comes from the Source Engine, which for all its faults has incredibly tight and crisp control in the air.  If I make a mistake in TF2 or CSGO it is my fault.  This game however... oh boy.  You run forward incredibly quickly, but side to side movement is almost nonexistent. Turning in the air is a nightmare and the sudden velocity increase when falling from any decent height results in you suddenly plummeting to the ground when you thought you might gracefully maneuver onto a truck.
So did I like anything about the game? The music for the most part is great. The last 3 worlds are a bit lacking and out of character but for the most part I enjoyed the music quite a bit. Now here's the real surprise coming from an elitist like myself: I actually quite like the abilities.  They give interesting options for movement although some are vastly better than others and there are some silly combos. Once I finished the game I went back and actually used the abilities to have some fun and probably will continue to do so from time to time in the future.
This is getting lengthy so let's wrap it up.  Would I recommend this game to someone who had interests similar to myself and would want to 100% the game if they played it?  No.  It is frustrating and stupid more than anything and I had to unlearn everything I previously knew about air control to work with the awful controls.  Would I recommend this game to a more casual person who will use abilities and probably has no background in air movement like I do? Yes.
So yeah, my enjoyment was crushed by the way I chose to experience the game.  If I could give the game a middle ground review I would because it does have merit for the casual fan, but for someone like myself this game was just horrendous to play through and I can't recommend it because of the issues I raised above.

Here's how I imagine how the idea for the game was made.
"Hey Scott you know the word cluster♥♥♥♥?" "Yeah Jim. What about it?" "Let's replace '♥♥♥♥' with truck and make a game called Clustertruck where it's a cluster♥♥♥♥ of trucks everywhere." "Sounds great Jim!"
All jokes aside, this game is really good with lots of content with very good level design. Even if you breeze through the official levels (which is going to be very difficult), there's always Workshop content.

Clustertruck is a very fun and addicting game where you use trucks to get from the start to finish of the track. This may sound easy, but you will find yourself having to restart levels often. Despite dying so much, I rarely found myself getting frustrated since the levels are fair and when you die it'll be because you didn't time your jump correctly or tried to land on a truck just our of reach. There is a wide variety between levels and you also can unlock abilities which can help you get through some of the tougher levels.
I recommend this to anyone who likes platforming games, if you enjoy surfing maps in Counter Strike or if you just think the game looks fun from the videos, then chances are you'll have a great time with this. Incredibly fun game. The upgrading aspect is great and the abilities that your crew unlock as they gain experience are for the most part meaningful (radio for recon? What does that really do? Still have no idea). The action is hectic, but addicting. It might as well be a small RTS with the amount of actions that need to be completed simultaneously, and as a life time fan of AoE2 and starcraft it felt at home. I’ve had at least 20 people die under my command, but after a point a golden grew will emerge that will somehow live to level 3 and you can stop the meat grinder and bother to put in parachutes into the plane.
The game can be punishing. If you lose your hydraulics in the middle of a swarm of fighters, you might as well boost your engines and manually abort the mission. The interface needs some work. Clicking on the ammo box to refill an empty turret when a dropped item is in the way is frustrating.  But the most important thing that needs to be implemented is an improved tutorial and a refined “How to play” section. Why should I pick First Aid as a secondary crew job? The game doesn’t even mention it exists as a position. Adding in small tips during the loading screens, like the fact that turrets at the start of a mission hold 2 ammo boxes, but the max that they can hold is 3. So every mission I’m sending them to grab that lone box before the bullets start flying.
TLDR: The game needs small reworks in a few places to truly be great. It’s a small thing here or there that once completed will make the game come in to its own. As of right now it’s a good game for the price. I’m at 8 hours in and only 3 critical missions through the campaign with 7 to go. This isn’t a short game.

ElderScrolls III: Morrowind will always have a special place in my heart. It was truly the last great RPG of the series, as later titles would become more noob-friendly, shaving off things like attributes, birthsigns, a multitude of skills, and practically destroying any kind of mage class.
In Morrowind, you will find yourself picking a series of "Major Skills" which will aid you in leveling up, "Minor Skills" which will help your character and add to subsections of your class, and literal hundreds of different spells (which don't need books to learn, and are mostly taught by buying them from a spell-vendor)
A slightly worrying thing to the returning player, is that 15 years after original release (2017), a lot of the modding community has vanished off the face of the internet. Gamespy went under, and the mods they had on planet elder scrolls have gone with it. A google search will help you find the mods you are looking for however, and TESNexus is still up and running.
I am very excited to own Morrowind once more; for the storyline, guildlines, and other interactions hold so much more canon and lore, and is all around more of a true to bones RPG.
Recommended whole-heartedly to returning players, and new players alike. If you have only played oblivion, or Skyrim, you will find the source for alot of references within this classic. Hope you enjoy!

--> As I creep though the familiar-yet-eerie corridors of Resident Evil, I can't help but feel terrified of Crimson Heads. Even 12 years after I first encountered them, it's genuinely frightening every time they spring back to life to try to tear a hole in my esophagus, but they're also a great example of why Resident Evil still holds up. While inconsistent art and persistent clipping problems give away that this is an update of a 1996 survival-horror game, the scares, puzzles, and atmosphere of the creepy corridors of Spencer Mansion are as potent as ever.
Ever since the tweaks made in the 2002 GameCube remake, Resident Evil has been a tense game of resource management. The makeover to the many rooms, puzzles, and monsters give it an edge that significantly surpasses the original game. Every zombie you spend precious ammunition to kill becomes a ticking time bomb that’ll turn into something much more deadly if you don’t dispose of them properly with fire or headshots.
That persistent danger is what makes the frequent backtracking through this labyrinth of locked doors something more interesting than typical busywork. As Resident Evil uses adventure game-style design to send you looking for keys and objects that have to be examined closely to solve puzzles, then brought back to the right location, you can feel the stakes rising as the chances of getting mauled or caught without the right resources increase.
Resident Evil is a gauntlet of twisted monsters and hard decisions. Make the wrong choice or take too long on some objectives, and sometimes you’ll pay for it with the death of a comrade or missing out on precious resources. It’s punishing at times, and managing the different inventories of two playable characters forces you to be smart and frugal with regard to what you carry with you. The constant pressure makes it a difficult game to play by design, but one that still manages to be fair.
This HD remastered edition of Resident Evil looks pretty good on the new-gen consoles, thanks to 1080p resolution and some nicely touched up backgrounds and textures, with the PC version offering the highest settings and a nifty option to switch between 60 and 30 frames per second. The biggest improvement across all versions is the ability to scale the experience the way you want to play it. You could choose between 4:3 or 16:9 aspect ratios, and you can swap the original “tank-style” controls for a more modern setup that moves your character in the direction you push the stick.
As an old fan I prefer the original controls, but the new controls help make Resident Evil accessible without sacrificing the tense nature of combat. You still have to stand your ground in order to shoot zombies and deal with the pressure of enemies getting closer. Since most face-offs happen in tight spaces, it’s not super easy to pull a juke move on multiple zombies, even with the new controls. Purists can have it the way the designers originally intended. Newbies can jump in and not completely break the game.
Dimly lit rooms with ambient effects like lightning or floating dust particles are some of the best to look at in this update. However, some backdrops look garish under a lot of light, and there are some noticeably blurry textures and pixelated art. I’m also disappointed that the major clipping problems still haven’t been fixed. Maybe in the next remake, Capcom?

This game is phenomenal...it immerses you full on into a visceral, eye-candy laden homage to the shooters that best defined the FPS, like Quake, Unreal Tournament and even Half-Life and adds to them. Normally I would wait to review a game like Bedlam, which is still in early access, until I at least had put more hours in...but because it's on sale as I write this, at an even better price then the Holiday Sale when I got it, I had to relate that I feel this game justified FULL price within the first ten minutes of playtime, and hasn't since let down, at least for me. It is challenging and engaging, and never feels like it copies too much from any of the games it salutes...it even mentions some by name, yet there is a fresh feel that's fun, exciting and there's still more to come...not to mention I also have a lot more yet to experience with what is already here. Best of all is there are areas, apart from following where the game leads you, that take you into what feels like a whole other dimension, and salute different games altogether, then take you back to where you would have been if you hadn't drifted off the main path. This game, Bedlam, is like a gift that keeps on giving, especially for those who have a particular fondness of first-person shooters and the games that defined the realm. Don't let my hours of play (at the time of this review, less than 2) take anything away from the extent to which I so highly recommend Bedlam...especially if you see it on sale...but it is totally worth the full price, even when in early access. Worth noting also, that even when my aged game card can't handle many of the newer releases, Bedlam looks awesome and plays awesome and adds to my recommendation. If you're going back and forth on whether to go for it, I say go full on, and enjoy Bedlam!

Prior to playing this game, I had tempered my expectations of it given the negative reviews.
Yes, this game does not feel like a classic RE game which will disappoint some people (I'm more of a classic RE fan myself). It is essentially a third-person, cover-based shooter (think a less intense Gears of War). In addition to the zombies, you will be facing off against many human enemies which is something I was not expecting and which got particularly irritating at times. With that said, here are my pros and cons for this game:
Pros
+ Gameplay can get pretty intense on higher difficulties (Veteran and Professional). My advice here is not to play on Professional until you level up and get better perks/weapons.
+ Brings back some nostalgia of RE2 and RE3 as you run into characters from that game and the setting is awesome.
+ DLC actually adds a lot to the game as it allows you to play seven new missions using another group (Spec Ops and is even better than the main campaign in my view).
+You get to play as Umbrella operatives which is pretty neat, but see my comments about the story below.
+There are a large variety of weapons and some perks to choose from, which can provide some variety in your playstyle.
+Graphics are pretty good and I did not suffer from any performance issues in my time with the game.
Cons
- The AI can be pretty stupid using up items when you would not want them to as evidenced by their going out into the middle of a warzone without going for cover. With that said, there were several moments where I would have died without their help (surprisingly they can do a decent job from time to time).
- If you plan on using keyboard/mouse, be aware that mouse acceleration seems to be turned on without any real way of turning it off. This makes it a pain in the butt to aim initially or to look around,
- The story is not memorable at best and non-existant at worst, which sucks given the amount of things they could have done with it. We finally get to play as the bad guys, but the characters and their motivations are not fleshed out. This is also true of the Spec Ops group in the DLC.
-GFWL integration. Hopefully, Capcom will take the effort to bring this over to Steamworks, but given the fact that the developer went under in 2013, this is unlikely.
-This game does allow you and your teammates to become infected, but it feels like wasted potential since you can kill your teammate after infection and simply revive them.
-A bit nitpicky, but there is a lack of variety among the zombies meaning you'll be shooting the same 4 zombies the entire time.
-Enemies feel a bit "bullet-spongey" which can be irritating when you begin the game (after buying better weapons, this becomes less of an issue).
All-in-all, I am on the fence about this game, so I cannot recommend it for purchase and certainly not at the $30 price tag; however, if it does go on sale again, I could give a cautious recommendation only to those who really want to revisit Raccoon City (albeit for a less enjoyable experience than previous RE titles) or who are looking for a semi-competent shooter.
Personally, after I complete the DLC (almost there), I do not think I will be going back to this title anytime soon.
*Note: I only played it on single player and was able to get some enjoyment out of it.

Pros:
- Classic RE survival horror.
- Controls can be changed to accommodate keyboard/controller (controller is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED).
- Switch between Tank Controls or Regular Movement (for newer players).
- Visually great, still holds up to today thanks to the pre rendered areas.
- Survival Horror to its fullest (item managment, ammunition managment, deciding between fighting or running, health management, puzzles, and minimal HUD information.
Cons:
- While the game itself is visually amazing, the cutscenes seem to be original Gamecube files, which have been blown up to fit larger resolutions, meaning blurrier cutscenes.
- Audio in cutscense can fall out of sync.
While it seems like there is very little downsides to the game, keep in mind the fixed camera angles, survival emphasis, and the tank controls. It can be a turn off for many new to the survival horror genre but the option to turn on "Regular Movement" over tank controls can make it easier on new players.

The art style is unique and fun, but doesn't take any of the seriousness away from the game.
Here's a little bit of my last flight on my main save:
I was 'flying' a barely held together wreck as 2 crew members lay bleeding out on the cold hard floor of the tail, no medkits left, as the last fully operational engine burst into flames, machine gun fire from enemy fighters ripped through my cockpit, killing my pilot, and as I grabbed the only chute onboard with my last remaining crew member, the tail rips off and sends us plunging towards the earth at breakneck speeds, impacting the ground.
If you like: Management, flying, WW2, intensity, persistant death, history or laughably grim situations, buy this game.
9/10. (Only because I would have liked to see more customisation for characters so you really feel their death and their story, although the memorial does a great job of that, and more bombers in the base game ie B17)

This game is a great time management and strategy game, combining the crew management aspect of FTL, with the persistency and difficulty of XCOM. This game is not meant to be easy. It gets hectic, and that's okay.
One thing I would like to see is rebalancing of altitudes. Medium altitude has some use in that it allows some use of ventral turrets, but the navigator cannot see the ground for some reasons (Though at higher levels it seems like the navigator can see a little bit). A revamp of the weather system would provided more challenge in that the player would have to determine conditions and choose the best altitude and way to play every mission.
All in all, this game is a 8.5/10. It's very fun to play, and I would recommend it to anyone, especially for the low price of $15

It's a fun game (at times), but it's tagged as simulation and strategy...
It's more an arcade than strategy. You won't have time to think about any tactic when you have to manually drop the bombs, manually select enemy planes (gunners won't start shooting until you point at the enemy). Manually tell the engineer to conserve fuel (and you need to repeat it as often as possible or you won't be able to go back).
It's micromanagement without active pause which can be sometimes fun but it has nothing to do with strategy.
To give an example - the crew has a number of skills. When you see an enemy on the radar you need to select the enemy planes by looking at each of them for a second or two, then it would be nice if you activate 'Focus' skill on your gunners to make them more accurate, and you could tell you pilot to take evasive actions once you're in range of the enemy... except that it's already too late as the enemy planes have reached you while you were still targeting them. There is no time to use any of the skills until after it's already late. If you happen to be near a target to bomb then your choice is to either fly past the target and start tagging the enemy planes, or ignore the planes and drop the bombs. Can't do both even if there are 7 people on board. And what happens when guns run out of ammo? You have to manually tell each guy to reload...
The controls could be better than well, especially flying. To tell pilot where to go you need to tag a navigation point created by the navigator (just as you'd tag enemy planes). Often there aren't any so you cannot change course at all. It seems like this part of the interface is counter intuitive just to make the game harder. It's like disabling the mouse in FPS games to make them last longer (as the player needs to repeat missions again and again).

Do not let the negative reviews scare you away - I've seen this compared to Dark Souls and thats frankly an insanely overblown comparison (and overused). My first campaign was a disaster because I had no clue what I was doing. I lost five planes, and around 20+ crewmembers. I was getting to grips with the game itself, and when you're learning new mechanics I think it isnt unreasonable to expect failure. My second campaign I ran the next day - I havent lost a single person. I'm now in the sixth section of the game itself, with over 50 missions flown. My plane is upgraded to the high heavens and I have 70,000 of exess cash saved. I've killed five of the ace pilots - three of them within seconds of them appearing on my radar. If anything the weakness of this game comes from how easy it gets when you actually understand the mechanics.
So what are the mechanics? At heart this game reminds me of an RPG - its about ability usage and timing. The bomber has incredible burst damage that will get you out of almost any situation. When the crew get experience you'll be able to do things like use AP, HE, and Incidiary ammo that DOENST even use your standard ammo, so you can keep pumping out shots for a long tmie. Your pilot will be able to evade flack, dive to low altitude to put out engine fires, and do evasive flying to avoid damage. Your navigator will learn to read the stars to direct your craft at high altitude during night, and how to set your own waypoints so you can have more control over where the plane actually flies. All of this is directed by you and its all about reading the situation and executing the right response. With a few hours in the game you'll be flying deep into enemy territory like it was a walk in the park, and boy is it fun.

I owned Morrowind on the first Xbox, and it was a mind-blowing title 15 years ago. The traditional Tolkein-like western RPG art, lore, and music with a wide open world was revolutionary. It made the dominant Final Fantasy JRPG's look... childish, effeminate, and downright bizzare at times. Even though the Elder Scrolls series was available on IBM DOS/Windows 95 style PC's in the 1990's, those PC's were ridiculously expensive, troublesome, very few owned one, and the Elder Scrolls had very little exposure to the public as consoles were popular. Nobody I knew ever heard of Elder Scrolls. A new king of RPG's was crowned when Morrowind came to Xbox and was part of a console launch line-up.
I played Morrowind a fair amount but never came close to even finishing the main quest. I found the game to be highly confusing. I was always lost and somewhat unable to locate quest objectives. I eventually became bored of Morrowind and became hooked on Halo 2 multiplayer, and traded the Morrowind disc in at Gamestop. That was a mistake. So I recently bought it again on a Steam sale, and now that I'm a veteran of Oblivion and Skyrim, I have a better grasp of how to play Morrowind.
Morrowind is for hardcore Elder Scrolls fans only. If you were born after 1990, you'll probably whine about the graphics, the unusual RNG-style combat, the slow sprinting speeds, very little voice-overs, no fast travel, the requirement to read alot, and the lack of any waypoint markers. Kids nowadays just don't have what Morrowind requires because they're used to a game holding their hand through the experience. Quests require following read directions with vague locations such as "Go north of Balmora, turn west at a cave, and your goal is somewhere near there." Prepare to use your brain, and physically trek to locations. I hope you know how to use a map and compass.
Also, the menu navigation is painfully slow with a mouse compared to a controller. Simple acts like looting crates takes longer than it did on consoles. Controller Companion can be used, along with X-Padder, but don't exactly streamline the experience like the Xbox did. Using ALT-TAB to switch applications while Morrowind is running in fullscreen can cause a crash. The resolution is annoying and dated, and a registry edit didn't work for me. I tried mods as well, but can't seem to find any that work properly. Save often, with at least 2 seperate files... you'll die alot.
People in their 30's and 40's who remember the crude titles of years past will adapt well however.
This is a great game for anybody who has a low-end laptop but wants an engrossing AAA experience. A cell-phone or toaster could probably run Morrowind. The combat is unusual by todays standards. You'll swing a weapon at an enemy a 100 times and hit nothing but air until your character is levelled up. There are many items to find, equip, steal, use, just like in other Elder Scrolls titles. Some are useful. Many are useless. The magic system however is far superior to Oblivion or Skyrim. Morrowind gives the ability to basically craft custom spells that could possibly allow players to fly anywhere in the sky, or breathe underwater. The combinations of what spells that could be created are quite impressive. Alchemy and enchanting are present. There are also more unmarked caves, tombs, and treasures to be found than later Elder Scrolls games which encourages more thorough exploration... even underwater...
Warnings and complaints aside, Morrowind will become probably one of the best RPG's you've ever played if you're patient enough to give it a chance, invest 30 hours, and be open-minded. I fully recomend it to anyone who considers themselves to be a more hardcore gamer.
I think the near $20 price is a bit steep for a 15 year old game. It should be $10 in my opinion, but the price is still high because the game is still popular with about 1000 people playing it on Steam at peak times. Even at $20 Morrowind is still money well spent considering you can easily sink 300 hours of your life into it or more. Mods only serve to further expand that time.
Thumbs up. Give it a shot!

First of all, I want to start this review with a negative. It's a fairly hefty one, but thankfully the only one since I would overall still recommend the game. I have a personal benchmark with games that it should provide an hour of fun per pound sterling. It's why I'm such a fan of indie games because they're cheap and usually break through that threshold. I completed the whole thing in 4 hours at the point where I was looking forward to whatever the next bit was and then "The Fall 2: coming soon". If you can get this on sale under £4 then you have an absolute GEM of a game.
+ Amazing atmosphere
+ Thought provoking storyline
+ The uncertainty of whether the pilot was alive or not forced some excellent choices
+ The action had the right stiff robotics/fun fluidity to give an excellent flavour of what hollywood androids would fight like without being frustrating
+ The amazing atmosphere (yes, it was so good I'm mentioning it twice)
+ The setting just drew me in and had me wanting to find out more!
-- Price/hours of fun ratio. Over too quickly
- Some of the puzzles just weren't logical and relied on the old adventure game strategy of "try every object with every interactable". However, I think possibly this was intended for story purposes (I won't spoil it). Buuuuut, that also means that my 4 hour playtime could possibly been down to 3 hours, making the price/fun ratio even steeper
All in all, I count this as one of my favourite storytelling/narratives in gaming alongside System Shock 2 etc. *had it have been longer*...

Bedlam is an original and fun take on the old school first person (multiplayer) shooters from the 90’s (and even before the 90’s). If you enjoyed playing Quake or Unreal Tournament back in the days (you might even play them to this day) then Bedlam is everything you want and more. No need to look any further. Here’s why:
Since this is an Early Access game – and therefore still incomplete – I can’t tell if the final product will be worth your money and time but the first few chapters that I’ve played so far are very entertaining to say the least. I won’t go as far as to say it’s brilliant, but I can’t remember a game that has tried this sort of story before. Not like this, anyway.
The basic story is as follows: your character is a scientist who’s volunteering to test some new brain scanning tech. The scan it makes eventually puts you inside a game, but you quickly realize that you can’t get out of it so the scientist is now experiencing the game herself. That’s correct; you are a female gamer, and a Scottish one at that.
The story is fairly to-the-point, so you’ll receive mission objectives and you carry them out. The girl will narrate as well, but this is mostly done for comic relief and a bit of a backstory.
Normally I’d write a whole paragraph about the gameplay, but the game plays like most first person shooters. So there’s a whole lot of shooting involved while completing different objectives. These objectives range from capturing checkpoints, blowing up towers, just plainly killing enemies and even winning an Unreal Tournament inspired low-gravity deathmatch. All made as a nice tribute to some of the older, but still great, games most of us used to play when they were young.
I haven’t yet played any of them, but there also seem to be a few levels that are a bit different as far as the gameplay is concerned; one of them seems to be a sidescrolling shooter (yup, it’s still all about shooting things). I think it’s a good idea to mix things up a little because not everyone might appreciate and enjoy this sort of repetitive gameplay nowadays. People keep looking for new things and ways to excite them and giving them an old school shooter might not just be the best solution/idea here. But there’s always an audience for things, no matter how silly, so I’m sure it will do just fine.
Bedlam is a game that references a lot of older games but it doesn’t seem to introduce anything truly new to the genre. Don’t get me wrong, because that isn’t really necessary in any way, of course; the game stands outs because of its fun voice-overs and over-the-top action, while it will also let you think back of the times when things were simpler. The Unreal Tournament-like level especially triggered some memories for me. Great times, and I’m certain there are a lot more people who will agree with me here, not just for that level.
The graphics can also be seen as a tribute with some old-school ugliness in there, especially in the earlier levels, but it gets increasingly better as you progress. It never becomes perfect or beautiful, but it’s all very serviceable nevertheless. Despite its (intentionally) ugly models and environments it all looks very sharp and clean. The developers have done a great job here, even if my review let you think that I maybe didn’t appreciate any of it.
The voice acting is charming but the Scottish accent can get a bit tiresome sometimes (no offense to Scottish people ;)). Sometimes it feels like she’s trying a bit too hard but overall I’m very satisfied with how it’s done. The rest of the cast also does a great job here.
In short; nothing wrong with the audio-visual experience here.
Because the game isn’t complete or even out yet, and levels are still being added, I can’t really tell you how long a playthrough will last you. I finished half of the levels in about an hour so I’d say that you can complete this Early Access version in 2,5 hours or so. I’m not sure about this, but I think the final product will last somewhere around 5 hours, maybe even longer.
Bedlam is all about bringing you a new old-school experience, and with success. It references a lot of the older shooters from the 90’s while adding some humorous voice acting and levels to complete the package. It might not do anything truly new but if you’re one of those people who doesn’t care about that sort of stuff then you should absolutely play this game. It’s a nice trip down memory lane, no matter what.
[Rating: 77/100]

Heroes & Generals is in desparate need of optimization, a game like so many others that found so much success in beta that development stagnated, favoring horizontal expansion (more guns and vehicles) over much more rudimentary development.
Pros:
-Multifacetted first person shooter gameplay
-Free to Play
Cons:
-Very buggy infrastructure. After latest updates, expect to need to try to connect at least five or six times before actually connecting to the server. Can get caught in endless loop of connecting, loading, then losing connection before you can start.
-Very poor optimization for multiplayer (which is the entire game) it doesn't matter if your machine can reach 60fps in gameplay on a good day, 9 games out of 10 your frames will be bouncing between 6 and 19 frames per second because the servers and game engine do not play nicely.
-Expect stagnant play after a certain point. After purchasing a fully upgraded weapon, you still have to maintain it. Ammo and maintenance costs for fully upgraded weapons can often exceed income.
-With only one war server for the entire world, expect 70% of all available games to have absurdly high latency.

This game is quite good in a lot of ways, unfortunately it fights tooth and nail to outweigh the good points with bad.
If you are looking for a simple drop in, kick around and get it done WW2 shooter, this is exactly the game you were looking for. Or not, because the cash and game economy are geared to ruin what is otherwise a very fun game.
Let me explain before someone comes up with the pitchforks and torches. Simply put everything in this game costs in game currency, repairs, upgrades, vehicles, the list goes on and on. Put more simply if it is in the game, you will be spending much if not all of what you earn from the in game economy on repairing it. If you go with only the most basic starter stuff, you can keep your costs down enough to actually build up a cash supply. This is because your economy rewards are based on time in match playing, not on things you actually do in match, and all your equipment and ammunition will eat into whatever you get from that at a very rapid pace. This means that unless you are spending large sums of time in match with nothing but the most basic gear you will not be buying or using any of that neat stuff you can unlock.
There is another way though. Everything, and I do mean everything, in the game can be bought for gold. As usual gold is the cash shop currency used by the devs to pay for their F2P title. Unfortunately the devs took all their cash shop and economy pages from the price gougers guide to pay to win economies. Not only can everything be paid for with gold, all the items locked behind the work of leveling and tasks for earning can be instantly unlocked with it as well. This, when combined with the extremely weak in game economy means it becomes quickly impossible to support anything but that basic starter gear, and makes the paying customers with their automatic weapons, bazookas, and Armored Personnel Carriers very obvious in every match you run into them.
Adding insult to injury, the gold itself is quite expensive compared to what you get for it.
On the whole, it is a good game, one I desperately want to like if not love, but I think not.

I can't really call myself a true Resident Evil fan, I've only recently managed to play Resident Evil 4 and have never played any of the original games (I.E Resident Evil 1-3). I will go ahead now and say I rather enjoy this game quite a bit, it's certainly got enough charm for a quick game every now and then but it doesn't have the lasting draw that most other RE games have. Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City did some things right, but did quite a lot at a mediocre level and some things plain badly, so I'll tell you what i think, and you can decide for yourself.
The Good
-The Character design: The characters and most enemies in this game are quite varied in appearance and personality, and I like that. Mainly I'm talking about Wolf Pack here, they each have an interesting back-story that is never mentioned in-game (you'll need an external source like a wikia for that) and they all look unique and interesting. Personally if they were a little more developed I wouldn't mind seeing them in other games.
-The Music: I'll say now regardless of how one-sided my opinion is, I love the music in the game. It's a mix of atmospheric tones to intense dramatic symphonies, all of them fit their respective situations perfectly.
The Okay
-The Cover mechanics: Cover in this game is a bit iffy, some things you can hide behind others you can't sometimes you can shoot from cover sometimes you can't. It's kinda like rolling the dice with your health and that's never a good thing.
-The Combat mechanics: Combat is arguably the main aspect of RE:ORC, and when the main aspect of the game isn't the best part of the game, you're not in for a good time. Recoil feels almost non-existent but bullet spread is a pain to manage, especially with the less accurate weapons. The meele combat is okay, however performing executions and special moves is unresponsive and it usually takes multiple attempts to perform one.
The Bad
- Enemy design : Enemies in this game can be easily described with the term "bullet sponge". They all take a hell of a lot of ammo to kill and that's not helping the face you hardly have any to begin with. This isn't a problem when it comes to the slow and easy to deal with zombies, but when faced with enemy humans, hunters and lickers it becomes a huge problem and is even more apparent in the harder difficulties. Additionally shooting enemies hardly causes them to react, they just take it like nothing has happened most of the time which is frustrating when it comes to already hard to kill enemies like the hunters or the final boss depending on what choice you make.
- The Story: Not much to say here, even for a spin off title in an alternate reality the story of this game is really weak and boring with no real development of characters.
All in all, RE:ORC is a game that's fun with friends, but not worth the given price-tag. Give it a shot if you can ever get it cheaper but don't expect to be amazed by the game.

Oh boy, One of my favorite all time games is finally on steam and im already hooked back into it. Dont let the time count fool you i played the original Guild for easily over 1k+ hours back during high school (minus all the patches...) and now we have a fully patched and somewhat great release of The Guild Gold on steam.
I wont ramble too much but heres the jist of the game: You are a poor boy from a poor family out in the forest that comes to the big city to make yourself into something. Sounds simple right? Nope! you cant make yourself super big and successful on your first character so youll be making a Dynasty in the city you'll be playing in to which there are several cities spread across Europe who have their own politics and events to deal with with one of them being other dynasties.
One of the great things about The Guild is that not only are you trying to run your business and not go broke, you also have to not only contend with other dynasties in the same town but also regional politics, everyone can at some point be eligible for every job in the game except for the Emperor/King itself, so while you are climbing the political and economic ladders your opponents and friends in other dynasties will be doing the same, it helps keep the game competitive as it wont take long for you and others to carve battle lines throughout the town (You and your allied Dynasties vs the others).
The game with the expansion pack which is part of the Gold edition allows for a variety of careers to play with, some are downright impossible to play due to being at the mercy of the marketplace or the one place that you and 5 other dynasties are buying stock from while others are so laughably easy that once you have several of these businesses running you only need to focus on politics or underhanded methods to screw around with other dynasties.
But as this is quite an old game it does have its problems, Gold does work on Windows 7 but for some it requires changing the desktop to 16bit to actually play, the game (as well as its sequels) were notoriously buggy at release and while the current final version of gold to my knowledge is bug free keep an eye out while playing as well as save often.
All in all a very enjoyable and comfy game, definitely worth a buy so you can chill out and build your business as the seasons roll on by.

During the Second World War, out of every 100 airmen who joined RAF Bomber Command, 45 were killed, 6 were seriously wounded and 8 became Prisoners of War.
Cute artstyle aside, this game stays pretty true to its historical inspiration by being f*cking nails hard. Enemy fighters come in thick and fast, flak shreds your fuselage and your crate drinks fuel faster than a thirsty man - making it back to your airfield is a genuine struggle and it's pretty damn fun. I do think the game could benefit from a bit of balancing however, as progress grinds to a halt if you get shot down and lose a decently levelled crew and plane. Although I appreciate it's supposed to be punishing, not having the money to upgrade everything again and being forced to fly missions underlevelled until you can grind your way back does suck the fun out of the experience.
It would also be nice if the devs added an option for your crew to exercise a tiny bit more autonomy - when I use an engineer to repair something which is damaged, it'd be great if he made his own way back to his station once repairs are complete rather than just standing there admiring his handiwork. Same deal for your gunners; maybe instead of point blank refusing to engage enemy fighters until you target them yourself, they could fire at will albeit with a damage or accuracy penalty until you're able to step in. I'd also love to know what the point of the mid-altitude option is - soon as you hit it your navigator gets lost. Annoying.
Minor balance gripes aside, I do rather like this game - the presentation is excellent, the core gameplay loop enjoyable and the customisation is engaging.

Bomber Crew offers great fun for a reasonable price.
The objective is to complete bombing raids against the enemy, earning you two currencies: Cash and R&D. These allow you to upgrade and develop your crews equipment and a wide range of components on your Lancaster Bomber, increasing your survivability and effectiveness throughout the campaign.
Initially you must decide where your priorities lay, this is WAR after all! Do you purchase hi-altitude gear for your bomber crew and avoid the majority of the enemy fighters, or let them freeze half-to-death at their posts? Or should you instead leave the fate of the crew up to Jerry and focus on the aircraft? Installing a more formidable arsenal of turrets will certainly allow you to reach out and touch the enemy aces when they come for you, but your Lancaster will end up being more of a "flying mattress" than a "flying fortress" without a stronger fusilage! Choices, choices! And that's before you even get to grips with the concept of aviation weight limit restrictions, hurah!
What if the worst comes to the worst and you have to bail out? Should you bring that Parachute this time just in case, or stick with the unsued Fire Extinguisher, just in case, you get struck by lightning? (note: this can actually happen). The period of existential crisis between not having enough money to really allow for these things early on, makes for some tense moments and gives you a real appreciation when you can finally afford not to worry about such trivial things...
In parallel to the main campaign missions, there are a number of other (only slightly repetative imo) raids and sorties that allow you to earn some cash and R&D with proportionate levels of risk and reward. These range from supply drops, intel gathering, intercept and support missions and standard bombing raids. Sometimes these non-critial missions will also offer an indirect reward by debuffing the enemy over the following two missions, which also stack, (e.g. Do less damage, have weaker armour, reduce flak effectiveness, etc). It's worth taking into consideration which of these debuffs will help you the most and queue them up before launching the toughest campaign missions. After all, you're only one Bomber Crew against squadrons of Luftwaffe!..
Bomber Crew also offers a lot of technical depth when it comes to expanding your tactical & strategic horizons... Eventually... Whether that's high-altitude "Zoom and boom" with emphasis on the zoom, or a more prolonged engagement with enough stamina to outlast the enemy... Initially however, your new recruits are restricted in their ability to do their job by their skill level. This leads to a bit of a linear experience. While arguably this is good for a first time player, as it helps to acclimatise (if you'll pardon the pun) them to the ways of engagement and evasion in the air, once you have previously experienced the difference that higher level crew members can make, (i.e. New game or new crew) you can be left feeling very restricted and frustraited.
Custom map markers for self navigation in particular is my personal gripe, surely that should be a mandatory prerequisite for being hired as a navigator, not an advanced skill that only unlocks after several missions? You're an aircraft, not a train.  Each of the other crew members have their own subconcious, pre-unlocked ability to function in their role, the navigator could do with a rework in that regard imo. That one point aside though, the skill tree for each role is well thought out and can all-to-often be the difference between returning home safe and losing it all...
I'm currently about 2/3 of the way through the game progress bar and have enjoyed my experience so far on the whole. I'm a fan of the XCOM series and this is in the same vein in some ways, as much as it is with FTL or Kerbal Space Program... Bomber Crew has scratched an itch for a fun, WW2 themed, bomber based simulation-manager-type game and the Developers should certainly be commended for their work. If youre thinking of getting it, its nothing you will regret due to poor craftsmenship on their part. Due to the low-poly fidelity of the game I would amateurishly assume that there could be potential for further iterations of this, perhaps a Pacific Theatre DLC focussing on the USAF in a B-25 or B-17 or something along those lines? So could be worth waiting for announcements if further development could swing it for you.
Overall, in response to some of the comments in the "not recommended" reviews, i would respond with this: Bomber Crew can be a bit difficult and frustraiting at times, but when you look at how many people bought Cup Head, you realise that it's a part of it's charm. And after all, Bomber Command and the RAF we're against higher odds than you face in this game and they made it look easy!

Update:
As of today's patch (27th Oct) I can say that most of my gripes with the game are gone. I really, really, really recommend playing this game - you won't be disappointed!
Original:
I wish that Steam would offer a better rating system then 'yes' and 'no'.
I really love this game, I've been following it since I first noticed it a while ago and I've been looking forward to its release. I bought it as soon as it came out and I played it a fair bit, it's a lot like FTL but with - in my opinion - far better pacing to a certain extent.
I'll start with the bad, because there isn't really much that I dislike. In terms of things that matter, I think the balancing could do with a bit of work. Your plane gets really, really messed up really quickly by aces and large groups of enemy fighters which is to be expected, but the frequency at which those planes appear can be really difficult to manage. It's not so bad if you manage to somehow keep the same plane all the way through because you'll be able to easily upgrade its components to handle that, and your crew will be experienced enough to take down planes in just a few bursts.
If, however, you lose your plane then you're in for a pretty rough ride. The same can be said for your crew - the worst case scenario is losing both. When your crew dies you'll have to hire new ones to replace them, the game kindly gives them a rank before you hire them (i.e. they'll be level 3 in navigation) so you don't have to start over from the very beginning but to be honest it might be better to start a new game anyway, as the grind is punishingly difficult. Going out on missions where aces appear almost constantly with a crew that has little-to-no armour or experience is a waste of a plane, but those missions are the only ones that give you enough money to get anywhere unless you want to grind the short and easy missions which, if you're unlucky, also might have an ace.
I realise that writing that I make the game sound far worse than it is - it IS a roguelike and it IS meant to be hard, I totally understand that and losing my crew and my plane should punish me for sure, but I think that the sheer amount of hostile planes and the money you get from doing missions in combination with losing all the gear and some plane upgrades is pretty tough to handle. Ideally, I'd prefer to start over if that's the case and I know that some others will agree with me.
The other thing I don't like too much is the lack of missions to do, you'll find yourself running the same 3 missions apart from the critical missions (which you can attempt as many times as you want, but if you succeed then you can't replay it). More missions would be really cool, performing missions with other AI planes such as fighter escorts or even other bombers would be pretty fun as well, I think.
In terms of things that don't matter, I think there could be more liveries or the ability to paint our own liveries. You can create your own wing and nose paints which is awesome, though, so here's hoping we can paint our planes ourselves later on!
Now, with the bad out of the way, I can guarantee that everthing else is great - it plays well, it's fun, you're never just sitting there just watching things happen, the upgrades feel very different to one another, the aesthetic is lovely and I really enjoy how chaotic everything can get in just a matter of seconds.
tl;dr things to take away:
- The game is very harsh with its punishments. It's like playing FTL on hard except you can't tone it down.
- There isn't a lot of variation in missions except for the unique critical missions, which you can only successfully complete once.
- If you don't plan on restarting after you lose your plane and/or crew, then you're in for one hell of a grind.
- Taking the bad things into account, the game is still really fun and really enjoyable to play. The upgrades are rewarding, dropping bombs is fun as hell, and watching as your gunners tear apart enemy planes is really nice.
- Also the damage models are beautifully done.
Overall: the game is fun, but I think that it could do with some balance adjustments for those who lose their plane and crew. I'd give it a 7/10, if Steam would allow more than 2 recommendation options.

This game is insane. Utterly utterly insane.

I put nearly five hours into this game, and finished the early access in one sitting. I'm genuinely disappointed there's not more to play yet.

However, the game is not without its faults too.
In the obligatory sewer level, there is a conversation with an NPC that triggers at a certain point. I was mobbed by zombies and died before the end of the conversation, and reloaded. This time, the conversation didn't trigger, and I spent a full 45 minutes in the sewer, attempting to find an exit that apparently only appears after the conversation has finished.
In the WW2 level, the enemy soldiers will sometimes run around in circles when you shoot them. I'm not sure if this is satirising dodgy AI, or is actually dodgy AI.
Overall, none of the problems are deal-breakers; and the game itself is full of dark, quirky humour, interesting concepts, and fast-paced, fun gameplay.
Worth every penny.

Early acces is a tricky proposition, so whenever you are tempted to buy one of those games there´s a little hesitation involved.  This is a game that tries to take old styles of FPS gaming to the front and add a modern sensibility, this usually is a complicated affair because the shooting is the easy part, is one of the most elemental forms of interaction in game design, what usually feels off about this kind of endeavours is the movement, the way you move in the game world is bastly different, if you are old enough you can  remember it, and usually there´s a disonance in what you remember and what you feel playing a game that tries to infuse modern movement in retro shooters and it can lead to some dissatisfaction, there´s some of this in Bedlam too, is unavoidable to an extent, but the game succeds in its graphic presentation and you can find your self smiling remembering old exploits.
The acting is pretty good, the weapons feel good to shoot for the most part, there´s some rough edges of course, but the game runs pretty well overall, right now you can easily end the game in under three hours, but the devs are pretty active in the forums and they are adding content, they have announced two more worlds, and are polishing the existing ones, i truly enjoyed my time with it and hope to continue doing it with the next additions, so far no regrets with this game, but remember is early access and if you have any caveats with it you may want to wait for the finished version, i for sure plan to keep playing and replaying it

Machinarium is an adventure game with a more than charming art style. It has got its fair share of challenging puzzles but for the experienced fan of adventure games should get through those as well. The game has a simple, yet charming storyline and a hand full of quirky, but lovable charakters. Most interesting point of this game is, that it needs absolutely no dialogue and still anyone should be able to understand it. In the end I think, the sellingpoint of this game is the interesting art style. If you are the type of gamer who enjoys that kind of thing, this game is a must have. If you expect another monkey island or broken sword, I wouldn't recommend it.

An "indie" game from before they were cool, Machinarium combines creative point and click tasks with excellent puzzles that briefly pop you out of the point and click interface to solve problems similar to classic real world mind benders like unhook the horeshoe/nails puzzle (but not that).  It wraps all this up in an immersive world of decrepit technology and cute little sentient robots.  One thing that works well in this game is the complete absence of dialog.  And I don't mean just spoken dialog - there is no spoken or written language at all.  The story and game progression is communicated through hand drawn diagrams and trail and error.  The game is entirely in flash, so your controls are usually limited to left mouse button and mouse movement.  Although, the game has a built in hint system comprised of a very short SHMUP sequence that allows you to use the keyboard.  Strangely an end game action sequence forced me to use mouse control which was the only real point where I experienced significant frustration while playing the game.
Overall, this game is easy to recommend even at full price.  The puzzles are challenging but not frustrating and the pace of self discovery is excellent for a point and click game.  The art style really makes you feel like you are discovering a new world, and invites you to participate in it with its quirky characters.

All the puzzles are truly unique and entertaining, some are also really hard.

Great story, great visuals, royally messed up by horrid gameplay and the developers being dishonest.
For the two most important points:
1. This game is incomplete. Unfinished. The long description mentions that by saying trilogy, but no other part of the Steam page even hints at this just being the first 3 hours of a story that'll take two more games to be completed. Given that The Fall was released 2014, that's gonna be a while. Wouldn't mind this if they made it unmissably clear on the Steam page, but they don't, and i don't reward dishonesty of this kind with recommendations.
2. The combat is unbelievably ♥♥♥♥♥♥. The controls are a very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥port from console controls (to the point that they actually still talk about "sticks" in the game), and the (luckily) few times you find yourself in combat the controls will work against you by keeping you from aiming, and by keeping you stuck behind boxes while 1-hit-kill enemies shamble up to you. And to top it off, the final boss fight requires the player to realize something is shootable that hasn't been shootable in a similar form anywhere else in the game.
The whole thing is sorta salvaged by the voice work, the story, the graphics, and the puzzles. In fact, the game would get a glowing recommendation from me if it were a relaxing story-focused puzzle adventure. I loved every second i wasn't engaged in combat, and the story was extremely engaging.
But as it is, i can only see average people being extremely frustrated by the sheer difficulty presented in getting through this game, and very disappointed by an incomplete ending.
Devs, in case you read your reviews still: I'm willing to change my opinion on this if you add god mode cheats to make the combat irrelevant, and make it unmissably clear that this is the first small part of a larger story, with no conclusion to be had.

DCUO is a little bipolar about its pay structure- it's free/microtransactions/subscription. The subscription is for multiple games, though, so certainly work it if you also play Planetside 2 or other Sony games. The microtransactions and DLCs are enticing, but not required for enjoying the game.To be honest, I never felt like the game was limiting me as a free player. I did have lots of cool content dangled in front of me that was paid content, but I could always keep playing for free with PLENTY of options and new gear and powers being unlocked in-game around every corner.
Getting a DLC is worth it just to raise your character, inventory, and money caps. You could still easily play and have fun for months before running out of quests on a free character, and you could then just start a new character with one of the 5 other mentors to get a whole new set of quests. The versitility of this game is wonderful. Character customization in this game blows me away compared to other games, even CoH.
If you are willing to pay for extra content, there are always new DLCs coming out with new powers and storylines. The DLCs are inexpensive and go on sale quite often.
Downside: the game takes up massive hard drive space. 20GB local storage. I couldn't do it on console because of that. Also, some of the features seem incomplete, such as an awkward and possibly broken chat system, poor voice chat options, and R&D items that seem to have no function in the game. I can deal with these because they can easily be ignored and at best are promises for future systems that might actually work.

So with a mediocre gameplay, surely the story would be its saving grace?
Nope.
The story, while midly amusing, is basically a "what if" plot for Resident Evil 2 and 3, and it's not very good. The only "oohs" and "ahs" you'll get are from the cameos of other characters in the series.
Overall: Unless you're a die-hard Resident Evil fan, then you're better off saving your money. The mediocrity of this game isn't worth it.

Type of Game:
Virtual Board Game
Version Played:
PC version through Steam
Similar Games:
Settlers of Catan, Risk, and to a lesser degree Monopoly
The Good:
An exact replica of the board game version, which means that the players get the same engrossing and competitive game they would play on a board
A wonderful multiplayer game (when it works – see below) that balances different strategy mechanics
Race and special power cards can really change the way that each gaming session is played and will also change the player’s choices
It is really nice not having to pull out all the physical pieces of the game to play a quick round with a friend
Being able to play against other players on different platforms ( iPad, Android, & Kindle Fire) is a definite plus
“Turn-by-turn” is a neat feature that lets players play their turns without having all players present. You can exit the game and continue at a later time once your opponent has finished their turn
Steam has a notification pop up when it’s the player’s turn
The Bad:
The online multiplayer is bugged and glitchy, which leads to dropped games and nonstarters
Seeing as most players will be picking up this game to play with friends, it seems as if it could have done with some more quality assurance testing in the online multiplayer department
The overall user interface is clunky and not very intuitive
Trying to get a game going has far too many steps and the lengthy registration requirements seem unnecessary
Sound design is awful and really could have helped with the immersion should some decent music and sound effects been utilized
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
Absolutely. Had a good time playing locally with my seven year old.
Did I make time to complete it?:
I played and finished five multiplayer games. I would have played a lot more, had the online multiplayer not had so many issues.
Recommended Purchase Price:
The gameplay is a blast just like the board game, but the online problems really hinder the overall experience. I applaud Days of Wonder for implementing the oft-requested feature for video game versions of board games (so many come out with just local play), but just wish they’d spent more time fixing the infrastructure before releasing the game.
