Let me start out by saying it is fun. I like the whole plane customisation thing and the leveling of the crew. Also equiping the crew with specific gear that makes thier job easier is really motivating.
But then the parts that really suck:
1) It is unreasonably hard. The game has you doing several actions at a time and at many occasions is just overwhelming, even unfair. This results in more frustration than a feeling of succes, let alone control.
Solution: A pause button and allowing to give commands during the game being paused
2) Managing the plane and the crew is more of a chore than that it adds to the gameplay in most situations. Why do I need to tell the gunner to get more ammo instead of the halfwitted idiot going to get it himself? I understand that I need to tell a crew member to help out an injured  buddy, no problem there but the whole ammo getting part is just stupid (Yes, there is an upgrade so the turret can't run out of ammo but it is stupid to have the player need to tell the crew to get more ammo, that is basic desicion making skills that a gunner can think of himself). The fact that the gunner is gone from his seat is already a drawback, no need to make it more than it already is by having to hold his hand all the way.
3) The part where I, as the player, need to mark the enemy planes for shooting is a bit over the top. It is already bad enough I can't give them a specific target to shoot at but having me mark the things before any of the gunners open fire on them is just silly.
4) Navigation is also rather annoyingly implemented. I really would like to have the option to give the plane a heading myself without having to wait for a node to pop up which I need to focus on for a few seconds before the plane changes course (this really get's to be terrible when in a fight and the gunners needing you to tell them to reload, having a injured crew member that needs help and a fire breaking out that needs attention. that is the game just taking a huge  ♥♥♥♥♥♥  in my face imo). It is even made worse by the flipping plane taking route through enemy fire instead of the player being able to set a straight route out of there. Just give the player that option with a cooldown or something...!!!
All by all I find this game more punishing than rewarding. It is unfair to the point where things feel like the motivation of being able to upgrade the plane or your gear is not weighing up against the BS the game puts you through.
It is a ♥♥♥♥ing shame I have played too many hours to find this out and can't get a refund for this great idea terribly executed.

For anyone that remembers cannonfodder, this is just for you. Dont let the cute art fool you, this game is hardcore. You have 7 people to micromanage whilst priortising between targetting enemy fighters, or dealing with one of the many potentially devasting effects currently afflictling your ship ranging from failing hydraulics (landing gear/bomb doors/ gun turrets wont work), electrical failure (radar etc wont work), running out of ammo, fires in any number of locations, or one of your crew carelessly getting themselves shot.
I love the pacing of the game and the fact there is no tactical pause option. Your decisions and actions are made in real time, you hesitate someone can and will die. You need to prioritise which of the above issues to deal with first, whilst also trying to complete the objective which is the whole point of being in the sky in the first place.
You will feel like you could do with a few extra crew members, as each one needs to multi task which adds to feeling of real pressure. You can level up your crew, which makes it unfortunate if one or all your crew get kia, but you can upgrade your plane and crew to improve their likelihood of survival.
The game is thematically spot on and for anyone who was even remotely partial to cannonfodder, or enjoys micro management sims this is definitely worth a try.

The oddest game design decisions.
Imagine FTL without the pause function or pacing. Imagine having to direct the crew that you have in the weapons bay to an Ammo cache a few feet away everytime you fire a misssle. Imagine doing that while also combating more than one ship.
Unfortunatly Bomber Crew trades in gameplay, for busy work.
I really wanted to love this game as it seemed like an awesome cross over of FTL (333hours in FTL) and WW2 in a good looking shell shaded 3d format. Unfortunetly it suffers from far too many minor horrible game design decisions that they glaringly take over. The game lacks pacing, the ability to slow down time when marking things out for your crew or a pause function would be the difference between night and day. Pressing space and slowing down the game to 0.25% would be a fine game feature. It would also make the game more suspenseful and give you time to actually take the visuals of the game in. Unfortunely whats left is not neccesarily frustration but indifference as you try and navigate each crews memebers personal UI.
TLDR; Game misses the point between crew interaction and crew busy work. There is a good game here a few design changes I'd certainly come back and give it another go, unfortunatly there's just better already out there. At this point I couldn't honestly recommend Bomber Crew.

-Good if you would like a nice little change of pace, but missing the variety and details to keep it from becoming a repetitive grind.-
So in this game you recruit a team of 7 crew in order to staff your Lancaster bomber as it flys sorties over the English Channel.  These missions play out in a strategic fashion where you guide the action, but have relatively little direct control over the action.   For instance, you don't steer the plane, but can direct the pilot to target a High, medium, or low altitude, or instuct him to perform specific emergency maneuvers.   The gunners perform a similar role where you identify the targets, but the gunners do the actualy aiming and firing.
Each mission really plays out the same way, you spend a couple minutes taking off and navigating to you intended destination (thankfully there's a fast-forward time feature), but ultimately each mission is a collection of varying amounts of ground flak, enemy fighters, and the occasional enemy aces that attempt to tear your bomber appart.
The combat is pretty rewarding, with chunks and bits of your plane coming appart as you try to manage to keep you gunners firing and keeping your crew alive while still managing to drop your few bombs, snap a couple intelligence photos, or both.   It can get pretty hectic, and it is worth it to point out that combat needs to be managed in real-time, as there is no pause function when managing your crew in combat.
If things go poorly however, a number of disasters can befall your merry band of sky warriors, and more often than not, can result in the downing of your plane with the loss of all hands.  You are then greeted in the post game synopsis of your mission with your number of MIA/KIA crewman, and your plane returned to a base level.  Save scumming might be the only saving grace of losing a plane with all hands, as the number of missions you will need to do starting from scratch to get back to an operational level capable of doing the later missions just isn't worth the grind.
The biggest mark against the game is the implementation of the crew.  As you complete missions, each crewmember levels up, unlocking extra skills, some of which are pretty essential to the more complicated missions  (a leveled pilot in particular is pretty indispensible).   The game wants you to care about the fates of your crew, however they are essentially little buckets of experience points that are rather painful to replace.   Even when recruiting replacements, it really doesnt matter who you pick, as their stat differences are small enough to be less than a basic pair of boots will provide.  In a game where losing one of your crew is designed to be a painful but memorable event,  there is curiously little to care about other that how long it's going to take to train a replacement back up to par.   There are no kill counts, statistics for sorties flown, or rap sheets detailing the missions accomplished for your fallen airman.
Other missed opportunities are the lack of additional bomber types (B17 in particular with a different payload and gunner crew would slot well here).  I would also like to see more emphasis placed on running different strategies for sorties.   Having to switch to a less armored, stripped down bomber in orderto make a high-altitude, stealthy night incursion would go a long way toward changing up the missions, however weight management of the bomber is largely rendered useless by simply upgrading engines, which allows you to armor up your bomber with little trade-off as there doesn't seem to be much sophistication to fuel-management/range beyond making sure your landing gear is up and the bomb bay doors are closed.

If you haven't played the 1996 Resident Evil, please, at least try it. The experience is way better if you remember the old mansion and it's old scares and puzzles.
I still don't know how they did it, but Capcom managed to make the best remake of a game ever. I realize it's a subjective opinion, but I guess everyone who played the original had a blast when playing this one.
It did what a remake should do, in my opinion, and went beyond. They remade all the graphics and audio, added new rooms while changing the design of others, included a side story that unravels as you play it and remade some puzzles while tweaking others and adding new ones. All the while, playing with expectations of players of the first one.
It's the same old school Resident Evil survival horror, but with added unexpected challenges and not as cringy dialogue. In my opinion, compared to the original, the bosses are easier, but the whole game is harder.
Inventory and ammo management, puzzles and manual limited saves are the staples of this series first generation so, if you don't like any of those, it's better if you skip it.
The only bad thing about this version is some the backgrounds. While Resident Evil 0 had the beautiful bagrounds rerendered at a higher resolution, this one had the original 2002 backgrounds upscaled, and it's really jarring, because they also put some really bad filters on it.
Warning, though. If you have a weak CPU, it might play at a low frame rate, because of the strange way that it renders the upscaled backgroungs in lower monitor resolutions.

The Fall is an interesting short adventure story where you're the AI of a powersuit trying to find a medic so you can help the human unconscious in your suit. You're stuck on a planet in an abandoned robot-creation complex, and along the way you befriend the facility's glitchy AI and try to thwart the facility's even glitchier security AI. This is frustrating, because the premise is amaaaazing - but the execution is shoddy. I know they're all logical AIs acting according to their programming, but they feel like they're trying to be as unhelpful as possible in every given situation. The facility itself is a joke - why on earth would you need to walk robots through sitcom-esque training situations? Can't you run a simulation with their programming or something? But I digress.
My quibbles with the story aside, the gameplay is bad. It's 2D exploration - run with WASD, use the mouse to look around - but you have to clunkily mouse over things with your flashlight, and it's just...awkward as you hunt for hotspots. I'd forgive this if the rest of the game were worth it, but the gameplay is adventure game puzzles: rub objects against each other until things unlock. Find new hotspots. Repeat, repeat, repeat. That's boring! It forces the game to rely entirely on the story to carry itself, and as I just said, the story is bad.
But....let me be fair, for a moment. I did enjoy the protagonist AI's stubbornness and pride. I was bothered by the final events in the game. I am curious about the sequel, whenever it drops. The graphics are pleasantly dark and spooky, with darkened silhouettes for everything. I enjoyed it, at first, before I got far enough in to be bored, and primus above the puzzles did not help. Not fun.
One last thing: the combat is tacked on, bad, and there to waste your time. Press shift to hide behind cover, aim to shoot, blah blah it's really bad.

If you're sick of the typical "modern" space strategy game, Solar War may well be your game.
Many modern space strategy games are designed around the principle of adding eye candy while removing mechanics. Solar War goes the opposite direction, using fairly minimal graphics while, at the same time, focusing on creating meaningful strategic and tactical decisions.
Here are just a handful of the things that happen in Solar War:
-Planets orbit at different speeds, so attack paths naturally open and close over time.
-Sometimes the heat sinks get shot off your ships, and you'll have to decide what systems to keep active, and how long to keep them active for, so that your ship can keep functioning as well as possible without overheating.
-Who gets the command position: the most competent person, or the person from the nation that contributes a lot of your funding and is thinking of cutting it?
-There's an enemy ship behind you. You designed your ship with front arc weapons, armor concentrated at the front of the ship, and thrusters optimized for speed rather than maneuverability. Now what?
The focus here is definitely more on tactics and ship design, with economics more of a consequence of battle outcomes than anything else. The economic game is not trivial by any means; the typical "build everything everywhere" strategy of many 4x will not work here, and the officer management and internal Earth politics sometimes require a good bit of thought. But it is in the ship design and the (turn-based, tactical) combat that the game really shines.
No, it's not flawless. Replayability is limited compared to more heavily randomized games, there's no multiplayer, and there are some cheesy strategies that the opponent has a hard time dealing with. And yes, it does look like what you see in the screenshots-- you can pick from a few things, but the overall appearance is pretty minimal. But, despite its flaws, it manages to be what many modern space strategy fail to be, namely, interesting.
Oh, and: if you thought the Antaran fleet in MoO2 was a bit of a letdown as an end-game boss fight, try taking down Solar War's alien mothership in direct combat. It's a pretty crazy fight.

This game is the digital adaptation of a board game that I had never played, so I was a little skeptical about purchasing it; and if I didn't have friends with which I could play the game, I probably would have regretted my purchase.  However, this game does something that most other Digital/Steam board-games don't: it pushes notifications.
During your game-play, you have a choice as to whether or not you actually want to be present.  You and your friends (I would not recommend purchasing this game for the single player) can play the game "live" or you can complete your turn and log off.  Your friends will have 48 hours to complete their turn before forfeiting the game.  This 48 hour window allows you to have a very "Words with Friends" style of game-play, giving you a 3-5 minute window of board game into your otherwise packed video gaming schedule.  You simply wait for Steam to alert you whenever its your turn, and you go about your business.
The actual game rules are pretty straight forward.  The rules are kind-of-sort-of similar to RISK, but with an element of randomness that prevents static strategies.  Every player selects a race with a random special power every game, and while the race bonuses stay static, the special powers are randomly assigned every game.  This can, unfortunately, lead to some relatively overpowered combinations; but so far I haven't encountered anything that has completely dominated the game.
Unfortunately, the Steam integration needs some work though.  While it does, for the most part, link a "Days of Wonder" account with your "Steam Account" (which raises some concerns), it does not import any of your friends.  So you must manually add buddies, who may not have the same Days of Wonder handle, and then invite them into a game through the game's multiplier console.  Once a game is created, players do not receive a notification that they've been invited until it is their turn.  You cannot invite players through the Steam Overlay.  As many accolades as the game got for the notifications, it lost for the lackluster integration.

I have mixed feelings, but overall I think it's a worthwhile experience with some clever story-telling and memorable characters.  This is first and foremost an RPG, unlike the  second and third renditions; where combat feels more streamlined to a wider audience and variety of platform. [Consoles]  The best comparison I can think of from personal experience is the way the combat contrasted between Fallout 3 and 4.  The latter requiring more dexterity and aim instead of pure timing of clicks and proper use of combat styles.  In fact,  Witcher 1 may have more appeal to a classic dice-rolling RPGer; who-may enjoy knowing when and how to use the combination of styles, signs, and alchemy Geralt has at his disposal.
As far as the gameplay goes, well, that's where it gets figuratively and literally murky in my opinion.  I absolutely loved and hated the beginning of the game.  It was unrelenting and boring and yet somehow getting through it felt sort of rewarding by the end.  It starts to feel more tolerable; once you're done grinding it out in the mud n' muck of the early phase.
Some quests are eye-opening, but ultimately a waste of time in comparison to the real meat of the game. The characters are often brilliant, dark, and simulatenously comedic.  I'm still debating if all of the humor is intentional, but the antagonists' in this game are sometimes... Well, you'll see, oh yes, you'll see.  *cackles*
Witcher will challenge you and provide a sense of accomplishment.  I used to be an antagonist of companies putting arrows all over the mini-map - telling me exactly where to go - but I don't mind following a guidance system when time is of essence in my waking life.  Going back to the Witcher made me realize how much of gaming has evolved.  Fast travel?  Not quite.
Again, this is a more linear, classic RPG experience. This is an absolute positive for some even if it can sometimes be a nuisance or not as intuitive as modern games.
One could argue the ingenuity of our classic games are simply being reskinned and squeezed dry at the expense of the consumer.  Yes, no, and it depends on the game and obviously the preference of the player. There's some things in the newer games I prefer and some aspects to the older games I wouldn't mind seeing again - like difficulty. (Edit: Dark Souls I have not tried yet, but hear it fills this void for some.)  Reskinning isn't necessarily bad, either:  Imagine, Jedi Knight II with new graphics, yet the same core and addictive saber-battle gameplay.  The formula was balanced and fun. No need to reinvent the wheel there.  Will it make as much money?  Well, maybe not initially, but a good reputation and a game that has actual substance empowers a company and creates loyal fans instead.  Better to lose a bit now and have a legacy to be proud of later.
*casts Axii sign*  I knew you'd agree.
The hope is these games many grew up with and developers going into the industry are allowed room to breath and create a variety of games not constrained by the de facto or industry standards.
In other words, we're gonna need a Witcher!
Word of Caution:  It may go without saying, but if there ever was a M-rating appropriate game - this is it.  Not for the faint of heart or incredibly young.  Although, I find Geralt often has rational choices, and seems to convey a sort of morale lesson if one so chooses a more paragon path.  Geralt often comes across as the most compassionate character on the screen; if you are able to look past the blood dripping from his steel and silver.

This game and its predecessor are two very underappreciated games.
There is quite a bit of strategy involved to meet the different goals every level.  Do you build-and-flip to get quick cash? Or build-and-rent for steady income? Do you acquire new properties or upgrade your current holdings? etc., etc.
This sequel's biggest addition is the concept of curb appeal. Certain improvements increase curb appeal, as well as neigboring installations like parks.  Other buildings such as workships and oil rigs can decrease the curb appeal of neighbors.  More often than not, your goal for a level will include increasing the appeal of the neighborhood overall.
Everything is so well balanced. The oddest game design decisions.
Imagine FTL without the pause function or pacing. Imagine having to direct the crew that you have in the weapons bay to an Ammo cache a few feet away everytime you fire a misssle. Imagine doing that while also combating more than one ship.
Unfortunatly Bomber Crew trades in gameplay, for busy work.
I really wanted to love this game as it seemed like an awesome cross over of FTL (333hours in FTL) and WW2 in a good looking shell shaded 3d format. Unfortunetly it suffers from far too many minor horrible game design decisions that they glaringly take over. The game lacks pacing, the ability to slow down time when marking things out for your crew or a pause function would be the difference between night and day. Pressing space and slowing down the game to 0.25% would be a fine game feature. It would also make the game more suspenseful and give you time to actually take the visuals of the game in. Unfortunely whats left is not neccesarily frustration but indifference as you try and navigate each crews memebers personal UI.
TLDR; Game misses the point between crew interaction and crew busy work. There is a good game here a few design changes I'd certainly come back and give it another go, unfortunatly there's just better already out there. At this point I couldn't honestly recommend Bomber Crew.

So in this game you recruit a team of 7 crew in order to staff your Lancaster bomber as it flys sorties over the English Channel.  These missions play out in a strategic fashion where you guide the action, but have relatively little direct control over the action.   For instance, you don't steer the plane, but can direct the pilot to target a High, medium, or low altitude, or instuct him to perform specific emergency maneuvers.   The gunners perform a similar role where you identify the targets, but the gunners do the actualy aiming and firing.
Each mission really plays out the same way, you spend a couple minutes taking off and navigating to you intended destination (thankfully there's a fast-forward time feature), but ultimately each mission is a collection of varying amounts of ground flak, enemy fighters, and the occasional enemy aces that attempt to tear your bomber appart.
The combat is pretty rewarding, with chunks and bits of your plane coming appart as you try to manage to keep you gunners firing and keeping your crew alive while still managing to drop your few bombs, snap a couple intelligence photos, or both.   It can get pretty hectic, and it is worth it to point out that combat needs to be managed in real-time, as there is no pause function when managing your crew in combat.
If things go poorly however, a number of disasters can befall your merry band of sky warriors, and more often than not, can result in the downing of your plane with the loss of all hands.  You are then greeted in the post game synopsis of your mission with your number of MIA/KIA crewman, and your plane returned to a base level.  Save scumming might be the only saving grace of losing a plane with all hands, as the number of missions you will need to do starting from scratch to get back to an operational level capable of doing the later missions just isn't worth the grind.
The biggest mark against the game is the implementation of the crew.  As you complete missions, each crewmember levels up, unlocking extra skills, some of which are pretty essential to the more complicated missions  (a leveled pilot in particular is pretty indispensible).   The game wants you to care about the fates of your crew, however they are essentially little buckets of experience points that are rather painful to replace.   Even when recruiting replacements, it really doesnt matter who you pick, as their stat differences are small enough to be less than a basic pair of boots will provide.  In a game where losing one of your crew is designed to be a painful but memorable event,  there is curiously little to care about other that how long it's going to take to train a replacement back up to par.   There are no kill counts, statistics for sorties flown, or rap sheets detailing the missions accomplished for your fallen airman.
Other missed opportunities are the lack of additional bomber types (B17 in particular with a different payload and gunner crew would slot well here).  I would also like to see more emphasis placed on running different strategies for sorties.   Having to switch to a less armored, stripped down bomber in orderto make a high-altitude, stealthy night incursion would go a long way toward changing up the missions, however weight management of the bomber is largely rendered useless by simply upgrading engines, which allows you to armor up your bomber with little trade-off as there doesn't seem to be much sophistication to fuel-management/range beyond making sure your landing gear is up and the bomb bay doors are closed.

So I love this game. It is difficult, requires actual brain power, and is fairly balanced. The biggest complaint people are having is that the game is too unforgiving, forcing the player to micromanage a lot and essentially has a permanent death mechanic, where losing crew and your plane is a VERY bad thing. While I can understand these complaints, they are very easily remedied by simple planning, doing the easier missions a few more times than normal, and patience. I would say patience is the number one skill needed in this game, and if you do not have it initially, the death mechanics will surely smack you around. The crew is super valuable, the plane is valuable, so why would you rush critical missions or attempt to do every mission with an ace in it?
Another complaint I can completely understand is the difficulty of some of the aces. A few could be considered OP, but once again, given proper planning and patience, you can always take them on with the proper upgrades and experienced crew.
Basically, this game has huge potential. It has a relatively steep learning curve, and admittedly kinda forces the player to play to the games mechanics, which some people are very disappointed with. Expect to lose a few crew members, maybe a plane or two, but learn from the mistakes and it will all be fine and dandy. I completed 25 missions before even attempting the first critical mission, and still failed on my first attempt, but loved every second of it.
On the topic of the micromanaging, yes it is a lot. Compared to other games, Bomber Crew has a ton of micromanagement. It does take some gettting used to, and I would recommend a few simple steps to make things a little easier:
-Adjust the Scan Mode sensitivity
-Upgrade Radar as quickly as possible
-Utilize crew abilities VERY OFTEN (Seriously, these things will save your a**)
-Use the crew panel to select crew members (Rather than hunting the plane for them)
-Use the number keys to select crew (Less mouse travel time results in quicker results)
- While you're zoomed out, you can hold [Shift] to temporarily bring up the interior of the bomber.
-If the time of day is not optimal, sit on the tarmac and advance time before taking off.
TL;DR
A great and challenging game that requires brain power, patience, and strategy. Harsh death mechanics kinda force the player to play a certain way, but only to a certain extent. Learning efficient micromanagement is critical to enjoying this game.

Based on the GameCube remake from 2002, Resident Evil HD Remaster is an admirable port to current gen consoles and PC. The remaster includes the original 4:3 ratio which displays the whole screen, with the 16:9 ratio zoomed in and the camera panning slightly up and down depending on which direction you walk in. The FMV cutscenes retain their original aspect ratio. Completing the game under certain conditions allow you to unlock hidden costumes (including some new ones previously unavailable on the GameCube original) and weapons, but probably the biggest addition is the inclusion of new game modes which only the most hardcore players will appreciate - Invisible enemies, anyone?
This isn't the most difficult or lengthy Resident Evil game, it has the usual cheesy dialogue and scare tactics. Overall, it's a great game for horror fans, and Resident Evil lovers in particular, and you'll certainly spend some time trying to unlock all the achievements in the games - who knew there could be so many endings?

I keep hoping Days of Wonder will improve, and they keep going in the other direction. For a free-to-play game port of a popular board game, this would be quite good. For its price, it's a bit of a letdown, still quite a few bugs (e.g.: complete crash when you accidentally send an empty chat message; random freezes), and clunky proprietary solutions that don't work as well with Steam as they should (no inviting your Steam buddies or joining their game, you need to register separately with DoW and then invite your friend player123456789xyz). The UI could use another patch or a few, and improved functionality, such as seamless switching, multiple instances running, not having the game overwrite your current action when something is happening in the game, more clarity on some functions and how to use them, less clunky, and for the Dragon's sake stop plastering ads for paid DLCs everywhere.
It's still a port of Small World, which is a fun board game in itself, and if this is the only way you get to play that game with your friends, you may want to put up with what you're getting for your money here.

I'm still of mixed minds about this game.  I've watched let's play on youtube and Wil Wheaton's Table Top review of it, and it looked like a lot of fun.  Thing is, I haven't had time to play this with others yet, and I wanted to really Learn the game first, so I've been playing only solo matches against the AI so far.  I expect when I finally start playing with others, I may like the game even more.
Basically this is a conquest board game for 2 to 5 players, any of which may be live opponents or AI.   A typical match shouldn't take even as much as a half hour and that's With the full complement of players.  The game rules and procedure resemble Risk somewhat, though in a fantasy setting rather than the real world.  It's all about conquering the world, though with a twist;  your 'army' only has a short lifespan and will inevitably be replaced by another army that you also control.  The goal is to build up gold units that you earn primarily at the end of your turn for holding territory, but also through special abilities your armies might have.  The armies are very diverse and represent fantasy races, from hobbits to skeletons, giants, and dwarves.  You get to pick which race you want to make 'active' but their abilities are randomized each game.
Strong replayability is built right in as no two games will ever play alike.  The graphics are decent, though the game map/board is a little 'busy' with all of the counters, symbols, borders, and artwork vying for space and That can make things a little confusing at times.  The music is fun and matches the light hearted tone set by the art style.
I don't have any major complaints, though I'm not fond of the nickle and dime aspect of the DLC.  It'd be nice if the developers had just bundled the dlcs rather than parcelled them out as they did, but I'm guessing it had something to do with rewards for the kickstarter investors.
TL:DR?  Bottom line, if you like board games that involve a good portion of luck, you should enjoy this.  It's easy to learn the basics but has enough 'meat' to make you want to invest some time in mastering the strategies.

This game for me is a simple combination of Master Of Orion ][ and Xcom Apocalypse. And when I say simple, I am talking about how easy it is to use, how simple but still beautiful and functional the graphics are, and also how much extra work could (and maybe should) be put into this game.
But the game is not simple when it comes to depth: you have a wide research "tree" and the game even takes visibility between planets and moons while they rotate around a sun or eachother into account.
The tactical part of the game however is a little bit too simple at the moment and I hope the developer will implement some or more of my ideas, or better ones :-). At this time, the tactical game is more or less shooting at eachother and coming closer to eachother. The only real tactical part of it is that you can choose which weapon you fire at which enemy. You don't need to fire everything at onces at one enemy (which the AI does if you use "AUTO RESOLVE"). An that makes the tactical part a bit boring at the moment. You need to play it yourself (not let the AI take over) or you lose too much, but it's not very exciting.

"So you've kicked alien invaders off Earth dozens of times, but always wondered what the next step would be?
Solar War gives you that scenario in a turn-based strategy game, combining some novel ideas with familiar concepts from different subgenres of classic strategy games. In the game, you will lead the effort to protect Earth from the aliens and battle them for control over the Solar System."
This actually sums it up pretty well. You play as the leader of earth's defenses, and your mission is to take over from where the Xcom boys left off.
Some good combinations of ideas here. The majority of the game takes place in a quasi-4X style strategic map that actually reminds me a lot more of Xenonauts or the older version of X-Com's  strategic map than an actual 4X game.  You have to get Earth's nations to provide you funding by meeting their needs (the U.S. likes you to be on the offensive all the time, Japan likes research, some nations only care if you put their officers in charge of ships, etc.), as well as building ships and defenses.
Fighting in done in the style of Master of Orion 2 (turn based, with a great deal of control over ship movement and weapons firing order), which is great, and also makes thinking about your ship and fleet designs important. It's a little management heavy initially (not so much once you get things set up), but that's something I kind of expect from games that play like this, so it's not much of a negative.
As everyone else has said, there aren't really any graphics, and there is no sound at present. I personally think the graphics fit the theme really well (you're a general looking at a map), though having different graphics for the ships would be nice - I don't mind the basic-ness of the display because it fits the game, but if you're going to have actual ships instead of representative radar dots, then there should be a bit of difference between how they look. I didn't really mind the lack of sound either because I usually play with it off unless required anyway - it's not exactly a demanding game on your system, and you can always play music in the background if you need some.
There's a few little menu things lacking (don't pay too much attention to what you find on youtube though, the UI has been made a bit friendlier since then), and a the tutorial just kind of drops off after giving the most basic of rundowns (though you can look most stuff up on the in game manual), but it's not really that hard of a game to get into from a 4X standpoint, or from a turn based tactical point of view either. It IS rather slow paced (I think, anyway. I feel like I'm perhaps not understanding the pacing properly), but that's not really a bad thing for this game and doesn't ruin the enjoyment.
All and all, it's probably the best 4X-lite tactical game I've played (maybe the only one). Only thing I'd really caution prospective buyers about is that this does not support all intel graphics setups - it is right there in the system requirements, but not something I noticed, and for the price, it's worth mentioning. That said, it's working fine on my intel laptop, but you may want to go try a demo or something to be sure before you buy,

I'm going to not recommend this game on a preliminary basis, not because I'm not enjoying it -- I am -- but there are some significant caveats that need to be said, or a number of people are going to be wasting their money.
First of all, there is no sound whatsoever in this game, which is very jarring. Secondly, the interface leaves much to be desired; controls don't always work as you might wish (in particular, the space bar sometimes acts as "pause" and sometimes acts as "click", meaning that for a while, if a popup happens, you may reflexively hit the spacebar and accidentally select whatever the default action is in the popup). Also, there is a fair amount of burrowing down and popping back up through popups, especially when shuffling officers around.
And there's a lot of that. This is the primary caveat: thus far, the game feels more like the logistics exercise of deciding who to promote and generally how run the admiralty, rather than the tactics of space combat. In other words, it plays a bit like dinking a spreadsheet. The thing is, I'm enjoying that process; so far, at least, there are enough interesting bells and whistles on the individual officers for me to want to build the perfect crew by proper career guidance. In that way, it reminds me a little of the class XCOM, more than it does of, say, Master of Orion (there is no exploration in this game).
One particular element that is unusual and highly satisfying to me is the mechanic of actual orbits. The entire battleground is simply the solar system, but there is no instantaneous travel (thus far?), meaning that the location of, say, the Earth relative to Mars or Jupiter matters, and changes over the course of the game. I don't know how realistic it is, but it's novel and adds a feeling of "reality" to the game that is often lacking in many similar games.
In general, the whole thing is lacking a lot of polish. I'm finding it a possible diamond in the rough -- satisfying, at least -- but I suspect that many people won't. Anyway, given that every last one of the reviews currently present is positive, I thought it best to add a note of warning to this. At the very least, buying this game should be done with eyes open.

When I first found out about Solar War, it immediately reminded me of the now obscure early 1990's Japanese series Regional Power by Cosmos Computer. With elements from early-type Romance of The Three Kingdoms and Civilization, the Regional Power games had left me wanting more of the same. So when I came across Solar War, it was with some excitement and trepidation - had I finally found a game I had been wanting to play but that had either not existed or lain undiscovered?
+Unique gameplay
+Highly moddable
+/- One-man developer
-No music & minimal graphics
-High price
The best element about it is the unique gameplay.
First and foremost is the officer and crew management.
You assign officers to ships in one of four designated roles: captain (Leadership), tactical, navigation, or engineering. All officers have stats in those four categories, and are enhanced or adversely affected by the captain's leadership.
All the officers have ranks and can be promoted, and their rank enables/disables certain roles. They can also have skills and be awarded, amongst other things.
Ships also have a crew, separated into several ranks, that gain experience and can be reassigned.
You manage relations with the countries on Earth, research technologies, build and outfit ships, bases and colonies, not to mention battling aliens.
Another element that is very well done in Solar War is the moddability of the game.
It is accessible and wide in scope - just about everything is available within the xml files.
You could add new countries, random officers, unique officers, technologies, or make new scenarios, to name a few things.

However, for me at least, there came a point when the game rang a little bit hollow and this is probably due to the fact that Solar War is a one-man operation.
First off, there is no music whatsoever in the game.
Second, the graphics while serviceable in quality are minimal in quantity. For instance, the inclusion of officer portraits and battle scenes would have increased the entertainment factor by many times.
And third, the officers can end up just becoming a bunch of names. There are a lot of them, but they die easily and have no official histories.
To conclude, Solar War has well-made and unique core gameplay mechanics.
However, it is an almost ascetic experience lacking the luxuries that makes a game what it is.
If you at all like turn-based strategy and sf, then I recommend it despite the high price just because there really are no other games like it currently for the western market.

This game needs a fair review. The cutesy graphics have done this game a great disservice - with folks confusing it for a kids game or an easy game. This is a great casual game, with some qualities that I think set it apart

- The controls are super simple. Just the arrow keys or a 4 buttons on the controller.
- Great for moments when you don't want to get into a complex game and want something simple, yet challenging and fun.
- There is little randomness in failure - its always your fault when you lose a piece. So you never feel cheated.
If they were to remake this with a Zombie theme, this game would do much better. But if you can get past that, gameplay is solid.

Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City is a gaiden game for the Resident Evil series. It's skirts on the "recommend" side of "recommend or not", but only barely. There's quite a few flaws in the game, but it's overall not a bad game.
A bit of background. You play as one of Delta Squad, an elite fireteam in the Umbrella Security Service. From there you take on increasingly harder missions assisting Umbrella in eliminating evidence of their involvement of Raccon City's outbreak and their "morally questionable" practices.
Now this is NOT a bad game. However, if you walk into this game expecting a "Resident Evil" (i.e. survival horror with zombies) game, you WILL be disappointed. If you do not treat this game as a "Resident Evil" game, you will enjoy it significantly more.
The good points,
It runs on a class system, where there are six classes to pick from (Recon / Demolition / Assault / Sniper / Medic / Scientist), where each class has their own uses and skill sets. Only one of each class can be in the run at any given time, so your team will ALWAYS be missing something. This, in my opinion, is actually good, but can shoo away some people. For example, at some points you run into armed mines. Demolitions are the only "safe" way of effectively dealing with them, but if you don't have a Demolitions, you could be slowed down severely by those mines. If your team is lacking a medic, you will ALWAYS be missing something important. Optimally, you'd set up a fairly balanced team to go into these missions.
The gameplay is fun. It's not "Holy crap, you have to play this game" fun, but it's fun. It's a passtime and enjoyable enough to play. There are some flaws in the gameplay, but that will be covered in the next section.
Now for the bad points.
It runs on Windows Live for some reason, so you'll need to get an account there to play the game online at all. It's especially redundant because looking at the grey / black background of this review window should give you the impression you're already on Steam. So why would we need Windows Live? I admit, this is incredibly minor. It's still a minor gripe, nonetheless.
The AI in general. The AI enemies seem to be programmed as zombies. As a result, most of the enemies will come after human players. AI allies are also really, really, really, REALLY dumb. As a result, I recommend you play this game with AT LEAST 3 people. If you can find 2 other people to play this game with (that can, of course, agree on who will play what role), it'll be a much better experience.
The cover system. It's terrible and needs a lot. The game is moderately schizophrenic on what qualifies as "cover" and what doesn't. Some "cover" doesn't protect you entirely and it can be a big hassle in the middle of a firefight. This somewhat ties into having more than just one player.
Overall
In spite of the more "bad points" than "good points", one of the bad points is almost completely negated by having friends you can play with and another is more of a minor inconvenience. If you want to play this game, I would recommend that you wait for a sale and make sure you have a few friends you can play this game with. Even with all the DLC, this game is NOT worth the $40 price tag.
TL;DR - Play with friends, wait for sale. Not a bad game.

This game is quite different from others that I have played.
You are flying, ready to bomb some small outpost of some sort. Then you see the dots on the radar, enimies. You tag them, and set up your crew ready to bomb and attack at the same time. You are about to bomb but you miss as you were to busy trying to tag the other fighters and forgot to open the door in the first place. You go around for your second attempt. This time you hit, you close your doors and put your bomber into the front gunner. Now another guy is out of ammo and you need to grab more, you forgot to tag some planes and now they are attacking.A few moments later, One engine has fallen off, a second broken and a third is on fire. The engineer got blown off the wing while trying to fix one of the engines. Fuel has leaked out of one of the fuel tanks and I forgot to transfer it and now I have to crash land over the ocean.
This game is nowhere near as cute as it seems it cruel. You lose your level 8 engineer and he has gone forever, you have to train another one. You lose your plane, the upgrades to that plane have also gone with it.
Like an actual WWII bomber, you WILL have to manage basically everything from fuel down to electrics failing.
The crew is heavily customisable which I do love and it changes the stats of each. For example, you pilot just stays in the pilot seat (unless he dies or something) meaning he doesn't really need to walk fast so you can put heavy armor onto him/her. But you engineer needs to run like a maniac around the plane so he needs to be fast at running but that means you will have to sacrifice elsewhere.
One issue with this game.
Missions are the same. Let me explain. If you crash and lose everything. Plane and all, you are basically back to the beginning. (There is no save function to go back to most games as it is automatic.)  This is fine, but not when u have to complete the same missions all over again. I wish the missions had a little diversity instead of dying and then repeating the same mission twice over. If this wasn't a thing this game would be great but I'm not going to let that give this game a negative review as I do enjoy this game a lot.

Engaging gameplay that gets stressful and chaotic at best, I've developed a newfound respect for the WW2 bomber crews, but at least they didn't need to be told what to do the entire trip.
No hotkeys mean everything other than switching in and out of tagging mode is done entirely by mouse. Micromanaging is essential, since it's your job to keep the plane in the air and bring it back to the mechanics one way or another with whatever is left after enduring German fighters, flak and the odd ace pilots.
More than once i've forgotten to raise the landing gear after takeoff, as by the time I've crossed the English Channel the Huns are already on me. I swear my Navigator is working against me, as he likes to bring up a new heading the very moment some hostile blips appear on my radar. If I don't change course I risk straying into an AA zone and waste precious fuel, as my Engineer keeps yamering over. But not tagging those fighters mean that my Gunners have nothing to shoot, and forget about trying to chase them with your mouse after they've already descended upon you. At least the Radio Operator, once he's firgure out how to, can automatically tag targets in the vicinity.
Swooping in at low altitude on the final approach on my target, a munitions depot, I have to focus entirely on the Bombardier's sights, praying that none of the engines get set on fire, the hyrdaulics don't fail, the oxygen tanks work, and the electrical systems are functioning, all the while hoping none of the other crew members take a nasty piece of shrapnel to the eye.
Bombs gone, it's time to head back the way we came, through the fields of flak batteries, fresh squadrons of German fighter planes and less than half of the fuel left. I just notice that one of the inner port engines is no more. And that's the one that contains the port landing gear.
What felt like hours but was actually just a few minutes, we skid onto the RAF runway The midsection of the fuselage is down to the frames, and the tail has more holes than a sponge.
But any landing you can walk away from is a successful landing.
Game is hard to really master (which I love), and it's a bit of a work overload sometimes. But overall, an awesome experience.

This game is a true gem.  I like a few others was nearly turned off by the cutesy Saturday cartoon style presentation. No other game has ever changed my mind so completely in so little time.  Beneath the adorable bobbleheaded exterior lurks an surprisingly fleshed out and deep survival managment simulator that reminds me a great deal of B-17 the mighty eighth crossbred with FTL.
Bomber Crew will challenge your mulitasking skills as well as your ability to prioritize cruical task in high pressure situations where the wrong call will effect not only the success of the mission, but also determine whether your plane and crew return to base in one piece.  This game pulls no punches, when you take off from base headed towards your mission objective you are fully committed. There is no saving during missions meaning if you screw up and wind up losing your plane and /or crew they are gone forever.
To me this permadeath aspect adds a tension to the game that elevates it from a arcade experince such as games like War Thunder and World of Warplanes offer to a nail biting tactical all or nothing gambit seen in the likes of Xcom. In Bomber Crew your decisions and actions really matter and will drasticlly affect both the current mission as well as the overall campaign depending on your level of sucess or magnitude of your failures.
If you are a fan of WWII or survival games and don't mind a steep learning curve there aren't many more satisfying ways to spend 15 bucks. Get it you'll love it.

I was waiting to review this until I had at least 10 or 15 hours in it, but I think this one needs to be reviewed.
This game is good. It's fun, addicting and such an unparalled board game experience. You startled by the bad reviews on Steam? Don't be, and here's why:
1. The second highest negative review is written by a guy who has poured in 4+ hours a day into a 'buggy' and 'overpriced' game.
2. The three main complaints are as follows: no fullscreen, high priced DLC, multiplayer crashes. One of those is fixed, one of those can be emulated by pressing the large box on the top right corner of the application, and one is true in almost every other Steam game in there. Oh, by the way, did I mention that it's DLC? And that the DLC are not shameless plug-ins, but based off the original board game expansions? And that you don't NEED to buy the DLC to play the game?
3. People have said that the SINGLEPLAYER mode of a board game is addicting. The SINGLEPLAYER mode. Of a MULTIPLAYER game. Does that not tell you how much fun you will have in the newly-improved multiplayer?
4. People complain about the people who abandon online matches, yet there is a system that allows you to play with Steam friends, and on the forums you can friend people who want to play with you.
5. The multiplayer is Asynchronous, meaning when you enter a match, you aren't forced to do your turn. Mum calls you to have dinner? Wait a moment, I'm not forced to rush my turn!
6. Multiplayer being Asynchronous means you can have more than one multiplayer game up at a time. Waiting for a slowpoke to finish their turn? Play a turn in another game! The opportunity is there for you.
To actually review the game: it's diverse, and you never feel like you're doing the same♥♥♥♥♥♥all over again. That was one of my main problems with such board games like Risk/Catan/Ticket to Ride: I could figure out a way to win that was pretty much the same every time. In this game? No such luck. Completely and utterly replayable.
The reason my hours are low is because I've had stuff to do, and I play this game called Dota in the times when I'm not free. But I assure you, I'm playing this game a helluva lot more in the future.
If you do get this, and you want to play some multiplayer with someone you know won't abandon the game, feel free to add me. I'm open for business in this marvellous game. I guess it is a Small World after all.

I really wanted to like this game, multiple times I've tried to play through it only to end up with bugs so bad it broke the game play. This isn't just with one system either, I originally purchased The Witcher in 2012 and have tried to run it across multiple PCs that I've had since then and each time encountered a different bug that made the game unplayable. Feels almost like some Bethesda level game breaking bugs.

(This review is quite long, but you can just read the first sentence of the numbered topics if you prefer, since the rest is purely my view of the mentioned aspects. I think this game isn't fully enjoyable if you just rush the reading, which is one of the points that I mention here!)
How to enjoy this game:
1 - Ignore the reviews when people complain about the combat. It's different, clunky and not easy to grasp- you'll get used to it after your second hour or whatever, so just ignore them. They work for Salamandra. They want to prevent Geralt from recovering Kaer Mohren`s stolen secrets and contribute to the hostility towards nonhumans (they also hate Leo).
2 - Don't skip dialogues. I strongly advise against follow that massive, almost unbearable impulse (we all have felt that) of clicking during dialogues to skip them, even when you've already read the subtitles; the whole thing becomes much more immersive if you just listen to the voice actors and allow the dialogue to play at its own rhythm.
3 - Be prepared to read a lot! You really shouldn't underestimate the Journal entries: the ones about Characters, Locations and Monsters, and the Glossary, they all have lots of useful data, little bits of information that are more than just flavor text; they add comprehension, life and detail to the whole game, making it such a rich and planned environment. Well, I admit that maybe I got a little overhyped here, but it's just because I really really liked the world of the game!
4 - Research, explore, kill things. Certain side quests cannot be completed after advancing through the main story, so... what are you waiting for? Yes, you have a main quest to complete, but don't you think that the monster contract about killing some human-eating specter dogs is a little more urgent? The main quest is there and has to be completed; it's not going anywhere. But if you complete a chapter and move to a new area, you can't go back to the previous one to help that guard with his ghoul problem, so explore everything;
5 - Gather ALL the herbs! (Ginatz Acid, Albar's Crystals and White Vinegar are the best ones to sell in the beginning, so stock them up!) And organize your alchemy bag. You'll notice that the bag has six rows, which is the same number of primary components. It will be much useful if you use one row to each one (I like to use the order that appears in the bag: Vitriol, Rebis, Aether, Quebrith, Hydragenum, Vermillion). Also there are three secondary ingredients, which can improve the effects of potions - I like to order them as Albedo, Nigredo and Rubedo. Special ingredients can go to the last line (you're not going to find much Vermillion in the beginning anyway). The alchemy system is interesting, and keeping your inventory tidy not only makes things easier, but gives a good feeling on it. But don't exaggerate - I personally don't like having 30 of four different ingredients that gives Vitriol and Albedo, there is no need for it. You can keep one type of each primary/secondary ingredient and sell the rest. Don't let your inventory be a mess!
6 - Play it on hard. I'm serious here. First of all, there are monsters everywhere, horrible beasts and creatures that terrorize the common people and prevents them from sleeping; it came to the point where people started to perform sinister rituals and experiments on children, mutating their bodies to the extreme and giving them superhuman endurance, senses and reflexes, so they can undergo extreme training in order to grow up and become the infamous Witchers, skilled monster hunters the that people despise, and yet they need them. Why would they have to do all of that if Geralt of Rivia (our most famous Witcher) was able to kill the creatures with a single swing of his sword? No. The monsters are not to be taken lightly, even for a Witcher, even for THE Witcher. If the combat becomes too easy, you may think "hell, THESE are the horrible creatures that make people scared at night? And they are giving me 500 orens to do something their farmers could do? Seriously?"
"Hard" is a difficult that can be beaten by anyone - "Medium" and "Easy" is simply unfair. Many people complain that the game is actually easy in the end, even on HARD. So...
7 - You can use Aard and Igni signs, of course, but don't SOLELY depend on them. The five Signs (think about them as "small, quick spells") are very useful, but these two (knockback and fire, respectively) are way too overpowered if you decide to max them right from the beginning. Remember, you have two swords, you're a WITCHER - the signs are secondary tricks. Burning everything with Igni is nice, but what's the fun in letting that meteorite sword resting by your back and letting magic do the job?
8 - Don't Load Game because you regretted a choice. Think seriously before making your decicions, accept the consequences of your actions. Imagine how Geralt (and here I mean YOUR vision of Geralt) would act, what he would not do, and if he could do that thing depending on the circunstamces; there are going to be dilemmas and hard choices. Sometimes, and more often than Geralt would like, it will about choosing the lesser evil.
9 - Prepare your potions. I like having at least 3 Swallow (my favorite potion so far, a real lifesaver) strenghtened with Rubedo (the Additional Ingredients page of the Glossary will introduce you to one of favorite small aspects of this game) Think about the witcher's preparations to combat, and how they have their equipments ready before fighting monsters; the potions are part of them, try to keep some of your favorite potions, oils and bombs ready when you need it!
There are some downsides observed by many people; the Inventory system is one, and the infamous swamp is another, and of course we cannot forget these two suspects from chapter two that demand more than some CSI episodes for you to fully investigate them. But try to think about those flaws as part of the game. They are not game-breaking, and if you just keep playing it, you learn they're not as big as an issue. If you really can't bear some of the downsides, there are always mods that can solve some issues without breaking the experience.
And, of course, remember that The Witcher 2 comes after this, and then The Witcher 3. There is a mechanic that allows you to import your save from TW1 to TW2, and the save from TW2 to TW3. Think that all the choices you've made today are going to follow you in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt!
(10 - If a woman in a witch's hut tells you she's selling an oil, buy it! You gonna need it)

Based on the 60+ hours play time, here's what I think about the game:
+ Graphic are cute, and there's lots of costume to make your bald white character look nicer lol.
+ There's skill (known as perk) to help your character do much more better and faster in this game.
+ Crafting is quite enjoyable and challenging. It's not really that simple, but not that complex either.
+ Getting resource is so damn easy here (compared to other sandbox game I played).
+ PVP is somewhat funny, not all serious and scary :D I lol-ed so hard when my friend using the shrink-wand on me.
+ Getting to other's people realm is easy (unless they lock the realm or it's only accessible for friend only). So when you got bored you can explore other people homes.
- Camera is really..quite an annoying issue in this game. Even though you can unlock camera for "better" view of the world, it still quite uncomfortable.
-  The no-cancel action. Like you mistakenly click for the wrong block. And there's really no way to cancel that action, not even moving your character can cancel it (unless you do the wrong click far away from your character).
- The perks have it's disadvantages tool. Each time you level up, you get a chance to pick 1 of the 3 random skill the system give you. Some tools needs certain skill so that you can use it to make items, and you will suffer a lot if you choose the less-important one (since leveling up become harder once you're pass 15 or maybe 20).
- The player(s) can be quite amazingly annoying sometimes. I'm not saying all players are like that. But really, some of them love to use caps lock so much it hurts, or try to scam using the old piggy tip method, or begging like their life really depends so much on your pity, and some of them doesn't even understand the word "no". And that's what I encounter on daily basis while I play the game.
-The quest. I'm aware that this a free-to-play game with a slice of Micro-transaction, but really, after you have done the basic quest, in order to get more quest you have to buy it with cubits. And there's only 2 quest in store, which one of them cost like 2000 cubits. It might be wiser to just make the quest equal to all paying player and the non-paying player.
---
I quiet enjoy the time I spent in this game, but that's because I have my friends also playing this game with me. On the other hand I also feel the game is quite boring due to lack of quest and the annoying player (and also that awkward camera...).
And the stress only got worse if you decide to play without using real money to buy the glorious cubits (because you need a lot of those to even craft some important item like doors, key (for personal/friend/or password-protect), cash register (to safely trade with your friends), etc.
I was expecting nothing. I still got dissapointed.

Pros:
1. Pretty good graphics
2. runs well (IF it runs at all - had an issue where it crashed to desktop every time I launched and one where it refused to launch), you get to pick from a variety of classes/characters
3. The enemies are kind of cool, as are the chapters. I like the environments. This game is aesthetically pleasing.
Cons:
1. This is my #1 biggest complaint for this game: you are playing COMPETITIVELY AGAINST YOUR FRIENDS. And it actually hurts your progress. I play this game with my boyfriend. I generally get the first few shots in and he comes along and steals them. He ends up with over 100 kills, I end up WAY beneath my target kills. He gets 15000 xp, I get 1/5 of that. He gets to buy awesome guns and skills. I get to buy nothing, chapter after chapter after chapter. First come first serve for bonus XP like data collection and camera destruction. He plays the guy that can easily see it, runs around and collects it all, I get nothing. This con alone is enough to make me not recommend this game to anyone. This is literally the one thing I cannot stand about certain games. There is NO reason to make a competitive co-op game. I'd be better off playing with the stupid AI, because then at least I'd get XP to progress. However... I don't play single player games very often. I hate them. I don't like playing by myself, but in this game you are forced to.
2. I hate how you can only carry two weapons and that a pistol is mandatory. Coming from other RE games (like RE5) this doesn't sit well with me. I hate being forced to use a pistol. Yes, I most likely would pick a pistol, but I'd like to have the OPTION to use a machine gun instead of it.
3. I think the collision barriers are WAY off at certain positions/times. I constantly have issues with my character's shots getting clipped by imaginary objects. I am clearly hitting him in the center of his chest. There is nothing blocking us in between. Why is he not dying??????
I'm playing this game because my boyfriend likes it. Otherwise I would not be playing and would consider this game a waste of money. If you have an issue with some of the cons I've listed, I honestly wouldn't buy it unless you are getting a super good deal. Don't pay more than 5 bucks.

This is a unique puzzle/2D shooter game with an interesting story. I have few complaints about it, but one of them is that I wish it was longer.
The puzzles are interesting enough. It takes on the style of games like Monkey Island where you find things and have to cleverly use them to your advantage. Figuring out a puzzle on your own is very rewarding, but at the same time you may need to look up a walkthrough once or twice.
The shoot 'em up portions are OK, not incredibly riveting but still fun enough. It's a basic cover shooter, just on a 2D plane.
I've read some complaints about the story, but I myself enjoyed it and found myself invested in it by the end of this short experience. You play as ARID, an AI in a military suit. Your pilot is unconscious and you must get to a medical facility (which is the overarching goal in the game). Along your way you'll meet other robots, some friendly and some not. I won'y reveal too much as much of the fun of the story comes from experiencing it.
Visually the game is nice, its art style isn't anything completely unique but it has some good visuals.
One complaint that I have about the game is that you have to turn your flashlight on and shine it on things you want to interact with. Although it's not really a big deal, it'd be nice if I could just hit a button without shining my flashlight on it.
Other than that, this is an interesting although almost painfully short experience. They are coming out with a second part though.
Get it when it's on sale, or if you really think this is your cup of tea, just get it now.

Clustertruck is basically what happens if someone takes the whole "look how goofy and kinda broken Unity's physics engine is!" genre, epitomized by Goat Simulator, and makes an actual game out of it. The result is a speedrun-focused platformer, with the platforms being trucks that obey wacky Unity physics.
The result is expectedly fun, and most of the levels are designed well enough that they don't become frustrating even when you keep dying to the slippery controls or unusual physics, but it shares a downside with many games like this where it's quite easy to get stuck on a single level and not really have fun any more, because the game is completely linear and all levels must be successfully completed in order to unlock the next.
(The "final boss" stage gets a special mention, however - Clustertruck mostly manages to not be frustrating despite combining slippery controls, wacky physics, and major errors requiring you to restart the run by having most stages be short. The final stage is... not, and suffers a lot from that.)
I would recommend Clustertruck to most people who enjoy action games and especially to people who have subjected themselves to Unity's default physics before, as seeing it become an actual game rather than just Goat Simulator was extra funny for me. It's not a terribly long game unless you want to replay stages to improve your score, but given its single gimmick, that's to be expected.

A charming, if sometimes confusing, puzzle-adventure game about a robot on a quest to save his city. The point-and-click system could have benefited with a little more clarity about what’s clickable and what isn’t, but once you get the hang of things it’s easier to figure that out. There’s a good mix of straight-up puzzles, logic games, and find/create the right item challenges. I used a fair amount of trial and error, but reaching the solutions was satisfying, and
of them made sense. (There is a hint system that’s available, but I ended up not using it because I’m stubborn.) In terms of story, there’s no dialogue in the game, but every now and then the characters will use thought bubbles with animated drawings to “talk” or recall background information. The art style reminds me of concept art - not polished, but instead focused on evoking feeling, and the soundtrack is written similarly. Overall it’s a very well crafted game best suited for players who are patient and want puzzles that make them think.

A strong game held back by a weak, confusing opening.
This game has a lot of strong points.  The graphics and 3D style are fantastic.  Beautiful and unique.  I've never played anything that looks and feels quite like it.  The soundtrack is fantastic, and is nicely integrated into the main story.
The only negative thing I have to say about it is that it really does flub the opening.  The game opens with a confusing sequence that doesn't really offer you anything to grab on to, and once that ends, you're dumped into a sequence that hints that the entire game will be some sort of a dry, retconed, alternate history that projects modern progressive values back onto the year 1851.  Making progress past all that feels like a bit of a slog, and doesn't give the player much reason to assume the entire game won't be more of the same.  But when the story finally gets moving, it REALLY gets moving.  You can actually feel the first moment when something interesting happens, because it's so striking.  "Wait, what?  Does that mean what I think it means?"  From then on out, the game is SOLID.
In fact, from then on out, the game moves so smoothly that the next thing you'll think to complain about is the cliffhanger at the end, as we wait for the conclusion.
In summary, you should absolutely play this if you're a fan of point & click adventure games with a strong story.  Just be prepared to give this one a very generous chance to get moving.  It will, if you let it.

It pains me to say this about a widely renowned and beloved game/series! However, I cannot recommend Witcher 1. Everyone says the story is amazing, giving me the initial motivation to push through. But after toughing it out for 16 hours, it's time for me to accept the fact that I do not like this game for a couple of reasons:
1) Combat. It's just so DRY. This is what did me in. The mechanics seem promising: You can select the most effective sword styles, weapon type, and spells against certain enemies. In reality, you're clicking your mouse at slightly different intervals to activate the 3- or 4-combo chain as per sword style. I'm down for action hack 'n' slash, but the combat is not robust, nor is it easy to execute.
Something seems off about the timing. I think it's that the animation for each part of the combo chain is rather slow. You can't misclick, or you will have to start all over again. I wouldn't have a problem with this combat system if enemies died more easily because killing them is neither quick nor fun, in my opinion. The enemies' considerable HP plus the long animation times for combat made me view fighting as a chore.
Meditation/skill leveling trees were interesting. However, the mere thought of having to go through swathes of monsters deterred me from exploring, looting, questing, and ultimately, from leveling up and progressing through the game.
Once again, there is nothing particularly wrong with this system. The game was designed to be played this way, and it likely made sense given the gaming climate at the time of its release 9 years ago. It's just not for me.
2) Drab characterization. HEAR ME OUT -- I know there is a lot of buzz online stating that the story in Witcher 1 is better than 2. You'd have to try to stay unaware of it! It's just that GETTING TO those moments in this amazing story were impossible for me. After I quit, I still felt like it was just okay, so I'm not sure if I had even gotten to the first plot development yet.
Furthermore, it doesn't help that the voice acting is dreary! Geralt sounds as lively as Robert Pattinson playing Edward Cullen. Completely ruins the writing, which was quirky at times.
Nevertheless, there were some things I enjoyed:
1) Roleplay. I got a real kick out of
It was also really fun beating people up during drunken fist fights.
2) Gambling. I may or may not have spent a third of my play time trying to beat every NPC I came across at poker.

let me start off by saying, i really, REALLY wanna like this game. and this is only my personal view.
the idea is good, a four player tactical ops. game, set in a resident evil setting, youre the bad guys so to speak.
but the problem is.. the different "classes" dont really have a balanced sync between abilities. many of them seem more like ego-classes, some have a somewhat beneficial ability, problem is you often forget to use it in the heat of battle.
there are a few major things that spoiled this game for me, and thats:
1) horrible, and i do mean HORRIBLE AI, i played this through with a friend, and the two AI's where worthless really, they take grenades, health sprays and anti viral sprays, but they never use them to help the group, even the healer class as AI often dont use the health sprays. so I decided to shift and be the healer, just to have that under control, problem is the AI runs away from you when you try and heal them, often resulting in you wasting the spray (or not completly wasted, cause you do heal yourself)
sometimes the AI runs into walls, getting stuck or glitch into a room behind a door that is locked, resulting in you not having that extra gun, well... hadnt it been for the fact that they more often than not decides to melee the enemy instead of using their guns, resulting in them being infected, and if you dont have the anti viral spray, they will turn to zombies and attack you, (luckily the medic can shoot anti viral into a team mate every 20sec, so thats often not a problem, if the medic is player controlled). and the AI will die and needs a revive, which can be hairy in the midst of zombies and soldiers trying to kill you.
AI (artificial intelligence) more like RS (Real Stupidity)
2) the sometimes unending waves of enemies, often accompanied by not enough ammo or health pickups, reulting in your team being ripped to pieces. i love it when its intense and on the edge, but its pretty anoying to get your butt handed to you like theres no tomorrow.
often the pickups are plentiful, but then sometimes the game 180's and you get nothing.
3) there are data pickups, for every piece of data you pick up you get 50xp, mind you this is a multiplayer game in intention, but data is not shared, so if one is greedy, the other will get no bonus xp. its easily fixed but agreeing to share, but come on, least have the bonusses be shared. same with special weapons, if one is greedy the other(s) wont get to try the special weapons. again easily avoided by agreeing to share, but i still think this should be shared.
4) many complain that the cover system is annoying, as you walk up to a crate and you automatically crouch behind it, this dosent bother me, i think it makes it easier to get into position for fights, what does annoy me is the fact that cover often dont work, like you being shot to hell through concrete barriers and iron plates. and the fact that if you try and shoot through an opening in a car for instance, you will not hit anything but the car, metal beam or alike, no matter how big the openening is.
5) the game becomes boring very fast, the story is boring and uninspiring. and as a Resident Evil fan, i find it so disheartening that it only partially follows the events from the second game, i know this is a spin off and non canon. but i mean, when they get up close to what i remembered from the second game, but decides to change a minor, but important thing, that makes me kinda annoyed.
this is really sad because the idea of the game is really good, it couldve been the game that brought something new and cool. problem is, its like the developers decided to drop the project and just go, "ah well screw it, this is fine"

Clustertruck is basically what happens if someone takes the whole "look how goofy and kinda broken Unity's physics engine is!" genre, epitomized by Goat Simulator, and makes an actual game out of it. The result is a speedrun-focused platformer, with the platforms being trucks that obey wacky Unity physics.
The result is expectedly fun, and most of the levels are designed well enough that they don't become frustrating even when you keep dying to the slippery controls or unusual physics, but it shares a downside with many games like this where it's quite easy to get stuck on a single level and not really have fun any more, because the game is completely linear and all levels must be successfully completed in order to unlock the next.
(The "final boss" stage gets a special mention, however - Clustertruck mostly manages to not be frustrating despite combining slippery controls, wacky physics, and major errors requiring you to restart the run by having most stages be short. The final stage is... not, and suffers a lot from that.)
I would recommend Clustertruck to most people who enjoy action games and especially to people who have subjected themselves to Unity's default physics before, as seeing it become an actual game rather than just Goat Simulator was extra funny for me. It's not a terribly long game unless you want to replay stages to improve your score, but given its single gimmick, that's to be expected.
