The game that has most been on my mind lately is
I've found myself humming the main theme a few times in the past month or so, and I always feel a saturated pulse of remembered emotion.
I first played Morrowind on the original xbox, which I kept alive for years past a natural end using a soldering iron and a dream.  It was a dark time for me, Atlanta in 2000s.  I was working 60-80 hours a week tending bar and barely pulling in enough to pay for my studio apartment, my cats, my phone, my food, an occassional xbox or ps2 game, and enough booze to suppress my as-yet-undiagnosed mental illness.
I would get home in the wee hours of morning and play Morrowind, often falling asleep on the couch with controller in hand.  It wasn't the story, exactly, though the story is not bad.  My life was so painful, and I felt so little control over my circumstances- until I entered Morrowind.

I remember little about that storyline and I kept playing my character for hundreds of hours after its completion.  In Morrowind, I had agency over my choices, and I improved at the things I chose to do.  When I felt unable to change my world or myself, when I felt unfit for my own goals and dreams- this aspect of Morrowind grew profound, became deeply important to me.
So many scripted characters going about their own business for their own reasons. So many stories to be told by the many individuals, so many books to be found and read in the world.  Morrowind felt populated by real people, so to speak.  Many of the characters have simple tales to tell that illustrate the vicissitudes and banality and struggle of everyday life.  This is a world in which everyone toils through their labors day by day, whether a hero comes or not.  I saw my life through the lens of toil, and I was comforted.
This is not your typical white-washed, messianic fantasy of a hero's journey set in an idealized medieval Europe.  This is Morrowind, and only Morrowind.  The Elder Scrolls have returned to a more mainstream fantasy vision and I believe they are weaker games for it.  Every step taken in the game was a journey of discovery of new and stranger wonders, and I was in love with each new one.  What better place to find solace from our world than in a world so alien to my expectations?
When I catch that music in my head and I get that thrill through my body, that wash of emotions from an immensely upsetting time, I reflect on Morrowind with a sense of deep gratitude for the role it played in my life.  In fact, the experience profoundly affected the way I understand and interact with video games, elevating the process from recreational narrative experience to

But that's what makes it fun.  I totally disagree with the other reviews saying this is too difficult to manage, it just takes practice.  I kept losing crewmembers or the whole aircraft at first but after getting in an hour or two of practice I started a new crew who have, as of today survived 46 missions without losing a single person.  Now that my aircraft is nicely upgraded and my crew has lots of nifty useful skills I am still finding it challeging on some of the tougher missions... and that's great, a good game should challenge you and still be fun.  I give Bomber Crew two electrically heated mitten covered thumbs up!

This game is terrific! I came into it pretty hesitant because I, like many of you, see reviews that say that the game gets insanely difficult after the initial easy missions. While there is a definite increase in difficulty, it's not impossible and I'm by no means that great of a gamer.
Be wise in what you spend your money on, develop your crew, and use your skills wisely during the battle. Additionally, do not just go willy nilly into the harder fights before completing the easier ones. This will allow you to give your crew better gear and you'll have a better plane.
However, even in the event that you do get show down, which is pretty inevitable, you are still able to try and rescue parts of your crew. If they survive, great. If they don't, there's always a recruit waiting for you on the horizon.
Eventually you will start to bond with these crewmembers. I was streaming it earlier for the limited number of viewers that I had and I renamed some of the crew members with their handles. It became pretty engaging and it was fun to see chat react to high tense situations.
All in all, this game is well worth the $12-$15 price tag. Good luck out there!

Firstly, note that this is my first Witcher game, havent played any others, so here is my review:
If you have never played any Witcher games, this is overall a good introduction, bearing in mind this is a 2007 game, dont expect too much graphically and gameplay wise. That being said, it is a solid game, especially on HARD mode, because otherwise its just not challenging at all and Hard Mode makes you use all you have and be versatile in combat, which is nice. Its biggest plus is the quests with a good story and overall story and characters in it. The dialogue is always interesting to do, and what you say defines your choices and can lead you on a different path than other dialogue choices. If you go on to play Witcher 2 and 3, you can import your last save game which will link the choices you made in previous game to 2 and 3, thus connecting all of the games, because essentially it is one story, which I think is very very cool.
The biggest con for me was poor character building, because when you get the basic skills, after that it feels like no matter what you pick it has no impact on the gameplay (with couple of exceptions). For example, your damage is improved, but it never feels like it does improve. Or you have a chance to incinerate an opponent with your sword, but it never once happened to me. And so on. This has an impact on the combat, because after Chapter 3 (from total of 5 chapters), you have basically done everything combat wise that you can, and after that its just repetitive even with new opponents, although its always cool to play as a Witcher, for me it didnt get too boring even through the grinding parts.
If you have played The Elder Scrolls games, you know how important it is to upgrade your gear, right? Armor, weapons, helmet and so on. Well, in the Witcher games its not that important, you can go through the whole game without upgrades and in fact if you do upgrade your weapons or armor it doesnt feel like much of an achievement, so that was a bit disappointing.
TLDR: I would give this game a 6/10 and recommend it only to big Witcher 3 fans, then play it on Hard mode, because its the most fun. For people who want to get into the Witcher series, but want a quick playthrough, play on Easy mode so you arent slowed down by repetitve combat  and can import your save game to Witcher 2 and later to 3.

Resident Evil (Remake) is a beautiful object of design which delivers a pleasurable and precisely managed play experience, but its mechanics and structure are stylized in the fashion of late 90s survival horror games. It's not for everyone.
The premise is a medium-length (i.e., the first playthrough is ~9 hours) single-player, linear 'survival horror' game played with fixed camera angles and set in a mansion populated with zombies and genetic aberrations. You need to kill a few things, understand the physical space, manage your inventory and use of items, and solve the odd puzzle. This game is very good-looking and powerfully scary. Fear here comes mostly from suspension of disbelief, and a very tense atmosphere, but there are a small number of contextual jump scares too. The hallmarks of later Resident Evil titles (quicktime events, over-the-shoulder cameras, fully rendered 3D environments, modular item management, and big action setpieces) are entirely absent. This game is much quieter and more delicate.
Like the many ornate keys the player accumulates in the game, this game feels bespoke and carefully produced. Every art asset is rendered lovingly, with an eye for detail. The mutated shark models have scars on their skin from where they have become aggressive with one another in their pool after having been abandoned. Each zombie's dress and injuries implies their backstory, and there are many zombie character models. The items the player collects are fetishistic totems, whose gorgeous polygonal models can all be examined closely in three dimensions. They include Yale lock keys, first aid kits, weapons (including a simulacrum of the Colt Python revolver), a large battery, piano scores, and X-ray scans. Every item has been crafted with obvious love and care. It has become a useless cliché to write of a game's 'fully realized world', but items, character models and lavish backgrounds are the core of Resident Evil (Remake)'s incomparable atmosphere. Because the game uses fixed camera angles, its backgrounds are pre-rendered textures, and there are relatively few 3D models on screen at any time. Spareness is presumably one reason for its high production values. The fixed camera angles give the level designers cinematic control over tone, which is rare in modern games. There is no capacity for the player to debase in-game suspense by constantly jumping or moving the camera during a crucial moment. A new room may open with the camera on the avatar, against the door, so you can't see what's ahead. In short, it looks great. This is a minor 'high definition' update to a game released in 2002, but the game has barely aged at all. Only graphics buffs or very superficial players will feel that they are playing an outdated title.
The controls and mechanics of the game are very much of their era. In this game, you control your avatar using so-called 'tank controls', which nominally resemble those of a traditional tank in that you cannot simultaneously turn and advance forward. Unusually for a 3D video game, pushing forward on the stick moves your avatar in the direction they are currently facing. This control system has always been controversial, and is now widely dismissed as a relic. There is an option to switch to a more conventional control system in the menu. Players will find their own most comfortable playing style, but the game was designed for tank controls, and I believe they are necessary for full enjoyment. This game is about suspense, ad hoc strategy, and uncertainty. The slight awkwardness and feeling of limitation which tank controls offer suit the setting. This game's fixed camera angles, which can switch between very different viewpoints, make conventional 3D world control systems unintuitive. The player can become disorientated easily as they move between screens. Tank controls alleviate this problem, because the player always has a sense of their current direction and momentum.
Plot barely features in this game. Cutscenes are minimal (although countless variations of scenes exist for players with different play conditions), and the optional backstory is explored mostly through text documents or exquisite environmental storytelling. You may find a couple of the characters irritating (personally I can't stand Chris, one of the playable characters), but what little dialogue there is can be skipped. As it is now fashionable to say, the story of the game is the story of your playthrough. I have found that I end up with a very particular relationship with certain rooms in the mansion. Ammunition and healing items are sparse, such that there are generally more zombies than you can kill in a given area, and unless they are properly disposed of (through fire or removal of the head), zombies will return, flush with their own blood and saturated with a more mature form of the plague virus, as the deadly 'crimson heads'. For these reasons, it is generally more desirable to avoid zombies than to engage them. But certain areas of the mansion are connected by narrow corridors, making escape difficult. The player therefore has to monitor their resources, managing ammunition, physical space, health and healing items, and inventory space, all of which are limited. Compromises must be made. That's a lot of the fun.
A few recommendations to maximise your pleasure: play it at night. Try not to seek help for the hard parts (unless a puzzle is totally stumping you, because a couple of them are very obtuse). Turn up the volume.
The HD Remaster is a delight. Every inch of curling wallpaper and dry rot is now visible! I just have a couple of complaints. A very select few of the master textures (such as the letter Wesker/Barry pins to the wall outside the East Wing save room) were obviously never designed to be seen at this resolution, and they really should have been replaced like other models have been. More inexplicably, great effort has been put into adding a 'physics boob jiggle' to Jill's walk. The effect is to dehumanize and overtly sexualize a well-loved character. Watching Jill animate is now an item of titillation for the presumed heterosexual male player. I think it's very myopic and dull of Capcom to add this feature. If nothing else, it is absurdly unrealistic. Jill's chest now undulates at a steady pace, independent from the rest of her body, whenever she walks or runs. It makes me more aware of the game as software, and harms its chief achievement: its extraordinarily tense atmosphere. This feature was missing in the 2002 release of this same game. Sadly, in every other way, this HD Remaster is the superior edition.
Please play this game. I don't normally go to bat for flagship releases from major studios, but Resident Evil Remake is a beautifully crafted artefact.

I've played much more of this game on a friend's tablet, so don't think this review is limited to the short playtime I have logged on Steam.  I'm severely neutral about this game, which is a shame given how enjoyable its atmoshpere is.  It is a pretty game, with an interesting touch of characterization on your little gizmo.  There are two reasons why I can't quite reccomend this game though, and while they don't make the game bad it definitely makes it worth less than the 10 USD price.
First is a more personal peeve, it's made to immitate old-school point and click adventures in that there's a thread of logic that usually makes sense in the game world but doesn't if the immersion is broken.  That thread of how to progress can feel arbitrary, like the developers have contrived a reason why you can't just do a simple solution here, or why this device's switch is in a nigh-unaccesible alcove.  And that adventure game logic has always peeved me, but it's perfectly fine so long as you're immersed.
Aaaaand that's the two of it: the immersion.  This game has a great soundtrack and needs it, because the gameplay is far from enough to pull (in my experience) the player in.  The tokenism and the obviously contrived puzzles are a big part of it, which encourages players to click around looking for what can and can't be used, but the other part is a bit more subtle.  Your character's competency changes, and that always pulls me out of a game.  Sometimes your character (Read: the game) will do something automatically that in a less-padded puzzle would have required you to hunt for an inventory item to do.  So occasionally I'm looking for what I believe is the last piece and then when I can't find it just rub my inventory against itself and give birth to progress.  That, or the gizmo guy can squeeze into or stretch to reach something that in a previous puzzle would not have been possible.
Two faults, yes, and two major ones that the 10 USD price cannot afford to have.

Books I& II of Herald: An Interactive Period Drama is definitely overall a win for fledgling developer Wispfire. It has a compelling story, with an interesting twist at the end. The only elements of the game which I weren't fond of were the slightly wooden 3D graphics and the mediocre voice acting. However, the engaging and well conceived plot more than makes up for this. Also, the 2D animations are beautifully done, and I enjoyed the musical score as well.  If you like the visual novel format, definitely check this one out.

I have to admit that history is not one of my strong subjects. For the most part I know the series of events and the main people involved but not exact dates of everything . And when most of our questions, both multiple choice and essay, have us pinpoint an exact date it does not go well for me. Despite this I love period pieces. Especially with the amount of research that goes into it and how it shows. Hearing possible ways the world would of been if certain events did not play out as they did is even more interesting, especially since there is a history book that is dedicated to showcasing it. With Herald: An Interactive Period Drama being alternative history, I just had to play through it.
Today we go back to an alternative 19th century in the shoes of a young man named Devan Rensburg. Opening up to him being in the hands of a mysterious woman who introduced herself as The Rani. Who, of which, also seemed to of saved him from drowning. Directing Devan to recount his story from his journal and why he is wearing the Protectorate blue captain coat. Not only paving a way for us to have an intro to the story but the structure the inner narrative will be from Devan. We do spend most of our time in Devan’s retelling. Being aboard the merchant ship HLV Herald with the help of the second officer, Aaron Ludlow, hand selecting him and eventually track down his parents when they get back on land.
As most of Devan’s surroundings is either the boat or the ocean it is not surprising we are around the same characters and slowly introduced to the different parts of the boat. Luckily the characters are strong enough to carry this weight. You get the sense of every character and you know they each have their own pasts. And with this having choices on what you can say, you also sculpt how Devan is. Is he one for change, does he become concerned, will he help others?
Not only are characters deep but they have great art and voice actors behind them. Each character had a great choice in a voice actor and I did not leave dissatisfied by any of the performances. When the characters talk a 2d drawing of them is put on screen, leaving the 3d model to do the body movement and not worry about facial expression. The art they show is great as well, with a little animation added, to show various expressions. And trust me some are hilarious.
I do like how they decided to do the conversation choices on the boat. We get the usual wording in The Rani scenes but we get more of “I decided to…” on the boat. It’s something little, but it goes in line with him recounting it to The Rani. This also goes into his narration on the various objects you can inspect. Doing it more as telling The Rani rather than thinking about what he saw. There is undoubtedly no way he can remember everything but they do balance it out somewhat with Devan’s journal. I can only assume our first tab, mostly used to tell you your objectives, would be more towards a diary deal. With the second tab just being quick notes and backstories on various subjects such as items and people, and the last tab being the map of the HLV Herald. Though the map is a tad confusing.
A huge thing with games giving you choice is how it handles them, with Telltale games commonly being brought up in this aspect. With Herald: An Interactive Period Drama, most of the decisions made have immediate, or almost immediate, consequences. Only some choices having a more long term consequence that will come into play in the last two books. And as of now they do seem like these decisions matter, especially with how the characters will probably react later on. Of course there are plot points it has to hit no matter what, but you still get some choices around those that do hold some significance. Some even are brought up as little jabs showing that characters will remember what you say.
This also focuses more on telling a story rather than the usual point and click aspect plays into the game as well. Bringing in more of a relaxed experience. Letting us look at the environment and focus on the characters and the story. There is really no challenge, other than finding your way around the boat, and most of your interactions other than with characters will be walking through the environments and giving items to various characters. The 3d world is somewhat lacking in terms of the character models, but they do try, and succeed, at filling the ship realistically. Also compensating with their soundtrack at the right times. If it was not for the 3d world we walk in, I would say this would be a visual novel.
One of the things I do wish is for the autosave to be brought to attention as I did not know if the game saved or not till I looked it up. I do totally get why as your choices seem more set in stone, but I wish it told you that it will autosave at every chapter. I do also wish we got more than three save slots. As we are eventually getting the last half, there are multiple combinations I can see happening and setting one down makes me reluctant to restart if I have all three slots filled. The replayability is there, but there are only a few save slots to use.
Even though the whole story has not been revealed to us yet, I do think the plot twist we were given at the end of book two happened too early. You can kind of tell the hints that supported it after you find out, but I think the want to know how Devan got to wearing a captain’s coat, how he ended up floating in the ocean, and other things that happened at the end of book two. With book three and four still to be announced, time will only tell how the reveal is handled and if it still seems too early.
+ Voice acting
+ Art
+ Well written plot and characters
+/- 3d models can be better
+/- Inspecting using a controller can be annoying as some items are so small one flick can go past the hit box
Herald: An Interactive Period Drama only contains the first two books out of the planned four, but even without this the experience seems like a full one. Everything is smoothly handled and nothing seems like they were trying to pad out the game with meaningless objectives or conversations. I do hope for the rest of the story to be released soon and highly recommend this.

The below review is taken from my original post at
The trailer of Herald exudes style and genuinely feels like something a little different. As far as I know I’ve never played a video game developed by a Dutch team with the exception of Killzone back on the Playstation 2 which obviously differs greatly from the visual novel genre.
Upon starting Herald, the craftsmanship on offer is clear and the fact that this is coming from a small development team of only four people is astonishing.
Wispfire has been working on Herald since 2014 and I’m pleased to say that it was worth their time and it is definitely worth yours.
The thought of playing an interactive period drama was instantly alluring to me as it felt such a unique premise, the period and place in which Herald is set is relatively unknown to me and so I was looking forward to broadening my knowledge.
After a brief introduction to the main character Devan Rensburg, who is being held ‘prisoner’ by a lady known as The Rani, the game flashes back to the beginning of Devan’s voyage and it is in this timeline that the majority of the game takes place.
The graphics continued to astound me as I played the game, the portraits of the characters that popped up when in the conversation were incredibly detailed and each portrait shimmers and moves to give a feeling of life to each person in the game, it’s a technique that adds an extra layer of involvement to the gameplay.
The in-game character models themselves are presented in a stylised way which reminded me of Escape from Monkey Island, which as everyone knows is a good thing. The backgrounds of the game and all animations are smooth and match the lulling, unobtrusive music which couches the game-play.
Herald is fully voice acted to an extremely high standard. Due to the nature of the game, there is a lot of dialogue but it is all handled well and I noticed no mismatches of speech to text which can sometimes be an issue in this genre.
The game uses a mostly static camera with occasional sweeping flourishes during cut scenes, this ties in nicely with the point and click gameplay with the focus being heavily geared towards dialogue choices which are well-constructed.
Whilst there are usually only three choices you can make, I found they were varied enough for me to always answer in the way I wanted to. In this regards the game reminded me of Deus Ex: Human Revolution as that game also had the knack of giving you dialogue choices that suited your style of play.
Narrative-wise, the game's’ focus is on moving forwards and telling a story as opposed to challenging the player with puzzles, this makes for a very breezy gaming experience in which you can focus on the tale being told.
The game has a lot of hot spots to click on but these are more for informational purposes to add to the thoroughness of the game world, these are interesting and give an insight into life at sea at the time. As you progress through the game, various items and areas are added to the in-game encyclopaedia which can be accessed by clicking on the top of the screen.
In-game objects of interest are highlighted when you roll the mouse over them, this avoids pixel hunting issues, which is a nice touch.
The game being set on a boat keeps the story tight and focused, each character also has a separate personality and voice actor which makes it easy to distinguish between them. Whilst the game is set in a time during which I’m sure there were intense class division and hardship, Herald exists in a world where that divide is somewhat romanticised. In the game there is no bad language and each character is quirky and has their own foibles but whilst there is the insinuation of racial and sexual divides, they are not the main thrust of the narrative.
Summary:
Herald is a wonderfully realised game and it’s branching narrative offers replay value. I completed the first chapters in a little over two hours and I would like to point out that there aren’t many puzzles in the game, as it focuses instead on plot and atmosphere but in my personal experience this can be preferable over forced sliding / lock-box puzzles to artificially extend a game.
If an interactive visual novel is something that floats your boat, I’d suggest getting a brandy ready and tucking into Herald. I eagerly await the next voyage!

I backed Herald on Kickstarter and was thrilled to finally get my hands on it. And the best part: Wispfire did not fail to deliver.
The game is visually an absolute joy, the story picked up right away and didn't let me off its hold until the credits started rolling, and I loved the diversity of the cast. The voice acting is (mostly) good and I didn't encounter any bugs or other technical issues.
I only wish I could sometimes walk faster (or run, when more appropriate to the story), since traversing the ship got old really fast after you learn the layout and already clicked on everything and everyone. That, and the camera angles on the deck don't always leave you a lot of area to click on when moving. Small annoyance, but still.
Overall, I enjoyed the game very much and can't wait to see where the cliffhanger at the end of Book II takes us in Book III.

Goodness, this game, It has such beautiful art, writing and voice acting, the twists it gives have actually left me speechless or gasping, I seriously cannot wait for the rest of the books. I love it so much.

Even though I'm still waiting for the whole story to unfold like the rest of you, from what I've seen so far, I'm pretty confident that they will continue to impress me with a quality narrative, believable characters, pleasing art style, intriguing background which would incur some thoughts about more serious issues like racism or imperialism in the rest of the books to come.
There's only minor negative things to say about the game, like one particular puzzle which involves discerning which item looks like a syringe or a bandage, and etc. It didn't really contribute anything to the gameplay, while successfully breaking the immersion by figuratively yelling at my face, "hey, it's an adventure game after all, so get ready for a puzzle!" - no, I don't want to see more of such puzzles in the rest of the books, as I don't think every adventure games need to be another The Monkey Island series.
The game relies on low quality models and textures, but when the overall art direction looks so pleasing, I don't think it'd be such a big issue for most of the people.
All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys playing such games which emphasizes more on story and characters, rather than actions or puzzles.
I was surprised to see that this game hasn't gathered more attention from gamers or review sites, but probably it will soon, if they can keep up with what they have done with the first two books of the series.

The game takes place in an alternate history where 1800's Europe and its colonies are unified under a single republican government, the Protectorate.
You play Devan, a young man in search of identity and adventure as you set out to sea towards the lands of the east where you born, but never got to experience.  Along the way, you'll make choices that affect events not unlike recent Telltale games.  Be prepared to encounter some weighty topics like colonialism, racism, feminism, and classism.
Animations are very stilted and robotic, but the hand-drawn artstyle still manages to bring everything to life.  The voice acting is also top notch and gives the characters some real, well, character.
As only Books I and II are released as of this review, be prepared for a very short game with a "to be continued" ending.  Books III and IV will be released at some point in the future to conclude the story.
Overall, worth the $10 I paid and I'm looking forward to the final two episodes.

Smallworld 2 is the digitalised version of the boardgame Smallworld.
This remake is very true to the original boardgame. It features online as well as offline play, aginst bots or Friends and has a huge amount of replayabillity through its sheer mass of possible combinations.
The Artstyle is very collorfull and high quallity, the Pictures for the abillitys are quite topical so they help you remember who can do what Trick
When you start the game you enter as one of the 28 Races that has been paired with one of the 35 random abillitys.
You then try to conquer terretory, that fits the special needs of your race, the Magicians for example score more Coins from terretorys, that hold a source of arcane power, while the Dwarfs prefere Goldmines.
The huge amount of variety enters the game when you factor in the abillity´s that every race gets randomly assined, you could for example get an Army of diplomatic  Skeletons wich enables you to go for one player while forcing the other to sign a truce with you, or you can rampage the countryside with pillaging orcs, that get more and more coins by invading other races.
Once you run out of Warriors for your race or you just feel like getting a new one, you can send your Race into decline and pick a new one next turn. The old one will stay on the board and still score points for you, but it will be weakened and easy Prey for a Fresh Race, maybe even your own.
The Tutorial is presented to you in the Form of videos and a Rulebook, just like the boardgame these Rules are quite clear and easy to understand.
Also the rulebook can be accesed during the Game to make sure you make informed decisions.
While the game does not have the incredible amount of deaph some other boardgames offer its great for a quick game aginst 1 other player, or for a longer one for up to 5 players.
All in all i reccomend this game for everyone that likes games that can be played in short bursts or just boardgames in general. My only complaint about the game is, that it features asynchronous play wich means you can make your turn, leave and come back later, this can drag a game out quite a bit but since you can start multiple ones at a time you can occupy your self otherwise.

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: 2D Point and Click Adventure
The Good:
+ At its core this game is a 2D exploration, point and click adventure game with some action segments thrown in.
+ Great atmosphere and lighting
+ Interesting story that adds to the atmosphere
+ Good puzzles that fit nicely within the context of the story and atmosphere
The Average:
A fairly short game that can be beaten in around 2-3 hours depending on skill level.
Because its 2D, there are times when you must run back and forth in levels to solve puzzles.
The action segments feel unnecessary and uninspired. Almost every action segment has you hiding behind cover waiting for the enemy to stop shooting and then proceed to shoot a few rounds before repeating the process over again. Luckily the action segments are few and are over with quickly.
The Bad:
- lack of any real graphical options
- Unless I missed it, no volume settings
Conclusion:
This is not a platformer, nor is it an action game. Its important to realize what kind of game this is. If you enjoy slow paced methodical gameplay, solving puzzles and getting yourself immersed in the atmosphere this is a great game to play.

I recently purchased this game on Steam but had originally bought this game back in 2003 for the original Xbox. I played it not knowing the history or significance of The Elder Scrolls series. I just thought the game looked cool by the cover of the box and figured I'd give it a try.
And boy am I glad I did.
Up until I played this game back in 2003 the only RPG I had ever played was the first Final Fantasy so my knowledge and experience with RPG's was very lacking to say the least. I figured I'd begin the game and start hacking and slashing my way through lickity split. That was my first mistake. This game humbled me. I was not prepared for the steep learning curve mandated by this game. I died. And then I died. Oh, and then I died some more. But once I understood the game mechanics and realized why I couldn't hit anything even though I was close enough to my enemies to hear their inner most thoughts and desires, I started to have fun.
Cut to several years later and hundreds of hours of playtime under my belt and this game has easily become one of my all time favorites. There is just so much to love about this game. For starters the setting is fantastic. It feels very alien with giant mushrooms for trees and giant beetle like creatures used as a way of transportation.
The story is extreamly engaging. The thing I love about the story is that it doesn't make you out to be this all powerful Demi God, savior of the the world right from the start like most modern RPG's do. You have to earn that title. You don't just kill a monster two hours in and get bestowed title of the chosen one with praise thrown at you by everyone you meet there after. You have to fight and claw your way to that title all the while everyone is looking at you like a piece of scrib jelly stuck to their boot. You have to convince people that you are the chosen and when you finally do, it is one of the most rewarding moments ever felt in a video game.
Another pro is the dialogue. More specifically the written dialogue. You see this game is primarily text driven meaning that when you talk to NPC's you have to read rather than listen. While this may sound like a con to some I find that the conversations are much more interesting and in depth. There are dozens of topics to discuss with an NPC with more topics that open up as you converse with them making the journey down the conversation rabbit hole an engaging one.
My last major pro for this game is the difficulty. I love how this game actually makes you have to think and work to accomplish your goals. You see there are no quest markers showing you where to go or who to talk to. You have to rely on your journal that your character updates by talking to quest givers. Often times you have to use natural land markers or ask random pedestrians where to go in order to reach your destination. Fast travel is also very limited which opens up the possibilities of stumbling into more random encounters or areas that may have otherwise been missed if performing fast travel all the time.
The game is not perfect though. No game is. Combat takes some getting used to and can be a bit of a turn off for some. Often times your character will miss it's target in the early game until you raise your combat skills high enough. Same goes for magic. Until you raise your magic skills high enough you will fail at casting a spell more than you will succeed. The game also does not tailor to sneak type characters very well making those character builds frustrating to use.
With all that being said if you are a fan of The Elder Scrolls games or RPG's in general this game is a must. Be warned though if you are coming from having played Oblivion and or Skyrim first this game is not those games. Morrowind does not hold your hand and it will require you to figure things out for yourself. This is a hard game and you will die. A lot. But if you give it a chance and take it for what it is you will find a lot of enjoyment out of it. I was fortunate enough to have been a teenager when this game released and was able to go into it without any preconceived notions are expectations.
The Steam version comes with the two official addons Tribunal and Bloodmoon.

TL;DR: Unless you are willing to spend A LOT of money, do not bother with this game.
Now onto the review.
This game is fun for the first hour or so. That is when everyone (all the beginners) are at the same level with similar performing weapons and gear. At this level, there are little to no vehicles besides the odd jeep or truck and bicycles. Everyone runs around with semi automatic rifles and the odd submachine gun user. It was fun as it felt like a World War II version of Battlefield where you can choose what faction you want to fight for.
Now that's where the good part ends.
After reaching a certain level, the Pay to Win wall smacks you right in the face. After crossing that threshold, you get put into matches with everything; every vehicle from bikes to planes and every weapon from bolt actions to machine guns. This would not be a problem or a complaint from me, but there is a really, and I mean REALLY big problem.
So backtracking a bit, I picked the United States to start this game with. It is currently my most played and most progressed nation. Now I felt that P2W wall but it did not bother me too much playing as an American soldier as I had upgrades to my M1 Garand, an M3 Grease Gun, and a Bazooka for the tanks.
But when I wanted to play the Germans or Soviets, I did not start back down where the beginners were and get the 'beginner' matchmaking for my unprogressed nations. The matchmaking I got was equal to that of my American progression! This means I got stock equipment (only a rifle with no upgrades) and I had to fight against tanks!
Of course you could get better equipment, but of course you have to pay real money for it. More times than not, I got killed by players that had far superior weapons and vehicles which are most likely payed for because the progression system is irritatingly slow and ambiguous. Ambiguous because it would say that you need 'X' amount of something to get 'Y'. I fulfill the requirements but I do not gain anything except stress. This is most likely a ploy to get you to pay money in order to get anything done. Speaking of money, the ingame credit rewards are pitifully small, even if you have a good match.
By the way, you have to buy (real money or ingame money) to buy vehicles as well so it is possible to just buy the strongest tank and mop the floor with enemy in every match.
The performance of the game is also bad. Everything feels floaty as if the game is taking place on the moon. Soldiers float around when they jump and some vehicles, especially the bikes, tend to spend more time on one wheel than two. When shooting, especially semi automatic rifles and bolt actions, it is completely random if you hit or not. This might be the case of my bad accuracy, but the feedback of whether you hit or not is very unclear which it makes it near impossible to be a sniper and hit moving targets. This is why automatic weapons reign supremacy as a hail of bullets will give you a greater chance of hitting something. To add insult to injury, the sounds of the guns are terrible. It can best be described as metal pots and pans hitting eachother or a curtain being opened and closed.
So if you want to spend the money, then go ahead and get this game. I do not recommend it at all. If you want to spend money, I suggest Red Orchestra 2 and/or Rising Storm.
Now I can hear you, "But this game has planes." Well planes in this game are next to useless as they can not capture objectives as the objectives are only on the ground. Sure the planes have bombs, but there are a lot of buildings to hide in.
This game is not worth it. Do not waste your time or money.

This game is amazing in so many ways, and a bit frustrating in others. It is visually gorgeous, with a very well-told story, albeit not a 'talkie'. The music and soundscape is truly masterful, and ranges from passively complimentary ambience to exceptionally crafted interactivity. The game is also quite difficult at times, as most of the puzzles are at least moderately challenging, and the hint and/or solution option usually present a quandary in and of themselves (the solution option just requires a little atari-style minigame, but is illustrated so cryptically as to be useless at times). If you are looking for something casual, this is not your game. Even if you consult the walkthrough, it can still be maddeningly hard. But when you solve puzzles in this game and as the story progressess and you see more of this strange world, all the tenuous stuff is worth it. The drawbacks of this game are glitchiness and obtuse interaction: glitches are glitches, and I need not clarify that other than to say they are not game ruining, but when I say obtuse interaction, I mean that a good portion of the game involves combinatorial or timely interaction with elements that are just not obvious. Case in point: (minor spoiler) in a certain encounter, the robot band's instruments are broken; what to do? Of course you go up a few flights of stairs in a certain direction, disrupt a few robots in very specific ways, accost an owl, and electrocute a cat, then take the cat and bring it over to the band robot dude's didgeridoo and stuff it inside so it can scare the small animal that nothing has indicated was present out of the robot's instrument. If I had not looked that up, I probably could have gone months without knowing what to do with either the cat or the didgeridoo robot-guy. All the same, I don't mind those inconveniences, as the game is an amazing and fantastic experience. I just can't give it the highest of recommendations, despite being extremely fond of it. [ 8 / 10 ]

Coming from someone who's never played the original Resident Evil (Only seen gameplay), Nor has really played Survival Horror game other than RE4. I'm really, really enjoying this game. I love the atomsphere and all the tension that's build up. I really like the gameplay, it's simple yet tough at the same time, as there is no UI at all other than the inventory and map. You have to look out for things whilst in game, such as the character looking hurt indicates low health. And you have to know when to shoot and how to aim the weapon without auto aim or crosshairs.
The game is challenging to say the least. The mansion is complex and almost maze like. The very limited item space and ammo as well makes things tougher. It really makes you plan out a route in the mansion as well as when to use your weapons. Especially how zombies come back as more powerful versions after a while if not properly downed.
I also super appreciate them sticking with 3d models ontop of pre-rendered screens, the fixed camera angles and even the door transitions. It emulates the original perfectly making it a brillant remake, One of the best i've seen actually.
The fixed camera angles is actually one of the core elements that make this game scary as it is. A lot of establishing shots of an area shows Jill/Chris facing the camera. You have no idea what's in that place until you move forward. It's a really good mechanic.
The only thing I'm not loving is the overall unclear nature of the game with the items and where to go; Which I understand is part of the genre, and I don't hate it as an idea, but as a first time player, I've spent countless hours walking all around the mansion getting lost. I geniunely needed to look at a quick guide a few times just so I made sure I did everything. It just was a little annoying. Obviously this becomes invaild after you've beat it, Just starting off blind can be tough.
All in all, I really love this game. It's a really good remake and offers a ton of spookes and classic survival horror gameplay. Go buy it!
Also Jill is just... wow. I mean she...

It seems that, in Herald, I am everyman and every woman. The script draws us in to experience the motives & thoughts of each character. The narrative, characterizations, art, & voice acting are incredibly well done.
The game plays out via simple p&c mechanics, where you use a mouse click to move through the ship. Controller options have recently been patched in, and are still being tweaked. The narrative is revealed in textboxes, where in parts it is just dialogue advanced by clicks, interspersed with sets of choices. Dialog is followed by cutscenes that are enjoyable and advance the story. I never got bored even after multiple games. The save system is convenient, making it possible to reload the chapter if you feel you made bad choices.
The soundtrack is lovely! One particularly haunting tune that appears in the theme is played on the piano by a character in one scene, who sings the words. This means a soundtrack would definitely be a plus.
Even with a good machine, the framerate never went above 30 fps for me. I felt like this was intentional, as it creates a not quite slow-mo effect, lending a dramatic flair to each scene. If lower framerates bother you, this may not be the game for you.
Most of the animations were done well, if simply. Most character movements seem true. There is one point where a character walks through a door, and then the irritating movements of the doctor helping a patient. Almost comical, the doc’s eyebrow moves side to side in one conversation.  But, in most other scenes, it is almost entrancing to see that simple can be elegant.

Herald is a mystery in its whole. At this point, only the 1st 2 books are released, so there is much to work with here and the writers seem to have taken full advantage of that, succeeding in every account.
✔  There is a revealer in the final scene of the 2nd book that changes what you thought you knew in very early scenes. This leaves you with a cliff hanger of sorts.
✔  Even multiple play-throughs add to and expand your opinions of different characters. Some things are never answered for us, but we are left to form our own opinions.
✔  Some apparent mysteries are left open at the end, hinted at only by shadows and shapes in the artwork.
✔  Ultimately, characters are left to being human with various interpretations of their behavior still being available after several replays.

I rate the choice in Herald a solid 8 out of 10. I played Choice of Robots, an excellent choice game that was totally text-based. I would rate that as a perfect 10, because your choices changed everything. The choice web was intricate, creating literally hundreds of outcomes. But, games like Firewatch, which I also loved but would rate a 5, presented only cosmetic changes with the choices. The players were all drawn back into the original plot line at collection points, so that ultimately your choices did not really change the story in Firewatch.
✔  In Herald, there is one story. The narrative rules as a mystery which you will reveal over the course of not only these current 2 books, but future books. But, your choices can affect the interplay of characters, and the outcome of scenes, and the appearance of different dialog trains. Information which you have not revealed is not later available in a conversation.
✘  Many decisions often affect only that immediate tier, and sometimes only in the emotional feel of the dialog. For example, whether you offer to do Ian's job for him or not, you get to do it. Regardless of how you respond to the Rani in the prologue, the results are the same. And, with the captain, navigator, & senator, I was accused of taking so long whether I stalled or took the direct text options.
✔  Numerous choices can change whether a character lives, dies, or is in the brig. Some characters can appear earlier in a scene, or in the place of another character, if your responses change. Interestingly, if you choose to start at the scripted start of the 2nd book, instead of in the 1st, I discovered that the script goes with the option of no characters being dead.
✘  No choice seems to have an effect beyond its immediate scene, with the exception of whether certain players exist or not. Because of this & the save system, it is possible to exit to the menu and restart a book multiple times, to get multiple achievies at once. Basically, some crucial decisions will pop one of 3 different achievements. No achievement requires more than one scene’s set of responses to resolve, with the possible exception of Mad Discourtesy, which requires probably 2 scene’s answers.
✔  Despite the save/ reload ability, multiple playthroughs will probably be needed to get all achievements. Also, you won’t get all info in the mystery without at least 3 plays. My 1st play took about 8 hours, with reading everything, even the letters that are unlocked at the end and the credits. The 2nd play took 4 hours, still reading choices and popping some achievements. After that, additional plays took about a half hour per book with skipping dialog & quick choices. So, after experiencing everything the story has to offer thus far… in every nuance, I have almost 16 hours.
✔  The dev team has made the art available in the trading card collectables.
✔   A large collection of concept art was made available free in earlier release notes. They don’t seem to be attempting to monetize every bit of data, as many devs are doing.
✔  They are responding quickly to comments and or email.
1. The log is helpful in-game, but access to what you’ve accumulated after the game would be a great addition to the menu.
2. Voice acting could be added for the letter collections in the menu. (Only half of them seem to pop after these first two books.)
3. Having musical options & even a musical library in the menu, as with the letter archive, would be even better. Alternately, a soundtrack would be a plus.

Okay, this is recommended for people who enjoy playing board games, and want to play either online with friends or by themselves.
If you want to know what the game is like in terms of play:
There's a Video of Wil Weaton playing it with Grant Imahara from Mythbusters and a few others. The game basically plays exactly like that but adapted to a computer.
It's a fast pased, 8 turn long board game with a suprising amount of in depth strategy inolved.
Now, some considerations. First, the game is complete in and of itself, there's no need to buy the DLC. But if you do wish to buy the DLC it can get a bit expensive.
Second, the game is slightly cheaper on Android Pads. If you want portability that's probably the way to go. if you want to play with your steam friends? this is probably a better bet.
Third, there's no full screen mode, but if you want, you can maximize the window for much better detail without losing any of the board to cut off.
Fourth, the "tome of Knowledge" also known as the glossary of terms and rules, is slightly buggy sometimes. the information is easy enough to read once highlighted, but initially it sometimes shows up obscured (particularly when showing races and powers).
Overall, this is a solid game well worth purchasing if you like board games in general, or the original Small World Board Game in particular.

My review is becoming riddled with updates, as the developer has been fixing stuff. Rather than keep trying to patch it, I'm just going to add my latest thoughts up here.
They've been very good about fixing issues quickly, and in particular the fact that it no longer pauses or resets when it loses focus is a massive improvement. There are some lingering issues related to the game's touch-interface-heritage (e.g. the requirement to drag tokens around, rather than being able to just click on a spot), but overall I'm much more satisfied with it now.
To be honest, I still don't heartily endorse it at the current quality and price (especially considering the price of DLC), but the steam rating system requires a thumbs up or a thumbs down and I think it narrowly makes the cut. Hypothetically, it should only get better from here.
I also should mention that at the moment, my review says 164 of 197 people (83%) found this review helpful. Those ratings were from before these updates, when I was giving the game a thumbs down, and that negative review. Hopefully my review is still helpful, but I don't want those people to feel like I hijacked their endorsements or something.
------ Mostly-original review below ------
Board games are my thing. I have almost 500 board games, and Small World is one of my favorites. I even kicked in for the collector's edition in the kickstarter that brought Small World 2.
And... I can't recommend this. Besides being overpriced (the Android version is $10; no idea what DLC costs for Android), it's really poorly designed for PC.
Doing everything requires dragging tokens from one place to another, which would be fine on a touch display but is a huge hassle with a mouse.
The game pauses if it ever loses focus, which means you can't browse the web and such during the computer's turn. Also, if you're playing an online game, and you leave the window's focus, even if it's played every other player's turn for you and it's your turn now, the game rewinds and plays back every turn again. What the hell?!
UPDATE: Quick play is now working, although the sub-minute estimates are quite optimistic. Took me a couple minutes to find a game. I'd previously written that only quick play wasn't working at all (and it wasn't, at the time).
There's support for a friends list, but it uses Days of Wonders' servers to manage your friends. There's no way of seeing your steam friends, as far as I can tell, which is particularly baffling since it already goes out of its way to tie your steam account to a Days of Wonder account.
That said, the quick play issues is the only real 'bug' I've encountered in the hour or so I've had it. All the other problems I have with it are design issues. Technically, it runs well. There's no full screen option, but the window resizes smoothly to whatever size you want (including maximizing).
I'm enjoying it, but I've already sunk the money for it. I don't recommend purchasing it until at the very least the online issues are ironed out, and ideally some more thought is put into how the game should work on PC differently from tablets.

+ Good story
+ Good exploration with a unique way to explore
- Awkward controls
The Fall is more akin to a point-and-click adventure game with a few action scenes here and there, contrary to the first impression you would get looking at the screenshots and trailers on the store page.
The game felt like it was supposed to be designed for another platform, such as mobile, or to be played with a gamepad, because the controls felt slow.  Mouse control was awkward and a little difficult to aim.  It required some getting used to.  Luckily, the fight sequences weren't difficult and don't require fast reflexes.  Platforming was also a little difficult to get right, but there were only about 3 platforming pieces.  99% of the time, the controls did not present an issue for me.
Animations relating to characters were buggy.  This became evident during the final battle.  I shot the enemy while it was in the air, and it caused a "ghost" image of itself to glitch out and stay there for the rest of the battle.  Jumping, running, and shooting in quick succession would cause awkward character animations, such as sliding across the floor.  Although most of the time the buggy character animations were not noticeable, and that they only affected the game aesthetically, they did however stick out to be something that was off and unpleasing.
The story and presentation were actually quite good.  You explore an underground facility, trying to discover what happened to it.  Evidence of the events that have transpired is shown throughout the facility for you to discover.  The developers have said that there was a lot of reading, but the amount of it was cut up into small pieces and strewn across the underground facility, so it never felt like there was as much reading as you would get in a traditional point-and-click adventure game.  The ending is also something I did not expect and took me by surprise.
I also liked the way descriptions of objects were shown.  Instead of randomly clicking to try to find interactive objects or clicking on already highlighted objects, you have to use your flashlight to have prompts show up and then shine on those prompts to have descriptions brought up.  This made the pointing and clicking part much more active and interesting than traditional games of this genre.
The game is rather short.  I finished it in 1.5 hours, completing all achievements in another 1.5 hours.  It is also not done yet; the ending is to be continued.  Don’t get me wrong, the story in this first game does end, but the overarching storyline does not.
In short:
Good story and a different approach to how you interact with the world made this game a recommend.  It does however have awkward mouse and keyboard controls and some buggy character animations.

Don't you
say this is a kids' game.
Because it is not.
Machinarium, in fact, is a great standalone from Amanita Design, a game development studio I am very proud of being from the same country as I am. It's a point-and-click adventure game about Machinarium - an ancient city of robots. You take control of Joseph, a robot thrown out of the city and dumped for untold reasons, and you'll lead him trough hours of great drawing and animations, story great yet simply told and soundtrack that you just have to love and admire as he makes his way back to the top, rescues his "girlfriend" Bertha, saves the city and escapes from it.
Point-and-click adventures are highly relying on their story, yet this game doesn't feature a single line of text (exception to main menu and credits). Instead, it explains it with simple comics which appear in classical speech bubbles. This adds to a feeling of really being a robotic being that doesn't need any words to explain it's thoughts, even though I don't believe the creation such a feeling would be truly intentional in it's nature.
The gameplay is simple as well, featuring locations with several puzzles and riddles you need to complete in order to advance further trough the city and the story. However, they aren't in any way dumb or repetetive, and can provide several hours of fun for those who enjoy solving these. And if you don't, the game always has a helpful guide for the location you can unlock trough fulfilling a simple minigame.
The graphics and design are the most awesome things about this game, providing you with beautiful sceneries, impecable characters and detailed drawings of the city and it's parts all along your path to the top. The city looks industrial and mechanical, creating a kind of a depressing feeling, with rust and metal pipes everywhere. The graphics are a true art, and that is not a statment I make lightly. Same of course goes for the soundtrack, so get ready to stay looking at the scenery and listening to a music, balancing at the edge of falling into depression or starting maniacally laughing. The feel is something many "horror games" of today miss - and yet this game doesn't even have to try to achieve it.
So my recommendation is simple - Go for it.

It might only say I have 0.2 hours on record, but I played this game before I even knew Steam was a thing.
Reviled at the time by many for its "Always-Online" gimmick that EA would still use for another decade afterward, Spore was a game that promised the literal "world" at its first preview showings, but did it deliver?
Honestly? No, but that's old history to most people, the game we got was, and still is, in my humble opinion however, a truly unique and creative experience that is paralleled by very few games.
The thing that makes Spore stand out, as with most Maxis games like The Sims, is its creativity. The Spore creature creator to this day is still one of the most interesting and in depth character customization mechanics in the gaming world.
Whether you want to go with some creepy, or somewhat realistic, or heck even phallic, your imagination is the limit.
Each stage of the game is based on a different stage of an organism, Single Celled, Primal, Tribal, "Civilization" (Quite literally), and Galactic.
You are going to spend the majority of your time in the Galactic phase as it is the proverbial "End-Game" to your adventure.
If I had to name any cons for the game, I'd say that each stage up to Galactic is fairly shallow, but in all honesty, this is a rather small complaint because although the game boasts having mutliple stages, it's not a "Civilazation" game, the stages are a "means to an end" so to speak.
My favorite stage is the Galactic stage, simply because once you've gotten to this point, you've kind of "grown" with your Creature race and Galactic boasts the most features of any of the stages.
The Galactic Adventures DLC essentially adds MMO-esque elements to the Galactic Stage, adding in Fetch-Quests, Escort Quests and the ability to get off on alien planets. While this is cool to break up the monotany of space trading and travel every once in awhile, even with community made quests, you are probably going to play the same 3 or 4 over, and over again.
Overall, Spore is a game that is very much remembered but often overlooked for how good it really was. 8/10.

I really love this game, so much so that the moment I finished one playthrough, I started the next. The genius of Herald is the way it blends everything that's almost comfortingly familiar about adventure games and comes up with something entirely fresh and exciting. Many of the character archetypes (stern statesman, whiny cabin boy, underappreciated officer) are immediately familiar, but as the story unfolds every single character is given depth. The plot surprised me at multiple times (especially the end of Book II, loved it!), but it never felt forced because there were always clues laying the groundwork for every reveal. It seems you are bound to go through the same basic plot, but your choices certainly matter in some significant ways, some choices opening up or closing options later. And both books so far end with high stakes conversations with dramatic effects. I was surprised after I finished playing to enjoy reading the archives (letter and document style backstory pieces), which add further depth to several characters and help to explain their motivations. This is a rich story with lots of detail accessible to flesh it out, but even if you skip clicking around the ship for extra information, there's a lot to enjoy.
Technically speaking, you can see the graphics from the preview videos and screenshots and they're nothing special. I love the character portraits though, which are very detailed and dynammic. Although many people consider this a horrible game, I find it to be fun and enjoyable if you know what to do.   FIrst off, the game has glitches and bugs that can definitely ruin the player experience; A.I. seems to be the most common but picking different teammates can fix that to an extent (having an all female team + the player makes the game easier) and sometimes the menu might tell you to press
for a second instead of
.  Medics especially have the best A.I. since they'll haul♥♥♥♥♥just to save you from death if you've taken too much damage (but they might heal you after you've healed yourself with and herb or First Aid Spray.)  You can also sometimes stick to cover when you don't want to and not stick to cover when you want to (I've only experienced the former.)
The campaign for the game can either be long and frustrating or short and enjoyable, depending on difficulty and player playstyle (this game really only gives the option to attack instead of sneaking, seeing that you're on an elite team sent to destroy evidence and kill witnesses, which is pretty damn edgy and feels like a bit of fanfiction) but you can turn the infected against your enemies by using a special ability by the team Scientist or making enemies bleed out.  There is also the Echo Six Campaign which seems a bit more fun (to me at least)
The game runs smoothly on my laptop on Max settings and at an always nice 60fps.  Mind you, this is a laptop from the Summer of 2013 and is non-gaming (Intel i7, 16GB RAM, 1TB Hard drive and IntelHD 5000)
The multiplayer seems to be dead and might not come back (even if it were given T-Virus) seeing as GFWL
, which is a shame as the multiplayer can be the most fun you can ever have on this game (which seems to be a trend with most games, but I digress.)  Though you can sometimes find someone to play with in co-op at rare times.
The Cosmetic DLC isn't really worth it at a normal price but on sale it's an ok buy (it changes the colour of the player's chosen character and gives them a slightly different outfit, at least in terms of Vector's.)  The Weapons DLC can make the game easier or harder (The Matilda and Grenade Launcher are horrible weapons since you can't shoot well at long range and have limited ammo, both in terms of magazine and resevoir; and not being able to pick up extra ammo, respectively) so just either pick and choose which weapon pack you want, buy the Complete Pack or just get the Weapon Stash for all eight weapons. The Campaign DLC has a slightly better A.I. than the base game but it still has some of the faults of the base game (getting stuck or stopping at a random area and sometimes just tanking bullets from enemies.)
Seeing as this game was only published and not developed by Capcom, there should be some similarities from games developed by Slant Six Games such as the SOCOM series.   Actually, it plays a LOT like them.  There might've been a sequel to this game but Slant Six closed down in June of 2013; it could be a blessing or a curse.
I really recommend this game ONLY if it's on sale and not a regular price, though I shouldn't discourage you from buying this if you really want it and want to play with a friend (or 3)

Machinarium, in fact, is a great standalone from Amanita Design, a game development studio I am very proud of being from the same country as I am. It's a point-and-click adventure game about Machinarium - an ancient city of robots. You take control of Joseph, a robot thrown out of the city and dumped for untold reasons, and you'll lead him trough hours of great drawing and animations, story great yet simply told and soundtrack that you just have to love and admire as he makes his way back to the top, rescues his "girlfriend" Bertha, saves the city and escapes from it.
Point-and-click adventures are highly relying on their story, yet this game doesn't feature a single line of text (exception to main menu and credits). Instead, it explains it with simple comics which appear in classical speech bubbles. This adds to a feeling of really being a robotic being that doesn't need any words to explain it's thoughts, even though I don't believe the creation such a feeling would be truly intentional in it's nature.
The gameplay is simple as well, featuring locations with several puzzles and riddles you need to complete in order to advance further trough the city and the story. However, they aren't in any way dumb or repetetive, and can provide several hours of fun for those who enjoy solving these. And if you don't, the game always has a helpful guide for the location you can unlock trough fulfilling a simple minigame.
The graphics and design are the most awesome things about this game, providing you with beautiful sceneries, impecable characters and detailed drawings of the city and it's parts all along your path to the top. The city looks industrial and mechanical, creating a kind of a depressing feeling, with rust and metal pipes everywhere. The graphics are a true art, and that is not a statment I make lightly. Same of course goes for the soundtrack, so get ready to stay looking at the scenery and listening to a music, balancing at the edge of falling into depression or starting maniacally laughing. The feel is something many "horror games" of today miss - and yet this game doesn't even have to try to achieve it.
So my recommendation is simple - Go for it.

Great remaster of what was and still is the best remake ever, and one of the best games of all time.
I owned and enjoyed the original on the GameCube, and I had just as much, if not more fun with this PC remaster. The character models got revamped with new textures as well as shiny new normal maps, and every area in the game takes advantage of that with nicer more-detailed lighting (on the characters) throughout.  Even though the pre-rendered backgrounds were just upscaled and filtered a bit (not re-rendered at a higher resolution), they still look convincing over 90% of the time. That eased my biggest worry with this remaster - that it would look dated in HD. I didn't end up feeling that was the case at all. It's aged surprisingly well.
I HIGHLY recommend playing this game how it was intended - with the tank controls. The game had the alternative, non-tank control option enabled by default when I first launched it, which I found odd. I guess Capcom is afraid modern-day gamers can't handle tank controls, but honestly, as long as you aren't playing on Hard, this game is pretty easy even with tank controls. I breezed through it on Normal mode with Jill, with dozens of healing items left over in my storage box. If I had such an easy time with it with tank controls, I can't imagine playing it with the new alternate control scheme. It likely makes the game WAY too easy to the point of being a snorefest. Do yourself a favor and play it with the original controls. It's a fantastic and enjoyable game that way, and one of the best examples of good pacing and game design in videogame history.

Brilliant game/remaster. As a long-time resident evil fan who played the first game shortly after it was released in the UK all those years ago, I was very happy with the remastered version which has managed to keep true to the originals story, play style and overall gameplay.
I feel the best way to review the remastered edition would be compare it to the original, so thats what I've done. As many of us are aware, remasters these days are usually lacking on some of the key aspects of the originals, and somewhat loose the alure and appeal of their original counterparts due to badly made graphics, gameplay, story modifications or additional content. This version however has managed to tick all the boxes a remaster should tick, and has brought forward many of the positives of the original game and delivered them in a very positive way. Many of the aspects of the game have been modified for the better, and all come together to form this masterpiece. Here is a list of improvements the remastered version has delivered.
# Kept to the original story and added content (for the better) that slightly expands on the original storyline in a non-intrusive way.
# Slight tweaks to character movement have been implemented, and alternate control setups are available. The original controls are also included if you wished to stick to what you know.
# A few adjustments and additions to the combat have been added, to bring the game up-to-date with newer modern-day resident evil titles. These additions are also very welcome and improve the gameplay further.
# The athmosphere of the game has been kept as it was in the original, deleivering that feeling which any decent horror game should deliver. This has been kept true to the original and deserves praise, as this was the part I was most worried about just before release.
# Graphical improvements. These are obvious even from the picture on the store page above. The graphics have been improved dramatically, and are delivered seemlessly with none of the bugs/issue many remastered version seem to adopt these days, (IE. bad texture mapping, lighting issues etc.)
All of these points above come together in harmony to bring you the end result, a very well made remaster of a timeless classic in the most efficient way possible, in my opinion. I couldnt have asked for anything more from a remaster of this game.
Any fan of the original series should play this game, and they will not be disappointed with this. I bought this game on pre-order at the time, at full price and was extremely happy with it. I personally think this game is worth more than the store price, when compared to other titles of the same price, so in my opinion even full price for this is a steal.
If I was to nit-pick at issues with the game, the voice acting is not the best, however saying that, the original had 'cheesey' voice acting so keeping true to the original I dont think this is a major issue. Some dialog has been added to the voice acting here and there, but its only really minor changes that dont defect too far away from the original.
So in conclusion, this is a brilliant game, and well worth every penny. I cant wait for the Resident Evil 2 remaster to come out and I hope it follows the same steps as this remaster has.
Thanks for reading my review.

My favorite thing about this game is that the Mansion gives you a chance to experience a true adventure to travel into the unknown in search for answers and progress. The game can be difficult at times, but that's what makes unlocking the next cutscene all the more rewarding. All the characters have been redesigned from the original so that the dialogue and lore can be taken a bit more seriously, thanks to this I was also able to enjoy this more than the ps1 version I had acquired years previously.
The set pieces in this game and how they tie into the gameplay is perfect. You will often find yourself more concerned with unlocking other parts of the mansion and solving puzzles than dealing with pesky zombies which gives a more rememorable experience.
The survival horror is definitely apparent. With the limited inventory and obtuse camera angles it will be best to avoid enemies. In addition, the new enemy type known as crimson head that was added into the game further drives the idealism that you should just run past enemies instead of mindlessly engaging them in combat. Lets not forget about the checkpoint system as well that is based off of you collecting ink ribbons, and finding a type writer to save your progress with. All these features become apparent within the first couple of minutes and should be noted that all these core survival horror elements is what makes the gameplay thrive.
I have yet to finish and complete the game, but as of now it is already amongst my favorites for the Resident Evil franchise alongside Resident evil: 4, and Resident evil: Code Veronica X.
Give the game a chance and buy it, if you're worried that you'll purchase it and leave it alone to collect dust I suggest that you buy it during a sale of sorts. Be it that it may, this game will not disapoint you if you're already familiar with survival horror.

An interesting game, if ever there was one. Mount & Blade: Warband sees the player, who starts from origins that are determined at the start of the game what his or her father was, and what he or she did during their childhood and teen years. And from there, your story begins and as for where it ends, well... that pretty much depends on what goals you set at the start of each new playthrough.
You see, you can be many things in this game, ranging from a thief to a noble, and several - but not everything - in between, add into this the fact that this game has no story aside from the questions asked to the player at the beginning of the game and whatever it is you do during that playthrough that determines the story might turn some people off.
The gameplay feels like a Frankenstein's Monster of gameplay genres (it's not, I just thought it would be funny to say that), and you can see inspiration from games such as The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, Uncharted Waters, and Romance of the Three Kingdoms (the video game franchise, not the novel). You hire troops, you can trade between towns through certain trade routes, you can (and will) fight bandits, you can join a kingdom or create your own! Really, there are SEVERAL possible ways to play the game, but to me, they always seem to end up at the same thing: trying to conquer all of Calradia. But you needn't go THAT far for your goals, whatever they may be.
The graphics, while not the prettiest in the world of video games, looks like they game straight out of a game from the Playstation 1 era, whenever that was, I don't remember, but they do look nice, yes.
The music will, at times, not come on at all and when it does, it is BEAUTIFUL! Likewise, the music, assuming it comes on, will occaisonally cut back out,
All in all, a very interesting game, and one I would suggest to anybody who may be a fan of the games mentioned above (TES II: Daggerfall, Uncharted Waters, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Nobunaga's Ambition, etc.).
