"Never go Full RAF" or, "How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Hate Everyone"
A video game review.
55,573* young men and boys died serving in British Bomber Comand during the Second World War. 55,573. Considering the fact that all of those lost souls were autonamous beings with functioning minds, that figure puts your little squirts in "Bomber Crew" in dire straits indeed.
As many people noticed when this game was anounced,"Bomber Crew" bares some resemblence to "FTL", a fantastic rogue-lite game where the player manages the crew and systems of a faster-than-light spacecraft on a desperate voyage against terrifying odds to save the galaxy from impending tyranny. The game is notoriously difficult, but regardless of how anticlimatic your failure of the final mission against the Rebel death ship may seem, on the journey there missions were completed, battles were won, new alien races were parlayed with and adventure was had all around.
In "Bomber Crew" the player assumes the role of incompetent hive mind to the crew of seven barely sapient stooges aboard a Lancaster bomber. This half-witted rabble is introduced during the recruitment phase of the game. They come provided with names, little gibberish radio voices, a randomized assortment of physical features, hobbies and a town of origin, all rather cheap ways to inseminate with "meaning" the tiny lives the game bludgeons you into expending with frightening regularity.

One should not grow too attached to the members of one's crew in "Bomber Crew." In fact, even attachement to one's bomber (which must be upgraded at the player's own expense, and is randomised upon replacement), the idea of progress, or even the point of the game, which eludes me somewhat, must be discouraged. It does, in point of fact, become increasingly difficult to view the silent, wide-eyed blur that one's constantly-replaced crew quickly becomes with anything but disdain, for they are utterly incapable of doing anything themselves, and must be shown enemy fighters to shoot down, (lest they stare disinterestedly into the clouds while the only structure keeping them aloft is disintegrating and their own bodies are riddled with machinegun fire), new headings to take so they don't get lost, to open the bomb bay doors before dropping the bombs that they cannot even select themselves... the list goes on and on. You even have to read maps.
As other players have pointed out, this tedium could be forgiven if the game had a feature that allowed the player to pause time while they selected crew members and tasks, spotted waypoints and enemy planes (which take about three seconds of pointed staring each to spot, and often appear in several flights of three fighters). But no, planes must be spotted, fuel mixtures micromanaged, and literal fires put out all in real time. The layered UI would be manageable with a pause button, but without one it quickly becomes the death of efficient action, and of your crew, your bomber and your fun. Played as is seemingly intended, the player is exponentially less efficient than the human crew of a real Lank, just by virtue of  having to micromanage everything in real time by themselves.
But if all this needless hardship is for it's own sake (and I think it is), what is the point of this game? Is it meant to harden the heart of the player to the facsimilated humanity of their crew, to demonstrate the wanton martyrdom of a war of attrition? If I wanted that, there's already a gut-wrenching, narrative driven little FPS based on "Heart of Darkness" which does just that. It's called "Spec Ops: The Line." But that game's realistic art style and dour, introspective tone couldn't be more different from brightly colored,  chibby, pixelly nature of "Bomber Crew". I know that deceptively cheerful nihilism has become rather popular with my generation's culture, but I don't think this game does a very good job of exploiting that while remaining an entertaining experience. That of course is assuming the point of the game, which I don't know. I haven't completed "Bomber Crew", and I don't much care if I ever do.

I've never really done a long review before, but here we go. I heard of this game when I saw TheDevilDogGamer post a video on youtube, the gameplay looked interesting so I hopped on Steam and saw the price and figured if it was bad I'd only be out 12 dollars. I've been hooked. I beleive I only have 8.3 hours at the time of this review but I have progressed well through the campaign and lost my fair share.
This game really is something unique. I see people compare it to a game called "FTL" but I have never played it so keep that in mind. After training I recruited my crew and named two of the seven pilots (I'll get to customization in a bit). After a few successful missions I had my first run in with an Ace, as I was feeling cocky at the time I believe it was a high risk mission. The mission started out great and after a successful bombing run, it was time to head home. The ace then showed up, the music changed and I thought I was ready but the Ace really showed me up. It was a close fight as it went from killing the Ace, Felix Feder, to a fight across the channel to get back home. As my crew races around the gunship, and my gunners exchanging fire with the Ace, My first casualty happened, Whittington. The tail of my plane was shot off and at that point I knew it was over.
My plane crashed into the Ocean. The only survivors were my pilot Alex and my second gunner, Justin. I then recruited a crew and started with a new plane, as my two experienced crew members helped guide the new crew to learn the ways. Eventually after many successful missions and experience, time came to face felix again. This time the Ace showed up to stop the bombing. Felix along with many other German planes tried taking down the "Virgineer". It was a rough battle. Justin, who was now rear gunner, was injured during the fight, two engines burst into flames and one stopped working in general. Donnie jumped out of the upper gunner seat as hope was dwindling, Ian grabbed the fire extinguisher and put out the flames to the engine as Madison, who was navigator went and began repairs on the malfunctioning engine. Donnie helped Justin up and then was shot. Ian and Madison barely made it back inside.
As Germans were swarming the plane Alex performed a risky manuever dodging many, if not all the enemy fire. Justin ran to the ammo box and sprinted back to the tail gunner seat as he saw Felix coming in for the final blow. Felix opened a channel and warned the crew they were not making it out alive. Felix, not knowing Justin was not killed, approached the tail. Justin focused and thought of his previous crew and now Donnie who risked himself to keep Justin from being killed. Justin pulled down the trigger and took out Felix with a final blow and watched as Felix crashed into the earth. The crew of the Virgineer finished their bombing mission and even completed vital intelligence photographs.
As the Virgineer flies over the channel, dramatic music begins playing and the crew lands. Unfortunately it was too late, Donnie who had sacrificed himself to give Justin his revenge died seconds before touchdown. Alex and Justin thanked their crew, and recruited a new gunner to carry on their missions in rememberance of their old crew and now Donnie.
That was within my first couple hours of playing.  So I hope that helped.

First off, I'm someone who easily gets bored with games; the second I lose interest I'm done.  There's so many games that I bought that I was like "Oh wow!  I'll love this game to death and I'll play it in the afterlife", but alas never was that the case.  So many games have gone unplayed or underplayed.  Even the games I do play regularly, I usually have a youtube video or podcast up cause honestly, I want to do something with my mind but my main attention is the video/podcast and not on the game.
With that said, Bomber Crew is completely different.  The music transitions and choice are fantastic; the Peanuts like voices are perfect; the game design, flow, pacing, ect. are all very well thought out.  The game is hectic, frantic, soothing, and cute all at the same time.  The graphics are simple that convey a clear and conciseness and the sounds are varied and distinct.  I actually started feeling like I was a part of the bombing runs that my crew do.  Hell, I still get a rush whenever I cross the English Channel in-game.
So let's talk about the gameplay itself.  It is a real-time resource management game based around 7 crew members on a bomber during world war 2 (for the allied side of course).  Most of your crew are semi-automonous, once they're at their station, they'll do their job.  But you're always somewhat involved to either kick-start their task or optimizing it.  T
Let's take the engineer for example, they just sit at their station doing jack squat, but you can time their abilities to improve gas usage or boost the plane to avoid flak and other hazards plus estimating fuel usage, moving fuel between the two gas tanks (FYI: don't try to land with all the fuel in one, lost my first bomber with that stupid mistake), activating the extinguishers over the engines (if/when you buy that upgrade).
Let's take the gunner as another example.  They'll shoot at enemy fighters automatically, but only after you've tagged the fighters and only if you've told them to stock their gun with ammo after they've run out (takes a minute or two to run out of ammo, so it's not like you're loading each bullet for them).  Tagging is just telescoping on the incoming aircraft and watching them for about a second then the fighter is tagged.  But to do that your radar needs to be working (though I think you can tag very slowly if the radar isn't working but I can't see crap without the helpful radar, maybe in the future I'll be able to) and manned and the radar can only be working if the electric box is functioning and if  the box is damaged enough and has low enough armor that it breaks then you'll need your engineer to repair it, but oh wait, engine #1 is on fire and we've already used half our fuel and we're not even to the bombing sight yet and where's those spite-fires we've called in with our super leveled-up radio operator who's almost dead and needs to go to the healing bed that OMG there's a fire there and.... and...  and thus the hidden deep strategy of it all shows itself in the game play.  This game is about triage, prioritization, short term and long term strategy all bundled up into one cute simple little game.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys FTL.  This game is FTL's distant cousin, they're related but not closely.  Bomber Crew has a more structured and narrow approach and a significantly more focused custimization of the vehicle and crew.  If you're even remotely into real time resource management games, I guarantee you'll enjoy this game through and through.
2 common questions in video games are: Is it 'worth' the price and how many hours of content is here?  Yes, it's worth the price, if you follow the 1 hour per $1 rule, you'll hit 15 hours before finishing your first run of the game and this game will hook/line/sinker you pretty quickly.  I don't know how much content there is cause every hour I see something new but I'm pushing on to see the final end cause I'm loving every minute with this game.
Of course, like any rouge-like games, don't get too attached to your crew or you're bomber; both will end up at the bottom of the sea sooner or later.  Sorry Hill and Hall, I did everything I could to save you :'(  At least the game has a memorial for you.

Many people state that this game is terrible. Well, is it? Do I agree with them?
Yes, it is and yes, I do agree. This game....is almost like a joke. A bad joke that is. First, good things. The music is actually pretty amazing, especially the menu song, which is really good to listen to. And I liked the fact that you actually can get infected by zombies, so in order to cure yourself, you need to drink some purple drink. And I liked the fact that you can play with 3 other people. I guess this miserable game is a little bit more enjoyable if you played it with friends.
And now onto the issues. optimization. HORRIBLE. This is like one of the worst PC ports I have ever seen. What were they thinking? It is jerky as hell sometimes, even though I am running the game on a medium quality resolution + low settings (I am not the only one complaining, many have reported the same thing on Metacritic). They obviously screwed up big time on the optimization process. Who made this? Amateurs? And my goodness.....the control is terrible. Basically those zombies swarm in, and a bunch of soldiers try to kill you, basically you are sandwitched and required for you to act fast, but the damn control is so bad, I had a hard time aiming and I don't even know if I am even actually damaging the enemy or not, as they are like sponges. I mean, fix the damn control, or do something about that messed up level. You can't even run right past your friends or zombies if they are blocking your way, when you SHOULD be running like crazy otherwise you will die, and this is just irritating as hell. And what's up with the gun shot sounds? Are those toy guns?
And this game only has like what, 7 missions? That's it. Way too short, and I only finished 4 of them and did not bother with the rest as it is just irritatingly annoying. The very concept was good, when I heard about playing as the members of Umbrella and fighting against the main characters of Resident Evil like Leon, I thought this game would be an amazing one. In fact, the voice acting is pretty good in this game, and only if the story was as good as it was meant to be, then I may not criticize this much, but pretty much, the voice acting and the music are the only things that I can praise them for. My goodness, Capcom really screwed this one up heavily. I would rather play Ride to Hell: Retribution than to play this, because at least Ride to Hell is actually well optimized, and is still an enjoyable TPS game. But this? is trash.

You know, Im in an Odd position reviewing Morrowind, I started playing the Elder Scrolls Games with Skyrim, and I will honestly say, I enjoyed Morrowind so much more than I ever enjoyed Skyrim.
The game hasen't aged well, thats for sure, but that isn't somthing which really drags down an expierence with the game, Just because its an old game doesn't mean It can't be a fun experince, this is the mentality I had going into Morrowind, and maybe because of that, I came out loving the game.
It told a story I felt I was so much more intertwined with than later games in the series, I was never treated as the chosen person to be this and that and pretty much the leader of everything, The game made you earn things, and I loved that, I loved how I was just some outlander who had to make his way into some form of respect, and even more work to climb higher than that, Even in the main story where your destined to become a great hero, you still have to earn it far more than later games ever made you.
As for mechanics, I can understand how it can be frustrating to some missing 9/10 of there swings or spells, but of course, with time you as a player can understand how the system works (Heres a hint for you new players, pace out your swings, don't spam it), and as a character to miss more like 1/10 of those swings or spells, and you can see that as your character improving as time goes on, lets be honest, your character is thrown off a boat knowing nothing, and of course your going to have to learn via trial and error, and I love how the game puts you through that, Rather than just being able to do all that right off the bat as later games allow you to. I also throughly enjoyed the ammount of customisation you had, how many skills there were to level up, though it may be more tedious, the reward is far more worth it because of it.
All in all, I loved Morrowind, I can confidently say its a great game that I would reccomend people try and give a chance to with an open mind, you'll certainly come out with a great experience if you do.
(Also, Hey look, a Positive Morrowind review from someone that doesn't have Nostalgia for it)

This is an excellent modernization of the original.  It stays very true to the original and adds a little extra flavor along with the better graphics, plus the voice acting is nowhere near as laughable as the original.  The atmosphere is what you expect for a mystery-horror thriller game, with some action elements mixed in.  Fans of the original won't be disappointed, and newcomers to the series really should start with this one.
There's really nothing about this title I would change, despite a minor complaint about how the fixed camera gets you stuck in a brief loop in certain rooms.  Those fixed cameras are part of the atmosphere and must remain as they are, as frustrating as it can be at times.  This is a classic that has ported well to the new millenium, and I do wish they would have returned to this formula as the series progressed.

This is based on a 20 year old game that, although being one of the most influential games of all time, really shows its age by now.
There is a reason developers have moved away from fixed camera angles, and Resident Evil, in both its original and remake form, makes that abundantly clear. Moving around is incredibly awkward even with the alternate control method, and with the camera angle constantly switching, you're gonna end up disoriented and heading the wrong way a lot.
There's also the issue of inventory management, where free slots are a rarity, forcing you to move back and forth between storage chests all the time to deposit and withdraw items. I see the point Capcom's trying to make, but it's more of an annoyance rather than actually adding something to the game.
Other than that though, the game still holds up pretty well in terms of graphics, sound design and overall atmosphere, and it's well worth a try if my previous points don't sound too horrifying.

While DC Universe is a good time of the surface, you will quickly find that you are incredibly limited in what you can do with a free account, which is to be expected with a Free to Play game right? Sure. Except that with a free account, DC Universe Online limits the amount of currency your PC can carry. Your money is capped at $1,500, and the rest you earn is sent to your "bank" which is locked unless you pay a "withdrawl fee" or pay for the game. This bars you from obtaining high quality gear, practically forcing you to pay. Maybe I would pay for the full version if the whole game didn't feel like a desperate ploy by DC to make some cash. If you are somehow not put off by these limitations, then by all means, play it. But honestly, this is borderline robbery.

Find You offers well crafted platforming puzzles, an inbuilt level editor and most importantly smooth physics that completely enable player control. Its antiquated presentation may be off-putting at first, but the gameplay is consistently on point with great level design and a gentle learning curve.
The main mechanics are nothing new but so cleverly put together and gradually introduced within 111 levels that they never feel monotonous. Plain logical puzzling, observing and planning lies at its core in all puzzles. Every possible aspect, even the most peripheral physical circumstance, is woven into a level. This makes some puzzles very finicky, requiring timing, precision and dexterity. However, the controls are tight and responsive so that it's always possible to fiddle a way through where intended.
While the graphics are certainly nothing to write home about, the clean sprites at the very least help focus on the gameplay. The music on the other hand can be distracting with a contradicting beat in levels where cadence is of importance. Usually though, the background music is unobtrusive.
Surprisingly polished gameplay renders Find You a worthwhile puzzle platformer with potential additional content thanks to the workshop integration and the easy to use ingame level editor.

An excellent action adventure side scroller with puzzles and a superb story. If you haven't finished it, please do and if you haven't bought it, please do. I picked this up for a measly 0,99€, but even if you buy it at full price I doubt you will be disappointed. To be clear, it's an episode, so it's on the shorter side (I completed it in 4.5 hours), but the ending is entirely satisfactory (don't sue me if you see it coming), so I've no qualms with the length. The writing is great, often witty and backed up by excellent voice work. Portal fans should definitely take a look.
Camera and player movement can get somewhat annoying as you try to line up for equipment interactions or grab onto ledges, which happened rarely, but it's the only unpleasant thing I can remember to point out. The camera jumps to the next area after you've crossed a certain point on the screen, but you'll get used to it. It's a side scroller. Puzzles are just of the right difficulty, though I did consult a walkthrough here and there. Though the gunplay is too easy, I think it warrants another playthrough for the story, cos the writing and voice work really are top notch. Either way you'll be missing some achievements on your first run, some of which are time-sensitive.
I've no idea if the developers are working on another episode, I would love to continue this story, but I think it's also nicely self-contained and well delivered, so I won't hold a grudge if this is where it ends. Over The Moon Games can be proud of what they accomplished here.
Edit:
As I checked their website, they announced Part 2 in August, with a Q1 2017 target date, so there you go. More to come. Sweet. It's nice to discover games 2 years after they've come out, with another episode not that far away.

Who should play:
- People who likes sci-fi stories
- People who likes atmospheric games
- People who likes side-scrolling action & adventure games

The Fall is an unexpected little sci-fi gem. It is a 3d side-scroller game which combines adventure and action elements.
The interesting part is, of course, the story of the game. We are controlling a space combat suit, programmed with a sophisticated AI named ARID. The directive of the ARID, and the purpose of the game is, to save the human pilot inside the suit who is critically injured after a sky fall.
Despite being a cliche AI theme, the progression and the dialogs are well-done. We are trapped in a robot facility which is gone wild. There are no humans, only some corpses. Robots behave a little crazy. It is almost as a robot asylum. The music and the sound effects also fuel this dark atmosphere.
The main NPCs, Caretaker and the Domesticon Mainframe are certainly interesting characters. And yes, they are AIs bounded by certain rules and directives. While Domesticon chooses to bend the rules as much as possible, Caretaker is very ridig with them. So it is not difficult to guess who the antogonist of the story is.
The progression is somehow ironic: as our protogonist AI Arid becomes more human with its decisions and sacrificies, the more "faulty" it becomes.
This is a short game. It has some flaws: controls are not implemented very cleverly. When you change your direction, there is no animation but instant movement, and I find this a little ugly. Some puzzles are irrevelant. Yet it is a nice and interesting game. I am eager to see what will happen on the following story of the ARID.

This game is essentially XCOM except instead of elite alien killers, you play as equally badass WW2 British bomber crew. You will have to keep an eye and order each crew member to do their job in order to complete a mission alive, so multitasking is a thing. This game is also incredibly unforgiving. Pros:
+ Customization is great, if not ridiculous at times. If you want a rainbow colored Lancaster bomber called the "Granola Gay" with all of your crew members named after your loved ones, then go right ahead! And that's not even touching the upgrades
+ Replayability is there
+ Game is cheap
+ Addictive and gets your heart pounding
Cons:
- Selecting crew members or selecting them to do certain actions can sometimes be a miss.
- The level of difficulty and mission designs can be brutally cheap at times
- Only 1 bomber type (for now maybe?)
- Can be repetitive
- No real reasons to use high, or even medium altitudes
- Damage model can be weird at times (you can literally land with 1 engine no problem)
- Gunners can shoot in the complete opposite direction of the enemy (no matter the skill level)

short description:
a rather minimalistic game about managing a lancaster bomber crew during late ww2. The gameplay mainly consists of assigning the crew to different stations at appropriate time and customizing them after combat. This game lacks polish but is very enjoyable. i recommend purchasing it specially if it is on sale
Technical notes:
The game does have a windowed mode.
The settings menus leave a lot to be desired. While not graphically taxing, more detailed video settings would be appreciated. Audio settings are even worse. I hope they improve this aspect of the game.
The menu and UI could use some overhaul. Not enough tooltips and it sometimes takes too many clicks to do what you want.
Long review:
To me, this game feels like a mixture of “FTL”, “X-com”, and “Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes”. Allow me to explain why by breaking the game into three parts
1) Crew management: The meat of the game involves moving your crew around the bomber to utilise stations and perform tasks. Much like “FTL”, you will always have more possible positions than the number of your crew, forcing you to make important decisions
2) Mini activities: as mentioned, each position in the airplane has a function, however you can't just assign people around and sit back. Depending on your preference you'll either see this as a good way to change things up a bit or just needless busywork, but you will need to tag every enemy fighter for your gunners, locate targets from your bombardier, press the release button at the right time to aim your bombs, etc. in short, you will be doing a lot of fiddling about instead of sitting back and just managing the general operation of the crew.
3) Customization and emergent drama: Those of us who have played xcom know that when you name your soldiers and meticulously choose their gear, they become important to you, you are more invested in keeping them alive and over time you might even assign personalities to them. While customizations in this game are nowhere near as robust, they seem to have gotten the soul of the concept down. In other words, the game creates emergent drama as your crew gains experience, gets gear and becomes valuable. Maybe you succeed the mission but that super skilled gunner you kept from mission 1 gets killed in the proccess, or maybe your plane can't make it back in one piece but a sole survivor somehow makes it out alive from the crash landing.
Conclusion:
So, should you buy this game? We all are different individuals and want different things from our games. All i can say is that after a bit over 5 hours of play i can say i got my 12 dolars' worth and that i can see myself continueing to play it for quite a while. That said, i don't think you would enjoy this game if:
1) Permanently losing valuable crew and upgrades seem like a waste of time to you and not a good way to build suspense and drama
2) You Have very low tolerance for unpolished and at times a bit clunky gameplay
3)Want a simulation. (this game is very arcady, you repair engines by climbing out and hitting them)
4) You dislike randomly generated missions (that are frankly all a bit samey), and dont want RNG in your game in general
Thanks for reading my rant :)

Bomber Crew is a game that I can certainly reccomend.  While the game is relatively calm at first, it quickly descends into chaos with you having to scramble your poor old flight engineer all around the plane (And usually have him fly off the wing while repairing the engine or fuel tank due to flak fire or god forbid, having your pilot manouver the plane.) and search for hostile fighter planes. The games difficulty isn't that bad. If you go looking for a high risk mission, you're going to get a mission filled with constant flak fire and constant fighter strafes. In those few moments of calm, you have to prepare for the next wave of fighters. Oh, and losing your crew is pretty tragic. Seriously, always bring atleast 2 medical kits. On my second critical mission (The missions that advance the campaign) my plane, the Jerry Bomber, was making its way back to Britain over the English Channel after destroying its target, but being heavily damaged. Right when it seemed as if it were calm, a BF-109 sprayed into my heavily damaged tail, and disconnected it from the plane. Luckily, we were at low altitude, so the impact wasn't too steep. My bombardier was killed on impact, my tail gunner was somehow saved, my top turret gunner was downed beforehand, the impact killed him, and my radio operator was also killed. The 4 remaining men were rescued.
Morale of the story: Always get survival gear.
Oh, and heres a bonus, The damage that your plane gets is completely dynamic. Any place where a bullet lands will make a hole. It isn't just a texture based on hitpoints. Infact, the only thing that has hitpoints in this game are hostile planes and your crew. Your plane can easily lose its flaps or alierons to fire if they are shot in the right places.

You know, Im in an Odd position reviewing Morrowind, I started playing the Elder Scrolls Games with Skyrim, and I will honestly say, I enjoyed Morrowind so much more than I ever enjoyed Skyrim.
The game hasen't aged well, thats for sure, but that isn't somthing which really drags down an expierence with the game, Just because its an old game doesn't mean It can't be a fun experince, this is the mentality I had going into Morrowind, and maybe because of that, I came out loving the game.
It told a story I felt I was so much more intertwined with than later games in the series, I was never treated as the chosen person to be this and that and pretty much the leader of everything, The game made you earn things, and I loved that, I loved how I was just some outlander who had to make his way into some form of respect, and even more work to climb higher than that, Even in the main story where your destined to become a great hero, you still have to earn it far more than later games ever made you.
As for mechanics, I can understand how it can be frustrating to some missing 9/10 of there swings or spells, but of course, with time you as a player can understand how the system works (Heres a hint for you new players, pace out your swings, don't spam it), and as a character to miss more like 1/10 of those swings or spells, and you can see that as your character improving as time goes on, lets be honest, your character is thrown off a boat knowing nothing, and of course your going to have to learn via trial and error, and I love how the game puts you through that, Rather than just being able to do all that right off the bat as later games allow you to. I also throughly enjoyed the ammount of customisation you had, how many skills there were to level up, though it may be more tedious, the reward is far more worth it because of it.
All in all, I loved Morrowind, I can confidently say its a great game that I would reccomend people try and give a chance to with an open mind, you'll certainly come out with a great experience if you do.

Before I begin, yes, Morrowind was my first Elder Scrolls game back when I was 16 years old and it left an impact on me like no other game has before or since.  So, of course, I may be a little biased in my opinion of it.  People who started playing with Skyrim often go back to check out the older games and wonder, "How can anyone like Morrowind?" It does have it's challenges and annoyances.  But no other game has ever felt more rewarding to me for the time and effort you put into it.  When you begin a character in Morrowind, it is extremely hard to start levelling up, and all of your skills suck.  You swing your sword 30 times and only make contact maybe 3 times.  You fail at casting a spell 6 times in a row and now all of your magicka is used up and you have to sleep or drink a potion to get it back.  You run slow and you can't jump more than an inch off the ground.  These things can be annoying.  But I also think it is one of the things that make the game so rewarding.  You really have to make an effort to improve the skills you want to use, and as you do, your character becomes more and more proficient with them.  Eventually you find yourself making contact with every swing of your sword, casting powerful spells and never failing, and running insanely fast.  My first character I ever played back on the original XBox, made it to level 90.  By that point my skills were maxed and I could jump nearly as high as a house,  cast powerful levitate spells and walk across mountain ranges, and deal insane amounts of damage with weapons I enchanted myself.  It is also very rewarding when you finish the storyline for a guild.  Unlike in Skyrim you are recognized for what you did and who you are, with people actually commenting that you are the leader of the guild.  Plus the quests are all insanely fun.  Another thing was difficulty and an element of fear.  Nowadays, when you see a Daedric ruin in ESO you run in, kill everything in a few hits, and leave with a skyshard and an achievement.  In Morrowind, I will never forget the first Daedric ruin I experienced.  It was terrifying and I got destroyed instantly.  From that point I steered clear of Daedric ruins until I was a much higher level.  And then there is the music, one of the best game soundtracks I have ever heard.  'Nerevar Rising' stills gives me chills everytime I hear it.  The environment, the characters, the music; it all has a magical way of making the world seem high fantasy yet familiar, strange, yet comforting.  Morrowind is, and will most certainly be, THE game that changed everything I knew about gaming and RPG's.  Those memories of staying up all night back in high school with my cousin, taking turns with our characters and arguing over the controller, will stay with me forever
Even for how old Morrowind is i would still recommend it.

A lot of people seem to forget that Morrowind is one of the finest RPG games ever made, and one of the most in-depth, pure TES games ever developed. Despite it's age, the in-game mechanics are far more complex than Oblivion's.
First and foremost, the game is much more difficult than both Oblivion and Skyrim combined. The combat system uses what's called a
system, basically this means that when you attack an enemy, you may or may not miss completely. This dice-roll system takes into account multiple variables from both the player and the enemy to ensure that it's fair and difficult at the same time.
Fast travelling? Forget it, Morrowind is the walking simulator of the TES series. Quest on the other side of the map? Better put your running shoes on. In reality, this can get really annoying and tedious at times but on the contrary, this allows players to absorb the environment and appreciate the effort that went into the level design in Morrowind.
In terms of stability, I'm saddened to say that this game simply hasn't aged that well. Before I continue, I will say that all the issues I faced could've been fixed using mods, but if you insist on playing vanilla, then brace for the following:
So in all, is this game worth buying? Sure, but keep in mind that you'll really need to mod the bajesus out of it to make it run and look modern. If you don't mind doing this, then you'll really enjoy the game.

I played this ten years ago and it was brilliant, my first proper RPG game. Oblivion seemed to blow the graphics out of the water, and Skyrim did that again.
Going back to Morrowind after 10 years was very interesting. It has the haunting foreboding of the island still intact, but the main thing I was happy to see again was the statistic system and the way skills progress.
The overall character set up and stats feels far more like an RPG than the later games. Something I think should have been carried through.
The level of lore present in Morrowind is pretty large and back then they were not afraid to just use text for the bazillions of minor NPC's that exist. Its great being able to walk up to pretty much anyone and ask them for gossip or a little about themselves.
Having 10+ choices for conversations with NPC's makes it feel as if you can have a conversation with anyone, even if just in passing.
I would love the series to port this to future games, give me more NPC's I can talk to. If they are minor NPC's and its going to break the budget, dont be afraid to use text.
Dont be afraid to play this game either, if you like old school RPG's this one has a great storyline and lots of playable hours.
It does require a good four hours of so of playing to start feeling like you can take on the world. Dont expect to be able to handle more than one bandit at a time at lvl 1...cause you wont.

For fans of parkour/speedruning who want to have their skills challenged in what might be the silliest setting possible, this game is for you.

First of all, I want to say I thoroughly enjoy playing this game. The speed and nonsense that happens during levels causes you to rely on your gut instinct, an element which I love.
And without any more, lets get into the pros and cons:
Pros:
+Quick, gut instict relying levels
+Makes you feel really cool about yourself
+I love how something so mundane (like a truck) is transformed into something so fun
+Some moments which make you say "What the f***?" which I ABSOLUTELY love!
+Happy and colorful art style which instantly puts you in a good mood.
There are many more, but for the sake of people not reading this forever (and for the sake of me running out of ideas) lets move on!
Cons:
-Some levels can seem similar to others
-Fail after fail makes you a little angry
-Some levels can be repetetive after failing multiple times
-Some levels are almost impossible without upgrades, so you have to download the dreaded "Easy Points!" workshop map.
The Clustertruck Editor:
Onto the final part of this review, I decided to give the editor its own section because it is... something special.
The editor is really cool in the aspect that you can make your own extremely ridiculous truck filled levels. You can even turn off lethality for certain objects meaning you don't even need trucks in your level. However, I've made it sound really good and flawless. In my opinion, it's 'decent' at best. There's enough tools to make a cool map, but if you don't save every 2 seconds there's a chance that your hard worked on map will suddenly disappear and be replaced with a truck in the middle of nowhere (the default 'editor' level). The tools can often break, too. I've experienced the rotation tools scaling or moving the objects, and the scaling or moving tools rotating objects. My mouse often also disappears from the screen at times.
Conclusion:
This game is very fun if you're into it's genre and if you're a calm person who enjoys a challenge. Just don't rely on the editor working.

This was pretty much my favourite go-to game. It has action combat, weapon combos, a semi-targetting system, feats/achievements which grant you extra skill points. Every power type has a dps role and a non-dps role, which the player can switch between at will. The other roles are tank, healer, or controller - the controller helps to restore power to the team, debuff enemies, and provide crowd control. Respeccing in this game is done easily, with in-game cash (not the real life kind). You can use armouries to basically store your build/gear, they can differ completely in skill/ability distribution.
However, there is a cash-cap for FTP players, anytime you go over the 2k cash limit, the rest of your cash is stored as "escrow" which requires a sub or cash-shop item to access. This is total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and essentially cuts off a large amount of players from auctioning. Once you reach level 30 your new "level" is measured by your combat rating which is calculated off your gear. You do alerts, raids, etc. in order to earn gear drops and "marks" which can be used to purchase new gear. Once you have enough gear to raise your combat rating high enough, you move on to the next tier content. All content past tier 3 is paid for, either you have to sub or buy some DLC. I loved this game to death and logged alot of hours on it, but I don't feel good about the obstacles free players will be facing. Subbing is cheap but i'm a casual player and subs make me feel like i'm playing on borrowed time - not a good feeling. My main character is now stuck at tier 5, combat rating 100, all dressed up and nowhere to go. Daybreak has made a bunch of changes, some of them were good, but some of the changes made it less rewarding to do certain things, like you no longer get any marks at all for doing content below your tier. Anyway i'm hoping they fix the game in future to be more FTP-friendly and a little more fun.

The Fall is a 2D sidescroller with light elements of puzzle and combat. You play as Arid, a combat suit tasked to protect the individual inside as they both fell from the sky into an abandoned facility. One of the most fascinating things about the game is how the game explores the relationship the suit or it’s AI has with it’s wearer (or pilot in this case). The game also explores what it means to be a machine and how much of a ‘machine’ they really are when they are gifted a degree of self-awareness only a living breathing individual might possess. Both Arid and the other AIs are constantly tasked to withhold their protocols while at the same time bending it if it means they are to achieve their goal, which for Arid — protecting her pilot at all cost. This forces Arid to intentionally put her pilot in danger only to open up certain protocols to better serve her pilot. I found this wrestle between being programmed for and self-awareness to change the programming parameters to meet her goals really fascinating.
The game is very atmospheric. The sound and visual art style are played to their strengths. The game does not use much color, however it uses the little color palette it is given to highlight the world to a maximum effect. Same goes with sound with only important audio cues related to gameplay are highlighted to give spatial awareness to the player.
The game has light puzzle elements which majority of the gameplay is comprised of. They aren’t very complicated, however often they are not very clear either and might induce a bit of trial and error when trying to solve them. There is a very basic layer of combat thrown in there and is one of the weakest parts of the gameplay. However there aren’t many instances of the combat to become cumbersome.
The biggest frustration came from the controls. The way you keep holding right analog to target and right shoulder button to enter inventory and finally press A to accept — all this just for using an item is incredibly frustrating. There are simply too many unnecessary steps for the player to do just about everything. Luckily the developers have acknowledged this issue and are working to resolve it for their next game.
So this sums up The Fall. A great sci-fi story wrapped around a game which took me by a surprise. While it is a shame the controls are very annoying, but it did not matter in the grander scheme of things. I am already looking forward to the sequel.

* Remember this is my opinion. It is up to you as a reader how offended you get by my opinion. Most likely you will be offended. Let me also clarify. I was unable to playthrough this game however, I watched an entire playthrough of the game just to understand what was going on. *
When playing a game that is ten years old you obviously should take into account how well or, poorly the game has aged. As you can see I have two and a half hours playtime for The Witcher and I will explain why. I am not the sort of person to abandon playing a game without a good reason however, whilst playing The Witcher I found it hard to find one good reason to play the game at all. I know this game series has a cult following and in the eyes of the super-fans CD Projekt Red can do no wrong. That's fine and I am sure the next two games in this series are significantly better (I will be playing them soon) but the first Witcher game has aged abysmally.
As I mentioned before whilst playing an older game you must consider the age of the game before being too critical on things like mechanics or graphics. As a result, comparing this first Witcher game to the third one and saying, "The first Witcher game has bad graphics." Would be an awful comparison. But you can compare a game made prior to The Witcher or within roughly a year of the games release. Let's start with the first Mass Effect game. Released on the 20th of November 2007 ten months before the release of The Witcher. Mass Effect bolsters beautiful graphics that have aged incredibly well, detailed dialogue that is very well voice acted and an incredible way to begin building a new game universe. On the other hand, I found The Witcher to have poor voice acting with no depth, textures that resemble the quality of Lionhead's 2004 Fable and a poor introduction to a new game universe. Sure, you can argue that The Witcher is being based off a book so there is less creative leeway when creating the universe but if you can't work with what is given with you and turn out something of a good quality. Then why bother?
I do not want to go into too much depth about the combat mechanics of this game they are just bad. Even if I was playing this game nine years ago I would still find them bad. You can compare the mechanics of this game to other games being released around this time that were just significantly better for their respective genre: Portal, BioShock, TF2, Uncharted: Drake's Fortune, Assassin's Creed. Hey! Even Super Mario Galaxy did a better job with its mechanics. Before the fanboys flip out that I am comparing the combat of an RPG to a platformer or an FPS. I'm not. These are all games that I either have replayed recently or have fond memories of. There is no denying that The Witcher has bad combat mechanics. You left click, double-tap to roll sometimes and maybe throw a few spells with right click. Truly thrilling.
Graphics and combat mechanics were the two largest reasons I could not force myself through this title. The third reason is one that A LOT and I mean A LOT of fanboys are going to get mad at. This game is so incredibly sexist. (Sorry I'm a SJW and I can't help it). Some fans would argue "Oh it's just because the game is based on Slavic Mythology" or that it is a "Period piece". Which is understandable - to an extent. However, it becomes very hard to remind oneself of this♥♥♥♥♥♥poor excuse when Geralt. The monotone, lack of personality, generic edge-lord seems to be banging every busty woman he speaks to. One of the personal favourite interactions is between Triss and Geralt. At the start of the game Triss becomes injured and is only healed by a specific potion that you must create. Once you have created the potion and Triss has drank it. She instantaneously is restored to full health and is up to go to pound town with Geralt. Just like real life when you face a serious injury.
Now calm down fanboys. I can hear your furious typing already. This is my opinion. It is okay for you to enjoy this game and have others think negatively of the game, it is only natural. This review does not reflect my opinions of the next two game titles.

The Witcher isn't a very good game.  Graphics and music are both passable for the most part.
Pros -  The plot, story, characters, and dialogue are interesting enough for the most part, though there are some serious flaws.  For instance, the bad guys could take Geralt by surprise several times and kill him but don't bother to, even after knocking him unconscious at one point.  Likewise, Geralt knows who one of the bad guys is but instead of just killing him, starts talking trash and let's him get away..... this is just prior to the part where he gets knocked unconscious, would've been really embarrassing for him if that guy had just killed him while he was knocked out.
Cons – The combat system is garbage.  Click on enemy, wait for sword icon to light up and click again to combo over and over and over and over and over until enemy is dead.  I was very confused by the way enemies attack during this.  Sometimes the combo completely prevents them from damaging you, but other enemies will damage you during the combos even though you can clearly see they aren't even swinging at you.  You can use several spells in combat but there are only 2 that are actually useful and thankfully speed up the terrible combat.  One spell lets you stun a single enemy and instantly kill it while another lets you cast fire at them, if you level the fire up enough it'll one/two shot most weak enemies and severely injure most sword sponge enemies in 3 uses.  The end boss of chapter 1 is broken, being nigh unbeatable unless you use the stun spell, get it to work at random, and then instagib it.  After that point, enemies and bosses are pretty much a cakewalk, even the final boss.  You'll get so tired of the combat system and pointless enemies that you'll try to run by most of them just so you can transition to the next area, but you can't transition if you're in combat, and enemies will follow you across half the map.
The inventory system is also garbage and for the most part pointless.  If you actually go around picking up stuff, it'll get clogged constantly.  The only things worth having in your inventory are potions and items for increasing weapon damage.  There are shops all over the place but the only things really worth buying are alchemy scrolls, some books about enemies so you can complete quests for them, and armor (though I'm pretty sure there's only 1 piece of armor you can buy throughout the game).  I never even bothered using the blacksmith.  The alchemy system for making potions is pretty bad as well.  There's a crap ton of potions you can make, but there're only 4 that even matter (health/endurance regen, see in the dark, and I forget the other, maybe it's only 3 that matter).
There are some interesting quests (usually related to the main plot) but most aren't very good as they're either 1. Go here and kill that thing.  2.  Kill this creature multiple times and bring me X number of things from their corpse.  3.  Go here and fetch that and bring it back.  The locations for the game aren't very big which is nice, but you will constantly be running back and forth through them over and over and over and over to do quests and turn them in, it gets annoying.  The game marks where quests will be at on your map as well as where NPCs will be at to complete the quest, but sometimes these marks are wrong, and it can be incredibly annoying trying to find those missing NPCs.  Some quests can only be done/turned in at certain parts of the day, so you're constantly having to go to firepits to sleep just to do a quest, then go to another firepit so you can turn it in, then go to another firepit so you can get the time right for your next quest, then use another to turn it in.  It gets obnoxious after awhile, especially in chapter 2 or 3 where there's only 1 firepit in the whole damn town.  There are also a couple sidequests involving fist fighting and a poker dice game.  The fist fighting is incredibly simple and pointless and the poker game is rigged against you.  Sometimes you can get information/quests out of certain characters by out drinking them.  Getting drunk is very annoying as Geralt then walks like a snail and you must then stumble incredibly slowly to wherever the nearest firepit is so you can sleep and actually move around again.
The game can get buggy at time too, so you're gonna want to make sure you save about every 5-10 minutes just in case.
The few interesting story bits, characters, and dialogue don't make up for the tedious combat & inventory systems, the repetitive and unimaginative quests, and the constant running around you will be doing.  I'm pretty sure I considered never playing it again about 15-20 times throughout the course of the game, I have no idea why I bothered finishing it.  This made me never want to play the 2nd or 3rd ones, so I'll never know if they're any good or not.

To first address the people who complain that you have to "spin too many plates" to stay on top of aircraft problems, yes, yes you do.  There are a lot of plates to spin and that damned electrical system just LOOOOOVES to short out at a moments notice right when you're fending off an ace and flying through a flak field while simultaneously fighting an outer port engine fire. It's challenging, it can even be quite demanding but by God is it fun. The graphics are adorable and cutesy which is kinda funny given how brutal and XCOM like (in that you recruit randomized crew members and watch as they get killed by sectoid/fighter fire) the game can be. Thankfully a total aircraft/crew loss doesn't mean game over. You start back at your airfield with a new Avro Lanc and can recruit a fresh crew to go out there. The missions variety is kinda samey with a few twists on the basic theme of "Fly here, manage defending your bomber from fighter while at the same time accurately bomb your target, and fly back home." Sometimes you have to blow up a tank factory, sometimes its a couple of munitions dumps, or three submarines (Im a big fan of B-17 Flying Fortress The Mighty Eighth and I never played it for its mission variety) so if you want to reenact the movie Dam Busters or pick a specific target other than the "Pick one of three randomly selected missions" you're out of luck. On another note, some people get freaked out about systems repair remember; you don't have to fix EVERYTHING. You have four engines, you can get by on 2 engines, maybe one if you're near your landing strip. You don't have to rush to put out an engine fire if your other engines are good. If an engines burning before you reach the mission area yeah I'd fix it but fair chance you can ignore it for a bit. The two most important things you need to know, always keep your turrets stocked with ammo. Have your turret gunners ferry ammo (in my Army unit we called that role the "Ammo Fairy" or "Ammo Ferry") when they're not doing anything and keep your engineer moving. He's your swingman or 6th man if you're a basketball fan. Now see, the bombardier is responsible for the forward gun turret AND the bomb sight. He can't do both at the same time so I "swing" my engineer to the forward ball turret during bombing runs so the plane doesn't lose forward facing firepower. Dress your engineer accordingly so he can stay mobile. And he's also the guy thats responsible for all major shipboard repairs. As to the other systems, you can ignore the oxygen system if it faults unless you're flying at high altitude. But NEVER ignore the hydraulics. You literally CANNOT land without it since it controls the landing gear. Oh and watch for Schrage Musik. German night fighters during WW2 realized that the Avro Lancaster can't defend itself from the bottom so the Luftwaffe started equipping their fighters with cannons that fire directly upward. So your crew will be chugging along, merrily bombing Rhine valley industrial complexes when all of a sudden the soft underbelly of your plane starts getting cut up. Usually your middle ball turret gunner is the first to go. This is my one complaint, Schrage Musik was very effective against the Lanc because it exploited a key weakness of the craft. The real world fix was to install a ventral turret underneath the plane. In real life it worked, in game, that ventral turret becomes a vestigial organ as the only man who can get to it in good time is the central turret gunner who by that time is bleeding out on the floor plate. Only an experienced pilots "corkscrew" move can get that pesky fighter out from underneath your plane. And even then, that fighter will probably just get back under your plane again. C'mon devs! Give us something we can use to counter that thing!
As a note to people who are worried about how damned difficult it can be in the early going, I say get cheat engine and get yourself the really high end plane upgrades if you just want to have a little light fun with it. It won't be nearly as hectic an experience for you.

"You sure my team aren't zombies?"
Set in Raccoon City during the events of Resident Evil 2 and 3, this game has you taking your team through streets, alleys and masses of zombies in order to complete your missions.
Story
You are part of an elite team sent to Raccoon City by Umbrella to retrieve samples of the G-Virus created by William Birkin. Later missions will have you taking down the power in the city and destroying any evidence about what Umbrella has been doing. Along the way, you will meet some characters you should recognize if you have played the older games. The events of this game are not part of the series though, which does make sense.
Presentation
This game is looking great. For a ruined city, this place is perfect. Raccoon City is wasted, just as it should be. Destroyed cars, dead bodies and burning wreckage all over the place. The indoor locations like Umbrella labs also look perfect. Moving onto the enemies, these are also as they should be. The zombies themselves look perfect for what they are.
Now we get to the sound, and that isn't so good. Forgettable music, poor voice acting and lacking sound effects all make me wonder if they tried here. Even the moans just aren't what they could be.
Controls
As a game developed with consoles in mind, it is best to stick with a gamepad. Even the HUD features a DPad to select your grenades and healing items. Playing with the pad, most of the controls worked decently, though attempting to make headshots with the analog stick was aggravating. More than once, I'd use my mouse to aim for those bits.
Gameplay
This game takes a massive departure from most of the other titles in the series, being a team based third person shooter with plenty of ammo to let lose at your enemies. Most enemies are bullet sponges though, and it will take time to clean up the mobs in your way. Nothing inspired here, it plays like many other team based shooters, such as the Left 4 Dead series.
There are six different character classes to pick from, each with their own active and passive skills to level up and use during gamplay, allowing different gameplay styles in your team. You have a Assault member, great with their guns, Demolitions who can set traps, a Medic for healing all your woes, a Scientist who can infect and control enemies, the Recon is all about stealth and finally the Surveillance member for boosting your ability to detect items and enemies.
The only problem with your team is that they are incredibly stupid, with me left wondering if even the zombie AI is smarter, since that lot don't get lost when attempting to hunt. This is easily fixed by having friends play, but unlike more popular titles, there isn't a lot of players around.
Lifespan
With a total of six levels, I found this game to be rather short. Once you have beaten the game, you have a few things to do, such as trying to get higher ranks in each level, powering up each of your six characters and finding enough intel in the levels to unlock all images in the Gallery.
There are a number of multiplayer modes, but like co-op, you aren't going to have many people willing to play with you. I wouldn't depend on that unless you want to gift out several copies to people on your friend list.
There are also a number of DLCs available, though I'm only going to mention the important ones here, the Echo Six content. This adds additional missions to the Free Play mode, in which you play as another group, working against Umbrella. This group is nothing more than reskins of the original team though, with the same skills available, but the missions themselves are different. If you care for the gameplay, these are worth purchasing.
Closing
While this game is nothing special, I enjoyed it enough that my purchase during a 75% off sale didn't feel like a rip off, as any early buyers would have felt. It has uninspired gameplay and isn't popular enough to fill a team for co-op, but it isn't bad.

Pros:
+ Seeing the Resident Evil universe from the view of the bad guys
+ Some enjoyment to be had here with friends
+ Variety of characters, weapons, and abilities
Cons:
- Poor controls
- Unnecessary difficulty spikes and frustrating enemy spawn locations
- Utterly bugged and glitched (animations, shooting, taking cover, etc)
- Poorly designed levels/environments
- AI relies more on cheating than any form of intelligence
The Bottom Line
It would be one thing to knock this game for straying from the usual Resident Evil model but when it utterly fails to be that which it set out to be - a third person shooter - something is incredibly wrong.
Despite the allure of having a handful of characters to choose from, an arsenal of weapons and abilities to unlock, and the enjoyment of seeing the RE universe from a totally different perspective Operation Raccoon City is broken, buggy, and ill-designed right down to its core.
It says a lot about a game when I can't bring myself to even complete it - and I've bit the bullet and powered through many a buggy, poorly made game just to see it to completion. ORC however is just not worth it in any way, shape, or form. Perhaps there is some fun to be had playing it co-op but unless you're really into that steer clear of this game.

A lot of people seem to forget that Morrowind is one of the finest RPG games ever made, and one of the most in-depth, pure TES games ever developed. Despite it's age, the in-game mechanics are far more complex than Oblivion's.
First and foremost, the game is much more difficult than both Oblivion and Skyrim combined. The combat system uses what's called a
system, basically this means that when you attack an enemy, you may or may not miss completely. This dice-roll system takes into account multiple variables from both the player and the enemy to ensure that it's fair and difficult at the same time.
Fast travelling? Forget it, Morrowind is the walking simulator of the TES series. Quest on the other side of the map? Better put your running shoes on. In reality, this can get really annoying and tedious at times but on the contrary, this allows players to absorb the environment and appreciate the effort that went into the level design in Morrowind.
In terms of stability, I'm saddened to say that this game simply hasn't aged that well. Before I continue, I will say that all the issues I faced could've been fixed using mods, but if you insist on playing vanilla, then brace for the following:
So in all, is this game worth buying? Sure, but keep in mind that you'll really need to mod the bajesus out of it to make it run and look modern. If you don't mind doing this, then you'll really enjoy the game.

The level of lore present in Morrowind is pretty large and back then they were not afraid to just use text for the bazillions of minor NPC's that exist. Its great being able to walk up to pretty much anyone and ask them for gossip or a little about themselves.
Having 10+ choices for conversations with NPC's makes it feel as if you can have a conversation with anyone, even if just in passing.

A game soley for people who have patience, a far cry from the other elder scroll's games. You're not going to be kicking♥♥♥♥♥right off the boat, no. You'll be walking as slow as a sloth, you won't be able to hit♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you'll have to find out where to go, all by your self. At first, I hated the game. I had played skyrim and oblivion earlier, and I had high expectations, I expected a carbon copy of the first two I played. Boy was I wrong. I hated it. It felt awful, and I ran out of patience for the game and uninstalled it due to its extremely hard difficulty early on. Years later, I came back to it. This time, with a clean slate. I lowered my expectations, and I didn't think of the other elder scrolls games. Over 35 hours later on the OpenMw sourceport, and I started to adore this game. Its the best Elder Scrolls game bar none. Far more interesting characters than in skyrim (my boy dagoth ur), and Morrowind already had the disadvantage of extremely limited voice acting. Exploration that rewards the player! Instead of some doofus marking it on your map and holding your hand through out, all you get is brief descriptions of where to go. No Map markers, no compass, nothing. Only crudely written notes in your journal. Because of this, you have the option of meeting and talking to other people, such as city guards, of more clear directions. I can't even recount how many times I accidently wandered into a completely different quest line when I was searching for a temple or a location I was trying to get to. Quests I struggled on at first, became dirt easy because I had gotten full dwarven armor from a random quest I stumbled on. It gives you one of the greatest feelings of progression, almost matching Dark souls and blood borne. The feeling of conquering a dungeon, or finding that puzzle box you've been hunting down for decades is so great. The atmosphere is amazing. Its not boring plains, or forests, its a weird alien and abstract looking world, making it much more interesting to explore than the future installments. To be perfectly honest, I'm kinda puzzled. I love Oblivion and skyrim, but they just feel like steps down to Morrowind in my opinion. Anyway, pick this up. Try not to compare the game to the new installments, and most of all: patience.

It's the floor is lava, but taken to the absolute highest level.
The gameplay at its core is a platformer, but the ability to strafe in the air and ride along trucks for extra speed makes it so much more. If you've ever tried surfing or rocket jumping in a source engine game it's somewhat similar to that. I can see it being difficult to get used to, but once mastered the gameplay is exilerating and extremely fast. Add in a multitude of different unlockable abilities(some of which are more humorous than useful) and you get gameplay that is fun, fast, and somewhat creative in a way.
The sound design is top notch, there's a neat little twitch integration if you plan on streaming the game, the levels and there mechanics are well designed(with a few glaring exceptions), and there's even a level creator which allows you to make your own levels and share them online so other people can play them.
My main issue with the game is that unless you're a speed runner or a perfectionist, the game may seem somewhat lacking in content. Including the 2 holiday theme worlds there are only 11 worlds and 105 levels. That may seem like a lot, but the game is so fast that those levels can past by in an instant if you're good enough. It took me about 4 hours to beat the entire game, and I'd wager that at least 1 hour was spent on the last level of world 9. I'll definately go back to beat some levels again for my daily dose of speed, but if you're someone who just wants to complete and game and not replay previous levels them $15 might seem a bit steep for about 3-5 hours of game (albeit an extremely fun one).
If however you are a believer that quality is better than quantity I'd recommend this game one thousand times over.

This game is somewhat disappointing.  The story is of a combat suit AI on a derelict planet with other dysfunctional AI, and goes more or less as you expect.  While presented well, it has a cliffhanger ending you can see a mile away.  The game has strengths in presentation and character, but lacks in enjoyable game mechanics and too many confusing puzzles for a light action / puzzle platformer.

It can be clunky as well, as a certain attack can only be performed from a certain position behind an enemy andgetting it to trigger can be finnicky.
I also ran into a few bugs.  One notatable bug involved moving back and forth between a menu causing the menu options to no longer work when clicked on, requiring an ALT-F4 forcequit.  Another caused loss of control and my character began slowly sliding across the screen until encountering a wall, where I regained control again.  The first occurred a few times, the latter just once.  The game otherwise ran well.
With unfufilling game mechanics and story, I can't really recommend this game.  The game is no more than 3-4 hours long and doesn't have replayability.  Perhaps worth a purchase on sale for an afternoon or two's worth of entertainment.

This is a good game.
It's a very atmospheric game, with enough creepy touches and somewhat unsettling things to keep things interesting, though I don't think I'd call it a horror game. It's just naturally eerie.
ARID, the robot, is actually a fairly sympathetic character. That was one of my favorite things about the game, how well they incorporated robot characters. It's really fun playing a robot and having to deal with other robots: the interactions and dialogue choices are just *almost* human but obviously just not quite the same. Having to view everything as a robot would is also fun; I loved how you get a dialogue option several times that was "tell the truth" vs "lie" and you're not able to select "lie" because...well, that's one of the robot rules, and you just have to deal with the consequences.
I only regret that I didn't notice the option to make the aiming control "toggle" instead of hold down the right mouse button constanty until the last few minutes of the game. Oh well.
Anyway. Way fun, looks like it'll lead to some cool things when they release the next part (apparently next year).

THE FALL's fabulous AI characters belong in the same pantheon as GlaDOS and Wheatley. You may have to run back and forth to the forums for puzzle tips (because man, some of them are obtuse!), but you'll keep coming back because you WANT TO KNOW what happens to these characters.
One of the reasons these droids get their hooks in you is because they're spectaularly voice-acted. I especially loved the rapport between ARID and the AI in the middle section. (You'll know 'im when you hear 'im!) ARID's performance is easily on par with GlaDOS'. Great subtleties going on there.
Story, atmosphere and characters are this game's strengths. The actiony bits (movement, platforming, and combat) are not. They're not so bad as to make it unplayable, but if you're not patient with these things, if you're trying to run and gun like you're Earthworm Jim, you're gonna be a sad, frustrated panda.
That said, I enjoyed the following so much that I forgave the game's action shortcomings, and I think you will, too:
- The aesthetic, which feels like someone smashed together TRON, LIMBO, LONE SURVIVOR, and the first two ODDWORLD Abe  games. The environments are spooky and mysterious without being dour and colorless.
- The offbeat humor in the second part. Oh. Man. It's robot humor, which is the best humor.
- THE FLASHLIGHT IS ON THE GUN. Which is how real-life military operators set up their weapons. Hollywood can't even get this right! (Maybe next time they'll add in a little crouch animation for when you're shooting?)
- Speaking of the flashlight, I SUPER enjoyed the way I had to inspect my environment with the flashlight. It really brought me into the world.
- Takedowns. They're fun AND they make the combat easier. Did you know when you vault over something, you get to trash the guy on the other side? Also you can shoot over your cover, which I wish I knew at the beginning!
- The emotional connections you'll form with these characters. One part made me SO ANGRY!! And I like that inna game. Because games that hit me like short stories get remembered like short stories, and become a part of me. Love it.
Can't wait to see what happens in PART 2!

The Fall is more or less a traditional "Point and Click" style puzzle game with an interesting story and atmosphere that has a little bit of a platforming/action vibe at times as well. If you're familiar with an older game called Blackthorne, the action component is basically a combat mechanism very similar to that game in nature.
In general you will be wandering between areas, reading/scanning key text, collecting items and using them (sometimes in combination with other items) in order to solve puzzles and advance the story. All of the puzzles seemed to have a very logical solution (within the context of the game and the character that you're playing), at least to me.
The action portions come at key points in the story and basically have you doing semi-tactical combat. While fun, this aspect doesn't seem to have very much overall danger attached to it in the game.
Start to finish the game took me roughly 5 hours to complete. To me it felt like the game was ending just as it was really getting rolling in the story. That said, the ending is very much a "to be continued" type of deal, and I think a sequel has been announced if not already in progress and I will definitely be picking it up as soon as it's available, if that says anything.
I appreciate the vision that the developer was going for overall including the action portion, but it seems like there should be either more action sequences or none (and just be a puzzle game).
Regardless, I would still recommend this as a great play if the genre interests you.

Not the best game I've played, but the story certainly seems more interesting than most games manage. On the lower side, however, there is very, very little story here... The game is just the first episode, and about 70% is game filler (you know, run around looking for whatever item you missed, solve several puzzles that don't really add to the story, etc. etc.).
My first impressions were mostly bad, but it got better. The main problems, initially, is how the animations don't really flow into one another, giving a game a very amateur feel. The interface and controls are also pretty bad. Even the standard mouse pointing is off the mark. You have to hold right mouse button to aim, instead of aiming at all times, as is usual. The other problem is the basic interaction: you have to hold Shift for a menu to appear with several option that you have to navigate to with WASD. I don't understand why this is the case. There are so many buttons, even on a controller... oh well.
Other than that, the game has some nice moments. I like the way it looks, in terms of atmosphere and aesthetic, but the graphics to look crude. The darkness hides it somewhat, so it gets the point across. The music what ok, nothing that stood out to me, either positively or negatively.
It's not a point n' click game (literally), but it's structured like one, with very similar puzzles. You're not ever trying to solve a problem with a set of tools you can explore - instead, you're mostly looking for the only solution that may or may not make sense. The game sometimes seems to take options away from you, forcing you to take a longer route to the solution for no reason... as I said, it's mostly filler, unfortunately.
The story, however, had some interesting things! You're an AI in a strange facility and you learn about as the game goes on. Your job is to protect your pilot, guided by 3 golden rules (like Asimov's, but with a more specific purpose).
The biggest fault is really how little there is to go on. I can't really say much about it, about the things I liked and disliked, because it seems only the first little bit of the story.
I wouldn't recommend it for the base price. I got it for 1$ on sale, and it was worth that much. But I'd advise anyone to wait for the second episode, since this one doesn't even come close to a conclusion, or get a point across.

Spore is a great game that I keep coming back to every few years.
You start as a single celled organism and evolve by adding and removing parts that effect what your organism can eat and how well it can defend itself.
You guide your critter from the primordial soup, onto land, through tribal village to city life, and eventually slip the surly bonds of earth and explore the stars. Bethesda has proven to be one of the best American companies in the gaming industry and much of its success is due to its close relationship with its vast fan base, particularly the modding community. Having said that, it is no surprise Morrowind still stands out as a unpolished gem that is a must for RPG fans. A classic and a must-have for any harcore players.
The game is undeniably outdated (not as much as Arena or Daggerfall, of course), as can be shown by the pointy character models, low res textures and a pletora of well documented bugs, but the modding community has came up to impressive solutions to pretty much any problem the base game had on its original release. The game is at is best when heavily modded to fix all this and add much more content.
In its current state, Morrowind is very unforgiving with modern players and that is partly because of clumsy mechanics and obscure stats-calculation in combat that is reminiscent D&D style role playing games. The game does not hold your hand through the first hours, which greatly contributes to building an atmosphere but it plays agains its accessibility. Not anyone will enjoy it but if one does see past the most obvious limitations, the game will be one of the best experiences in gaming. As other Bethesda games, it feels like part of something way bigger and its vast land, the lore, and a huge amount of detail that developers and modders pays in a very thorough experience.
I would not recomment it just for the curiosity of how the Elder Scrolls was before current entries in the saga (by the way, Arena and Daggerfall are completely free on Bethesda's website). It is a rough gem of another time era but very good and enjoyable nonetheless. On its day I would have given it a 95/100 butby current industry standards it would be still  a 70/100.
