This is one of those games that's so good that you own it on more than one platform. I have fond memories of the Resident Evil franchise that go back to 1996 and with this one, 2002. Maybe it's because of my nostalgia for the original Resident Evil games, but I seriously think this game is one of the best ever made.
In 2002 this game was seriously unreal. The graphics were insanely better and the game felt more fleshed out. I still play the original PS1 Resident Evil at least once a year, but this is definitely the better version of the two games.
For the (most likely) few people that have never played this game, it's throwback survival horror. This isn't like most modern Resident Evil games that consist of more action than horror. In this game, there are many factors that contribute to the overall sense of horror. Besides being trapped in a huge mansion with numerous monstrosities trying to kill you, there's also a limited number of items that can be used throughout the game. For the most part, those items are ammo and health.
Despite having played through this game and the original PS1 version more times than I can count, there are still instances where I have to carefully plan out what items I use and when. If you play as Jill, this isn't quite as bad. She gets more weapons and with the two extra item spaces, there's not so much backtracking involved. If you play as Chris, you get 1 less main weapon and two less item spaces. As a result of this, you have to carefully plan what to carry or else you'll find yourself running back and forth to item boxes.
Besides this somewhat general description of the gameplay, there are many things that make this a truly amazing game. As I previously stated, when this game was first released in 2002, I considered it groundbreaking. With this remastering, it's even better. The graphics are more crisp and there are a few more modes added to change things up.
To cut this review short, I definitely recommend it and I give it a 5/5.

Faithful Port of the Gamecube Remake - a remake of the good AND the bad that is
I really don't need to say anything about this you don't already know but here's my Two cents...
The Good -
This is pure, unadulterated nostalgia.  Lets face it even with all the action and graphical quality of the Post RE3 era we are all secretly missing the days when we actually needed to engage our imaginations, people need stimulation not just heart pounding action.  The early RE games were more like reading a book than pretending to be Rambo (of whitch there is a TON other games out there for that) and for this reason these early offerings will never grow old.  The artwork, sound, feeling and the story are just as we remember it way back then.  It will still impress you visually after all these years, scare you witless and delight you with it's classy construction.  In fact I would say that it has slightly crisper visuals than its Gamecube Parent and evidently a great deal of time has been spent on it.

Yeah, what to say about Roogoo? I admit that the high rating does surprise me, it's a nice little game but clearly not "close to 80%"- talk about Metacritic :D
It's a puzzle game. Coloured shapes drop from the sky into a tower of rotating disks; your job is to spin them so that the shapes slide into the matching holes all the way to the bottom. Drop em all down and you win. Miss too many and you lose the level. Things take up some speed after a while and it can be pretty hard to match the perfect ratio, but it's mostly a chill-out game. It's clearly not about thinking ahead and planning moves, the challenge is speed and reaction time.
The whole thing is wrapped into an utterly cute little story with child-friendly silly monkey creatures, complimented by catchy tunes and silly voices. Makes it all look like a children's game- but actually it might be a bit too hard for those.
So... yeah well, it's fun. In small doses. I can't see me playing Roogoo for hours on end and I actually enjoy stacking/matching games. For the price it's fair enough to say you should go and see for yourself. I... got it during a sale for 40cents. Can't say I didn't get my money's worth :D

There are four separate games in this bundle, and they're all from the same company and quite similar. That said, they are also all quite different. The names of each were utterly forgettable to me, except that the Atlantis game has maybe 5% of its gameplay actually take place in Atlantis, and that's in the first 15 minutes of the game. The rest of the game actually takes place on a human colony built on Mars in the future.
Alright, so my play time is going to look funky on this one because I played one of them and watched the other 3 played live on stream with 2 other friends. Another friend and I took turns clicking and such, while we both tried solving the puzzles. It was pretty entertaining and fun that way. We used Discord with screen share and it was great. The puzzles are pretty enjoyable in all four games, for the most part. There were definitely some odd ones in each which I didn't think were great, but it's basically like you told a point and click adventure game, removed watching your playable character walk around to do things, and added some Where's Waldo and a couple of puzzle minigames.
This all worked well enough in 3 out of the 4 games. The storylines in all of them were generally just laughably bad. The vampire one (Sins of the Fathers), however, stands out as being awful, not only in the plot, but in the gameplay. The "hidden object" portion of that particular hidden object game (the Where's Waldo-esque) part is a little
much like Where's Waldo, in my opinion. By that, I mean that the other games feel more like a fun search for objects, whereas the vampire one has poorer graphics, making it harder to spot needed items and to differntiate between certain items easily, and it rehashes the same piles of items about 4 times each. The other games typically have you search the same pile of stuff 3 times or less.
I understand why they have you search the same piles so many times, but I think 3 should have been the limit. 4 was going too far. Everything you're searching through is grayscale or and brown much of the time, so it's not attractive to even look at for lengths of time. In the other games in the bundle, there are more attractive items and colors in most of the piles of stuff you search.
The music is fine and  the voice acting is pretty bad in these games, and my friends and I typically talked over the voices, or made our own if there weren't any, simply doing deliberately goofy and poorly fitting voices for the characters. These games are mostly just visually attractive, with the positive reinforcement feeling of quickly getting items and solving puzzles, as if you're playing a traditional point and click game, but designed to give you your dopamine nonstop while sacrificing plot, voice acting, and other aspects for the gameplay. Other than the vampire one, the other 3 items definitely make this bundle worth getting, in my opinion, unless you don't like point and click adventure games at all.

I wasn't a big fan of the New Atlantis game that's included in this bundle ONLY because it forces you to run around a lot, but if you use the map to teleport to areas, it's not as annoying. Honestly, out of all of the games I played in this so far, (I didn't play House of 1,000 Doors yet) the New Atlantis one is probably the best value with the most interesting story, even though it still has bad acting and plot holes.
Overall a great buy, great value, and definitely pleases my inner puzzle solver and hidden object lover.

Remembering that this is a ten year old game, I'll adjust my review accordingly. I have never played any of the Witcher series (and I'm assuming you are reading this because you haven't either), and only played this game so I have story continuity for Witcher 3.
Over all, very adaptable game play. It could give a bit more information about alchemy and mutagens, but it isn't a deal breaker. I did spend way too much time wondering about specific potions and there was very little need for it. Combat was interesting, let me feel like I was in control of the character, and no boss was too tough that I couldn't figure out what I was doing wrong eventually to beat it. Not gear-heavy, which was great, but relied on knowing how to avoid the damage and which tactic to take to defeat the boss.
The closer one gets to the end of the game, the more cut scenes appear. It became a bit ridiculous in the end, but there you go.
Graphics, though a bit choppy in places (some of the hair just went crazy and that has more to do with compatibility issues, I imagine), were fantastic. I can imagine playing this game ten years ago I would have been over the moon.
As for the story, well, it could use work. The overlying story was good, but the delivery was choppy. Our main goal is salamandra, but we have to choose between knights and rebels which has nothing apparently to do with salamandra, and there's a kid who just vanishes, and death is chasing us down asking us about our destiny. The connections could be a bit more seamless, feels forced.
The ending of the story leaves you with a bit of a wtf feel. You have achieved your goal, killed the main boss. But then there is no tying off loose ends, you're paid and you move on. The medallion the boss is wearing isn’t even explored, with a clear connection, and nothing says there’s a follow up game coming like the main character saying “I guess we’ll never know”.
It is a great game. If you’re hard core about seeing how your decisions would affect the outcome, it warrants a second play through, but I likely won’t be playing it again.

Surprisingly engaging, diverting and terrifying or should I say terror flying.

Strive to have a quality crew and plane to find yourself a few missions later agonizing over who of the two bleeding on the ground gets the last medkit. Do you risk the fuel leak to land at base or emergency land now? Oh did the skilled pilot just take a bullet to the head? Who will fly now.
Now a moment of silence for our fallen.
Then get new crew or even a new plane to carry on. The war isn't over you know.
Now to compare the game to earlier ones it isn't a super hard core sim. You don't manually aim the guns or bombs. You are more a manager or director giving commands to the crew. You do hit the final release on the bombs but don't have deal with the Mighty 8th game's need to precisely adjust a Nordenfelt sight.
The M8 game was prone to a problem of huge empty times prompting to use a time compression which then ran through critical moments as well. In this game there never seemed to be those dull pauses. Mission flight times are 10ish minutes and you will be high strung all the way. Only when you get the rare lightly damaged plane and healthy crew back can you relax over England. Several times I have still had fighters tapping holes, wounding crew and breaking things.
What looks to be child's play will embrace you in the horrors and peaks of the bomber war. Welcome to Bomber Crew.

text:
You know, I keep meaning to get into sci-fi; it's such a fascinating genre that I wish I were better versed in. Well, this game's as good a start as any. It boasts a thematically rich story that's veritably drowning in symbolism and allegory, while holding your interest with compelling characters, creepy atmosphere, and a plot that's equal parts mystery and tragedy. If any of that sounds good to you, I highly recommend this game...
...just make sure to keep a guide handy. As good as the story is, the gameplay is mediocre at best. It combines the worst aspects of metroidvanias - mediocre combat, an arbitrary unlock system, and way too much backtracking - with the worst aspects of point-and-click adventure games; or, rather, the single worst aspect: the puzzle-solving. These "puzzles" are so freaking obtuse and convoluted in their solutions that I have to wonder if anyone actually playtested this game. You pretty much can't solve half of them without a guide, and even the solvable ones are a chore to actually complete. To be fair, the gameplay is a good thematic fit for the story, but that's just about the only good thing I can say about it.
Still, the story is worth the crappy gameplay, especially because it is the kind of crappy gameplay that can be made a lot less crappy if you use a guide. And the story really is that good.

While it is a fairly short game (I finished it in one 3.8 hour session), I would say that it's well worth the money. Even though I got it on sale for a fraction of the cost (something like £0.79), I would absolutely have been satisfied with my purchase had I paid full price!
Gameplay-wise, it's a blend of simple combat and adventure game style puzzles that, in classic adventure game format, rewards experimentation, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. The graphics look a lot better in-game than they do in the trailer, and I quite like the general darkness that pervades the game, and I also very much enjoyed the atmosphere that the music and sound effects brought in.
Story-wise, it's simple, you've fallen into a cavern, you don't know where you are, all you know is that you need to get your human pilot medical attention, no complaints from me on that front! I enjoyed the general mystery surrounding the whole thing, and the ending especially has left me eager for the next in the series!
There's always gonna be bad things though, of course, and in particular the controls were a bit clunky right out of the gate, although I did get used to them quite fast! In addition, barring a boss fight at the end of the game, combat was pretty repetitive, although combat's really not the main focus. It certainly wasn't a deal-breaker for me, although I do feel that the game would have performed equally as well if they'd removed the combat altogether.
To sum up:
Graphics - Good!
Sound - Good!
Story - Good!
Price - Good!
Gameplay - Mixed, but still more good than bad!
Controls - Bad :(
Combat - Bad :(
Recommended? Heck yes!

I can recommend this game on the story, music, characters, and dialogue alone. However, some issues with the game make it a bit more difficult to stomach than it should be.
Let's start with the good. The music is wonderfully done. Every note, every pitch, every tone is really well done. Plenty of times I felt immersed and even felt attached to the game despite it's flaws. The dialogue was fitting and interesting, and I even felt emotions. Over robots. Tin cans that follow programming made me feel somber. That's a new one, but I'm impressed.
The dialogue was very well written making the characters far more interesting than the metallic bodies they really are. The protagonist seemed a bit more lively for a robot than she ought to have been but it really helped shape her throughout the game, and it was a constant rather than a quick evolution over the course of the game. Like some life-altering events suddenly took place and she became someone else entirely or something
The story was awesome. And at the end I actually didn't expect the twist I witnessed, but it made me even more interested in the sequel or update, whichever the devs decide to go with. It started out innocently enough, making me think it was going to be a simple tale. But that quickly changed and evolved as the character experienced many things, and we the players are along for the ride.
However... The bad really stung a little. The combat. The combat is simply clunky, unintuitive, and unchallenging. It felt more like I was playing a 3D flash game rather than a new indie title with potential (It has plenty, don't get me wrong). Simply draw your weapon, pop into camouflage or cover, and click when the enemy shows their head. That's pretty much it. Click until you win.
The controls are... Sub-par at best. I understand this is a 2D side-scroller, but there's a clear need to have a visible cursor of some sort indicating where my mouse is. You know, since the game keeps track of it's location. It felt disappointing having to aim based on feeling around for my cursor, sliding it around to finally get enough movement to aim all the way up or down.
And finally... The puzzles. A core mechanic of the game. These suffer greatly as they're hardly conveyed to the player properly and are instead "click everything until something works." This isn't a good puzzle mechanic. There isn't any penalty for just clicking and shooting everything. You could literally beat the game with your eyes closed if you had enough patience. There's no reason for me NOT to just wander around aimlessly trying to figure out where the disembodied head goes, or where to use a robotic arm I found. It also doesn't help the game doesn't give you any real hints as well, asking the player to simply feel around and press buttons until something works.
To make an example, a spoiler:
All in all, I'll be playing the sequel and do recommend this game to anyone looking for a good story that changes it up a little with well written dialogue, story elements, and well performed music. But the combat and puzzle solving needs work. My only complaints are puzzles should be less difficult if there's going to be a lack of direction and 0 penalty for clicking on things like a curious child, and the combat could benefit from upgrades beyond shooting faster and aiming for the head.
Overall, 7/10. Really good. Doesn't suffer from any serious bugs, good story, music, and dialogue. Walkthroughs will not likely cheapen the experience if you get stuck as you can simply click things until something works anyway. Combat is simple and easy, which makes up for it being clunky.

Morrowind is the best game in the Elder Scrolls franchise hands down. The gameplay is second to none, as for the graphics, you could download a mod to upgrade them, or you could play the game how it's supposed to be played. I chose the latter. The game itself can be a bit aggrivating at times, missing most of your swings in the beggining (upgrade your agility and that won't happen, random mobs hindering your ability to heal, and it took me awhile to get used to not being able to fast travel. But, the selling point in this game is it's compelling storyline (not found in skyrim or oblivion); from starting out a prisoner, to defeating Dagoth Ur and fufilling your prophecy this game is a rollercoaster. It's worth the ride, but it's not for everyone. Once you get used to the graphics, you'll be in for the story of a lifetime.

As a life-long fan of the two Atari ST games, "Alternate Reality," and "Dungeon Master," I've waited my whole life for a game like this to be created. Upon reading about Morrowind, I eagerly awaited almost a year for this game's release. After finally playing it, I fell in love. It single-handedly began my long-standing love affair with the entire Elder Scrolls series. I bought both the original, then evetually, the "Game of the Year" edition for the first X-box console, and played it for many, many hours, on end. Upon joining Steam, I found myself placing the game on my wishlish, and I was compelled to buy it, once again, as soon as it went on sale. Of course, I also own Oblivion, Skyrim, and Elder Scrolls Online. However, this game, in particular, signifies the beginning of one of the most immersive, intense, open-ended RPG series I've ever played, with some of the best graphics of its time, along with a very dynamic "first-person slasher"-based combat system. I have a very sentimental attachment to it. It may be over a decade old, but I would still easily recommend this game to anyone!
Morrowind is the high point, in my opinion, of The Elder Scrolls series. I would highly recommend it for travelling as most laptops can easily run it these days. :)

Perfectly recaptures what made the original Resident Evil such a excellent survival horror experience.
Resident Evil HD Remaster features the older style of Resident Evil games with a fixed camera angle, gorgeous backdrops, absolutely intense as hell atmosphere as you make your way through the mansion and fight your way through a huge array of enemies such as zombies, zombie dogs, giant spiders & hideous mutants.
Not only has the graphics been one upped with the HD remaster, but there has also been added additional subplots within the game, which only further enriches the story of Resident Evil. That of course also means that there has been added a few new areas for you to fight your way through. There has also been added a new form of zombie that completely changes your approach as to how to deal with zombies in general.
The only issues I had was with error messages such as "Memory overrun" which is often caused by alt tabbing from the game. This happened on 2 occassions out of my 30 hour gameplay. It set me back quite a bit the second time, which was very frustrating. Don't alt tab unless you're fine with potentially losing your progress.
Another very minor issue is that once I'd walk through a door, I'd experience ocassional slow downs. The way to fix this was to alt tab, which isn't very efficient considering my previous issue.
The game itself is a 10/10 for me, but the technical difficulties might take it down to a 9.5/10, not that there is much of a difference. Would recommend this game anytime if you're looking for a true survival horror game.

I must say, I was pleasantly surprised by this. The game is mostly faithful to the original RE on ps1, but several of the little changes/additions add some nice atmosphere to the game, up the difficulty a bit and expand the gameplay (although the crimson heads might be seen as a bit of chore to those used to the original experience). The changes also made sure veterans had still something to throw them off a bit, when playing it.
I will say I had some minor problems with performance (I had to find a fix and limit the game to 30fps to ensure the audio didn't desync from the visuals or the game didn't slow down too much) as well as "trick" the game into picking the lowest quality for the videos (I copy/pasted the lower quality ones over the others, this too in order to avoid desyncing issues). While my PC is frankly subpar, some people have reported performance issues on more robust machines, so keep in might this might be a possibility. When I solved this issues, I had a smooth experience, and I would say that the visuals and the art direction in general are actually really good, and the atmosphere managed to genuinely scare me early on (of course, I eventually settled down in my old routines, but I think that if it managed to keep me on the edge despite my experience with the original, it must have done something very right).
As for the game itself, it's classic RE for the most part, with some new touches here and there. You can expect the same camera angles (which have aged really well, by the way, the photography is really expertly done, and adds to the tension whenever the sounds of a monster off-camera is heard), the same clunky combat (it does aim toward enemies automatically, though, which wasn't a thing in the original, if I remember correctly), the same resource/inventory management (killing everything that moves is never a good idea, and the inventory is a real issue to work with, especially with Chris), puzzles everywhere, and a really creepy mansion which seems set on killing you. The dialogues are still rough around the edges, just like the various notes you find and the descriptions you can read around the house still make a good job at building a creepy atmosphere.
I would recommend it to anyone who liked the original trilogy, and to people looking for something different from current survival horrors (only if they can be patient enough with inventory management and aren't upset by fixed camera angles which are there expressly to unnerve you).
I honestly wish we got more horror games in this vein, the fixed camera angles, not being shy with deadly traps, and stringent resource management all contribute to create a scary experience to me, having limited saves make it so there is a real suspence when walking dangerous hallways, and the temptation to waste some ammo to have an easier time in the future when we'll have to go back through the same areas is much more real. In case it wasn't clear, I really enjoyed my time with it, it had been years since a game managed to make me feel this way.

Hello, and welcome to my review to the Witcher 1. I hope I can give you a good reason to give these series a try, because its one of a kind and I think if you gave it a chance, you won’t regret it.
First lets start with the graphics. The game is from 2007 and its kind of dated,but there are beautiful landscapes and environments which you will love and will help you believe the world.
Second the music. What can I say ? The music is amazing, its my highest point of this review, because every track of the OST is great,and memorable – and will greatly help you get immersed in this great Game/World. From the menu you can fell the atmosphere, the despair and darkness which lingers in this game.
Third is the Story. The story is interesting and you will want to know more of the backstory of the main character,and the other characters which he is connected to.And you will want to hear every piece of dialogue – the side quest are also interesing there are of couse generic ones like – go kill some monsters bring proof – but that is also made interesting and will tell you how in my next point of this review.
Fourth is the Gameplay. The gameplay is quite unique and I haven not played a scheme like this in any game – you have 3 kind of weapons. Steel sword for normal enemies, Silver for monsters and Third one which you can choose from different weapon types,but those are not interesting for me,because they don’t use the 3 different styles of witcher combat. Yes you heard me right – 3 styles (which means you have 6,including the silver one). Is quite satisfying to change between styles mid combat. Another great part is – you are a Witcher, you get your income from completing tasks of killing monsters – you get the task,gather information of the monsters so you will know which part of the monster to take for your quest and prepare for long and tough battles with alchemy – which takes a bigger role in higher difficulties.
I can go on and on about this game – but if you really want a interesting,unique and immersive RPG with a great story and setting you wont get dissapointed.

Review's limited to singleplayer:
Really tried to enjoy this one because I got into the series very late and enjoyed Resident Evil 5, but it's a dying struggle. It definitely doesn't at all play like the recent titles, putting a prime focus on four-player (squad-based) shootouts. Unforunately, that killed the horror factor (which is pretty much dead already) and instead set a higher focus on firefights.
The above would be fine if more work was put into making the title more fun instead of different. However, it falls short, as most every other player might've complained.
-Mismatched horizontal/vertical mouse sensitivity
-Higher difficulties seem to only multiply enemy health, dragging out fights and bosses for far too long as you spend much of the time filling an enemy's head with more bullets than they have brain cells.
-Campaign felt rather short and anticlimactic, with the already iffy gameplay ruining encounters.
-Executing zombified teammates had no weight or tension since you could resurrect them a second later
-The healthy selection of characters doesn't make up for seemingly uninspired abilities and pretty much no character development, if that was even to be expected.
-Optimization was incredibly..not there. My framerate shot down before even exiting the elevator in the very beginning of the game.
I would only suggest playing without high expectations and with friends. It's not amazing, but playable, however not exactly worth playing.

I bought this game expecting a not so great experience despite having Resident Evil in the name. I can safely say that it’s much better than I expected :) That being said, I can still see why people and critics tore the game apart. It doesn't play like any other Resident Evil game and the attention to detail is lacking.

Nothing surprises me in terms of level design, a lot of things look quite samey and there’s a distinct lack of graphical fidelity that Resident Evil 5 had. Gameplay is also somewhat lacking. The guns feel under powered when fighting the various enemies and the weapon firing sounds are among the worst I’ve heard in a game :S I do enjoy the level progression and co-op features which allow you to unlock several new weapons and upgrades for each of the six characters to play as. The Umbrella squad are absolutely bad♥♥♥♥♥and each character has a unique look and attitude.
The AI in ORC is terrible. Probably the worst feature of the game. My teammates enjoy running around in an elevator and running straight into enemies line of fire. This of course would be fixed if I was playing online, but I want to have the same quality of gameplay in single player or co-op and not feel more tempted to play one over the other. The co-op can be played throughout the whole game which is probably why the AI is so stupid.
The enemies are varied and along with Resident Evil classics, there are a few new enemies to fight. The zombies attack in massive hoards sometimes and the human soldiers take cover and lob grenades at you. I can’t really find any problems with this part of the game. Even boss battles are interesting.
Overall the game has that Resident Evil feel, it just doesn't have the best engine or the most well thought out gameplay. The developers should have put more time into the PC version in particular because it definitely feels like a direct port. I mean there’s even an X-Box 360 D-pad icon as part of your HUD where you select different grenades. Performance wise it meets expectations, but I feel it needed some more time to work out where it could be improved. Despite these flaws I’m enjoying this game so far and look forward to experiencing everything Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City has to offer!

I really loved playing this game. The atmosphere reminds me a bit of later stages of Portal 2, with it's dark, underground, dilapidated scientific compound-and somewhat helpful mainframe AI-which you navigate with very little clue of where exactly you are. However, the gameplay actually varies quite a bit, instead relying on observation and connecting objects that you pick up throughout the rooms to overcome obstacles. I will admit to using a walkthrough for a few puzzles, and some solutions were fairly hidden or unintuitive, but most became apparent after retracing my steps or simply stopping to think. The controls were also unfamiliar, but after a few minutes of playing, I got used to them and appreciated the fairly unique combination of keyboard and mouse. Finally, I really enjoyed the story aspect, both the grim and humorous bits, through both dialog between characters and the setting and details around them. I was actually expecting a scarier game, but while darkness and creepiness was definetly present, the story leaned much more towards suspense than horror. Overall, The Fall is a very incredible game that I greatly enjoyed and would recommend to anyone who likes story-based, puzzle/problem-solving science fiction games, or even anyone thinks it looks even vaguely intriguing (don't be afraid to step out of you comfort zone: it will probably be worth it!).

I've read other reviews, the general consensus is that the gameplay is really bad but the story etc. make up for it.  It depends on how much you're willing to put up with, I suppose.
Combat consists of clicking on enemies to chain combos together.  About half the time, however clicking on an enemy will not start the attack chain, Geralt just stands there like a lemon until you give him a poke.  Apparently you can only attack if you're facing the opponent directly or are out of melee range and have to move, causing you to face them.  If you're in range and try to attack something to your side, nothing happens.  When it works properly, combat is pretty bland, it's not challenging and there are no tactics to be employed.
The voice acting isn't the worst I've ever heard, that accolade belongs to the Gothic series but this comes a very close second.  The script is as dry as a week old baguette and you can tell the actors aren't invested in it.  There's a lot of talking too.
The graphics are functional but there are only a handful of NPC models which can be a little jarring when you keep seeing the same person over and over.  There aren't even different face, body size/shape, clothes etc. like Morrowind had to distinguish NPCs, and that came out five years earlier.
The epic story we're promised is composed of killing things and fetch quests.  You'll do about 50 laps of the starting village before moving on.
There's a certain boss fight which you have to prepare for but aren't told is coming; you need to stack up the necessary buffs before it starts.  Otherwise it's only winnable by accident after many tries.  You can't actually beat the boss in a fair fight, they just die suddenly and nobody knows how or why.
There's a dice poker minigame whose RNG makes the AI win ca. 90% of the time.  It's not even remotely fair on the player and has nothing to do with skill, it's just a time sink which makes you reload many, many times.  If you get a good hand in the first roll, the AI will beat it, no matter how unlikely.
There's so much faffing about in this game.  If the story everyone harps on about were actually happening, I might have a different oppinion.  After ten hours I don't feel I've accomplished anything at all, I'm no farther along the main plot and everyone I meet is a complete dullard.  I could keep playing and save the world but honestly, I hope that monstry dog eats every last one of these cretins.
Edit:
So I continued playing, cheated my way past the monster pooch and made it to chapter 2.  A lot more seems to happen in chapter 2, at least at first.  There are a bunch of pest control and fetch quests to hoover up your time but the main plot is actually moderately engaging.  It revolves around searching for the main bad guy, gathering evidence and deciding who's in league with him.  The big plot twist is pretty easy to spot even before it's spelled out for you.
There are way too many conversation pitfalls which lock characters up and make quests either unfinishable or leave you with only the most tenuous of plot threads.  I had to use a walkthrough to avoid getting to the end of the chapter and finding I'd messed everything up.
The main irritation in chapter 2 is the constant flipping between day and night.  Seriously, you'll do one or two things, then rest until midnight.  Talk to one person, knock over some monsters, then rest until morning.  Talk to another person at work then rest until midnight to talk to them again at home, then back to midday to talk to them at work again etc. etc.  I'm not exagerating, this is actually what you do.
Chapter 2 ends with a fight with two people who don't take any damage.  After a minute or so it just ends and they run away.  If they were going to run, why didn't they just do so in the first place?  If they can incapacitate Geralt, why didn't they just do that earlier?  Why did they just leave him there?  They could have finished him off but no, instead they tell him where their hideout is and teleport away.  This is Saturday morning cartoon level of storytelling.
I made it to chapter 3 but I haven't enjoyed getting there.  I might continue playing to see how it ends but I'm not buying into the paper thin story, nor the cardboard cutout characters.  For now I give up.  I was hoping to finish so I'd have some context going into the sequels, also that the sequels are not so agressively boring.
Maybe this game is only for fans of the book, those who enjoy particularly low quality fan fiction.  If somebody made a game like this about a book which I like, I'd be terribly disappointed.
TLDR - The writing is bad.  The gameplay is boring.  The characters are shallow.  The quests are repetitive and easily broken, leaving you stuck.  Dice poker is BS.  It's like the programmers decided they could write the plot and characters themselves instead of getting a professional script writer to do it.

Score: -2 (out of 10 or -10)
For H&G:
+2 Moderately good gunplay, weapons are precise, mostly effective, and limited to a realistic range
+3 Good maps, gameplay changes from day to day depending on the defendable positions on that day
+1 Tanks are incorporated moderately well, and, while being destructable, can shape the game
+2 UI is easy to use and all of the controls are intuitive
+2 Players are moderately well able to coordinate through squads
+1 It is easy to friend and play with other players, and servers frequently have strong connection
Against H&G:
-4 Matchmaking sorts new players with old ones, making the older ones with gun customizations (1 hit kill rifles) farm new players with stock weapons (3 hit kill rifles)
-2 Matchmaking makes vehicles either vulnerable to rambo players with anti-tank weapons or dominant over players without tanks, rocket launchers, mines, or grenades
-4 There is no learning curve, as players using stock equipment are far inferior to players using modded equipment
-3 Grinding (no explanation needed, I have 400+ hours in the game)
H&G is a fun, easy-to-play game, and, though poorly optimized, is as good as a f2p game can be. Its main shortcomings lie in the matchmaking (mostly due to the lack of isolated new, average, and veteran playerbases) and the amount of grinding it takes to reach moderately effective weapons. Furthermore, since there are usually 18 player max servers, there aren't enough players to balance the gameplay, so one vehicle is either unmitigated or completely stifled.

I'm going to group the games together for their mechanics until the end of the review because they're very similar/the same. You have all the classic types of puzzles in here: memory games, spin-and-match, etc. For the most part, they don't seem to be very challenging but are time consuming. They're still fun (besides a few puzzle types I don't really care for in any game), but you may hit "Skip" on a few just to keep moving.
The graphics are pretty decent -- mostly standard fare for HOGs. Don't expect excellent quality, however, as most HOG companies focus more on puzzles and story than graphics. Some computer animations will look like circa 2000s technology, but that never really bothered me. The voice acting was pretty decent for the most part, but there were a few characters who made me cringe a little.
House of 1000 Doors:
~I enjoyed the different settings you go through and the different themes. The story was okay but the ending was obviously cut off. You're promised an explanation and then the credits roll. The end. I've read that there's a collector's edition of this game that has the real ending and a few bonus levels. I was shocked that Alawar would do such a thing, but I guess they can do whatever they want with their games.
Eternal Journey:
~I played this one last because I didn't think I'd like it and I was totally wrong. This particular game was my favorite of the four and is easily in my top five favorite HOGs. I've never considered myself big on sci-fi so when I found myself really getting into the story, I was surprised. I wouldn't call it realistic sci-fi but I wouldn't call most HOGs realistic either. Even if you're not big into this particular genre, give it a shot.
Dark Strokes:
~Yes, I giggled at the title for a few minutes. Yes, I cringed at one particular voice actor who just couldn't act anyway but bored. Yes, I spotted the ending halfway through. I didn't hate the game but it was my least favorite. I don't normally harp on about a poor plot, but this one was legitimately bad. Every time something happened, I spotted a plot hole that could've been fixed with a little tweaking. I don't want to spell out spoilers, so I'll say don't bother unless you don't really care about that stuff.
Stray Souls:
~This one was weird. I really liked the dark atmosphere and design, but the story was so strange. The heroine, too, was very gullible to...everything. She liked to just accept things at face value with little coercing or argument, even when a desperate person would go, "Wait, what? No way." The "twist" about the bad guy was so obvious I wouldn't even call it a twist. I enjoyed enough things in this one that it's not the worst of the bundle, so it sits above Dark Strokes (teehee) and below House of 1000 Doors.

A bundle of 4 HOGs containing:
House of 1000 Doors: The Palm of Zoroaster
Nice graphics, the HOGs scenes are beautiful but the difficulty is very low. 46 morphing objects to find. The story is fantasy style, with magic and fire spells and a very classic construction. Also it's a sequel and I didn't play the previous game(s?) so it felt a bit awkward. The characters and the cutscenes are nice. The ending was a total let down though: the cutscene lasted 3 seconds! It's the game I liked the least in the bundle but it's still a good game and I do recommend it.
Eternal Journey: New Atlantis
You're an archeologist exploring an underwater city, then end up exploring the future. This one is more original than the usual run of the mill: you'll dive underwater, repair solar panels, use space suits etc. There's also 18 collectibles to find and the map is very handy. The graphics and the music are nice and the future is clichéd but well done. The mini games are very good. I liked it a lot. The best game in the bundle IMO, the most innovative and the Sci-Fi setting is pretty rare within HOGs.
Stray Souls: A Dollhouse Story
Creepy and so well done that I've already replayed it a second time. There's a lot of good ideas in this one, like a live doll clone of Number Nine, a creepy doll house, with creepy dolls, a creepy little boy and 36 morph objects to collect! If you like horror theme then you'll surely like it. The only con is the res that seems lower than the other games, so the image is a bit blurry. The second best game in the bundle IMHO.
Dark Strokes: Sins of the Fathers
I had already played that one previously but I enjoyed replaying it. Graphics and characters are gorgeous, music is okay. Didn't like the mini games much, tedious and not original at all. The HOG scenes offer a bit of challenge, being dark and cluttered. Again there's a boat model and you find little dolls to fill it but it only unlocks videos, no small featurettes with the dolls like in Stray Souls. The videos you unlock are rather bland. And no special collectibles to find. A dark setting but all in all it's rather classic. But I liked how the story unfolded and how the player is guided toward the next scenes. Third best game in the bundle.
Conclusion: all the games are good and you won't be deceived! Each game lasted 4 hours (5 for a leisure playthrough) so it makes this bundle really worthy.

After the 5 in 1 bundle, Alawar released anoth batch of hidden objects, though this time, they released only three new games on Steam. Indeed, House of 1000 Doors: The Palm of Zoroaster was already released as a Collector's Edition. It means that for anyone already owning it, it's not a complete surprise. However, for the rest, it's a nice addition.
Kate Reed is called back to the House of 1000 Doors: a gem spread a plague in it and every resident, particulary Gabriel, is in a grave danger...
You understand, this game is the second in a series of four (the first is also on Steam) but you don't need to play the previous one to understand the universe.
While the game is pretty standard in terms of gameplay, what's great in that game is the universe itself: you're travelling between different worlds, through the house. And this time, you'll learn more about Gabriel, the guardian of the house. The graphics are very good too, which is pleasant.
For more information, read this review:
After an accident, you're waking up into the future, thanks to new technologies and because your knowledge was important. You don't know what happened to your fiancé, making you sad about your new life. Sent to a mission in space, you're crashing into a planet... How will you manage to save yourself? And will you discovered what happened to a previous crew of the base?
When the game is showing clearly a sci-fi adventure in space, you don't understand why you're beginning in the present, with an underwater experience. However, given the twist at the beginning of the story, I feel like this part could have been avoided. However, the rest of the game is very faithful to the sci-fi theme. You're arriving into an abandoned base and your journey will be full of dangers, though at the end, a familiar face will appear. The gameplay isn't innovative as it's the same as any other hidden games.
In other words, you search for items, you use them, you clear hidden objects scenes and you solve puzzles. Everything is pretty easy. You can search also memory cards, explaining about the future. And with all the video cards around, you can also know more about life on New Atlantis and the secrets hidden there.
However, what I loved with this game is the graphics, very sci-fi, with some sounds making me think about Doom.
Anyway, it's my favorite among the three (I don't count House of 1000 Doors, as it's already a favorite of mine) new hidden objects in this bundle. If anything, I wouldn't mind to see this one as a collector's edition.
Ethan and Clair are visiting the young man's father but she's kidnapped by The Faceless One. Ethan, decided to save her from them, is making his way into a decimated city. However, all the kidnapped persons are tied to a tragedy and the death of a boy on a boat...
The game is also a good one: the plot is really well-written and I didn't realize the truth before nearing the end. While it's shocking to discover who the Faceless Ones are, the title make a reference to Ethan's father and to the boy's one. The graphics are also good, as you're navigating through a city that is diving into darkness progressively. The gameplay is still the standard one: hidden objects to find, puzzles to solve, etc..
Your husband is in danger and you need to save him. However, the town seems to be the home of a terrible spirit and the orphanage may be the key to stop it...
Stray Souls has an interesting plot: your husband being the "damsel" in distress, a young sad boy, a sad clown and a mysterious woman, everything related to your man's past. Besides, what's good is that you have a little companion: a doll that can talk and can help you to discover the truth behind everything. Besides, the concept of cleansing some rooms of the evil is very nice as you can discover new items in them.
However, the gameplay is still the same as any other hidden object game: find items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes and solve very easy puzzles. The hidden objects scenes are kinda reminiscent of the early era: with objects being in the same tone of color as the background or with a very small size.
The graphics are what I like generally: a town plunged in darkness, with everything around making you understand that evil is watching you. However, I wished that perhaps, the locations were a little more original than the mandatory cemetery or police station.
The soundtrack was also good.
I enjoyed the game, that's a fact but I feel like something is missing. I don't know, maybe more interactions for the doll?
Anyway, this is also a good pick for the bundle.
This bundle is way more worthy than the 5 in 1. I can't judge for the 6 in 1 as it's a new release and that I'm in the first game. Every game has good graphics, good sountrack, a gameplay, while being standard, polished without too much brain frying.
Any lover of HOG can buy this bundle and any person wanting to discover the genre can too, as there are no "weak" games like in the 5 in 1. Go ahead!

The Theodore Adventures is a platformer that unfortunately feels unfinished, and is both short and extremely long...
You can find about 10 minutes of gameplay amd commentary here:

You play as Theodore, who wants to fly to Juicy island - an island full of fruit - but he needs to buy a plane to get there. The goal of the game is to trade 100 coins per stage for gold ingot and when you have enough ingots, to buy the plane.
Lets begin with the positives and work our way down. Art wise, I feel the game is done well. To overcome flat looking stages in a 2D style, the stage backgrounds are drawn in layers, allowing for depth in in the levels that it would otherwise be missing. This detail can also be seen in the enemy types which vary in look and are in line with the level environment. They all move in set paths and are destroyed by jumping on them (except one type that cant be squashed), but this variety keep the stages interesting during the initial run through.
The music is an 8bit synth style and is fine to listen too while playing. There is no way lower the volume of the game music or turn it off that I have found, so hopefully you enjoy it if you buy the game. :)
Control wise, it is a simple platformer, with left - right and a jump key. It can be controlled by either keyboard or a gamepad, but for some reason the game has been designed that you need to press a button to transfer control from a gamepad to keyboard or back again. I don't understand why it was designed in this way, and initially I did not have my controller connected so when I ran the game I could not actually start it. It wasn't until I reloaded the game with a controller attached that I found I needed to press the enter key to move controls to the keyboard.
In game physics is a bit off, on early stages if either foot is not on a platform you fall off, but as the game progresses you can stand with one foot off a platform and stay on it. Also enemy hit boxes are noticeably larger then they are drawn, so you can take damage if an enemy has not touched you or you can destroy an enemy sometimes by landing next to it. Inconsistencies like this don't make for an enjoyable playthrough.
Finally is the game length. There are a total of 10 stages, each of which can be completed within 3 minutes provided you don't die and have to start over. This means you can see all the content in half an hour, but you get one gold bullion per level and need to buy the plane for 600 ingots. Going for this final goal would result in repeating each of the 10 stages at least 60 times, at 3 minutes a stage you would be looking at doing the same levels for 30 hours. I cannot understand why the plane is so expensive, or why anyone would play the same 10 stages for that long just to get it.
As it is on release, I cant recommend this game as I while feel it is an OK platformer in gameplay (putting aside the few game bugs) it comes across as unfinished in design.

Reading through some of these reviews has forced me to write a review of my own.  For those who grew up in the late 80s/90s, some of you will remember a game called Cannon Fodder.  The game was ridiculous, with permadeath all over the place because you ALWAYS lost soldiers on EVERY mission.  And you had to do EVERYTHING for them.  And it was fun...because it was worth having a SSG and three FNGs and your hillside with crosses littered all over it from the previous missions.
Anyways, this is about Bomber Wing, a flying spiritual successor to Cannon Fodder.  The artwork is effective, and the gameplay is brutal.  You ahve to manage your crew's tasks while simultaenously figuring out if you should shoot at the fighters or bomb the target.  However, as your guys level up, additional items will become available that do make your job easier.  From fuel management, to having your pilot gain altitutde so he can dive to put out the fire on the wing without you having to send out one of your people.  Learned that lesson the hard way as John slid right off the wing while attempting to put out a fie on the engine after I did a corkscrew maneuver to evade enemy fire...oh, and without a parachute....
If you enjoyed cannon fodder while growing up, then Bomber Crew is right up your alley.  Its cute, brutal, addictive and just frustrating enough that you read the memorial on the menu and wonder what could have been had you just figured out to take some simpler missions first prior to attempting the big one, instead of your crew bailing out over france and your pilot kissing the ground with the plane...

Possibly the best game I have ever played!
Gameplay:
Bomber Crew initially reminded me of three of my own favourite games of old :
- B-17 Flying Fortress
- Cannon Fodder 1+2
- Commodore 64 game called Dam Busters (thank you) where you release a bouncing bomb from your Avro Lancaster.
Initially I felt the game was priced too high, for what I could see of the game and what it appeared to offer it just seemed too much.
I didn't look elsewhere for a better price but often Steam overprice everything and on this occasion I just felt compelled to jump in.....so far I am very glad I did!
Overview;
- The tutorial is good but a little short, it’s easy to figure everything out but you have to learn by your mistakes.
- The graphics are nice, bright and enjoyable.
- Game runs very well, no issues except when mouse disappears off screen.
- The obituary and crew selection (with character background) gets you emotionally involved (Like Cannon Fodder).
- The game mechanics are unique, and work very well.  Easy to Learn & Difficult to master.

Okay I should just say this. The game is a lot of fun from the start. You get to make a crew.
Customize your own Lancaster Bomber and such. I have played for a while now and I do see some issues, it is at this point of the game where the difficulty sharply turns from a 2 to an 11. Destroying Aces early on can give you a small boost cash-wise but will only make later game more difficult. Losing your crew is not an easily acceptable thing. For example, a highly trained gunner can at curtain times mean the difference between life and death for your crew. Losing a single plane late game without enough funds can in a way be the same as ‘GAME OVER’. If this had happened early game then it would be a completely different story. Because not only will you not be in a sense not losing much but because the ‘easy’ level mission mean that you can rapidly re-train them. Unlike the sending them through hell on earth taking on highly skilled aces and/or heavy Concertation’s of flak fire.
I would also like to ask if there is a bug in the way the gunners shoot. For as long as I have been playing it so far the gunners would randomly shoot into the sky, I guess ‘leading’ an enemy fighter. Shooting in the path of the fighter without once hitting the fighter. It annoys me because I see it as a waste of ammo. Ammo which I need to use the engineer to get because of the flak vest’s speed decrease which is realist but at times annoying.
Talking about the Aces I will mention that I have met all 8 of them but I have not defeated all 8 so I can’t tell you what happens after all 8 are killed. Aces in the game are very much like mini-bosses in other games. Each Ace has a reward of what can be seem at the time as a lot of easy, fast money. But don’t be fooled. As each Ace is defeated a more harder Ace will replace Him/She. I do like the Aces in that they have different views of their might in the sky, to the point where they can be seen as the ‘8 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s high on LSD and ‘black magic’ BS that make no sense and even flee like cowards’. On the 8 th Ace which is the Kaiser. Where a reward of $25,000 for his death isn’t much detail of how much of… of… just his will to f*** you and kill your entire crew. I do have a complaint about the Aces in the game however. The Aces in the games fly out to intercept you pretty early on ALONE. Yes, that is right, alone. You would think that the Aces would have for example a small crew of other fighters to dissect your crew and make it harder. Nope. Now I know that many Aces during WW1 and WW2 fought alone. But it comes to a point where 4 gunners each armed with .50 and .303 rounds all opening fire at you just becomes easy money. Hell I did not even manage to pass the first major mission before I have knocked out 4 Aces.
I am going to give this game never the less a thumbs up. Why? Because in a way it is a game which by no means is easy. It is very hard, demanding focus on more than one thing and above all the specialising of the crew to be able to perform more better tactical shooting or path finding with the stars and even bouncing a bomb. Personally I’ll give it at least 7/10

Machinarium is and adventure game from the hands of developers from Amanita design (who are my fellow countrymen) who are responsible for couple of very well accepted adventure games. Machinarium is another one of those and it can boast a very cute, original and !lovely! art followed by a very decent soundtrack.
Adventures are usually a story driven games and Machinarium is no exception, though compared to other adventures it is quite exceptional. There is not a single line of text (spoken or written) and the story is narrated with the use of comics bubbles showing thoughts of characters in pictures. I would not like to spoil anything and my memory is also a little fuzzy since I have been playing the game with months worth of pauses so I will not dig deep into the story, but to outline it a little I will say at least a bit. You are a small, male robot who has been separated from his sweet robot "girlfriend" and you have to find her. To do so you have to travel through a robot town doing the usuall adventurist stuff like using and combining items.
As for the art itself, as I have said, it is really cute however overally the locations and characters are actually depressing, very dark and negatively industrial. This leads to pretty mixed feelings because on one hand you admire the cuteness of the drawings, on the other you feel sorry and sad.
What I cannot vouch for is the design of the puzzles. They are not insanely hard, actually you will probably be able to guess what you are supposed to do pretty fast, or that was at least my case, however the steps needed to get it done seemed pretty much random and I did often struggle with them. There is nothing more frustrating than knowing the answer and struggling with finding the right paper to write it on. Because of that I often had to resort to using the build in hint system.
The hint system has two levels. Upon using the first level, your little robot will pop a thought comics bubble and give you a small hint usually pointing out what it is you should do in the current room and you are to find a way to do it yourself. This may help you, but as I have already said, figuring out what to do is not much of a problem, but how to do it, that's the question. And that is what level 2 hint is for, if you are really desperate you can use it, but in order for it to work you have to finish a small mini-game which involves navigating a key through areas and monsters in kind of a side scrolling shoot-them-up (like Space Impact on old Nokia cells). Upon finishing it (and you will probably hate every second of it, because it has terrible hitbox and is just no fun) you will be given a comics like page in a book showing you step-by-step walkthrough.
So to sum up, I did like this game to an extent mainly because of the art and soundtrack. Story was good enough but I was really annoyed with puzzles and the hint system. I do recommend you to play this game, but I would say, don't feel a shame if you want to grab a hint or two, or rather get  a walkthrough on the internet (if you hate the minigame required to complete for the hint as much as I did) when you are stuck for unreasonably long time.

is a collection of four fun games for a bargain value, three of which are not available on Steam outside of this bundle. This is a great collection to pick for fans of this genre.
The first game in the bundle that I played was
, I was attracted to the title’s name and the preliminary artwork of the protagonist Ethan and his fiance Claire. The story starts off with the two of them being summoned by Ethan’s father to come visit, simple enough. Though, as soon as Ethan utters the words “Everything will be fine” players are thrust into a world of supernatural mystery and family secrets. Claire soon finds herself kidnapped, shock, and Ethan must save her from the clutches of a mad man.
The game itself plays like a basic hidden object game. Finding items in a variety of different scenes with puzzles and mini games thrown in. One feature I enjoyed was that you could find more than one useful object at a time during the hidden object scenes. So instead of having to replay a scene countless times you could say pick up the knife and puzzle piece needed in one go through. Artwork was lovely in the game and the audio was good as well, voice acting was a bit on the cheesy side though but that added to the charm.
I next jumped into
again, based off the title. I was expecting a mystical journey through the lost city of Atlantis, instead what I got was a space odyssey. The story starts off with Amrite, a famous archaeologist, going to explore the newly discovered ruins of a temple from the fabled city of Atlantis. However, tragedy strikes as the excavation site is destroyed taking all mortals with it. Fast forward over a century later, Amrite is on her way to a Martian archaeological site to lend her expertise. After being suspended in cryogenic sleep, it’s time for her to use her skills to help mankind find a new home as they flee Earth.
The game’s story is rather far-fetched but refreshing as Amrite wanders around a deserted space station with only a kitten as company. While I wouldn’t look for deep inner monologue or reflections of the emptiness of space itself, the game does present a very good mystery element as you try to figure out what happened to the crew. The artwork is alright, I feel it’s a bit weaker than the other titles in the bundle but not bad at all, it certainly feels other worldly along with the music. The game also has voice acting which is a plus, and it’s not bad either. The game plays smoothly but be prepared for quite a bit of backtracking, thankfully there is a map.
In my opinion the weakest of the four titles, I played this one last because it had a creepy clown in it. You play a woman named Danielle who has just witnessed her husband Sam being kidnapped. A talking pin cushion doll instructs you that you must return to the town that Sam grew up in to find him. As is the case with many protagonists in these games, Danielle shows the minimal amount of shock at her current situations and rushes to find Sam. The story is weird, involving magic, orphans and clowns. The story is also slightly predictable, many twists being obvious before they happen. The biggest example being the clown, never trust a clown people.
What the game lacks in a compelling story and interesting characters it makes up with good gameplay and artwork. The artwork matches the setting of the story, it’s dark and moody along with the music. The visuals draw players in and the puzzles and hidden object scenes keep them there. Tasks move from one to another smoothly and it’s usually easy to figure out your next step, the game also isn’t too difficult either which can make it a little short. I wasn’t even prepared for the sudden ending of the game as things seemed to wrap up very quickly despite the slower pace of the rest of the story, though I found the ending to be one of the better parts of the entire game.
I saved this one for for last because it’s the only one of the four games available on Steam separately. The difference being that the separate version is the collector’s edition which has bonus content as well as a bonus chapter for more gameplay. I played the game again to see if there were any other differences between the two but there are not. The issue with this game is the story, you play Kate who is returning to the House of 1,000 Doors for really no reason, she isn’t summoned and she never outright states why she’s going back after her adventures in the first game of the series, also available separately on Steam. Once you arrived you’re sucked into supernatural escapades. The story offers no real sense of urgency, however, as you try to stop a mysterious fireball you only find out is the Palm of Zoroaster at the end of the game. The unfortunate part is that the bonus chapter, not available in this bundle, adds more story than the main game offers.
The game is still fun, however. It is hidden object scene heavy with a few puzzles as well. The artwork is good and the game has a great map feature which makes the backtracking less tedious.

Update: The game has been getting worse and worse and I think it's funny how the trailer says 'millions of players in one grand war' when the entire player-base is around 6000... At this point I have to say my rating has dropped to a 4/10.
300+ hours of the game have taught me a few things. Most important being that this game is grindy - 0% doubt in that, but in my opinion that is the aspect of the game that makes it stand out from other FPS games (that, and the fact that it's one of the few WW2 themed MMO FPS' around). Sure, when you start the game with your horrible SA rifle which takes 3-4 hits to kill someone, you will die a lot. A lot. But! One day you think: 'Okay, I'm getting better at the game, I have figured out some decent strategies with my starter weapon!' So you go in and try them - die a lot again. But you try again, you die a little less. And after a while (50-75 hours +), you start to get the hang of it. It's really these first couple of steps that separates people who are used to COD and CS, where there is little-none grinding, and then these people might post some pretty angry reviews just because it's different. Of course, another important fact is that stronger weapons can be bought with real money - another thing people complain about. However, hours and skill generally go hand in hand, so even someone with a purchased gun is beatable if you are more experienced then them. A good way to go about these people is to:
1. Kill them.
2. Steal their gun.
3. Kill them with it.
4. Repeat step 3 until satisfied.
So, to conclude, I recommend this game for people looking for a different experience to traditional FPS games where everything is available right off the bat.

I've read other reviews, the general consensus is that the gameplay is really bad but the story etc. make up for it.  It depends on how much you're willing to put up with, I suppose.
Combat consists of clicking on enemies to chain combos together.  About half the time, however clicking on an enemy will not start the attack chain, Geralt just stands there like a lemon until you give him a poke.  Apparently you can only attack if you're facing the opponent directly or are out of melee range and have to move, causing you to face them.  If you're in range and try to attack something to your side, nothing happens.  When it works properly, combat is pretty bland, it's not challenging and there are no tactics to be employed.
The voice acting isn't the worst I've ever heard, that accolade belongs to the Gothic series but this comes a very close second.  The script is as dry as a week old baguette and you can tell the actors aren't invested in it.  There's a lot of talking too.
The graphics are functional but there are only a handful of NPC models which can be a little jarring when you keep seeing the same person over and over.  There aren't even different face, body size/shape, clothes etc. like Morrowind had to distinguish NPCs, and that came out five years earlier.
The epic story we're promised is composed of killing things and fetch quests.  You'll do about 50 laps of the starting village before moving on.
There's a certain boss fight which you have to prepare for but aren't told is coming; you need to stack up the necessary buffs before it starts.  Otherwise it's only winnable by accident after many tries.  You can't actually beat the boss in a fair fight, they just die suddenly and nobody knows how or why.
There's a dice poker minigame whose RNG makes the AI win ca. 90% of the time.  It's not even remotely fair on the player and has nothing to do with skill, it's just a time sink which makes you reload many, many times.  If you get a good hand in the first roll, the AI will beat it, no matter how unlikely.
There's so much faffing about in this game.  If the story everyone harps on about were actually happening, I might have a different oppinion.  After ten hours I don't feel I've accomplished anything at all, I'm no farther along the main plot and everyone I meet is a complete dullard.  I could keep playing and save the world but honestly, I hope that monstry dog eats every last one of these cretins.
Edit:
So I continued playing, cheated my way past the monster pooch and made it to chapter 2.  A lot more seems to happen in chapter 2, at least at first.  There are a bunch of pest control and fetch quests to hoover up your time but the main plot is actually moderately engaging.  It revolves around searching for the main bad guy, gathering evidence and deciding who's in league with him.  The big plot twist is pretty easy to spot even before it's spelled out for you.
There are way too many conversation pitfalls which lock characters up and make quests either unfinishable or leave you with only the most tenuous of plot threads.  I had to use a walkthrough to avoid getting to the end of the chapter and finding I'd messed everything up.
The main irritation in chapter 2 is the constant flipping between day and night.  Seriously, you'll do one or two things, then rest until midnight.  Talk to one person, knock over some monsters, then rest until morning.  Talk to another person at work then rest until midnight to talk to them again at home, then back to midday to talk to them at work again etc. etc.  I'm not exagerating, this is actually what you do.
Chapter 2 ends with a fight with two people who don't take any damage.  After a minute or so it just ends and they run away.  If they were going to run, why didn't they just do so in the first place?  If they can incapacitate Geralt, why didn't they just do that earlier?  Why did they just leave him there?  They could have finished him off but no, instead they tell him where their hideout is and teleport away.  This is Saturday morning cartoon level of storytelling.
I made it to chapter 3 but I haven't enjoyed getting there.  I might continue playing to see how it ends but I'm not buying into the paper thin story, nor the cardboard cutout characters.  For now I give up.  I was hoping to finish so I'd have some context going into the sequels, also that the sequels are not so agressively boring.
Maybe this game is only for fans of the book, those who enjoy particularly low quality fan fiction.  If somebody made a game like this about a book which I like, I'd be terribly disappointed.
TLDR - The writing is bad.  The gameplay is boring.  The characters are shallow.  The quests are repetitive and easily broken, leaving you stuck.  Dice poker is BS.  It's like the programmers decided they could write the plot and characters themselves instead of getting a professional script writer to do it.

Bomber Crew is a cute little strategy/simulator where your objective is to micromanage your crew and plane to ensure their survival. Despite being quite a casual game, it is in no way easy, you will be frequently get caught up in chaotic situations as enemy fighters tear your bomber to shreds. As your crew improve you'll gain access to various skills and abilities that you'll only truly appreciate after the crew members innevitable death. Your Lanster also has many upgrades available, allowing you to customise your planes strengths to your preferences.
Simple controls
Basic concept - the micromanagement is difficult due to the hectic style, rather than a complex system
Pleasant art style
Upgrade/Skill system helps keep the game interesting
Your vulnerable crew make you care about their survival - they're not just souless drones.
Missions can get repetitive - At the time of writing they all involve flying to a location under fire, dropping some bombs, taking (optional) intelligence photos, and returning to base. While not being an awful formula, it does become a bit of a grind after 10-15 missions.
Crew survival can be a little too harsh - a crash landing in friendly territory, near your airbase, can still lead to your crew getting marked as missing in action.

Bomber Crew is a fun/frustrating game. I was expecting a few more "tutorials" before the game proceeds with dropping you in the drink (this is likely a more literal statement than you realize). The learning curve can be brutal and some simple things--things that make you feel dumb once you realize where they are or how they function-are tucked away and left for you to find on your own. (SHIFT Key is your friend)
That being said, the gameplay itself is a little rough around the edges. If you load it up and don't like it at first, just give yourself a few missions to get the hang of things and you'll end up feeling better about your purchase.
And when you do gain some momentum and aren't flailing around--usually after finally surviving a mission that you thought was doomed, landing with almost no fuel and with your engineer out on the wing holding your last engine together with duct tape and paperclips--Bomber Crew begins to shine in its own low-pixel, cartooney kind of way.
R.I.P to my first crew, I thought we'd have more time together....I didn't even get to know your names.

Machinarium is and adventure game from the hands of developers from Amanita design (who are my fellow countrymen) who are responsible for couple of very well accepted adventure games. Machinarium is another one of those and it can boast a very cute, original and !lovely! art followed by a very decent soundtrack.
Adventures are usually a story driven games and Machinarium is no exception, though compared to other adventures it is quite exceptional. There is not a single line of text (spoken or written) and the story is narrated with the use of comics bubbles showing thoughts of characters in pictures. I would not like to spoil anything and my memory is also a little fuzzy since I have been playing the game with months worth of pauses so I will not dig deep into the story, but to outline it a little I will say at least a bit. You are a small, male robot who has been separated from his sweet robot "girlfriend" and you have to find her. To do so you have to travel through a robot town doing the usuall adventurist stuff like using and combining items.
As for the art itself, as I have said, it is really cute however overally the locations and characters are actually depressing, very dark and negatively industrial. This leads to pretty mixed feelings because on one hand you admire the cuteness of the drawings, on the other you feel sorry and sad.
What I cannot vouch for is the design of the puzzles. They are not insanely hard, actually you will probably be able to guess what you are supposed to do pretty fast, or that was at least my case, however the steps needed to get it done seemed pretty much random and I did often struggle with them. There is nothing more frustrating than knowing the answer and struggling with finding the right paper to write it on. Because of that I often had to resort to using the build in hint system.
The hint system has two levels. Upon using the first level, your little robot will pop a thought comics bubble and give you a small hint usually pointing out what it is you should do in the current room and you are to find a way to do it yourself. This may help you, but as I have already said, figuring out what to do is not much of a problem, but how to do it, that's the question. And that is what level 2 hint is for, if you are really desperate you can use it, but in order for it to work you have to finish a small mini-game which involves navigating a key through areas and monsters in kind of a side scrolling shoot-them-up (like Space Impact on old Nokia cells). Upon finishing it (and you will probably hate every second of it, because it has terrible hitbox and is just no fun) you will be given a comics like page in a book showing you step-by-step walkthrough.
So to sum up, I did like this game to an extent mainly because of the art and soundtrack. Story was good enough but I was really annoyed with puzzles and the hint system. I do recommend you to play this game, but I would say, don't feel a shame if you want to grab a hint or two, or rather get  a walkthrough on the internet (if you hate the minigame required to complete for the hint as much as I did) when you are stuck for unreasonably long time.
