Well son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ if this wasn't actually pretty good.
It's a fairly standard point-and-click-esque with cover-based shooting thrown in. There is substance in these humble beginnings; some puzzles caused me to pause, a bit perplexed but with solutions that inspired and, in many later cases, entertained me to actual laughter. Action segments felt decent - I was very much in control and there was satisfaction to be had. These segments are infrequent, reacting well with their choice of use in specific parts.
Of course, what makes The Fall shine like a diamond in the rough is its premise, and the way that it unfolds.
There are no humans in this world; cold, severe logic drives every character in ways that is both easy to follow and intruiging. We see the conflicts unfurling from a distance as we approach but find them fascinating when presented by the few characters seen. At no point does the story not make sense - it's both watertight and accessible, so you may wade in freely and find the speed to which the game picks up much shorter than usual.
Framing the plot is the UI, which uses a Unix-like terminal that emphasises minimalism over complexity. Come to think of it, there's actually no HUD in the game, at all. Everything that shows up is a result of your scanning over the ruined depot, a cunning move to reward investigation using light. We have precisely what the designers intended, because of this: players moving through dark, devastated areas sweeping their light from the ceiling to the floor, controlling their speed to drink in both the surroundings and any analysis of the area we can find. It works. It feels good, and the A.R.I.D suit's robotic movements are the perfect compliment to tie these moments to the overarching story.
One of the most notable things that drew my applause was how "abilities" are unlocked. Put simply, I have never seen it done better than The Fall. The AI controlling the suit is denied access to functions such as networking with other machines and greater firepower, but these functions have failsafes that activate them when their release is required to safe the occupant's life. Therefore, you are able to activate these by intentionally putting your pilot in danger, a colossal AI protocol moral quandry. These represent contradictions to the running protocols of the suit, to such a point that I wonder why I've never thought of the concept before. The Fall makes it seem so natural and obvious that this would happen for AIs in general, and for it to have achieved that as a story about AIs shows its fortitude as a pure story, let alone a story attached to a game.
Of course there are some rough edges to be found - some moments when the suit seems to float along the ground, hands that don't connect with ladder rungs, some floating objects here and there - but their arrival was noted and discarded, as by the point I'd encountered them I was wholeheartedly sold on the entire experience anyway.
For the 69p I bought this for, it's beyond any measure of value for money and a standout success for showing how Kickstarter projects can bring otherwise-impossible projects to life. The Fall tells a strong story using minimal assets set to a soundtrack that seemed almost perfect for every moment it appeared. It's much like a shot of something strong, but goes down smooth - you'll be at the end of the experience quickly, but it'll feel like you've just drank something well worth the money.

Machinarium is a point-and-click adventure game with heavy use of puzzles and brain teasers. It’s created by Amanita Design, a small, independent game developing studio based in the Czech Republic. The game was released in 2009, but that something is “old” doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s bad. “Old” in this case means that us patient gamers can get it on sale. “Old” in this case also means that the game is written in Flash, but we’ll come back to that later. Machinarium tells the story about Josef, a little robot who finds himself dumped on a scrapheap. After re-assembling himself he sets off towards the city to look for a friend. The story, which is told without the use of text or dialogue, unfolds as you play, and even though it’s not the most intriguing and creative story I’ve seen – you’ll probably feel it’s very familiar – it’s very well told.
The story’s backdrop is beautiful, hand-drawn scenes accompanied to a lovely soundtrack by Floex, Amanita Design’s own in-house “sound maker”, as he is entitled on their website. The soundtrack is available
if you want to listen to it. If I’d have to label it, I’d call it “industrial chill”, which is perfect for Machinarium – except for some plants and a bit of water, everything in the game is mechanized and industrial, including the local wild life. The game design is extraordinary well thought-through and the attention to detail is impressive.
The puzzles you stumble across in Machinarium are mostly about pattern recognition. How to interact with the environment is also often part of the puzzles, which are very well balanced and just challenging enough for Average Joe. I got stuck once, but even if that happens, there is hope. Josef will have a small clue for you most of the time and if you find yourself feeling like an idiot for not being able to solve a puzzle even with his help, you can play a little mini-game that will reveal the solution, or at least give you some very good clues on how to solve it.
But Machinarium, like all games, has its flaws. The game is written in Flash, and clicking the right mouse button brings up the Flash menu with its “About Flash” and whatnot. Since clicking the right mouse button is usually some kind of action in other point-and-click adventure games – for instance that you automatically put whatever you are holding back in to your inventory – the Flash menu got a bit annoying after a while. It’s mostly my own fault though, for not being able to memorize that I could not use the right mouse button to return whatever the little robot was holding in his hand back to the inventory. Instead the inventory had to be opened before the item could be returned. Point-and-click adventure games often involves a lot of pointing and clicking – hence the genre’s name – with items from the inventory, a process that got rather tedious.
The game lagged considerably on my computer when played in fullscreen. It have to be said that my hardware isn’t what you would call state of the art, but it should be able to handle a game from 2009. Hardware acceleration was turned on in the Flash settings, but that didn’t help at all. I ended up playing the game in windowed mode, which worked a lot better and was fine since fullscreen didn’t really add anything to the game: The resolution used in both fullscreen and window mode is the same. The immense detail of the background images also proved to be a challenge: In one of the scenes, it was virtually impossible to see that the main character could interact with an object on the screen, and it was only by accident I clicked on it.
But in spite of these minor issues, Machinarium is a great game. If you like puzzle games and brain teasers, you should go right ahead and buy it. It won’t entertain you that long, it took me only 6 hours to complete the game and I really suck at puzzles, but at the asking price of USD 10 it’s certainly worth it.

Morrowind is the only game that I seriously dedicated every bit of 2 months of my life to.
It was early 2004...I went on my lunch break at my crappy job and I decided to never return, I was living with a slob of a roommate, we ate ramen, I was using a credit card to get by and I was somewhat depressed. I heard about Morrowind from a friend, who sold me when he said "It's a rpg that's kinda like GTA in a fantasy setting" (boy was he dumb)!, I bought it used for about 10 bucks that day, popped it in my Xbox as soon as I got home and began my journey...
The addiction was real, "♥♥♥♥ the job search" I said to myself, as I also skipped some showers and meals. My routine was as follows: Wake up at about noon, play Morrowind for about 14 hours, sleep, repeat, with a few quick breaks in between of course. I was hooked.
Morrowind amazed me to say the least and took me away from the BS that was life. Sure, some could say I was a "loser" during those 2 months but I didn't care and I don't regret it one bit, Morrowind was the most amazing experience I've ever had with any form of art or media. It took 3 long years before I found somewhat the level of enjoyment in a video game (there was Fable in late 04 but it was short lived) that I had in Morrowind, which was Runescape (believe it or not) but nothing came close to my love of Morrowind.
I persevered through the game freezes (losing hours of game play), starting over with different characters because I couldn't make up my mind which race I wanted to be, playing entirely in the 3rd person view, and that huge and incredibly annoyingly hard to navigate city (Vivec) while the characters, the level progression system (the sense of getting better with every step), the huge open world, the graphics (I would often move the camera towards the sky at ingame night to look at the stars),.and the incredible music, sucked me in.
The possibilities seemed endless with this game, as I could do whatever I wanted (ohhh shiny! I'll take that!) and there were surprises around every corner...I'm just casually walking along and all of a sudden someone falls from the sky and plops on the ground, "Did that seriously just happen?" Later, I jump up a mountain only to find a lone orc on top wearing badass armor I so desperatly want to have. "Can I take him?" was the question I was asking myself. It was these types of discoveries that made Morrowind so different.
Most of the time I would ignore the quests and just roam the world to see who or what would pop up. Silt Striders were for "marks", I thought, as I spent hours traveling the land on foot, making sure to occasionaly jump or swim to level those acrobat and athletic skills. Often I was ever so swiftly r a p e d by a blighted Cliff Racer.
Something this fun had to eventually come to an end, I couldn't stay in Morrowind forever.
After 2 months, the journey was over...I finally decided to go out with friends (they begged me) one night. I finally became unglued from the game for a few hours. I had a great time (got to see a girl I was interested in) that night and I realized living in the real world wasn't so bad and that I could make it better for myself.
It's almost as if Morrowind played a part in my transition into full blown adulthood, as I was finally saying goodbye to the carefree days of being a child or teen with little to no responsibility, Morrowind was the finale...and it sure was grand!
The rest is history. I got a job a few days later, moved soon after that, and began dating that girl I saw that night. I played Morrowind again a few years later (PC physical copy) and sunk another 80 hours into it, but that was it, I was done, I walked away never beating the game. It already served it's purpose.
Although sometimes I deeply miss the characters (Fargoth), the world, the music, and 2004, I can happily say that I am done with the game, a closed chapter of my life,  but I'll always have fond memories of Morrowind. I enjoyed Oblivion and am currently playing Skyrim SE & ESO, but they can't compare. Nothing can compare to Morrowind.
Not gonna lie, I look forward to Skywind and I watch the Morrowind store trailer sometimes for that nostalgic trip, and just hearing the main theme song damn near brings a tear to my eye. Like most people who have experienced a most joyous event, my time with Morrowind in 04 evokes pure happiness.
Even if it meant that my character's end game was to be deleted from existence after being brutally fisted by a lowly scamp (of all things), I would still relive those 2 months in a heart beat.
After typing all of this, I feel the urge to play it, but I'm spolied now with Skyrim's improved engine, and I know the experience will never be the same...2004, unemployed, my whole life ahead of me with just Morrowind to worry about is long gone...but I'm thankful to have had the experience.

This is one of the most epic games I have ever played. From the moment you disembark the boat, you feel the enormity of the world of Morrowind. From the get-go you can choose your own path, whether you want to follow the main quest and save the world, or spend your days looting dungeons and bandit caves for gold, it's up to you.
Sometimes open world games like this can be daunting when all you want is a linear experience, but don't let this freedom discourage you. The world is filled with people you can interact with, and so many of these can offer you quests to keep you busy instead of mindlessly roaming the countryside.
At some point you should take on the main quest, which is a fantastic story in of itself. This game is so deep and interesting, and has the entire Elder Scrolls mythology fuelling it every step of the way. Sure, it's 99% reading text instead of actual hearing the NPC's talking, but this is how they have managed to cram so much backstory into this game. Add the amazing soundtrack and you have an immense experience, where you feel just like the lonely outlander the peoples of Morrowind refer to you as.

I think one of the three best things a game can do is sell you on the legitimacy of the world it puts you in. Guess what Resident Evil did -- it didn't. nah jk it totally did. That's something really great about Half-Life as well, and when comparing the two of them and trying to reason as to why both are both as immersive as they are, I came to one conclusion: control. Resident Evil's a game with stellar atmosphere (and le meilleur parfait environment art & sound design), creepy and dangerous enemies, and fitting mechanics. What makes it stand out though is how much control over the game's progression it gives to you, which is complete.
In horror games like The Evil Within 2 or Resident Evil 7, you just sort of run around places until the environment (or some character, gadget, etc.) gives you a blantantly obvious clue as to where you should go, or outright opens up a pathway for you, and you progress. It's something GIVEN to you. Resident Evil operates on the complete opposite. Every clue or direction you get from Resident Evil is comes from something YOU find, and the connection you build between dots when thinking. If you entered and exited a room having glanced over a crucial item, your progression would stop to a grinding halt. That's why Resident Evil is scary, and why it's easy to feel as if the world is 'real'. The atmosphere is ominous and the enemies are unsettling, but what adds to the pressure is the responsibility that's soley placed on you of figuring out your way out of the mansion. The biting questions of "Did I check every room?" "Is this used in that room?" force you into the danger of manuevering around zombies, but also make way for amazing dopamine hits whenever you figure something out, and put one puzzle piece in the perfect way it was needed to. On top of this you have item management, with adds another layer of planning and tension. You have no idea how much of X you're going to find, and how much of Y and Z. You have to play very carefully all while the game throws one surprise after another at you. It's simply thrilling, and the game rewards you for smart, strategic thinking.
I don't mean to downplay the importance of the atmosphere and creature designs, though. The zombies are genuinely scary. They have a genuinely monstrous look to them, whereas most zombies look like dumb induced with some kind of inhibitor. The zombies in Resident Evil genuinely look, act, and sound like different creatures, which grinds so perfectly against what you read in the memos you find that detail their thoughts before having their humanity robbed from them, and that's where the existential horror comes into play. They're not just monsters, or just 'dumb people' in the general context -- they're people. "Maybe the zombie right outside in the hall is the guy who wrote this note..." The mansion's aesthetic is excellent as well. There's a really good blend of genuinely very satisfying looking interior design with interesting and strange angles, complimentary details, and old, abandoned looking areas. They all share a desaturated, cold color pallette and an almost disorienting, surreal lighting, making long, stretching shadows.

This is a fantastic game!  I can't recommend this game more.  No, I didn't get the game for free... and yes, I bought the game like everyone else.  Here's what you need to know:
PROS:
+ It is a roguelike in the vein of FTL
++++++  BUT THERE's NO FLEET MAKING YOU HURRY EVERYWHERE!
+ Like a RL WWII bomber, you have to manage your fuel, mechanical situation... and if you can get around to it, the lives of your crew.
+ Crew and aircraft alike can be customized with a healthy amount of stat enhancing gear.  The aircraft has a weight limit per the type of engine you use.  You can max it out to be a flying tank... a slow, flying tank with limited fuel supply.  Or, you can max it the other way for ultralight speed and range.  Of course, you can mix things up!  Armored engines and tail gunner and lightweight everywhere else... because really, who needs a radio operator all that much? ;-)
** This game is difficult.  On purpose.  If you're the type of gamer who plays games on easy mode... there is no easy mode in this game.  There's no magical, "stop time so you can think" button.  You are presented situations, you must react.  If you react poorly, people die or engines explode.  This is a game for the type of gamer who thrives on challenge and overcoming great difficulty.  It isn't as grognard as Dark Souls or that stupid mobile game, "Dumb Ways to Die," but if you go into this casually and think you can just set it on easy and bask in victory.... well.  There is no difficulty settings in the game.  You get the real deal, all the time.  And you're going to die.  I play FTL on the hardest setting and I've lost 3 bombers so far and I've only gotten past the first "critical" mission point.
CONS:
- The game could maybe give more information to the pilot... things like easier to read fuel supply for planning whether or not I will have to ditch in the Channel or chance it on home?  Now, you're given a readout that says, "You have 4 minutes of fuel left."  But, that doesn't really mean 4 minutes.  Time is accelerated somewhat and plane performance affects fuel rate.  You can't manually control the pilot and sometimes they like to make high power turns for no damn good reason... bye bye fuel.
- You can't prioritize fighters to focus on.  Example:  An enemy ace attacks you while you're swarmed with 6 other fighters.  You can't "clear" the targets of the less dangerous fighters to let your gunners focus on the 1 guy who is flying around over western France with $3,500 in his pockets.  So, you have to plink at him and hope he dies, but usually your gunners shoot anything else but the ace pilot.
- Wearing fingerless gloves make you run faster, apparently.  I don't know why this irks me... maybe it's because the game does take a good amount of detail into things... so when I saw there's a glove item that makes your guy run faster... it makes no sense.  I'm nitpicking here.  That item give a little move speed, no damage reduction and a little bonus to cold protection.  It's a nice hybrid item for someone needing a little of two stats I guess... but, GLOVES THAT MAKE YOU RUN FASTER?
Lastly, a tip for you.  If your starboard inboard engine is on fire, don't send your engineer out on the wing to put it out with fire extinguisher while your pilot is using corkscrew maneuvers to try and shake off enemy fighters.  Although this game is like FTL... there are no teleporters and this isn't zero G.  That engineer is gonna fall off and end up being remembered for all time on the memorial to your lost crew...

Your Star is a hand drawn horror-survivor adventure in RPG maker format. This is perhaps the most punishing and cryptic game you will ever play. There are a lot of problems with glitches and game design which you would have to overlook to enjoy it. Overall Your Star was a chore to play through but I feel that originality of this game alone could possibly make into a cult classic. Saying all that do not buy this game if you not very forgiving toward unintuitive mechanics and puzzles.
I was experiencing a lot of game breaking glitches that kept resetting my progress. Developer fixed some of the issues so I was able to get though the game eventually. You will likely run into some bugs that may force you to reload save files such as invisible text. I am sure there are more problems to be found but I think Developer is very proactive if you can help him identify where bugs happen.
Perhaps my favorite thing about Your Star is a psychological aspect of the game design. Your character has 3 resources which are mind, light, and will (basically health, ammo and armor aura). I think Mind is the one that drains overtime as in your character is going insane (even if you just stay still) The game sort of implies that crazy events have the effect on the character and it also impacts gameplay. Your Star has a very unsettling atmosphere as a horror game should. I experienced loneliness and sadness playing this game with some relief toward the end. It is very easy to get lost in the mood.
Nearly everything you do and don't do slowly kills you. So basically the game is timed and if you not quick enough you will eventually die. There are enough items to barely get you though assuming you not using the guide. Without a guide, you will do a lot of backtracking which slowly kills you so you will need to leapfrog on your safe files. Enemies toward the middle of the game respawn few second after you kill them so you have no time to fart, let alone explore the area. I am somewhat experienced with these games so I managed to pull through by the skin of my teeth. Not exactly casual game. Made even harder by some design problems and dark environments.
It is kind of like a wird mixture of Silent Hills and Witch's House. There is some combat, resource management, and obviously puzzles. I had to use pencil and paper for some of the riddles that require math so don't expect it to be straight forward. About 60% of the game is logical and the other 40% is convoluted, to say the least. There is a neat alternate world mechanic where things are different. You will also find different kinds of power-ups, some of which hidden in secrets and side-quest.When you kill enough enemies you will even level up your attributes and get items. Very weird game which is why I kinda like it.
Your star has a mature story that was well paced and explained toward the end . There are side quests, secrets, and even several endings.  I am a little skeptical that someone would make the effort to beat this game several times just because you so happy to even beat it once. It took me 8 hours to beat the game without a guide but do to glitches it was closer to 14 . So with several endings I would say game has about 15 to 20 hours worth of content .
You have to give credit where credit is due. Not everyone can make RPG maker game with their own drawings and I appreciate that . It is a pretty dark game so it might be hard to tell where things are. The tone overall suits the story so I did not really mind it. Not exactly a gorgeous game but I dig the gloomy art style and gore .
Unfortunately, I think this is one of the weaker attributes of the game. I did not find soundtrack very enjoyable and the sound was not used particularly well when it was needed. You will probably find that a boss song feels very out of place for example. There are many areas that have no music. Perhaps you could argue that horror game can get away without music but I prefer something ambient in all places.
I really debated with myself if this game was worth for someone who is not as masochistic as I am. Normally I would not recommend a half-broken game but there is something special here . For $4 this game was worth in WTF moments for me at least .
Your Star has a lot of good elements and combination of those that you will not see in other games. There is a good Core idea but it needs a lot of glitch fixes and more intuitive mechanics. Some of the things will hopefully get fixed but I still see it as a cult game which only the most persistent RPG maker fans will enjoy .
Update: Developer fixed some of the problems and added extra features that I asked for (like gamepad and better inventory) so I bumped score from 6 to 7... I plan to beat the game for another ending and I appreciate that developer still puts time into this old game .

===
Have you lost your mind, boy?
===
===
Your Star is essentialy a Puzzle-Based Adventure mashed up with Survival Horror style gameplay. The story revolves around a young boy who lost his memories and is now stranded in a huge mansion, on a quest to find what he lost of himself and also to find Maya, his sister, that for some reason yet unknown, has been separated from him. On this quest he is not alone, as some friendly characters, like his magical teddy bear, which is sentient, and others will help him, but there will also be enemies on his path, ready to get what they want and stop for nothing.
The first thing that catches your eye when opening Your Star is a very peculiar art style. The developers chosen a hand drawn style for all the elements we find in the game, from backgrounds to characters to environments. The color palette is almost always very darkly toned: dark brown, black, deep red and similar colors are what is most predominant in the ambience. From this we can understand that this title is focused on giving out a gritty, dark, unnerving atmosphere from the very fist moments of gameplay, and in this it succeeds quite well.
Not everything about this style is positive though: this choice of art also has problems that fall on gameplay, as many times the player will have difficulties in discerning what is what around the game world. Doors, drawers, boxes and other key items which contain story and progression elements are often very hard to spot, because of the very dark and imprecise drawing style they have been portraited with. Secondly, even if the art style is acceptable for this kind of game, you don't have to be an art expert to see it is clearly the work of amateurs, as many of the cutscene images and character portraits are not drawn very well.
To partially counter the object-finding issues, the player's Teddy Bear has a function that when activated briefly highlights any interactable item in a certain radius around the boy. But this function costs Light or Mind if light is depleted.
Moving on to the gameplay, let's start sayin' that Your Star has two main components: one is puzzle-solving adventure, and the other one is survival horror. The main character will have two main statistics, which are Light and Mind. Light is the magical power embedded in the Teddy Bear, the boy's only weapon against the Shadows, evil dark figures that will attack him and spawn constantly all around the mansion: every time he uses the Light to defeat Shadows, a part of it is consumed, as it is when he gets hit by enemies. If all the Light gets depleted, then the boy's Mind will be damaged, and if that reaches zero, it will be game over.
Luckily, Shadows sometimes drop Stars, that when collected will replenish part of the Light or Mind, depending on the color. Certain items found in the game world can also do this, or have opther beneficial effects, but they are rare. There are also other types of enemies to be found, stronger and more dangerous. Aswell, there will be means for the player to get "upgrades" that will render the boy's abilities stronger in different ways.
Other than defeating enemies, the boy will have to solve various puzzles and find items to unlock doors to progress deeper in the mansion. There will be good variety of gameplay, as puzzles have good diversity, and span from mechanical puzzles, to logic problems, to riddles. The game will not hold the player's hand, and there will be no clues on where to go or what to do next. Around the world you can find Map segments that will help with determining your location in the mansion, but not tell you your exact location.
Even with a good variety of puzzles and enemies, the gameplay is affected by several problems, first of which is the limited number of savegames in a playthrough. At the start you will be given 10 inkpots, each savegame consumes one. Other ones can be found but are not common. This, combined with the fact that the game is generally not very reliable in terms of stability, in fact crashes can happen rarely when defeating enemies and very commonly during puzzles, can lead to massive frustration, as savegames must be used wisely because limited, but at the same time, instability means having to save often or a crash could revert lots of progress.
The second problem of this game is that the puzzle-survival horror mash-up formula does not really work well. Enemies constantly spawning and giving nothing most of the time, always consuming the player resources, are just annoying and do not even represent a challenge per se, they just exist to deplete resources. This, combined with the fact that maps are hand drawn and as said before, inaccurately represent many key items which are hard to spot, makes up a combination that easily leads to player frustration and not satisfaction in overcoming difficulty as it should be. The main challenge for the player will be to spot things while dodging monsters and running around, so much for atmosphere indeed.
===
- Good atmosphere...
- Original art style...
- A combination of different game genres...
- Challenging Puzzles...
===
- ...but not really enjoyable.
- ...but cripples gameplay.
- ...that does not work well.
- ...that crash most of the times if failed or reset.
===
Your Star has some promising concepts at the base of its idea, and an original art style not seen everyday in nowadays games. This being said, the game still has many problems in its gameplay design, and is a mash-up of two genres that could work well but does not. It has a good atmosphere that cannot be fully enjoyed because of the reason explained before.
I suggest purchasing only if you are a diehard fan of puzzle solving games, and are prepared to face game crippling crashes that will multiple times revert your progress.

Update:
As much as I liked the game at first, the more I played the more the issues were made apparent. I think what initially drew me in was the mystery-oriented game in the vein of a classic SNES concept with a feel of Amnesia. But the deeper I got, the more difficult it was to proceed. I realized I was forcing myself to like the game in the last bit of play, because I really wanted it to be something I could love. The guidance is more limited than I thought, to the point where some of the puzzles are trial and error rather than something that can be clued together and figured out. Besides all that, what I think finally did it in was when I realized I had to cut my lights out to be able to see the screen, and even then I had to strain to make out some details. That made me pull back and objectively look at what I'd been playing more critically.
The game is a still a beautiful concept, but the design of the puzzles needs work, a brightness/gama option for players to customize their experience would be a huge help, and more interaction with the player outside of major story events. I wish you the best of luck, Natahem.

If you have played computer games for longer than the past decade (or if you have a taste for the classics) then you have played one or more of those old point-and-click adventure games, like those of old-school Lucasarts fame. Machinarium really brings you back to that time, when games did not have to be about leveling-up, taking the shot, making that jump, or fighting your way to the next checkpoint just in case that one annoying enemy takes away your last few hit points. Machinarium is a hallmark of this old-fashioned game style. In a time when few studios focus on this type of game, it is amazing to see an indie game with this level of artistic development. Every screen is unbelievably beautiful and breathtaking. The simple, hand-drawn characters have depth and personality that even the greatest mo-capped, celebrity-voiced charicatures cannot match. The puzzles are just right: not too easy, not too hard. Most of the time, the solution will come to you and you will think, "Why did I not think of that before?" THAT is what makes a great point-and-click adventure, and Machinarium is definitely a great game.

Phenomenal game, no other way to say it.
Game play is amazing, while I know this is a controversial one (first x-com game with the option of real time ground combat, and real time air combat), I'd say this is easily the best x-com game.
I mean, look at it, we're talking 1997, a solid 20 years ago, and all of the environments are *FULLY* destructible.   Base building was entirely modular, and when your base was attacked, the map was your actual base, exactly as setup, with your exact staff, combatants and non-combatants and all, fully destructible as you went.  What other game boasts this?
The level of detail involved in all aspects of game play is something that I've never seen before this game, or after it really.  I wish more games were crafted to this sort of template, it's easy to imagine how awesome this would be, if brought to current standards, something every developer is *still* struggling to produce.
If you've never played Xcom-Apoc, do yourself a favor and give it a go.  The graphics aren't bad for a 20 year old game, stability issues will obviously exist (you're running on gear 20 years newer than the game, can't reasonably expect otherwise), etc.  I'd say this was a genre defining game, but sadly it was not (or we'd see more of these elements about).

Operation Raccoon City is a game that was developed by the 3rd party developed Slant Six Games, and naturally like any IP that you lend to other people it becomes an aborted child.
So let's start with what you see on the store page, you see a 3rd person shooter with more action elements than RE5 such as diving, character abilities, an easy melee combat, and loads of DLC... say these things sound pretty familiar. It's almost like this game inspired RE6's action aspect oh wait.
Moving on, Operation Raccoon City's gameplay is a standard cover shooter with about one survival aspect, for starters it's really easy to burn through ammo, but that's ♥♥♥♥ing nothing. If you get hit by certain attacks by infected enemies you will become infected yourself, there are antidotes and an antidote ability which will cure the infection, and the punishment for failing to cure a player is that the player will turn into a highly aggressive zombie, infected players are also vulnerable to friendly fire so if you know you're ♥♥♥♥ed and dont want to burden you team, ask them to put you out of your misery. I don't remember if it's pure death or just getting put into a downed state though, it's still pretty crippling to be down a player.
Next is the characters, you play as Umbrella Corp's Security Service, highly skilled guns who have been tasked with two objectives, obtain the G-Virus, and eliminate any and all witnesses, and evidence of Umbrella's involvement. There are 6 characters who play unique roles, there cannot be duplicate characters so if someone takes your character you better have levels in another character, otherwise you're going to have a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.
Lupo the Assault she is a damage dealer, not much to it.
Vector the badass on the cover art is a stealth/recon character with his optic camoflauge clothes he can hide as anything.
Bertha the medic, you're going to need one of these in your games because she's got the cure for infection as well as buffs for other players.
Spectre the minimap detector, no seriously his entire reason to be there is to give you minimap blips for everything.
Four Eyes the Virologist, she can manipulate the battlefield with the T-Virus by infecting human enemies turning them into zombies or controlling other infected enemies.
Last is Beltway the demolitions expert, capable of setting up traps and disarming enemy traps, don't underestimate him.
What's wrong with the game? If I can remember correctly: Bosses are a slogfest, Leon is literally invincible at the finale, they didn't cover brutal takedowns aka instant kills in the melee tutorial, GFWL and nothing was done about it, plenty of games haven't had anything done about GFWL, and now the fact that they have the audacity to charge you for a 2nd campaign TWICE.
One of these days I'll end up replaying this game just to remember how utterly disappointed I was in the final product.

From my prespective, still the best game of The Elder Scroll series, might unfortunately remain so, and maybe the best RPG single person sand box exploration title ever published.
I love the immersiveness and complexity of the gameworld, background lore and especially the underlying race / faction / personality reaction adjustments. The race selection is actually more than just a cosmetic choice especially in the beginning when your fame is low, with dominant Imperials having the easiest start and the enslaved beastie-races having the hardest get-go.
I've actually gotten attached to the Imperials because that was first CHAR I ever created in Morrowind to give myself just that slight edge with the learning curve I expected to be pretty steep, which it was. I just kept on exploring and stubbornly figuring ways to get around my initial limitations, and am ever since faithfully enamoured.
One such trick I particularly vividly recall was using Scroll of Icarian Flight - acrobatics +1000 if memory serves - when at some point I got a bit stuck not having yet figured out that "Levitate" is really a must! Or trying to frantically remember what I did with my sucky imperial armour, because I could not get my next assignment without knowing "where was my uniform."
Also, the different regions feel distinct, as well as the most important factions actually have a network of outposts in the contient, requiring more than doing a few odd tasks to raise through the ranks.
I personally strongly prefer the major/minor skills and attributes character build up: pimping up your character if you choose to is surely part of the TES legend!
Graphically Morrowind vanilla version is obviously somewhat dated, but that has never personally bothered me.
Would rate the main questline above both Oblivion and Skyrim perso. The soundtrack is "typical superb TES" as well, composed by good ol' Jeremy Soule.

Deep, rewarding, and flawed - just how I like my games.
Flawed, ey? Yeah, well, I don't mean the game-breaking type, no, this game is pure bliss most of the time. I mean the kind with that lovable janky intriguing personality you just can't stay away from. There's a certain charm about this game I really can't put my finger on. It's part of the overall package, I guess. The atmosphere, writing, environmental design, and attention to detail is mighty impressive. Among the best I've ever seen, to be frank.
The only real faltering point is the combat, but let's not pretend it's a make-or-break part of the overall experience. You do engage in it, quite a lot. And it's clunky and old school, indeed. That sure is a matter of getting used to. Nothing I persoanlly had any trouble with, but I know some will.
But, the other ~82% of the game are at times damn flawless - combat is just one of the many ways of exploring this game. I have a hard time coming up with another world I like to indulge in as much as Morrowind's.
Morrowind stands the test of time - without a doubt. What it does good has nothing to do with technical prowess (although the skybox is still among the best I've ever seen to this day - fancy that).
This game is easily one of my favorites of all time, and I whole-heartedly recommend it to anyone interested in RPGs, the TES series, or just the exploration of a well-crafted, and well-written setting and world.
So, go play it!

Resident Evil is the originator of the survival horror genre, and kickstarted the successful commercial franchise that it is today. Survival horror is a unique take on the 3rd person action adventure genre which was common to the fifth and sixth generations of games, combining the inventory puzzle adventure game mechanics of 90's point and click games with resource management combat and some 3D action adventure puzzling as well. Puzzle is the keyword, as Resident Evil is less a zombie apocalypse combat simulator than it is a giant puzzle box, the combat figuring into that as well. Since keys and puzzle items are stored in the same limited inventory as weapons, ammo and health supplies, a conflict is presented in balancing progression items with tools necessary to survival in your inventory, as well as leaving space in said inventory for future items that may be encountered. Combat is less a skill and reflex based challenge but a tactical decision of whether to spend supplies on the enemies encountered.
The Resident Evil remake graphically retouches the original, while also adding and changing environments and scenarios and adding new mechanics as well. What is notable about this remake is that other than some graphical and mechanical additions the core gameplay from the original game is left untouched. This is truly a remaking of the original game, rather than a reimagining. So in essence you have a 90's ps1 game with a modernized presentation. For those who expect modern 'features' in the games they play they may find this game antiquated or lacking. Conversely, one could argue that Resident Evil has features of its own which many modern games lack. In an age of increasingly homogenized 3rd person action games, the prerendered action-adventure brings qualities of its own to the table which makes the genre unique to this day.
To start with, Resident Evil is not so much a 3rd person game as it is a 2nd person game. A 3rd person game grants a somewhat distant view of your character while giving you agency over their actions and omniscience over the character's surroundings. This omniscience of the character's surroundings in some ways means that 3rd person grants even more agency to the player than first person does. Resident Evil is not about absolute agency however. This is where the game benefits from it's 2nd person perspective, which some games such as Super Mario 64 have used to cleverly characterize the camera, but Resident Evil uses to make the player a passive agent to the game world. Not passive in the sense that the player is not the driving force of the game, but that their autonomy over the game world itself is limited. In Resident Evil the player's autonomy over their vision is limited, they themselves are a far off viewer of the events which unfold over the player character. This static camera has the ability to make the player feel like an audience and helpless to determine what lurks in the surroundings, and to give the player a sense of being watched, as intrusive and lurking camera angles give the player a sense of being spied upon by some unknown.
The movement and control functions are built around this static view point, which some may call limiting. However, the game is not crippled by these functions since the mechanics of the game itself are built around them. Combat, as mentioned earlier, is designed to be a cost benefit analysis for the player, not a real-time trading of blows. Resident Evil is a slow methodical game built around problem solving and risk assessment. The ink ribbons are an insurance against gaming this system, forcing the player to calculate the risk of saving frequently after ideal turn-outs versus the risk of waiting longer to save data in the future. The static camera angles also mean that the developer is free to put a greater amount of detail into the level environments, enhancing the adventure game aspect by creating a more dense environment to investigate and problem solve within.
Aesthetically, having static camera angles with prerendered environments means that every single room, setting and 'shot' can have an engaging and distinct look, something which is almost impossible to pull off in a traditional 2D or 3D game since even the most visually impressive 2D/3D games must reuse tiles, color palletes or textures. Having been remastered in HD, Resident Evil shows how effective this technique is in creating an engaging and memorable setting, with every room and 'shot' a unique vista. The black magic of prerendered environments means that the game feels like it belongs to 10 years ahead of its actual origin.
Resident Evil, and the pre-rendered action adventure genre in general, fulfills a niche for video game experiences which the current industry ignores. Despite this genre being 20 years old(Happy Anniversary!) there has yet to be any other genre or design formula which provides the same experience which these games provide. Ironically despite being old in its origin it would be a very fresh and original game type to make in this current industry. Capcom has the opportunity to give this genre new life with the Resident Evil 2 remake, but it's uncertain how Capcom in its current state will proceed with that game, so it's a very real possibility that the Resident Evil remake of 2002 and its sister prequel Resident Evil 0 are the last that we will ever see of this genre. Either way, I would recommend Resident Evil to anyone interested in the unique alchemy of genres that is survival horror. Resident Evil is not only a substantial interactive experience, but possibly the swan song to a generation of games. Some could argue that the reason this genre died in the first place is because of how antiquated and inconvenient the genre was compared to newer game design philosophies. But then, maybe the point of a video game isn't always to be as convenient and unimposing as possible, but to provide challenging and engaging interactions. The success of retro-hard 2D indie games and the Dark Souls franchise certainly shows that there might be a market for "old-school" design philosophies. Maybe Capcom will show how daring they really are and making a prerendered action-adventure out of the RE2 remake, as opposed to a first person jump scare simulator, because nobody has ever thought of that before.
Addendum: I highly recommend playing this game with the classic control scheme as opposed to the 'modern' one. All of the combat in this game is built around the classic control scheme which is completely broken with things like frame cancelling never being an intended part of the gameplay. You also miss out on the setting since the prerendered scenes were never meant to be  sprinted by on a first playthrough and you miss out on the atmosphere which is organically presented through the camera angles. If you want to play with the modern control scheme you don't actually want to play Resident Evil, you're looking for Resident Evil 4.

It's a cross between an adventure game and a metroidvania, but more the former than the latter. There's slight platforming and a bit more simple shooting, but for most of the game you're solving puzzles. Overall it works really well, particularly because of the thick atmosphere and interesting plot. It might look like Limbo when you start it up, but it doesn't do the artsy-fartsy gimmick like it. This is a solid adventure game with a plot that hooks you in, especially if you're a SF fan. Won't say much else because that would be spoiler territory.
The only thing you might struggle with are the controls. You move with the keyboard in typical platformer fashion, but you hold the right click on the mouse to aim your flashlight and see what you can interact with (as nodes in many other p'n'c games) and then press and hold shift and the movement keys to interact with objects and use the inventory. Additionally, you can switch from the flaslight into a lasersight for shooting with F, but of course you can't interact with the lasersight on. It can be frustrating at times. Also, some objects you can interact with are either small enough to miss or blending in the dark backgrounds. There's around 2 or 3 of those that could have been better highlighted.
The positives outweigh the negatives, and I highly recommend it!

Let's not mince words here: this game did not age well at all. I bought this game as part of the X-COM: Complete Pack after hearing a lot of good things about the old school X-COM games. I decided to start with this game since I had spoiled myself to the first two games and I wanted to actually be surprised of what was going on throughout the game. So I started a new game and it took me to a city and a dialogue that said "Welcome to X-COM Apocalypse" and then I was left with the game with nothing else to go on. The User Interface itself is so confusing that it made the game almost unplayable as I had no idea what was going on and had to figure everything out on the fly.
It was only later that I learned that I needed to read the manual to understand what was going on in the game. Thankfully, this was accessible through Steam but a digital copy of the manual would not do you much good when you're playing the game. This means that you would have to print out the manual. However, if you're like me and like to play a game with only a keyboard/controller at hand while facing a screen/monitor this is going to be a problem. Having a manual in your hand in case you need to understand some part of the game will only impede your enjoyment of the game.
I understand that this game is over 20 years old and I may be a bit harsh in this review. In fact, I am willing to admit that this game is probably good for its time. However, judging by how present day gamers would find this game, I would say that they would have a hard time enjoying this game. I myself could not play this game for too long and I admit that the old 1990s graphics played a part in this. While graphics in a video game is far from being of paramount importance to me, when I had no idea what I was doing and the user interface is downright confusing, I am not very inclined to continue playing a game with 1990s level of graphics.

Machinarium is a Flash based point and click adventure game that is unique in its execution.  Each area has readily accessable hint and a full walkthrough of the area at the cost of playing a somewhat tedious mini-game to keep you from looking at it unless you're really stuck.  The robot you control can be stretched shorter or taller with a mouse drag which gives you the ability to reach areas you couldn't without it and adds complexity to many of the game's puzzles.  Most of the puzzles are pretty simple and produce, at most, a moderate challenge.
The real appeal of this game though is its art.  Almost everything is made of metal and the way it's drawn and painted gives the abstract looking structures a touch of realism that shows each ones age through how rusted or weathered it looks.  The ambient music helps to set the darkish tone of the game with mechanical and lo-fi sounds. While I'm on the topic of tone despite the dark atmosphere, the character you play as, and many of the ones you meet, are quite peppy and charming which gives an interesting contrast that made me feel as if the robots were living it a different paradigm.
It might just be nostalgia, but I miss adventure games, and I really feel the medium still holds up today; at least on PC's.

First thing to take on board; this game isn't COMPLETELY historical.
Some of you might be wondering why Bomber Command aircraft are being used for Air/Sea Rescue and ASW. Some may be wondering why the Germans are launching V1s in 1942. Some may be wondering why the Lancaster doesn't have a four gun tail turret as standard, or why none of the missions seem to be Gardening (minelaying) despite the fact this was a common Bomber Command task. Most of you should be wondering what a purpose designed NIGHT BOMBER is doing flying solo daylight raids.
You are thinking too hard :)
Second thing is that this game is not that easy. There is no pause. Some of the mechanics take finding out the hard way (First aid kits are ONE USE?!? But I have two critically wounded crew and... oh... fine... sigh... Hello new recruit.) The game is frantic. The game is ruthless. The game is quite willing to kill your entire crew.
On the other hand when you get it to work it is incredibly satisfying. Returning to base and realising you have unlocked some better equipment for your aircraft or crew gives you just that small hope your next mission will be easier. It is, in painful sort of way, a lot of fun.
Thumbs up. Well worth the price.
On a side note it is interesting to note the game includes Operation Chariot as a critical mission, and one assumes the deeper you get into the campaign the more 'historical' events you will come across. Historically Bomber Command were not tasked with ASW or suppression of coastal batteries, but with flying a distraction raid over the port a few hours before the naval forces were due. Unfortunately for the raiders the orders were to linger over the target and drop single bombs for an extended period. Being very different behaviour for RAF night bombers over a target the suspicious German commander kept his troops on full alert, resulting in all guns being fully manned when the commandos arrived. While the larger HMS Cambelltown managed to muscle through the German fire and successfully ram the lock gates as planned, most of the smaller motor launchers carrying commandos suffered heavily.

I know what you may be thinking: "but Bill, you've only put in a little bit of time into this game, how could you really weigh in on whether it's good or not?"
Hear me out.
The combat is left clicks. That's it. That's the combat. Left click, left click, left click, left click, left click. There, you just slayed the beast.
The story is great, go watch a summarization on Youtube. Even they will say "since the game is bad, I did this so that you don't have to play it like I did".
The questing system is awful. The maps are always slightly off, whether it be objective markers or invisible walls. It's really (REALLY) frustrating to have no earthly clue where you have to go. The majority of side quests I did manage to finish, I literally had to guess where I had to go. Before you ask, "well why didn't you just ask the NPC to remind you of where you had to go?" Well, for 2 reasons: 1) They won't tell you. 2) If you accidently say something they don't want to hear, it won't matter anyway (which I'm about to go into further detail about, so strap in).
The NPC's are probably the worst part. Many quests require you to talk to people to acquire information, but the game has dialogue options that will make the NPC ignore you PERMANANTLY. Meaning you can go through hell to do something for someone, but then you can't finish it because you accidently said something rude. I could possibly forgive this if there were some way to know when it's going to happen, but they just drop it on you at random times, and sometimes during/after inescapable cutscenes that you can't save beforehand to prevent messing up. This was a huge oversight, and a huge letdown.
Another irritating thing is the illusion of choice, a pet peeve of mine. "Pick a side" constantly happening and never actually changing a damn thing. Why even include it to begin with?
All of this, and I'm not even going into detail of the awful camera, the awful controls, the awful alchemy system, the awful inventory system, the awful leveling system, the awful trading system, and the fact that every single NPC in the game (except for about 15 of the important ones) are the same exact character models as all the others. So you end up meeting the same exact person hundreds of times. Really breaks the immersion, since even games like Baldurs Gate and Neverwinter Nights (both games that came out years before this one) didn't drop the ball on that.
To end my review, let me just say that this game was so frustratingly bad that I felt obligated to write my first steam review EVER. I'm off to play the 2nd title now, knowing that it couldn't possibly be worse. I'd say, in fact, that 2 and 3 are a million times better. But a million times 0 is still 0, so I won't.
Save your money.

While I don't have many hours in this game, I have something to say.
I enjoy the game -
The graphics aren't the best, but they certainly aren't bad. The weapons feel like they have power behind them, and I have no problems with the sound.The grind, while... 'modest' is tolerable, as long as you play this game for fun and not just to get the next unlock.
As an example, within 27 hours I have eached rank 5 on one of my soldiers, and am close to reaching rank 5 on another. Rank 5 is important because once you reach it, all of your characters from that point on will enter tier 2 battles. At tier 2 you play against better players and are able to enter the war, where you earn extra experience and credits compared to staged battles.
In these 27 hours I have also gotten close to a MP40 and Thompson - Which are some of the best SMGs in the game, so don't worry about the grind too much, ok? Just make sure to hold off on weapon modifications and grenade spamming until your a higher rank, those things cost a lot of credits to maintain.
Now that I've talked about that, I have to move onto a major... 'problem' I have with this game - The community.
The community is extremely toxic. If you don't have at least 200 hours in this game, anything you say will be ignored. Try to add something to a discussion and you will be spat upon and called a 'Noob' (Or things I can't mention here) by 'Superior' players.
I`ll say this - Just because one has 200 hours in a game, doesn't mean they are any good at, nor does that mean they are knowledgable about the game. Anyway, I digress - I`ll say this for any of you thinking to try this game, NEVER in my entire online career have I EVER wanted to quit a game because of the community. Not even League of Legends was so bad.
That's all I have to say about that - For those of you who didn't read it, here you go.
TLDR:
Pros:
-Graphics aren't great, but they are good.
-Weapons feel good, they feel like they have power behind them.
-The sounds are good
-The game has a somewhat large playerbase, so you`ll get into games quickly
Cons:
-The community
Neutral:

Alright, here it comes. After so many years, I got to play this masterpiece again.
To begin with, I had only played the PS1 version and not the gamecube one, so this game brought many new puzzles for me to solve. Everything is so much better, and I am really glad that CAPCOM decided to hear us fans and start remastering RE games of our childhood.
I bought it on PC some days ago, and decided to write a review after I finish it at least once. The replayability value is amazing, as it was back in the PS1 days. Not only did it feel satisfying to properly finish this game, it made me want to play again, and again. Everyime, it brings the horror atmosphere I like seeing in games.
Yet, this 20 year old game scares me over 9000% more than these new sci-fi and whatnot games that have been released the last 6 years.

Resident Evil strikes a great balance between puzzling and combat. The puzzles are well-presented and feel like an integral part of the world while also not being overly cryptic, and the combat is hectic and satisfying as all hell. You're constantly low on ammo and if you're not careful, every enemy can kill you. A big part of the gameplay is inventory management, as it severely limits the amount of weapons and ammo you're able to carry, that way every enemy feels significant and every bullet is costly.
While the story and voice-acting are somewhat cliché and campy, they're still well done and presented in an interesting manner. Aside from puzzling and fighting zombies, you also find documents that hint at past occurings in and around the manor. Environments are beautifully designed, visual effects and character models look pretty good on 1080p and everything runs at a buttery smooth 60fps. There are some grainy environments here and there, but that I can forgive easily since everything else is just really well done. Considering that this is a remaster of a game that's well over a decade old, they've done a really great job.
For achievement hunters there's a commendable variety of achievements that force radically different playstyles. I usually don't care too much about achievements, but I still enjoy it when they're done well. I have a hard time finding flaws with this game and can definitely recommend this to anyone as it has made me a fan already. My tip for new players though: Keep a pen and some paper nearby, that way you won't get lost quite as much.

From my prespective, still the best game of The Elder Scroll series, might unfortunately remain so, and maybe the best RPG single person sand box exploration title ever published.
I love the immersiveness and complexity of the gameworld, background lore and especially the underlying race / faction / personality reaction adjustments. The race selection is actually more than just a cosmetic choice especially in the beginning when your fame is low, with dominant Imperials having the easiest start and the enslaved beastie-races having the hardest get-go.
I've actually gotten attached to the Imperials because that was first CHAR I ever created in Morrowind to give myself just that slight edge with the learning curve I expected to be pretty steep, which it was. I just kept on exploring and stubbornly figuring ways to get around my initial limitations, and am ever since faithfully enamoured.
One such trick I particularly vividly recall was using Scroll of Icarian Flight - acrobatics +1000 if memory serves - when at some point I got a bit stuck not having yet figured out that "Levitate" is really a must! Or trying to frantically remember what I did with my sucky imperial armour, because I could not get my next assignment without knowing "where was my uniform."
Also, the different regions feel distinct, as well as the most important factions actually have a network of outposts in the contient, requiring more than doing a few odd tasks to raise through the ranks.
I personally strongly prefer the major/minor skills and attributes character build up: pimping up your character if you choose to is surely part of the TES legend!
Graphically Morrowind vanilla version is obviously somewhat dated, but that has never personally bothered me.
Would rate the main questline above both Oblivion and Skyrim perso. The soundtrack is "typical superb TES" as well, composed by good ol' Jeremy Soule.

Deep, rewarding, and flawed - just how I like my games.
Flawed, ey? Yeah, well, I don't mean the game-breaking type, no, this game is pure bliss most of the time. I mean the kind with that lovable janky intriguing personality you just can't stay away from. There's a certain charm about this game I really can't put my finger on. It's part of the overall package, I guess. The atmosphere, writing, environmental design, and attention to detail is mighty impressive. Among the best I've ever seen, to be frank.
The only real faltering point is the combat, but let's not pretend it's a make-or-break part of the overall experience. You do engage in it, quite a lot. And it's clunky and old school, indeed. That sure is a matter of getting used to. Nothing I persoanlly had any trouble with, but I know some will.
But, the other ~82% of the game are at times damn flawless - combat is just one of the many ways of exploring this game. I have a hard time coming up with another world I like to indulge in as much as Morrowind's.
Morrowind stands the test of time - without a doubt. What it does good has nothing to do with technical prowess (although the skybox is still among the best I've ever seen to this day - fancy that).
This game is easily one of my favorites of all time, and I whole-heartedly recommend it to anyone interested in RPGs, the TES series, or just the exploration of a well-crafted, and well-written setting and world.
So, go play it!

For the record, I've completed the entire campaign without losing a single crewman. And I can safely say, Bomber Crew as a game is amazingly good at it's current price.
The gameplay is fairly unique in my opinion, many will compare it to FTL, but the removal of the tactical pause, changes the way the game is played entirely. FTL is about perfection, pausing, queuing up orders, unpausing and watching them play out. Bomber Crew is chaotic and hectic, orders have to be given out as bullets whizz pass, courses plotted as you struggle to repair enough to stay in the air.  I wholly reccomend you try it.
However, there are a few minor issues I'd like to mention in no particular order;
- Tutorials, or rather the lack of adequate guidance, there was nothing beyond a text guide hidden in the Esc Pause Menu that would explain some very important mechanics such as altitude. This is a minor spoiler, but Altitude, temperature and Oxygen played a particularly large role in my Campaign, to survive night missions, you had to be at the highest altitude to make use of the Navigator's ability to guide via stars. Low Altitude and all the dangers that lurk there was certain death. And yet, it was never mentioned in the tutorial missions.
- The grind, oh gods the grind was long and hard. By the end of the game, you quite literally need the best equipment to complete missions due to the foes you face. Money was no concern I had well over 300k of in-game currency laying around, what gated my progress was "research" it is given out in pitiful amounts at the start and the optional objectives reward the same amount no matter what part of the campaign you're at, it was hardly worth the additional risks towards the end.
- Balance, I can't quite say the game was unfair, but certain enemies gave me immense fustration. Again, spoiler, the Me 163 and 262 almost seem impossible to hit in flight with the best turrets available in game, the .50x4 Mk4, I'm almost certain the bulk of my kills of the 262 came from when it was lining up to use it's rocket barrage. The rate they spawn in might need some tweaking as well, I regularly found myself overwhelmed by them even with the Spitfire Ability active.
That said, the game is still very fun, especially once you get the hang of it.

I've had a lot of fun with this game, and think it is a great deal for the price.
Pros:
+ A fun twist on the juggle-management genre (definitely has an overcooked-style vibe imo)
+ A very good "Just one more time" game.
+Fun Aesthetics: Just look at the screenshots.
+Cutsomizing your plane: Balance different upgrades and choose or make your own decals/paint schemes.
+ Very simplified: The game is pretty easy to understand, information is delivered pretty well visually.
Cons (a lot of expanded text, but only 3 listed):
-UI: It's not terrible, but it can be a little clunky which can be annoying when you have fighters buzzing all around you with half of your plane onfire.  More assignable hotkeys and getting rid of some of the micro would be nice (have a person auto-grab a fire extinguisher if i tell them to fight a fire).
-Repetitive: I don't have a problem with duplicate mission types, but the missions will not deviate one bit.  A mission where you bomb a target/targets will ALWAYS put them in the same place.  It would be nice if they put targets in different areas while mixing up the missions a bit (throwing in last minute objectives, randomizing gun emplacements/intercepts along your path, etc etc.)  It would give a better feel of not knowing what is over the horizon and make the player wonder if they are a bit over their head this time.
-Missing information: Even though it does a great job conveying information, it does leave out some things that you will probably eventually pick up along the way by process of elimination or guessing.  Example: I had no idea that the parachute item was a parachute until I told my crew to bail-out, and only one person picked up the parachute...since I only had one parachute aboard.  I also had no idea what some icons meant for the longest time since it never explained them to me.
Overall, I think it is a great game and the negatives really aren't that big.  Just understand that the game has fairly fast rounds, upgrading between them, and a lot of repeating.  It's grinding for more experienced crewmembers and better equipment, but it's a game where I enjoy the grind and find it to actually be fun which a lot of games fail to do.  I've also read a lot of complaints about a lack of a tactical-pause feature (FTL) but I haven't had too many problems with managing it since I got down the routine of the game/how to minimize risks, more capable crewmembers, etc etc...but I haven't gotten towards the end of the game yet, so maybe the need for one becomes more apparent later on; it probably wouldn't hurt to just throw one in the options to enable/disable the feature.
If you are looking for a more casual management game (easy to learn) but one that can still get hectic, intense, and challenging, then this game is a pretty good choice.  I highly recommend it and have loved playing every second of it.

As a Double Dragon fan I have mixed emotions about writing this unfavourable review; I love the arcade game but don’t care much for this port.
I'd also like to point out that I got this game in the Steam sale so I didn't pay full price of it, and I'm glad I didn't, here's why:
I've been  a hugeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee Double Dragon fan ever since I was a kid, I spent many an hour down my local arcade pumping serious coinage into my fav game. (Despite being able to beat it using one credit using the infamous elbow cheat, that’s because the wall section on the last level didn’t work for some reason lol).
I purchased this game on different formats over the years; Commodore 64, Sega Megadrive (Genesis) - now whilst I enjoyed these versions they weren't exactly 'arcade perfect'.
I missed out on the opportunity to buy it on the Xbox 360 arcade, shame really as that looked like a good port. (I won’t cover MAME emulation for legality).
When I seen this on Steam my eyes literally lighted up, filled with tears of nostalgia. With it being on sale too it was a no brain-er!
Blinded by my love for the game and ignoring the negative reviews I decided it buy it, a decision I immediately regretted – what is wrong with the audio?!
The graphics and presentation are fine, gives you a few options to tinker with them which I like. Though the new health bars look ‘ok’, why wasn’t there an option to include the originals? The intro music as you start the game from the car garage is wrong (It uses the last level final boss music instead!). In other parts of the game it is also missing sound effects and music, for example the 2nd boss who comes up to fight you from an elevator.
These could be perceived as small things to the average gamer, but on a game like Double Dragon with it’s loyal fan base these are big issues. I really did mar the enjoyment for me and subsequently I haven’t played it again (I haven’t bothered playing the other 2 games in the trilogy – the 2nd Game in the arcades was a bit meh, but still had some charm. I don’t even consider the 3rd instalment a DD game if I’m being honest).
To summarise:
If it was arcade perfect with a few extras throw in it would easily be worth the money (I’d even pay ‘double’ – pardon the pun), but this is but a pipe dream. If you’re the normal gamer and can get this cheap in the sale it ‘might’ be worth considering. True Double Dragon fans and anyone thinking it purchasing it full price then I personally wouldn’t bother.

I love the Samarost-y style of adventure game. There's a screen, there's stuff you have to do on the screen, and then you move on to the next screen when everything's done. And the art, oh the art. I love the style. In most cases the sounds are great, too, and in Machinarium's case, the soundtrack is super-good. But I don't much care for pixel hunts. While Samarost's got some, the puzzles are simple enough that the hunting becomes part of the fun. Machinarium's puzzles are much more involved than Samarost's, and the pixel hunting and trial and error of testing different combinations of actions to see what happens is more like a chore to me. I've gotten to be kind of a wimp when it comes to adventures, in that I'm more interested in moving the story along than clicking and waiting and clicking and waiting. Give me a long story with simple puzzles and I'm happy. Don't get me wrong, Machinarium is a very good game, but I'm not feeling enough reward quickly enough to finish it, and that's very much my difficulty level preference talking. Yes, I know there's a walkthrough available inside the game, but it's cleverly set up to take some time to get to the walkthrough for each area, and then there's still some trial and error. If you like some tough logic puzzles and the art style, Machinarium is a must-get. If you don't care for pixel hunting and trial-and-error in your adventures, you may want to pass. I'm happy enough with the game for its look and sound that I might keep it installed for a while to plink away at it.

The Resident Evil HD Remaster is great, however the quality of the port makes it unplayable.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Though meeting the reccomended specs, FPS tanks are common in random areas despite settings on lowest. It appears animations are tied to frame rate therefore when the FPS tanks the game enters slow motion mode and it's unplayable. This leaves audio out of sync if FPS drops during cutscenes.
In the community it's reccomended to download an unofficial patch called the resolution lag fix v2. I tried this and it seemed to be working well, but I encountered FPS drops again soon afterwards despite all settings off or low. I'm not sure how this is even possible as the game environments use pre-rendered scenes, so very little resources should be spent on the rest.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Despite these issues, the game itself is an excellent remaster that stays true to Resident Evil. It is with a heavy heart  that I say I had to refund it.

For hardcore RE fan the game will be good or very good (or awesome with the right people). For others it will just be an average shooter with some RPG elements (unlocking character skills and weapons). Versus multiplayer mode are something new and if you are bored of all the other games of the genre, you will spend few hours here and won't regret it. Game is not ground breaking, graphics are rather bad (for PCs it's like 5 years ago, consoles sux heh) and maps design are average. I wish there was a meduim for reviews, or a get it on sale box for recommendations, but there isnt, so i will just give the game a no, with one VERY BIG DISCLAMER: Get it on sale. simple as that.
My reasons for not reccomending it UNLESS ON SALE is that while the game is very good as a story game, as a puzzler, and its very atmospheric, the story did indeed impress me, however, i had many problems through out the game. For one, the combat. Its horrible. The cover system, atleast for me, was useless. While in low cover, you cannot aim low enough to hit targets who are also in low cover, this combined with bugs such as when you come out of cloak and try to draw your fire arm, it doesnt actually draw the fire arm, instead you shoot the floor a few times, realizing this bug is happening AGAIN, and either die or cloak again, wait, decloak, bug out, try it again and go through the animation so it works, get shot 5 times, kill the enemy. unless they dont die, in which case the process repeats. The controlls feel very off, as when you try to stop, you actually take a few more steps than you should have, almost like theres a lag between you stopping and the character stopping. In general all, and i mean ALL of the controls feel off, however that may just be me for all i know. next up, again, might just be me, but the game is LOADED, and i mean ABSOLUTLY. LOADED. With bugs. Bugs and poor design choices. For one, during one puzzle, i was stuck between a wooden board and a set of stairs, attemping to draw my gun caused it to just sit in the holster and shoot the ground. Or where while i was on low health a elevator put me in the line of fire of 2 tougher enemys and a melee instant-kill enemy with very little time to do anything, as the instant kill enemy would reach me before i could kill it if i cloaked and shot at the enemys, but the enemys with guns would kill me if i didnt cloak, in which case i died, restarted with more health, thankfully, and managed to finish it the next time. The game is very short, unfortunatly not short enough to get a return but it was only 99 cents anyway, tbh, if you dont have all the problems i had, or if you quickly solve the puzzles, you could probably do it in under 2 hours. IT IS NOT WORTH $10 THOUGH. At most, this game is worth 99 cents, maybe $1.50, unless it comes with the sequal for free and a bunch of patches that fix the entirety of this game, then 10 dollars is fine. However, a part 2 is doubful, 2 years down the line, so, who knows.
