Double Dragon WAS my 1988.
I spent a lot of that year in arcades (back when they were operated with 10p coins) and played a LOT of button mashers and coin gobblers of the era. Double Dragon got most of my money and was the first side-scrolling beat-em-up I never played. The anime aesthetic and pumping soundtrack made it stand-out from the competition and the game went on to be a classic (thanks to many dodgy home console ports) with fans.
This collection of the first three games might ruin the nostalgia for you. The legacy is not as spotless as you remember.
Double Dragon (1987) 4/5
As Billy and/or Jimmy Lee you battle through a post-apocalyptic city (with wildly different environments hilariously segueing into each other) to rescue your shared girlfriend Marion from gang (bang?) boss Big Willy. The usual hand and foot combos are aided by bats, barrels, whips, knives, and boulders. The game is fun until you reach the last stage and are actually murdered by the lancing statues and smashing stone beams.
Double Dragon II (1988) 3/5
I first came across this one in an arcade in the Florida Mall in summer 1989, six months after it debuted. I was beyond excited to see it but I didn't get very far, not only because I wasn't very good at video games back then but because the game is sadistically hard. As with the first you can just elbow smash your way through the entire game and this is actually recommended since if you attempt to punch and kick the enemy everything you do will be in vain as they lay waste to you non-stop. Collision detection is very poor and the level design is virtually a carbon copy of the first game. Still cannot finish it, even on easy mode.
Double Dragon 3: The Rosetta Stone (1990) 1/5
An absolute abomination of a game and one of the most miserable gaming experiences I have ever had. If you thought that the  Mega Drive port was bad try playing the arcade original. It's utterly appalling and irreparably broken. Enter this game at your despair, I mean it!
Sadly, this collection is a bust. It improves on the arcade in regards to the increased RAM, so there's no slow down when lots of characters are on screen but the controls are terrible with serious lag and sensitivity issues. You'll accidentally commit suicide many, many times and I once wasted six lives, count 'em...SIX, trying to get across that broken bridge in the first game. If you don't want to hurl your controller at the TV screen then I'd avoid it. The collection advertises the original soundtrack or a "brand new, remastered one" but it's not brand new. For the original game they've worked in the arranged soundtrack from the 1988 Japanese CD single, for Double Dragon II they've used tracks from the long out-of-print soundtrack CD but without the awesome "Dead or Alive" vocal track, and for Double Dragon 3 tracks from the old arranged CD are used. None of this music, or the remix of the theme tune on the title screen, have been made available for download, which is a shame since the CDs go for huge prices and a digital soundtrack release could have kept them contemporary. However, considering how popular these tunes are I'd expect a vinyl soundtrack release sometime in the future.
There are 15 trophies/achievements with this Steam release (I only managed 10 as there is not a herd of wild horses on this Earth that can drag me back to Double Dragon 3) and 11 trading cards.

The graphics and music remix is a great mix to retro acrade triliogy of Double Dragon. However the main controls are delayed if they register at all. Single button clicks work fine but any combination combos like jump kicks or elbows you can forget about using.
If it wasn't for the poor controls these games would be perfect. In the current state, do not recommend buying.

First played a demo for this game. Way before its release. It was awesome, the music was awesome. The game looked and played awesome.
This is actually my favourite classical XCOM game. I like it for its liberating real-time option. Played it at first in a turn-based mode, but it is actually way more fun to play it in real time. There is a more genuine feel to it, where you don't cotrol your soldiers to the tiniest degree, i.e. when in combat they can move around based on the aggressiveness settings. Plus it often causes total armageddon on the map, especially when you get the piggy gun. The Devastator Cannon is really what it says. You can level whole buildings and not have to worry about finding the aliens. You can sort the rubble later. The company will be enraged, but this is fun.
Oh yeah, this game had planned a more detailed political gameplay on the city-scape. I am afraid that besides Transtellar being mad at you because you are destroying the roads during alien incursions and Cult of Sirius being generally hostile, there is nothing remaining from that aspect of the planned game. Too bad. Maybe openApoc will solve this problem.
Also, the ending of the game is weak. Once you start invading alien dimension (oops, spoiler), the aliens stop comming to the city and there is nothing for you to do then. Maybe except another raid on the Cult. This is another thing: you can raid anybody and keep on doing that for fun, but no matter how many raids you perform and how much in the negative the corporations balance is... this does nothing bad for it. They can still field soldiers, buy/sell weapons. Another thing for openApoc.
In all, the first 95% of the game is good/great. Rest is you needn't bother.

Resident Evil Remake Remastered is a survival horror game, created by Capcom and the director is the father of survival horror himself, Shinji Mikami (Creators of Resident Evil Zero - 4, The Evil Within and Vanquish). This game is a remastered or reworked, placing with high quality textures, volumetric lighting, shadows and other graphics fidelity related improvements (animation and the character details, more so). It's the same Resident Evil Remake from Gamecube. To be honest, I have never played the Gamecube version, I played the Playstation version and it's massive difference between Gamecube and Playstation version. Other than that, it is the same Gamecube version with better graphical changes. The gameplay is still the same old classic; item management, riddles to solve, exploration, heavy backtracking, fixed camera angles to create suspense at every corner and ammo conservative. The game is still scary, even I got jumped out of my seat when the dog came into the window (Oh, that classic jumpscare still got me XD). There are some technical issues, where the background music keeps cutting out for a second (it happens rarely, so it's not a big deal), the movement controls changed due to fix camera angle changes and the controls for PC are not recommended (I think you can change the controls if you can but aiming is annoying though). Other than that, it's a great survival horror game, I miss these kind of survival horror games. There are multiple endings to get an outcome based on your choice you have made.
For the final review, I definitely recommend this game if you are an old Resident Evil fan like myself (whether Playstation or Gamecube version). I am hoping there will be a survival horror game like this. The item management, riddles to solve, heavy backtracking, exploration, fix camera angles to create a suspense moments. I am hoping that the next Resident Evil game brings back to its roots. The issues are not game breaking or anything, it's just the movement controls are frustating. This game is 9 out of 10, a solid recommendation.

The gold standard for all Survival Horror games. It's just perfect in literally every way- it's controls are tight, gameplay fine tuned and polished to a mirror sheen, perfectly paced and constructed around the players thoughts and actions (and a few gags at the expense of the expectations of the original PS1 RE1 players) and back on the GC it looked absolutely beautiful, with excellent animations and beautiful, pre-rendered backgrounds.  It's a highly rewarding experience to play this game, as well, as it's one of the games where you can feel yourself getting better at it. An average playthrough will take 9 or so hours, but consequtive ones will only take about 5, and if you're really good, 3. It feels great to blast through the game like this, and the action, amazing atmosphere and fantastic game design still hold up to this day as not only the pinnacle of the entire Survival Horror genre, but also as a damn excellent game.
For $20, you get a lot of bang for your buck.
The only really bad thing is that the HD uprezzing on a lot of the background art looks pretty bad at times, especially on moving backgrounds with lights. Despite that, this is easily worth $20 or less, and it's a great game every survival horror fan should play.

This is probably my new favorite adventure game. It's beautiful, charming, funny, and very clever.

I also played this with no less than three non-gamers, and they all enjoyed getting into it as much as I did.
I have read many people complaining about the game's length, saying it took 6-8 hours on average while using the in-game guide for the tougher puzzles. I am a decent puzzle solver (not great), and it easily netted me 10 hours of gameplay time without using a guide at all. That having been said, knowing the solutions can make a speed run of an hour or two very easy.
Machinarium is innovative and brilliant, and I like it.

Personally, I started playing the series with Oblivion, but I still think Morrowind is superior to its successors in certain aspects, and I do not regret buying it one bit. The game has excellent role-playing mechanics, combat mechanics that allow for customization (light or heavy, depending on play style or class), and an interesting faction system and story that kept me going even through the not-so-fun parts of the game. So, on its own merits (not comparing to Oblivion or Skyrim), here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
27 different skills allow for a lot of variation in play style
Storyline is usually engaging, especially to someone who has never played an Elder Scrolls game
Almost every character has a name, and every character that talks to you has something to say
The world is vast and full of interesting Easter eggs and sidequests. You never really know when you might find someone in need of assistance on the road.
Every single character you come up against can be killed. (The game also warns you afterwards if that character was necessary to the main quest, then leaves it up to you whether to reload an old save or live with the consequences of your actions.)
The Journal keeps track of your conversations and quests in a way that makes it feel like you are an actual adventurer writing in your own adventures.
Tons of spells to keep you entertained, with effects from basic fire damage to full on levitation
Cons:
My Biggest Beef: Travel is Slow. Very slow. So slow that the game was borderline unplayable for me without an enchanted item (Boots of Blinding Speed) that drastically increases your speed. Running (or rather jogging) uses fatigue for a speed boost that is barely noticeable without a massive speed stat. What happens if your fatigue is low? You can't attack (at least effectively) and your magic is prone to failing. The game tries to make this more tolerable with travel between cities via silt striders and boats, but these features are inaccessible by the other characters in another aspect of the game...
Escort Missions Galore: Remember having to take care of Ashley in Resident Evil 4? Prepare to do that a lot. It seems every 3 faction quests is an escort mission at some point, and many of the side quests on the road involve escorting someone to another person or a town. This would be more bearable if the AI was smarter or faster. Even with a speed of 40, my character would often have to stop (while walking) for the escort character to catch up (while running). During one quest, I thought the game broke because one character didn't know what these newfangled "stairs" were.
Managing Magic: Morrowind does not have a magicka regeneration feature other than resting. Also, if you had the misfortune to pick the Atronach birthsign, better stock up on potions, because resting doesn't work, either. The biggest downside of having to rest to regain magicka is that you cannot rest while enemies are nearby. Makes sense, right? Only the game typically requires you to clear every enemy from an interior map before allowing you to rest. (Something difficult to do for a "true" mage.) Spells also have a chance to fail, depending on how high your skill, luck, willpower, and fatigue reserves are, as well as how much the spell costs to cast. If the spell fails, it causes you to lose magicka, anyway. (Some may like this; I do not.)
Finding Quest Objectives: The Journal is a bit of a double-edged sword. While it does keep track of tasks in an organic way, it also can get quite cumbersome. It's incredibly easy to reach 40 pages and have to search through everything if you don't know the name of a quest (the journal lets you find information within it relevant to the quest). Finding locations or items can also be difficult, as only major locations are marked on the map, and having to delve into a cave is rather hard to do when you can't find the cave. Sure, there are directions, but all too often, they are directions like: "Go east from [city]. Turn right at the next intersection towards [other city]. Make a right when you enter the mountains. then continue straight, taking a left, then a left, then a right at the intersections until you see swamps. [cave] will be on the left." The directions are sometimes worse, with vague landmarks. Mountains? Those look more like hills. Or maybe they're bluffs?
Massive Changes in Difficulty: The game loves difficulty spikes. You can go through an entire dungeon, kill everything in it with one hit, and then the last enemy for some reason has a massive pool of health, armor bestowed upon him by the great Daedra lords, and a spell that throws you across the room like a rag doll. Sometimes this extends to an entire questline, where everything seems easy until the last mission, where one guy kills you with two hits.
So if I recommend this game, why do I focus so much on the cons? That's because you should know what you're getting into. This game is great, overall. But minor annoyances can take away from the experience, and if I would have known it would be worth it to stick through those annoyances, I would have played Morrowind a lot more when I first got it, instead of now. If you expect to get anywhere fast, you're gonna have a bad time. If you expect your magicka to come back on its own, you're gonna have a bad time. If you think quests are going to take an average of 15 minutes to complete, you're gonna have a bad time. But stick with it. It's worth it.

Don't let the 14 year old graphics turn you away from one of the best role playing games ever made!  If you are reading this on Steam, chances are, you've played its grandchild Skyrim or at least its child Oblivion.  Now, with the release of The Elder Scrolls Online, Morrowind is the middle act of an epic tale told of a mythical place called Tamriel. A continent-wide empire with many provinces.
Most of each of the Elder Scrolls games take place in one of these provinces. Daggerfall takes place in High Rock, Oblivion in Cyrodil etc.  This game takes place in the province it is named for. Daggerfall and Morrowind are quite open 'sand box' RPGs which make almost no effort to railroad you along a plot and even less effort to keep your character alive.  In fact, in Morrowind, you may very well die the first time you tangle with a lone bandit in a cave.  If you can avoid dying, you get to wander huge maps, even bigger than the ones in Oblivion and Skyrim.
As I said in the opening, the graphics may take a bit of getting used to if you've been playing 'modern' CRPGs with the latest in graphics tech behind them.  Still, once you stop comparing the look of Morrowind to a claymation cartoon, the look and feel of the game grows on you.  It is quite a cohesive game, as most Elder Scrolls games are, with its own style and culture. I've always found Morrowind to be the most 'alien' feeling of the ES games with its strange creatures and plant life. But that's good in a way as it really transports you to another world rather than reminding you of some place here on Earth you may have visited.
The characters may move more like animated department store dummies compared to the nearly lifelike movements of the new ES games, but they are infused with personality through their wonderful dialog.  Less of what they say is voiced, but the game more than makes up for it in the sheer volume of what they do have to 'say' in text.  Between that and the books, scrolls, signs etc. you find, there's enough here to fill a rather thick novel if it were all printed out in prose form.
None of the ES games can necessarily be called 'combat simulators' as their fight animations are nowhere near as realistic as some other games, but if you don't save constantly (in this game, its up to you to remember to do so, unless you turn on the setting for 'save on rest' and make the time to sleep in the game, you'll still be kept quite busy trying to keep from having to start the game over. As much as the combat may resemble little kids swatting at each other on a playground as I've heard it described in some circles, it's still come a long way from the static turn-based combat representations such as the ones in early Dragon Quest games.
Morrowind is certainly worth playing. Especially if you are like me and can't afford to buy or build a new gaming rig with 64 bit OS, more than 2 GB of the latest speed of RAM, quad core processor, video card that cost almost as much as the rest of the PC put together, etc. etc. like many of the very latest video games are now requiring.  Rather than breaking the bank to play those, why not go back in time and discover gems from generations past like this one?  If your computer has the hardware to match the recommended specs for original Skyrim (not the latest version of it being advertised now) then it will run practically any game made before 2010, with the possible exception of the insanely high spec demanding games from Crytek. :)

Awesome concept carried out decently. The combat is good and is mostly fluid, and PvP is a lot of fun. The quests can get a bit dull, but they break the regular MMO grind by throwing in boss fights every few missions and lots of rewards for exploration and story completion. The story itself is decent enough, especially in Gotham where you take on Bane and Scarecrow. The only major flaw in the story is the HORRENDOUS voice acting for the Brainiac characters and most of the cops in the nightclubs and police stations. The voice acting on those characters is so laughably awful it completely breaks immersion and sometimes actually makes me laugh aloud. However I will say that the voice acting on the hero and villain NPCs (Joker, Superman, etc.) is fantastic. It's really awesome to fight alongside Batwoman to take down Scarecrow, or Superman to take down the Brainiac horde. There are also some annoying things that should be addressed:
1) When flying/running near enemies, if they attack you just once it slows your movement speed drastically, making navigating the city below the rooftops nearly impossible.
2) Sometimes stun abilities just won't work on certain enemies with no explanation as to why. There was a boss fight in which we fought Power Girl and she was regular size, no outstanding special abilities, but was completely immune to being stunned or knocked down, which was annoying because my character was control and that's the entire point of my build.
3) The flow of melee attacks can be awkward at times, mostly due to desync between players.
4) Enemies that have stun and knockdown use it CONSTANTLY, and you have to sit there spamming shift to get out of it.
Overall I give the game 7.5 out of 10, and would give it an 8 if they patched some of the player desync issues.
ALSO, forgot to mention, the game has a decent community and a lot of older players are helpful to new players.

TLDR :
If you like the X-Com style games then this is something absolutely worth trying, its an old one though so the UI and graphics will not be up to todays standards.
I love this game, it was one of the first PC game I bought. In other words nostalgia probably has some influence on how I look at this game,I keep returning to it every so often and I love it. Wish more games would try to combine a strategic city/world map with turn and the option of real time strategy layer, its not perfect but I have yet to play a game I would say was perfect, it is however a diamond in the rough.
So what is this game all about? If you are familiar with the X-Com series then I probably can leave it at saying its similiar enough to its predecessors that you will feel right at home, it also have a bunch of new elements that might confuse and excite you. The Geoscape or overworld/land map is a city filled with destructible buildings, the strategic map is similiar enough to the other X-Com games that it will feel very familiar but it has a difference in the fact that you can choose between turn based (Time Units) style and real time control of your soldiers.
Earlier I mentioned destructible buildings, why would that matter? in this game you are protecting a city filled with factions that is funding you to protect their assets, so when a alien dimensional portal spews out UFO's that you are suppose to destroy and protect the buildings from getting invaded by foot soldiers that get beamed down by said invading UFO's.
While in the City scape, you can launch vehicles, both ground and air ones that you use to shoot down the UFO's or send soldiers to repel invaders.
While fighthing on the Geogscape there is a high likelyhood that a stray bullet or laser beam will end up hitting a building that can either damage or destroy it, if this happens then you get penalized and eventually the faction that suffers might even withdraw its funding that you need to survive, in other X-Com games this would spell the end for you, in Apocalypse you can and probably will raid some of the factions that are littered through out the map to steal gear from them that you can sell or use.
Probably should mention that besides the whole defending the city from aliens you also have to manage research and manufacturing of stuff that you either use for improving your base, your soldiers or vehicles.
The AI of the enemies is suppose to learn from your actions in combat and to some degree this works, as in if you hide around a corner every time and shoot them down when they keep crossing then after a few matches they might just start chucking grenades or use explosives once the first one falls, but they do not react to every strategy.
Guess I have covered the important stuff, it ended up longer than planned so I'm adding a TLDR at the top.
This might be partly nostalgia, but this is my favourite of the X-Com games, and the one I am most likely to randomly go back to.

So a couple hours in and I feel I can already confidently recommend this game.  A very good value for the cost vs the fun factor!  Like any review, good news and bad news.  But the bad is simple so I will start there.
Reasons not to buy this game?  Well I cannot think of any reason not to, but I can point out things that might bother some people.
The most noticable part of any game.  It is low poligon.  Much of it is fun and done well.  The planes, the crew, the base interiors, all quite comically enjoyable.  It is above standard in those areas for low poli.  The crews all have unique looks and readily distinguishable at a glance when not in the plane and all geared up.  Rare for low detail graphics.
The negatives I have for it visually consist of land detailing and damage.  The ground, buildings, etc just feel too space, even for a low poli plane based game.  Additional work to environment would really up the appeal.  Second visual negative I have is how some damage is displayed on the plane.  Holes in the fuselage is a bit rough and makes the plane seem to lack any structure and depth.
The way the plane moves at times can feel very clunky.  It sometimes will bob like a boat when changing altitude and turns a bit too fast.  Like with graphics, some smoothing would improve this one pretty decently
So of all negatives, this is the one part of gameplay that bothers me most.  Specifically mouse looking between two views.  There is a scope view for spotting and targeting planes so your crew can shoot back, and there is general look view.  When you toggle spotting, it is look by mouse.  When you are in general look, you must hold down the ctrl button to pan about.  I would really like the option so that it is default mouse look, and ctrl allows you to move cursor.
And that is about it my short term negatives.  Not much, nothing game breaking and all improvable if the dev wills it.  Time for the positives.
If I was to compare game, I would give it the feelings that one gets playing FTL, Rimworld or a turret defence game.  You can get set up and get going right, make decisions, but the final outcome can be out of your hands if wrong choices.  Randomness making it just as much reactive as proactive.
Your crew and your plane have a diverse selection of equipment able to be unlocked and put on.  This is also again, only with a couple hours of play in so far.  I fully expect there to be even more.  It isnt just power, but also that there is nothing that is one thing does all.  Do you want your crew able to respond and move about quick to repair and reload, or more for armor and survivability.  There is considerable selection even at this early stage.  What you choose, how you outfit all will affect how you approach missions.
I am still early in game, but am finding the difficulty is continuing nicely.  The game starts simple enough, but you get more enemies, more things to manage with the plane, it just keeps growing and giving more to do until it can become difficult to manage everything.  Eventually you will be shot down or have things not go according to plan.  It isn't possible, it is inevitable that something will thwart your survival.
Hrm... survivability as well as comparing to FTL/Rimworld.... that can only mean one thing.  Permadeath.  That is right, there is a permadeath in the game.  Your plane is shot down?  It is gone.  Your crew?  Might die of exposure.  How you equip affects their odds of survival and rescue.  That is determined by a roulette wheel of sorts.  But wait.   You can be rescued?  Why yes you can!  This is war.  Many pilots few out and accomplished their missions, but never to return.
This gives the game a perfect sort of difficulty curve.  While you may lose your upgraded plane and crew, you have not necessarily lost progressin the campaign or unlocked.  You can recruit new crew, there are more missions to do and can get more practice, get better and configure differently without having to unlock everything again.  Just need the money to buy it.
The permadeath side I think is one of the most attractive parts of the difficulty.  It gives an attachment to the crew and ensures you keep focus, but the fact you maintain your unlocks and old equipment in storage means that if you learn from your mistakes, you can recover your progress quite quickly.
I would like to comment on replayability, but because it is a mission based game, I consider it is more one of just enjoying the progress over time and playing it different next time.  Perhaps their is end game content, but I do not know.  Until I get more time in and clear the campaign, I will not be able to address it.
For those concerned about the difficulty and progression as well as how it plays, I highly recommend watching the "Bomber Crew" videos currently done by Blitz
Family friendly episodes.  The game is more challenging than the initial videos show, but episode three that went up on day of posting this review  shows how the missions increase in complexity and multitasking requirements.  It also shows how just because it goes bad, it doesn't knock you out of the campaign.  You can rebuild and be right back.

You will hate this game.
Either you will love-hate it or just completely hate it. It's definitely not for everyone, and I have a difficult time recommending it for the people who would likely like it.
The game feels a little incomplete and a bit unbalanced, but after the Halloween patch the game has become bearable enough to get a positive review. Do note that this was previously a negative review of the game.
So I suppose I should try to explain this game as best as I can, and what is good and bad about it.
So Bomber Crew has you taking your 7 crewmembers in missions over Germany and France having you get shot to pieces and hopefully returning intact. The game feels similar to FTL, except without procedural content, without multiple different vehicles to select from, without a pause button, with more micromanagement of the crew, with more ways to die, and without permanently losing your campaign progress on death.
Bomber crew's missions are all pre-built, and 3-4 will appear for you to choose from at a time. Early in the game there will be 3 regular missions plus a campaign mission. When the campaign mission appears it will stay for you to select. The regular missions will cycle as you complete them. The more campaign missions you complete the more regular missions will be added to your "pool" of possible missions the game will let you choose from.
If you lose your plane and/or a/your crewmember(s), you will get a plane and/or crewmember(s) of slightly lower levels (although I have lost a lvl 9 to recruit a lvl 10 afterwards). You are set back a few missions monetarily (probably a couple of hours), and may lose some crew abilities. Some of these crew abilities are pretty important, such as the ability to set custom waypoints, multiple abilities to increase the damage output of your gunners, and the ability to auto-target all planes in radar range. The monetary used to be a lot worse, and was the main reason I originally gave the game a thumbs down (combined with a lack of procedural content, forcing hours of repetition of content), but has since mostly been fixed.
Weirdly enough, this actually makes the early game, past the first campaign mission, and up to maybe the 3rd or 4th, the worse point in the game to die, as you (may) lose skills which are critical for your survival while having to repeat a limited pool of missions to get back to where you were. Although the Halloween patch may have partially fixed this, and I could see losing a plane in the lategame when you don't have a good cash reserve more punishing. At least there is more mission variety then.
There will be times you die which are entirely preventable, but other times it really feels like there isn't anything you could've done to prevent death, other than to order an abort while your plane and crew were still in good health. If you get swarmed by fighters you better hope they don't hit too much important stuff. Them knocking out a crewmember means you're down to 5 as you have to have another one fetch a first aid kit. If both your fuel tanks go you'll soon find yourself out of fuel unless you can repair one quickly. If you lose all 4 engines you'll also be doomed, unless you can get one fixed while you still have one. And your Lancaster doesn't really do the thing called "gliding." So if, for example, you lose either both your fuel tanks or all 4 of your engines while you have multiple crew members, better hope you can equip parachutes and bail (or emergency land if you still have power) before you nosedive into the ground.
Yes, death in this game can be really frustrating.
In addition to your bomber not being able to glide in the slightest, there are other annoying things the game doesn't tell you. Such as not getting gear on corpses back. And to not bail someone out who is near-dead. Aces seem to regenerate health (unconfirmed). And (although this one is obvious and I haven't done it) don't emergency dive or corkscrew with anyone on your wings. There, you just learned 3-4 things the easy way.
I will admit, the game is decently cheap, it has really solid core mechanics, and, for a small update, the Halloween update has given me faith in the development team again. They've made huge steps to fix the main issue with the game, while simultaneously finding a really nice middle ground with those wanting a pause button and those who thought the game was fine without it. The devs are proving themselves to be both listening to the community and capable of making logical decisions about the game themselves from this feedback.
So, do I recommend it? Honestly, it depends. If you like your games being tough and full of micromanagement, and are OK with a little bit of a grind, then I'd say go for it. If you want a "fair,"
but still tough, game, then you might want to wait and keep an eye on future updates. If you don't like micromanagement or grindy mechanics, or lack the time to do a grind of a couple to a few hours, then this game really isn't for you.
And my message to the devs: I really want this game to succeed. I really want to be able to point to Bomber Crew and say "this is an example of how to make a great game." The core mechanics are all there, but you still need to balance the game to be a bit more fair to the players. More hotkeys, better balancing regarding losing your plane and crew (including the ability to kind of glide the bomber for a bit, long enough to crash land or bail out at least), better balancing in regards to the late game missions (including the maximum upgrades you can give your bomber), and a greater diversity of missions, especially in the early game, would all help the game become much, much better. And if the Halloween update is anything to go by, even if in the present this game isn't the greatest, this game has a bright future.
Let me know in the comments if there's anything I missed. I definitely feel like this review flows worse than my last one, but I hope it's just as informative, if not more so, about the game.

I would only reccomend this game if you are interested in the atmosphere of the world or a decent short scifi story. The game takes roughly 4 hours to complete. The story and intrigue were enough to keep my interest and justified the price of the game for me (which I bought on a steam sale). However, as a game, I felt like it fell flat.
My problems with the game are all in the gameplay:
1) The game keeps giving you new abilities that you barely ever utilize again.
2) The combat is very stiff and often comes down to luck. It's not fun at all.
3) The game is inspired from metroid puzzles but the puzzles do not have the same level of polish (or anywhere close). The Fall requires that you do  things in a specific order. It would spawn in new things when you finished the previous step. However, these things would often spawn illogically in places you had already explored. This takes away from the puzzles. In metroid you were constantly remembering little pieces that you couldn't access until you got a new ability and when everything fell into place you felt really good. In the Fall, you just have to keep walking around and searching with the flashlight in case something new spawned after the last step. In a couple moments, I found myself simply retracing  my steps again and again until I figured out the puzzle.
4) I personally didn't like having to point my flashlight at everything to examine it. This mechanic seemed to be designed to save some money on the art budget. A lot of the art seemed to lack detail which would have helped bring me into the world. Some of the puzzles involved seeing difficult to spot objects rather than actually figuring out a complex mechanism.
5) The game is very short.
6) Ending is extremely predictable and contrived.
Conclusion: The gameplay hindered my immersion into a wonderful story. I hope the team address some of these issues in the upcomming sequel.

Remember the puzzle-like Red Alert missions where you started out with a small amount of men, and had to use your resources cleverly to accomplish your goals? Remember the story starting out with Einstein traveling back in time to kill Hitler?
Original War takes these ideas, turns them to 11 and adds depth and charm on top in the form of RPG elements. You play as a group of soldiers with unique capabilities who are not replaceable, although of course you can build as many (customized!) vehicles as resources allow. During the campaign - with features branching missions - you get to keep and level up your crew chosen from a variety of soldiers in an available pool, some of which can also be lost or gained through the CYOA events of the game, and some of which have unique roles in the story - but the latter is for you to figure out during several playthroughs.
The setting is just as original as the name suggests, at least I can't remember any other RTS game set during the Pleistocene epoch. Yes, you read that right. The story of the game is essentially that a group of American soldiers travel back in time to move "Siberite" from Siberia to Alaska, while in an alternate resulting future Soviets travel back in time to move "Alaskite" from Alaska to Siberia. Clever, right? Oh, and there's also Arabs with European mercenaries who try to grab their share of the cake - I won't spoil how they enter the story. You can tame local apemen and even mastodons, although the latter is not possible to do in the campaign.
The American and Soviet factions are very charmingly and stereotypically presented, with lots of voice-acted dialogue during missions. The protagonist in the American campaign get cutscenes in the form of narrated sketches in his diary, while the Soviet protagonist watches some sort of Communist C64-like computer with video clips encoded as characters on the screen, which I always thought was very cool and original (get it?).
All in all, this game is a must-play for people who like RTS and RPG games. Even more so if you like beautiful 2D graphics, and if you have enjoyed the US vs. USSR setting in other games and movies.

Let me start off by saying I am a creationist, and don't believe in Darwinian evolution. But that aside, it IS fun to have in a video game, that's for dang sure!
To start, you choose a planet and name it. (You have all of them, though, each basically like a different "file") You choose whether to be a carnivore or herbivore, and start out as a cell in the ocean. Right then, it's basically an arcade style sidescroller, where you move in 360 directions. You eat and you eat, and stay clear of op enemies. You keep eating to "rank up" until you can then find a mate to upgrade your species. You can choose different mouths, eyes, and other "accessories." You can even shape the creature, choose colors, and name it and give it a description. (On one of my planets, I am the species known as the N00blets, and it's description is "Trolololol," lol)
After long, you eventually grow to the size of a fish, and eventually get bigger until you get feet and can move to land. Now, it becomes a 3D sandbox game where you roam about, discovering other species, and finding bone remains to get new body parts available to upgrade. You can choose to befriend other species, or attack them, via the social buttons. But watch out, as they also have that decision....sort of. You see a face next to them, and if it's mad, then they are hostile. Also keep in mind there are GIANT creatures from time to time just freely roaming about....all of which are SUPER hostile and way too op to mess with. STAY CLEAR OF THOSE GUYS! You have to find food via fruit on trees, or other creatures. (Depending on if you have a herbivore mouth or carnivore mouth.....or both)
The next "game type" is when you become sentient. Now, it becomes more of a birds eye view strategy type game. You are the leader of a tribe, can tame other creatures who are not yet sentient, (Or "animals") and so on. You can befriend other tribes of creatures, too. All in all, really fun game. And it holds up well after all these years.

After watching the news coming out of e3 2016, I got excited when I heard that it is going to be a big year of releases for the Resident Evil franchise. RE1 was the very first survival horror game I ever played way back in the days of PS1, and is pretty well single-handedly responsible for my love of the genre, and my measuring stick for other games that claim to belong there alongside it. There is no doubt that the Survival Horror genre is one of the largest in the industry, but like Metal music, I firmly believe that there are some key differences between Survival Horror, Thriller, Psychological Thriller, and plain Horror. I’m not going to write an anthropological essay on the nuances between them all, but suffice to say that I when I look at Dead Island, for instance, I see more in common with RE1 than I do with the likes of Penumbra or Outlast.
One of the keys to a good Survival Horror for me, is the balance of resources and enemies. Resident Evil HD Remastered does this in a way that not only adds to the tension of the gameplay as you increase the difficulty, but completely changes the way that you have to play if you want to survive. For example, if you play through the Jill campaign on easy, you can kill every single monster you come across and still have enough ammo at the end to fire shots in the air like it’s the Wild-Wild West. If you swap to Chris on hard though, you’ll be bobbing and weaving like Ali, saving every bullet for only the most dire of situations. Likewise on easy, you’ll find so much herb that you can patch yourself up if you even get a mozzie bite, whereas on hard you’ll be weighing up how much you need to heal compared to how long ago your last save was. RE takes it a step further here too, even limiting how many saves you can have, which again, can add another degree of resource management to an already stressful situation.
If you didn’t play the original, you’re probably wondering why a lot of people like me talk about RE being the original and best game in the genre? Well it’s pretty simple really (in my mind anyway): One, nobody seems to know about, “Alone In The Dark”. And two, you don’t know what’s around the next corner. Literally. Resident Evil is one of those games that did something truly unique and original, and did it well enough to spawn an entire generation of cult followers in the process. The first three (in terms of release date) games are shot in a frame-by-frame manner with fixed camera angles, essentially creating a game that is played in hundreds of hand-crafted scenes where the player can never get the full picture of what is happening, both literally and figuratively. Some of the best horror moments in Resident Evil HD Remastered result from little more than a fixed camera angle, and the sound of hurried footsteps over a carpeted floor.
It really wouldn’t be right to review a remastered edition of a game without looking at some of the things that have been done differently, so here are some of the things I noticed:
Obviously the graphics have been amped up to a more modern standard, with the lighting being the clear standout for me. Some of the balcony and basement scenes amazed me by how far things have come from the turn of the century. The rendering of some movable objects is still not 100%, but it’s a lot better than the original, and in some cases was not even noticeable. All-in-all though, the feel is much more in line with the Biohazard series now which has the effect of starting to tie everything together in a more comprehensive graphical style, as well as giving a whole new generation of gamers the opportunity to see where it all began, without having to play some horrible port that doesn’t do the game any justice.
The remastering of the sound is very welcome. You could actually play without subtitles now if you wanted, whereas in the past doing so would mean that you would hear nothing but the music and the occasional, “Barry!”, or, “Chris!” (This actually really excites me considering that RE2 Remaster should drop this year, and I’ll actually be able to understand what Leon is saying). Best of all, are all the familiar tracks like, “Safe Room”, which have become as iconic to me as the track for the town of Tristram.
The addition of Crimson Heads is a great success in my opinion. They fill a niche that was maybe over-compensated for by Cerberus’ and Hunters in the first edition, and add a whole other level of lethality to the regular Zombie which is an excellent surprise on the first playthrough. In fact, I spent two thirds of the first playthrough thinking that they may have replaced hunters with these things altogether! Part of me was disappointed at that, but for someone who had already played the original, I was also drawn in by it. I wanted to know why? I wanted to find that next set of research notes. I wanted to get to the bottom of what was going on in the mansion. And for me, THAT was a very subtle, yet very successful way of drawing an experienced player back into a story they thought they knew.
There are new areas to explore!
And lastly, defensive weapons have been added. Now for me this one is a little contentious, because I can’t decide whether it was a good or bad idea. On easy, for instance, they should not be allowed at all; You have more than enough healing items to counter for the odd bite or scratch. But on normal/hard, surely a, “shove”, button would have sufficed? Would it not be more realistic to just push a zombie in the chest with both hands, rather than fend it off with your off-hand (while avoiding being bitten, mind you), then pulling out a dagger or a taser (wtaf?) to deal with the intrusion of your personal space? However, I won’t deny that there was more than one occasion where I didn’t really feel like dying, and I was glad for my collection of ridiculously ornate, mass-produced, trusty daggers.
All-in-all you’d be crazy not to play this game over if you’re a fan of the original. It’s prettier, sounds better, and best of all it gets you pumped up for what looks to be an awesome year for all of us who have followed the franchise from the beginning. It’s highly unlikely that you will be disappointed.

To say that The Witcher is just an amazing game will do it no justice. There is no good or evil, just the choices you make and the consequences that follow. The first game in the series has gotten some people to over look it or skipping it entirely. I can understand that. The graphics are somewhat dated but still looked great, even for it’s time. The battle system is one thing that a lot of people tend to complain about. It is outdated and it is a clunky but after an hour or two of it you may grow to love it like I did. The battle system is a cross between real-time strategy rpg and hack and slash with timed movements. It’s not bad but I dont know any newer games that use this battle system. Because of this battle system, many people tend to skip it entirely despite the great story that is to be told when playing. Now the story does start off slow and you have to be half-way into the first chapter to get things rolling which is another problem. The pacing in the beginning is horrible but if you can get past that, you will enjoy this game entirely. It’s a great game if you give it a chance. It’s an 8.5/10 for me.

The graphics appear a bit dated since the game is from 2007, but it still has its beautiful moments.
Sound design is pretty good.
Music is fantastic from start to finish; the credits music is an additional unique track I really enjoyed.
I completed roughly 95% of the content, and it took about 60 hours while hoarding loads of items I never really needed. Just a quick tip: you won't even need a quarter of the items you find.
There's tons of dialogue among countless characters and every single line is voice-acted.
Many quests with multiple choices leading to different results and story paths; it was clear that a lot of effort went into this game.
Combat isn't very good, and it clearly doesn't
to be, but it's not bad either; there are a lot of problems with it and you'll often find people simply misunderstanding it.
A live day/night cycle where certain things only happen at a certain time of day helps make the world feel more alive.
You move around the world quite slowly. There's very minimal teleport options, no "fast travel" system, no horses or anything, and you move faster with your sword unsheathed in a fast combat style. In some towns in the day, you aren't allowed to unsheathe your sword so you're forced to move around more slowly.
There's lots of side quests, and trying to finish most of them is what took the most time. Fortunately the side quests in this game are of decent quality, not all just "
" though it's near-impossible to completely avoid that, most have stories with voiced dialogues.
The game has subtitles for 99% of its dialogues, which is great.
Performance optimization is not great; I guarantee you will lag when there's many NPCs in the area, but it always remains playable even though this game hates my particular CPU architecture. (Tip: Reducing draw/render distance helps the most)
Sometimes the game crashes for no reason, but it's very rare. Just save your game when you make progress if it hasn't autosaved recently.
Extensive information in the player journal about characters, monsters, history, lore, locations, formulas, ingredients, tutorials, etc., as you discover it of course.
Bet on dice poker and fist fights, and inevitably exploit the fist fight mechanics.
There are 3 difficulty options and medium is easy enough as it is, so I highly recommend you don't choose the lowest difficulty.
I just remembered that there's 7 additional playable mini-stories in the 'New Game' menu that I haven't finished.

I am clueless on this one. I know a lot of games are not very logical but this one totally baffles me. Everything was fine until the enemy ships were introduced. Why would enemy ships steal the jewels and then return them... allbeit in a different location but still... why return them?
Aside from that I found it very boring waiting for the ships to drop the gems so I could move them. This is definitely a "hurry up and wait" game. And why does the game only save at chapter ends or checkpoints (every 4 levels so far). It's not like it's a big deal to save at least at the end of each level.

I wanted to like the game, for less than a buck, how can you go wrong after all. In truth, the "enemy switching gems" kind of mechanic is interesting, but it gets old VERY fast. I'm quite glad when I see the "harder" fast enemies, since at least they will drop the gems more quickly. I kept hoping the game would get more interesting with time, but all that happened was more gem types, very slight variations on enemies (neat, an even faster fast grabber) and more waiting for them to drop the gems so I could switch them.
To it's credit, the game is well made, seems quite reasonably done, and has some inventive mechanics that build well on the core. However where it fails for me is the core mechanic simply isn't interesting, and while the additional mechanics serve to make it more difficult, those same mechanics simply slow down the rate I blow through the levels and don't introduce any challenge beyond thoughtless frustration. Puzzle games are supposed to be frustrating because I _should_ have been able to figure out the solution (within a time limit, move limit, etc.) but this is simply frustrating while watching the clock run down waiting for the enemy to drop the last piece in place for me because it's the only location left to drop one.
Note, there don't appear to be any game breaking bugs, for example I kept waiting for enemies to pick up another gem when I had it effectively beat, thus prolonging the level even further. It never happened, nor did the enemies clash with each other at any point in terms of gems picked up to make an unwinnable condition within the timeframe. The mechanics are solid, the AI appears well done and well tested, and the mechanics for what they are appear fully fleshed out. It's simply not something I'd recommend given the lack of depth or interest in the core mechanics themselves.

The idea of the game is simple:  Get all pods with 4 like gems.  To move gems around, you click on two pods "connecting" them, and then click on a gem in either pod you'd like to move and that gem will instantly swap with a gem in the connected pod.  When 4 in that pod are the same, it's complete and gets locked.   Get all the pods locked and the level is complete.
The challenge starts with the alien ships which transport gems from pods that aren't locked.  The challenge increases when the space stations get larger (from 5 pods to 15 pods) and with additional gem types, and then with additional alien ships (ones that move faster to ones that carry multiple gems).
Overall, it's certainly a neat idea and I did enjoy the game, and I liked the graphics.  But once you get the space station expanded to the larger size, it's very repetitive and the challenge doesn't really ramp up any more; it just gets more annoying
.
+ Nice idea
+ Nice graphics  (Though I'd like wide-screen graphics, and more variety in backgrounds.  But what's there is nice)
+ Music was pretty good
I believe there are 68 levels, but how many are identical?  Appears to be a lot.
The backgrounds are not-widescreen; nor is there many variety of them.
Considering the resolution is not all that high in the game, and also that ALT-TAB'ing takes a good 30-40 seconds for the game screen to come back up when trying to return to it, this is one of the few games that I
wish had a Windowed display mode.
You have the 5 pod space station, and the 15 pod station station.  (I made it to about Level 45 and only saw those 2 layouts anyway...)
I'm not entirely sure why there's a timer.  For score and bonus purposes sure, but to end your game if it reaches 0?  Not a fan.   Not when I lost on level 40-something because the final jewel of the final pod was being carried around for ~20 seconds when the timer finally ran out.

The only reason why I didn't refund the game is that it costs below 1€, so why bother.

After having a C64 for many years back in the '80s and music tracking the hell out of it as well as playing there the ancestor of all UFO games a lot called 'Laser Squad', the release of the very first UFO game was a strong reason to purchase my very first PC. It was a workstation to record / edit audio, soon with equal UFO and UFO2 playing time.
When the 3rd game came out somewhere late '90-something without hesitation I purchased a CD box version that I've been playing to ruins on a regular level since that.
With its hybrid turn-based strategy and realtime game concept, X-COM Apocalypse was (and still is) the best X-COM game as well as the best strategy game to me. I do a complete playthrough every year or two, I guess I burned more hours of playime that I'd like to admit and it still never stops producing new situations.
The goal (just like in all of the UFO games) is to ultimately defeat the alien invaders. X-COM Apocalypse gives incredible freedom of choices in doing that. You can train cloaked ninja specialists who can single-handedly wipe out alien ships or raid and raze the buildings of enemy fractions. You can fire lazy scientists and technicians. You can combine armor parts. You can keep on raiding and repelling enemy attacks so your bases must have a defendable layout. If a fraction is too annoying you can throw them into a debt. Do you have financial issues? Steal valuable stuff from the nagging companies. Do you have a difficult opponend behind cover in a house? Burn it down then make it collapse on him. Or destroy the floor under and let the opponent freefall a little. You can build strategies and counter-strategies to the actions of the enemy as the game goes on and you try to follow the aliens technologically who will be always some steps before you.
I really like the new X-COM games but when it comes to depth, variety, creative solution of situations and freedom of choices and in general, this ancient game bests them, by far. To this date, there is no alternative to it.
Loved the realtime combat, no other XCOM had it this good. City Scape was amazing. I'd give my left nut for a remake.
My favorite installment in the XCOM franchise, feels the most whole and rounded.  I just wish they had continued with some of the mechanics from this in the series reboot.

This is one of the greatest strategy games of all time. I have owned this for what feels like forever, and ended up getting it again on Steam as part of a classic X-Com bundle (from the days when XCOM was X-Com). I have spent more hours of my life playing this game than most teenagers have spent sulking. Yes, I have played it THAT much.
Apocalypse is a funny old game. The graphics, while appalling (from interviews it seems that even the game's developers were a bit stunned by the incompetence of the artwork), are overloaded with 50s retro sci-fi charm. This game looks weird, make no mistake about it, and its visuals are highly Americanised, which is odd because I believe the game was developed in Britain.
Instead of fighter aircraft you get a giant drum with stubby wings, hovercars that look like a Cadillac shagging a Merc and one-man hoverbikes. Hasn't everyone wanted to attack an alien mothership that looks like a muffin while riding a flying motorcycle with a missile launcher in its nose? The aliens are some of the most laugh out loud funny designs you'll ever see, but it's still as satisfying as hell when your squad lays waste to them.
Unlike modern XCOM, in X-Com Apocalypse you can extensively customise your bases, vehicles and troopers. While you can't change the way anything looks (unfortunately), you are responsible for buying or producing every single piece of equipment including different armour components. Limited stocks are available on the market and if you start flooding the market with captured alien tech, prices will start to nosedive. This does unfortunately mean you will run out of grenades, armour, medikits and maybe other equipment soon enough. Treasure your stun grenades, if you're playing turn-based these will win you the game.
The geoscape plays in real-time which can be paused or changed to different speeds. Combat missions are very interesting as you can pick real time, in which case the average mission lasts two minutes and costs 90% of your ammo reserves, or the traditional turn-based in which one of your troopers can simply walk into the middle of the enemy and shoot three of them in the face. While this sounds easy, the game gets very challenging later as the aliens develop new teach and come at you with vastly more powerful ships, to the point where it's safer to cower in your bases until you develop Retaliators to blast them back to their own dimension.
New ships take quite a while to get and even longer to be able to deploy them in any numbers, and all the while the enemy is growing stronger.
The absolute best thing about this game is being able to fight other human factions. Sometimes these will aid you, flying to the rescue as your outclassed hovercars strive to battle invading alien bombers (yes, they field bombers, but they seem to think launching their ammunition at your fighters is funnier than dropping it on the city). Human factions range from pathetic to surprisingly tough - while constantly raiding gangs will make you very popular in the city, the gangs will send holy hell your way. In fact sometimes the aliens, who are considerably tougher than the gangs, become a distraction from the looting and judicial♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking you will need to unleash.
If you are tired of the original Enemy Unknown and find Terror From the Deep to be too frustrating or too much of a retread, and if you aren't so keen on the brilliant but dumbed-down new games, Apocalypse is a superb choice. It's quaint, it's deep, it's gripping, but most of all it was the last classic X-Com that actually felt worthy of the name.
This might actually be my favourite game in this franchise, and coming from a very long-term TFTD veteran who is also a huge fan of XCOM 2, that is high enough praise.
What are you waiting for? It's time to get out there and cancel the apocalypse.

In theory this collection should be a great experience. That's what I thought when I booted it up. As soon as I tried to adjust the resolution, the game proceeded to crash, forced me to verify files and turn off my virus protection as a content lock occured.
Once I got it back up and running with controls set comfortably on my 360 pad, it worked well. Well enough for what feels like a lazy attempt to wrap three arcade roms into a stand-alone executable.
The Time and Score text overlay is really weird and doesn't mesh well with the rest of the visuals. The options feel kind of barebones, there's no intro videos or explanations or anything for any of the games, nothing. People coming into this without knowing about the games will have no idea that you can do super moves, like hitting punch and jump together in DD1 for the game-breaking backwards elbow. Or how DD2's controls are odd. Or how you can flipping run in DD3 by double tapping move (the previous two games didn't have it, so unless you did this by accident how would you know?).
The games themselves are hit or miss. DD2 in particular is masochistic and unfair as hell. DD3 feels weird, clunky, and slow, but it's also the easiest of the trio. DD1 is decent, provided you abuse the elbow.
DotEmu tried to spice things up with three difficulties and "Story + Arcade Modes!" for each game, but this is shallow. Difficulty just means how many lives you get and how much damage enemies have to take before they die. One elbow versus four. Easy? 4 lives. Normal, 5 lives. Expert? 3 lives. And the difference between the two modes themselves? No continues in Story, but you have a level select where you can start from any level you've made it to. Arcade is a single run, but you get two continues (at least in DD1).
Limited continues in very hard arcade beat 'em ups. No indication or explanation for getting any more. No explanation or details on controls, game back story, none of it. DotEmu just took three roms, slapped them together so they'd work, and added a fancy UI wrap around to sell. Unless you're honestly torn up about emulation, you're better off skipping this purchase and just using MAME. At least then you can pump in however many quarters you want and play by your rules.
Game might be good, but what kills it is that you cannot play it with controller. Good opportunity missed because game makers wont test the things they create. Stupid I say.

DC Universe Online is a super-hero MMO that makes you feel you're the next Superman or Wonder Woman as you're a hero helping your comrades against the opposition and the main threat, Brainiac.
The story brings an underrated villain, Brainiac, into the Hero vs Villain fray and decides to start destroying Earth after he obtains all bits of intelligence (which also means humans). Lex Luthor, who saw Brainiac invading, left the rest behind to be destroyed and travelled to the past, warning the present heroes of the upcoming threat. Using Exobytes, technology stolen from Brainiac that was stolen from the heroes and villains of the future, he allowed the entire of Metropolis and Gotham to have superpowers to defeat Brainiac.
Aside from the story, the gameplay is very diverse and gives you plenty of opportunities to display yourself. In character creation, you choose from plenty of powers (some requiring DLCs), weapons (one currently requiring DLC), and three movement modes (Flying, Super Speed, and Acrobatics). You can also choose side, personality, and mentor. Choosing a side means you're either a hero or a villain. Your personality reflects how your presence affects other players (how they think of you), and mentor (which kind of hero/villain you are). Depending on mentor, you can be a magic, meta, or tech character, and you will do two mentor quests in the entirety of the story (which is not much, but it's better than listening to Oracle or the Calculator all the time) and fight the nemesis of your mentor (Lex Luthor, Circe, or Joker). The story in this game is pretty much known to the community as the tutorial. It shows you around, has you geared up, and ready for the main part of the game: Increasing combat rating or PvP combat rating.
On the topic of PvP, there are five kinds of ways to PvP: Worldwide PK (PvP phase), Ring War/Diamond Heist, Arena PvP, Legends PvP, and duels. Dueling, at this point, only helps with a few feats, the most you'll get feat-wise would be Arena or Legends PvP. Legends PvP is different to the others as you use a character from the Legends roster. You can be Doctor Fate, Kyle Rayner...heck, even Classic Batman in Legends PvP (note that gear and traits won't make you better in this kind of PvP).
Now on to feats. Feats are like achievements, but they actually account for something. Feats come with feat points: the harder the feat, the more points you earn. Every 100 feat points will earn you a Skill Point (so you don't feel like you're stuck with 15 SP the entire game). The more feats you do, the more skill points you earn, and the easier for you to increase combat effectiveness.
The next point to note is alerts/raids/duos/solos. These are pretty much dungeons/instances where you go and do missions related to the instance to earn Marks of Triumph (later tiers will have something different). The higher the tier, the more Marks of Triumph you will earn, and an added bonus if you complete ones with a star beside them. Duos and solos can be fairly easy, as you can do them seperately from your peers, but alerts/raids require you to engage in strategic fights with your allies. If you're not able to engage in conversation and strategize, you won't make it far.
The only issue I have with this game, for personal reasons, are the DLCs. Understandably, they do need a way to earn a profit, however to make a game Pay 2 Win (P2W), is a fairly bad way of making a profit. To engage in anything from tier 4 and up will require legendary membership or the purchase of certain DLCs to be involved. Other than that, if you do get a DLC, you're treated to it's benefits.
Pros:
• Original story
• Nostalgic characters
• Legendary voice-acting (especially Mark Hamill's Joker voice)
• Immersive and enjoyable gameplay
• Engaging and strategic boss battles
• Near-infinite customization possibilities
Cons:
• Pay 2 Win
• Spawn killing can be abused in PvP
• Friendly mobs involved in a mission can be killed by enemy players (which leads to delays in progress)
• Spawn killing while in PvP phase
• PvP isn't exactly balanced
• A few bugs here and there (like Cape Carmine Lighthouse lvl 9 mission on solo, being very hard to complete)
Conclusion: I would recommend this game for the fans of the DC comics and for those who just love to enjoy a taste of being a superhero or supervillain. If any of you read this and require assistance in-game, do feel free to message me if you're on USPC. ~Permafrost Imp

I am writing this review after playing the game for 8 hours and having watched about 5 hours of YouTube Let's Play content for the game from a couple of different channels.
I don't often write reviews, but I really, really enjoy this game.  Lemme break it down:
Pros:
- WWII Bombing, without the terrors of war.  Yep, the game is about WWII - and that always comes with a lot of baggage.  You play as a plucky British aircrew and you're always up against those cunning Jerrys of the Luftewaffe.  You're always bombing strategic targets - you're never firebombing cities or doing something that makes your crew ever look like villains.  And when you're trying to cheer for your crew, I think it's important.
-Style:  The game art is pixelly, which might not be for everyone, but I loooove it.  It's chipper and bright and consistent through the game - their artists did a bang up job and they should feel good about themselves.
-Inclusion.  Your crew isn't just a bunch of white dudes with moustaches.  I know that's the trope of all war movies, especially ones featuring the UK, but it's just not accurate.
-You can paint your plane.  I mean, there are at least 5 custom slots that you can use to make your own livery for your plane and put it all over.  I immediately drew a bunch of immature graffitti on mine, and felt immediately happy about it.
-Hectic, challenging game.  Especially in the first two sections of the campaign, expect to come home limping and on fire with no fuel, if you come home at all.  I WILL say that if you're smart about grinding out some easier missions when they come along, you can kit out your plane and crew to be able to handle most of what the game throws at you, which we'll see on the con list below.
-No pause.  I like this choice, it's not just "FTL in a Lancaster" - because you can't just pause and give orders (you can technically pause by pushing the ESC key, but it brings up a menu and doesn't allow you to issue commands).  My last mission, I had 2 people unconscious, a fire in the tail, and fighters surrounding my plane - I really had to prioritize things quickly in order to sort it all out without losing my plane or my crew - and when I was able to do so, it felt VERY rewarding.
Cons:
-Just the Lancaster.  Ok, I LOVE the Lancaster bomber - it's iconic and it's beautiful ... but the game is so much fun, I want to play it over and over, and it would benefit from having additional plane types.  I wouldn't mind seeing a patch, DLC, or expansion that allowed for playing different bombers through the war.
-Learning curve plateau.  I'm at the halfway point now, according the campaign map, and because I carefully played my cards... my plane is as upgraded as it can be (there are more upgrades, but I have capped the current available).  And I have all my original crew as well - so things are a little bit easier than I would like.  Don't get me wrong, it can stll be hectic at times, but I find myself missing the first two sections of the game where I really felt like I could die at any time.
-Music.  The music that is in the game is great... I just wish there was more of it.  I barely notice the music during missions - and games like FTL did so well because of a great score.  I wish there was more good to say here.
Final Thoughts:  It's a fun little game.  It's a great game to play a mission and then get some work done and then come back and play another mission.  It was only a couple of bucks, and I think it's well worth the price.

I love when a gem of a game comes out of nowhere!
The moments this game creates are very unique to itself. Flying high above occupied Europe, trying to slip past the Luftwaffe and flak cannons. Keeping a hard eye on the oxygen levels, temperature, map, radar, fuel, and the bombers readiness; trying to prepare my mind for the enevitable sh!t-storm that is going to take place at any moment. I've never clenched so hard.
One wrong move and it can spell disaster for the entire mission and, more heartbreakingly, can seal the fate of your veteran crew and the bomber you have invested all your time & resources into. The latter being a truly horrible feeling, I feel genuinely sad for the death of any crew member. Was it my fault? Could I have saved them? I often go to the memorial plaques, saying each of their names to pay my respects.
Though often times I feel the mechanics and the RNG of the game are to blame for a failure. A cluttered UI leads to miss-clicks, and the RNG of a 'low-risk' mission ends up shredding your bomber leading to a total loss.
Things can get VERY hectic, and even though you have a crew with duties they perform, you more or less have to do them all. So you end up being a one-person crew with a TONNE of mechanics to keep under control or things could end badly.
If you become overwhelmed and forget to spot new bogies? You die. Don't notice a fire? You die. Don't manage your fuel? You stall, and you die. Don't notice you need to reload your gun(s)? You die. Forget to utilize your crews 'perks'? You die. Miss a new heading? You go off course, run out of fuel, and you die. Among other scenarios.
I don't necessarily want this game to be easier, I'm too lazy to get into each issue, but I feel somethings could be ironed out or refined to remove the feeling that it was the game's fault. For me though, it's more often than not my mistakes that lead to the death of my entire crew.
I have not yet mastered all the mechanics, most notably, improving the survivability of your crew if you go down.
You don't lose all your progress if you die, you do slowly get replacement bombers with better starting gear, and you can hire new members with better and better experience. But you need to re-outfit them all with gear, and need to prepare the plane with better equipment by grinding lower risk missions to get currency, which I mentioned could quickly end up being a total loss once again. You have to decide when you are ready to take part in a major operation.
Overall, this is a difficult, unforgiving, fast paced, simulation, managment rogue-lite...
and I love it.

Original War is not your run of the mill real time strategy games, it is a difficult one to describe, you still have the base building and resource collection that you are used to, with one of the resources randomly appearing on the map as they are sent back through time to you. But there is a big catch with the most valuable resource in that it is finite, in most RTS games you just make all the soldiers you need but in Original War your soldiers (I include the engineers, mechanics and scientists in the) are finite, if they die that’s it for them.
There is a nice level of role playing elements with this as when your soldiers perform tasks in a specialisation, they will earn the usual experience and level up to make them better and you will find that you have to juggle what you need on a map by map basis, so I have always found it is never too wise to have too many specialists as if you lose these then you are set way back.
OW is a RTS game that is set in the past where you are securing the most important natural resource on the planet either as the Americans or the Russians.
You build bases, perform research, build defences, send soldier out to visit the enemy, build vehicles, decide on what propulsion, chassis, weapon these vehicles need, all limited by what resources you can gather.
It may be a dated looking game these days, but I have found it to be a very enjoyable game, frustrating when you lose some of your prize soldiers or make the wrong decision that sends you down a different path.
Unlike other RTS games you will need a different strategy then sending all your soldiers out and not caring about the losses, each loss can hit you hard.

Clustertruck is 90% fun, 10% awful. So it merits a purchase.
The 90% fun include a great soundtrack, a fun concept and about every nine out of ten levels that are really enjoyable.
The remaining 10% include moving instakill obstacles in a first-person platformer where you, as a result, can't tell where your character's head, legs or back stop, and the randomness. Whatever physics engine governs Clustertruck includes a pretty big chunk of RNG, which means that in some levels, you might flub an attempt simply because zero trucks made a necessary jump or they all dogpiled halfway down the track.
I appreciate that there's SOME randomness, since it helps keep things fresh, but when a given level doesn't let you waste a split-second if you want to catch the next convoy so you can actually beat it, having that split-second be governed by randomness in the trucks' steering, colliding and flipping... is a pretty unfun thing.
Still, I don't regret this purchase. Make sure to get the OST, though, if you get Clustertruck, the OST is awesome.
