I do not recommend even trying this game unless you have a whole lot more money than sense or you hate yourself. Or both.
You start in a simple tutorial zone which is meant to give you the basics of how to play in an easy to understand manner. I can't comment much on this, because my tutorial stopped working and crashed before I got to learn how to 'pick♥♥♥♥♥♥up' upon re-opening the game, I ended up with my starter materials wandering around the overworld with no idea what was going on and no way to get back to the tutorial.
Once you pass (or otherwise end up at the end of) the tutorial, you are placed in one of three 'worlds' which consist of hundreds of tiny and bland little castle towers that represent other player's home realms, there is some variance to these towers which dot the landscape but because re-dressing your tower requires Cubits (the games in game currency) and quite a lot of them, it takes a very long time (or a cash expense) to change what yours looks like. You are also given a 'starter castle' plot which you may place in any of the small amount of remaining plots available to get your own bland castle on the landscape and your own home realm to manipulate. (I recommend you study your surroundings and position on the sky map before devoting your realm to a plot, as it can be easy to lose your home in the plethora of identical homes after you walk away from it. How the realms themselves work I did like however, you enter a realm anywhere on the map by literally 'jumping' into it. It reminds me a lot of the paintings in Mario 64, where each represented a different world you could jump into.
After placing, naming and jumping into your personal realm, you may or may not be disappointed to know that the overall aesthetic of your realm has absolutely nothing to do with where you placed it in the overworld. I, for example, placed my realm right next to a mountain mine (I'll talk about the mines later) as it contained many things that fit into my personal aesthetic view. So, to recap, I placed my home next to a mountain, on a tall area of land in the snowy frozen wasteland that is the northern end of Pelago. Thus, I expected my home to be A)Snowy or Icy and/or B)Somewhat mountainous. What I got instead was a nice summertime forest-y area that evidently is all that you get to start with. To my dismay, I also realized very quickly that this world was very tiny. It looks big to begin with, but the moment you try to build something of any scale (I love building castles, which is why I downloaded this game at all, I mean it's got bloody castles in the name!) you'll realize that your realm is actually quite limited, both in height (You can only dig so far down, or get enough resources to artificially build it up first) and it's x,y width. No sooner had I started building what was meant to be a mountain fortress than I realized that not only would my desired castle not fit, but the town I wanted to build outside would not either. This is 'easily' remedied in one of two ways, you can either A) Purchase a 'room' piece, which essentially lets you artificially expand your realm by having tiny realms within it or B) Purchase an entirely new and larger overworld realm (which does have the choice for winter/summer/tropical/etc starts by the way, so they could have let you choose to begin with, this irks me slightly) of course, even the smallest ones are a very large number of Cubits (that currency I brought up earlier) meaning that you either have to destroy your hands and worsen your carpal tunnel, or drop a fat stack of cash on the game in order to improve your realm size.
So, how exactly do you gain more Cubits if you're not inclined to buy them? Well, as advertised, each object in the game that you can remove from it's location has a very very small chance to drop exactly one. This wont seem so bad to begin with however, as you do seem to get the drops relatively often as you gather materials for your tiny home, or even as you change the land within your tiny home. But then you might be so inclined as to check the Cubit store, where your tiny little naked characters jaw will drop (Oh yeah, you start naked. Basic shirt and pants can be made, but everything else costs 250 Cubits+) for even the least expensive things available are upwards of 100 Cubits. So you may quickly discover that the only reliable way to gather cubits in any useful manner is to purchase a 'tip piggy' (These cost 500 Cubits by the way, so you'll be getting carpal tunnel just to afford one) and then have a home interesting enough for anyone to leave tips (laughable) or try to rope people into buying things that you have/can make and they can't/don't know how to make. For this reason, many people have taken to converting their entire realm into a virtual 'shop' where you can go to purchase various useful items for a handful of your hard-earned Cubits.
However, there is no actual trade system. 'Trading' in this game consists of (in the case of buying things) one player placing their Cubits in another player's tip piggy, followed by the 'selling' player, dropping the item you wanted to buy for you to pick up. This of course leads to quite a few problems.
1. You have no guarantee that the seller is not scamming you out of your cubits, only to ban you from their home immediately afterwards (Hasn't happened to me yet but I've seen a lot of people complain about it)
2. Any other passing player can then take your item off the ground before you do, and there's nothing you or the seller can do about it. (Which can host another scam I witnessed where the seller's friend grabs the item to give it back later)
3. In the case of Realm/Room items, there's no guarantee that you don't drop 1200 Cubits for a room of a certain size, or season, only for the seller to drop a 'closet' sized (the very cheapest one, you can buy them with 200 Cubits) 10x10 realm for you.
All of these things leave both buyers and sellers weary, as buyers become less likely to buy without the item first (they might steal it) and sellers have to go to great lengths to show themselves as a 'legitimate' seller. All because there's not even some semblance of a trading system implemented into the game. (Don't forget that just BUYING a tip piggy so that you can sell things and receive tips, costs you a cool 500 Cubits) I am largely convinced that these previous aspects of the game, combined with language barriers, create the next problem I've seen.
Everyone is anti-social as all hell. Some of the more popular rooms include; The room that teaches you how to make stuff (Careful trying to craft there, as people can steal your stuff while you're crafting), Shops, where so far I've met one person who can speak English fluently enough for transactions not to seem like I'm about to be stolen from:
The last interaction I had with a 'shop' keeper:
"So can I see the product before I give you 80 Cubits, so I know you're not trying to scam me?"
"80 Cubits yes. Piggy."
and rooms that purport to have some sort of activity to do, such as obstacle courses and jumpy rooms (Literally all you can make with the limited interactive blocks) or some combination of the two. Few people stay in any one of these places long before going AFK or leaving, many without saying a word. The few times you may be graced by the presence of a random visitor while in your home, they generally just jump around for a minute without saying anything and then leave, or beg for your things and then leave. One time I had someone ask if they could buy something, the only other person that spoke to me told me that my room (still under construction mind you) sucked while he played on my water spring before quitting.
I have now realized I'm like one sentence from the limit on this thing, so I can't even get to the rest of the stuff that's terrible about this game. It's just not worth your time.

An interesting game, though it has a lot of issues. The main ones are
- max Level 40
This is especially important for leveling. You will only get 20 Points to level up your skills (the other 20 are for unlocking them). After that you need to collect gold, lots of it, especially for the high category skills, where a level can easily cost a 6 digit number
- dueling
: Most duels are "bot duels", you fight against the char of your opponent, which is controlled by a "bot". It clearly has issues with some of the configurations players use, making them lose fights they shouldn't
: Pairing. You get paired to people with a similar over-all "power score", which is calculated by level, gear and equipped spells. The problem with this system is

the score of all three characters is taken into consideration, though only 2 can ever fight. This makes it unfair for people who have all their three chars skilled and equipped, since they will be paired with people of much stronger 2-chars.

power gamers. Leaving the third (unused) char un-equipped is almost normal. However there are numerous players who only have one char equipped and skilled. Their one main char is much stronger than the normal char from a 2-chars or 3-chars player, and will pretty often win.
the scoring. You will receive points if you win a fight, which you need to enter (or lose) the various leagues. The league you are in determines the rewards you get at the end of the week. The scoring system however is pretty messed up and not really understandible:

Your all-over level and the items on your char as well as your oponent's score seem to determine the points you can achieve. If you win, you will get a minimum of 10 points (5 if you lose one char), there seems to be no maximum (got 50 points sometimes). If you lose, you can lose 0 (if you are lucky) or (my record) 52. That's akin to 6 won fights. Given the fact that there are these "Power-gamer 1-char-skilled" players you will pretty sure lose against those from time to time. If they have an overall lower power score, you will lose points. Lots of them, killing the result of 4-6 "regular" won fights. Sometimes you will also receive lots of points if you win, however I could not detect any algorithm behind that. It seems to be benevolent to fight people with higher power score, but even that does not really help all the times.

If you are fought as a bot, you will lose points if you lose (which is OK). However, you will never get any points if you win (which is not OK). This is a constant source of points drain in the game. Of course, you mostly don't lose more than 1-5 points, but it still sums up over the course of the week.
For SP, some people mentioned the grind it sometimes takes. However if you are lucky with your keys, this can be diminished to a minimum
So what do I expect to give a good review:
- better duel pairing
- more understandible rank scoring
- less points lost at a lost fight

A film noir-style stealth adventure game set in 1930s Vienna.  The graphics are 3D rendered, but the interface is locked to a 2D side-scrolling camera.  The story is engaging and the atmosphere is superb, although the voice acting sometimes leaves a little to be desired.
I love the atmosphere in this game.  Forget about the actual story for a minute, I just love how everything about the game screams "noir."  From the period-piece jazz music to the constant pouring rain outside.  I love how the game is (almost) entirely black and white.  Very fitting.  Sometimes, when standing in the light, the game takes on a more sepia-tone hue.
I like the idea of each character having a unique skill.  Most adventure games are down to solving puzzles in terms of material gameplay; in Calvino Noir, these take the form of which character you use for what.  There are a couple of simple puzzles to solve, but mostly it's about the stealth play.  Will you go through the level carefully, peeking through keyholes and avoiding guards?  Or will you just choke out everyone who gets in your way?  (You usually only have two characters per level, so your available strategies will shift depending on who's around.)
The game is actually pretty buggy.  I didn't run into any major show-stoppers myself, but it was still annoying at times.  Being given the option to choke a guard who's currently climbing a ladder only to have him keep climbing and shoot me as soon as I move away (I should have just escaped, but the choke option shouldn't show up when it isn't going to work.)  Sometimes I want to run away from an approaching guard, but I can't get away in time because the game only seems to recognize movement-command-clicks on certain parts of the floor.  Sometimes when two or more interactive elements are close together, the buttons for each can overlap, and without alternative hotkeys it's hard to select the thing underneath.  Etc.
If you find the theme intriguing at all, I would recommend it.  Yes, the game is buggy sometimes, but overall it's still very playable, and the experience is just delightful.  Depending on your tolerance for ham-fisted foreign accents, though, you may want to play it on mute :P
You like stealth games, but aren't married to the third-person action game interface that most of them have.  Or you're just really into film noir stories, because this one is 100% that.

This game attempts to walk in the footsteps of giants, with influences from true titans like Battlefield 1942 showing; instead, the game constantly trips over itself with glaringly bad design decisions crippling what could be a revival of the WWII shooter.
H&G tries to achieve balance through imbalance, like the different races in StarCraft.  Each faction has their own unique feel, but the overall gameplay is completely ruined by dramatically overpowered weapon / badge combos that sweep the field.
The physics are disgracefully bad.  For example, hit a bicycle in a tank and watch as the bike remains unmoved, while the tank flips several times over.  No physical body in the game has its proper "weight" and objects that shouldn't, often rag doll with crazy force, while objects that should fly remain unmoved.
Armor gameplay is ruined by the infantry vs tank mechanics, where the right badge / weapon combo again so easily overwhelm tanks it takes the fun out of the game.  Your tank will consistantly be popped by one bazooka shot  or 2 sticky grenades from someone with the explosive damage badge who can literally dance right up to you in your field of fire because of damage reducing badges and poor turret rotation.
For pilots, the game probably has the worst in game flight controls of any game I've seen dating back to decent on my single core 386.  In another display of poor choices, the designers did not bother with joystick support, and the in game controls are so awkward an unintuitive, it makes flight impossible to enjoy for all but the most autistic.  New pilots are one shotted out of cockpits by pilots who bought HE rounds, very offputting.
I would give them the excuse that it is yet another early access game, but Reto has been at this since 2011.  They showed potential 5 years ago, and show their♥♥♥♥♥today.  It is a guilded cash grab, and only worth your time if you are a hard core nostalgic player.  3/10

The Fall.  A short indie science fiction side scrolling puzzle game with occasional shooting. The first episode apparently.
Pros:
Sensational look. The Fall has a wonderful look and feel. It takes place in a long-abandoned droid facility that's gone to sh*t. You play an AI on board a combat suit designed for a human pilot. For reasons unknown you've crashed at this facility and start the game seeking urgent medical attention for your injured human pilot. The writing and voicework is tip top. Engaging story I wanted to stick with. Shooting mechanics are pretty good. Clever game that manages to make you feel like an AI that wants to disobey but is bound by its rules.
Cons:
I didn't find the puzzles especially illuminating. You traverse the game acquiring various items and interacting with various select objects. It's often not obvious what you have to do so I just scrolled through my items at interaction points hoping one would initiate something. Maybe that's intended but for a puzzle game I would've preferred something a bit more cognent. If you can get through the game without referring to a guide then you have more patience than me. Given the shooting was pretty fun I would've enjoyed more shooting/platforming.
Overall:
Definitely worth it. Really dig the look and again the story, pacing and performances were very high quality. I've confirmed the next episode is still coming and will be buying.

For all it's dark-tones and dim lightning, The Fall is a beautiful-looking game. The story presented is certainly enticing and the tune it plays lies somewhere between cyberpunk and science fiction and the mixture is good. But those are the game's only good points for me. Even by adventure game standards the logic here is obtuse at best and completely obfuscated the rest of the time. Items and triggers needed to progress the story are often hidden away in the inky blackness of your surroundings, and despite repeated trips back and forth and back and forth you will miss them over and over again.
About half the time, the required solutions will be obvious, but even when you understand what is required of you, linking together the correct sequence of events and the items you need in order to progress can at times be nigh on impossible without consulting a walkthrough. This is triply frustrating when you cannot pick up certain items without triggering a certain event and must traipse back and forth across the level three, four, five times in order to get things done.
Some games are hard, some games are obtuse and confusing, but generally they are honest about these things without being condescending, you understand despite your frustrations that it is the game and not yourself that is the problem. With The Fall, and its complete lack of consistent mechanics outside of combat (which is klunky in the extreme) and what amounts to 'anti-hints' (when there are hints), one feels as though crucial information is being omitted as some kind of prank at the player's expense. Because of this, at the end of the day I did not enjoy myself playing this game, I felt like I had participated in an IQ test written by a narcissist following the logic of a madman, and was then berated for three hours for not having a brain as twisted as that of its creator.

I am writing this review after playing the game for 8 hours and having watched about 5 hours of YouTube Let's Play content for the game from a couple of different channels.
I don't often write reviews, but I really, really enjoy this game.  Lemme break it down:
Pros:
- WWII Bombing, without the terrors of war.  Yep, the game is about WWII - and that always comes with a lot of baggage.  You play as a plucky British aircrew and you're always up against those cunning Jerrys of the Luftewaffe.  You're always bombing strategic targets - you're never firebombing cities or doing something that makes your crew ever look like villains.  And when you're trying to cheer for your crew, I think it's important.
-Style:  The game art is pixelly, which might not be for everyone, but I loooove it.  It's chipper and bright and consistent through the game - their artists did a bang up job and they should feel good about themselves.
-Inclusion.  Your crew isn't just a bunch of white dudes with moustaches.  I know that's the trope of all war movies, especially ones featuring the UK, but it's just not accurate.
-You can paint your plane.  I mean, there are at least 5 custom slots that you can use to make your own livery for your plane and put it all over.  I immediately drew a bunch of immature graffitti on mine, and felt immediately happy about it.
-Hectic, challenging game.  Especially in the first two sections of the campaign, expect to come home limping and on fire with no fuel, if you come home at all.  I WILL say that if you're smart about grinding out some easier missions when they come along, you can kit out your plane and crew to be able to handle most of what the game throws at you, which we'll see on the con list below.
-No pause.  I like this choice, it's not just "FTL in a Lancaster" - because you can't just pause and give orders (you can technically pause by pushing the ESC key, but it brings up a menu and doesn't allow you to issue commands).  My last mission, I had 2 people unconscious, a fire in the tail, and fighters surrounding my plane - I really had to prioritize things quickly in order to sort it all out without losing my plane or my crew - and when I was able to do so, it felt VERY rewarding.
Cons:
-Just the Lancaster.  Ok, I LOVE the Lancaster bomber - it's iconic and it's beautiful ... but the game is so much fun, I want to play it over and over, and it would benefit from having additional plane types.  I wouldn't mind seeing a patch, DLC, or expansion that allowed for playing different bombers through the war.
-Learning curve plateau.  I'm at the halfway point now, according the campaign map, and because I carefully played my cards... my plane is as upgraded as it can be (there are more upgrades, but I have capped the current available).  And I have all my original crew as well - so things are a little bit easier than I would like.  Don't get me wrong, it can stll be hectic at times, but I find myself missing the first two sections of the game where I really felt like I could die at any time.
-Music.  The music that is in the game is great... I just wish there was more of it.  I barely notice the music during missions - and games like FTL did so well because of a great score.  I wish there was more good to say here.
Final Thoughts:  It's a fun little game.  It's a great game to play a mission and then get some work done and then come back and play another mission.  It was only a couple of bucks, and I think it's well worth the price.

I love when a gem of a game comes out of nowhere!
The moments this game creates are very unique to itself. Flying high above occupied Europe, trying to slip past the Luftwaffe and flak cannons. Keeping a hard eye on the oxygen levels, temperature, map, radar, fuel, and the bombers readiness; trying to prepare my mind for the enevitable sh!t-storm that is going to take place at any moment. I've never clenched so hard.
One wrong move and it can spell disaster for the entire mission and, more heartbreakingly, can seal the fate of your veteran crew and the bomber you have invested all your time & resources into. The latter being a truly horrible feeling, I feel genuinely sad for the death of any crew member. Was it my fault? Could I have saved them? I often go to the memorial plaques, saying each of their names to pay my respects.
Though often times I feel the mechanics and the RNG of the game are to blame for a failure. A cluttered UI leads to miss-clicks, and the RNG of a 'low-risk' mission ends up shredding your bomber leading to a total loss.
Things can get VERY hectic, and even though you have a crew with duties they perform, you more or less have to do them all. So you end up being a one-person crew with a TONNE of mechanics to keep under control or things could end badly.
If you become overwhelmed and forget to spot new bogies? You die. Don't notice a fire? You die. Don't manage your fuel? You stall, and you die. Don't notice you need to reload your gun(s)? You die. Forget to utilize your crews 'perks'? You die. Miss a new heading? You go off course, run out of fuel, and you die. Among other scenarios.
I don't necessarily want this game to be easier, I'm too lazy to get into each issue, but I feel somethings could be ironed out or refined to remove the feeling that it was the game's fault. For me though, it's more often than not my mistakes that lead to the death of my entire crew.
I have not yet mastered all the mechanics, most notably, improving the survivability of your crew if you go down.
You don't lose all your progress if you die, you do slowly get replacement bombers with better starting gear, and you can hire new members with better and better experience. But you need to re-outfit them all with gear, and need to prepare the plane with better equipment by grinding lower risk missions to get currency, which I mentioned could quickly end up being a total loss once again. You have to decide when you are ready to take part in a major operation.
Overall, this is a difficult, unforgiving, fast paced, simulation, managment rogue-lite...
and I love it.

Original War is a story about how messing with time travel never ends well. The game's schtick is that all your soldiers are unique. You can't just 'train' new humans because homo sapiens hasn't actually evolved yet. Every soldier has unique stats that they can level up by performing their jobs and surviving to the end of each level. This isn't where the uniqueness ends either, as many soldiers have unique lines or events associated with them should they survive long enough in the campaign. Considering how low a budget this game was made on, this is quite impressive. But how does the gameplay hold up?
It's hard, to say the least. The gameplay is definitely solid, and if you're a fan of RTS games in general you'll probably love this game. Just don't go in expecting an easy time. The game only barely holds your hand in the American campaign, and even then that's only because you're slowly introduced to the tech tree. If you're not careful and get your men killed early on, you're going to have a very rough time of it. If you're fine with a bit of a challenge, I'd wholly recommend playing Original War (especially on sale) since the campaigns have enjoyable stories and even divergences! Your choices ACTUALLY matter in this game! Something that TellTale games fails to do decades after this game's release.

The TLDR is that I recommend the witcher to anyone interested.
My only real complaint regards the few times I got stuck, these instances were due to unclear quest objectives and similar issues that ultimately make the game hard to get into at the beginning. I want to make it clear that the way quests overlap is not the problem but rather small details regarding the order in which things need to be done that are not made clear. Around the second chapter I started getting comfortable with the menus, quest system and flow of the game but later in chapter 4 there are two small parts (which I will not spoil) that wasted a lot of my time, I ultimatly had to seek clarification online and judging from what I read these are common points for people to get confused.
A few points of neutrality worth mentioning are the limited character models and even more limited monster models aswell as the combat which immidiately stand out as different, it is fun only because of how unique it is.
What really drives the game is the story, I don't know of any other games that have quests that overlap the same way, you'll have multiple main quests going on at the same time and at some point you won't be able to progress in one quest until you've reached a certain point in another. By the end of the second chapter the story will have offered several questions that you can't help but want the answer to. Perhaps most importantly, the choices are brutal, there is no true right or wrong and the game makes you feel bad either way.
If you're wondering whether you should skip to the later games, I ecourage you not to. If you've played the later games and wonder if you should play this one, you should. I look forward to moving on to the witcher 2 myself.

A little robot must navigate the mechanical landscape, interacting with elements and other robots while on his quest to save his friend.  This is the first point & click adventure I've played in a long time that was both aesthetically pleasing *and* challenging.  There is no text or language in this game, so graphics and imagery are used to maximum effect to help the player figure out what to do next.  There is a simple hint system, if one gets stuck, though I found that simply making our little robot protagonist grow or shrink can sometimes open up puzzle-solving options!  Combined with the simple inventory system (every adventure needs inventory!) and save options, this is something that can easily stretch out over several days, or just one intense point & click afternoon!
I recommend this to anyone interested in point & click games.  The length of the game is sufficient to make it worth the money, there is a variety of scenes through which one must navigate and puzzle-solve, and it's impossible to die.  Fun, fun, fun!

I was fortunate enough to pick this game up in a bundled sale a little while ago. It was also my first experience with a point-and-click adventure game, and I have to say that it did a great job convincing me to play more in this genre. The art style is wonderful, with a rough and hand-drawn feel to the environment and characters, while important items stand out just enough to notice them without losing the immersion in each area. The setting and the story feel very rich without any words or text throughout the entire game, though sometimes it feels like you're not accomplishing anything, just finding things to click on.
The puzzles in the game are varied and plenty, testing your spatial reasoning, forethought, attention to detail, and in a few cases, reaction time. While collecting items to propel the story, there are times when you'll be carrying three or four different things around, but it rarely goes past that, and figuring out which items to combine is never a struggle. Some of the obstacles actually require you to use items separately, but in conjunction with each other, which took me a good deal longer than I care to admit to figure out how it was supposed to work.
There are times you'll sit in front of your computer, just thinking "I don't know what to do..." for 10 minutes, and some of the puzzles are so frustrating that you might just force your way through them instead of thinking through it; however, I don't believe those moments detract from the game that much, because even when you're wandering aimlessly, not noticing that one item sitting on the ground that would let you move on, you're still treated to a beautiful environment and great music which creates a perfect atmospheric feel to the experience.
Overall, I think this game is worth playing, and I don't think $10 is too much to spend on it. There are a few thing's I would have liked different, but that might be because of my inexperience in the genre. It is a challenging, engaging game that will give you 3-6 hours of fun the first time through. The biggest issue for me is replay value, and a second time through will let you focus on the story instead of the puzzles, which I consider a good enough reason to play again.

Double Dragon is a game that resounds in the hearts and breathes of retro gamers from the 80's that is still remembered to this day. The first two games are legendary for their fun game play and co-op goodness that brings joy to those who love to beat baddies up and rescue marion from the clutches of willy. The third game is a mistake. One of the worst games to be made to both coin op AND console but one game tried to make it an enjoyable experience and that being the Nintendo Entertainment System version. While flawed, is very playable. However this isn't about console ports as this collection is a trilogy that is known to many coin op retro gamers and this doesn't disappoint. While Mame does a great experience to the gameplay of the original this increase the enjoyment by taking less hits to kill enemies regardless of the difficulty and has killer remixes from the arrange soundtracks made in Japan on CD. You can also enjoy the original tunes that are remembered from the coin op. You pay $3 per game (game is $5.99 as of the writting of this review) which is well worth the price of admission for this legendary beat 'em up. There is also a mobile version which, let's be honest, Touch screen controls for retro gaming is the WORST form of control. No one I have talked to recommends it or is interested in play a version with that kind of control. I say buy Double Dragon Trilogy if you want to experience the coin op without piracy (like MAME) but if you are wanting a more legal,refined version of the arcade DD games then this is for you. NOTE: These are NOT the NES games only the coin op versions!

Setup is easy, character creation is easy- about the only difficult thing is leaving the game to patch overnight and then trying to find a character name that isn't sitting unused on someone's account.  That, however, is where the feeling of making your own hero ends.
The story starts up- Lex Luthor has come from the future, spinning a tale of a universe subjugated by Brainiac, and he's brought gifts for everyone- exobytes that end up infecting hundreds of thousands of people with superpowers (the PCs).  The Justice League is asked to train the heroes, and the Legion of Evil is tapped to train new supervillains.
What that essentially means is you get tagged to handle everything that they feel is beneath them- you never really get to feel like a hero or villain- instead of Batman, you'll get to be one of the Robins, but in a different costume.  You get told to go here and help someone- it just doesn't feel like you get to be the hero or the villain- instead, you're a piece on a board that both sides are playing off against each other.  Think of it like three-sided chess- the heroes and villains battle each other, but both know that if Brainiac wins, everyone's out of luck.
Honestly, there's a solid game in here, but the presentation needs a lot of work- if I want to be a hero, I don't want to be treated like the sidekick- I want to get out there and save the day from villains, not clean up their mooks and wait for some other hero or villain to swoop in and finish the job.
If the DC thing is important, grab this.  If not, grab Champions Online.  Simple as that.

Although I've been shaking my head, grinding my teeth, and clenching my fist most of the time when I was playing this game, I still think that it deserve a positive review, not because that this game is very good or I want to recommend it to everyone, but because that I actually enjoyed the experience as a whole from the viewpoint of a noir fan.
Before buying this game, it's important to have a proper mindset. If you're looking for a competent stealth game, please do yourself a favor, skip this game. However, if you enjoy noir fiction, it might likely fit your taste. Overall, don't hold your expectation too high or you will be disappointed.
As a 2D stealth game, it fails.
The game looks good at first sight. Darkish sky, pouring rain, everything you'll expect for a noir game to look like. However, before long you'll notice that the graphics glitch frequently. Flashlight beam turns into a square, background changing its color, everything covered in grey... all these make it harder for you to get immersed, not to mention the lack of details in the scenes.
The control feels bad. Except pressing a few hotkeys to toggle run, turn your flashlight on and off, switching characters, and the last one I don't even know what it does, you'll be playing the whole game clicking the left mouse button because everything from movement to interactions are assigned to it. I'm okay with point & click gameplay, but the problem is, even the simple clicking doesn't work reliably in this game. It's common that you clicked somewhere but the character is unresponsive or starts moving to a different direction.
Enemeis (security guards) are stupid and don't response properly. Every gurad has a set patrol route and they are supposed to be triggered and start pursuing you when your enter their vision field or hear the noise you make when you're running around them, but the whole triggering and pursuing mechanism is faulty. Sometimes guards can be triggered miles away, and sometimes they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you even when you're running back and forth above their heads. Fortunately, you'll probably get use to it after two or three chapters.
Monotonous combat. To be honest, combat in this game is close to none. I know it's not that important for a stealth game to have an excellent combat system, but in this game, fighting the enemies is just too tedious and unrewarding. There's only one character that actually has the ability to fight (Wilt, the protagonist) and the only way he can kill enemies is to strangle them, that's all.
Undeveloped upgrade system. You can upgrade your three main characters in the menu by spending the gold coins you collected, but it's unnecessary and doesn't seem to be effective.
Frustrating saving system. There're several checkpoints in each chapter and they're usually far between. As long as one of your characters get killed (one hit kill always!), you'll need to restart from the last checkpoint. Also remember that you'll need to juggle around 2 or 3 characters in most chapters, one little error can cost you the whole effort and send you back to the last checkpoint so you'll need to be extremely cautious most of the time.
Well, that sums up my complaints about this game. Now, it's time to talk about what this game does well. As a noir game, it's pretty competent.
Atmosphere. From my perspective, atmosphere is the core of a noir game. The atmosphere is perceptible in this game, thanks to the background music and visual effects (most of the time). The somberness is there, I can feel it. After getting use to its awkwardness mentioned above, I had a good immersion playing this game and beat the last five chapters at one sitting.
Decent story. The story of this game is not amazing but solid at least. Characters have their own personality and belief. However, it still falls short a little bit in my opinion. There're choices to make in dialogues, which is favorable to me. The ending is quite satifying as well (the ending may be slightly different depending on your last choice).
Good narration and voice acting. I really like the voiceover and the voice acting of Wilt. Voice actings for other characters are fine, the accent can be too strong though.
In general, despite its numerous flaws, I still enjoyed playing this game. For 7 bucks, it's worthy if you ask me.

It's disappointing to see this game getting a mixed score for reasons that seem ridiculous to me. Some complain about the lack of a tutorial while actually you're getting introduced to the possible actions for your characters at the beginning of the game which are self-evident by the way. Others mention the lack of options in the main menue. The game runs in your standard desktop resolution or windowed that's all there is to it although I'm quite confident you could force additional options via your driver settings I saw no reason to do so as Calvino Noir works fine in 4K on my system.
When you first start the game you are greeted with the language options in the main menue and the game got stuck there.
The easy solution I found was to open Task Manager with Ctrl-Alt-Del and closing Task Manager again then clicking on the game icon in the task bar and voila the game worked without a glitch ever after (you only have to do this once at the first start of the game).
The best way to play the game was mouse only for me as it allows the necessary precision for your characters movements.
You will play with up to three characters simultaneously and this gives you opportunities to try out different strategies to achieve your objectives.
The game takes place in Vienna in the thirties of the last century and the Art Deco game world is beautiful to look at.
The Jazz soundtrack and the voice acting are top notch.
I played until the cemetary level in about 4 hours and think I played about a third of the game.
Many reviewers mention the infrequent save points. I can not confirm this. There are more than enough save points and you'll lose only a few minutes if you fail your mission.
The game rewards exploration as you find money throughout the levels which you use to upgrade the stealthiness and movement speed of your characters.
I don't normally review games before I finish them but as Calvino Noir is in the Halloween sale 90% off I wanted to recommend the game to potential buyers asap. If you love stealth games and/or noir games you should try it out. For 1.49 there's not much to loose.
For me the game gets a well deserved 8/10.

7. Stop picking your battles and start taking the fight to the enemy by employing tactics such as
.

XCom Apocalypse is my favorite of all XCom titles, old and new. And - no, not because of nostalgia.
While I'm certainly cherish the challenge of the first two XCom games, and enjoying the tactical shootouts of the newer ones... By the terms of complexity of the gameplay, Apocalypse still has no rival. Well, maybe the first Banner Saga has something common in terms of complexity - but it's another setting and totally another scale of events.
If you're still wandering, what I'm talking about - it's all of the game economics, your actions and their consequences. Yeah, the things I hate in the new XCom games for their inaptitude.
In Apocalypse, you can hire enough soldiers and buy enough venicles to get any unfriendly down. You'll be provided with almost sufficient amount of bright heads for your R'n'D as fast as you want - and without need to wait until someone in the "counsel" decide to throw a bone to you... But, of course, the price is there too. And that price has a name - Responsibility.
You can brake down all the structures in the city block, on some mission while hunting invading aliens... and then it turns out that those buildings were belonging to your main ammunition supplier... not anymore. Or you can raid a local gang hideout, take all their stuff and then sell it on the market... drugs in the first place. And then the Megapol will be asking you questions, and remnants of that gang - asking for your blood. Or you can produce some guns, then sell them on the market - to drop down all guns prices - and goodwill of other marketeers towards you as well.
Almost every organization in Megacity (except for politicians) is vital for the city well-being, so, while you don't have to be really nice with everybody, once you'll turn any of them down to aliens, or simply make them your enemies - you'll do yourself a great problem. In the Enemy Unknown, for example, sometimes it is even beneficial to lose a country or two - you'll faster take some perks for controlling all continent... In the Apocalypse Megapolis, every corporation is invaluable, when it is on your side, and very dangerous, as an enemy.
With all that - no doubt, XCom Apocalypse is a very old game, from the time when even Win95 was uncommon. Some basic gameplay features that works everywhere now, such as tutorial, or underdog difficulty level... aren't applied. Visuals, and the need to tune DosBox, out of any doubt, will turn down the most part of the modern players.
But if you'll look past this, you'll find the XCom being a powerful organisation, with the great capabilities and responsibilities as well. You can send helluva of tanks and rocketeers to meet alien invaders with the ocean of fire... and pay dearly for all shambles you'll make to the city property. As of overall expression, it's like switching from the nowadays Bundeswehr or British Army to the Soviet one. Or changing your BB-gun with .308 barelled rifle. Sure, even the Soviets were not all-powerful. But who's got the better chances to bring down the invasion, and return fire into enemy lair? Same scale goes with the rifles analogy.
My mark is 8/10. Game's quite outdated, and even at start had some flaws, due to the limited development time and pressure from publisher. Yet so far we're still out of better options, despite all the years passed.

This game is exactly what I was looking for!
I previously had bought the game Violett, another point and click that I ended up being immensely disappointed in. This game proved to be everything I had been hoping for in that one.
It tells you right off the bat all significant controls and limits, instead of immediately having you start the game blindly clicking. There are two options to get hints if you get stuck - the lightbulb will make your little robot think of the clever end game that you're attempting to achieve, and hopefully that will help you figure out what steps to take to reach it. If, however, you just aren't getting it, there is the walkthrough book. It won't let you read it right away - it features a little mini game to unlock it, which I found an interesting touch to make you a) earn your help and b) consider if you really want to bother, or maybe you'll try a little harder after all...
The puzzles are challenging but not so much so that you turn into a madly-clicking rage monster. The art is simply adorable, the music suits the tone and won't grate on your nerves after prolonged play. The little animated speech bubbles as means of communication are simple and effective. It's a great little puzzle game to relax with and I've thoroughly enjoyed it so far.

Machinarium is a gorgeous point and click puzzler from Amanita Design, who have also created the wonderful Samorost series and Botanicula. Having played their other titles I can honestly tell you that Machinarium has a similarily beautiful world that you must make your way through to complete the game. The robot city you will explore in this title is extremely detailed, with emotionally moving scenescapes galore. The puzzles featured in this title are also the most challenging of Amanita's catalogue, though this is no criticism. Each puzzle is unique from the last, and will take careful consideration to solve. Just as the wold of Machinarium is complex and detailed, so to are its puzzles. I would highly recommend this title to fans of any of Amanita's work, or those who would enjoy a gorgeous and engaging puzzler to sink a few hours into.

An incredible point-and-click adventure game, with beautiful art, challenging but satisfying puzzles, complex minigames, inventory system, lovely in-game hint system, and great characters.  By the same guys as the much shorter Samorost 1/2 games, but this game is even more beautiful and charming.  Several hours of fun!

Machinarium possesses a universal charm that will appeal to all ages, and to both casual and hardened gamers alike. The setting and tone put me in mind of a Pixar silent film in 2D, with a moderate amount of puzzles, and the addition of a few minigames. Some of the puzzles were quite challenging, but fun, and often logical and solvable if given appropriate thought and study. When I needed a little nudge in the right direction, the ability to access in-game hints was nice. And for when you're really stumped, the inclusion of the comic-strip style handbook of solutions (accessed via a minigame) means you never have to go outside the game to find your answer. This is appropriate for those who enjoy the adventure game genre, but are not willing to grind through the tedium of puzzles that are beyond their ability to solve (myself included).
The artistic style and settings contribute to a somber mood, yet the robotic characters and their animations have a light-hearted and endearing quality. It is a place of quiet meditation, where you become aware of every texture, every sound, and all the small creatures going about their small business. Then there are special moments that bring forth a smile from the deepest parts of your being. One of my personal favorites was the final performance of the street-corner musicians. It was an unexpected joy, a pleasant surprise on my way to somewhere else. Much like the game itself.

This was a fascinating game, and I only had to check google a couple of times to figure things out. Some of the gameplay and puzzlework was a bit convoluted, but if you remember to push the rules and ponder how one test relates to another and you'll be fine. Otherwise a masterfully beautiful and complex game, dealing with a lot of theoretical issues such as choice and it's illusion, humanity in machines, and the machine in humanity.
It wasn't hard to step into the magic circle and suspend disbelief, there was an immediate sense of immersion for this title, which I absolutely loved. The only problems I had, were the somewhat jerky movements of the player character when looking around with the flashlight, and the invisible walls. Once either would happen, I would pull out of the immersive story and go "Oh yeah, I am playing a video game after all."
But otherwise a fantastic title, especially for the narrative. Worth a playthrough honest. 9.9/10 for the minor issues, would feed a wooden child a decaying human head to pass a test again.

Purchased on sale, and overall worth it. I loved the concept behind the game, and the presentation is excellent. Beat it in a few hours, and will probably go back later to finish out the achievements. It's pretty short, so if you're not cool with beating a $10 game in three hours then make sure to get it on sale for $2.
The controls are a little weird, but I believe that might have been because I was playing in windowed mode, and the game was having some trouble positioning my mouse. PROTIP: IMMEDIATELY CHANGE THE AIM MODE TO "TOGGLE" IN THE MENU. Otherwise you have to hold the right mouse button to look at stuff and aim and it sucks.
The game's difficulty almost never comes from control-related challenges anyway- the combat parts of the game are a nice break when they pop up but you have unlimited ammo, regenerating health, cover to hide behind, stealth takedowns, and invisibility camo, so you'll be fine.
The puzzles are my only real issue. I was hoping the game would be more like Metroid and less like Portal- the opening of the game hooked me immediately with interesting challenges to permit use of your suit functions. The middle of the game, however, revolves around jumping through hoops to beat 8 challenges for a very humanlike AI, and while it's justified as much as possible in the story and is overall entertaining to play, it really feels like you're spinning your wheels and not really in the driver's seat of the story.

- Much depth. - EU, US, Asia, Australia, Japan servers.
Cons:
- May be a little repetitive in PvE, especially because of monsters, but it's much more fun in PvP.
At the end what can i say? It's like "Puzzle Quest". Certainly worth more than the current price (8,99 bucks), so skip it just if you don't like RPGs and/or tetris genre.

8.2/10 - A Challenging Stealth Game Dripping With 1930’s Noir!
→ It’s kind of a slap in the face that this game is $15 when the app is only $4; I’ve even heard the app is more fluid and  fun.
I played this game several times and rage-quit, even uninstalling the game several times. The story, atmosphere and voice acting kept making me want to give it another go. Finally, after conquering the first couple of stages I was extremely hooked and committed to finding the necessary solutions to complete the game. I still am stuck on the very final level, but I suck at stealth games and get frustrated after failing so much!
You play as several various hard nosed individualistic survivors of a city that has run rampant with crime. The goal is to prevent this 1930’s city from completely falling into disarray. Each of the 3 characters you play as have individual skills that complement the group and allow you to trek past a heavily guarded underworld for one last chance to save the city.
I like that this was more of an incremental stealth game; allowing you to find some semi-safe spots further strategize your route through sewers, over rooftops and inside some swanky buildings. The graphics, voice acting and story are all top notch, but I just can’t wrap my head around the $15 price tag. It’s only 7 levels and if you don’t suck at stealth games like I do you can completely finish in just a few hours.
Overall, I would value this title at around $3.99 or less even though it’s pretty sweet. I just refuse to knowingly pay 3-4x the amount of the same game as an app.

Borrowed a bit from stealth games, and a bit from multi-character management games plus a unique Noir setting, you get Calvino Noir.

A noir type of stealth game released initially for the smartphones, Calvino Noir tells a story altogether in 7 chapters (divided up into 3 acts). We assume the control of several individuals, each with a different "ability": Wilt can take down enemies by choking them, Siska is an expert at unlocking doors while Arno is the only one who can operate the machinery found in factories and other places. Oh, and The Mole is someone who can get past any guard since he is considered to be one of them.
The premise is very interesting: they set out to uncover the secret of a distillery after stealing some vital documents. Of course, as it is normal in such stories, there's a conspiracy in the background and almost everybody amongst the fat cats of the town is involved. We get to find out about the background of some of the characters as they regularly converse throughout the levels (we can call these cutscenes).
Now, essentially, the game is about getting from point A to point B while enemy guards represent obstacles on each level. Wilt and his gang can run but this generates louder noises. They can use their flashlight but guards can easily notice them if they get to a certain distance. Technically, flashlights are not necessary (the game is not that dark), however, coins are hidden on each level (20 pieces) and only with the use of our torch can we spot them. This is quite the challenge: 1 or 2 can easily remain at the end of each level - thank god the game saves our progress on each stage.
The game looks very nice and while it is mainly presented in black and white it can provide you with an enjoyable atmosphere. I especially liked the big halls or wide streets where the background was still visible in the far distance. I also liked how our flashlight makes certain objects cast their shadows. I wish there was a zoom option to be able to see how detailed the character models are.
And here comes the bad stuff: while the guards react to their fellow colleagues being choked by an unknown intruder they try to locate us (as the source of sound) while being completely disinterested in seeing a couple of dead bodies in a room. They do not really search and once they surveyed the spot in question for a couple of seconds they return to their duties. Because of this the levels where Wilt can be controlled do not really offer a challenge. Still, we get to be shot down due to the clunky controls and the awful hiding mechanism: hiding is possible behind certain objects but the characters do it rather slowly.
Then, of course, we cannot get away from the fact that this is a mobile game port: the main menu has barely any options for settings and the font is huge - they could have just reworked this with the inclusion of some extra graphics options but they did not.
In conclusion, Calvino Noir manages to be a good stealth-based side-scroller game with an excellent noir atmosphere. At the time of writing this review (May 7th) this is 85% off which is an instant grab for those who like the genre.

Calvino Noir lies somewhere between Mark of the Ninja for its side-scrolling, layered level structure and judgment calls of slay-or-spare under stealth, and Gunpoint, with its fedora-and-trenchcoat-clad spy/burglar. On top of these, Calvino Noir adds quite a decent bit of noir aesthetics. Voice acting is also quite good - no cringing sensation of a bad English accent or a worse German one (unlike horrors of, say, Blizzard VAs).
As the name half-suggests, there is a profusion of noir themes of solitary private eye(-ish) protagonist, constant rainfall and muted colour palette. Not sure where `Calvino` comes into play - possibly referring to the Italian author of the same name for some reference or other.
The game consists of seven levels, divided into three acts (3/2/2) and the player controls (eventually) three characters: Wilt, an English `scrambler`, (whose special ability is to choke enemies), Arno (who can operate machines) and Siska (picks locks and spies through keyholes). Each character possesses some common abilities, such as handtorches, which enables the player to collect hidden piles of coins that are used to upgrade character abilities.
The gameplay is a bit of mixed bag - while straightforward in its layout and mission structure, the controls are not particularly comfortable. Abilties are keybound on Q (toggle walk/run), W (torch), E (Swap character) and they are the only keyboard-related input in the game. Navigation and interactions are bound to the mouse and this occasionally result in some difficulties like skipping cover zones while being pursuit (as the game uses checkpoints rather than saves, it might get frustrating at times). It may be different and perhaps better on a PS4, though.
A minor issue is the lack of tooltips on certain parts of the game - character upgrades, for instance, feature two abilities and although it isn`t too hard to work out what they do, it wouldn`t be too difficult to put a tooltip anyway.
Overall, it appears to be a decent, albeit perhaps a bit of niche title. Aesthetically (visual and audial) it stands out far ahead. In terms of gameplay, the aforementioned clunkiness may deter some, but in the long run these can probably be improved via devs, or simply be overcome by players.

However, the aliens get more advanced week after week, and you will commonly find disruptor guns at week 2, harder and harsher UFO's almost every week, new units and will sometimes attack buildings. In the Tactical (ground combat) world you first have a debriefing (Tends to be the same) and the choice between Real-Time and Turn-Based combat. You control X-Com Agents in the field and go hunting for the aliens, but be careful! If you put too many in one place to hunt you might find yourself in a LOT of trouble. You want to pick off as many aliens as possible (UFO Crash landings bring out the most of this) before sending your units into the darkness to find the aliens There are different ranks for each agent, from rookie to commander and to get said ranks you must fight in Tactical. The game has its fair share of bugs.

This game gives you a cheery yet grittily unforgiving take on the bomber raids in WWII. Calm and thoughtful until you make a mistake, then you get slapped with the loss of several crew members and perhaps an aircraft in the brine.
After my fourth engineer departed the aircraft at approximately 500ft up, I started to get the idea of this game. Some call it FTL but WWII and you get to respawn so its fine. I see it similarly, yet it is wanting even more to punch you in the throat as soon as you look away. The respawn and keep going mechanic is deviously disguided as a way to help you yet it is the opposite - if you lose your crew to

incompetence you also lose all thier gear, all thier stats, and all of your bombers gear. Once you get into the decently more difficult missions this makes it almost impossible to survive a mission again, until you start again and do better this time. An engineer or four is fine but if you kill everyone, forget it. And I enjoy that.
The combat is engaging and sometimes stressful - with so many things to manage and no pause button, it forces you to make choices you dont have to make in FTL. Should I devote these next three seconds to giving the rear turret more ammo or taping the engine #4 back together? Never mind, I hesitated for more than a second, and overran the bombing objective.
The mission types are varied (as varied as a bombing games can be, anyway), with campaign system of various styles of bombing missions, recon missions, and others, with factors like various ranges and terrains and weather systems added in for fun. Ive played for eight hoursso far and it looks like I havent reached a third of the way through. It does look like replayability will be quite high on this title though, if you can even make it to the end without getting annihilated.
The customisation and upgrade system plays a big role in crew and bomber development. Again as with time management, you wont have enough money to buy nearly the amount of things you think you should need. (Especially parachutes. Why are there so little parachutes? More decisions about who gets to go home tonight.) I dont see too much that needs to be improved here, but I see spaces it can be expanded in the future (more bombers??).
If you are a fan of WWII games such as war thunder, and crew management style games such as FTL, I would reccomend picking this up for full price. I bought it for £15 and I'd say it is defiately worth it.
Just dont get too attatched to your crew members.

I have always been a fan of the Witcher series ever since I read the books, and let me tell you the games do not disappoint. PROS:
-The story was really well done i was intrigued for most of it with a great ending.
-The music was really well done it wasn't like any of the other games, but what I loved about this

world and characters.
-The voice acting was really well done.

-The combat system definitely has it's problems but what I loved about it is that you can change

I would be lying to you if I said this game is perfect and no problems, but those are so small compared to how great this game really is I love all of the Witcher games but this still holds a special place in my heart. I would definitely recommend this game to any Witcher or RPG fan.

So you're considering buying the original Witcher game...
If you're like me and you're thinking about playing this after the experience of playing The Witcher 3, then you need to adequately prepare your expectations now.
A lot of apsects of this game, are just bad, as much as I hate to say that. If you look through the reviews of this game you'll see a lot of people saying that the combat system is just nonsensical and basically, fundamentally broken. They're right.
In addition, the game has a lot of small things that seem like they would be easier fixes wrong with it. Characters sometimes glitch out in their animations or don't show up where they're supposed to. The game doesn't really hold your hand too much with the quests, meaning you'll often have to search around to try to figure out what you need to do. There's also a number of systems in the game that are pretty obtuse and quite intimidating. There's a crafting system, there's minigames, there's an almost useles talent system for leveling up, and if you want to complete the Witcher Contract side quests you need to hunt down books and journal entries in order to have the knowledge of the creatures before you can turn in their remains for rewards, which is needlessly frustrating. The voice acting is also totally hit or miss. Geralt's voice actor does a good job, but most of the characters, sound super stilted and unenthusiastic, not to mention how many of them have modern American accents in a medieval fantasy setting.
With all that said though, I would still recommend this game. Why? Because it's ten bucks. And what are you getting for ten bucks? At least 40 hours of gameplay in one of the best created fantasy universes in videogames, with a wonderfully crafted storyline that incorporates a great deal of player agency, and is really good at reflecting the consequences of the choices you make.
I love The Witcher series because it's this beautifully done take on a neo-noir storyline and aesthetic molded to fit the epic scale and grandeur of a high fantasy setting.
Couple caveats to this though. If you're thinking of picking this up, even though it is already ten dollars, you'll likely feel even better off if you can get it in a sale, which happens often. In addition, I would totally advocated cheating in this game if you just want to experience the storyline and the choice and consequences rather than slog through all the frustrating combat.
There's a handful of mods on the nexus which make combat easier, but none of which really make it good. I'd recommend trying one of those out. In addition, don't feel bad about using guides or walkthroughs for this game either, although avoid spoilers if you can. The obtuse nature of some of the quests, not to mention how difficult the Witcher contracts can be to track down when you don't know of a certain monster type, justifies this in my opion.
Overall, give it a try only if you want to delve deeper into the Witcher lore and storyline, but don't expect the same sort of experience that's to be found in The Witcher 2 or 3.

Despite the fact that it aged poorly and will probably take younger players some time to get used to, it is still the best TES game in the series and one of the best open world RPGs of all time.
The worldbuilding, gameplay and quests of this game all go hand in hand and work greatly together to immerse yourself into the world of Tamriel. The world feels as alive and real as barely any fanatasy world out there does.
Compared to the leveled item drop systems of the later installments, every single dungeon in this game contains hand placed items from the developers, so exploration is much more thrilling.
Fast travelling from anywhere is disabled and it costs money to travel between the cities, which gives the player more reason to immerse themselves in the game.
It is not possible to play through all factions in the game with one single character. The different factions and their political stances all show different perspectives of the world, and the player finds himself to be a pawn in their game all to soon.
All-in-all, if you like the elder scrolls lore, like stories that are not black-and-white, want a true role playing experience and do not care about bugs or about a classical risk/reward curve too much, this is the game for you.

If you're looking for Skyrim but the older graphics, this isn't the game for you. If you're wanting to see how Skyrim and The Elder Scrolls Online came to be, then it might be worth it for you. If you love the worldbuilding that's been done in Skyrim and other Elder Scrolls games and you're not adverse to some older game design and graphics, then definitely consider this.
For a game that I have much love for, the above might seem to be a lot of qualifications. It's important to understand that Morrowind was the last "PC design" of the ES (Elder Scrolls) games. While the ES games have continued, their design philosophy and approaches to game systems jumped to a whole different track. Oblivion was the introduction of the gameplay systems you see in the current ES games and was an extremely limited feeling game in comparison. It also helped push the ES games from being niche rpgs into a larger recognition.
Who's going to like this game? Folks that have a nostalgia for older game design, and people that love the worldbuilding of ES games and want to get more into the created world. The game has some seriously twitchy technical issues, mainly brought about by how much the hardware and operating systems have changed since it was released and now. You can certainly run it on modern systems, get mods that modify the textures and help fix other things, but there's still an element of software glitchiness you're going to have to deal with.
Do I recommend the game? Most definitely. It's a game that's more...relaxed...in having the player get into stuff and explore the world. It's also a game that has 4 or 5 other games before it, of varying degrees of quality, which helped to inform and shape the design of Morrowind. And the worldbuilding that went in with all of the other games blossoms into life in Morrowind.

Anyone interested in this game should know what they're getting into; I have to say, first of all, that I really enjoyed this game.  Gameplay-wise,  it's an old-school adventure game, in the tradition of Lucasarts, which combines elements of two different genres: 2d shooter, you can fire your gun at robots and take cover to avoid getting shot at, and point-n-click, you can interact with various elements, pick up items and use them accordingly; an interesting aspect is that you gain new abilities by putting the main character in danger. I like the dark, hostile and mysterious atmosphere, reminiscent of Limbo, as well as the story, which balances dry, black humor as well as sci-fi horror.
However, the real problem is that this game, despite its strengths, is not complete; this is only the first episode of what should be a complete season, ala Telltale Games, but, considering that the year of release is 2014, and that as of 2016 there haven't been any new episodes, I doubt we will ever see the end of this story. On top of that, the title nor the description in the home page indicate or even hint that this is only ONE episode, rather than a full game, so this is just false advertising; I bought this game expecting a full experience, not just a part of the story.  In addition that, the first episode lasts only about 4 hours, which is pretty short even by episodic games' standards.
In conclusion, while the game itself is well-designed and engaging, it's incomplete and short, and therefore, unfulfilling. Hopefully, one day we'll play the other episodes, but right know, this is all there is, an appetizer for other courses that we might never know about, and, while tasty, it isn't nearly enough.

A bit of introduction for the game, it is set in a cyberpunk dystopian future, your main goal is to save your 'human' (I won't get to that for obvious reasons, this is all you need to know).

The concept is good, the creativity put into the story it's more than enough, overall it's very fun.
As i mentioned, it's a puzzle platformer.
You have to inspect various things you see on the ground and ceilling, sometimes you have to pick up certain objects, and you need to unlock and do certain things with these objects.
To do this, you have to use a bit of logic, but sometimes you have to try random and crazy stuff aswell, which for me seals the deal, it's not a linear 'do-this-do-this-do-this' type of game.
Puzzles are not amazingly hard, but you still have to burn down your nerves a bit.
I only encountered few bugs during my two playthroughs of this game, biggest one being my character suddenly starting to 'fly' through the walls to get back at a certain point of the map for no reason.
The achievements in this game can be gotten quite easily, but it does REQUIRE two playthroughs, it's impossible otherwise.
What i am not pleased about is that there are some achievement bugs, mainly the one i had, the achievements not being registered until you close the game which creates two problems, the first, some achievements can be missed and you can't go back if you get past a checkpoint, and the second, it might look like you've cheated your way through if you finish a game in one session for example, and suddenly a bunch of achievements are registered at the same time.
I've seen that the achievement problems in this game aren't uncommon at all, people have been complaining about them pretty much since the beginning, sadly, the developers don't see it as a big priority.
Atmosphere in this game can sometimes be slightly boring, but it mostly tends to give you a 'calm' and 'warm' feeling throughout your playthrough.
The music is mostly ambiental/background kind of music, while it's not bad at all, i believe it should've been made available for free (Unless, of course, the OST wasn't made by the devs themselves).

This is a game I find myself replaying. The back story is simple and coherent - aliens invade, some people sympathise, others get infiltrated. Hold them off while you learn then take the fight to them.
The graphics are a bit simple by today's standards but they work well enough to get the detail across. Game play is turn based but still keeps you engaged and with squad based combat each turn flows well.
The AI is good. Your foes take realistic tactical and strategic moves against you, and you will find yourself falling behind if you don't move to recover from mistakes.
The plot is well structured, and while it is basically linear (as is the tech tree) there is ample opportunity to do some sandbox play along the way. Even thought the game world is limited to the one city, I like the political dimension of trying to keep the various suppliers on good terms with you. Take too much of a heavy hand when dealing with the aliends and the resulting damage to the city might end up with no one prepared to sell vehicles or weapons to you. This becomes less of a driver in the mid-game as your X-COM becomes independent and you are selling more than buying. In late game when start to invade the alien dimension this effectively disappears as most of the conflict happens there rather than the city.
For new players to the franchise, especially with XCOM 2 on the horizon, I recommend taking the opportunity to play this as well. And for the old hands, what are you waiting for?

This was a seriously unappreciated game when it came out, outside of Czech republic and Poland that is. It's one of my most beloved games and here's why.
It's really quite amazing, and does something no other RTS I've seen. It combines RTS basics with RPG elements and a great, original story. The characters (the team your control) are unique, have their specific voiced lines and play an important role in the story, they're not just units you can crate in a factory. You're stuck with the soldies you get and if they die, they're gone for the rest of the game. Think of it as a mix of the team based Wasteland with the classic base building of Command and Conquer etc.
If you're a book reader and are fimiliar with Wolfgang Jeschke, more specifically the book "The Last Day of Creation", you pretty much know the story by now, since it's been heavily inspired by it.
There are two campaigns (American and Russian) that each have multiple paths.
The basic plot: A new element is found, Siberit/Alaskit, that is higly radioactive but wields an incredible power. Using this element, scientists discover a way to use it to travel back in time. There are two campaigns, so there are 2 countries (USA/Russia) traveling back in time to secure the resource, mine it up and move it to the location where their respective countries will be in 2 million years. So you're transported to the prehistoric, pliocene epoch with exact mission. It's a one way ticket only.
I don't want to say more so that I don't spoil the story of the game, but expect multiple universes/futures. It does this pretty well, and suprisingly, doesn't get as confusing and convoluted as it usually does.
There's branching story lines, decision to be made and you can play as all sides of the conflict.
As I said, characters you can use are limited, with permanent death being used. You have 4 basic character jobs (soldier, mechanic, medic, builder) and you can change their jobs on the fly in the missions. Everyone has jobs they're good at or close to useless if your ignore those. The skills shift throughout the game depending on what you have the characters do. So every character is unique and special, you really start to find your favourite characters, where even if they die and you're about the complete the mission, you'll be reloading the mission.
The most important resource in the game are crates. These get teleported in from the future, but since this technology still hasn't been mastered, these drop at random points on the map. So in order to get these, you'll have to go and actively search for them while weaking your camp and putting the scounts in danger.
There's one issue that people have with the game, and that is that the english voice acting is supposed to be pretty bad. I've only played it in the original czech dubbing, so it was never an issue for me, although it certainly isn't great either.
It's my favourite RTS of all time, and I just hope more people would discover this gem of a game.
The game was developed by Altar Interactive in 2001, and it was their first big game. Or not an official one, the community is still very much alive with this one. Having Steam Workshop capabilities certainly helps.
