Okay, I'll admit it now: I own the "collector's edition" from PC too, so my hours played is WAY under-reported on Steam.  Probably something like 1k hours played, and I'll go back to it plenty of times.  I even have an older computer still built to PLAY said game.
X-Com Apocalypse is probably the defining idea of what an X-Com game should be.  The designers are all gaming deities who did the best game that might ever exist for the RTS genre.  Now on to a proper review:
Graphics: Okay, this game was made in 98 I think.  It LOOKS it.  But there's still a lot of details to be found in it.  And you didn't really buy it for the graphics now did yo u?
Sound/Music: Again, it was made in the late 90s.  I usually play with the sounds on and the music off.  But for a while I did play with the music on.  It was suitably creepy at times when it needed to be.
Overworld gameplay: Oh where to begin?  Fantastic.  This is the strategy side of things.  You have the options of buying additional bases, training your troops, starting/cancelling research jobs. make friends out of the govervment factions and playing with the in game economy (because your government is a bunch of stingy folks who start out mildly hating you, go figure).  The economy is important to make you enough money to hire more troops, build more bases and equip your aircraft (which go through missiles at an alarming rate).  Plus, this is the side where you WILL have to fight UFOs from.  Which takes a lot of firepower at the midway point.
Tactical gameplay: This is the slightly micromanagy part of the game, and I have seen a few issues from time to time.  You can either go with the traditional X-com turn based option, or you can go with a full RTS combat.  Whichever you pick is up to you.  The aliens tend to be aggressive enough to warrant a defensive arrangement.  Humans (alien controlled or just people who you decided to hit up for some money...) generally range from aggressive to fleeing in terror at the sight of you.  The major downsides are that Psi powers have only 4 functions (more would have been nice, but it's an older game) and that your troops even in armor tend to want to stand and shoot (but again, it's an older game).
Some odd bugs: Occasionally I send out 18 troops to hit a downed UFO, the tactical map shows me only having 13.  Go figure.  YES, Steam has a wonderful DOS client analog for this game, but it still will crash usually after 45 minutes to an hour.  SAVE OFTEN.
TLDR: What the hell are you still doing reading this review?  BUY THIS GAME NOW!

Where do I even start? X-Com! this one was probably the very best!
The amount of detail they put into making the world, all the items, weapons, equipment, vehicles, aliens, enemies, entities, factions, right down to level design and overworld design - this game will have you totally immersed, whether or not you care for the graphics.
You can carry out raids on enemy factions/gangs for some vigilante justice, you could even choose when you want to go on a mission, either by pre-empting an alien alert in a building, or letting the alert call you in, and even then, you could totally ignore it and let the aliens infest the building and ultimately, let the aliens take over that faction!
There's a working economy, you'll start off as a buyer in the market, in order to equip your troops, but the gains you make from raiding enemy factions, and collecting alien technology means that you can eventually turn a profit on top of your organisation's (X-Com!) income from the Senate. Prices do change depending on supply (albeit only a little, but it was great they put it in); and of course, the world reacts to what you do on the market too, if you sell dangerous alien weaponry en-masse, don't be surprised to see it being used against you on the streets!.
Combat; you will want it to be slow-paced and turn-based, even if there is an active real-time mode, because you want to think every action through, and make sure your squads are prepared to react to whatever contingencies arise, and proceed effectively and efficiently to gain the best mission outcomes.
Do too much damage to the building, or injure or kill civillians, and expect it to show up on your bill, as well as a reflection in your relationship with that faction (a totally hostile faction can mean that they may outwardly attack your bases or personnel on the overworld, or if the faction is an infrastructure provider or an arms dealer; you'll find that their services will be denied to you - i.e. taxis will not deliver your new recruits, ship manufacturers will stop selling you ships, Android alliances will stop allowing you to recruit androids, hospitals can stop providing you medkits); of course, if you blast enough craters into the building, it could simply crumble down around your squad, wiping them all out. This of course, also means that there are destructible environments, every block on the map can be flattened to dust and ashes.
The research tree is another magnificent mechanic in the game, from quantum physics, to xenobiology, every bit of research leads to meaningful discoveries of powerful technology and understanding of your enemies, where you can harness the power of their weapons against them, to discovering weakesses they have, or possibly even develop bio-weapons that will be lethal to them only! D: Research enough tech, and you'll find yourself being able to manufacture enough weapons to outfit a small army, with your very own engineering division.
All the flavour text about any research you do, to the lore of the world, as well as any factions and entities have intriguing information about themselves that will keep your interest endlessly.
If you like turn-based, squad based strategy, mixed in with a management sim, look no further :D

Like all games i played when i was younger, i'm still not entirely sure if it was a really good game, or if it was just the fact that i was much younger.  In any case, i do remember also having played bad games when i was younger, and i remember having a blast playing Original War (over and over and over again), so i guess the fact that i was impressionable didn't make everything seem much better than they are.  Think what hooked me to this game was:
- the fact that some characters are persistent: if they do well in one mission, they'll be better when they appear later; if they die in a mission, they're gone,
- the starts and branches of the game are interconnected story-wise,  (although the story itself isn't all that great)
- and you only ever have a limited number of characters and resources to play with, so strategy actually matters.
Well, and it's a really good game.  I tried playing RTSes and didn't enjoy them for very long for the most part (C&C Red Alert was fun, for example, until everyone figured out that it's just a race to a tank rush), but really enjoyed this one for a pretty long time.
All that said, it's also a really old game.  The gameplay is still there, and can't help but feel nostalgic for games where the only instruction you receive is "Survive" and if you don't, game over.  But the graphics are dated and a lot of things we take for granted in modern games (like detailed step-by-step guidance as to what to do next and well-nigh impossibility of failure or even penalty of any real sort) are simply not there.  Although, to be honest, i find that refreshing and kind of like that.  No idea if you will.

The core of the game is solid. The missions are fun and the upgrade system is interesting enough to keep playing to see the different upgrades. However, it feels like an early access game not a fully finished. Don't get me wrong, the game is good I'm having a lot of fun playing it, but a few updates could take this from a good game to a great one.
- The ability to pause would be very nice. It can get overwhelming when there are 4 different things happening at once; engine is on fire, unmarked fighters, a crewmember is injured, you're approaching the target. Pausing works great in FTL and I think this game could benefit from it too.
- Different aircraft, I assume this would take a lot of work, but it would be awesome to play this game with a B-17 or B-29.
- More mission variety. I realize the game is about a ww2 bomber, so there's not too much you can do, but the missions can get repetitive after a while. Could do a mission you have to escort a VIP to North Africa/ Russia, etc Maybe some long distance missions where you go to bomb Germany and would have to worry about fuel. Or missions in the North Atlantic bombing uboats to protect convoys. Similar to whats already in the game but a change of scenery would make the missions feel like less of a grind IMO.
Overall I like it a lot. If this kind of game interests you, it is done very well.

Calvino noir, is a fun little Black and white stealth game, where you are controlling different characters through the game with each their own abilities. Switch between them to get different tasks done.

Amazing. If I had to pick a word. That's what I would use.
Dripping in atmosphere, drama, grit, good writing, meticulous details everywhere and wonderful voice acting.
If you love film, 1930s era pieces, art, casual adventures, or exquisite nostalgic homages then this is a must buy for you. There are some issues, controller issues, no option screen, little quirks - but they pale to how fanastic this title is.
Our Video Gameplay/Commentary is here:
Our full detailed review is here:

Calvino Noir is fun but also has some severe flaws.
The art style, music, narration and voice acting are all good ( bar Siska's ), and they blend in rather well. You quickly get use to the greyscale art style, where some colour is only added to help attract your attention to certain objects and places.
Even in some cases the colour can be rather subtle, like a hint of soft yellow in a sea of grey.
The story isn't bad either, although some of the dialogue can be rather cringey at times. This is mostly due to the fact that it's a Noir game set in the 1930's.
The main issues are the checkpoint system, and the character movement mechanics; and that it seems to have been designed for iOS and tablets first. As a result you need to do everything with a single mouse click. You move with a click, you stop, you open doors, select items, and change characters that way.
There are no real options either.
Some parts of the game can easily take 30+ minutes and accidentally dying or being spotted because of the slow character movement and clunky system is horrible. As the checkpoint saves can mean you're suddenly set back that 30+ minutes.
It's extremely annoying, as the characters can't make turns or go up and down stairs rather well. They walk, stop, turn, stop, then move. In that time the guards would easily have spotted you and shot you. They are rather trigger happy, as they shoot the second they see someone.
If you can get by the controls and checkpoints the game is rather enjoyable. Especially if you like stealth Noir games. It's rather fun.
I only wish I could choose a third option for the review though, such as MAYBE. The issues either make or break the game for many and I hope the little PC Gameplay footage below can help folks decide.

The moody black and white thriller is inspired by film noir, based on exploratory and sneaking through dark and post-World War I Vienna during 1930’s.
You are taking control of four different characters during game where main character is supposed to be Wilt, written with dark poetic monologues filled with hate against city along with everyone else. Story is starting out of the sky with a single phone call where mistery lady is asking for a man with particular set of skills where Wilt jumps in with his espionage and blackmail knowledge looking for money and nothing else. As in movies, an easy mission turns into conspiracy filled with twists and turns where innocent Wilt is drawn by accident.
Now there is a slight disparity between 2D platformers and these kind of games settled in this ambient so overall immersion is lost since begining, though dark and mistery story followed by events and reveals of new characters keeps you occupied.
Through game you will discover new people and their backside stories where further into game you can make choices suited to those or only for your desire, outcome will not change but getting more info and a bit more of story behind is always interesting. Fact that your main plot character Wilt will literally dissapear after couple chapters due to slight disagreement with mystery lady “Siska” is making whole situation a bit more confusing where you can clearly feel gaping hole during progress.
Siska, young but determined lady to destroy corruption and underground criminal along with Arno, old military Wilt life-friend even though they meet in unpropriate situation comes with unique skills which will help you to make progress and get unnoticed from guards and usually only guards. As I mentioned Wilt will dissapear from game for a while so knocking out enemies is not a option anymore although eventually we get into control of moll from that same underground criminal organization which will be helpful since we can move through world without being noticed, with him ofcourse while rest of crew need to follow on their own stealth way.
Bad side comes up with frustrating feeling after dying every time along with incosistent AI where sometimes you can get killed by one shot on sight or you can simply sprint through guards despite you being noticed. Checkpoints in some bigger levels are rather few and far in between while some of mechanics doesnt work smooth as they should and it will depend on RNG factors will you succeed or not. Wilt and his knockdowns will need to be perfectly accurate in terms of when you sprint to get faster to guard since getting closer even from behind doesnt make your knockdown faster along with fact that characters will often get stuck on ladders or unexpected places. You cant go over feeling that simply this genre with this kind of gameplay is not made for stealth game and yet every new chapter will delivere nothing more then already seen.
Concept art on the other hand is more then amazing, always rainy and dark Vienna with many buildings and structures including small indoor objects deliver what they are supposed to do. Dialoguess and monologues are sometimes poetic yet still original with different accents where you can feel how natural conversation would be, well aside from repetetive sentences when you try to direct them.
Controls on PC are rather simple and they are making click and point genre from this title despite developer claiming that this is not that and its recommended to be played with controller. Problem occurs with fact that you need to control 3 different characters most of the time concurrently and that can be done only with mouse since you have enough time to choose second one while you direct your primary character at the end of the screen. There’s a lot of backtracking which makes you play same area even 3 times with really slow moving around fairly large facilities. Some of you will probably overlook these cons due to interesting and intriguing story but only if you are prepared for what is waiting you.

The third entry in the Xcom-series tries to do something different from the first one (unlike the second entry), and while it fails in many ways it also succeeds on some important points.
The bad things are that the alien design and atmosphere of the game is weird, bad-weird. The aliens look like some kind of dr. Seuss-creations, and the graphics are full of vibrant colours, likening the game to a childrens book in look would not be far off the mark, which is weird considering that it probably hopes to evoke a mood of suspense like the first two games.
The game also offers a choice between real-time or turn-based combat, but both versions are worse than if they had just focused on one or the other. The turn-based combat is not as crisp as in the prior games, and the real-time combat is clunky as well.
However, the game offers a large city full of corporations with their own agenda, so there is a lot of interplay going on between various factions, which is impressive and fun. The levels are complex and fully destructible with a rudimentary physics-engine, so shoot outs are often interesting.
The complexity of the strategic playing field married with the tactical combat makes the game interesting, however, it is not as good as the first game. It is not a step forward from the second, but a step sideways, introducing both good elements and bad ones.
PLAY IT.

If I had to describe Morrowind in one word it would be uncompromising.
Morrowind feels like a game the developers wanted to make instead of a game made for mass appeal. It is hard to pin down why this game was, and for many gamers still is such an incredible game, especially since the combat and graphics did not age very well.
The best parts by far are the story and the world of Morrowind and the exploration within it. What makes exploring so great in this game is that you can do it at your own pace. You didn't need to talk to every NPC and accept every quest out of fear that you can't open a door or an item won't spawn. You could walk around with a quest item without ever realizing its importance, you could even sell or lose an important item making it impossible to complete a quest.
And that's why Morrowind is such a phenomenal game because you could fail, because you could walk around for over 20 hours with a quest item as your strongest weapon only to realize that you have to choose between keeping it or compleating an important quest, and most importantly because you can play it your way and experience the game in a different way than many other gamers.
The only thing I regret after playing Morrowind is that I can no longer play it for the very first time.

I don't tend to like point and click games. Mostly because if the puzzles and controls aren't perfect then you can waste alot of time trying to find a solution that you already found. For example, an early puzzle invoules putting something on some train tracks. This was the very last step of the puzzle, and I spent maybe 5 minutes putting this thing on the tracks, trying to solve the puzzle, and having it fail. After many annoyed clicks I discovered that if you lower your mouse down to the other side of the tracks you can put it there. The problem is the click box for the wrong side of the tracks was so big, that you would assume that that is all you could do with it. Suffice it to say, I was very annoyed at this. I played through, and figured that was an one off event.
In the very next screen I figure out the puzzle in a reasonable amount of time, but the very last step was bugged. As in I would click on the thing, and it wouldn't work. After maybe 10 minutes of cursing at it, I quit out of the game, and come back to it the next day. The exact same action I was trying to do before works the first time. It was just that the game wasn't reading my clicks correctly.
On the very next screen, I get stuck again. This time because the puzzle wanted me to stand if a very exact spot for it to work. After reading a walk through, and finding out that I was doing the right thing, I tried different spots and quickly was able to continue.
I play the game for about another 45 minutes until I run into the same bug of the game not reading my clicks. At this point I've had enough of the game.
I really wanted to like this game, but the fact that the game could ruin the experience in many different ways put me off in a very bad way.

Awesome concept carried out decently. The combat is good and is mostly fluid, and PvP is a lot of fun. The quests can get a bit dull, but they break the regular MMO grind by throwing in boss fights every few missions and lots of rewards for exploration and story completion. The story itself is decent enough, especially in Gotham where you take on Bane and Scarecrow. The only major flaw in the story is the HORRENDOUS voice acting for the Brainiac characters and most of the cops in the nightclubs and police stations. The voice acting on those characters is so laughably awful it completely breaks immersion and sometimes actually makes me laugh aloud. However I will say that the voice acting on the hero and villain NPCs (Joker, Superman, etc.) is fantastic. It's really awesome to fight alongside Batwoman to take down Scarecrow, or Superman to take down the Brainiac horde. There are also some annoying things that should be addressed:
1) When flying/running near enemies, if they attack you just once it slows your movement speed drastically, making navigating the city below the rooftops nearly impossible.
2) Sometimes stun abilities just won't work on certain enemies with no explanation as to why. There was a boss fight in which we fought Power Girl and she was regular size, no outstanding special abilities, but was completely immune to being stunned or knocked down, which was annoying because my character was control and that's the entire point of my build.
3) The flow of melee attacks can be awkward at times, mostly due to desync between players.
4) Enemies that have stun and knockdown use it CONSTANTLY, and you have to sit there spamming shift to get out of it.
Overall I give the game 7.5 out of 10, and would give it an 8 if they patched some of the player desync issues.
ALSO, forgot to mention, the game has a decent community and a lot of older players are helpful to new players.

If you're an avid player of the brawler genre (yes, we still exist) Double Dragon Trilogy is a no-brainer. At $5.99, young gamers can also now experience the history of the virtual mean streets during the late 1980's. The old school can even meet the new school online for cooperative play. What else do you need?
Not much. Double Dragon was never complicated- street punks kidnap girlfriend, must get girlfriend back. This simple premise was flawlessly presented with no dialogue at the start of the original in a matter of seconds. Azz-kicking ensues thereafter.
There’s been plenty of sequels, remakes, and reworks over the years, and none of them were too shabby (save for the terrible one-on-one fighting entry that was Double Dragon V). With Trilogy, you should expect more arcade faithful versions of the original three, rather than the fondly remembered and popular NES ports. I’m sure we can all agree that Double Dragon II for NES is the superior version, but the original was a great game in its own right.
The very best in the series, Double Dragon Advance, incorporated skills from previous entries like the headbutt, spinkick, hyper knee, mount, stomp, wall jump, grab, and parry to name a few. These powers complimented each other for a furious festival of flowing fists and feet. You won’t find such a diverse arsenal of moves in Trilogy- only the simplistic fighting styles that graced arcades back in the golden age.
That being said, don't assume the most recently released homage, Double Dragon Neon, is the superlative entry. While it did wield an impressive move list and an insider's nostalgia, it never felt quite like a Technos game. For those looking for the genuine experience starring their beloved super-deformed characters and pick-up-and-play controls, Trilogy is the way to go, even if the platforming has aged beyond rationality by today's standards.

Ever felt like jumping from truck to truck while you were staring out of your window on a car ride? Then this game will do the truck for you ... I mean the trick. Clustertruck will have you dreaming of trucks. And jumping from truck to truck while standing on a truck and looking at trucks. In Clustertruck, the truck drives you. Crazy. I just cant stop trucking of trucks. Wait until you see the ability in the truck that will let you backtruck to the last truck you truck truck trucktruck. Dont truck the trucks. Truck me. Trucktrucktruck TRUCK!
Clustertruck is all about skill and enjoying the gameplay. No story, no stats, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I enjoyed clustertruck because it allows a lot of freedom in how you play it. You can pick between abilities and you can choose your own pace in most levels. It often rewards you for taking risky jumps and going fast but it always felt like it was possible to take the slow path too. It is possible to find a cheaty route through stages on the first playthrough and I like that they left that kind of thing in the game. I often tried to get a good time on my first playthrough, so it took a lot of attempts but it always felt good to take a quick route through the stage.
I found the game a bit more challenging than it looked from just watching videos and even some early stages had me trying for a bit. There are speedruns of it out there and since there is no story, it will only spoil you the graphics and level designs, but I highly recommend watching the beginning of a speedrun to get a feeling for the game. It took me about five hours to beat the game, but the speedrun beats all the stages in less than 25 minutes. Did I say it was all about platforming skill? Dont pick it up if you've never played a 3d platformer in your life.
The music is just great, it makes the game so much more energetic. The graphics are minimalistic, but somehow it still looks gorgeous in its own way. The developers have made two updates so far that added new levels for free. There is an integrated level editor, but a lot of the game assets seem to be missing in the editor right now. Custom maps can be shared through the game itself but currently there are very few high quality maps in the workshop. This is the one thing I am really sad about, although I guess the developers are only partially to blame, but I really hope this will be better in the future. The other shortcoming is that it is kind of a short game, can be finished in 3h - 10h depending on skill. Got it on sale, not sure if I would pick it up for the full 15$. But the content it does give you is very polished and certainly worth your time.

Like all games i played when i was younger, i'm still not entirely sure if it was a really good game, or if it was just the fact that i was much younger.  In any case, i do remember also having played bad games when i was younger, and i remember having a blast playing Original War (over and over and over again), so i guess the fact that i was impressionable didn't make everything seem much better than they are.  Think what hooked me to this game was:
- the fact that some characters are persistent: if they do well in one mission, they'll be better when they appear later; if they die in a mission, they're gone,
- the starts and branches of the game are interconnected story-wise,  (although the story itself isn't all that great)
- and you only ever have a limited number of characters and resources to play with, so strategy actually matters.
Well, and it's a really good game.  I tried playing RTSes and didn't enjoy them for very long for the most part (C&C Red Alert was fun, for example, until everyone figured out that it's just a race to a tank rush), but really enjoyed this one for a pretty long time.
All that said, it's also a really old game.  The gameplay is still there, and can't help but feel nostalgic for games where the only instruction you receive is "Survive" and if you don't, game over.  But the graphics are dated and a lot of things we take for granted in modern games (like detailed step-by-step guidance as to what to do next and well-nigh impossibility of failure or even penalty of any real sort) are simply not there.  Although, to be honest, i find that refreshing and kind of like that.  No idea if you will.

I can't think of an example of a game, that is so brilliant like Original War, and yet receives barely any attention.
The story follows an armed conflict between the world's superpowers, which fight over a control of a newly-discovered natural resource called siberite, with the twist that they sent their soldiers to fight two million years into the past by using an alien-constructed time machine, which uses that same substance they fight for as a fuel. While this sounds like a cliche B-movie (and it kinda is), every other aspect of this game is rather unique (some might say, pardon the pun, original)
The game could be characterized as RTS. You build bases, in those bases you explore new technologies, build vehicles, defense towers etc. The game however features many RPG elements. As sending people to past is demanding, you only get a set number of soldiers for each mission. They all have names, personality, and skills, and they are at your disposal for the entire campaign. If you lose a soldier, you won't get a replacement, you are one man short for the rest of the mission. If you lose a skilled soldier that has been fighting with you since the beginning of the campaign, not only does this hurt your performance (you no longer have that guy that could all by himself clear out a small enemy base), you also lose a person that talked to you and other soldiers, made jokes, expressed concerns and otherwise interacted with the entire unit.
There are many more aspects of the game and it's gameplay, that could be considered innovative, but I will leave exploring those to people reading this. If you are considering buying this game, then I can only recommend that you do. You won't get just another Red Alert or Age of Empires clone, I can guarantee you that you will get a game that is unlike anything you've ever played.

If you are new to the plot of Resident Evil then I'd say you're excused only if you were too young or not even born back in '96 and missed any info about it since then: anyway as a member of STARS you get sent on a mission to find out what's exactly happening in a mension outside Raccoon City and things go bad quickly, very bad.
This "remake of a remake" features a few more graphical improvements over the 2002's GC version while still retaining most of its old school feel.
-improved graphics really make the game shine, with nice 3d models and pretty sharp backgrounds
-the good, ominous soundtrack is still effective
-new control mode provides a more responsive and fluid experience, old tank controls are still there though
-still sports a great atmosphere, especially in the mansion level
-the mix of exploration, combat and puzzles remains very satisfying
-offers a decent length if you're not powergaming through it, I'd say around 5 hours per character
-ok story, pretty flat characters as per usual in the series
-the inventory management can get a tad tedious, same goes for the need for backtracking and the plethora of unskippable door animations...but then for most it's all part of the charm
-some fixed camera angles can feel awkward, and sudden camera changes can be annoying
-voice acting feels a bit so-so overall
-slow paced menus for saving, item boxes etc can be dull
The fact Resident Evil can still provide a very effective survival horror experience after 20 years is a testament to its quality: even past the rose tinted glasses there's no denying its gameplay is simply good whether you're exploring the mansion, trying to not be killed by a nasty bioweapon or solving one of the game's infamous puzzles. It simply works, and works well: sure the game might not be "scary" but it has a strong atmosphere going for it and can still surprise you a few times.
The game is still as old school as ever though apart from the new coat of paint and improved controls. So expect to have to manage your inventory quite often and, when you fail to do so, be forced to trek back to an item box to free space or simply get a puzzle item you've forgotten behind. Also the titular "slow-unskippable-door-animation-for-every-room" can get dull after a bit, but if it gets on your nerves too much there seems to be a mod for it. Still, well, changing these mechanics would take away some of Resident Evil's charm itself or lower the sense of danger.
Whether you're looking to experience the game for the first time or simply want to jump in it again this HD remaster is simply the place to be and is worth the purchase; it's pretty much faultless if you can go past its sometimes clunky mechanics.

Bomber crew is a charming little WW2 bomber sim where you control seven crew members of an Avro Lancaster, From the pilot, to the gunners, to the bombardier. It's blocky artstyle is cute, functional, and lends itself well to the game. Crew members names can be personalized to your liking, however their looks are randomly generated. All in all, There's a lot of potential here for this game, but there are some things that the Devs should add to make the better.
As it stands, Bomber crew is not an easy game. Especially in it's current state. The first couple missions are easy enough. Go here, bomb target, shoot down a couple planes, take some reconnaissance photos, return to base. Pretty fun. But soon, (Very soon) the game spikes in difficulty. Throwing waves and waves of fighters (That all need to be individually marked by you for your gunners to fire at them) and walls of flak at you, while you struggle to have your engineer run around repairing all the damage and healing the gunners, if they're not already dead. (Yes, there is Permadeath) Not only that, but you also have to keep targeting waypoints for your pilot to follow, less he fly off in the wrong direction and Whoops! There goes all your fuel. There's been talk of adding a "Pause" or "Time slow" button to help with these frantic moments. Only time will tell if that much needed feature does get added in. Personally, I'd rather have an "Action queue" mechanic like it most other RTS's, where you shift click multiple orders to a crewman and they do them all in the order you clicked them.
Here's a concise list of Pros and Cons I noticed during my time so far with Bomber Crew.
Pros:
-Charming Art Style
-Lots and Lots of customization and upgrades, both in plane and crew.
-Addictive gameplay
-In-depth management
-TONS of potential
Neutral:
-Soundtrack is nothing special
-Extremely arcadey physics, but what do you expect? DCS?
-Not a historical representation of WW2 aircrews. Please don't take it as such.
-No real story. It's WW2. Sometimes you bombs historically significant targets.
Cons:
-Large difficulty spike within the first couple hours, which can lead to frustration.
-Only one bomber, being the Lancaster (Possibility of more being added later)
-Management is not efficient. Everything needs to be done individually, and in some cases simultaneously
-Missions get samey. Bomb this depot, bomb this artillery location, deliver supplies to this pilot.
-Crew member's appearance cannot be customized. Who you get is what you're stuck with.
-Not enough feedback to the player. I always seem to die because somehow a fire starts in the cockpit and the pilot jumps out and then the plane just nosedives into the sea.
This is a very hesitant recommendation from me. I want to love this game. I REALLY do. But there's still a good amount of things that the devs should look into before this I feel I can wholeheartedly recommend it. But I recommend it here anyway, because I want the game to be successful, the more succesful it is, the better chance of having these issues fixed.

I really wish I could click that "Yes" button under "Do you recommend this game?" more than once. This game is just, whoa. This is the peak of this game's franchise. Its successors fail to live up to Morrowind's greatness. Steam only shows I have played roughly twelve hours of this game, but before I got it on Steam, I played this nonstop. Around 500 hours or so. I couldn't even pour a hundred hours into Oblivion or Skyrim combined. Morrowind's successors fall flat. Anyway, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Story
+ Lore in general (lots of lore, of which is all interesting)
+ Tons of detail
+ Lots and l o t s of sidequests, that all grab you in (Skyrim had boring sidequests and there were too many of them)
+ The main quest is actually good
+ Super extensive enchanting and potion making (seriously you can create some really ridiculous things, that are otherwise impossible to make in the later titles)
+ Lots of freedom (no invisible walls, you can permanently kill whomever you want, etc.)
+ Honestly, this is a true RPG. You cannot deny that. (Skyrim isn't even a real RPG, and Oblivion is just a watered down RPG)
+ This game actually allows you to roleplay (you can create a Shrek-esque character and live in the swamps of the West Gash Region for Christ's sake)
+ The game world feels huge, even though it actually isn't
+ For a game this old, it has a lot of pretty impressive mods (HIGHLY recommend Tamriel Rebuilt and the graphics/sounds overhaul)
+ Has a construction kit for mod developers (for some reason the Steam version doesn't come with it, but you can download it here:
)
Neutrals:
+/- The combat can put some people off, but I honestly like it. It sticks to the roots of its predecessors. This is the main reason why this game is so hard for some people to get into.
+/- The fast travel system, where you pay for Silt Strider (or boat) rides to available areas. I personally enjoy this method of fast travel, but as for people coming from Oblivion or Skyrim, I can see why this would put them off. (I like it because it's both realistic and it promotes on-foot exploration)
+/- The graphics onbviously do not age well, but honestly, graphics don't mean everything. Besides, there's always the overhaul mod, if your PC can handle it.
Cons
- Modding the game can sometimes be frustrating, as sometimes mods will easily cause the game to become more unstable. (as if it wasn't unstable already)
- I haven't noticed many compatibility problems with Windows 10 on this game except the resolution issue. When I got this on my gaming PC, it would still show the toolbar (with the exit, minimize, and enlarge buttons) at the top of the window despite being in fullscreen. This is easily fixed using MGE (it allows you to play at your native resolution; I'm not sure about multiple displays, as I have not tested that.)
- You're an n'wah from the start. (not a real negative, just being humorous)

Spore is basically what No Man's Sky should've been: creative, charming and just straight-up fun. Even though this game is an old fart by today's standards, it's still a damn good game, if a bit flawed. You're basically allowed to create your own species and civilization as you go from a microorganism in a space-faring civilization in a positively GARGANTUAN sandbox. Not really much to say other than this game is very fun and very entertaining.
However, there are two big flaws with this game: due to EA severing ties with Steam and forming Origin, the Steam-version's online capabilities are pretty much gone for good, meaning you're either gonna have to be content with the Maxis-created creatures, or make a lot of creatures of your own. That, and the game is severely buggy and unstable: there's a whole WIKI PAGE dedicated to all the glitches in this game, and while that's understandable, given the scope rivals and even surpasses The Elder Scrolls and Fallout for sheer byte usage, it's still extremely annoying if you're save file for the civilization you worked so hard for ends up corrupting and forces you to restart.
Otherwise, it's an amazingly fun game and central part of my childhood. If you have a kid who would like to play a fun, creative, kid-friendly game, or just want a universe to explore, I recommend this game, especially since $20 is a steal. Far better than anything No Man's Sky got, anyway.

DotEmu has done other great retro compilations before like the fantastic Raiden Legacy but this package (which was ported over from mobile phones) is lazy and does badly by the legacy of Double Dragon. The games are artificially sped up to compensate for the slowdown that was normal in the arcade versions and you can't toggle that off to play the original way. The original music is not emulated properly and the available re-mix music is awful and sounds like it was done on a mid-90s MIDI keyboard. They also removed any ability to coin up which breaks Double Dragon 3 as that game uses additional credits as a means to buy powerups.
There are modern resolution options, local and online multiplayer (though
is playing this online and you can rebind all your controls, though the Xbox 360 controller buttons are not properly represented in-game.
If you just want to play Double Dragon and aren't a retro enthusiast who wants the original games properly preserved, this is OK I guess. The Fall is a side-scroller action puzzle-based adventure game set within a dark and atmospheric environment and story where exploration and knowledge of your surroundings is key.
Mechanics that are used to play through this game are minimal. You find objects within the environment to interact with by using ARID's flashlight, or you can switch to ARID's gun with laser-sight in hostile environments. There is also a very small inventory system used within the game - you can pick certain objects up to interact with other objects, all done by using the flashlight.
The puzzles are well thought out and reasonably obvious in their solution if you have explored well enough - and explore you will, as there is a fair amount of back-tracking through environments in order to find the solution to solve some of the puzzles. I do have to admit that I had to look up the solution to two puzzles as I spent an awful lot of time trying to work out how to get around the problem, and on reading the solution would have absolutely never come up with the answer myself. That said, though there is some difficulty with the puzzles, there is also (for the most part) a sense of logic to it and, other than the two puzzles mentioned, it didn't take me long to work out what I was meant to be doing in any given situation.
Combat, though a relatively small part of the game, doesn't feel like an over-sight at all. Using just a pistol with laser-sight, you have the option to duck behind cover or run wildly at the enemy to finish them off, also taking into account that headshots are more effective than just shooting wildly at your foe.
Progression through the story is this games biggest achievement. The writing and voice-acting is incredible, and though I can't discuss the story here as it would ultimately result in spoilers, it is a fascinating journey with an ending that I did not expect at all.
If a good story-line is important to you in a game, I would strongly recommend a play-through of this, particularly as it is quite short. Excellent voice-acting, stunning and gritty visuals, a superb story, interesting game play mechanics, progression and puzzles - I'm not sure there's anything about this game that I didn't enjoy (even the back-tracking!), and I wouldn't hesitate in recommending it.

The fall was a short game and the puzzles were near impossible for me to solve intuitively. Yet despite having to look up a walkthrough when I hit a rough puzzle, I really enjoyed it. The story was interesting and it kept me entertained for the 2-3 hours it took to beat. I wouldn't play it again simple because it's a one play game. Grab it if it goes on sale.

Back in 2002, this game ushered in the era of more realistic graphics. Now, it serves as proof that no matter how much time passes, console games can, and are, ported to the PC. This particular one was remastered most excellently. The graphics are certainly as enhanced as the comparisons show. The atmosphere and the sound effects are among the most lifelike in any video game to date. The lighting, both from the moonlight and the candles and the contrast of the shadows  is very impressive. In Resident Evil HD Remaster, the line between video games and cinema is much thinner than it was before. In the original game, there was no lightning or thunder, no running water or leaves moving in the wind, but there are in this version and they create a great ambiance.
The gameplay is modelled after the classic stop and shoot design, but somehow that makes the experience even more suspenseful. The fixed camera angles add great tension and dread to the atmosphere. The shooting mechanics are crisp and the autoaim is a very welcome feature that will appeal to the early Resident Evil fans who were frustrated by having to turn and face the enemy manually. Also, the self-defense technique of sticking a hand grenade in the mouth of a zombie, cerberus or hunter, offers a very inventive and spectacular way to blow their heads off, either by running away and letting the grenade go off, or shooting it with a weapon.
For the fans and newcomers to the game, you'll find much to like about the port of the Resident Evil remake. The least of which will be a more elabourate Spencer Mansion. Many new areas have been added to it, making the building more believable and complete. The larger library, the enlarged and new balconies are particularly noteworthy. Don't miss out on this game. If you value sophisticated level design, mystery and action, I think you will enjoy what this remastered port has to offer.

Apocalypse, what a raw and unfinished gem. This game is something else and unique, the basic framework is there and the potential for a great tactical X-Com style game but it was not critically acclaimed as it's predecessors. So, is this game bad then?
Not by any means. You could call Apocalypse a somewhat dated and unpolished, graphics look extremely odd. The interface is not that well thought out, micromanagement can be a hassle and the map can be quite useless. Basically it is not very user friendly on the first glance. There are other minor things that might annoy you but once you get past that, you will find a very refreshing game.
The unique concept and draw of this game is the huge city that you have to defend against alien forces. You manage a specialized organisation and need to trace any sign of alien activity, research them, capture them and even fight off huge invasions, be it on the ground or airborne. The city has it's own intricacies like the many factions or economy. The city is filled with various factions and corporations and your relationship with them might change the prices of some goods. Factions fight against eachother in this turmoil and your job is to keep the city alive and defend against the impending alien threat. It all feels very interactive and alive compared to other games.
Your duty is to manage the base, personal and equipement of your organisation. Fight, research and engineer your way to victory. Most of the time will be spent in the tactical ground battles against aliens or in the city screen while trying to fight off ufos. Battles can be very intense due to the high difficulty and tactical options.
There is much to talk about but I recommend this game for anyone who likes the concept of X-com with a unique twist, it just needs some time to get used to due to the somewhat unfriendly user interface and dated graphics.

Overall: 10/10
If you are on the hunt for the ultimate tactic game, look no further X-COM Apocalypse is it. I purchased this game 3 times, on release, 2 years later after I had to install it on a new PC and the original disk was broke and then on Steam, just for having it. This ranks amongst my all-time favorites and is in my eyes the best title of the franchise.
What makes it so great? Never has tactical combat been deeper and never had a game a greater range on tactical approaches and significant shifts of how you play over the course of its campaign. There is a technology life-cycle here that will keep the game fresh, whenever the aliens show up bringing new toys, you have to adapt quickly, research if your survive to stay on technological eye-level with your foes until the next cycle. This is the basic principle of all X-Com games, but here are much more of these technology cycles and their impact is much greater.
Speaking about impact, the environments are completely destructible and you can literally bring down whole buildings in the tactical missions, as well as in the strategic city view instead of hunting the aliens one by one. But you might♥♥♥♥♥♥of the owners that are funding your operation. If they are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of already, then why not raid their building for resources, even if there are no aliens involved, yes you can even do that. The feature depth out of combat is massive, you only have a city as playing field, but every building has an owner and every misguided missile during an interception attempt has a political impact. You can buy buildings, station vehicles and agents all over the place, raid and attack organizations. Research and Development as well as budget management are complex, but easily learnable and even when you are in tight spot, the game has desperate measures available to turn things around.
Sure, the graphics where not that god, even at release, the optional real-time mode is not much more than a gimmick (quite useful when you are confidently overpowered to accelerate things) but it is not hard to appreciate the “inner-beauty” of the gameplay once you get into it. All the other franchise trademarks like customizable soldiers, inventory management and UFO base building are at their feature-filled best.
I played most tactic games since the good old DOS days, from Ufo Defense over Jagged Alliance, Fallout over titles like Silent Storm up to last year’s great XCOM – Enemy Unknown. But none ever could compete to X-COM Apocalypse, if you have the slightest interest in the genre, you absolutely owe it yourself to play this! If Firaxis is working on a sequel to their re-imagination, I wish they would go to Apocalypse for inspiration. It might be too complex for today’s streamlined standards, but it gets so much depth out of this complexity, that keeps it interesting even after all these years.
Pros:
- true tactical depth
- strategically complex
- all franchise tropes in effect
- fierce technology lifecycles
Cons:
- complexity requires ramp-up time
- boring graphics

I really wish I could click that "Yes" button under "Do you recommend this game?" more than once. This game is just, whoa. This is the peak of this game's franchise. Its successors fail to live up to Morrowind's greatness. Steam only shows I have played roughly twelve hours of this game, but before I got it on Steam, I played this nonstop. Around 500 hours or so. I couldn't even pour a hundred hours into Oblivion or Skyrim combined. Morrowind's successors fall flat. Anyway, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Story
+ Lore in general (lots of lore, of which is all interesting)
+ Tons of detail
+ Lots and l o t s of sidequests, that all grab you in (Skyrim had boring sidequests and there were too many of them)
+ The main quest is actually good
+ Super extensive enchanting and potion making (seriously you can create some really ridiculous things, that are otherwise impossible to make in the later titles)
+ Lots of freedom (no invisible walls, you can permanently kill whomever you want, etc.)
+ Honestly, this is a true RPG. You cannot deny that. (Skyrim isn't even a real RPG, and Oblivion is just a watered down RPG)
+ This game actually allows you to roleplay (you can create a Shrek-esque character and live in the swamps of the West Gash Region for Christ's sake)
+ The game world feels huge, even though it actually isn't
+ For a game this old, it has a lot of pretty impressive mods (HIGHLY recommend Tamriel Rebuilt and the graphics/sounds overhaul)
+ Has a construction kit for mod developers (for some reason the Steam version doesn't come with it, but you can download it here:
)
Neutrals:
+/- The combat can put some people off, but I honestly like it. It sticks to the roots of its predecessors. This is the main reason why this game is so hard for some people to get into.
+/- The fast travel system, where you pay for Silt Strider (or boat) rides to available areas. I personally enjoy this method of fast travel, but as for people coming from Oblivion or Skyrim, I can see why this would put them off. (I like it because it's both realistic and it promotes on-foot exploration)
+/- The graphics onbviously do not age well, but honestly, graphics don't mean everything. Besides, there's always the overhaul mod, if your PC can handle it.
Cons
- Modding the game can sometimes be frustrating, as sometimes mods will easily cause the game to become more unstable. (as if it wasn't unstable already)
- I haven't noticed many compatibility problems with Windows 10 on this game except the resolution issue. When I got this on my gaming PC, it would still show the toolbar (with the exit, minimize, and enlarge buttons) at the top of the window despite being in fullscreen. This is easily fixed using MGE (it allows you to play at your native resolution; I'm not sure about multiple displays, as I have not tested that.)
- You're an n'wah from the start. (not a real negative, just being humorous)
I rate this game 9.5/10. The best game in the franchise. The best way to start this game off is with the code patch, Tamriel Rebuilt, and Overhaul mods. Honestly my favorite RPG of all time.

Bomber crew is a charming little WW2 bomber sim where you control seven crew members of an Avro Lancaster, From the pilot, to the gunners, to the bombardier. It's blocky artstyle is cute, functional, and lends itself well to the game. Crew members names can be personalized to your liking, however their looks are randomly generated. All in all, There's a lot of potential here for this game, but there are some things that the Devs should add to make the better.
As it stands, Bomber crew is not an easy game. Especially in it's current state. The first couple missions are easy enough. Go here, bomb target, shoot down a couple planes, take some reconnaissance photos, return to base. Pretty fun. But soon, (Very soon) the game spikes in difficulty. Throwing waves and waves of fighters (That all need to be individually marked by you for your gunners to fire at them) and walls of flak at you, while you struggle to have your engineer run around repairing all the damage and healing the gunners, if they're not already dead. (Yes, there is Permadeath) Not only that, but you also have to keep targeting waypoints for your pilot to follow, less he fly off in the wrong direction and Whoops! There goes all your fuel. There's been talk of adding a "Pause" or "Time slow" button to help with these frantic moments. Only time will tell if that much needed feature does get added in. Personally, I'd rather have an "Action queue" mechanic like it most other RTS's, where you shift click multiple orders to a crewman and they do them all in the order you clicked them.
Here's a concise list of Pros and Cons I noticed during my time so far with Bomber Crew.
Pros:
-Charming Art Style
-Lots and Lots of customization and upgrades, both in plane and crew.
-Addictive gameplay
-In-depth management
-TONS of potential
Neutral:
-Soundtrack is nothing special
-Extremely arcadey physics, but what do you expect? DCS?
-Not a historical representation of WW2 aircrews. Please don't take it as such.
-No real story. It's WW2. Sometimes you bombs historically significant targets.
Cons:
-Large difficulty spike within the first couple hours, which can lead to frustration.
-Only one bomber, being the Lancaster (Possibility of more being added later)
-Management is not efficient. Everything needs to be done individually, and in some cases simultaneously
-Missions get samey. Bomb this depot, bomb this artillery location, deliver supplies to this pilot.
-Crew member's appearance cannot be customized. Who you get is what you're stuck with.
-Not enough feedback to the player. I always seem to die because somehow a fire starts in the cockpit and the pilot jumps out and then the plane just nosedives into the sea.
This is a very hesitant recommendation from me. I want to love this game. I REALLY do. But there's still a good amount of things that the devs should look into before this I feel I can wholeheartedly recommend it. But I recommend it here anyway, because I want the game to be successful, the more succesful it is, the better chance of having these issues fixed.

So.... Bomber Crew. What do I think of it?
Well, I think it's QUITE HARD to be honest, and quite satisfying as well. (Get your mind out of the bloody gutter, I know that sounded off but come on..)
The gameplay itself is quite nice, although you have to learn a bit it does well to give you a feeling of satisfaction when you have a crew that has lived for a while. Do not misunderstand when I say this, that is a rare occurance, and even then, crews can constantly die.... No, I am not joking. The literal main aspect of this game is that it is similar to a rouge-like, with the way it plays, it basically says if you crash the bomber, and your crew dies? There's no getting them back. All those hours and hours of grinding on one team of bomber crew-members, just gone within the few minutes you were on that one mission WITH ALL THE F$@^ING FLAK GOD FU*$ING D@MN IT!
Ahem.
Anyway, as well, this also applies to the bomber as well. Any upgrades you decided to get? Oh, those are long gone. This isn't the same bloody bomber. Especially if you had to make a crash landing, which even then there's no exact way of saying if your crew will actually LIVE or not. Given that most times when you CRASH, it's going to tear the bomber apart, and most likely kill the crew within it. Infact, some have even begun spreading tales of their fallen crews, and bombers.
Yes, this game is frustrating due to some of it's quirks especially the part about losing hours upon hours of effort in a single giant fireball that is now embedded in the dirt. But instead of me talking about just the crew dying, what about the "missions"
Well, you are the british in a campaign against the germans. The basic idea here is that you will need to go out, bomb or recon stuff, and return to base after doing the objective, these missions are standard, and sometimes you re-do the same missions, just with higher difficulty and reward. (Frankly, I'd prefer more missions, because doing the same stuff over and over makes the game feel like literal deja vu.) As well as these normal missions, CRITICAL missions are the essential missions to move forward in the campaign. The more you do, the more difficult the missions, and the more ACES you'll encounter.
Yup. You saw it right. Aces.
Aces are basically "pro" pilots who are germany's finest, you can actually shoot and destroy these little buggers, and end their reign of terror on your bomber crew. If you sucessfully do destroy one of these pilots, you will infact get a nice cash reward. (The more difficult the ace, the more cash you'll get.)
Now you might be asking: "What do you do with all the cash you earn from these missions?" Well, you use them for upgrades of course! Mostly everything on the bomber itself is customizable, even the crewmembers gear is able to be customized. No, this is not just for visual appeal, if you change stuff on the bomber, or on the characters, things change on the bomber as well.
For instance, say you wanted your gunners to be better protected from flak and incoming enemy fighter fire. You could equip them with a flak vest and a helmet. This does protect them, but has a speed reduction which can cause your crew to become slower. This is also very bad for gunners, especially since they need to RELOAD their gun after 3 ammo clips have been used.
What about a bomber? Well, you can upgrade your engines, the armor on your plane, the guns the gunners use... Even add a ventral turret if you feel it's necessary. (It is VERY necessary when dealing with certain ACES that decide to FLIP UPSIDE DOWN AND SHOOT YOU WITH THE BACK GUNNER) Along with these upgrades (there are more than I have listed) you can even add cosmetic stuff to the exterior, changing the paint-job, adding some nice wing art, or engine art. Hell, you could even make your own! Basically this makes your bomber feel more like... y'know, actually YOURS instead of it just being some random print and press bomber with no character at all.
There's one more thing about this game that I like: Stats. Yes, your characters have stats. So you may be asking: "What type"
Well, these stats are not stuffs like "faster reload" nono, that comes when you level them up as a gunner. THESE particular stats give them better resistance to heat and cold, even extra speed , as well as possibly giving them a survival bonus in certain areas.(Land and Sea.) As well, they can also have different levels of experience, as you progress their levels will start to rise by default, so you dont lose "EVERYTHING" after your previous crew have hit the dirt.
In conclusion: What do I think of this game? Well, I think it's a d@mn good game, even though it is frustrating to lose your crew, I'd suggest you play it. It's a nice game.

Not an exact arcade emulation...
These games are not ports of the original arcade games. They're recreated games using the sprites, backgrounds, and music ripped from the arcade game. If you have played the original arcade versions of these games you will know where all the enemies are placed, how many hits (elbows) it takes to take out the enemies, and also including button layouts.
Double Dragon 2 is the prime example of exactly the reason these games are recreated and not even emulated. The control scheme for Double Dragon 2 is Left Attack, Jump, and Right Attack. On Double Dragon Trilogy there exactly like Double Dragon 1 control scheme (Punch, Jump, and Kick) only switching out the kick to always do a back kick no matter which side your facing instead of meaning if your facing right you would press the left attack to back kick and vice verse. Also they don't even have the original hud of the game and instead made a "modern" hud with a generic font.
I guess for nostalgia purposes these games serve their purpose. and for $5.99 you do get pretty good recreated games (including the awful controls of Double Dragon 3). Also note that they have it set to a certain number of continues for each difficulty as well as how many lives you start of with. And they don't even show you how many credits you have either. So don't expect to be able to insert coins or even have infinite credits.
Final verdict is if you like a classic beat-em-up style game then this game can satisfy for the price. But in all honesty nothing beats the original arecade games (although this does come kinda close).

TL:DR Great story and atmosphere though the poor controls and combat let it down a bit. This is only the first part of the trilogy and probably not worth buying at full price right now. I'd recommend waiting to pick it up on offer or for part 2s release.
Full Version:
The Fall see you playing as a mechanized combat suit AI called ARID who takes control when the suit pilot is rendered inconscious. ARID crash lands in an abandoned facility and in compliance with her programming has to find medical aid for her pilot. The story for this game is brilliant as well as the incredibly atmospheric setting. The gameplay is a bit of is a combination of puzzle solving and metroidvania style exploration of the facility.
There is combat but it is the biggest weakpoint of the game with it being very clunky and awkward though not to the point where it ruins the game. This is also the first of a trilogy and so the game is only about 2-3 hours long with a cliffhanger ending. This is worth considering if you want to buy it as its been 2 years and part 2 in still unreleased though it may be released soon.
Good points:
- A really gripping clever story that had me hooked
-The setting is really atmospheric and unnerving
-I really liked the visual style of this game which makes good use of shadow and lighting to add to the unsettling atmosphere of the setting
Bad points:
- Clunky controls and combat
- Puzzles are a bit uneven. Its usually finding an object and using it on another object but some of the items you need to collect can be hard to find or in unobvious locations
- This is only the first part of the trilogy and thus it ends quite suddenly on a cliffhanger so it maybe worth waiting though given its been 2 years since release and still no episode 2 it may be a long wait.

The Fall plays more like a point-and-click than the action-adventure game it appears to be at first glance. There is plenty of adventure, certainly, but the bulk of the game is spent shining a light around and learning, not spent in the brief - but not out of place - combat sequences. This is not a complaint as the story is what's important here. The famous 'Three Laws of Robotics' concept is explored with a slight twist: the triad of laws each AI is bound to is different from the laws other AIs are bound to. The game's three characters, none of which are human, serve to play out the resulting thought experiment brilliantly and manage to do so while inspiring emotional investment, all within the game's relatively short run time. More installments are planned and despite the two year interim between The Fall's release and now, the next part is actively being worked on. However, the impact of the The Fall is not dependent on the story continuing as the ending screen declares it will, it's plenty strong and plenty complete as it is.

It's very rare to play an RPG that does
feature a globe trotting, world saving, massive journey taking main character--And yet, here we are with The Witcher: Enhanced Edition, the first of the Witcher trilogy. In this Polish developed CRPG, you take control of witcher Geralt of Rivia, whose task is to investigate the city of Vizima and its outskirts in an attempt to apprehend members of a treacherous organization known as the Salamanders, who have stolen secrets from the witchers--secrets that should never fall into the wrong hands. Throughout the five chapters featured in the Witcher, Geralt butts heads with religious orders, investigations clues and leads, learns about fatherhood, hunts monsters and beasts, and, well... bangs a
of women. As an NPC can be heard exclaiming, "A Witcher! Hide your women!"
If anything else, the Witcher is infamous for its rather unique, bizarre rhythm based gameplay. Distilling the gameplay loop down to its most base form, you draw your sword and click on the enemies to begin swining. Geralt automatically deals blows, and it's on you to click on the correct timing to create combos and wreak havoc. Of course, that is simple, but, again, it's in its base form. Being a CRPG, there is quite a bit of strategy involved. You have many different types of weapons to choose from, and, from there, many sword "styles" that work well on certain enemies but not with others. Alchemy assumes a big role in combat, as the right combination of stat buffers can make or break certain encounters, and that simply won't happen without experimentation or the necessary leg work to discover recipes.
Ultimately though, the combat
pretty wonky. If you can adapt, you're in for a great time. If you're completely turned off, perhaps you should look elsewhere.
Storywise, the Witcher shines brighter than
. The mature writing and themes are evident from the very first few conversations you have, and it quickly becomes obvious that the Witcher is not a classic tale of good vs evil, but rather, a series of gray shades dominating a political landscape. While the story begins simply enough, with amensiac Geralt setting out to get revenge, he soon finds himself a pawn for those willing to control him, and the player must face their own set of ideas and morals when choices rear their heads--for there is never a correct choice--merely
choice. Additionally, the plot stacks itself with nearly every chapter, revealing layers of layers of intrique and questions as the veil is pulled behind the city of Vizima and its inhabitants.
As for a few short remarks, the music is very atmospheric and fits in well with the land of Temeria. The voice acting is
good, with the occasional bizarre encounter or two along with Geralt occasionally forcing out a line that could've been better retaken. The lore is incredible and I personally encourage anyone who starts out playing to consume knowledge wherever they may find it, whether it be a person of interest or a stray book they come across, as the world of the Witcher is vast. Finally, it should be stated that there are more than a few weird moments as a result of awkward silence and weird animations, but if you can overlook these moments, your immersion will hold strong.
Overall, The Witcher is a very great CRPG with minor flaws. Its story is intruiging and mature, peppered with choice and consequence. It's gameplay is tactical and interesting, but many may find themselves divided on whether or not they can accept the combat for what it is. If you are  entering the Witcher series, consider starting with the very first of the trilogy--you just might not be disappointed.

The survival horror of the 90s is back! This is an HD Remaster of the 2002 Gamecube Remaster of the 1996 Playstation Original: Resident Evil. Confused? You should be! Well not really, this is an HD upgrade of the Gamecube version of the same name.
Compared to the Playstation original. Besides the upgrade in graphics. The game was vastly expanded, with the mansion having more secrets, more traps and more Resident Evil!
Gone is the bad voice acting that made the Guinness World record 2008, but back is what is Resident Evil in a nutshell. A slow paced, cheesy, creepy horror survival game where you control either S.T.A.R.S Members Chris or Jill. By this point, most of you should've already know that.
Unlike Resident Evil Zero. You don't control both characters at once, you select them at the start of the game, with the other missing. You play the games in the perspective of one of them. While story wise, events unfold pretty much the same and both characters are basically Identical except for a few tweaks. Bare in mind, this is still a 90s / Early 2000s game at heart and the game is short and kept mostly simple without getting too deep into it.
The obvious upside to this HD version of the game is the once again updated visuals, this time sporting 1080p+ amazingly detailed and gorgeous areas. 60FPS game-play, new alternate controls, two new costumes and a ranking leader-board system to show off how much you cheated get 00'00'00 on Hard mode.
Even though this one came before the Resident Evil Zero HD remaster. I can't help but feel that some more love was added to the later game. RE0 has costume DLC packs, even a new Wesker mode. The leader-board system is not included in RE0 but this one comes with the Soundtrack. You can change the controls here on the PC version to pretty much anyway you want. Yet that is locked in RE0. What's with the lack of consistency here?
The visuals are great, but for some reason when compared to RE0. It seems that not as much attention was focused on it. I understand this was the first of the two HD remasters but I can't help but feel at some areas in this game, they got a little lazy.
Also, what's with some of remixed music? Again, not found in RE0. That's fine in all in fact some of them are great. Except for one at least. But I find it a bit odd they didn't do the same for RE0.
You can change the controls and technically the graphics to mimic that of the Gamecube / Wii version. There is not much I can say without going too in depth but I'm not the in depth kind of reviewer. This is simply a great trip down memory lane to a simpler times where Resident Evil was Resident Evil. And not something that is trying to copy another franchise that is totally unrelated to what made the series loved in the first place.
Huh, where did that last part come from? Anyways, if you enjoy Classic Resident Evil or Old school games. Or you want some cheesy 90s horror. There is nothing better than Resident Evil in 1080P+ 60FPS! Though if you enjoy RE4 or later. You might wanna skip this one, might be a little too slow for you guys.
And hey, it's $20! C'mon give this old sucker another round. It still has teeth to chew off your brain dead gaming corpse...

While Alone in the Dark is remembered for being the forefather of survival horror games, Resident Evil is considered one of the best founding titles of the genre; the game is highly revered across the world, and it has spawned many successors which have turned one game into a complete franchise. The original Resident Evil made its debut on the first Playstation console in early 1996, and since then the series of games have captivated audiences with the unique approach to zombies, complex story line, and array of well-rounded characters. Not to mention, the opening live action sequence to the primordial release is absolutely hilarious. The remake of this classic title made its first appearance on Gamecube back in 2002, and that is the version that qualified for this high-definition upgrade that was released in early 2015.
The game takes place within a giant mansion on the outskirts of Raccoon City. At the beginning of the game, you are allowed to pick between two main characters to play as; either former-US military pilot Chris Redfield, or explosives expert Jill Valentine. At this time in the series, both characters belong to Raccoon City's own special force, S.T.A.R.S. (Special Tactics and Rescue Service). The player will experience a mildly different set of events depending on which character is chosen, and there is added replay value in going through the game at least a second time with the opposite person. The gamer will then explore the many corridors, rooms, and hallways of the massive mansion, all the while solving puzzles, fending off grotesque abominations, and managing a tight inventory space.
Seeing as this is the first Resident Evil title, the story line is pretty bare bones in comparison to later games. You will find out about the T-Virus and the wretched enemies that have spawned from it, along with a small glimpse into who and what makes up Umbrella Corporation. Going into this game without the knowledge from prequel Resident Evil 0, some questions are left unanswered; which is expected, if a game is expecting a sequel. There are also only three major bosses and a handful of enemies, and this might seem lazy for a game made in 2002. However, we must remember that the remake was based off of the 1996 game, and the limitations of data storage on a disc were much more confined back then. Rather than having a large number of enemies, the main focus of the original Resident Evil is exploration and survival rather than fighting many battles.
With the basics out of the way, we can now discuss the actual Resident Evil HD Remaster. Capcom have done an amazing job with bringing the 2002 version of Resident Evil to life in brilliant high-definition. The character models are crisp and sharp, the spotless floors of the mansion gleam, water has outstanding reflection, the backgrounds are clear, and the monsters look great. The atmosphere in the game breeds death and decay, the fog in some areas is so thick and pronounced that you can almost feel it soaking your skin. Likewise, the audio is completely immersive and crystal clear, the 5.1 surround sound breathes incredible life into the title. To boot, the game itself does not suffer from any glitches, bugs, frame rate issues, or crashes; at least in my experience.
I've never seen Resident Evil so deliciously alive as it is in this HD Remaster. From the aesthetic character model visuals, to new high resolution textures, atmospheric development, and completely immersive 5.1 surround sound audio, everything is overwhelmingly stunning. One thing that may put some people off is that Capcom decided to leave in the door animations; for those that are unfamiliar with early Resident Evil games, each time a door is opened a small cutscene plays showing the door opening. This also goes for some elevators and ladders. Originally, these were used in lieu of boring loading screens, and while it would be a nice option to be able to toggle this feature on and off, the inclusion keeps the dark, cult-classic vibe of the game within the HD Remaster. If you're a fan of Resident Evil, or even if you're new to the series or have been interested in playing it, I highly suggest picking up this HD Remaster; for $20 CAD, you really can't go wrong. I do also highly suggest picking up Resident Evil 0 and playing it prior to this game.
