Resident Evil 1 is amazing.  Not only is it a great concept and rather well executed given the time, but the actual gameplay and aesthetics hold up rather well.  The infamous phoned-in voices are finally gone (Flour Bunny made a mod to bring them back, if you're interested) and with clunky combat only adding to the tension, it manages to be rather tense when you're surprised by an enemy.  While most people remember this game for the first zombie, I remember it by the Art Closet... absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying.  Moments like these make the game, and the puzzles in between basically turn it into the most stressful LucasArts point-n-click you'll ever see.
Really, you owe it to yourself to give it a chance.  Once REHDHook is set up, and you've manually changed the resolution via INI, the game's perfect.  The remastered visuals get the job done, and the game's been visually overhauled without taking away the effect of the original game.  Now, if you'll excuse me, will somebody tell me where that damn sword is?

Would definitely recommend this game! Main negative point to make: it's a bit short for an RPG.
Pros
+Wonderful, cartoony graphics (think KoA: Reckoning or World of Warcraft).
+Lots of fun, very light-hearted game
+The 'morality' system
+Fun combat, and plenty of options to choose from (see next point)
+Very useful leveling/experience system; two types of XP - one general that can be spent on any type of upgrade, and the other XP type, which is awarded based on the type of attacks you use in combat (ranged/sneaking, melee or magic), to upgrade that skill tree specifically.
+Leveling is very easy because of the combat multiplier system
Cons
-Morality system is very simplistic, same goes for the story itself
-The game is quite short, and there aren't many side quests available
-Various in-game activities like romance, buying/renting property, finding ways to open demon doors etc. are fun, but not very well developed (and don't really add to game time)
-There are VERY few weapon and armor 'tiers', and few items to choose from in general. There are recolours of some sets (for good/bad characters), but still.
-It's relatively easy to max out all skills and buy the best equipment rather early (it is a short game, though).

No reason to get this over the cheaper, original Lost Chapters version of the game. This isn't nostalgia. This is a sheer  objective stand point.
Anniversary = Lost Chapters
The textures aren't all that better, they're just different.
Content is the exact same.
Story is the same.
Cut scenes, general gameplay, and voice acting is the same.
Different character models are not better, just different. Arguably worse depending on person.
Anniversary > Lost Chapters
Super high resolution support, though the original worked in 1080 just fine except for main starting menu.
Mod Support, but there's only about a dozen mods in total after so many years. "Modding" is basically non-existant for this game.
Lost Chapters > Anniversary
Controller Support is supposedly better but it's not. You have two set schemes and you can't change anything about them. It's better just to use Big Picture Config for controller and map keyboard buttons to it for Lost Chapters as you have way more freedom than Anniversary.
The original version of the game is actually better lit, more colorful and the faces have more emotions and character to them.
Lost Chapters runs a lot better, obviously, and has way more graphics options.
Overall, despite it being a PC game remaster, it has LESS features than the original PC version and feels more like a port of the console version which means less freedom with settings and an awful new ui menu that is just counter intuitive. SPORE™ is a
combination of Agar.io, Rust, Starcraft and Sid Meir's Civilization. - elements from all the greatest videogames orchestrated into an evolutionary masterpiece. In my opinion, SPORE is the best game ever made, at least in concept: SPORE™ is about playing a role in the history of life, out on an alien planet, and the game does this well as it is, however it seems that the scale of this concept made it difficult to completely encapsulate the bits and pieces of the individual god-spectacle games which SPORE™ borrows from: If your game is planned to have four stages, with each of which grand enough in concept that they could be filled with completely different games, that each took YEARS to make: so why not just distribute 1/4th the effort into each of the four sub-games, so that the final game could be completed in a reasonable time? This is the one flaw of SPORE™; each of these four sections (Cell, Organism, Tribe,/Civilization, Space age) seemed just to big in their counterpart games to execute into one. Appart from this, you should have a great time with this game, and not regret it like i have for most steam summer sale games.

I've always loved the older Resident Evil games, however the last one I actually remember much about was Resident Evil 3 as I owned that one growing up, and only played the previous games at a friend's house.
This Remaster/Remake is just was I was hoping for.  The newer Titles RES 5 and RES 6 focus way too much on action, and you often end up with a small asenal at your disposal with a ridiculous amount of ammo.
This is not the case with this Remaster/Remake.  Ammo is limited, Inventory space is limited, and even your vision is limited depending on where the camera is situated. (this is a good thing)
It makes you use caution when moving somewhere, often you may want to rely on your senses... can you hear a zombie groaning in the other room? or was it just your imagination?
I started out playing this game on hard mode, just to see what it was like.  I died from the 2nd or 3rd zombie I encountered.  It was a brutal experience, the zombies were tough as nails eating most of  clip from my hand gun before finally dying.
I was stuck relying on my knife almost immediately due to not having enough ammo to take care of the zombies, and since I needed to get around the zombies to proceed, there was little choice.  Due to being in close melee range, it also meant they could grab and eat me.. which is what usually ended up happening.
Hard mode was INTENSE..  It was terrifyingly amazing how useless and weak I felt.  This made me actually FEAR the zombies.  Everytime I entered a new room I was a tense situation not knowing if there would be a zombie to greet me as soon as I stepped though the door..
After a couple of deaths I decided to switch to Easy Mode and progressed through the game much better.
While it was Easy Mode, I still thoroughly enjoyed the experience.  It wasn't a walk in the park, the game was still challenging but the player can take more hits before dying, and there are more healing herbs and ammo scattered around the mansion.  This was greatly benifital to me as I had no idea where I was going, or what I was to expect up ahead and it allowed some room for error.
There were still times where I died, but often it was due to being ill prepared.  There are multiple traps in this game, and while they look like they would probably be insta-death I managed to avoid all of them by being cautious or just seeing ahead.
I finished the game after about 20 or so hours.. This was actually a pretty long play through and could have been done much shorter.  This was widely because of not knowing where I was going.  Not to say that you are wandering around aimlessly.. (although you kind of are in a sense)  There is a map, and its the key to progressing.  Some areas of the mansion are unaccessable until you find a certain objects.. like keys, or items used for puzzles that open way for new areas.
There is a lot of back tracking involved and the game doesn't direct you at all by giving you a marker to move towards or a mission objective to complete.  Its all up to you, and it feels great!
After finishing the game and making sure I had 100% of the map and item progression I decided to check online to see if there was anything else I could unlock or do in the game.  In fact there was.. but I had to play on Hard Mode.
I was still a bit in fear of the experience I had with Hard Mode the first time around, but I decided to come back and try it again a couple of weeks later.
Having learned a lot from playing and finishing the game on Easy Mode, I figured I had a better chance at survival than when I first attemped Hard Mode.
While the zombies were MUCH harder to kill, you take brutal amounts of damage, and ammo was scarce.  I did indeed have a better grip on the game..  I was ready.
Unlocking the Samurai Edge Pistol. (beat the game in under 5 hours)
Unlocking the Anti-Tank Rocket Launcher. (beat the game in under 3 hours)
Given how it took me over 20 hours to beat the game on Easy Mode, I clearly had some work to do if I was going to even get close.
The first thing I did was find out if there were any safe places where the game clock did not tick.. like in a menu, or pausing.. during cut scenes.. etc.  There was not.
The moment you load the game, there is no pausing the timer.. PERIOD.  This means you really have to be careful when you save the game.  Thinking a head is critical, you have to know where you are going and where all the monsters are.
I decided I would do some trial and error with some runs.. I'd take a path, get the items I found to be valuable in order to progress the quickest without having to back track too much.
The game needs to be done in segments, figure out a path that leads you to get some importent items and then gets you back to your safe house to save/deposit items to clear up your intentory.  Planning was integral to success, as I didn't want to go through the game and fail just short of the required time to get my unlocks.
My brother and I decided to digitally draw the mansion using mspaint by tracing an online map of the mansion.  I was then able to mark rooms that were locked with a certain key, or needed something special to progress.  Making a path to follow was also easier as you could now visualize the whole processes before going through with it.
Through a lot of trail and error, I completed the game in about 2 hours and 30 minutes.  This was a great success for me, and I unlocked both weapons in one run.  While I finished the game with an in game clock of under 3 hours, in reality it probably took me longer to complete than the first play through since I often was not happy with my segment times and would redo them.
This process turned me into a zombie dodging ninja, as often the fastest way through a room wasn't to clear it by gunning zombies down.. it was to simply step around them somehow.  Completing this time trial challange has essentially turned Hard Mode turned into Easy Mode.. and it was a lot of fun.
The games over now right?  Wrong.
There are 2 characters you can choose to play as.
Chris
Higher max HP
Higher damage output using a Knife
Starts with the Lighter item
Jill
Larger inventory capacity
Starts with a lock pick
They have different story progressions and you explore the masion taking different paths.
If you finish the game with both Chris and Jill on at least Normal Mode, the next time you play, the game will throw a new zombie into the mix.. This zombie has a bomb straped to it's chest and killing it will result in an explosion that will always kill you.
Not enough?
Invisible Enemy Mode - Yeah.. its what it says, the enemies are invisible.  I haven't even attempted this yet as I am certain how it will turn out...  but one day..
There are also different costumes you can unlock per character.
Lastly.. there are also Steam Achivements to strive for.. like
Beat the game without saving.
Beat the game using only a knife. (no other weapons, not even counter/defensive ones)
Amazing game, worth every penny.  I hope RES 7 will take a note from how well this game has sold and try to stay more true to it's roots.
Can't wait for RES 2 Remake/Remaster.. will buy day one. (this one is actually being worked on!)

DISCLAIMER: I am writing this review after playing the game for less than an hour and requesting a refund. Obviously, this means my experience is limited in scope, but that I felt sufficiently strongly about it to request my first-ever Steam refund.
I will first summarize my view of this game, and following that, I will provide more specific details on why I feel that way.
From what I understand, this game is made by a small dev team on a small budget. This definitely shows in the production value of the game. On the other side of this, as with many of the better indie games on the market, it genuinely feels like the devs loved their game and put effort into it. However, from what I experienced, it is just not enough to translate into a fun or satisfying game experience, at least not for the $15 price I paid (at the time of this writing, that is a 25%-off sale on the $20 full price. The comparisons I see on the reviews to bigger games like Ace Combat are not necessarily inappropriate, but do not convey this significant difference.
The first major issue I had with the game came to light immediately after the tutorial, and had to do with the game's language. Despite being set EN voice/EN sub, there were a lot of people yelling at me in Thai with no subtitles. I ended up resolving this after messing around with it a bit, but the first impression this created is a significant component of my having felt the need to refund the game. (Edit: It is worth noting that right after posting this review, within an hour of posting something similar on the forums, I got a response from a developer politely acknowledging the bug and stating an intention to fix it, so that was nice).
The other two significant (non-bug-related) problems I had with the game were the camera and the lack of feedback from the player's actions/reactions.
Firstly, the default camera is problematic in my opinion. I felt that it was zoomed out way too far so that it was difficult to see what was really happening, and there is no way to adjust the third-person camera as such. I did find out, by browsing the forums, that there is a cockpit view, however I could not find any explanation in-game on how to access it, and only managed to do so by pressing every button on the keyboard, starting from F1 and running down to 'V', which finally did the trick. I also had a somewhat nit-picky issue regarding the visibility of the enemies' missiles, which are very difficult to see and identify.
My other, more significant issue was the lack of feedback from the player's actions. At least in the first mech, there is not really any feeling created by firing the weapons  in the game. Even more lacking is the feel of being hit by the enemies' weapons. If I were to play the game muted and not pay attention to the health gauge, I would probably never know I was hit, whether by missiles, cannons, or running in to an object. Whether this is due to the sounds or the animations, or some combination of factors, I am not qualified to say, however this issue is the primary reason that I keep referring to the game as "unsatisfying".
All in all, as much as I feel the devs have drive, and despite being a fan of anime, mecha, and Ace Combat, I believe that this game was not for me. I may consider picking it back up at a lower price at some point in the future, but not any point that is presently foreseeable.

This is a fun mech game. We don't get enough of those. I haven't played through the entire thing, but here are my thoughts.
Positives:
+References aplenty. The game starts with a Robotech/Macross reference, and that's awesome.
+First person cockpit. I was suprised to see this, since most japanese mech games (at least I assume the creators are japanese), since first-person perspective games don't seem to be popular over there. The game is third person by default, however.
+Decent voice acting. Gets a bit engrish every once in a while, but good for the most part.
+High mobility. Oh god, very much so. Armored Core is a bit sluggish compared to this (I've only played Silent Line, though), and that's saying a bit.
+Easy interface. If you didn't like Armored Core's weird numerical health bar, and you feel like something a little simpler than Mechwarrior's, than you'll like it.
+Female player character. I don't usually care for playing as male characters (especially in Japanese games, where they're often a bad combination of all the worst aspects of Amuro and Shinji, without the character development of either), even though the guy in this game is basically Roy Falker, it's still a good feature in my book.
+Combat is very, very fluid, quick, and deadly. If you stay still, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. In the first mission, the fight you have with a squadron of tougher and shootier enemy mecha felt a bit remniscent of how the fight with the rival pilots felt in Star Fox 64, and that definetly had a nostalgia moment (keep in mind I'm playing on Prepare To Die difficulty).
+The hardest difficulty, Prepare To Die, is especially good.
+Animu artstyle. Yes, this is a good thing.
Negatives:
-On the first mission, when I boosted to the left, I rammed into a building, and took no damage. A bit immersion breaking.
-Lack of customization. The Mecha are solidly designed, look cool, and are well-armed enough to hold their own, but if you're lookingfor anything close to Mechwarrior, Heavy Gear, or even Armored Core, this'll be a negative.
-First Person Cockpit design. It doesn't seem like the Cockpit view is directly linked to the third person model, and it feels somewhat weird to take a hard turn and not see your arms or shoulders, even though in third-person you can tell they're perpendicular to the cockpit, or at least visible enough to see the edge. Also, their is no pilot model in the cokpit, so that might mess with your immersion a bit.
Overall, a solid, fun game.
Neat/notable details/observations:
>Squishy mecha. They are very squishy, and make up for their low durability with their agility. Remember to just keep moving.
>Ammo expedenture. You go through a crap ton of ammo and missiles. It's interesting to note that in real life, the majority of rounds fired in a combat situation won't hit. This is why most militaries began the switch to assualt rifles and carbines following World War 2. in the first mission, on PTD difficulty, I doubt even ten percent of my shots connected.
>Macross Missle Massacre. So many missiles will be fired. Missiles are your friend. Missiles are your saviour. Lock on, and fire some missiles.
>In the third mission, when you fire your "Psycho Drone Missiles", the character says that's what she is doing. It was cute at first. It became redundant after a while. This isn't really a negative, but it's not quite a plus. They do this because this is based off of animu, and animu teaches that it's highly reccomened to announce your attacks. Imagine if a soldier, in real life, said "TRRIIIGGGERRR PUUUUULLLL!!!" every time he discharged his/her weapon.
Nice :3

Coming back from school, and firing either Fable: The Lost Chapters or Black & White 2 in your old, clunky PC, then spending the day playing them, those were the days, and oh, how great they were.
This review will be simple, for players that already played The Lost Chapters, and are feeling nostalgic, this is a must, basically an improvement over the original game, just putting it up to date with better graphics and fixes, just buy it and enjoy again those days.
Now, if you've never played The Lost Chapters, nor any Fable:
This is third person adventure/action game combined with RPG and the premise of: Will you be a hero, or a villain?
Indeed, the choice is yours to do whatever you want to do. Kill villagers that are traveling to the city to buy stuff and steal their precious posessions? Go for it! Want to defend the poor villagers from robbers? Oh, you sure can. In fact, lots of missions can be accepted in 2 ways, example being 2 missions that are either; robbers that need help stealing from a farm and will hire you to defend the farm, or guards needing an extra hand with the security of said farm. Now, actions have consequences, if you're truly bad people will be afraid of you, your skin will shatter and horns will grow out your head, and if you're good, your eyes will turn blue and a halo will be put above your head. Of course, it's not as simple as good or evil, your choices have direct impact on your character and they'll show a bit of horns if you're just being a bit evil. Also, want to mention about dying; if you die, you'll forever receive an scar in a random place in your body that is impossible to remove.
The story is alright, you're a kid with a great family in a village, and you start the game in the birthday of your sister, you need to buy her a gift, which is a chocolate box if I don't recall badly, that is 5 coins of gold, and you need to get 5 coins, and this is basically a tutorial that doens't feel a tutorial at all, you can choose a few things to do. You will see a woman angry that her husband isn't home, and you need to find him, and then decide wether or not to be good or bad (I don't want to spoil), and then twist! You're in a hall of heroes, and you'll need to train and grow up to be a hero, and then choose your path.
Gameplay is not really dated, it feels great to use your bow to kill enemies from far away, and with a simple touch of a key, you're holding your 2 handed sword ready to blow them off, or you can always use magic. Lots and lots of magic abilities to choose from, leveling up is so good because as I said, actions have consequences, and the more strenght you put in your character, the more he'll look like a bodybuilder, and there are quite a few secrets in which you'll need certain amount of strenght/speed/magic abilities :).
Sounds and graphics are nice, nothing extraordinary, they're excellent if you think of a game that is this old, but they're only good if you take into acount that we're in 2016 already.
Overall; buy this game and feel for yourself what everyone has been speaking about for years. You WILL have fun.

Morrowind was the first Elder Scrolls game I ever played.  I thought the game was fantastic at the time, and I still do.  There is some warning which should be given to people who have played the newer games first, and want to go back in time to try this one.  There are differences which you may find annoying.  This review is targeted towards people who have played the newer games but not the older ones.  If you are completely new to the series, and are thinking about starting with Morrowind, then there are older reviews which can summarize the experience without comparing it to anything else.
I will refer to many things as a "change" even though this game did them first.  This is because I am making the comparison as if the newer games were played before this older one.
Lets start with the
.  I will be vague about this since there are so many things that make the Elder Scrolls amazing, and the majority of the pros are shared across all games in the series.
-
:  This has the same immersive story and quality that you have come to love in the other games.
-
:  Morrowind has the most varied and exciting environment of any Elder Scrolls game to date.  From burnt, ashy volcanic regions, to  snowy northern islands, to the swamps in the south, and everything imagineable in between.  Vvardenfell is superior in every way to any other location ever used.  It's something which you need to experience to appreciate.  Once you explore Vvardenfell, you will realize just how boring and repetitive the locations in Oblivion and (especially) Skyrim are.
-
: Morrowind has more weapon categories than newer titles like Skyrim and Oblivion.  Favorites of mine are spears and crossbows, but there are a few more.  To be fair, Skyrim has crossbows, but as a part of a DLC.  You get them as part of the game right off the bat in the case of Morrowind.  There are also throwing knives, darts, and stars, throwing weapons which don't make an appearance in Skyrim and Oblivion (to my knowledge).
-
: You can fly!
Now we can explore some differences which are quite broad and affect many parts of gameplay, meaning they can have both
effects.
-
: This is a big one.
1) In combat, there are many, many instances where you will swing at an enemy and miss, regardless of how well you are aiming.  Morrowind uses your character statistics (and the stats of whatever you are attacking) to determine what percent of your attacks will hit.  This can leave combat feeling VERY disappointing during early game while your stats are low.  As you progress and these stats get better, there is a great feeling of power as your hours of practice pay off and you find yourself landing nearly every hit and inflicting massive damage on your foes.  There are rarely miracles in Morrowind.  If an enemy is just too powerful for you, you need to come back to them later when you are stronger.  You wont be able to use trickery or exploits as much as you might think, because the stats don't lie.  If your character is too weak, you will lose.
2) Weapons in Morrowind truly feel special.  There are noticeable differences in the way each one behaves.  Short blades are fast, extremely close range weapons.  If you are good, they are great for landing many fast hits and dealing small amounts of damage repeatedly until your foes are defeated.  Long blades are slow and powerful, spears even more so.  These will require knowledge of how quickly your enemy swings, so you can time your attacks between theirs, and retreat when necessary.  These are slower, more methodical weapons, and they have incredible range.  Bows and crossbows behave as you would expect, but remember to keep in mind that you need to be good with these for your attacks to actually connect.  Bows allow for more input, allowing you to use the appropriate balance of power and speed for the situation.  Crossbows are simple, one power setting, a slow reload, and a lightning fast projectile.  Fantastic.
-
:  Character creation gives you more freedom as to the backstory of your character.  You can change Race (as usual), select a premade class (absent in Skyrim) or create a custom one yourself, and choose a star sign (also absent in Skyrim).  The combination of these three things can lead to some extremely unique and customized characters.  You can fine tune them a lot more, which is a welcome change to personalize who you play as (and I missed the freedom in Skyrim and Oblivion).  Star signs are very cool because they do so many things, from passive, always active abilities, to temporary abilities and spells you can use once a day.  And you get all this, ready to go, the second your character creation is finished.  So what's the catch?  Well, there are no sliders to fine tune your characters body and face.  As someone who plays with first person camera on, I don't see my character all that much anyways.  This is not a game which uses cutscenes, so I find myself more appreciative of the ability to fine tune performance over appearance.
-
:  Morrowind has a lot more dialogue than you are probably used to in the other games.  This means that a compromise had to be made somewhere along the lines.  Probably the most jarring switch from a newer game like Oblivion and Skyrim to an older one like Morrowind, is the lack of voice acting.  There ARE some lines which are audible, but be prepared to do a lot of reading.  If you find yourself pressing the skip button during conversations with NPCs in Oblivion, Skyrim, and Fallout, this is a welcome change, as you can read the dialogue at your own pace, and you can even save it for later if you wish to read your journal.  If you hate reading on the other hand, and want information spoon fed to you, you wont like this.  Personally, I zone out when I listen to characters drone on and on about where I need to go and what I need to do.  Reading keeps me alert.  And the best part is, you can absorb the info you want.  If you want to be immersed, you can enjoy the lore.  If you only care about the objective, you can just read that bit as well.  Take in the info you want, and leave the rest.  Another benefit of no voice acting is that the dialogue feels more real.  There are fewer shared lines as a result of no voice acting.  Speech is more believable.
-
:  Morrowind does not have a compass.  Navigation must be done by using a map, and listening to the directions of others.  If an NPC is giving you directions to a house on the other side of town, you better listen to every turn they tell you to make, because you cannot just point your character in the right direction and run.  This is an inconvenience at first, but if you want to be fully immersed in the world, its a welcome change.  You need to actually explore the land, and look at where you are going.  Your eyes aren't glued to an arrow on a compass bar.  This is a change I love.
-
:  In Morrowind, there are no loading screens to enter and exit a city.  This is fantastic because your immersion is never broken as you seamlessly explore Vvardenfell.  This also saves the pain of some instances where you accidentally enter a large complicated area by accident, only to turn back and deal with the loading screen twice.  Something to keep in mind is that because of this, a few of the cities and towns seem abnormally small, likely due to performance.  You wont find the same scale that is present in Skyrim because there is no loading screen to hide a massive world behind.  Cities are by no means tiny, just slightly smaller than you may expect.  It is something which is easy to get used to.
And now, the only
I can think of:
-
:  You cannot own a house in Morrowind.  You CAN take one from someone else though.

Morrowind:
This is my favourite game of all time, and I just can't put a finger on why. I guess it's just because of the atmosphere, and the ability to go do anything you want.
You probably know that there are some characters in Skyrim you CAN'T kill, or are simply not permitted to die E.G. Ulfric etc.
In Morrowind, this isn't the case. If you meet someone who really pisses you off (Helseth), you can (and probably will, kill them.
This game isn't perfect, and it shouldn't be, that's what makes Morrowind so special. You know the little flaws and oddities you find around the world, they help shape your adventure.
I certainly don't expect anyone has had the same experience I first had when I played this game (however similar it may have been), but that's exactly what makes it so special to me: It's YOUR adventure. YOU decide what to do. And NOT some old guy with a beard that says "Wise man stereotype" (although you'll find those too).
Morrowind is special, in it's own very unique way. So I encourage everyone to pick it up and try it out, you might not like it and that's completely fine, you're allowed to have your opinion, but I urge you not to give up before you've begun.
Btw this game is seriously old, so I'd recommend a graphics mod like MGSO if you're gonna play this on a newer machine

Yes, it's enjoyable, especially the arena fighting, BUT I'm really frustrated because I love the fighting mechanic's but they need a lot of working on, so many schemes to choose from I can't really find the right scheme to give me a decent fight.   Blocking is hit or miss when you need those movements to count, especially when you have 3 or 4 AI's targeting you at the same time.
If they improve that mechanic, because there's nothing bugged that I see, just needs improving, to deliver a decent 1 on 1 abiity to send your attack however you intend it to go in whatever direction you want, that goes for blocking as well; I may consider installing it again!
I used to be so good at this game, then I realized maybe it was because the controls may have been set to "automatic", but that takes the fun out of developing the skill through the mechanic, which I haven't found in any other game.
Another thing they could improve is the Arena, make it more entertaining, such as give us the choice to spawn with what ever weapons we want.   I prefer the heavy sword and the bow, as it is now, Arena fighting is as dry as it was in the original game, you'd expect more from a sequel, in the area of creativity.
I can't give the game a bad review because I like the game, and have put countless hours, but I sincerely wish they'd work on the fighting mechanic's so that when you swing your sword it connects where you want to go, and explain the control options for fighting and blocking, rather than just allowing us to pick the options without an understanding of what they do in the options screen.
Block by mouse movement... Block by movement keys... attack b relative position of enemy...
Combat needs to be fluid and you don't have time to study arrows on the screen when you have numerioius ai's attacking you from every direction, I'm thinking the Computer gets confused and doesn't know which enemy I'm engaged with when there are so many swinging at me.

All in all, it's worth a buy, and worth playing if your not broke and want to have some fun, they did a good job with this game.

This is one of those games with such a brilliant concept that you kick yourself for not thinking of it first.  I'll spare you the details as I assume you can read the store page for yourself.  I played the first hour and got through about 75% of the main content.  Most of the time you're at the mercy of whatever the physics feels like doing, and while that might seem like a knock against the game, the unpredictability is really the entire basis for the game and its "charm", right up to its title.  Personally I found the early content to be ridiculously easy, and it's goofy and pretty fun at first.  I think the right mindset is important here, and I wouldn't go into it with serious expectations and look for some ultra-hardcore challenge.
But my second hour consisted of increasing frustration, and not the "good" kind.  Don't get me wrong, I tend to enjoy masochistic games that are impossibly hard, but when you fail in this game, it's more of the "that was unfair" kind of hard rather than the "I goofed up, let me try again!" hard.  I really don't like the way this game handles.  Let me outline the two major failings that I think hold this game back:
1)  You have very limited control over your jumps.  You can alter your direction and speed just slightly, but not enough to really react or course-correct.  I get it, in a platform game you probably want players to make calculated jumps rather than flying by the seat of their pants.  But isn't that what this game is all about?  The chaotic nature of it kind of necessitates having more ability to control where you land and be able to respond when things go crazy.  This starts to become a problem when the game has you making longer jumps where you're in the air for a while, only to have the truck beneath you suddenly swerve away at the last second.  Sometimes you have to make blind jumps at odd angles and land on trucks in motion which are also prone to veering off or getting pushed off course.  It's tough to get it right, and when you do it often feels like dumb luck more than anything.
2) There's some funny business with the truck friction.  They're slippery.  Most of the time you'll stay in place, but sometimes the truck you're on will get knocked and you'll slide off.  Sometimes you'll be falling through the air lined up for a perfect landing and it doesn't stick.  If you instinctively jump to try and stay with it, you'll usually get thrown at some odd angle and because you have no control in the air, it's over.
Ultimately in the more difficult levels you just feel cheated, and because I don't think this is the sort of game to take seriously, I just stopped.  It doesn't feel rewarding when you push through it because the game doesn't really give you the tools to overcome the challenge.  It's not a bad game by any means, but I think it's probably not worth the price.

I usually like to recommend games when I get 1 hour of playtime per dollar, and well I did it!  I got this game about 1 and a half weeks ago, and luckily I had a long break this past weekend, so I got to play this game a lot and enjoyed most of it. This is a really fun game, but it is a little outdated (which should be expected because it was released in 2010).
What is good:
Fighting - I enjoyed this more than combat systems in other medieval games, such as Elder Scrolls games or Chivalry
Not Fighting - The non-combat aspects of this game were great.  You get to manage your troops, villages, and castles.  I think you can do some political stuff, but I haven't really tried that too much yet
Content - I like games that can keep me occupied for $1 an hour, this game has done this.
Mods - So many mods.  I've only tried one, which was supposed to enhance gameplay.  I haven't played the game without this mod, but I plan to try some more later
Music/Audio - I really like the soundtrack for this game, it fits very well with the game's theam
Art Style - I really liked it, it reminded me of Age of Empires III
Meh (I'm not really sure if I can mark this as good or bad):
The writing - The writing itself is not bad, but there's not enough of it. This means a lot of the text is reused, making a lot of the NPC interactions feel the same.
What's not so good:
The graphics - They aren't great (again because this was made in 2010)
Grindy - This is probably an effect of the lack of writing.  A lot of text and quests are reused making tasks sometimes feel repetitive.
Lacks polish - I'm  not really sure if I can just chalk this up to being made in 2010 because some of these problems look like they could have been fixed with a few more hours of bug tests and fixes.  Some of these problems include:
- Battles not ending, forcing me to restart my game (this only happened once for me)
- The intro video opens, then closes, then the game opens in a new window (I found a way to shut this off online)
- Walking into spikes, instead of killing you, forces your character to be stuck there forever, or until an enemy shoots you to death
- If you walk into a town after finishing a battle, the people in the town (like shopkeepers) will sometimes puch the air or swing their weapon as if they were fighting someone, realize they're not actually fighting someone, then stop.
Stuff I haven't tried yet, but are probably good:
Multiplayer (if people still play this game, this seems like it would be fun)
The DLC

I've always loved the older Resident Evil games, however the last one I actually remember much about was Resident Evil 3 as I owned that one growing up, and only played the previous games at a friend's house.
This Remaster/Remake is just was I was hoping for.  The newer Titles RES 5 and RES 6 focus way too much on action, and you often end up with a small asenal at your disposal with a ridiculous amount of ammo.
This is not the case with this Remaster/Remake.  Ammo is limited, Inventory space is limited, and even your vision is limited depending on where the camera is situated. (this is a good thing)
It makes you use caution when moving somewhere, often you may want to rely on your senses... can you hear a zombie groaning in the other room? or was it just your imagination?
I started out playing this game on hard mode, just to see what it was like.  I died from the 2nd or 3rd zombie I encountered.  It was a brutal experience, the zombies were tough as nails eating most of  clip from my hand gun before finally dying.
I was stuck relying on my knife almost immediately due to not having enough ammo to take care of the zombies, and since I needed to get around the zombies to proceed, there was little choice.  Due to being in close melee range, it also meant they could grab and eat me.. which is what usually ended up happening.
Hard mode was INTENSE..  It was terrifyingly amazing how useless and weak I felt.  This made me actually FEAR the zombies.  Everytime I entered a new room I was a tense situation not knowing if there would be a zombie to greet me as soon as I stepped though the door..
After a couple of deaths I decided to switch to Easy Mode and progressed through the game much better.
While it was Easy Mode, I still thoroughly enjoyed the experience.  It wasn't a walk in the park, the game was still challenging but the player can take more hits before dying, and there are more healing herbs and ammo scattered around the mansion.  This was greatly benifital to me as I had no idea where I was going, or what I was to expect up ahead and it allowed some room for error.
There were still times where I died, but often it was due to being ill prepared.  There are multiple traps in this game, and while they look like they would probably be insta-death I managed to avoid all of them by being cautious or just seeing ahead.
I finished the game after about 20 or so hours.. This was actually a pretty long play through and could have been done much shorter.  This was widely because of not knowing where I was going.  Not to say that you are wandering around aimlessly.. (although you kind of are in a sense)  There is a map, and its the key to progressing.  Some areas of the mansion are unaccessable until you find a certain objects.. like keys, or items used for puzzles that open way for new areas.
There is a lot of back tracking involved and the game doesn't direct you at all by giving you a marker to move towards or a mission objective to complete.  Its all up to you, and it feels great!
After finishing the game and making sure I had 100% of the map and item progression I decided to check online to see if there was anything else I could unlock or do in the game.  In fact there was.. but I had to play on Hard Mode.
I was still a bit in fear of the experience I had with Hard Mode the first time around, but I decided to come back and try it again a couple of weeks later.
Having learned a lot from playing and finishing the game on Easy Mode, I figured I had a better chance at survival than when I first attemped Hard Mode.
While the zombies were MUCH harder to kill, you take brutal amounts of damage, and ammo was scarce.  I did indeed have a better grip on the game..  I was ready.
Unlocking the Samurai Edge Pistol. (beat the game in under 5 hours)
Unlocking the Anti-Tank Rocket Launcher. (beat the game in under 3 hours)
Given how it took me over 20 hours to beat the game on Easy Mode, I clearly had some work to do if I was going to even get close.
The first thing I did was find out if there were any safe places where the game clock did not tick.. like in a menu, or pausing.. during cut scenes.. etc.  There was not.
The moment you load the game, there is no pausing the timer.. PERIOD.  This means you really have to be careful when you save the game.  Thinking a head is critical, you have to know where you are going and where all the monsters are.
I decided I would do some trial and error with some runs.. I'd take a path, get the items I found to be valuable in order to progress the quickest without having to back track too much.
The game needs to be done in segments, figure out a path that leads you to get some importent items and then gets you back to your safe house to save/deposit items to clear up your intentory.  Planning was integral to success, as I didn't want to go through the game and fail just short of the required time to get my unlocks.
My brother and I decided to digitally draw the mansion using mspaint by tracing an online map of the mansion.  I was then able to mark rooms that were locked with a certain key, or needed something special to progress.  Making a path to follow was also easier as you could now visualize the whole processes before going through with it.
Through a lot of trail and error, I completed the game in about 2 hours and 30 minutes.  This was a great success for me, and I unlocked both weapons in one run.  While I finished the game with an in game clock of under 3 hours, in reality it probably took me longer to complete than the first play through since I often was not happy with my segment times and would redo them.
This process turned me into a zombie dodging ninja, as often the fastest way through a room wasn't to clear it by gunning zombies down.. it was to simply step around them somehow.  Completing this time trial challange has essentially turned Hard Mode turned into Easy Mode.. and it was a lot of fun.
The games over now right?  Wrong.
There are 2 characters you can choose to play as.
Chris
Higher max HP
Higher damage output using a Knife
Starts with the Lighter item
Jill
Larger inventory capacity
Starts with a lock pick
They have different story progressions and you explore the masion taking different paths.
If you finish the game with both Chris and Jill on at least Normal Mode, the next time you play, the game will throw a new zombie into the mix.. This zombie has a bomb straped to it's chest and killing it will result in an explosion that will always kill you.
Not enough?
Invisible Enemy Mode - Yeah.. its what it says, the enemies are invisible.  I haven't even attempted this yet as I am certain how it will turn out...  but one day..
There are also different costumes you can unlock per character.
Lastly.. there are also Steam Achivements to strive for.. like
Beat the game without saving.
Beat the game using only a knife. (no other weapons, not even counter/defensive ones)
Amazing game, worth every penny.  I hope RES 7 will take a note from how well this game has sold and try to stay more true to it's roots.
Can't wait for RES 2 Remake/Remaster.. will buy day one. (this one is actually being worked on!)
Can't wait for RES 3 Remake/Remaster.. will buy day one. (I can hope they eventually make this)

Lemme get this out of the way first: this game can be fun, but it just doesn't fit what I am looking for.
In Project Nimbus, you take control of a high mobility mech with a host of weapons and defenses to combat other mechs, as well as ships and some ground emplacements. Combat is extremely fast paced, with a booster you can use to accelerate in all directions.
For me I've been looking for a solid mech game for the PC, and have been left wanting for a while now. I was extremely hopeful when I found this game. But, it did not have what I was looking for, in both customization and combat.
CUSTOMIZATION: One of the things I want from a mech game is the ability to customize my mech and make it mine. Being able to adjust the color, the weapons, the look and feel of the mech, I was looking for all of these. Unfortunately, in Nimbus you take control of premade mechs without any ability to change them. If you are not looking to make your own mech but to jump straight into piloting, this shouldn't affect you. For me though, I want my own mech, and not someone else's.
COMBAT: The combat in Nimbus is extremely fast, too fast for me. The majority of fighting takes place at far ranges and fast speeds that you have to rely on your auto-aim to hit the target, and the distance is so far that you usually only see the enemy mech as a few pixels, and instead spend a lot of the game shooting at the green targeting reticals. They attempted to remedy this by having a window pop up showing the target zoomed in, but even that is too zoomed out at times. Against the larger bosses that you are big enough to see from a distance, the fighting felt a lot better. If they toned down the speed and the distance so that you could actually see the mechs, it would feel more like a mech vs mech game instead of mech vs green targeting box.
Now, I don't hate the game. There are some things I like about it.
One, the cockpit view looks great to me. It actually feels like I am in the pilot seat, with the screens and consoles around me. Very good there.
Two, I appreciate the ability to shoot down missiles without have to rely on flares. I really hope other games pick up on this as a valid form of missile defense.
Three, I like a lot of the mech designs. They are extremely varied, which I appreciate in any game that has multiple factions. Though, this makes it even sadder for me that there isn't an extensive customization system.
Four, voice acting is pretty good for an indie game. I never found myself pulled out of the moment due to a character with a bad voice.
So for people that are looking for extremely fast combat without having to worry about tuning your mech to be effective, this game should fit your needs. For people like me, however, that like to go toe-to-toe with your personal mech against others, this unfortunately won't sate your thirst.

Morrowind:
This is my favourite game of all time, and I just can't put a finger on why. I guess it's just because of the atmosphere, and the ability to go do anything you want.
You probably know that there are some characters in Skyrim you CAN'T kill, or are simply not permitted to die E.G. Ulfric etc.
In Morrowind, this isn't the case. If you meet someone who really pisses you off (Helseth), you can (and probably will, kill them.
This game isn't perfect, and it shouldn't be, that's what makes Morrowind so special. You know the little flaws and oddities you find around the world, they help shape your adventure.
I certainly don't expect anyone has had the same experience I first had when I played this game (however similar it may have been), but that's exactly what makes it so special to me: It's YOUR adventure. YOU decide what to do. And NOT some old guy with a beard that says "Wise man stereotype" (although you'll find those too).
Morrowind is special, in it's own very unique way. So I encourage everyone to pick it up and try it out, you might not like it and that's completely fine, you're allowed to have your opinion, but I urge you not to give up before you've begun.
Btw this game is seriously old, so I'd recommend a graphics mod like MGSO if you're gonna play this on a newer machine

Morrowind is hands-down one of my favorite games of all time and well worth a look for any lover of RPGs with the time to spend on it.

Machinarium is an adventure game in the classic point & click style. A genre that by now only lives in the indie development scene. Whether that is a good or a bad thing is still up for debate.
You play as a little lovable robot that seems to have been made out of mostly trash. As an entirely mute protagonist, as are every character in the game, mute that is, you experience the entirety of the storyline through little memory bubbles that pop every now and then to explain your connection to a particular item or individual. You may or may not understand them however.
Gameplay is entirely point and click. You click on an object in the world to interact with it and on occasion pick it up. Items you collect can be used to interact with those same objects and occasionally can be combined with other collected items to form a new object. It is all very tried and true having been done this way for ages. Unfortunately Machinarium always keeps around some the failings of this genre. Many times you will find that you have to interact with a very specific part of a larger object with no discernible way to see which small place on the screen you have to click to make it work. The logic of the various puzzles, in true point and click fashion, marches to it's own drummer and if you approach the puzzles without being able to adopt this often bizarre method of thinking you will find your stumped quite often.
Machinarium is quite a pretty game, despite being made entirely in flash it manages to produce a beautiful steampunkish environment that is very pleasing to the eye. Being made in flash however means that the occasional accidental right click can often ruin your day.
All in all Machinarium is a fun little game if you're a fan of adventure point and clicks. It is however not a game that stands out in the genre or makes any attempt at even being playable for someone that is not a fan of the genre already.

The game starts out really fun. You start off as a simple rifleman and have to fight in battle to earn better gear and it really gave me one of those old Call of Duty (the good WWII ones) and Medal of Honor vibes. In the beginning you're on a seperate ranking where you are pitted against people the same level as you.
After level 5 the game goes downhill fast. At this point you're put into matches with anyone level 5 and up. You can and will get into matches where the other team has tanks and you don't have anyone on your team who does. You've lost that match already. I get that war is never 'fair' and this game wanted to capture that feeling but a game is supposed to be fun and I don't find losing a match because I never had a chance in the first place compelling.
The game is incredibly grindy as well. You want a bolt action rifle for sniping? That's going to be about 10 to 20 hours of playing matches to gather the currency to afford it. Ammo and weapon repairing will take a toll of your currency too. Used all your grenades? well have fun playing 3 or 4 matches without them to be able to save up enough money to buy more.
Also after you hit the 'real game' after level 5 your queues become longer and the matches become smaller. I can only assume because people realise how grindy and unfair the gameplay is and quit.

Huniepop is a dating sim mixed with candy crush, to put it simply. The story goes that you are apparently so horrible with ladies that a love fairy that is well over 350 years old says that you will be her "greatest accomplishment yet". Ouch. So she teaches you that the key to getting a girls heart is to match up a bunch of colored spheres/jewels/whatevers and apparently if you do it right you're in the clear.
Now that you know the true, secret ways of dating, your job is to go around town and bang literally every girl you can. Remember how I said 'your job...' and all that? That was literal; apparently after some time these dates you take these girls on are SO amazing that they will pay you thousands of dollars.
Anyway, onto the pros and cons of the game:
Pros:
+ The story, although kinda bland, still has a decent charm to it.
+ The characters are all unique, and none of the girls really are "boring" in a sense. Each one has their own unique way of presenting themselves.
+ On easy/normal the puzzles are not difficult by any means and can even be relaxing after some time.
+ The designs of the girls, voice acting are beautifully designed.
+ The game doesn't take itself seriously, and makes lots of funny jokes here and there.
+ You can give a latino girl maracas and a sombreo, a black girl watermelon, and an japanese girl sake/a bonsai tree and not offend anybody.
Cons:
- Considering that this game is more or less softcore porn, more than likely you're going to get patronized by your friends a bit online/irl about playing this game (in my case, having 4 friends synchronize their texts before the game even loaded up)
- It gets kinda repetitve. Find girl, ask questions, go on 5 dates, bang,
, go on more dates, move to another girl.
- Not much replay-ability. I might be wrong, but aside from different intial dialouge, there's only so much to do.
- As you play the puzzles, there are purple "broken hearts" which if connected together, will rip out huge chunks of your "affection bar" (basically what you need to fill each date) and those numbers can get kinda ridiculous.
- The game apparently secretly takes place in an alternate reality where a bagel costs $200 and a glass of whisky costs $600. What?
- If you're single and play this game at night, it might make you question yourself in many ways.
- A bit pricy at it's base. At the time of this review (6/29/2016) it's 69% off.

Don't let the graphic fools you, give it extra hours before you dropped it.
Several minutes into the game I myself was put off by the graphic, it certainly hasn't age well and the combat felt weird at first. Still, we should keep in mind that this is CD Projekt Red first title and it is a small budget game.
Knowing the problems I had, I still played it till the end and ENJOYED IT.
After several hours into the game, the graphic became more acceptable. Once I understood the content more, I felt that the graphic wasn't that bad and the style actually brings out the nature of the world that feels dark and gloomy and it certainly supports the story and mature content of the game that sets The Witcher franchise apart from other RPGs.
While the game seems unpolished in lots of aspect, the story and role playing experience are definitely worth it and I consider it to be in par with BioWare's titles (As BioWare is one of the greatest RPG developer in my opinion). That being said, the world of The Witcher is based on a novel and CD Projekt Red did a good job setting up the lore in game which is a joy for us RPG fans to explore.
Now it is already a common knowledge that Witcher 3 is undoubtly one of the best RPG of all time and there's no reason not to play it, but before playing the sequel I recommend you to play the franchise starting from this one not only because of the save import feature (So your choices made in the first two titles will affect the third) but also because this game alone is a solid RPG that you need to try.

Superflight is amazing for what it is. It captures the feel of "falling with style" quite well and the maps are usually great and not buggy.
However there is one annoying problem that other games like this one also suffer from. A problem that will mostly effect casual players that pay $3 and expect just a relaxing, distracting game.
After you become half decent (about 5 minutes of play will get you there), the game becomes waaay too long. For a casual and relaxing game to have "runs", the runs need to be short (10 minutes tops). However you can really just go on and on forever. There is no real change in difficulty and the only challenge comes from how daring and greedy you get with combos. That means unless you like to constantly crash into things every minute, the game becomes way too easy and boring.
It's a problem worth not recommending over because games like Superflight need to be short, sweet and relaxing. Not long, boring and repetitive.

The epitome of survival horror. If you enjoyed any other game in the series, and have yet to try this one out, definitely give it a shot. If you're new to the series, this REmaster of the 2002 REmake of the 1996 original is a great place to start. I always particularly enjoyed the art style and atmosphere of the REmake and RE0 (also getting an HD remaster), and now with the upgraded resolution, textures, and lighting effects, it's that much more immersive. Even after playing through as both characters, there are plenty of extra game modes that require you to change up your strategy in order to progress. The amount of content you receive for the price makes the purchase well worthwhile. A common criticism of the older RE games (although one that I personally don't find problematic) is that tank controls are difficult for beginning players to get a feel for. Fortunately, this version features an optional Silent Hill 2-esque alternative control scheme, in which the character moves in the direction pressed. So go on and grab your Samurai Edge and try not to smoke too many green herbs.

Quite simply, one of the finest examples of survival horror out there.
The brooding atmosphere, deadly enemy encounters and the limited resources make for an oppressive game that never lets up. There's no hand-holding here, it just throws you in the deep end and expects you to cope.
As for the port itself, the updates for this remastered version are largely welcome editions. Everything that is expected of modern-day ports is here: Widescreen support (which works flawlessly), 60fps (or uncapped framerate), V-Sync and Anti-Aliasing appear for the first time in the game. The original game from 2002 still looks beautiful even today but this remaster gets that little bit extra out of it, with new lighting, higher resolution textures and higher quality audio. The port is also very stable; I only had one crash to desktop in 26 hours (7 playthroughs). The only thing I can't comment on is the (optional) newly designed controls. I stuck with the original control layout as that's what I'm familiar with from the Gamecube version.
The achievements are also a nice little extra, especially if - like me - you have previously played the game on Gamecube/Wii. These achievements dare you to try new things, such as completing the game using only your knife, not using any ink ribbons (saves), or even playing the game with all the enemies invisible.
In short, one of the greatest horror games ever gets a fantastic port. There's plenty of unlockables and achievements to work towards, so there's loads of replay value here.

One of the better free to play MMO options (other than the severe currency restriction).
(updated after the ProSeibenSat.EU server debacle finally ended, lost my characters due to a limited-time transfer window in 2015, luckily my purchases were saved)
It's a free to play & subscription based MMO with a cash shop and all the gated content and limited choices that implies.
TL:DR play it for fun for free (it's great for a weekend of casual play once a month). maybe spend a month or two on subscription to try the gated content, quit once you have had your fill.
The progression system is 30 standard character levels, skill-points (earned through character achievements/feats, you can get 150+ points eventually) and gear-score to access new/tougher content. Easy to get into and simple  to progress in.
Level 30 gets you 15 ability points (spell unlocks) and 24 skill points (enough points to fully unlock 2-3 weapons combos and start on passives).
The weapon based combat is inspired by 3rd person brawler games (devil may cry/dynasty warriors/Tera), 10 weapons plus the DLC shield weapon to use.
You can equip any weapon (once unlocked with skillpoints) but swapping is done throught the inventory screen. Weapons have clear combat differences and ranges but all combos are a mix of tap/hold melee/ranged buttons with occasional directional imputs.
The powersets are themed so you can fill the 6 available hotbar slots with a decent mix of active abilities. Every powerset has 2 trees containing 12 powers each, plus the iconic pool of 22 famous abilities (superman heat-ray, shazam blast, batarang volley, wonder womans lasso) and passives.
The voice acting aged well (the cast is the known voices).
The cut scenes are passable but the instance reward scenes are well made (short but effective).
The setting is (mostly) well used, 2 open cities plus DLC content I have not tried yet and usual themed MMO holiday events.
Travel skills (flight, super-speed, batman gagets) are suprisingly well implemented.
Acrobatics starts slow with wall-climbing but ends up as a grappling-hook/rocket-hang-glider combo.
Single hotbar loadouts. It's also a contole game so 6 active abilities, one heal, and one trinket slot (DLC expandable to allow 4 trinkets later on) is all you get. One DPS loadout, one role loadout, swappable only out of combat.
Restrictive power sets, 6 basic and 8 DLC. Split by trinity tank/heal/control roles.
You pick a power/role at character creation and are locked-in forever (can pay to swap to another power in the cash shop). no fire healers, munitions tanks, or sorcery tanks possible.
The game is stunlock/CC/combo heavy and the break-out mechanic is to mash the block button. The only defence is to hope you don't get hit again immediately.
Personally I refuse to PvP due to the escalating passive benefits of long time players (acchievements unlock skills are put into passive numerical upgrades once you have your chosen weapons combos unlocked) and the easy to apply irritating to break stunlock nature of PvP combat.
The questing is the usual MMO affair, fetch, kill, click, escort.
The free to play limitations.
Usual MMO bag-space lmiitations
In game credits are limited to a pathetic 1500 or 2000 unless you subscribe (overflow stored in escrow) some houses, gear items and auction house items are beyond your reach.
Amazing artwork, sound and puzzles.

single-player 3D-4X RPG.  The game starts on the island of Vvardenfell in the Dunmer kingdom of Morrowind.  You the Gamer are free to create and develop your Player Character {PC} in many ways to suit your desired play style.  Your PC may be any of several available Races, such as Human {e.g.: Imperial or Breton}, Mer {e.g.: Dunmer or Bosmer}, or Beast-race {e.g.: Khajiit or Argonian}.  You also choose the PC's "occupation" such as battle mage, warrior, thief, rogue, etc., and even the astrological birth sign.
Through game-play experiences, the PC can develop and improve various characteristice which will enable your PC to prevail as you strive to complete the many quests in the main storyline.  However, you do not have to follow the storyline at all.  After clearing "Customs" in Seyda Neen, the PC is free to roam, interact with the many NPCs {non-player characters}, explore the wilds of Vvardenfell, dungeon dive, or even do some of the story line quests as you prefer.

While very simple, Superflight accomplishes what it sets out to do - provide a relaxing experience based on gliding down procedurally generated levels with the goal of earning as many points possible during your run (which ends upon crashing into a solid surface). The game is also very simple to control and may be something you let younger kids play around with (I imagine my nephews would enjoy it).
My only complaints are that there doesn't seem to be a way to view the full leaderboard (you can see your ranking based on your top score and top combo) and the weird 'click' noise when you hit play and start a run (it just annoys me).
If you enjoy having a game to play while doing something else (like listening to music, podcasts, etc.) or enjoy trying to continuously beat your high score, I highly recommend it, especially for the current sale price of $1.49.

I am going to be completely up front. This game isn’t for me. The reason why I’m featuring the game is because I contacted the developer through Steam and he agreed that he’d like me to feature the game here. Really cool guy. The game is the sequel to Spaceman Sparkles 2 which was released last year. Now I thought that the game would be my cup of tea. It’s space and I’m a lover of space games. But the game is just too frantic for me and the flashy lighting and the controls do funky things with my head. That’d be awesome if I was in any position to experience a non-drug induced trip out but I’m not.
But you know what? This game will appeal to many people. The graphics – as basic as they appear – are pretty darn cool and spectacular. Those who can get to grips with the concept and who love challenging gameplay will find something deeply meaningful and enjoying in this game. Ainslie enjoyed the game but couldn’t think of anything to justify an Ainslie’s Little Pearls segment other than to say that the game was experimentally exciting and that it’s the type of game that her colleagues that are gamers would get an absolute kick out of.
As Bootleg Jones said on the Steam discussion forum for the game you really do have to appreciate a developer who will spend the time to make the game that they want to make. And I love the honesty in recognizing that the game isn’t going to be for everyone and that the Steam refund system is a neat feature that will give you your money back if you don’t find the game to your liking. And really it is one of those games. You’re going to either love it or you’ll refund it.
At the end of the day it’s a risk free no obligation. Spend the $4.49 the game currently sells for (or $4.99 at full price) and give the game a go. It’s well worth the download and the try and I can say that with full integrity and honesty even if it wasn’t for me.

For the most part, the puzzles are fine, but some of them require some very specific logic and noticing very subtle changes in the environment in order to solve without a guide (I got stuck in three places during my playthrough). Combat's a bit clunky, but the game's more of a 2.5D adventure/puzzle game, so I feel like combat wasn't the main focus. Also, the game is part of a planned series, so if you're expecting full closure at the end, you'll be somewhat disappointed.
The voice acting was solid, as was the animation. Definitely has potential, but I think--based on my experience with The Fall--the rest of the series won't really be my cup of tea (so take my lack of recommendation for what it's worth).
Not sure I'd recommend getting it at full price, either way, as I clocked in at about 3 hours for a complete playthrough.

The Fall is a short side-scrolling title which -does- involve tiny amounts of shooting and jumping. The majority of the game, however, involves exploring a shadowy underground facility which appears to be derelict and abandoned. You play as an artificial intelligence commanding a suit intent on saving the human that wears her. The voice acting is all excellent, the story is interesting, and I had a good time playing it.
The most surprising thing about this game to some might be that it is effectively an adventure game. Y'know, like King's Quest, etc., though there are very few characters and interacting with things involves rightclicking while aiming your flashlight at them, holding shift, then using your directional selection buttons to choose to either network with something, take or use it, or interact an item of your choice with it. It works pretty well once you get used to it, and the majority of the game consists of little puzzles. Nothing is terribly difficult to figure out, and I completed the game in under four hours. I believe it actually only took me about 2.5 hours, though, because I stopped to watch a couple of TV shows while playing and left the game running.
Despite its brevity, I do recommend this title if you ever enjoyed adventure games. Don't go in seeing the side-scrolling with a gun in a sci-fi setting and expect Metroid, because you will -not- get Metroid out of this game at all. So yeah, adventure games, robots, A.I., sci-fi, if that stuff appeals to you, pick this game up.

Morrowind was my first Elder Scrolls game and my first PC game. Initially I played it on the Xbox and loved it, but once I found out about how much better it was on PC, I had to try it out. This is one of my favorite games of all time. Even after playing the hell out of Skyrim, I can still come back to this game and have loads of fun (unlike Oblivion). It is one of the ultimate RPG experiences out there and I honestly don't think you can call yourself an Elder Scrolls fan if you haven't played this one. Graphically, it hasn't aged very well, but it is still a gorgeous game and one of the few games that genuinely made my jaw drop. The combat system takes some getting used to, but there is so much history/lore in this game, so much variety in playstyles/classes, just so much of everything all in one game.

Terrible game because you can't rebind the controls on a gamepad. Jump is the A button on an xbox controller but you need to use the right stick to turn your character. It makes the game unplayable with a gamepad since you really can't turn at all because you need to be constantly hitting jump at a precise time so you're basically just limited to jumping in a straight line with a little bit of lateral movement because of strafing with the left stick.
Seriously, I don't understand how the devs 1) Didn't realize that a default control scheme where jump was on a shoulder button or trigger would be infinitely better and 2) DON'T JUST MAKE THE CONTROLS REBINDABLE. How hard can this be? I don't think it's asking too much. It's like no one on the dev team even tried to play it with a gamepad because 2 minutes into the game I realized it just doesn't work how it's setup.
There was a steam discussion thread with people asking for rebindable controls for gamepads and the devs only response was something along the lines of "Well what kind of control scheme would you like to be using?" like they would just create an alternative scheme instead of, ya know, MAKING THEM REBINDABLE so you can just make it how you would like it. Even then, the thread was old and it seems they chose to do nothing anyways.
Would probably be a fun game otherwise but it's unplayable with a gamepad in it's current state.
PS - You shouldn't need third party software because of lazy devs.

This game needs work, but has potential.
During large battles when too many models like missiles and enemies are on screen the frame rate tanks to unplayable levels. There are  missions where there are too many enemies to focus on at once, and the fight becomes more frustrating than exciting. Act III has a lot of this.
The targeting system needs fine tuning and some adjustments. While a feature of this system is to lose targeting when the enemy is out of range, it is extremely frustrating in boss fights especailly later in the game. Many bosses out speed your craft and to retarget them to fire your weapons proves to be more of a challenge than dodging their attacks. If you target an enemy it should stay locked until the player chooses a new target or the target is eliminated.
While the game scales with difficutly, some missions/ boss fights like *spoiler* the one with Yuliana in Act 3's final mission are just plain hectic and impossible. This fight in particular is the most frustrating due to her speed, seemingly non-existant cooldowns, and the targeting system losing her all the time.
Water physics should be added for those levels it applies to (i.e. if you skim the surface of a body of water, there should be sprays).
In Sekai no Zange, there is a spelling mistake when the HUD boots up for Skull-1 (begib should be begin), and the sub-titles do not always match the voice script. The latter comment is prevalent throughout the game.
I have been reccomending this game to friends, but that was before I was deep into Act III. Act I and II play well for the most part. For a low budget AC clone it does well otherwise. My complaints are mostly to show that the game needs some clean up, balancing, and has potential to be more visually appealing. If the devs can work on these issues and others that I may not ahve mentioned I will change my review.
