the HEROES game (1st person shooter)
STICK WITH IT, STICK WITH IT, STICK WITH IT, Got  it?
NOT PAY TO WIN
This game is NOT PAY TO WIN (sorta) in my opinion. I do not play premium as a practice and I finish in the top 3 in points routinely. I dont see it as a game changer.
There is a small advantage to paying players by use of an extra boost slot. But that is really it. I encourage you to pay if you want to, because it supports the game. I have played close to 1000 hrs at this writing, and I have not paid for stuff with real money with the exception of I paid a one month membership as a thanks to the developers for their hard work, and I have bought a couple exp boosters for the banners to level up my M1/m2 SMG but thats it. If you are not lazy and are willing to work at it, You can just grind up and buy everything you need in game with patience. Just grind it up. Or pay and dont grind. Both things are good. The game needs money to survive. People who dont want to pay dont have to and can do exactly as well.
EARLY GAME PLAY
THIS GAME IS NOT EASY. If you like easy you will hate this game. But if you work at it and learn the game it is absolutely an AWESOME FUN GAME. It is very hard early, but this game gets much better with experience and levels as your weapons and gear improve. STICK WITH IT. Grind it out. The game gets easier and much more fun as you go and grow into new things. Early you are going to get killed alot and feel VERY inneffective. STICK WITH IT. I have leveled 2 soldiers to Officer, I have a tanks commander at Lt Colonel and an infantry officer to Major, soon I will have a para Officer. MY pilot is geting close as well, and my recon will be last. I did it all with hard work from level one with each soldier, and tons of determination and alot of deaths.
NEW PLAYERS
I found that tank play allowed me to make the most money with all tanks except the Chaffee. I recomend levelling the tank tree first. Be agressive especially in pub matches (standard battles) that is the place to learn and experiment. Grind your HE rounds as fast as you can HE is deadly on troops. If you go infantry and go American fire your M1G from the hip as much as possible and always at close range it becomes very effective as you upgrade it and learn to use it. Smg's are typically better in a room, but not by much. Skip the planes early unless that is just really what you want to do. Flying is tough to play as your only toon. I would wait until later to level your pilot.
THE OBJECT
Cap Cap Cap. Guys you have to cap to win. At least when you are attacking, but generally always. If you cap you will score well, good exp, and you will win the game. GO find the cap get on it. Hide, fight, learn the tricks of capping and you will rule this game. Tanks understand that your main goal is to support your team to cap. Period. Sometimes a tank can push open a path for people to cap behind. Tanks need the infantries support, and visa versa. Work together. Protect the tanks when you are playing infantry by keeping anti tank infantry away. Get on cap. Watch your lives.
THE WAR
Guys, this game has a full war going on a huge map of Europe. Every troop in the war is being directed by other players. When you play the Heroes part of the game you are playing one of the Generals (Officers) troops. Which he has bought and paid for with his Warfunds. When you fight in the war you gain War Funds which you can use to fund your generals game play. If you are playing in the war don't ♥♥♥♥♥ the generals. It is their war, they are paying, and only they have the big picture in mind. Often the players in the battle don't understand why they are facing very uneven odds and things like that, but don't worry about it. Do your best. And If you can win a battle by out capping the other team when you only have 250 infantry on motorcycles against 2000 or more troops, it is incredibly rewarding to know you probably just captured a city against very unlikely odds. And those 1000's of troops you displaced are now retreating and needing to reinforce all because you didn't quit based on what you perceived as an unfair battle. If you cant win, drain as much of their resources as you can and level up.
Also the troops that you start with may not be the troops that you end up with in a war battle, and often you will get reinforced as the battle progresses. It takes time to move troops on the map and you may end up with many more troops at the end of the battle than you started with and new lanes opening up and so on as troops arrive to the battle.  Just do your job as best you can. DONT WASTE RESOURCES IN THE WAR. Protect your resources and you will be a long way on your way to winning.
LASTLY BUT MOST IMPORTANT WORK TOGETHER DONT BISH AT EACH OTHER. YOU ARE ON THE SAME TEAM. FOCUS THE ENEMY, and help to teach those who know less than you by encouraging not name calling.
GENERALS
I didn't play the Generals game until very late. But it is fun too, and again I have paid for nothing more than a single month of premium. see above. I now have two officers with a total of 3 assault teams. I have a medium and a light tank assault team. And a Motorized Infantry assault team with infantry and jeeps. Armor is key to winning on the map, and it can very easily tip the tide of battle to have armor in the battle especially when your opponents have only infantry.
Google - Heroes and Generals - Generals game, there are many very good guides on YouTube.
BOTTOM LINE PLAY THE GAME IF YOU LIKE A VERY FUN GAME THAT IS NOT EASY, AND that  REWARDS PLAYERS WHO STICK WITH IT!
Have fun and see you in Battle.

I really wanted to like this game. From what I did play, I was really enjoying the story. However, overall the game feels very dated. Controlling Geralt is pretty clunky, the combat is somewhat uninteresting, the graphics are unremarkable (even keeping in mind that it's a low-budget 2008 game), character models are reused all over the place (even for important characters), the voice acting is pretty shoddy at times, and the first few hours are a bit of a drag.
From what I've gathered, the game does seem to get much better once you get out of the swamp area, but I couldn't get that far. Due to a bug in the game, I didn't get a certain item that I need to progress in the story. I don't know how far back I would have to go (or if I'm even able to), and I really don't want to start the whole game over again, so I gave up.
A lot of people really love this game, and I understand why. It's not a bad game, it's just really hard to get into.

I've heard many things about this franchise, most of it stemming from the third entry into the series.

The combat is more akin to point and click RPG with active combat thrown in to pull back the dice rolls. The interface and mechanics are very rough as the game was created in the early 2000s but it is serviceable if you are willing to find an edge. The story is gripping but also hard to follow due to odd writing choices and shoddy voice acting.
However, you should play it see the series' roots and enjoy a oddball story with a unique perspective.

The combat isn't for everyone and is pretty dull. There also seems to be a general consensus that the first two acts of the game are incredibly tedious, and is where many people give up on the game, especially in the swamp area. Once you get to the swamp part, just know that there is so much more to the game after this section that completely makes up for it. If you're wondering if you can just skip this thing and go straight to The Witcher 2, I would say you can, but you should do yourself a favor by at least giving this game a shot. It is extremely cheap, especially during sales.

I just bought this game, after having it on my wishlist ever since it came out, but after playing it for less than half an hour, for the first time ever, I applied for a refund. This game, unlike any other RPG or FPS I have ever played, uses fixed camera angles all the time. There is no first person or third person view. Resident Evil/Biohazard HD Remaster (Resident Evil REmake) is an excellent addition to the library of any survival horror fan.
An HD remaster of a remake of the original Resident Evil, Resident Evil REmake brings the classic survival horror game into the 21st century with updated graphics, a new control scheme, and a refinement of various puzzles and encounters from the original.
The game looks brilliant, all things considered. Bringing about the look of modern horror games only serves to further improve the atmosphere of Resident Evil REmake.
If you're familiar with the original Resident Evil, you may recall the "tank" controls that it sported. While the original control scheme is still available, Resident Evil REmake introduces a new control scheme that allows Jill (or Chris) to move and turn freely. While this is a vast improvement over the original tank controls, it is sometimes hindered by the fixed camera angles, which are still present and, from time to time, present issues with aiming and navigation.
Unlike more recent installments in the franchise, you cannot run and gun your way through REmake. The Spencer Mansion, in which the game is set, is a maze that requires careful navigation and will have players fighting to survive as they move from room to room, attempting to progress. Ammunition is scarce, as are healing items, and, as such, players will have to manage their resources, know when they should kill an enemy, and know when they should run.
The atmosphere stays spot-on nearly all the way through. Time and time, again, you will yourself unnerved and forcing yourself to progress. Encounters with enemies are tense as you try to survive, managing your ammunition, and attempting to overcome various monstrosities that, almost always, have the upper hand. But it is in the quiet moments that the game really comes to life. As you pass from room to, seemingly, lifeless room, it's hard not to hold your breath for the next trap or encounter, breeding a fear of the unknown and anticipated.
As for the story, it's a Resident Evil game. Umbrella is cartoonishly evil and it's up to you to clean up, or, in this case, survive, their mess. Still, journal entries and atmospheric story-telling throughout the game provides some interesting and, at times, meaningful back story, as you try to piece together the history of the Mansion's captives.
In terms of performance, I did notice some drops in frame rate, despite playing with the graphics settings and having a PC that should have no trouble running the game on its highest settings.
A brilliant game that delivers on all fronts, with only some minor hiccups, Resident Evil REmake is an exercise in true survival horror, and an example of what a remake/remaster should be.
I highly recommend it. 8.5/10

Incredibly fun mechanics, clever level design and a decent difficulty ramp make Clustertruck one of the best games I've played all year. It's hard to describe the immense pleasure I felt playing this game. Absolutely worth anybody's attention.

This game is actually a subtle commentary on the abuse of stimulants by many of America's truck drivers and the horrible effects it has on their lives, as well as the risks to those around them.
The truckers in Clustetruck are an exaggerated analogy used to communicate this idea, as they are clearly hopped-up on some sort of cocktail of amphetamines that has driven them into a hideous murder-rage which consumes all of their thoughts. Their sole purpose, their entire function in existence, their raison d'être is to drive as fast as possible, towards the ambiguous "goal", while competing with other truckers - most often by killing them. At their drugged state, the only way they can feel anything is to enter into this terrifying world of diesel-soaked mayhem and Lynyrd Skynyrd mixtapes. Forever chasing their objective, doing terrible things to fellow truckers they once called friends, all for the sweet release from the daily hell of motorized labor, but almost always failing to reach it as their lives are more often consumed in a conflagration of exploding semis and laser beams.
Compounding this social tragedy is the part of the player, who must traverse the trailers of these homicidal road warriors in an attempt to survive and reach your own goal. This is a representation of how the average American consumer relies on truckers as a vast majority of foodstuffs arrive at American grocers and markets via trailer - making the plight of truckers even more relevant.
The soundtrack is pretty great but if you want to enhance your experience, throw down on a bunch of pre-workout and listen to Slayer while you play. Riveting.

The storyline is famous, and there's good reason for it. Intrigue, mystery, political turmoil and living gods all contribute to this game being far ahead of its time.
This is a game that may not appeal to those who are used to the flow of modern RPG's, but I believe it should be played anyway.

Morrowind is, arguably, tied with Oblivion with being my favourite game in the Elder Scrolls series. While Oblivion and later procedings to the series depict environments not too dissimilar from florid landscapes that can seem tantalisingly similar to our own - Morrowind is a strict outlier. A bold thrust into the unknown with an utterly alien art style that is immediately apparent from the beginning up until the very end.
For the sake of this game's unique story, I will keep spoilers to a minimum. Players can select one of the many iconic species of the Scrolls series and are dumped into the world with barely any guidance or hand holding involved. The game lacks quest markers and the easily accessible fast travel system players might be familiar with from Skyrim or Oblivion. It is tricky to weigh this as either a pro or con - for it can be either. It encourages exploration, yes, but when you surface from a ruin overburdened with loot it may seem quite the opposite. Fast travel is not non-existant, however, for there are various ways to traverse Vvardenfell but only from certain points; such as dockyards or the bizarre fauna travel of silt-striders.
It can be an overwhelming game at first play, but it is for this very reason that the game has a heartwarming and vast sense to it that seems vacant or overlooked in later games. It is true that Morrowind has the smallest land mass of the Scrolls games, but it feels anything but. Quests are everywhere and being left to one's own devices after leaving the initial area is all part of the experience; and it is a unique one at that.
Morrowind has aged considerably since it's release in '04, but still has an active modding community that can patch holes  in the hull long after the initial developers moved on from the project.
A major con which is immediately apparent is the outdated combat system - even for it's release date. It relies on a superfluous and complex system of dice rolling, factoring in countless algorithms for whether an attack hits or not. Armour, weapon, fatigue, skills, spells and those of the target all fall into a hopelessly headscratching equation. But, nothing a mod cannot fix.
Last, but certainly not least, is the game's soundtrack - produced by the same Jeremy Soule who worked on earlier and later editions of the Scrolls series. The compositions fit a game with so unique an artstyle flawlessly, with an almost equal amount of uplifting tracks which seem to encourage the exploration of this unique environment.
TL:DR Version:
I enjoy it a lot. It's something everyone should experience for themselves.

I've always wanted to play a medieval themed role playing game. I saw my friend playing it, so I decided to give it a go. It was one of the best decisions I've made in a while.
The premise of the game is that you start out alone in the kingdom of Calradia where numerous factions fight for the ultimate throne. You can join a faction as a mercenary then work your way up, or help someone overthrow their king. Once you are affiliated with a faction or already own one, you'll be at war against other kings sooner or later.
For you to conquer Calradia, you need to seige the enemy forts and towns to conquer them one by one. You have to recruit your own men from various towns for war. After battle, you and your men will gain exp and eventually be able to upgrade.
The game itself is very heavily focused on combat, so it feels to me as if it lacks depth to other aspects, such as kingdom management. If you're a fan of combat based games however, this is a great game for you. The melee fights are very responsive, the hitboxes are good, and it just feels right. You also have a fairly diverse range of weapons to choose from, such as crossbows, throwing axes, lances, maces, and longswords.
This game does have its downsides though, For the most part, the game can be very dull and repetitve when you near the end of the game. You can do quests for the townfolks and talk to various characters, but you are going to be fighting someone at the end of the day.
But don't let this deter you from buying this game. I've already spent well over 100 hours playing this game, and I haven't even tried out workshop contents or multiplayer. Despite its lack of content in other areas, it still does great in what it focuses on. If you like medieval action, you should definitely give this game a try, especially during sales!

Enjoy Project NIMBUS for what it is: A high-speed 6DOF mecha action romp.
I'm a big fan of Mobile Suit Gundam:00, so the storyline and tone hit my yummy buttons straight out of the gate.
The Campaign is a series of sequential missions that (sort of obliquely) tell a story of conflict between Haves & Have-nots in a post-apocalyptic future. If you put the effort into following it, the story is pretty cool.
It's worth mentioning that all the campaign missions are available at any time, so you can be a rebel and play them backwards if you like. Very punk.
Suvival is the standard pick-a-mech (called 'battleframes' in this milieu) and try to survive waves of progressively more challenging enemies. I've found it fun for mechy-blasty action.
Also worth mentioning is that there are no customization options for the battrlerframes or their loadouts. Not a big deal for me, but if you rully-rully-rully need that kind of thing, consider yourself informed.
I've been enjoying it so far, and I can see it being a go-to for quick casual fixes of the aforementioned mechy-blasty action with a definite Gundam vibe. A very impressive indie production!

Imagine if Ace Combat and Armored Core had a baby and you'll have a good idea what to expect.
That being said, this game DESPERATELY needs polish. I have no idea how some of the weapons actually work and some just need some kind of explination. I'm still trying to figure out what the particle shield does. Are you supposed to hide behind it? Activate it and run? Use it like a decoy?
The weapon reloading and usage mechanics also mean that you often don't use weapons based on what's best for a given situation but rather what's loaded at the moment. Weapon cycling becomes a must and as a result you spend disproportionate time
Also, the voicework needs some work. Yes, bow as in the front of a ship and bow as in that thing that shoots arrows are spelled the same but they're spoken entirely differently. I know, english is stupid like that but it's one of those things a larger team would catch.
That being said, I occasionally forget that this is an indie game. The action is so frantic and fluid that I could swear that only a AAA company could have made it. Indeed, I'd happily play this over whatever crud gets thrown at me by EA.
Here's to hoping for more.

I kida stalled with playing this game because I was afraid it wouldn't meet my expectations. I love those indie sci-fi puzzle platformers because, if the creators are sensible enough, they are just the right mix of deep, ambitious storytelling and down-to-earth, classic platforming and puzzle-solving. Like Swapper, which is one of my favourite games of all time. Let's just say I love the genre and the potential it carries. But all too often the games just fall flat because they are either too ambitious and story driven which makes for a very confusing afternoon, or too casual and mainstream which makes for a very disappointing afternoon.
This one is the winner in my book. It's just the perfect love affair between mind-bending storytelling and brain-churning puzzle-platforming. There were a couple of times where I was ready to throw in the towel and cry my way towards the nearest walkthrough, but just at the right moment the puzzle revelaled its secrets and everything was good again. And it felt good too. And the story? Wow. Very well paced and with some unexpected plot twists. Before long you start to think like an autonomous war machine on a mission to save its pilot by all means necessary. Or do you? ;) There are some feels too. Nothing tear-jerking but you do feel like you've witnessed something meaningful.
If you look for negatives very hard you could probably point to the fact this game was clearly made with consoles in mind and the porting team didn't even bother removing the oh-so-helpful "Use your Right Stick" tutorial messages, let alone redoing the UI so that it is actually semi-usable when playing on a PC. As it is, the interface is probably the biggest facepalm-inducing thing in the game. Other than that, the sound didn't make a big impression on me (then again I was playing on a sub-par headset). The cover system and combat in general felt kinda tired and "trope-y" with all those waist-high walls and "silent takedowns" but it's by far not a major part of the game so I guess it's fine.
In closing: If you like puzzle-platformers - buy this game; If you like thought-provoking storytelling - buy this game; If you like indie sci-fi games - buy this game. Hell, just buy this game and either way you won't be disappointed, and you might even be happy. Like I am. I'm happy I got to play this game and I'm looking forward to the second installment.

I've heard of this game for a long time now but never got a chance to buy and play it until last winter sale, I finally tried it, and it's an awesome game so far, worth more than what I paid for.
It's a sandbox medieval RPG/tactical/strategy/empire-management game. You start out with a character, whose 'background story' can be customized, that can affect your character's starting location, equipment, stats, and reputation.
You level up your character, assign stats and skills, customize his looks, equip gear and weapons, acquire followers. the battles are in real-time, similar to Chivalry and Skyrim but with more units, Imagine Total War-like battles but you get to join and command your army in battle. Once you get more known in the land, and have a lot of reputation, kings and lords might get interested in your service and ask you to join them, or maybe refuse them and found your own kingdom! or just make your own business empire and earn money the civilian way, or be a travelling merchant,. be a bandit in the wilderness raiding villages, selling prisoners to slavers, and preying on passing caravans, Many possibilities.
What you do in the game depends on your choice, You can completely do almost everything you want, be a bandit, a merchant, a businessman, a mercenary, a soldier, a commander, you can even make your own faction, and conquer the whole land.
Not mentioned the multiplayer is fun as well, like Chivalry but better. and the modding support is great, tons of new content to play if you somehow get bored of vanilla gameplay. Since the game is out for many years already, the game has a lot of total conversion mods already, aside from the usual mods that enhance the gameplay, there are ones that completely add new land, factions, lore and backstory, some mods adapts a popular work-of-fiction like the lord of the rings or game of thrones, or moves the game into a different era and setting, like feudal japan, roman empire, american civil war, medieval europe, etc.
Luckily, I only played it recently and a sequel is coming out soon (2016), not much waiting for me. Play it now while the sequel isn't out yet, or you'd miss out on a lot of things.

The first title in The Witcher trilogy of games (no Gwent, you don't count) isn't for everyone. It will feel busted and unpolished throughout most of the game (heh, unPOLISHED) however if you can look past the "eurojank" you will find that you are playing one of the best modern action RPGs.
The combat style is unique, it may feel strange and dumb at first but it will grow on you.
World building and story telling is where the game shines however, and I know a lot of you will be rolling your eyes at this. IT'S A GAME, WHO CARES ABOUT THAT, I WANT MY DARK SOULS PVP SHENANIGAAAANS. Yes, yes you're not wrong, however the investigation, the conversations, the roaming around the dark fantasy world are part of the gameplay.
Gameplay doesn't mean combat or platforming necessarily and The Witcher's gameplay and worldbuilding go hand in hand.
I recommend that you play all three games in release order if you're interested in them due to the incredible popularity of the GOTYAY, Witcher 3.

I came very late to the Witcher series, and decided to start at the beginning - and I'm very glad I did. Though the original Witcher suffers from a few problems as a result of some strange design choices and its age, it is, arguably, one of the best games I've ever played - and certainly better than the game that followed in the series.
Sadly, its first four hours are the worst. The entirely brown landscape of the castle you're introduced to and the initially incomprehensible combat system left me thinking that I should probably just have started at TW2, like everyone said.
If you can stick it out though, there's a moment in the second location you're taken to where everything just... clicks. Suddenly, the way the quests are structured makes sense. The combat system actually becomes quite enjoyable, and the game finally finds its voice.
After that moment, The Witcher suddenly becomes impossible to stop playing. The story ramps itself up to an addictively inriguing level, and the whole atmosphere of the game changes and deepens. Indeed, I don't think that any other game has quite managed to create the 'feel' that the first Witcher has in abundance.
There are a few standout moments of storytelling - and one that totally suckerpunched me, and that I still think about months later - but if nothing else, its the characters that you should stick it out for. A lot of what happens in this first game is very important for what comes later on, and I can't imagine going on to TW2 and 3 without having played this first. Even basic elements of the later stories are informed by the first game.
For its very low price and long playing time, it's an absolute bargain.
So - if you've come here wondering whether you should start at the beginning, my advice is: do it. I can't recommend it enough.

Machinarium continues the unfortunate trend of enticing worlds dripping with character that offer very little in terms of actual content. The majority of the game takes place in a small part of what is clearly a massive city, and the story tends to be a simplistic telling of what was intended to be a heartfelt tale of reuniting lovers.
However, what there is to the world is all presented in a highly artistic, "handmade" style with hand-drawn environments that nearly engulf the little robot in scale and sketched cartoons in place of dialogue or text. It's soundtrack mixes unorthodox instruments and old Czech radio transmissions into wonderfully varied ambient music. In all It's a gorgeous work of art with plenty to enjoy, but more to desire

This game makes me wonder why we rarely see point and click adventures.
Machinarium is full of life, the developers really succeeded in creating an immersive world.  The music, characters, and scenery are all so well done that they make you feel like you're really there.
The puzzles are solid as well, you'll be getting very familiar with the world that's been built, struggling to figure out how to get further.
Whether you want a good brain teaser, or just feel like indulging in a good fantasy world, Machinarium delivers.

I want to like it, and it has its moments, but overall I can't recommend the game.
On the positive side, the game-play that I've seen is slow and semi-tactical. The lack of real spotting makes it possible to actually flank and ambush people, and there's some satisfaction in headshotting people at range or mowing people down with a mounted gun on a halftrack because you know it may take a minute for them to get back to the fight. It's a nice change of pace.
On the negative side, the gameplay feels like you're controlling a block of wood. Movements are stiff, gunplay is stiff and uncoordinated, context action and keys don't work well. I couldn't find a way to report people for teamkilling after they shot rockets into trucks leaving our spawn. Most of all, the game is grindy as hell. It's Play for Free modelling, but man do they want to encourage you to pay real money. I was looking at unlocking the grease gun, but the cost to unlock it was around a solid week's worth of gametime for me.
You get an amount of in game credits based on time in battles, but this amount is very small compared to what things cost. In addition you have to pay for literally everything. Your weapons degrade, and you have to pay to maintain them, and you have to pay to resupply ammo. It felt like the game would be impossible to play without spending real money.

Its Mechs, Its Fast, Its Fun ?
Sadly this game has alot of problems that hold it down compared to titles like Armored Core.
First of this game left Early Access this Week so it cant be used as a execuse anymore for the horrible performance issues that plagues this game, often it runs with solid 60fps yes but once things get a litte bit more heated the frames start dropping hard to 40-30 depending on how many Enemys and particles are on the screen, this happens despite what Graphics settings you have.
This can be best seen in the last Mission of Act2 where the Frames drop immediatly at the start of the mission and with a I5 6600K and a R9380 that should not happen with the Graphics the game offers.
Now the Gameplay on the other hand ranges from Very Fun to frustrating.
It does a good Job at making you feel like an overpowerring Killing Machine like the Dynasty Warriors games do, you move fast and most Mechs have a wide variety of Weapons to use like Rockets and Machine Guns which feels fun to use,
But the game is way to fast for its own good, in later missions it turns into a Catastrophic Cluster♥♥♥♥ with you Dashing around and mindlessly pressing the attack buttons to win, every death feels cheap because most of the time you dont even know what killed you in the first place, its impossible to dodge attacks that arent Rockets because you cant even see them coming at you, which makes you question alot of times why you just died,
Shortly said the Battle System is as deep as a puddle and gets very chaotic the longer the game goes on.
The "Story" is almost nonexisting and feels very disconnected from mission to mission making me wonder whats even going on there.
The Mech designs are great, ranging from Gundam looking ones to straigt up Metal Gears, but yet they feel a bit lifeless at times because of the lack of animations they have.
The Soundtrack is also great.
It fists the Situations, doesnt sound too generic and gets you pumped during the fight.
I love Mechs and i love games like Armored Core and Zone of the Enders but Project Nimbus fails to grab me the same way these games did.
Dont get me wrong Project Nimbus is not a terrible game or a complete failure, there is alot of potential lying here, but at its current state it leaves alot to be desired and sadly i cant recommend it.
I hope the Devs work on fixing the Performance Issues and build up on the foundation of the Battlesystem to make it more fair and enjoyable, once that is done i gladly try out the game again and hopefully can enjoy it to its fullest. :)

The great writing here – a dark sci-fi plot on the nature of identity and duty/morality, convincing dialogue and characterizations, plus some (again, dark) humor – carries the experience.  Worthy assistance also comes from the subtlety of visual and aural elements that inspire the imagination without showing every detail.
Unfortunately, the short length (I completed the game twice in less than four hours) means that much of the gameplay feels restrictively linear.  And despite novel variations on the standard adventure game formula and some decent puzzles, the control scheme feels (intentionally?) clunky and frustrating.
Overall, as much as I enjoyed it, I can't wholeheartedly recommend The Fall as a standalone experience.  As the first chapter of a larger series, however, it is excellent and will leave you wanting more.  The next chapter is already in the works, so I’ve heard.

I also don't know what it is about this game, but I always feel encouraged to try to beat my friends in the levels, though I believe the game still suffers from hackers breaking the global scoreboard. Finally, the level editor and steam workshop let you share epic levels you've created and keep you entertained between seasonal updates.

[Note: this review has been written at the end of the second act I will update it later if I feel it is necessary. No spoilers for the campaign will be included]
Overall I can very much recommend this game if you're a fan of the Mecha genre, or if you just like fast-paced shooters in general and don't dislike the anime aesthetic.
Controls are intuitive and combat is fast-paced. There are a lot of things to keep an eye on in the more advanced mechs, but in my experience there’s just enough to keep the dog-fights tense and hectic, without making you feel like you’ve lost control of the situation.
The game isn’t without faults, however, though most are on the technical side of things, and will likely be ironed out in future patches. The game occasionally freezes for 0.5-1 seconds, which is annoying, but doesn’t occur often enough to be a real hindrance. If/when the developer has the time and money, I think they should also make a second pass on the English script and voice acting. The voice acting isn’t bad, but it’s quite clear the script hasn’t been written by a native speaker (for example, there are several factions that, in normal sentences should be referred to as the [faction name] , but that aren’t, which just sounds a bit weird).
One other thing I’d like to see implemented is a more granular difficulty setting. Right now there are 3, and the lowest setting is too easy for me, while the middle setting is a significant step too difficult. However, this really is a minor nitpick.
So, overall, I can recommend this game. There are some minor issues, but I expect these to get ironed out over time, and the core gameplay is fun and engaging, while the story up to now has been interesting.

October 26th edit - the game is getting frequent updates, and the devs are friendly and responsive. Some parts of my review may no longer apply. Go read other reviews for more reliable information.
Decent budget mech game if you're itching for a lite Armored Core/Zone of the Enders-style game. It looks like you can choose what level to play at any time, so you can go back and switch the difficulty if you need to. The normal difficulty is actually pretty easy, so I would recommend putting it on Die mode (except for the escort missions - screw those, your friendly NPCs will always be slaughtered too fast).
Graphic options are nonexistent - it just says "low - medium - high - very high - GPU melt", with no indication of what changes. Even with GPU Melt turned on, it seems like the game doesn't have V-Sync. So, you might have to force VSync in your GPU panel. Also the game can lag like crazy during bossfights, even on the minimum settings with a good rig. The boss fights can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because of how fast they are.
Multiple-perspective storyline. There are audio tapes between missions that give a bit of backstory. I can't tell if there are story consequences yet if you're too slow to blow something up or protect something, but I don't want to spoil anything. Maybe I should go back and try certain missions again to see. Game is fast and fairly fun with you spamming missiles, dodging missiles, and strafing enemies, though flying in the Jet mode is a bit awkward. Overall a decent way to spend $11-$15 for a few hours.
If you're an Armored Core fan and you're wondering about customization -- there is none. You're given pre-determined mechs for each story mission. The plot itself is completely forgettable (and a bit too recognizable, if you've played certain other games). Overall 6/10.

The Fall is a side scrolling, almost point and click style adventure game.  It was released in early 2014 on the PC, and then later released on the consoles in July 2015.
Plot wise, The Fall is focused on A.R.I.D, which stands for Autonomous Robotic Interface Device (a good mouthful right?), you navigate through a destroyed industrial factory looking for a medical aid for the human inside of the suite you are in control of.
The gameplay is similar to that of Metroidvania style games, you aim with the right analog stick and shoot. You are equipped with a torch and a gun (eventually), you can switch between your laser sight on the gun, and your flashlight. This game is extremly dark, so you will need to use your light ALOT. Thankfully you don't have to running out of batteries like most games seem to force on you nowdays, your flashlight will never run out of juice.
Parts of this game feel like you are playing a point and click adventure, you have to locate certain objects in the game world by highlighting them with your flashlight before you can interact with them. You can combine objects to make new ones to aid you with puzzles, all of these are common found mechanics found in adventure games. There is some very basic shooting action to be found - when I say basic, it is very basic; don't expect to go into crazy gun battles with the androids, you have one weapon throughout the whole game, it has unlimited ammo, and all of the enemies die in the same amount of shots, apart from the end boss.
Graphically, The Fall is not exactly top of the range graphics; the atmoshere is so dark that they actually get away with having amazing graphics, the game puts alot of effort into the lighting to create the decaying atmosphere that you are set in. If anything, I think it may of been a little too dark, as sometimes it made it a real challenge to be able to see what you are looking for, especially since the flashlights arc is so small anyway.
Much like other metroidvania type games, all of the levels are non-linear, allowing you to explorer to your hearts content, there are a few locked doors which you have to work around, but the majority of the time you can go where ever you want; at first, the vast amount of rooms and corridors you find yourself in is very overwhelming, but you will soon be able to work your way around with ease, even without any sort of map/mini map.
A fullplay through of The Fall took me just under four hours. It starts out quite slowly but soon picks up pace once you are thrown into completing certain tasks in order to get merit points. I managed to get through the game with minimum deaths, maybe 5 or so through the whole game, so it is by no means a difficult game to finish.
I am going to simply just recommend The Fall, it's by no means a bad game, but it also doesn't blow me out of the water. I did enjoy playing it, and there is some really interesting moments in the game; there is a sequel in development, and I am eager to find out where they intend on taking the plot as it stands now. If you go into The Fall with the expectations of it being a point and click adventure game, you will enjoy yourself; however don't go into it wanting a really action filled playthrough as it is not that at all.
1) Stay away
2) Only recommended when on sale
4) Highly recommended
5) This is a must play

This is one of those games: should I recommend it or not? It's cheap, mediocre and fun for a short time but grows old before you're finished.
Reminiscent of a blend between tower defense and action arcade games, in
you place cannons in the field and shoot any enemies that parachute their way towards them.
Graphics are really simple and dated. There's no animation to speak of, the main screen has a blatant typo in the English version (
instead of [/i]waves[/i]) and options are rudimentary at best. Even the game name looks misspelled.
At least you can switch between windowed and fullscreen and choose your resolution, but apparently the windowed mode does not work correctly, because in the forums it is the go-to reason to suggest using fullscreen when you have trouble with the controls.
Yeah, the controls. While the Unity launcher shows you keyboard options, KB is not used.
can
. This is fine, but KB would have been extremely useful, if one could press a button to shoot a particular cannon. Instead, you have to click on the circle that says "Fire" every second or so to keep firing.
Each level begins with waiting for a cannon to become ready: why not start with one ready? Once it is, you may drag it to its place. The tutorial shows how this is done, but for some reason you can only grab the cannon by its base or its barrel, not its center that is the most logical place to click (you know, being the center).
You may move the cannons around the 3 or 4 allocated slots. You have to hit the slot or the cannon gets reverted back to its original place, which can be frustrating. Moving cannons can be used to dodge bullets or prevent enemies from invading your base.
This is also the actual game phase: after you have filled all the slots, there's nothing else to do but spam "Fire" until the level is completed. You might have to replace destroyed cannons but not much else.
Enemies are stupid and uninspired: most of them just blindly fall towards the cannon and inflict damage on impact. But some shoot back, or can take several hits before dying.
Ninjas and drones were the most interesting enemies: ninjas disappear for a couple of seconds so they can't be hurt. This doesn't matter because if you just shoot constantly, they'll eventually die anyway. Drones fly zigzag, so you actually have to time those shots. Game would have benefited from more of these interesting enemy types.
Completing levels gets you medals that are used to buy permanent upgrades to your cannons: damage, health, speed and recharge. I never learned the difference between speed and recharge so I just maxed everything. After that the end game was very easy.
There's also a bunch of special modifiers that have to be unlocked and then bought separately in each level: things like piercing bullets and armor negating.
Honestly, it would have been simpler and better to ditch the special modifiers or even the whole upgrade system altogether and keep the modifiers only available within certain levels.
One hour to 3-star each level and to get 100% achievements. For its merits,
is adequately priced as a $1 game. Myself I got the game from a bundle.
I only played it because it looked simple and I was up for something like that. For that matter it did do its job. But to recommend or not? Ultimately, there are many better and more enticing games at this same price. If you get it, get it for the achievements/cards but otherwise, skip it.

My issue with the game and why I got stuck is the controls. A lot of the combat is down to timing. You hit combos and the last of the 3 hit does the most damage. This uses up adreniline and a single 3 hit combo will use up nearly all your stamina. Meaning you can't get away if there's multiple enemies as you slow down when you have low stamina. The main part to avoid being hit is a dash/dodge button which (as default) is left ctrl or hold down and press jump, the latter being what the tutorial says. Which often means you will jump instead of dashing and therefore take a hit. But it gets worse. You dodge/dash away in the opposite way to the way you're facing. Or you could try running away from an enemy, in which case if you then dodge you'll go into the enemy. Or if you're already facing the wrong way, you need to walk into the enemy to then dodge away. I couldn't get my brain to decide whether to run or to dash, and would end up getting confused and frustrated and taking hit after hit. This is where I gave up with the game.
There's apparently inventory management, but I didn't get that far. There's also spells and doors to come back to after you unlock abilities, but again I didn't get that far.

This is my review for Heroes & Generals.
Heroes & Generals is a very good game, small size and easy to learn.
You start off picking a side in the war as either Russian, American or German.
When you've "finally" picked a side in the never-ending war you then queue up for a battle.
You can only play staged battles until level 5, which takes quite some time. But don't let that discourage you! You can get to level 5 within about 15 hours of gameplay (If you know a good way to farm to it.)
You get new weapons by leveling badges and ribbons which rewards you with new types of skills (Passives) that gives you bonuses to Precision, less blur when aiming down sights etc...
I've played the game alot. (In my opinion.)
Which is about 50 hours of gametime.
I've switched around the sides several times, and experienced alot of patches etc. I even played the game before it hit Steam! And back then it was easier I suppose because you only had to get to level 3 to play War battles and get the tank crewman training.
But nowadays you have to get to level 5 to be able to train your infantry soldier to be able to buy Tanks and Heavy Artillery.
The game is a solid FPS with bullet drop and bullet travel time, much like the Battlefield series. It takes some time to learn the ropes on how to farm ribbons/badges the fastest and getting the gun you want as fast as possible.
If you want a solid FPS with proper history of war (World War 2) you should definitely get this game! It's free and it's only 1,5GB so it doesn't take that much space on your PC!
And now let's proceed with Pros & Cons!
-Easy to Learn.
-Doesn't take over 10 minutes to find a battle.
-Everything can be achieved by playing the game.
-Stealing cars as the opposing factions.
-Many "pay-2-win" players at low level. (Players that have invested money into the game and has better equipment at low levels)
-the Squad menu can't be tabbed down if you want to buy ammunition or repair your gear, you have to leave the party.
-Players can report you for dealing the slightest of team damage, example; You're throwing grenades into a heavily-populated area of soldiers and you accidentally hit a teammate, and what do they do? They press F1 and you get a 1/3 reports in that battle. (When you reach 3 reports you get kicked from the battle.)
7/10 - Play the game! It's a fun experience but even better when playing with friends!
P.S: I don't understand what the developers mean with the game still being early access when it's really polished even at this stage.

Spore is less of a "simulation game" and more of an "adventure through evolution". The vision of Will Wright's epic "Universe Simulator" didn't turn out quite as many sims fans might expect. Now hold on, while I do not think Spore met its very high expectations set back circa E3 2005's demo, I did enjoy and love Spore.
Spore is one part creation tool, one part action/adventure game and one part RTS game. The game is split into five stages, cell, creature, tribal, civilisation and space. The cell and creature stages play like a simple action RPG game, eating plants or killing/socialising with other creatures to raise your  "level" and unlock new parts as you evolve. Eventually your creature gains greater intelligence and moves to the tribal stage and civ stage where they play out like very simple RTS games and the Space stage return to a more action RPG format with some diplomacy sprinkled in. Each of these five stages are very simple, in fact they feel like far simpler versions of other games in the same genre. One could equate the cell stage as a very simplistic version of pacman, except with the lack of mazes. Your goal is simple: eat, grow big, and avoid ghosts - well in this case, predators, unless of course if you play a carnivore where your mission is to instead others. As a creature, the game shifts to a third person action RPG style game, depending on how your creature evolves, you gain different attacks and abilities to use as you fight of predators, socialise, or hunt down prey. At the tribal and civ stage, the games are very simple versions of Battle For Middle Earth. If you never played that very awesome Lord of the Rings based RTS game by EALA, you should definitely check it out.
Ultimately though, each of these stages feel very bland and personally, lacks variety. While you creature creator allows you to make a variety of different creatures, the ability variety and units/building variety at civ stages are just too few. There's very little option for different strategies in any of these four stages. What makes up for it for me, is two things - the creature creator and the space stage. The creature creator is one of the best selling points of spore - who doesn't like to see your favourite fantasy creatures move and come to life? It is also nice to look at the timeline which your creature evolved, to see how they started from a single worm like cell with a glowing electric butt to a ferocious dragon thing wearing a top hat and sporting a beard (at least that's how my creature turned out) lel. The Space stage is perhaps the most fleshed out, and most satisfying stage to play in Spore. It is clearly the stage that Maxis put most time into. While there is no longer any evolution taking place, what makes the space stage so great is the blend of diplomacy, where you have to ally or fight off neigbouring alien empires, look for resources, spread your empire, abduct creatures from lesser civilisations for study or alternatively, lift them up to the space stage, terraform planets, or just drop a planet buster and blow them to bits. Space stage is most satisfying due to the greater level of difficulty, the things you have to manage and the variety of things to do. The first time you drop the atmosphere machine to pump a desolate planet full of air before throwing a down a blizzard machine to cool it down to the right temperature is so satisfying. What's  even more satisfying is deterraforming a planet - i.e. finding an alien empire and messing up their ecosystem and cause them to go extinct, I mean Why not!? Ha! (Goddam Zealots and their goddamn Spode....)
Individually, each stage of Spore is quite weak, but put together, Spore is definitely a very good game. And since most stage won't take you more than an hour to beat anyway, the lack of variety of the first four stages won't get too much in the way and you won't be bored by it because once you're done, you are doing something different in the next stage. I also recommend that if you get Spore, get it with Galactic Adventures because it introduces the adventure creator which is great fun and adds more variety to the missions you get to do at Space stage while simulataneously allowing you to land on certain planets to do missions controlling your character like during the creature stage.
But, however I have only one final criticism, and this is aimed squarely at EA. Although I absolutely love Spore and want to give it greater praise, at the end of the day, I feel Spore is just very very poorly supported. The online search is absolutely atrocious. The in-game Sporepedia (which is a library of creatures and creations that users can upload) takes forever to load, there's frequent disconnections and for Galactic Adventures only, the points and ranking system for new adventures are completely and utterly broken. This is sad because Spore DOES have an active, albeit small, community who still creates great creatures and adventures.
The verdict? Spore is a great game as a whole package where each stage works in unison to give a fun experience. As I said, the game doesn't take too long to move through each stage and seeing how your creature evolved over time is a satisfying experience. Ultimately however, had the game have better online functionality, like say Steamworkshop integration directly with Sporepedia, I would give this game a solid 8. Criticism of each stage being too simple aside, I did enjoy my hundreds of hours on this game creating things, and messing up and blowing up planets in space stage, finding secret space objects and flying through wormholes. It just made my inner science nerd fangasm as I live my sci-fi dreams. I just adore this game. However the poor online and very old community makes it very hard for me to reccommend today and ultimately I must drop a point and give this game a 7.
tl;dr should you buy this game? Only at a sale and if you are okay with EA's terrible (or actually, completely nonexistent) support for this game. I'm still recommending it, but just barely and ONLY if you are okay with the nonexistent support from EA.

Excellent story, writing, and voice acting. The game is worth playing on these grounds alone IMHO. The biggest complaint against it is that the dark atmosphere does not lend itself well to puzzle mechanics. A good portion of the game will be frantically looking everywhere for hidden items, and since changes in your environment reveal more items, you'll be sure to scan the same area over and over again. Having to use the flashlight is also somewhat annoying, since this means you'll be holding down the right mouse button anywhere you go. However, if you are really stuck, there are very straightforward guides available that can get you through. Overall, it's a game with great atmosphere and characters that you will enjoy playing, and I'll be looking out for the sequel.

While The Fall does throw occassional moments of combat at you, you'll spend the majority of the game exploring the environment looking for any item or clue that may help you solve problems (I can't quite bring myself to call them puzzles) in order to progress.
The game is dark, which not only adds to the creepy atmosphere, but forces you to inspect every inch of the game with your flashlight to ensure you haven't missed something (I'll also note that the only way to interact with your environment is to first aim your flashlight onto an object, so you literally can't play the game without constantly shining your flashlight onto everything anyway). Some might find this annoying, I didn't mind the mechanic personally, and once I got used to the awkward controls I found myself very immersed in the gameplay.
Combat is fairly simple, take cover (or cloak) until enemies pause between firing at you, then lean out (or uncloak) and try to pop them in the head for maximum damage. You can also perform stealth takedowns, though they require little effort, and tougher enemies are introduced as you progress, which adds just enough to keep combat from feeling like work but doesn't add enough to consider the combat deep or particularly interesting. Luckily, as I already mentioned, the combat is occassional in this game, so it never really has enough time to make you feel bored or annoyed by it.
The Fall is a small game, and by small I mean there are only a handful of areas in the game that you'll explore and none of them could be considered large. HOWEVER, the nature of the game will have you spending a lot of time in each of these areas rather than just moving through them once or twice. Progression will require you to seek out and find items that you can utilize to solve problems, and sometimes an item you find early on won't be needed until late in the game, or an item you find late in the game needs to be used in an earlier area. There's a lot of backtracking, so if that's something you dislike in games, this isn't for you.
The game world in The Fall is mysterious and interesting. You're kept out of the loop for most of the game, learning bits and pieces about what's going on through conversations or finding messages. The characters are well done and each have a unique personallity from one another. Some of the dialogue and voice acting could've been better in places, but by no means do I consider any of it to be bad. I really enjoyed the atmosphere of the game, and I think a great job was done in putting it all together.
Overall, The Fall is simple in design, but delivers challenging content (I admit I needed to refer to a guide a few times because I was totally stumped). The visuals are creepy, the music is creepy, the characters are creepy, and I loved it. At $9.99 its definitely worth it if you like exploration and problem solving, and if you manage to grab it on sale then its an absolute must play. At around 3-4 hours long, I'm confident you'll be satisfied (and apparently a sequel is in the works, so there will be even more The Fall to come in the future. I look forward to it).

The Fall is a unique take on the point-and-click adventure genre that all fans should give a shot. The way that the game handles puzzles in relation to the character's conflicts creates a very unique dynamic that I have never experienced in other entries in the genre.
There are some problems with the game, sometimes I could not solve some puzzles because of a glitch or two. So it can cause some serious frustration when the solution you are looking for actually doesn't exist, but simply restarting the game can resolve that.
If you want the best experience while playing this game DON'T READ SPOILERS. There is some story beats that are exciting and you would only be making it a lesser experience by finding out what those are before the time you reach the end.
For those who aren't interested in puzzle games or adventure point-and-clicks, using a guide while playing through may not be a bad thing either, the story is a different take on AI becoming independent and emotional attachment between them.

You don't need to spend money on this game to enjoy it, though to be honest if you spent money on some things it'd be worth it because it takes 1hr 30 minutes roughly to get 150 cubits (ingame currency) and with that you will have mined about 2000 blocks.
While you can get 4000 ingame currency for $2.99. So unless you live in a third world country where you get payed less than $3 an hour it isn't worth your time to mine thousands of blocks for cubits. I've got about 730 cubits in my playtime of 19 hours, though a lot of that time was spent talking to people. I've barely even touched my own base yet but I've got thousands of blocks and all of the tools you can get in the game. Which I've made myself.
I wouldn't waste cubits on the stores ores or blocks or anything like that you can get from mining. You can just ask around and you will surely be able to buy the stuff you need from people for cheaper prices. I traded 5 chests earlier for a viking helm (insanely good deal). Though trading atm is putting your trust in the other person not to rip you off. Hopefully they will get the trading menu in sooner rather than later.
Cabinets/chests can be opened by anyone within your realm so make sure they are hidden underground (at least one block over them and on the sides (I've seen hackers, which can clip outside of walls). You'll want to go to the tropical mine through the sky portal (I think it's called that) and pick up some rubber trees ( you just place one of the rubber tree logs on the ground and it will produce rubber) and some cotton plants if you want to have some of them.
TLDR: If you want to get nice things without lots of tedious mining you are going to have to buy cubits and if you want ores/blocks/ anything you can make ingame you should buy them from players as it will be cheaper. The trading system is pretty much based on trust atm so remember what your mother told you about talking to strangers. (don't trust anyone) Sure there's plenty of trustworthy people but there's lots of non trust worthy people (I haven't been burned yet but I don't take chances) I'd also suggest you look up the receipe list
Most things aren't hard to buy and things don't really require many resources to build. Of course you can't build any clothing other than pants and a shirt atm. So you will either have to trade or buy them with cubits. You can also travel to other peoples realms and use their workshops if you don't have one yet. Other people can and will take items out of the workshops when you are using them that you've put in them. Chests can be opened by people who do not own them so cover them when not in use or people are around (covering them does not close the screen for them if they've been opened by someone). You don't need to spend 7000 cubits on a 100x100 plot as rooms are way cheaper and you can get a 100x100 room for either 2000 cubits or 4000 (I don't even have close to it so I don't remember) Check out the steam forums if you have questions.
The game is a little buggy atm with quite a few crashes and disconnects but I've never lost any progress or items because of them. When the game hangs just use task manager and exit the game.

- If you are looking for a complete game that challenges you and is free of all bugs, look elsewhere and come back to check on this game later after they add monsters.

Game Concept: 9/10

Cubic Castles is a 3D game that is only playable in top down view mode. There is no way to change to a first person view like Minecraft does by default. This makes it impossible to create tunnels, houses with roofs, etc. because my view is blocked. This is a severe limitation on what I would like to build. It's like going from a modern first person shooter with completely 3D levels to Doom 2 which can't support things like the ability to go over a bridge and under the same bridge.

Momento Temporis: Light from the Deep gameplay at first seems to be your typical platform adventure game.  You can jump and attack and there is an inventory system so it seems like a typical metroidvania...but then you discover that there's actually a stamina-stagger system and combat is a bit timing-intensive.  This makes fighting way more engaging than I expected for a game in this genre.  On top of that, the world is large and fun to explore where you're eager to see what's on the next screen, hoping it will answer some of the questions about who you are and how you got into this situation.
Gameplay:

+ The combat system is surprisingly enjoyable. It's very similar to a brawler as you punch, kick, block, and dodge while being ever watchful of your energy meter to not get staggered.
+ The levels themself are pretty huge with MANY rooms to find and explore
+ Visually the game looks pretty good with pixel-art sprites, similar to games like Terraria or Starbound
+ Good background music and ambient sounds
- The game currently lacks a story or any clear sense of direction. You suddenly appear in this world and tell yourself "I should find someone to talk to"...after traveling all over I could not find anyone to talk to, and still don't understand where I am or where I'm going. The objective is unclear.
- Most enemies in the game can be easily skipped or jumped over. Stopping to fight enemies is often unrewarding as they rarely drop health. (Suggestions: Make enemies drop coins to buy items at a shop, or perhaps earn experience to increase your hp / stamina meters)

BUILD: Beta 1.0.2
Momento Temporis is a metroidvania 2D action adventure platformer featuring pixel-art graphics. Explore the world and learn spells, fight bosses and lots more in this magical universe. The game was made by Burning Ice Games and published by 501 Industries.
I received the game for free after writing a feedback article on another 501 game; Pro Gamer Manager. I was then sent the Steam code for the game and after watching the trailers I couldn't wait to get to play it, I downloaded it as soon as I could and gave it a try.
I haven't got very far into the game yet but in my experience the game has been very good; the soundtrack is rather good and the gameplay it self is pretty good too, I personally love the combat system and how simple but challenging the game is; it takes what classic platforming should be and makes it great; keeping the retro feel while it's at it. I haven't got into any big puzzles that the game promises yet or faced any of the bosses and I can't wait to get further into the game to see some of those things.
Personally I love the graphic style. The 8-bit graphic style makes the game run on any PC and is still very attractive while doing so. The retro style is also attractive to almost everyone; older gamers love that the retro feel is there and younger gamers can get straight into it as the gameplay is easy to play and looks great too. The one thing that I absolutely loved was the 8-bit lens flare which occured when I was playing. It looked amazing and it just sums up why I love the style.
One notable thing is that the game throws you straight into the deep end as it currently features no tutorial. This left me a little confused when playing the game as I had to look at the controls before I could get straight into it. I was also stuck when the character (who I haven't learnt much about yet) talks at the very start of the game; a little "Press () to continue" would be nice so that people didn't have to go through every key.
Of course, remember that this game is currently in Beta. I will most likely come across bugs while I play but these will surely be fixed in the future when the game is fully released. I currently recommend this game as it's a great 2D platformer which is sure to evolve in the future. The price is a bit high and I'm not sure if I would pay 7.99 while it is still in Beta but I would 100% pay full price in the future when the few issues are fixed and more things are added.
Pros:
- Loveable 8-bit graphics
- Classic and great gameplay; great combat system
- Awesome platforming mechanics
Cons:
- Needs a more in-depth tutorial
- Throws you straight into the deep end
In conclusion, I can't wait to play more of this game and see it evolve. Good job so far!

ZombieRun is an action platformer that has it's problems.
The screenshots and information shown on the store page for this game initially had me very interested, I haven't seen many platformers take on the theme of Zombies before so was eager to play. As with all other platforming games;  I plugged in my Xbox controller and sat back in my chair to play. Sadly upon loading up, I was faced with my first problem; I was unable to navigate through the main menu with the controller. While this isn't a massive issue, it is the sort of thing I have come to expect from games like this, especially when they are marked as "Full controller" support on their store page.
I navigated through all the menu options as I always do, wanting to check out the controls, this is where I found my second issue. The controller page is just horrendously messy.  I didn't know what actions were referring to which buttons, it was just all over the place. This option may as well be taken out as it stands as it will be no use to anybody, other than a hindrance.
So I start the game, thinking the controls can't be that hard to figure out as I can always test buttons as soon as I am in the game. NOPE, as soon as you load into the first level, you have to effectively move out of the way of an enemy more or less straight away otherwise you die. While you may not think this is a problem, it is, especially when the controller doesn't work...sadly it is just not me who has the problem, many people online are also complaining of it too. I'm sure you know, playing a platformer game with keyboard is challenging at it's best, but I tried, sadly again the controls were even more of an issue. In order to move around you have to use the arrow keys, and you shoot with your WASD keys, who'd a thought it? This to me is completely backwards.
The actual game play is very basic too; this may as well call it self a rogue-like too, because you only have one life and if you get hit by a zombie, you go right back to the start; it's brutally hard. I managed to clear a few levels before managing the controls and completing jumping puzzles became too much of an issue.
So in conclusion, ZombieRun has major controller issues which virtually makes the game unplayable after the first few levels, and even though it's a really cheap game, you'll still feel ripped off if you pick it up and try it.

I've played up to where the developers have finished which was Act IV: Chapter 1.
Pros:
-Wonderful and Bloodpumping Soundtrack that hits the correct notes when in combat, especially during explosive and vital moments.
-The English VAs are great and do a wonderful job. Keeping everything within acceptable and simple standards for even the beginner into the Anime Mecha Genre.
-The Story, while still being developed, is intriguing and has a visible path that you can see, while still throwing unexpected events to keep you guessing.
- Combat; It's superb. Its responsive and quick to pick up. Yet hard to master. (I've played all three difficulties, Normal with Regen, Hard, Dark Souls Reference)
- Graphics are very nice and shiny, Mechs are well-designed and you can see parts move around when deploying different weapons or subsystems
- Decoys actucally do their job
- The AI on both sides are realtively smart and can pull off some pretty amazing things
- Characters are nice and relatable
- You don't see the Anime too early (Unless you look at the main menu closely)
- Mecha fights are really fun
- Diverse set of Mecha with their own strengths and weaknesses
- The OP Mechas can easliy be killed if they try to go solo or aren't used to their full potential
- Maps are wonderfully designed and have unique aspects to each of them
Cons:
- The Console can be accessed by accident and commands can be inputted.
- Sometimes the AI can't path properly and will continously smash themselves against a wall until a few-thirty seconds when they can find their own way out
- Sometimes the Characters seem flat at times
- Plot can be predicted at times
- Not a lot of Options to work with,
- No ability to make a Custom Mecha (Yet)
- Survival Mode is a bit too easy even on Dark Souls Reference Difficulty
- That Coma Mission was a pain with the breathing (Suggestion: Not so loud)
- Lore Tidbits (The Transmissions/Audio Logs) are easily ignored and while having important information players don't have a libary or something to review later on instead of replaying a mission to get the audio log again.
- One Character doesn't get a lot of Screen time even though they are with the pilot of one of the Named Mecha throughout the game as that pilot's co-pilot (Or Voice time, all in all they don't even get a Character Art other than a voice)
Overall Review:
A fun, fast, and flashy Anime Mecha fighting game that pits you against hordes of enemies or difficult bosses. Players get to see both sides of a over-arching and escalating conflict with a storyline that is somewhat predictable but also throws random wrenches at the player at the same time. However, this game is in Early Access and while I refrain from expecting and setting a bar too high, I will nevertheless expect a game that is enjoyable and brings a new light to the mecha games on Steam right now.

Right now it is a very fun finely tuned early acess game, I cant wait to see what this turns into.

Long overdue review. Still my favorite Elder Scrolls game.
Morrowind is the height of Elder Scrolls RPG crunchiness. Daggerfall had some more mechanics, but fell short in translation to a computer game in some ways (let's face it, the UI and graphics have not aged well). Oblivion had physics and improved graphics (minus faces), but dumbed down a lot of mechanics in compromising ways. Skyrim had good graphics going for it, but that's about as nice as  I can be. The game mechanics are watered down, the dungeons are reduced to loops, and it, ahem, poops on the lore of the earlier games. Yes, I realize it's a controversial position for such a popular game, but it's little more than a poor console port of an action game, not a built-for-PC RPG masterpiece, like Morrowind. In fact, I think Morrowind's UI on Xbox was better than Skyrim's.
But back to the point. Morrowind has an insane amount of customizability in terms of skills, magic, items, quests, factions, you name it. It's all deep, it's all good, and it'll keep any hardcore RPGer entertained for years. The story is incredible, and without revealing too much, really sets you up for an interesting progression where your choices matter against the backdrop of an incredible lore, spelled out through dialog, books, events, and locations. The books in game alone could fill tomes with the amount of information they contain.
But the game has only gotten better since release. Have you seen the mods? Incredible! They bring the graphics up to modern par, allowing the amazing world design to shine in a new era of computer horsepower. Bugs are all but eliminated, features are added, and everything is polished.
Give this game a go. This long after the release (2002!) it's still a contender among the best.
Still amazing, no matter much time passes.

-Massive open world
-Multiple factions with deep stories
-Replayability
-Epic plotlines
-Deep story and worldbuilding
-Wide Character customization
-It's Elder Scrolls
-Potato Graphics
-Buggy (There's a massive community patch to fix several issues)
-Quality of life issues (fast travel, rng fiesta, NPC escort quests, etc.)
Morrowind is old.  Really old.  And this shows in so many ways.  So many systems that seem logical in Oblivion and Skyrim are missing here.  You will find yourself running across the map often, because the location you need to get to doesn't have fast travel service.  This is easily the buggiest Elder Scrolls game without the community patch.  The graphics are pixellated and grainy.  And the journal is painful.
But it's still Elder Scrolls.
You can still court daedric lords for their superb magical artifacts.  You still start the game off as a prisoner about to be released.  You still have countless factions you can join, and you can still own property and become a living legend.  The main quest is outstanding, and the three great houses are each so different and awesome in their own ways that you have to play each one out.  You can romance a khajiit, and frame a mage's guild head as a spy.  You can meet a younger Master Neloth, or work with the author of Lusty Argonian Maid.  You can even kill
(with one exception) and still complete the game.
Morrowind is rough around the edges.  Really rough.  But the experience is still breathtakingly wonderful.  The world is full of countless quests, with plot lines that are some of the most memorable.  If you can get around the game's low points, it's well worth the effort.
Recommended at any price.

Fantastic story with bad gamepad controls.
The Fall is a unique and interesting story with remarkable voice acting and generally well-designed puzzles. There was only one puzzle that I didn't think gave enough information (finding the board) and one that required too much pixel hunting (the re-introduction of a jar), but otherwise with some exploration and time to think you can solve everything.
This is part 1 of The Fall and while it ends with a to be continued, it feels mostly self contained. You definitely have strong desire to continue the story, but I was satisfied.
While I have minor complaints with the puzzles, the real disappointment is the controls. Playing with a gamepad, you use the RS to aim at a point of interest, then hold RB to interact, then use RS to select your interaction mode. The problem is that you have to hold all three of these at once. You release RB to select your interaction. Playing with the mouse has the concession of "Toggle Aim", but it's non-functional with the gamepad. Since you spend a lot of the game looking around you as you walk through the game and there is little benefit to unaimed mode, being able to aim once and release the stick but continue aiming in the same direction would be a blessing to my tired hands. Additionally, the face buttons are generally unused and (I think) X and B could have been reserved for the two main types of interactions.
Another negative is the camera. It's great that the camera always shows a lot of space in front of the player. However, it adjusts very quickly when you switch facing directions. I often tried to change facing directions quickly and some players may get motion sickness from the rapid movement.
The narrative was strong enough to keep me playing despite my frustrations. I still wholly recommend it and hope the developer improves the controls and camera in future iterations. Took me about 4 hours to complete playing with a gamepad.

To sum it up: Brilliant.
No fancy graphics. No nonlinear open world. Most objectives have just one solution. No motion capture, no voice acting, no HD textures, no HDR lighting, no integration to central online servers, no trendy gimmicks, no pandering to the lowest common denominator.
Despite the game's outward simplicity, the gameplay is fun and challenging, and has more hacker cred to it than Watchdogs2. The story, shown (not told) by little more than crudely textured polygons and a few sound effects, is not your latest Hollywood thriller, but is far from bland. I did not learn all the playable characters' names until more than halfway through the game, yet I feel I learned alot about them from their style of problem solving. While many triple-A games often make you feel that you are playing a glorified thug with fancy toys, this game gives you the role of highly ambitious, intelligent, meticulously calculated (and only slightly insane) lifelong learners.

I don't exactly know how to describe QC.
It's a very charming, very engaging puzzle game. But not like you think. It's sort of like Portal, but... different. There's some super basic pseudocode programming involved, but the game holds your hands pretty good to explain how things work.  The story is told through your interactions with the world, and the old-timey soundtrack (playable via in game records - old timey I suspect to use some royalty free tunes) fits the missions well, though I did get mad and throw a virtual radio across the room once or twice when I got tired of the song.
If you like things like TIS-100 or Human Resource Machine or Shenzen I/O - definitely give this one a look. It's oozing with character. I just wish it were longer.
